text: I kept my umbrella angled toward the road, though the rain was coming sideways beneath it. The bus stop stood outside the shuttered pharmacy, and every few seconds a car hissed through the puddles, making me jerk my head up. My phone showed no signal. At the far end of the shelter, a man in a gray coat had been watching me without moving. I tried to read the route map, but the letters swam as my fingers tightened around the strap of my bag. When the bus finally appeared, I stepped toward its headlights before it had even slowed. The driver opened the doors, and I climbed aboard, leaving the umbrella behind. Only after the doors folded shut did I notice my hands trembling in my lap.

Mina, seventy-two and newly settled in the city, waited beneath the narrow awning of a bus shelter on a wet Tuesday morning. The street smelled of exhaust and soaked leaves. She clutched a paper with her clinic address, checking it so often that the ink began to blur. A delivery truck stopped nearby, its engine rumbling hard enough to rattle the shelter glass. Mina took two quick steps backward and pressed her shoulder against the timetable. She had heard that buses sometimes changed routes during storms, and the empty road ahead offered no one to ask. When a young cyclist pulled up, she rehearsed her question silently, then swallowed it. At last the bus rounded the corner. Mina climbed aboard and sat close to the driver, still gripping the damp paper.

The rain tapped the metal roof above me like handfuls of gravel. I had chosen this stop because it was closest to the warehouse, but at dawn the surrounding lots looked unfamiliar and vacant. A dog barked somewhere behind the chain-link fence. My shoulders jumped; I turned so quickly that my coffee sloshed onto my sleeve. The bus was already six minutes late. I checked the schedule, then checked it again, as if the numbers might change into an explanation. A shape moved behind the fogged window of the closed laundromat. I backed toward the curb, keeping my eyes on it, and fumbled for my keys. When the bus arrived, I boarded without looking back, then stayed standing beside the driver until we reached the brighter main road.

At sixteen, Darius usually filled quiet moments with jokes, but that rainy morning he said nothing at the bus stop. His school backpack rested between his shoes, and both hands stayed buried in his sleeves. Across the road, a dark sedan had been idling since he arrived. Each time he glanced at it, the windshield wipers swept away the water and revealed a face turned his direction. Darius tried calling his older sister, but the phone slipped against his wet palm. He tucked himself behind the shelter's advertising panel, peering through a torn corner. When the sedan's engine revved, he flinched and stepped into the open, waving at the first bus he saw. It was the wrong route, but the driver let him board while he called his sister again.

I stood at the bus stop with my violin case tucked beneath one arm, listening to rain drum on its hard shell. The morning was still dim, and the road dipped out of sight around a bend. I had promised my teacher I would arrive early for the audition, but my attention kept snagging on the footsteps behind me. They stopped whenever I stopped. I glanced at the shelter's scratched glass and saw a tall figure several paces away. My mouth went dry. I moved closer to the timetable, where the light was brighter, and pretended to study the routes. When the footsteps came nearer, I lifted the violin case in front of me. The approaching person only asked when the next bus was. I answered in a whisper, then boarded as soon as it came.

Noura waited for the number 8 beneath a shelter beside the river road, her bakery uniform already damp at the cuffs. A warning on the news had mentioned rising water, and the brown current below the embankment seemed much closer than usual. She kept glancing from the river to the bus timetable, tapping one shoe against the pavement. A gust drove rain under the shelter and scattered the receipts in her pocket. When a siren sounded upstream, Noura's breath caught. She gathered her things with clumsy hands and walked toward the higher ground by the corner shop. The bus appeared just as she reached the doorway. Its driver opened the doors and called to her. Noura climbed in, then watched the river through the streaked window until the road carried them away.

I was waiting outside the courthouse, trying to keep the envelope of documents dry beneath my coat. Rain blurred the traffic lights, and the bus stop's glass panels reflected a version of me that looked much calmer than I felt. A police car rolled past slowly. My stomach tightened; I wondered whether the papers in my envelope were enough, whether I had missed some form, whether the person I was meant to meet would appear. I counted the coins in my pocket three times. Across the street, a man raised his hand, and for one awful second I thought he was signaling to me. I stared down at my shoes until the bus brakes sighed beside the curb. Once aboard, I placed the envelope on my knees and held it there with both hands.

Eli, a night-shift nurse heading home, waited at a bus stop in the first gray light of morning. Rain streamed from the shelter roof in silver ropes. His phone buzzed with a message from an unknown number: a photograph of his own front door, taken moments earlier. He read it twice, then looked over his shoulder at the empty street. The cold seemed to creep beneath his collar. He called his roommate, but the call went straight to voicemail. Eli moved beneath the brightest streetlamp and kept the phone ready in his palm, thumb hovering over emergency services. When headlights appeared, he leaned toward the curb, squinting through the downpour. The bus doors opened. He gave the driver the address of the police station instead of his apartment and sat near the front.

My first morning in town began at a bus stop beside a field of wet, flattened grass. I had the right address written on my palm, but the ink was running into blue veins across my skin. Somewhere beyond the field, a loud bang cracked through the drizzle. I dropped my suitcase handle and crouched behind the shelter bench before I understood what I was doing. A moment later, a flock of birds burst from the hedge. I stood up slowly, heart punching at my ribs, and brushed mud from my coat. The road remained empty. I searched the horizon for the bus, then listened for another sound. When it finally came, I nearly missed it because I had been staring at the hedge. The driver waited while I hauled my suitcase aboard.

Ravi waited beneath a leaking bus shelter with a lunch tin balanced on his knees. He was on his way to a job interview, but the envelope containing his certificates had become soft at the edges. A woman at the next bench kept checking the road, then looking at him. When she stood and approached, Ravi's fingers locked around the tin clasp. He could hear his pulse above the patter of rain. She only wanted to know whether the bus had passed; he shook his head, unable to make his voice work at first. A gust blew her scarf into a puddle, and he retrieved it for her. They exchanged a brief smile, though Ravi kept watching the street behind her. The bus came at last, and he boarded with his documents held close beneath his jacket.

I waited at the stop near the elementary school, rainwater dripping from the brim of my cap. The message from my daughter said she was already on the bus, but the route had been diverted and I couldn't tell which direction it would come from. Every engine made me lift my hand. Every passing car left me staring after its red lights. I pictured her alone among strangers, searching the windows for me. My phone battery blinked at one percent. I paced from the shelter to the curb and back, counting the seconds between the traffic signals. Then a small face appeared behind the glass of a bus moving through the intersection. I waved both arms. The driver stopped at the next corner, and my daughter ran to me through the rain.

Greta, a retired cartographer, waited for the bus outside a closed garden center. The rain had erased the chalk markings on the pavement, and the familiar route seemed suddenly difficult to read. She had left home without her walking stick, certain she would manage the short trip. Now the road shimmered under a thick gray sky, and the shelter's bench felt too far from the curb. A gust pushed a branch down with a sharp crack. Greta grabbed the timetable pole, her knuckles paling as she stared at the fallen limbs. She considered turning back but could not remember whether the next bus was the last one before noon. When it arrived, she waited for the driver to lower the step and took his offered hand. She did not release the rail until she was seated.

I signed the lease on the fourth floor because the rent was low and the windows faced a row of maples. By dusk, my boxes were stacked beside the kitchen, and the old radiator began knocking in the wall. I stopped unpacking with a mug halfway to my mouth. Three knocks came, then a pause, then three more. I called the landlord, but my phone showed no signal. With one hand gripping a heavy saucepan, I crossed the room and pressed my ear to the plaster. A faint scraping moved behind it, traveling toward the bedroom. I backed into the hallway, keeping my eyes on the wall, and found the building’s emergency number taped beside the elevator. When the superintendent arrived, he opened a panel and a pigeon burst out, flapping into the stairwell. I laughed once, too loudly, and held the saucepan until my fingers loosened.

At sixty-eight, Marisol moved into a small apartment above a bakery, bringing her sewing machine and a box of photographs. On her first night, footsteps crossed the ceiling, stopped directly above her bed, and began again. She sat upright, clutching the quilt around her shoulders. The building manager had said the upstairs unit was empty. Marisol switched on every lamp and kept the television murmuring while she searched the hall for a neighbor. No one answered. At dawn, she heard the same measured steps and followed them to the rear courtyard, where a maintenance worker was testing a loose staircase. He waved when he saw her. Marisol thanked him, though her mouth felt dry, then asked him to show her the work order. For the next few nights, she slept with the hallway light on and her shoes arranged beside the bed.

The apartment looked harmless in daylight: pale walls, a view of the train tracks, and a lock that clicked neatly into place. After midnight, I heard the lock turn from the other side. I stood frozen in the kitchen, keys pinched between my fingers, listening as the handle dipped once and sprang back. My new neighbor had mentioned that the doors were old, but I had not expected mine to move. I called my sister and whispered while I wedged a chair beneath the knob. Then a second scrape came from the hallway. I crept to the peephole and saw a small dog nosing my door, its leash trailing behind it. The owner hurried up the stairs and apologized. I let out a breath that shook, then checked the deadbolt twice before returning to my boxes.

Nikhil’s first apartment was a narrow studio above a closed tailor shop. He had moved from a village to the city for nursing school and was proud of the key in his pocket. That pride thinned when the elevator stopped between floors during his first trip upstairs. The lights blinked out. Nikhil pressed the alarm button, then pressed it again, though the silence offered no reply. He sat on his suitcase and counted each breath, keeping one palm against the metal door. Somewhere above, a cable groaned. He imagined the car dropping and stood so quickly his head struck the ceiling. After several minutes, a maintenance worker called through the shaft and restarted the lift. Nikhil stepped onto the landing with his knees trembling. That night he carried his boxes up the stairs, one at a time, and left the elevator untouched.

I moved into a basement apartment near the harbor, where the rent included a small patch of garden. On my first evening, rain began tapping the window, then water seeped under the front door. I dragged my suitcase onto the bed and watched the dark line widen across the floor. My landlord’s number went straight to voicemail. I packed my passport, medication, and cat into a laundry basket, then climbed onto a chair to reach the buzzer. When I pressed it, every light in the apartment went out. The cat dug its claws into my sleeve. I kept talking to it while I felt along the wall for the stairs, my voice climbing higher with each step. A neighbor opened the building door before I reached it and helped us upstairs. By morning, the landlord had brought sandbags, but I slept at my cousin’s.

When Beatrice moved into the apartment beside the elevated highway, she expected traffic noise, not the steady hiss coming from the bedroom vent. She placed a chair beneath it and climbed up to listen. The sound seemed to stop whenever she moved, then return as soon as she sat down. She called her son and kept him on speaker while she checked every window latch. At last, she shut off the heating unit. The hiss continued. Beatrice gathered her purse and stood by the front door, unable to decide whether to stay or go. A plumber arrived after the superintendent found a leak in the neighboring unit’s radiator. He opened the vent, and warm, wet air puffed into the room. Beatrice watched him work from the hallway, arms folded tightly. Later, she unpacked her cups but left the chair angled toward the vent.

I got the keys to my new apartment on a Tuesday, two days after arriving from Manila. The hallway smelled of paint, and my door opened onto a room with one bare bulb. When I reached for the switch, the bulb flickered and went dark. I heard a soft thump behind me. My suitcase tipped over, spilling clothes across the floor, and I crouched beside it instead of turning around. My phone flashlight showed only the open doorway and the long hall beyond. I called my cousin, but the connection kept breaking. Then the thump came again, followed by a little scrape. I edged toward the sound and found a loose window shutter beating against the wall in the wind. I fastened it with a belt from my suitcase. My hands still shook as I texted the landlord to ask for a brighter bulb.

Eli, a retired bus driver, moved into an apartment near his daughter after his house was sold. He liked the balcony, but the first morning he opened its sliding door, the railing shifted beneath his hand. He stepped back so quickly he struck the table, sending a cup rolling to the floor. For several minutes, he remained inside, staring at the narrow gap between the railing and the concrete. He called the building office and repeated the address twice to make sure they understood. While waiting, he moved every chair away from the balcony and shut the curtains. A repair crew arrived before noon and found two rusted bolts had come loose. Eli watched them replace the hardware from the kitchen, one hand resting on the counter. That evening, his daughter suggested dinner outside. He smiled, then asked her to test the railing first.

My new apartment was on the ground floor, beside a courtyard where the residents kept bicycles. On the first night, someone tried my doorknob. I was brushing my teeth and froze with the toothbrush still in my mouth. The handle turned once, stopped, then rattled harder. I backed into the bathroom and shut the door, holding my phone with both hands. A message from the landlord said the front entrance had been sticking, but that did not explain my lock moving. I called the police and stayed silent while the dispatcher asked questions. Then I heard a child crying in the hall. I opened the bathroom door a crack and saw a little boy beside the wrong apartment, searching his pockets for a key. His mother hurried over and apologized. I waited until they were inside before I touched my own door again.

Sofia had saved for years to move into a bright apartment near the university. On the first night, she noticed that the smoke detector flashed red every few seconds. She pulled a chair beneath it, but the blinking continued after she removed the battery. Her throat tightened as she stepped into the hallway and knocked on the neighbor’s door. No one replied. She returned to her unit, gathering her laptop and coat in case she needed to leave. The detector gave a sharp chirp, and she dropped the coat. A technician arrived after the building manager answered her call. He found a second battery lodged behind the unit, left by the previous tenant, and replaced the whole detector. Sofia watched from the doorway, gripping her sleeves. Later, she unpacked her books, but each time the refrigerator clicked on, she glanced up at the ceiling.

I moved into a fourth-floor apartment after a divorce, carrying my plants up the stairs because the elevator smelled of hot wires. As I unpacked, the ceiling light began swaying, though the windows were closed. I stood beneath it, staring at the fixture until its motion slowed. Then it swung sharply again. I grabbed my coat and hurried into the corridor, leaving the front door open behind me. A neighbor came out, holding a laundry basket, and asked what had happened. We watched the light through the doorway together. The building shuddered as a truck crossed the street, and the fixture swung in answer. He explained that the old structure moved with heavy traffic. I nodded, but kept my coat on. That night I slept on the sofa, with the lamp from my bedroom beside me and the curtains drawn across the window.

Tomas, a widowed baker, rented a small apartment near the market so he could walk to work. The place came furnished, including a tall wardrobe that leaned slightly toward the bed. He wedged a folded newspaper beneath one foot and went to sleep. Before dawn, a deep creak woke him. The wardrobe had shifted several inches, its door hanging open. Tomas backed into the kitchen and stood there in his socks, listening for another sound. He called his nephew, who arrived with a toolbox and a level. Together they found one loose wall bracket and secured it to a stud. Tomas kept the hallway light on while they worked, handing over screws with careful fingers. When the wardrobe finally stood straight, he examined the wall twice. He slept in the living room that night, with his coat folded beneath his head.

I practiced my presentation on the empty bus ride to school, whispering facts about coral reefs while the windows shivered in their frames. At home, I had arranged my note cards by color, but now they stuck together in my damp hands. When Ms. Alvarez announced that I would present first, my mouth went dry. I stood beside the projector and watched the class settle, each chair scrape sounding unusually loud. My opening sentence vanished. Then I spotted a photograph of a reef on my first card, the one I had taken during a family trip. I described the fish darting through the coral, and the memory gave my voice somewhere to begin. I still stumbled over a difficult word, but I finished the final slide without looking down. Afterward, my knees kept trembling as I returned to my seat, though my classmates clapped.

At twelve, Imran had built a cardboard model of the water cycle for his science presentation. He carried it into the classroom with both hands, keeping the cotton clouds from slipping off. Before his turn, he watched one student forget a line and another drop a sheet of notes. His own tongue pressed against the back of his teeth, and he rehearsed the first sentence silently until it lost all meaning. When the teacher called his name, he walked to the front so carefully that the model barely wobbled. The class looked up. Imran’s fingers curled around the edge of the desk, but he began by showing how sunlight warmed the painted blue ocean. His explanation gathered momentum as he moved the paper arrows from sea to sky. A cloud finally fell off. He laughed, set it back in place, and carried on.

My presentation about my grandmother’s bakery was scheduled for the last period, which left the whole day for me to imagine everything that might go wrong. I checked the flash drive twice, then once more outside the classroom. At the front, the screen stayed blank, and a hot flush crept from my collar to my ears. I pressed the button again. Nothing. My teacher offered to help, but I could barely make my fingers release the device. Then I remembered the photographs I had printed for my display board. I turned toward them and began describing the flour-dusted counter, the ovens, and the little bell above the shop door. The details came easily because I had spent Saturdays there. When the slides finally appeared, I continued without stopping. My voice sounded thin at first, but by the end I was smiling at the picture of my grandmother’s cinnamon rolls.

Lena, a new student who had moved from a fishing village, prepared a presentation about local tides. She had drawn careful diagrams, yet the classroom felt larger each time she practiced before it. As her turn approached, she rubbed the corner of her first page until it bent. The teacher smiled encouragingly, and Lena’s shoulders rose toward her ears. She walked to the board and set down her notes. For a moment, she could hear only the clock ticking above the door. Instead of reading the planned introduction, she described how her uncle watched the water before taking his boat out. That familiar scene steadied her pace. She used a blue marker to trace the rising tide across her diagram, explaining the moon’s pull as she went. One classmate asked a question about storms. Lena took a breath, considered it, and answered with a small, certain nod.

I had to explain how to make a simple animation, and I knew every step until I stood beside the classroom computer. My palms left faint marks on the printed instructions. The first slide opened, but my pointer jumped wildly across the screen while I tried to guide it. A couple of students shifted in their seats, and my face grew warm. I wanted to retreat behind the projector cart. Instead, I placed the pointer down and used my hands to show how one drawing changes slightly at a time. That part had always made sense to me. I demonstrated with two paper figures, sliding them across the desk to create a tiny walking scene. A quiet laugh rose from the back row when the paper person bumped into a pencil. I began speaking more clearly after that. My final example worked, and I gathered the sheets with fingers that still wouldn’t stay quite still.

Before presenting her report on desert plants, Safiya waited in the library corridor with a rolled poster under one arm. The paper kept uncoiling, and she tightened her grip until the edges pressed into her skin. Through the open classroom door, she heard the previous speaker’s confident voice. Safiya’s own prepared introduction seemed impossibly long. When she was called, she carried the poster inside and pinned one corner crookedly. A classmate reached up to straighten it, giving her a moment to settle her breathing. Safiya began with a photograph of a cactus her father grew on their apartment balcony. She explained how its thick stem stored water, then pointed to each labeled drawing. Her voice wavered whenever she looked directly at the whole room, so she focused on the poster and the kind faces nearest the window. By the end, she was answering questions without consulting her notes.

I had chosen the history of the neighborhood train station for my presentation because I passed it every morning. The night before, I practiced in front of my little brother, who kept making the toy train whistle whenever I paused. At school, though, the note cards felt slippery and the classroom smelled sharply of dry-erase markers. I stood at the front, staring at the first card until its words seemed jumbled. The teacher asked if I was ready. I nodded too quickly. Then I remembered an old photograph of the station in my folder and held it up. People leaned forward to see the horse-drawn carts in the background. I started describing the picture, and the rest of my research returned in pieces. I spoke about the station’s changes over time, glancing at the audience only now and then. When I finished, I sat down and carefully flattened every bent card.

Mateo had never spoken into a microphone before his presentation on rainforest sounds. The school auditorium swallowed the small practice voice he had used at home, and the microphone gave a sudden pop when he adjusted it. He flinched, then fixed his eyes on the notes in his hand. His first line came out so softly that the teacher asked him to try again. Mateo’s throat tightened; he could feel several rows of faces waiting. He stepped away from the stand and played a recording of rain striking broad leaves. The sound filled the room, giving him a few seconds to collect himself. He explained how insects, frogs, and birds used different calls, then played each clip. As the familiar recordings followed one another, his hands unclenched. He spoke louder for the final example, a low monkey call that made the class laugh. Mateo grinned and bowed his head.

My class presentation was about the phases of the moon, and I had made a model with a ball, a lamp, and a shoebox. While I waited for my turn, I kept checking that the ball was still attached to its stick. When I finally carried everything to the front, the lamp cord caught on my shoe. The light flickered, and several people turned toward me. My cheeks burned as I untangled it. For a second, I considered skipping the demonstration and reading from my report. But I had spent two evenings making the model, so I switched on the lamp and started with the new moon. The ball cast a clear shadow against the box. I showed how its bright portion changed as it moved around the light. The teacher asked me to repeat one step, and I did, more slowly. I returned to my seat with the model intact and my hands tingling.

At ten, Beatrice was the youngest student in her class and had been assigned a presentation on family recipes. She brought a tin of lemon biscuits, but the lid rattled whenever she shifted in her chair. Her index finger traced the paper label again and again. When her name was called, she stood so quickly that her chair scraped backward. At the front, she looked at the rows of desks and forgot the story she had planned to tell. The teacher nodded toward the tin. Beatrice opened it, and the sweet citrus smell rose into the room. She explained how her aunt measured ingredients without a scale, using a chipped blue cup. Her voice grew warmer as she described the flour on the kitchen table and the recipe card stained with butter. She offered a biscuit to the teacher, then finished her final point with a small laugh.

I prepared a presentation about making a garden in a small space, but the classroom windows looked out onto a bare brick wall. My slides showed bright tomatoes and green leaves, and I kept glancing at them as if they belonged to someone else. The clicker was cold in my palm. When I reached the front, I heard my breath snag on the first sentence. I pressed the button and nothing happened. My thumb hovered over it while the silence stretched. Then I set the clicker on the desk and pulled out a packet of seeds. I passed it around, explaining how I had grown herbs in a recycled yogurt tub on our fire escape. A student asked whether the plants needed much sunlight. Answering that question felt easier than reciting the script, so I described my sunny windowsill. The slides began working again, and I finished with a list of useful plants.

In a classroom above a busy market, Yuki prepared to present her research on the history of paper. Outside, vendors called to customers, but inside she could hear the soft tap of her pencil against the desk. She had practiced every evening with her father, yet the notes in her hand seemed to belong to a stranger. When the teacher invited her forward, she nearly left her notebook behind. At the board, Yuki drew a sheet of paper and marked the path from ancient plant fibers to modern mills. Her voice caught on the first date. She paused, looked at the picture she had drawn, and continued by explaining how paper changed daily life. The dates returned as she described them. A pencil rolled off the desk, and she jumped at the clatter, then smiled at herself. She answered two questions and walked back to her seat, shoulders still tight but chin lifted.

I was presenting a short report on mountain rescue teams, and I had brought a bright orange rope as a prop. Before class, I tied and untied it beneath my desk until the fibers roughened my fingertips. At the front, the rope slipped from my grasp and landed in a loose coil. My stomach seemed to drop with it. A few classmates leaned forward, waiting. I crouched to pick it up, then decided to demonstrate the knot instead of pretending nothing had happened. I showed how rescuers secured a line, explaining why each loop mattered. My voice shook when I began, but the steps gave my hands a job. I asked for a volunteer to hold one end, and a student near the window helped. The demonstration worked on the first try. I wrapped the rope around my arm and finished with the safety rules, speaking steadily enough to hear myself.

At the night market in Penang, I kept my noodle stall open after the other vendors began packing up. A man in a wet gray coat had been standing across the lane for nearly an hour, watching my hands. Whenever I glanced up, he turned toward the lanterns. I counted my cash twice, then slid the knife beneath a folded towel. My brother was supposed to meet me, but his last message said the train had stopped. The man finally crossed over and asked for hot broth. My fingers fumbled with the ladle, spilling some across the counter. He looked at the knife-shaped lump under the towel, then at my face. “Long evening?” he said. I nodded and kept the pot between us. He paid, took his bowl, and left without looking back. I waited until his coat vanished beyond the gate before I let out the breath I had been holding.

Mira had sold dumplings at the Seoul night market for six months, but the sudden crack of a transformer made her drop a tray. The lamps along the lane went dark, leaving only blue emergency lights and the hiss of rain on canvas. Somewhere nearby, a child began crying. Mira reached for her phone, but its screen showed one bar of battery and no signal. Then a heavy scrape sounded behind her stall, where she kept the propane cylinder. She froze with one hand on the counter. Her lips moved through the safety steps her father had taught her: turn the valve, check the hose, find the exit. A shape shifted behind the hanging tarp. “Who’s there?” she called, though her voice barely carried. A neighboring vendor answered, and the shape proved to be a toppled crate. Mira’s knees still trembled as she relit the lantern and began gathering dumplings from the wet ground.

I took over my aunt’s little taco stand at the night market in Oaxaca while she visited our sick grandmother. Near midnight, a gust tore the menu from its string and sent it skidding beneath a parked truck. I crouched to retrieve it and saw a pair of boots planted on the other side. They didn’t move when I called out. My throat tightened; I backed away, gripping the metal spatula until its handle bit my palm. The market’s music thumped on, cheerful and distant. Then the truck’s engine started. I stumbled against my table, knocking over a jar of salsa, as the vehicle rolled forward. The boots belonged to a tired delivery driver who had been checking his tires. He apologized when he saw my face. I laughed too loudly, swept up the glass, and put the menu back in place, though I kept watching every vehicle that passed.

At the Marrakesh night market, Youssef served mint tea from a narrow stall wedged between a spice seller and a leatherworker. A courier arrived with a sealed envelope bearing his name, though Youssef had never met the sender. The courier insisted that someone had paid him to deliver it before closing. Youssef’s thumb hovered over the flap. The crowd pressed past, shoulders brushing his, while the tea kettle rattled on its burner. He glanced toward the market entrance, where two men stood beneath an arch and appeared to be waiting. Instead of opening the envelope, he tucked it beneath the till and called the spice seller over to watch his counter. Then he walked, slowly and carefully, toward the security booth. The guards opened the envelope there: it held an old photograph of Youssef’s stall and a note with no name. He left the tea service untouched until morning.

My fish-cake stall at the night market in Taipei usually drew a cheerful crowd, but tonight the alley behind it smelled sharply of smoke. I looked over my shoulder and saw a thin ribbon curling from the electrical box. The switch was mounted near the back wall, beyond a stack of oil tins. My hands went slick. I shouted for the neighboring vendor, but the music swallowed my call. A spark snapped inside the box. I pulled my apron over my fingers and edged along the counter, counting each step under my breath. When the vendor finally heard me, he ran over with an extinguisher. Together we cut the power and smothered the small flare before it reached the awning. Customers applauded as if we had staged a trick. I smiled, but my knees knocked beneath the table, and I kept checking the darkened wires between every order.

At the night market in Lagos, Kemi sold pepper soup from a blue cart beside the bus stop. A little boy ran up and said a man had fallen behind the stalls. Kemi left her ladle resting across the pot and hurried after him, then stopped when she saw a dark shape near the rubbish bins. The lane was narrow, and the market noise seemed to fade at once. She called out. Nothing answered. Her heartbeat thudded against her ribs as she backed toward the lit food row, keeping her eyes on the shape. The boy grabbed her sleeve and pointed to a hand moving beside it. Kemi yelled for help. Two vendors came running with a lantern and found an elderly porter tangled in a fallen tarp, awake but unable to rise. They freed him together. Kemi returned to her cart after checking the lane twice, and served the porter a bowl on the house.

I sell grilled corn at a night market in Manila, where the ferris wheel turns slowly above the stalls. Just before closing, a woman left a parcel under my bench and hurried into the crowd. I called after her, but she vanished between the bright umbrellas. The parcel gave a soft ticking sound. My mouth went dry. I didn’t touch it; I waved over the security guard, then moved my customers across the lane with an excuse about a spill. Each second seemed to stretch while the guard examined the bundle from a distance. When he opened it, a cheap kitchen timer was ticking beside a wrapped birthday cake. The woman returned, breathless, explaining that she had hidden the cake from her children. I managed a small laugh, though my fingers were still curled tightly around the corn tongs. After she left, I checked beneath every bench before packing up.

Linh’s small bánh mì stall stood at the edge of a night market in Hội An, where lanterns swung above the river. A sudden shout rose from the pier, followed by a splash. People surged toward the water, leaving Linh alone with the open flame and a line of customers. She stared toward the railing, unable to see who had fallen. Her hand shook as she turned off the burner. Then she snatched a coil of rope from the neighboring boatman’s hook and ran to the pier. A young tourist was clinging to a post below the boards, coughing as the current tugged at his jacket. Linh dropped flat and reached down while another vendor held her ankles. Together they pulled him up. The tourist was shivering but conscious. Linh returned to her stall with muddy knees and a trembling jaw, and gave away the sandwiches that had gone cold during the rescue.

I set up a tiny pancake stall at the night market in Reykjavík whenever the winter festival brought visitors. That evening, a gust slammed the side panel against my wrist, and the entire canvas roof began to lift. The propane flame danced beneath the griddle. I could hear the metal supports groaning, but my assistant had stepped away to find more napkins. I pressed my shoulder against the frame and shouted for the other vendors. Snow whipped into my eyes; the market lights blurred into streaks. For a moment the roof rose high enough to expose the burner to the wind. I reached for the valve, missed it, and tried again with numb fingers. Two stall owners grabbed the poles while I shut off the gas. Once the canvas was tied down, I sat on an overturned crate. My hands kept shaking long after the storm eased.

At a night market in Mexico City, Arturo ran a modest stall selling cups of roasted corn. A customer paid with a bill that looked genuine, then lingered while Arturo checked it beneath the lamp. The paper felt unusually smooth. Arturo glanced toward the nearby police booth, but the customer’s eyes followed his. “Everything all right?” the man asked, smiling without warmth. Arturo’s tongue stuck to the roof of his mouth. He set the bill on the counter and called to the vendor beside him, asking her to confirm the watermark. The customer shifted closer, one hand disappearing into his jacket. Arturo knocked over a stack of cups as he stepped back and shouted for the guard. The man bolted into the crowd before anyone reached him. Later, the vendor showed Arturo how to spot counterfeit notes. He practiced with every bill, though the lesson had left a tight ache beneath his ribs.

My little soup stall at the night market in Bangkok sits near a canal crossed by a narrow wooden bridge. A child dropped a toy boat into the water, and I leaned over the railing to point it out. Then the bridge gave a sharp creak beneath my feet. I gripped the post, staring at the black water between the slats. People behind me kept walking, their steps making the boards flex again. My breath shortened. I crouched and shuffled toward the bank, refusing to look down until my shoes touched solid ground. The boat drifted away, but a nearby vendor retrieved it with a long bamboo pole. I returned to my stall and stirred the soup until the steam clouded my glasses. Customers asked whether I was cold. I said the night breeze had found a gap in my coat, then moved my cooking table farther from the bridge.

Nadia had just opened her small falafel stall at a night market in Amman when a stray dog wandered between the tables. It was limping, and a length of wire trailed from one paw. Nadia set down her tongs and crouched, but the dog bared its teeth and gave a low growl. Her heartbeat stumbled. She stayed very still, hands open, while the crowd parted around them. A boy tried to shoo the animal with a cardboard sign, and Nadia told him to step back. She spoke softly, though her voice shook, and slid a bowl of water across the pavement. The dog drank, then lowered its head. A market cleaner brought a blanket and called an animal rescue volunteer. Nadia watched from behind her counter as they secured the wire and carried the dog away. When she returned to frying falafel, she kept the water bowl near the stall entrance.

At six in the morning, I signed out after twelve hours on the pediatric ward and stepped into the empty stairwell. My car keys slipped from my hand and clattered down three steps. I froze, listening. Somewhere below, a door clicked shut. The hospital’s night sounds had followed me out: a call bell, a cart squeak, a child coughing. I bent to retrieve the keys, but my fingers would not close around them at first. When I finally reached the parking garage, the lights seemed farther apart than I remembered. A man stood beside the elevator, looking down at his phone. I took the stairs instead, though my knees trembled on every landing. Outside, dawn had turned the sky pale blue. I sat in my locked car with both hands on the wheel until the sun cleared the roofline.

After an exhausting overnight shift in a rural clinic, Maribel packed her lunch tin and headed for the bus stop. A storm had washed branches across the road, leaving the shelter deserted. She checked the arrival app; it showed no signal. Behind her, the clinic’s motion light blinked on, then went dark. She spun around, the strap of her bag cutting into her palm. Nothing moved beyond the glass doors. Maribel called her brother, but the phone gave a thin electronic chirp and died. She walked back toward the clinic, counting each step and keeping her keys threaded between her fingers. At the entrance, she fumbled the lock twice. Once inside, she pushed a chair under the handle and lowered herself beside the reception desk. The first bus finally groaned past the windows as the clouds began to lift.

I finished my overnight shift in the city emergency department just as the elevators began filling with morning visitors. On the ride down, the lights blinked out. Someone exhaled sharply, and the car stopped between floors. I pressed the alarm button, then pressed it again, harder. My scrub top clung to my back. I tried to remember the calm instructions I gave patients, but each breath snagged in my throat. A child in the corner began humming, and I counted along with the tune, losing my place whenever the elevator shuddered. When the emergency light came on, everyone’s faces looked washed in green. I kept my voice steady while I told the others help would come. After the doors opened, I stayed in the lobby, watching the elevator numbers rise and fall before I dared walk away.

Rohan had worked the overnight shift in a crowded transplant unit, and his legs felt full of wet sand as he crossed the hospital courtyard. Near the fountain, a security alarm gave one abrupt chirp. He stopped beneath a bare tree. A maintenance cart stood alone beside the doors, its plastic cover lifting and settling in the wind. Rohan’s badge tapped against his chest with each shallow breath. He tried to call his partner, but his thumb missed the screen twice. The automatic entrance opened behind him, though no one appeared. He turned toward it, then backed toward the lit guard booth, keeping his eyes on the glass. The guard came outside and walked him to the staff parking lot. Rohan thanked him, sat in his car, and waited until his shaking hands could fit the key into the ignition.

My last patient was stable when the night shift ended at the rehabilitation center, but the walk to the train station felt unlike the one I knew. A stray dog stood beneath the platform clock, staring at me without moving. I stopped near the ticket machine and pretended to read the schedule. The dog’s ears lifted. My mouth had gone dry, and I could hear my pulse above the station announcements. I stepped toward the stairs, then heard claws scrape the concrete behind me. I gripped the rail and climbed, one step at a time, glancing back at every turn. At street level, a bakery worker was unlocking the shop. I waited beside him until the dog wandered off toward the tracks. My train arrived, and I chose a seat near the conductor instead of my usual empty car.

Eun-ji clocked out of the neonatal unit after a long overnight shift and found a folded note tucked under her windshield wiper. No name, just a time and the words, “Come alone.” She looked across the nearly empty hospital lot. A delivery truck idled by the loading bay, its driver hidden behind the windshield glare. Eun-ji retreated to the lobby, where the receptionist was stacking forms. She asked him to call security, keeping her voice so level that he glanced up in surprise. While they waited, she watched the note tremble between her fingers. A guard searched the lot and found no one near the car. Eun-ji asked for an escort to the bus stop and sent a photograph of the note to her manager. On the bus, she held her bag against her chest and checked the window reflections until the hospital disappeared.

By the time I left the overnight shift at the long-term care home, snow was falling thick enough to blur the street signs. My bicycle lay on its side where I had locked it, one tire flattened. I pulled out my phone to call a cab, but the battery showed one percent. A crunch sounded behind the row of parked cars. I backed toward the bright entrance, trying to keep my face turned toward the noise. My hands shook so badly that I dropped the phone. The night custodian came outside carrying a shovel, and the sound proved to be his boots crossing the lot. Even so, I asked him to stand with me while I called my sister from the front desk. She arrived in twenty minutes. I rode home with the heater blasting and watched each intersection pass in the side mirror.

After a long night in the hospital’s surgical ward, Petra changed out of her scrubs and stepped into the staff locker room. A locker door stood open at the far end, rocking slightly though the air was still. Petra had closed every locker during her rounds. She stopped with one sleeve half on, listening to the ventilation hum. A dull knock came from behind the open door. She backed into the corridor and called the security desk instead of investigating alone. While she waited, she kept one hand on the exit bar and stared at the polished floor, where a pair of shoes appeared around the corner. A guard arrived and checked the room with her. The locker held only a loose metal hanger. Petra laughed once, too sharply, then asked the guard to walk her to the staff entrance.

I had just finished an overnight shift at a community health center when the power failed on my block. The sidewalk vanished into darkness, and my apartment building’s front door would not open without its electronic latch. I stood under the awning, still wearing my badge, and listened to the wind push a loose sign against the wall. My key card slipped from my damp fingers. When footsteps approached, I pressed myself against the brick and held my breath. It was Mr. Alvarez from the second floor, carrying a flashlight. He let me into the lobby, but the stairwell remained black. We climbed together, his beam jumping over the steps. At my door, I kept the light trained on the hall while I turned the deadbolt. I left every lamp on, then sat at the kitchen table until the lights returned.

Nadia finished her overnight shift at a coastal hospital and walked to the ferry terminal beneath a moonless sky. The last boat had been delayed, and the waiting room was locked. A shape moved near the water’s edge. She stepped back from the railing, her shoe scraping loudly on the concrete. The shape moved again, then disappeared behind a stack of crates. Nadia called the terminal number, but only a recorded message answered. She carried her bag to the brightly lit ticket booth and knocked on its glass. The attendant opened the side door and let her wait inside. Nadia kept glancing toward the crates while she wrapped both hands around a paper cup of tea. When the ferry finally arrived, she boarded with the crew and chose a seat beside the lit cabin door.

My overnight shift in the oncology ward ended with an unfamiliar sound coming from the supply closet: a slow scrape, then a pause. I was the last nurse on that corridor. I stood outside the door with my hand around the radio, unable to make myself turn the knob. The hallway clock clicked through three seconds. I called the charge nurse, who was still upstairs, and told her what I heard. My voice came out thin. We waited together until a custodian arrived with a master key. The door opened onto a mop bucket rolling gently against the wall; one caster had broken loose. I laughed, but my stomach stayed tight. The custodian walked me to the staff entrance, and I checked behind me twice before the outer doors closed.

At dawn, Tomas left the overnight shift in a busy maternity ward and drove toward his apartment. A road closure forced him onto narrow streets he had never used. His navigation screen went blank, and the fuel warning lit up. In the rearview mirror, a pair of headlights remained close through three turns. Tomas pulled into a well-lit gas station and parked beside the cashier’s window. The other car continued past, but his hands stayed fixed at ten and two. He went inside, bought water he did not want, and asked the cashier to check a map. She marked the main road and watched until he had pulled back into traffic. Tomas kept the station receipt on the passenger seat, its printed address visible. When he reached home, he sat in the driveway with the engine running until a neighbor came out to collect the mail.

My brother Eli and I had barely opened the first carton when something scraped across the attic floor behind us. The sound stopped as soon as I turned. Dust floated in the beam of my phone, and every corner looked deeper than it had a moment earlier. Eli laughed too loudly and asked me to check the next box, so I kept my eyes on the cardboard instead of the dark stairwell. Inside were my grandmother’s knitting needles, tangled in a ball of gray wool. The wool twitched. I dropped the box and backed into Eli, knocking his elbow against the rafters. He grabbed my sleeve. Then a tiny mouse shot from the yarn and disappeared through a gap in the boards. We left the boxes for morning, carrying the phone between us like a lantern.

At fourteen, Nia had promised her little brother she could handle the attic. Now she stood beside him among the boxes, listening to rain drum hard against the roof. A sharp crack came from above. She shoved Mateo toward the stairs and held up a hand for silence, though her own fingers were trembling. A thin line of water began to snake beneath a trunk marked WINTER. They dragged it away from the leak, uncovering a loose floorboard. From below came a muffled thump. Mateo clutched her jacket. Nia swallowed and called their father’s name, louder each time. The thumping answered once, then stopped. Their father soon climbed up from the kitchen, explaining that a cupboard door had blown shut. Nia laughed with him, but kept one hand on Mateo’s shoulder as they finished sorting.

I was sorting old boxes with my older sister, Sora, when the attic light blinked out. She told me not to move, which made me want to move in every direction at once. My palms slid against the cardboard, and the little flashlight on my key ring wouldn’t turn on. Somewhere near the chimney, a slow tapping began. Sora whispered that it was probably a branch, but she was gripping my wrist hard enough to leave marks. We edged toward the hatch, feeling for the ladder. The tapping followed us, steady as a fingernail on glass. Then the hatch banged open and our cousin’s face appeared below. He had come looking for us with a fresh bulb. The tapping turned out to be a loose metal vent flap, but I let Sora climb down first.

When the twins opened a long cedar chest, the smell of mothballs filled the attic. Jasper found a sailor’s coat, while his sister Mina uncovered a small wooden music box. She wound the key, and a wavering tune began. From inside the wall came a second tune, lower and slower. Mina’s smile vanished. Jasper set down the coat and stared at the plaster. The melody stopped when she stopped turning the key, then began again after a pause. Mina backed toward the hatch, knocking over a stack of newspapers. Their father called from downstairs, asking what had fallen. He climbed up and found a wind-up toy wedged behind a loose panel, its spring moving whenever the floorboards shook. Jasper showed Mina how the mechanism worked. She still insisted the music box stay closed while they sorted the rest.

My sister Layla and I were hunting for our mother’s recipe cards in the attic when the roof groaned overhead. I froze with a box in my arms. The whole house seemed to hold its breath, then a shower of grit sifted down between the rafters. Layla set down her stack and put her arm around me, but she kept glancing at the ceiling too. We hurried toward the stairs, stepping over old suitcases and a broken rocking horse. Halfway there, a second groan rolled above us. I clamped my hands over my ears. Layla called for our uncle, who was repairing the roof outside. He shouted back that a ladder had shifted against the gutter. Once we heard his boots cross the porch, I returned for the recipe cards, though I carried them tucked under my coat.

Tomas and his younger sister Ines were sorting their late grandfather’s boxes when the attic hatch slammed shut beneath them. Ines tried the pull cord, then called down. No one answered; their aunt had gone to the market. Tomas forced a grin and said they could wait, but his throat felt tight and he kept wiping his damp hands on his jeans. A box tipped over near the chimney, spilling faded maps across the floor. One showed a narrow service ladder drawn behind a shelf. They shifted the shelf together, each listening for footsteps below. Behind it was a little door, swollen with age. Tomas pushed until it gave way onto the landing. Ines went first, clutching the map. He followed, then shut the attic door gently, as if it might make another sudden move.

I told my brother Benji that sorting the attic would be easy, but the first box held a bundle of old masks with cracked, painted faces. One slipped onto the floor and landed looking up at me. My mouth went dry. Benji picked it up by one strap and said it was from our school play, yet he kept standing close to me. We put the masks aside and opened a carton labeled CAMERAS. A flash popped from inside, bright enough to leave spots in my vision. I stumbled backward and knocked into the chimney. Benji found a disposable camera with a faulty shutter, its button caught under a strap. He showed me the jammed mechanism, then took the camera downstairs. I stayed by the open hatch, counting each box we still had to sort.

Amina and her brother Rafi had nearly filled a donation pile when they found a box of their mother’s childhood drawings. One picture showed a tall figure standing beside the attic window, though the glass faced a blank wall. Amina turned the page quickly. Behind them, a floorboard creaked. Rafi grabbed the nearest broom and held it out with both hands. They stared toward the stairs, waiting for another sound. Their cat, Pepper, padded into view, carrying a strip of paper in her mouth. It had slipped from the box and snagged beneath her collar, making her drag it across the boards. Amina crouched to free it, but Pepper’s tail puffed when the rain rattled the window. Rafi kept hold of the broom until their mother called them down for tea.

My sister Esther and I had been sorting boxes in the attic of our new farmhouse for an hour when I noticed a smell like burnt toast. The outlet beside the chimney gave off a faint buzzing sound. Esther reached for the cord of an old lamp, and I caught her sleeve before she touched it. My heartbeat thudded against my ribs as I backed away, watching the dark plug. We called our landlord from the stairs and waited outside in the yard, still wearing our dust masks. He came with an electrician, who found frayed wiring under the insulation. The lamp had not been plugged in for years, but a nearby wire had begun to heat. After they shut off the circuit, Esther and I brought the boxes down in careful trips, leaving that corner untouched.

Eleven-year-old Pavel was sorting attic boxes with his sister, Zoya, when they found a glass jar packed with tiny teeth. He dropped the lid, and it skittered across the boards. Zoya picked up the jar, then stopped when something rattled inside the wall. Pavel’s knees pressed together. He asked if they could finish downstairs, but Zoya wanted to find the rest of the collection. A second rattle came, followed by a soft scrape near the chimney. Pavel climbed onto a trunk to see over the boxes, his breathing shallow. Their grandfather appeared at the hatch and told them the wall shared a vent with the kitchen. A spoon had fallen into the duct. The jar, he explained, held old baby teeth from their family. Pavel climbed down and asked to put it in a closed cupboard.

My brother Noah and I were dividing our father’s attic things after he moved into assisted living. We found a small radio, and Noah turned the dial until a voice crackled through the speaker. It sounded like someone whispering our names. I backed into a stack of boxes, sending one tumbling open. Noah switched off the radio, but the voice continued for a few seconds. We stood shoulder to shoulder, listening as it faded into static. He examined the dial and found a station barely coming through beneath the noise. The broadcast was a call-in show, and a caller had mentioned two names that happened to match ours. Noah unplugged the radio. I could not stop looking at its dark speaker while we carried the boxes downstairs, one at a time.

Sofia and her brother Emil were clearing their aunt’s attic before a renovation. Behind a row of trunks, they discovered a narrow window covered by a wooden shutter. Emil pulled it open, and a gust shoved dust into their faces. The shutter swung back and struck the frame with a bang. Sofia flinched so hard she dropped a bundle of linens. Then something pale moved outside the glass. Emil reached for the latch, but Sofia caught his arm and asked him to wait. The shape drifted past again, fluttering in the wind. Their aunt came upstairs and identified it as a torn plastic sheet caught on the gutter. She tied it down from the roof. Sofia helped gather the linens, checking the window after every few pieces, while Emil carried the trunks toward the stairs.

I walked the north rows with a canvas sack of seed corn bumping my hip, though the planting was finished weeks ago. The radio had called for hail after sundown. Above the orchard, clouds crowded together like bruises, and each gust pressed my shirt flat against my back. I tested the ditch gates, then tested them again, pulling each lever until my knuckles blanched. At the low corner, water already trembled in the furrows. My phone showed a message from my daughter asking whether the old barn roof would hold. I typed yes, erased it, and typed, “We’ll see.” A loose sheet of tin clapped overhead. I ducked before I could stop myself, then stood still, listening to the metal rattle. In the dimness, I hurried toward the house, counting the seconds between distant thunder and the next flash.

At seventy-two, Belen knew every rise and hollow in her barley field, but the black shelf of cloud made the familiar ground seem strange. She carried a lantern though dusk had not yet come, its handle swinging against her wrist. Before the storm, she checked the irrigation pump, the grain shed latch, and the narrow culvert beside the road. When the pump coughed, she flinched and dropped the wrench into the mud. Her neighbor called from a tractor, asking if she needed help. Belen lifted one hand, but it shook enough that she tucked it beneath her apron. A gust drove chaff into her eyes. She blinked hard and kept moving, speaking each task aloud as if the list could hold the weather back. At the far fence, she turned toward the farmhouse, watching the sky over her shoulder.

I had been back from military service for only three months when the storm warning came over the kitchen speaker. The squash leaves were already turning upward in the wind, exposing their pale undersides. I took a flashlight and checked the crates stacked beside the packing shed, tapping each one to make sure nothing had shifted. My hands moved quickly, but I kept losing track of what I had done. Had I closed the chicken run? I went back and tugged the wire gate twice. Thunder rolled behind the ridge. The sound made my breath catch, and I pressed my palm against the fence until the boards stopped seeming to sway. My father used to say the farm could take a beating. I repeated that while crossing the field, though the words came out thin. Near the house, I looked once more at the clouds before going inside.

Niko, a new farmer on the coastal plain, had never seen wind push rain sideways before it even began to fall. He walked his tomato rows with a clipboard pinned to his chest and marked which stakes might need bracing. The pen slipped from his fingers when a gust snapped a plastic cover loose. He chased it only a few steps, then stopped as the sheet sailed over the fence toward the marsh. His jaw worked while he studied the sky. He called his sister and tried to sound casual, asking her to keep the truck near the house. A low rumble crossed the fields, and he crouched instinctively beside the irrigation pipe. When he stood, mud clung to one knee. He checked the greenhouse doors, pushed each bolt into place, and left his hand on the last one, listening to the wind gather strength.

I was checking the rice paddies when the storm siren began its slow, wavering call. My grandmother had taught me to read water by its shine, but that afternoon every surface flickered under the restless sky. I moved along the bund with a bamboo pole, clearing leaves from the drainage cuts. At the third channel, the earth gave way beneath my heel. I grabbed a stake and hauled myself upright, then stood bent over, breathing through my teeth. Across the paddy, my younger brother waved from the storage hut. I waved back too quickly and nearly dropped the pole. The clouds hid the hills, and the path home looked narrower than before. I checked the sluice one final time, though my fingers could barely turn its handle. Then I walked toward the hut, placing each foot carefully and keeping my eyes on the ground.

Marisol had promised the schoolchildren that the pumpkin patch would be ready for their autumn visit. Now the storm warning crackled from her truck radio while she inspected the vines. She wedged a crate beneath the gate and gathered loose tools, stacking them with unnecessary care. When lightning flashed behind the water tower, her shoulders jumped and a pruning knife clattered into the dirt. She picked it up, wiped the blade on her trousers, and checked the barn roof from several angles. Her son asked whether they should leave for town. Marisol answered that they had time, but she kept glancing at the road. At the far end of the patch, a broad leaf had torn loose and plastered itself to her boot. She peeled it away, swallowed, and hurried back toward the truck, holding the radio close as if its faint voice could guide her.

I was due to deliver the last crates of apples in the morning, so I went out to inspect the orchard despite the darkening sky. The old trees stood crooked on the hill, their branches grinding together whenever the wind rose. I checked the ladders, then moved them into the tool shed, though I kept looking back at the clouds. A gust slammed the shed door against its frame. I jumped and knocked my shoulder on the jamb. For a moment I could not remember whether I had latched it. I walked around to test the handle, then tested it again with both hands. My dog stayed close to my knees, nails clicking on the path. I told him we were only finishing our rounds. The lie sounded cheerful enough until thunder answered from somewhere beyond the valley, and I started toward the farmhouse at a near run.

At sixteen, Tessa was trusted to check her family’s sunflower field while her parents repaired a fence on the opposite ridge. The clouds had turned greenish at the edges, and the stalks bent in restless waves. She carried a coil of twine and tied the weakest plants to their supports, fumbling each knot as the wind tugged her sleeves. Her phone buzzed with her mother’s message: Get inside if it starts. Tessa typed that everything was fine, then hid the phone in her pocket without sending it. A crack of thunder made her drop the twine. She stared at it in the weeds, unable to make herself bend for a few seconds. Then she scooped it up and hurried to the water tank, checking its cover and the nearby gate. She kept her face turned toward the farmhouse, measuring the distance with every step.

The storm was moving inland, and I had one last job before heading back: check the beehives beside the clover field. I wore my veil and gloves, but the mesh brushed my cheek each time the wind pressed it inward. The hives rocked on their stands. I wedged flat stones beneath two corners and listened to the bees’ muffled vibration. A sudden gust lifted the lid of the nearest box. I slammed it down, then held both palms on top while my heart beat against the suit. My uncle’s pickup was parked by the barn, but he had gone to town for feed. I called him and heard only static. The clover lay flat toward the west, pointing the direction the worst weather was coming from. I collected the loose straps, checked each hive once more, and walked back without taking my eyes off the sky.

Old Mr. Okafor had planted cassava on the hillside after retiring from the city, and he still treated every field check like an examination. That evening, he tested the fence wire and inspected the young stems for damage. Wind rattled the dry leaves overhead. When a branch snapped somewhere behind him, he froze with one hand gripping the fence post. His mouth had gone dry. He looked toward the village lights, then down at the muddy track his small tractor would have to cross. A neighbor shouted that the storm might arrive within the hour. Okafor nodded, though the man was too far away to see it. He gathered his tools into a bucket, spilling two screws into the grass, and left them there. At the shed, he locked the door and pulled the handle several times before making the slow trip back to his house.

I checked the vineyard rows in a borrowed raincoat, the hood flapping against my ears. My family had spent all spring tying the young vines, and the forecast called for heavy rain before midnight. I walked from post to post, tightening loose wire with a pair of pliers. The metal seemed to slip whenever thunder rolled over the hills. At one point, I looked up and saw a limb swaying above the shed. I backed away so fast that I stumbled over a bucket. My brother laughed from the tractor, but I could not join in. I kept my eyes on the branch until it settled, then finished securing the last row. The wind smelled of wet stone. As I drove toward the farmhouse, both hands clamped the steering wheel, and I took the bends at a crawl, watching the tree line for movement.

Pavel had spent the day harvesting onions, but the storm clouds arrived before the final bins reached the barn. He hurried across the field to inspect the tarp covering the remaining crop. Its corner had come loose, whipping above the rows like a flag. He grabbed the rope and wrapped it around his palm, wincing as it burned his skin. A flash lit the distant ridge, and he ducked behind a loaded wagon. For several breaths he stayed there, listening to rain begin ticking on the metal roof. His daughter called from the barn door, asking him to come in. Pavel raised a thumb, then checked the knots one more time. He could not make his hands stop trembling, so he shoved them into his coat pockets and walked toward her. Behind him, the tarp strained against its ties, snapping in the rising wind.

The rear wheel of my bicycle buckled on the empty road just as dusk swallowed the fields. I rolled it beneath a highway overpass and set out my wrench, but my hands kept slipping against the cold metal. Each passing truck shook dust from the concrete ceiling. I checked the chain, then checked the road behind me, though nobody was there. My phone showed one bar, then none. When a shape moved near the far pillar, I dropped the wrench and crouched beside the frame, holding my breath until it resolved into a torn plastic bag. I forced myself to work, turning the axle a quarter rotation at a time. The wheel finally spun straight. I pedaled toward the nearest lit farmhouse without looking back.

At eleven, Nia had never opened a bicycle hub, but the wobbling front wheel stood between her and the school race. Her older brother had gone to fetch their mother, leaving her alone in the garage with a tray of tiny bearings. The wind rattled the door. She lined the pieces up on a rag and followed a repair video, pausing whenever the speaker moved too quickly. A metallic clatter from outside sent her wrench skidding beneath the bench. Nia froze, shoulders raised, listening. Nothing followed. She retrieved the tool and tightened the cone until the wheel turned without scraping. When her family returned, grease streaked her cheeks, and she held the bicycle upright with both hands as if it might tip over again.

I found the crack in my bicycle frame outside the closed ferry terminal, where the last boat had already pulled away. Rain ticked against the awning while I studied the split near the seat post. My camping kit held epoxy, but the label warned that it needed an hour to cure. A horn sounded across the water; I flinched so hard the tube rolled from my palm. I pictured being stranded on the island road after dark, with the marsh on one side and no houses on the other. Still, I cleaned the metal, mixed the resin, and wrapped it in cloth. Every few minutes I tested the bond with a careful thumb. When it held, I pushed the bicycle rather than riding, keeping close to the terminal lights.

Mateo was halfway through repairing his bicycle in the apartment courtyard when the motion-sensor lights blinked out. The loose pedal lay beside him, its threads stripped, and the only replacement was in a toolbox upstairs. He listened to footsteps crossing the corridor beyond the gate. His screwdriver slipped from his damp fingers and rang against the paving stones. He waited, jaw tight, until the sound faded toward the street. Then he used a file to smooth the damaged threads, working by the glow of his phone. The screen dimmed twice. He kept glancing at the dark windows above, expecting a neighbor to call out or a door to open. At last the pedal caught. He tested it with one slow turn, then wheeled the bicycle inside.

The chain snapped on my bicycle while I was crossing a forest trail, and the nearest road was several miles away. I opened my multitool, but a twig cracked in the brush beyond the trail. My fingers closed around the chain tool so tightly that its edge pressed into my palm. I stared into the trees, then made myself count the links instead. The quick-link was still in my saddlebag; I had practiced using it at home, where the birdsong never sounded like something following me. I joined the chain, tugged twice, and wiped my hands on my jacket. A second crack came from farther off. I packed everything without checking what caused it and pushed the bicycle toward the open trail, keeping my eyes on the pale strip of sky ahead.

When a storm tore the brake cable on her bicycle, Celeste pulled into the shelter of an old bus stop. She had promised to reach her grandmother’s house before nightfall, and the road beyond the shelter ran beside a steep ravine. She examined the broken wire, but the gusts kept lifting the repair manual from her lap. A branch scraped across the roof, making her jerk upright. Celeste pressed both palms to her knees until they stopped trembling, then threaded the spare cable through the lever. Her phone buzzed with a weather alert, and she nearly dropped it into a puddle. She finished the adjustment and squeezed the brake again and again. It held. She chose the slower village road, riding with one hand near the lever and the other gripping the handlebars.

I was fixing my bicycle beneath the fluorescent lights of the underground parking garage when the elevator doors opened behind me. The back tire had gone flat, and I had already removed it, so there was nowhere to go quickly. A man’s shoes crossed the concrete, stopped, then turned away. I kept my head bent over the tube, though I had lost track of where the puncture was. My breath came in short pulls. I ran water from my bottle over the rubber and watched for bubbles, willing the task to give my hands something exact to do. At last, a pinprick hiss appeared near the valve. I patched it, reassembled the wheel, and checked the tire pressure twice. I waited until the elevator swallowed the footsteps before leaving.

Priya had borrowed her cousin’s bicycle for a delivery shift, and now its handlebars twisted loosely in her grip. She brought it into the courtyard behind the restaurant, where stacked crates made narrow shadows. The shop’s closing bell rang inside, and she looked toward the rear door, expecting someone to discover the damage. Her cheeks warmed as she searched the tool pouch for the right hex key. A bottle clinked in the alley; she crouched behind the bicycle, then scolded herself under her breath and stood again. The stem bolt was barely finger-tight. She aligned the front wheel with the frame and tightened it in small turns, checking after each one. When it stopped shifting, Priya rolled the bicycle around the courtyard, listening for any new rattle before returning it.

My bicycle’s front light flickered out on the mountain pass, and when I stopped to inspect it, I noticed the fork had loosened. The road was empty, with a drop-off just beyond the gravel shoulder. My knees locked while I took the small wrench from my bag. I kept imagining the wheel turning sideways on the descent, so I avoided looking down the slope. Instead, I braced the bicycle against a stone marker and tightened the fork bolts by feel. The wind pushed at my jacket, and each gust made the frame knock against the rock. I paused, counted five slow breaths, and tried the wheel again. It spun true. I walked the bicycle downhill until the road widened, then rode only as far as the next ranger station.

At the edge of the night market, Omar’s bicycle chain jammed between the gears. He dragged it behind a row of closed stalls and laid it on its side. The vendors were packing up, but a shout from the far end of the lane made him duck behind a stack of baskets. He waited, gripping the frame, while footsteps hurried past without stopping. The chain was twisted around the derailleur, and every attempt to pull it free tightened the knot. Omar took a small breath, followed the links with his finger, and eased the metal backward one tooth at a time. His knuckles scraped the gear. When the chain released, he wiped the blood on a napkin and turned the pedals slowly. The bicycle moved again; he pushed it toward the busy, brightly lit avenue.

I had just started repairing my bicycle outside the desert observatory when the wind erased the track behind me. The rear rack had snapped, leaving my water canteen dangling by a strap. I unpacked wire and pliers, but the sky had gone the color of rust, and fine sand stung my eyes. A sudden gust toppled the bicycle. I sprang back, then stood motionless, listening to the low whistle across the flats. The observatory’s dome was still visible, though its lights blinked through the blowing dust. I twisted wire around the rack stays, checking the knot with shaking fingers. It would not carry the canteen safely. I strapped the bottle to my own pack instead and walked the bicycle back toward the dome, stopping whenever the wind swallowed its outline.

Lena found a bent spoke on her bicycle just before the bridge over the canal. She wheeled it beneath a streetlamp and opened a repair kit, though the passing water made the narrow path feel smaller by the minute. A bicycle bell rang somewhere behind her. Lena clutched the frame and turned; the path was empty. She set the wheel upside down, then struggled to locate the spoke wrench in the crowded pouch. Her fingers kept missing its handle. Once she found it, she loosened the neighboring spokes and tightened the replacement until the rim sat nearly straight. She spun the wheel, stopped it, and listened for a scrape. The sound had vanished. Rather than cross the bridge in the dark, she walked the bicycle toward the station, holding the handlebars close.

I set my clarinet on the chair and rubbed my palms against my trousers, though they were already dry. The community hall held only twenty folding seats, but every one seemed to face my music stand like an accusing eye. My first note came out thin. I stopped, checked the reed, and tried again, counting each breath as Mr. Alvarez had taught me. From behind the curtain, someone dropped a tray; I jolted so hard the clarinet slipped in my hands. “Just the sound check,” I told myself, quietly. I practiced the opening until the melody settled, then the difficult run, then the opening once more. When the caretaker asked whether I wanted the lights brighter, I said no and watched him leave. The empty seats waited. I lifted the instrument again, keeping my fingers moving until the stage door clicked shut.

At sixty-eight, Hye-Jin had played violin at weddings, funerals, and once on a ferry in rough weather. Still, the library’s intimate concert made her bow hand tremble. She tightened the screw, loosened it, then tightened it again. A child peered through the rehearsal-room window, and she lost her place in the score. Her mouth went dry. She turned the page back, though she knew the passage by heart, and marked the measure with a pencil. The accompanist arrived carrying tea and asked if she was ready. Hye-Jin nodded too quickly, then made a joke about needing a second pair of hands to hold the bow. They began the piece at half speed. When the violin’s first clear phrase crossed the quiet room, she drew a longer breath and let the next note follow.

The basement smelled of wet coats and old paint, and I kept checking the lock on the side door. In an hour, my three-piece band would play six songs for the neighborhood fundraiser. I had promised to sing the first one, but the microphone looked taller each time I glanced at it. I tuned my guitar, missed the low string, and turned the peg too far. My brother offered to take the opening verse. I shook my head, then wiped my hands on a towel and tried the chord progression without singing. On the next pass, I added one line, barely above a whisper. The heating pipes knocked behind the wall, making me flinch between verses. I laughed at myself, but my shoulders stayed raised. When the others arrived, I asked them to start from the beginning and kept my eyes on the fretboard.

Malik arranged his trumpet mute, spare valve oil, and water bottle in a precise row on the piano. The café’s back room could hold thirty people, and the concert would begin as soon as the tables were cleared. He had never performed without a music stand, so he kept glancing at the pages clipped to a chair. A waiter slid a glass across the counter; the scrape made Malik’s breath catch. He pressed his thumb against the valve casing until its edge left a pale mark. His teacher suggested playing the first phrase with his eyes closed. Malik tried, but stopped after three bars and opened them at once. “Let’s take it slower,” he said, though the tempo was already gentle. He practiced the ending until each note landed cleanly, then stayed beside the piano, listening to the room fill with chairs being moved.

I had played accordion at family gatherings for years, but the retirement home’s sunroom felt different with its rows of waiting chairs. My red shoes tapped an uneven beat beneath the keyboard.
