The expedition leader asked if she was all right. She nodded too quickly, then sat by the window and counted the stations on the timetable.

I heard the train start as I stepped onto the platform, carrying my father’s old camera in a paper bag. He had asked me to photograph the mountains from the northbound line before his eyesight faded further. I had promised, then delayed until the final day of his visit. Now the carriage was pulling away, and the camera’s strap poked through the torn paper. I ran beside the train, whispering, “Please, just one more second,” though nobody could hear me. The air scraped my throat. My fingers felt numb, and the bag shook against my leg. A guard at the rear door leaned out and caught the handle. I climbed aboard, then sat down hard on the nearest seat. My father’s message glowed on my phone: Don’t worry if you can’t. I stared at it until the scenery blurred.

Sanjay was halfway across the plaza when the platform announcement named the train to the border. His daughter was on it, bound for a scholarship interview she had insisted on attending alone. He had meant to wish her luck at the station, not watch the train leave without him. He ran, clutching the envelope of documents she had forgotten on the kitchen table. His breath came in noisy bursts, and the envelope slipped from his damp hand. Papers skittered across the pavement. A stranger helped gather them while Sanjay kept glancing toward the shrinking train. At the platform entrance he shoved the papers under his arm and rushed on. The carriage had nearly cleared the station when his daughter spotted him through the window. She opened her palm against the glass. Sanjay lifted the envelope. He remained beneath the departure board, shaking, until the next train was announced.

At the first gray hint of morning, I pushed my skiff from the reeds and heard a sharp knock beneath the hull. The lake lay smooth, but my hands tightened around the oars until my knuckles blanched. I told myself it was a floating branch. Then the knock came again, directly under my seat. I stopped rowing. Across the water, the shore lamps blurred in the mist, and my mouth had gone dry. My phone showed no signal. I lifted the anchor rope, ready to drop it if the boat shifted, and kept watching the black water beside me. A loon called somewhere beyond the fog. I nearly shouted back, then clamped my lips together. When the sun edged over the ridge, a split log drifted into view, its submerged end tapping the boat with every small wave.

Marta had fished Lake Winona for decades, but that morning the fog erased the far bank before she had rowed a hundred yards. She kept one hand on the gunwale and the other on the compass, checking its trembling needle every few seconds. A bell rang from somewhere behind her, though the marina had been empty when she left. She turned so quickly that her tackle box slid across the floorboards. The sound came again, faint and uneven. Marta swallowed and called out, her voice smaller than she intended. No answer followed. She rowed toward the last patch of visible shoreline, counting each stroke under her breath. When daylight finally thinned the fog, she found a red buoy rocking beside her boat, its little bell chiming whenever the waves nudged it.

I was twelve when Grandpa let me take his aluminum boat onto Birch Lake by myself, just after dawn. He watched from the dock until the mist covered him. I kept glancing over my shoulder, expecting his cap to appear again. Halfway to the fishing grounds, the motor sputtered and died. The silence felt enormous. I pulled the starter cord once, then again, breathing through my teeth while the boat drifted toward a line of dark pines. Something splashed close to my elbow. My shoulders shot up, and I grabbed the paddle so hard it bent against the seat. I wanted to call for Grandpa, but my voice caught. A beaver surfaced beside the bow, chewing a twig. Its tail slapped the water, and I nearly dropped the paddle. The motor started on the next pull.

Elias, a retired baker with a stiff left knee, launched before sunrise because the trout fed best in cool water. He had barely baited his hook when a low engine growl rose behind him. No boat showed through the mist. He reeled in fast, the line scraping his thumb, and stared toward the sound. His pulse beat hard in his throat. The growl stopped; then came three slow knocks, as if someone were rapping on a door beneath the lake. Elias shifted to the center of his boat and reached for the flare tucked beside his lunch tin. He could hear his own breath rasping. As the sky brightened, a chain of bubbles crossed the water. A diver’s orange hood broke the surface near the old quarry marker, and a gloved hand waved an apology.

I left the landing at dawn with a thermos, two rods, and my father’s old map folded in my pocket. The lake was so still that my paddle made a sound like tearing cloth. Near the eastern point, I saw a pale figure standing among the trees. I stopped rowing. The figure seemed to lift one arm, though the branches shifted at the same moment. My stomach tightened, and I backed away from the shore, letting the boat turn in circles. I tried to whistle, but only air came out. After several minutes, a gust cleared the mist. The pale shape was a birch trunk split by lightning, its loose bark fluttering. I laughed once, too loudly, then kept my eyes on the tree line all the way to my fishing spot.

Niko had moved from the city only a month earlier, and the lake’s morning quiet still unsettled him. He guided his narrow boat past the last dock, listening to the oarlocks squeak. A sudden splash struck the stern. Niko spun around, nearly tipping the boat, and found no one there. He wiped his damp palms on his jacket and checked the rope twice. The fishing net lay tangled at his feet, so he worked it loose with stiff fingers, pausing whenever a ripple crossed the water. A second splash sounded near the reeds. He backed toward open water, eyes fixed on the dark stems. Then a muskrat emerged carrying a mouthful of grass. Niko let out the breath he had been holding and settled the net carefully across his knees.

Before dawn, I took my father’s wooden dory onto Lake Ash, though the weather report had promised calm. The clouds gathered quickly, turning the water the color of slate. Each gust pushed the bow sideways, and I gripped the tiller until my forearms ached. A flash of lightning showed the far shore, then vanished. I counted the seconds, but thunder rolled before I reached five. My bait tin rattled against the bench. I turned toward the landing, rowing hard, yet the shoreline seemed to slide farther away. When rain began, I hunched over the oars and muttered directions to myself. A small harbor light appeared through the downpour. I aimed for it, missing the first dock and bumping the second. A woman in a yellow coat caught the bow rope and steadied the boat.

At seventy-three, June still brought her own boat to Lake Loon at dawn, though the narrow channel had grown harder to navigate. That morning a foghorn sounded close by, loud enough to make her drop the thermos. She could not see a single vessel. June shut off the motor and listened, one hand pressed against her chest. The horn groaned again, now seeming to come from behind her. She reached for the radio, but her fingers slipped on the wet dial. For several minutes she sat perfectly still, watching water beads gather on the windshield. Then a breeze opened a gap in the mist. A maintenance barge appeared near the dam, its horn still sounding as it reversed. June retrieved the thermos and steered toward the public dock, taking the long route around the barge.

I had promised my sister I would bring home enough perch for supper, so I launched before the sunrise despite the strange knocking in my engine. The boat coughed twice and carried me beyond the reeds. Then it went silent. I pulled the cord until my shoulder burned, while the hull drifted toward a stump field. One stump rose ahead like a hunched shape, and I leaned back, scraping the oar across the water to steer away. My breath came in short bursts. I checked the fuel line, then the spark plug, fumbling each step as the boat nudged a submerged branch. At last the engine caught with a roar. I flinched and almost fell overboard. By the time I reached shore, the sun was above the hills, and my sister was waiting with a spare motor.

Rafi, a school custodian, rowed onto the lake every Saturday before his shift. He chose a sheltered cove and cast toward a patch of lily pads. A distant crack echoed over the water. His rod slipped from his hand, and he stared toward the ridge where the sound had come from. Another crack followed, then a third. Rafi crouched low in the boat, pulling his cap down as if it could shield him. He reached for his phone, but the screen showed no service. The woods remained still. He began rowing toward the landing, keeping the shoreline between himself and the ridge. At the dock he found a posted notice: crews were removing dead trees nearby. As he tied up, a worker waved from the hillside, and Rafi’s shoulders slowly loosened.

The lake was still dark when I eased my canoe away from the public ramp. I had never fished alone before, and every creak seemed to come from something moving behind me. Near the middle, the paddle snagged on a line beneath the surface. I yanked, and the canoe lurched sideways. My heart hammered so hard I could feel it in my jaw. I tried to free the blade, but the line tightened again. For a moment I sat frozen, staring at the water around my hands. Then I leaned forward and cut the line with my pocketknife. A yellow fishing float bobbed up, attached to an old net. I paddled back with the severed line curled in my lap, checking over my shoulder until the ramp came into view.

Beatriz had borrowed her neighbor’s motorboat for a dawn fishing trip on Lake Cinder. She knew the shoreline well, but a sudden vibration ran through the steering wheel as she passed the island. The engine pitch dropped. Beatriz pulled the throttle back, eyes flicking between the fuel gauge and the dark water beneath her. A thin ribbon of smoke curled from the motor. She shut it off and fumbled with the emergency radio, her fingers clumsy against the buttons. When a voice answered, she gave the location twice because the first attempt came out too softly. She waited near the island, wrapping her arms around herself while the boat rocked. A rescue skiff arrived ten minutes later. Its operator found a loose fuel hose and towed her safely to the landing.

I arrived at the gallery before sunrise, carrying the last three paintings and a paper cup gone cold in my hand. Tonight’s opening would be my first since the fire that destroyed my old studio. I kept checking the smoke detector, though it had been tested twice, and chose a place for each canvas far from the exit signs’ red glow. When the curator asked whether I was ready, I nodded too quickly and smoothed the same corner of a label until it curled. Then I noticed a faint haze near the storeroom door. My mouth dried. I set down the cup, called the building manager, and stood outside while he checked the wiring. Nothing was burning; a humidifier had leaked onto a hot vent. I went back in with shaky knees, moved my paintings to safer hooks, and opened the doors for the guests.

At sixty-eight, Devika had spent a year stitching scraps of her mother’s saris into a hanging work for the city museum. On installation morning, the rigging crew raised it above the main hall, and one metal clip gave a sharp, small click. Devika’s hands clenched around her folded program. She asked the technician to lower the piece, then watched him test every attachment twice. He explained that the clip was secure, but she could not stop measuring the distance from the fabric to the marble floor with her eyes. When the doors opened, she stayed beneath the work, scanning its seams instead of greeting visitors. A child pointed out a patch patterned with tiny green birds. Devika followed the child’s gaze, and a laugh escaped her. She stepped aside at last, though she kept the spare clips in her pocket.

The gallery’s walls looked too white, like a blank page waiting to judge me. I had painted the portraits of people from my fishing village, but none of them had seen the finished show. My uncle had warned me not to put his portrait beside the entrance, where everyone could stare. I had done it anyway. As the opening approached, I shifted the frame, then shifted it back, listening for footsteps in the corridor. When a car door slammed outside, I dropped the hammer. My fingers would not close properly around it. I considered taking the portrait down before anyone noticed. Instead, I called my uncle and asked him to come early. He arrived in his work boots, stood before the painting, and studied it without speaking. Then he straightened the frame. “You got the scar right,” he said. I let out the breath I’d been holding.

Nico’s exhibition was built from photographs of abandoned train stations, and the final print showed a platform where his older brother had vanished from his life years earlier. He had not told his family it was included. On opening night, he kept the image turned toward the wall while guests wandered among the other photographs. Each time the entrance opened, his shoulders rose. His sister appeared near the refreshments, studying the captions. Nico’s tongue stuck to the roof of his mouth as she reached the last room. He started toward her, stopped, and rubbed his thumb over a strip of tape on his sleeve. She turned the print around herself. For a long moment, neither spoke. Then she touched the frame and asked when he had taken it. “The year he left,” Nico said. Her eyes stayed on the platform. She did not walk away, and he moved to stand beside her.

I had arranged my glass sculptures on low plinths, each one catching the gallery lights like a trapped piece of afternoon. The forecast promised high winds, and the old warehouse windows rattled whenever a gust crossed the street. I kept walking the room, checking the plinths for wobble, although they were bolted down. At noon, a branch scraped the largest window. The sound made my stomach seize. I called the gallery manager and asked whether the storm shutters worked. He demonstrated them, then showed me the emergency plan posted beside the door. I read it twice, holding the paper so tightly it bent. By evening the wind eased, but I placed extra padding beneath the most delicate works and moved the crowd barriers farther back. During the opening, a guest admired the way the sculptures trembled with light. I smiled, still listening to the windows.

Mariam, a printmaker who had recently moved from Aleppo to Montreal, spent weeks preparing an exhibition about the sounds of her new neighborhood. Each image paired a street scene with a handwritten phrase in Arabic and French. She worried that a translation error might turn a private memory into a public insult. Before the opening, she checked every card against her notebook, then asked the volunteer at the desk to read them aloud. The volunteer stumbled over one name. Mariam’s pulse thudded in her throat; she pulled the card from the wall and compared each letter. The spelling was correct, but the pronunciation needed guidance. She wrote a small note in pencil and placed it beside the label. When visitors arrived, she stood close enough to help without hovering. A woman recognized the phrase from her own childhood and began to tell Mariam a story.

My first solo show filled a narrow room above a bakery, and I had spent the week painting tiny birds onto canvases almost too small to notice. On the afternoon of the opening, I discovered that the gallery’s front door would not latch. Every draft pushed it open a few inches, letting street noise and cold air spill inside. I imagined someone brushing against a painting or a gust sending one tumbling from its hook. I tested the latch until my fingertips hurt, then wedged a chair beneath the handle. The owner promised a locksmith, but the minutes crawled. I kept my coat on and watched the doorway rather than the work. When the locksmith finally arrived, he fixed the strike plate in ten minutes. I laughed at the chair, though my knees still felt loose. Then I took off my coat and turned on the lights.

At twenty-two, Jun was the youngest artist invited to exhibit at a downtown gallery. His installation used hundreds of paper boats suspended by thread, and he had spent the night before the opening picturing one falling into a visitor’s drink. During setup, a maintenance worker wheeled a ladder through the room, brushing close to the lowest boat. Jun stepped between them, palms lifted. The worker stopped and apologized. Jun tried to explain the fragile arrangement, but his voice came out thin. He inspected every knot while the others finished hanging the labels. When the gallery director suggested raising the boats, Jun shook his head; they were meant to hover at shoulder height. He asked for a rope barrier instead. At the opening, guests leaned in to study the folded paper, keeping their distance. Jun watched the installation sway gently above them and finally unclenched his hands.

I prepared my exhibition in the back room of a library, where every painting showed a different version of the town’s demolished swimming pool. I expected a few old neighbors to come. Then the mayor’s office called to say he planned to attend, and my stomach folded in on itself. I had painted him as a child, diving from the high board, though I had never asked permission. I nearly removed the canvas. Instead, I rearranged the room so it was not the first thing anyone saw, then rehearsed three explanations in front of the dark window. At the opening, the mayor arrived with his coat still buttoned. He stopped at the painting and leaned close to the small figure on the board. My hands went cold. “That was the summer I broke my arm,” he said. He looked at me, not angry, and I managed to offer him a chair.

Sofia’s exhibition of embroidered maps was scheduled to open the morning after a minor earthquake. The gallery’s old plaster walls had developed a hairline crack, and her work was pinned directly across them. She asked the building inspector whether the room was safe, then followed him as he examined the ceiling. His calm report did little to quiet the tight flutter beneath her ribs. She removed the maps one by one, wrapping each in tissue while the curator called a structural engineer. The engineer found no danger, but recommended moving the display to a newer room. Sofia spent the evening rehanging everything, checking each pin with the flat of her thumb. Visitors arrived the next day to find the maps arranged in a brighter space. A child traced one stitched river in the air without touching it. Sofia watched the walls instead of the crowd, then joined the child’s mother to explain the route.

I was preparing a gallery show of portraits painted from memory, and the final face belonged to my father, who had died before I could ask him about the years he spent away. The canvas sat wrapped in brown paper while I worked on the labels. I kept finding reasons not to unwrap it: the lighting needed adjustment, the frame looked uneven, the title might be wrong. On installation day, the curator asked where it should hang. My palms slickened, and I told her to wait. Alone in the room, I peeled back the paper. The painted eyes seemed to meet mine, and I stepped into the hallway, breathing through my mouth. I called my cousin, who had known our father better. She came over and stood quietly beside the canvas. “That’s the way he looked when he was listening,” she said. I carried it to the wall myself.

Ravi had spent months collecting discarded electronics for an exhibition about planned obsolescence. The sculptures were wired to blink in uneven patterns, and one had begun making a clicking sound during the final safety check. He switched off the power strip, then stared at the sculpture’s tangled circuit board as though it might start again by itself. The gallery electrician was delayed, so Ravi taped off the corner and moved the opening reception table away from the work. He answered the curator’s questions in short bursts, glancing back whenever the lights flickered. The electrician eventually found a loose relay and replaced it. Ravi watched the repaired piece run through three cycles before letting anyone near it. When guests entered, the sculpture blinked and clicked on cue. A visitor called it playful. Ravi smiled, but kept the electrician’s number saved on his phone.

I waited until the hallway was empty before knocking on Mr. Vale’s door. Water had been dripping through my kitchen ceiling for three nights, and a brown stain now spread above the stove. When he opened up, I held my phone with the photos ready, though my thumb kept slipping on the screen. “Could someone look at it today?” I asked. He glanced toward the stairs and said the building’s plumber had quit. My mouth went dry. I pictured the ceiling giving way while I slept, then hated myself for imagining it. I asked if he could at least shut off the pipe. Mr. Vale studied the pictures, finally picked up his phone, and called a repair company. I stayed in the doorway until he told me when they would come.

Nia rehearsed her request on the bus, then folded the paper with the repair estimate into smaller and smaller squares. The front lock had jammed twice, leaving her outside after late shifts. In the landlord’s office, she kept one hand on the strap of her work bag while she explained. Mr. Dunn said the lock was old but still usable. Nia’s cheeks warmed; she imagined another night on the step, calling a neighbor who might not answer. She asked him to test it himself. The key stuck halfway when he tried. His expression changed, and he wrote down the address of a locksmith. Nia nodded, though her knees still felt loose. Before leaving, she asked for the appointment time in writing and tucked the note safely into her pocket.

I found a crack in the bedroom wall after moving my bookcase, a jagged line running from the window to the floor. I called my landlord, but when he said he would “get around to it,” I nearly hung up. My fingers had gone numb around the phone. I told him the window frame shifted whenever trucks passed and asked him to come see it. While I waited, I sat on the bed with my shoes on, listening to every creak in the building. He arrived with a level and pressed it against the wall. The bubble slid hard to one side. He stopped joking, took several photographs, and promised a structural inspection the next morning. I wrote the promise on my calendar before he left.

At seventy-two, Hector disliked asking anyone for help, especially the landlord who had dismissed his messages about the loose stair rail. On Tuesday, he climbed the stairs slowly, gripping the wall with his free hand. At the top, he found Mrs. Pike near the laundry room and explained that the rail had pulled away again. His voice thinned as he showed her the screws in his palm. She asked whether anyone had fallen. Hector said no, then looked down through the stairwell opening. His shoulders drew tight beneath his coat. Mrs. Pike called the maintenance worker and stayed with him while they waited. When the worker arrived, Hector watched each turn of the screwdriver, asking that the rail be secured into the studs. He tested it only after the worker stepped aside.

The heater clicked and went quiet just as the temperature dropped below freezing. I wrapped a blanket around my shoulders and called Ms. Chen, my landlord. She answered while I was standing beside the radiator, listening for any sign of life. “It’s probably the thermostat,” she said. I had already tried that, but the words came out in a whisper. My breath showed faintly near the window. I told her my toddler was asleep in the next room and asked for an emergency repair. There was a pause long enough for me to count the clicks of the cooling pipes. Then she said a technician was on the way and gave me his name. I repeated it twice, writing it on the back of an envelope as the radiator began to hiss.

Sasha had only lived in the basement apartment for a week when sewage water bubbled up in the shower drain. She called the landlord, keeping her gaze on the dark water as it rose around her slippers. He asked her to send a video. Her hand shook enough that the first recording showed mostly the wall. She tried again, narrating the gurgling sound and the smell spreading through the room. The landlord stopped asking questions and told her not to use the plumbing. Sasha carried her cat upstairs in its carrier and waited on the front steps, coat unbuttoned in the rain. A plumber arrived within an hour, followed by the landlord with towels and a temporary room key. Sasha held the key in both hands until the door clicked shut behind her.

I brought a jar of the plaster that had fallen from my ceiling to the landlord’s office. It sat between us on his desk while I explained that more pieces dropped whenever the upstairs tenant ran a bath. Mr. Rios leaned back and said old buildings shifted. I could feel my pulse in my jaw. I asked him to inspect the ceiling before anything heavier came down. He began to object, then noticed the dust on my sleeves and the fresh split above the doorway. I wanted to leave, but I stayed with my hands flat on my knees. He called a contractor and arranged for me to sleep in an empty unit until the ceiling was checked. I carried the jar with me, careful not to spill its chalky contents.

Miriam, a nursing student from Kenya, noticed sparks at the outlet beside her desk. She unplugged her lamp and went straight to the landlord’s apartment, rehearsing what to say on each stair. When he opened the door, she held out the scorched plug without stepping inside. He initially said an electrician could come next week. Miriam’s lips pressed together; her desk was beside the only outlet in the room, and she needed it for her laptop. She explained that the socket had flashed twice and smelled burnt. The landlord looked at the blackened prongs, then called an electrician and told Miriam to leave the breaker off. She returned to her room and stood in the hallway while the lights remained on. When the electrician arrived, she watched him replace the outlet before plugging anything in.

I found mold behind the wardrobe after my son’s cough kept waking him at night. The landlord said he could stop by Friday, four days away. I stood in the kitchen with the phone pressed to my ear, staring at the damp patch on my sleeve. “Could you come sooner?” I asked. My voice sounded smaller than I meant it to. He asked for pictures, so I moved the wardrobe just enough to show the black spots spreading along the wall. The room smelled sharp and wet. After a long silence, he said he would bring a specialist that afternoon. I packed my son’s pajamas and favorite book while we waited, though I wasn’t sure where we would sleep. When the specialist arrived, the landlord helped carry the wardrobe into the hall.

Owen’s apartment door had begun sticking in its frame, and one evening it would not open from the inside. He called his landlord through the narrow gap, phone held near the latch so she could hear him tugging. His chest tightened each time the handle stopped. The landlord said she was ten minutes away, but Owen kept checking the clock and trying the lock with a coin. He left the phone line open, listening to her footsteps approach from outside. When she arrived, she worked the key while he pushed the door. It sprang inward all at once, and Owen stumbled into the hall. The landlord apologized and called a carpenter. Owen stayed outside while they examined the frame, watching the open doorway as if it might close again.

The balcony railing moved when I leaned on it to bring in the laundry. I stepped back so quickly that a basket tipped over, sending socks across the floor. My landlord, Mrs. Bello, lived downstairs. I knocked, then almost turned away when I heard her footsteps. I told her the rail was loose and asked her to come look. She followed me up, and I pointed from several feet back. A gust rattled the glass door. My stomach clenched as she reached toward the railing, so I asked her not to touch it. She listened, then called a repair crew and blocked the balcony entrance with a chair. I spent the evening checking that the chair had not shifted. The crew arrived the next morning and replaced the entire rail.

When the ceiling fan began wobbling, eight-year-old Laila ran to tell her father, who was at work. He called their landlord, Mr. Keene, and asked for a repair before the fan fell. Mr. Keene said he would send someone after lunch. Laila sat on the couch beneath the fan, tracking each uneven sweep with her eyes. Her father asked her to wait in the kitchen, but she kept glancing back through the doorway. He moved the couch and unplugged the fan at the wall. When the repair worker arrived, he found a cracked mounting bracket and carried the fan down carefully. Mr. Keene came by afterward to apologize for delaying. Laila’s father thanked him, then asked for the other fixtures to be checked. Laila stayed close to the kitchen door until the tools were packed.

When the food bank’s freezer alarm began chirping, I was alone in the basement with three crates of chicken. My hands went slick against the clipboard, and I read the temperature twice without taking in the numbers. If the food spoiled, the director had said, the Thursday families would go home with less. I called upstairs, but the sorting room swallowed my voice. Then I noticed a thin ribbon of water beneath the freezer door. I backed away, bumping a shelf hard enough to rattle cans, and nearly dropped my phone. Instead of guessing, I followed the emergency card taped beside the light switch. I shut the freezer circuit, called the repair number, and hauled the crates into the walk-in cooler one careful load at a time. When the director came down, I was still gripping the clipboard with both hands. She checked the food, nodded, and handed me a clean towel.

At sixty-eight, Salma had volunteered at the neighborhood pantry for only two weeks when a man at the distribution window began demanding a box she could not find on his list. He slapped the counter, and the waiting line went quiet. Salma’s throat tightened. Her thumb pressed into the edge of the inventory sheet until the paper bent. She wanted to call for the coordinator, but the coordinator was outside unloading a delivery. Salma kept her eyes on the list and asked the man to spell his surname. He muttered it, then glanced toward the door. She found his name under a different household number and explained the mistake in a steady, low voice. His shoulders dropped. He apologized, almost too softly to hear, and she carried the box around the counter herself. After he left, Salma noticed her knees trembling beneath the table.

The first time I drove the food bank’s van, the route sheet sent me across a bridge I had never used. Rain blurred the lane markings, and the van’s wipers squeaked in a rhythm that made every passing truck feel close. I kept both hands fixed at ten and two. At the far end, a detour sign pointed toward an industrial road, but my phone had lost its signal. I pulled into a gas station, checked the paper map, then asked the attendant for directions. My voice came out thin, so I repeated the question. He drew the turns on the back of a receipt. By the time I reached the church kitchen, the volunteers had set out soup and bread for the families. I unloaded the crates slowly, letting the solid weight of each one settle against my arms. Nobody mentioned my late arrival; the coordinator simply showed me where to park next time.

I was sorting cans at the community food bank when a small boy slipped away from his mother and vanished behind the storage shelves. The woman searched the lobby, calling his name, while I stood with a crate tilted against my hip. My breath caught. I set the cans down and checked the narrow aisles, trying not to knock over the stacked boxes. Each empty corner made the building seem larger. Then I heard a faint scrape near the loading dock. The boy had crawled under a folding table to retrieve a toy car. I crouched several feet away and asked whether he could roll it toward me. He did, and I passed it back before calling his mother. She hugged him so tightly that he squeaked. I returned to the cans, but my fingers needed a moment before they could work the labels loose again.

Mina’s first shift at the food bank coincided with a surprise inspection from the county. The inspector asked for temperature logs, cleaning records, and proof that donated produce had been checked. Mina had been shown the filing cabinet only once. She searched the folders while the director spoke with the inspector, aware of every second ticking from the wall clock. A bead of sweat slid beneath her collar. The green binder was missing. She pictured the whole delivery being rejected because she had misplaced it. Then she remembered carrying a stack of papers to the break room after a spill. The binder sat beneath a pile of aprons. Mina brought it back and opened to the correct page, though her hand shook enough to blur the signature. The inspector found everything in order. Later, the director thanked her for remembering where she had put it.

I signed up to pack grocery bags at the food bank because I thought the work would be quiet. Then the power cut out, leaving the warehouse dark except for the red exit signs. Somewhere across the room, a metal cart rolled and struck a shelf. My shoulders jumped, and I gripped the packing table. A few volunteers began talking at once. I could hear someone near the freezer calling for a flashlight. I found my phone in my apron pocket and switched on its beam, keeping it pointed at the floor so nobody was blinded. We followed the wall to the supply closet and found two lanterns. Once they were lit, we counted heads and moved the refrigerated goods into insulated bins. The generator started after twelve minutes. When the lights returned, I laughed too loudly, then went back to folding bags beside a volunteer who hummed while she worked.

At the rural pantry, Hector was asked to drive a box of groceries to a house at the end of an unpaved road. He knew the route, but fresh snow had softened the shoulders, and the old pickup fishtailed on the first bend. He eased off the accelerator, jaw clenched, and watched the trees pass inches from the passenger window. Turning back meant the family might miss dinner; continuing too fast could put the truck in a ditch. Hector stopped at a wide spot and called the pantry manager. Together they decided he would leave the groceries with a neighbor who had a plowed driveway. Hector carried the boxes through the snow instead of risking the final stretch. The neighbor signed the delivery sheet and promised to take them the rest of the way. On the drive back, Hector kept below the speed limit, his palms still damp on the steering wheel.

I was labeling donated jars when the front door banged open and a dog bolted into the food bank. It skidded across the tile, knocking over a basket of apples, then disappeared into the storeroom. People backed away from the entrance. I could hear claws scrabbling behind the rice pallets. My pulse beat hard in my ears as I looked for the animal’s owner. A teenager outside was calling a name and holding a leash. I asked everyone to stay clear, then used a rolling bin to block the aisle without cornering the dog. It emerged slowly, ears low, and sniffed the apples. The teenager clipped on the leash. Nothing was broken except one bruised fruit. I gathered the apples while the owner thanked me. My hands shook as I rinsed the dust from them, but I finished the labels before taking my break.

Rina had worked in the food bank kitchen for months, but the industrial mixer still unsettled her when it shuddered. One afternoon, while she prepared dough for the shelter’s dinner rolls, the machine gave a sharp clank and stopped. The metal bowl rocked on its base. Rina stepped back, knocking her hip against a counter, then reached for the red power switch. She unplugged the mixer and called the kitchen supervisor before touching anything else. The supervisor arrived with a maintenance worker, who found a loose guard and a bent attachment. Rina stood by the doorway, twisting her apron hem while they repaired it. They tested the machine empty, then asked her to run a small batch. She watched the bowl closely, ready to cut the power. It turned smoothly. Rina portioned the dough and sent the rolls to the oven, where the warm smell gradually filled the room.

At the food bank, I was assigned to explain the new sign-up tablet to visitors. The screen froze while an elderly man waited, and a line began forming behind him. I tapped the button again; nothing happened. My face warmed as people shifted and checked their watches. I had practiced the instructions, but not this. I asked the man if he would mind waiting while I restarted the device, and he nodded without looking up. The tablet took a long time to reboot. I fetched the paper forms from the office and offered them to the people in line. That got everyone moving. The coordinator later showed me how to enter the forms by hand. I wrote the steps on an index card and taped it beneath the counter. The next time the screen stalled, I reached for the card before my fingers could start tapping at random.

Niko was stacking produce boxes when a ceiling tile sagged above the sorting tables. A dark stain spread across it, and a drop landed on the floor. The building had flooded once before, and the memory returned in the smell of wet plaster. Niko stopped the volunteers from placing more food beneath the leak. He moved the boxes to the opposite wall, then called the facilities manager. While they waited, the drip quickened. Niko dragged over a clean plastic tub and positioned it under the tile, listening to each splash. The manager arrived with a ladder and found a leaking pipe overhead. No ceiling sections fell, and the produce stayed dry. Niko filled out an incident report, writing slowly so the pen would not slip from his damp fingers. Before leaving, he walked beneath the repaired ceiling twice, checking for new stains.

The instructor’s name was Mr. Vale, and the car smelled faintly of peppermint and warm vinyl. I kept both hands locked at ten and two while he explained the pedals for the third time. My right shoe hovered above the brake, trembling whenever a truck passed the empty lot’s fence. “You can take your time,” he said. I nodded, though my mouth had gone dry. When he asked me to start the engine, the key rattled against the steering column before it turned. The motor shivered alive. I pressed the accelerator too hard, and the car lurched a few feet. Mr. Vale calmly pointed to the brake. I stopped, cheeks burning, then looked at the painted line ahead. This time I eased forward until the hood crossed it. The instructor marked something on his clipboard. I could not tell whether it was praise, but I let out a breath I had been holding since the key first clicked.

At sixty-eight, Pilar had spent decades riding buses through Albuquerque but had never sat behind a steering wheel. Her instructor, Dev, chose a quiet school parking lot and placed a paper cup of water in the console. Pilar’s fingers kept slipping on the smooth rim of the wheel. When a shopping cart rolled across the pavement, she jerked so sharply that Dev reached for the dashboard. He did not scold her; he simply asked her to name three things she could see. Pilar listed a blue sign, a crack in the asphalt, and his striped tie. Her breathing settled enough for her to move the car between two rows of cones. On the return, she stopped well before the chalk line. Dev said the distance was fine. Pilar studied the gap, then inched forward until the bumper rested exactly beside it. She smiled only after the engine was off.

I had practiced the route on a map all week, tracing every turn with my thumb, but the real road climbed above the harbor in a series of steep bends. My instructor, Tessa, sat beside me with one hand near the brake she could reach from her side. I watched the stone wall slide past my window and felt my shoulders rise almost to my ears. “Keep looking where you want the car to go,” she reminded me. I fixed my eyes on a yellow mailbox rather than the drop beyond the guardrail. At the bend, my foot pressed the clutch too quickly, and the engine coughed out. Behind us, a delivery van waited. I swallowed, restarted, and followed Tessa’s slow count: clutch, gear, gentle gas. The car climbed again. At the viewpoint, I parked crookedly, but I stayed in the seat long enough to notice the boats below moving like bright paper scraps.

Marlon arrived for his first lesson wearing a pressed shirt and carrying the same folded permit he had checked on the bus. Instructor Rina asked him to drive around a quiet industrial block. A forklift beeped somewhere behind a warehouse, and Marlon’s head snapped toward the sound. The car drifted close to the curb. Rina gave a brief steering correction and asked him to pull over. He sat with his hands still clamped to the wheel while a bead of sweat slid beneath his collar. “I thought I had this,” he said, voice barely audible. Rina pointed out that he had noticed the hazard quickly; they would practice balancing attention between the road and unexpected noise. They drove the block again, slower. This time Marlon kept his eyes ahead when the forklift beeped. At the end, he parked between the lines. His fingers remained curled around the wheel, but he managed to unfasten his seat belt without fumbling.

My instructor, Jo, took me to a wide, empty stretch beside the county fairgrounds. The dashboard seemed crowded with glowing symbols, and every passing cloud changed the light through the windshield. I kept asking whether the car was centered. Jo answered patiently, but my voice grew thin each time I checked the mirrors. Then a gust pushed a plastic bag across our lane. I gripped the wheel and tapped the brake, stopping well short of it. Jo said my response had been sensible and had me practice pulling away again. I tried to laugh, but it came out as a short squeak. We drove toward a row of orange cones, and I steered around each one at walking speed. On the last pass, I left a neat, even distance on either side. When Jo asked if I wanted another round, I nodded before I could talk myself out of it.

Nia’s instructor, Hal, began with a lesson on the quiet streets near a botanical garden. The windshield wipers clicked back and forth, though the rain had nearly stopped. Nia kept checking the rearview mirror, where a bus seemed to grow larger with every glance. “Let it pass when we reach the turnout,” Hal said. She signaled too early, then corrected herself when he pointed to the painted arrow. Her knuckles had turned pale against the wheel. At the turnout, the bus swept by, sending a fan of water over the side window. Nia flinched and shut her eyes for one beat. Hal waited until she opened them, then asked her to describe the road ahead. She named the puddles, a cyclist, and the garden gate. They continued at a measured pace. By the time they returned, she was still sitting rigidly, but she had remembered every signal and stopped smoothly at each crossing.

The instructor’s car had a manual transmission, which made the lesson feel like a test with too many moving parts. I was seventeen, and my older brother had already passed, so I could hear his cheerful advice in my head whenever I stalled. Ms. Alvarez took us to a level street beside a closed library. My left foot shook as I eased off the clutch. The engine died with a blunt click. I stared at the gearshift, waiting for Ms. Alvarez to sigh, but she only asked me to reset and try again. On the fourth attempt, the car rolled forward without a jerk. A cyclist appeared at the corner, and I stopped too early, leaving half a block between us. Ms. Alvarez said stopping was better than rushing. I restarted after the cyclist passed, then drove to the end of the street. When she praised the smooth gear change, I looked out the window so she would not see my eyes watering.

Eun had learned to ride a scooter in Seoul, but the instructor’s sedan felt enormous on the narrow roads outside her new town. Mr. Burke chose a residential lane with no parked cars and asked her to make a three-point turn. Eun watched the curb approach in the side mirror, then corrected too sharply. The front tire mounted a shallow patch of grass. She froze, both palms pressed flat to the wheel. Mr. Burke spoke in an even voice and guided her through reversing a few inches. The tire dropped back onto pavement. Eun’s cheeks flushed as a woman walking a terrier glanced over. They tried the turn again, using a driveway entrance as extra room. This time Eun moved in small, deliberate steps, checking each mirror when prompted. The sedan ended up facing the other direction. She wiped her damp palms on her trousers and asked if they could practice one more. Mr. Burke handed her the signal controls.

I had never driven on a bridge, and the lesson route included one crossing over the river. My instructor, Beth, explained that we could turn back if I needed to. At the entrance, the metal grating made a low rattling sound beneath the tires. My stomach tightened, and I stared at the white stripe ahead instead of the water. A gust nudged the car toward the center line. Beth told me to make a small adjustment, not a sudden one. I moved the wheel barely an inch and kept the car steady. Halfway across, a truck approached in the opposite lane, its mirrors seeming to fill my windshield. I sucked in air and held it until the truck passed. Beth asked me to exhale slowly. By the far end, my shoulders had dropped a little. We pulled into a riverside lot, where I sat quietly and watched the bridge traffic continue without me.

At twenty-six, Jalen was the only person in his friend group without a license, and his first lesson began before sunrise. Instructor Pavel met him outside a bakery, where delivery vans rattled along the curb. Jalen adjusted the seat three times and still sat too close to the wheel. When Pavel asked him to merge onto a broad avenue, Jalen’s foot hovered above the gas. A car behind them honked. He flinched and turned toward the sound, nearly crossing the lane marker. Pavel calmly asked him to keep his eyes forward and wait for a larger gap. They circled the block until the avenue grew quieter. Jalen checked the mirror, signaled, and eased into traffic. His breath came in short bursts, but the car held its lane. Afterward, Pavel noted the successful merge on the lesson sheet. Jalen folded the paper carefully and tucked it into his jacket as if it might blow away.

The driving school placed me in a small electric car, so there was no engine noise to cover the ticking indicator. I found the silence unnerving; every click seemed to count down to a mistake. Instructor Farah took me through a business park on Sunday, where the broad lanes were empty except for a groundskeeper on a mower. I held the steering wheel so tightly my wrists began to ache. At a roundabout, I stopped even though there was no traffic. Farah asked me to look left, then ahead, and tell her what I saw. I listed two signs and a delivery gate. “And the circle?” she asked. I gave a nervous little laugh and watched the empty roadway. She coached me through the turn at a crawl. The car glided around without a sound. On our second lap, I entered without stopping, then let my hands loosen as the quiet motor carried us toward the exit.

Sol’s instructor, Miki, took him to a snowy practice lot in northern Vermont. The sedan’s tires crunched over packed snow, and Sol’s scarf brushed his chin whenever he looked down at the pedals. Miki demonstrated a gentle stop, then asked him to repeat it. Sol pressed too hard; the car skidded a short distance before the tires caught. He went rigid and stared at the windshield, where flakes gathered along the edges. Miki explained how to use lighter pressure and leave more space. Sol tried again, starting from the far side of the lot. This time he eased the brake down gradually. The car stopped without sliding. He glanced at Miki, searching her face for a verdict, and she pointed to the clear stretch ahead. They practiced until the lesson clock chimed. When Sol stepped onto the snow, his legs felt unsteady, but he carried the ice scraper back to the school office himself.

When Inez’s ankle healed enough for the track, Coach left a starting block in lane four and told her she could try one sprint. I tied my shoes twice, though the knots were already tight. The other runners’ spikes clicked against the floor, and every sound seemed to land beside the place where the bone had cracked. I stepped into the blocks, then backed out. My hands had gone slick. Coach didn’t hurry me; she asked me to walk the curve first. I did, counting each footfall until the lane felt less like a test and more like a strip of rubber. On the next lap, I jogged. A sharp tug flickered at my ankle, and I stopped so suddenly my breath snagged. The trainer checked it, then nodded. I ran again, slowly, finishing one straightaway. I didn’t celebrate. I sat on the track and let my shaking hands rest on my knees.

At sixty-two, Tomas had never expected a broken wrist to keep him from his curling club. The doctor cleared him to practice with a lighter stone, but he stood at the rink’s edge while the team swept and called instructions. His injured hand remained tucked close to his ribs. When his turn came, he gripped the handle with both hands and stared at the target until the painted rings blurred. The stone slid crookedly, stopping far short. A teammate offered to adjust his stance; Tomas swallowed and asked to try once more. This time he released earlier. The stone traveled cleanly down the sheet, though it missed the center. He looked at his wrist, flexed his fingers, and waited for pain to announce itself. Nothing did. His shoulders lowered by a fraction. He joined the others at the far end, still moving carefully, and accepted a broom.

I was the youngest goalkeeper at the academy, and after surgery on my knee, the goal looked enormous again. Coach placed soft balls close to the line so I could practice dropping without diving. I kept my weight on my good leg and watched each ball roll past, embarrassed by how quickly my pulse climbed. The physiotherapist reminded me that recovery wasn’t a race, but I still heard the old team chanting from the next field. When she finally rolled one toward the corner, my body started moving before I could reconsider. I lowered myself, caught it against my chest, and landed on the padded mat. For a moment I stayed there, listening to my knee and the whistle of wind through the net. Then I stood. The joint held. I asked her to roll another, and she did—not harder, just a little farther from my reach.

Sana’s shoulder had been out of its sling for three weeks when she returned to the climbing gym. She chose the easiest wall, a route marked with wide yellow holds, and studied it from the mat. Her fingers twitched against her chalk bag. The first two moves went smoothly; at the third, she had to reach across her body. She froze with one hand on the wall and the other hovering. Below, her brother said nothing, which somehow made the silence louder. Sana lowered herself carefully and sat down, rubbing the stiff joint. After a drink of water, she tried the move from the ground, stretching her arm in small increments. The next attempt carried her past the hold. She reached the top without rushing, then descended with her eyes fixed on each foothold. At the mat, she smiled briefly and shook out her arm, as if surprised to find it still hers.

I’d trained for the regional swim meet all year, then fractured a rib during a bicycle fall. Six weeks later, the pool smelled exactly as it had before, but I stood at the ladder with my toes gripping the wet tile. My coach suggested one length at an easy pace. I lowered myself in, and the cool water pressed against my chest. On the first stroke, a small pinch stopped my arm halfway through its arc. I grabbed the lane rope and waited, jaw clenched, while the other swimmers turned at the wall. The pinch eased. I tried again, keeping my strokes short and steady. By the far end, I had forgotten to count them. I rested with my forehead against the tiles, then swam back. It wasn’t a personal best, or even close. Still, when I climbed out, I left my goggles on and asked whether I could come back tomorrow.

Marek’s hand had healed after a cycling crash, but the first race back brought him to the start line with his thumb pressed hard against the brake lever. The downhill course twisted through pine trees, its sharp turns familiar from years of practice. He watched the other riders clip in and roll toward the gate. When his name was called, he checked his helmet strap twice, then tightened it a third time. The starter raised a flag. Marek pushed off, keeping his speed low through the first bend. His front wheel brushed gravel; his breath caught, and he squeezed the brakes. He nearly stopped. Then he remembered the physical therapist’s drills and shifted his weight as practiced. The bike straightened. He finished well behind the pack, but crossed the line upright. His coach held out a bottle. Marek took it with both hands, studying the scraped dirt on his tires before looking up.

My fencing coach said the repaired tendon was strong enough for footwork, not sparring. Even so, when I entered the salle, the clatter of blades made my left hand curl against my side. I wore the padded jacket and practiced lunges toward a target on the wall. The first few were shallow. Every time my repaired finger brushed the grip, I pictured the blade slipping from my hand. I adjusted the glove, then took it off and checked the scar. It had faded to a pale line. My partner, Jules, offered to stand still while I tested a touch. I lifted the foil and stepped forward. The tip tapped the jacket with a soft sound. No one cheered, which helped. We repeated the drill, gradually adding a retreat and a parry. When practice ended, I packed my gear slowly, my hand aching but steady around the zipper pull.

At sixteen, Noura had returned to volleyball after surgery on her knee, but she still ducked whenever a hard serve crossed the net. Her coach started her with gentle tosses, then invited her to join a short scrimmage. Noura’s teammates called her name as the ball rose above the court. She bent her knees, then stiffened, unable to commit to the jump. The ball landed untouched beside her shoe. She pressed her lips together and rolled the knee once, a habit from the rehabilitation room. On the next serve, she moved two steps and passed the ball with her forearms. It flew high enough for the setter to reach. Noura blinked at the clean arc, then glanced toward the sideline where her mother was watching. She didn’t wave. She returned to her place, breathing in through her nose, and asked the server to send another.

I broke my toe during a rugby match in a town where I’d only lived for a month. When the team invited me back to practice, I nearly turned around at the clubhouse door. The grass looked uneven, full of small dips that might catch my foot. I laced my boot loosely and joined warm-ups at the edge. Each time someone kicked a ball toward me, I stepped aside. Then our captain rolled one gently across the field and waited. I trapped it with the inside of my boot. The impact sent a brief jolt up my foot, and my stomach tightened. I checked the toe through the leather, as if I could see it there. It felt fine. I passed the ball back, then jogged after it. By the end of practice, I had joined a passing drill. I still chose my steps carefully, but I no longer stayed beside the clubhouse.

Elise’s first skating session after a fractured collarbone was supposed to be easy laps around the rink. She wore her old jacket over the protective padding and kept one hand close to her chest. The boards seemed farther away than she remembered. A child zipped past, and Elise’s skates scraped sideways as she tried not to collide. She caught the rail, heart hammering, and stayed there while the child’s laughter faded. Her instructor suggested pushing off for just one curve. Elise looked down at the ice, where the overhead lights broke into trembling stripes. She bent her knees and moved. The first curve was stiff; the second flowed more naturally. Near the gate, she slowed and stopped without grabbing the boards. Her instructor gave a small nod. Elise rubbed the spot beneath her collarbone through the jacket, then asked to do another lap, this time with the rail out of reach.

I had won three judo tournaments before a torn ligament put me on the mat for months. On my first day back, the gym smelled of canvas and disinfectant, and every thump from the practice area made my shoulders rise. Sensei paired me with a patient beginner. We started with grips, no throws. When his sleeve twisted in my hand, my injured knee shifted under me, and I let go at once. I sat on my heels, cheeks hot, while he waited without asking questions. Sensei showed me how to turn from my hips instead. We tried again, slowly, then practiced a careful step and reset. My knee held through each repetition. At the end, I bowed to my partner and stayed on the mat to watch the others. Their throws sounded heavier than I remembered. I packed my belt away neatly, already planning the next practice, though I knew I’d begin with grips.

After a stress fracture, Daniel returned to the basketball court carrying a list of exercises from his physical therapist. He planned to shoot from the free-throw line, but the familiar squeak of sneakers and pounding rebounds made him hover near the bench. His teammates waved him over. Daniel tested his weight on the recovering foot, then shifted back to the other one. He bounced the ball once; it rattled against the floor and sprang into his hands. The first shot struck the front rim. His jaw tightened, and he rubbed his shin through his shorts. The coach asked whether he wanted to stop. Daniel glanced at the exit, then rolled his shoulders and took another shot. It dropped through the net. He didn’t jump or shout. Instead, he passed the ball to a teammate and joined a slow shooting rotation, leaving the running drills for another day.

I had been in the benefits office line for nearly three hours, clutching a folder whose corners had gone soft beneath my fingers. When the clerk called my number, I stood too quickly and the room tilted. My daughter’s inhaler prescription was tucked among the forms, and I could not remember whether I had brought the doctor’s letter they required. At the counter, I arranged every page in a neat stack, then rearranged them when my hands began to shake. The clerk asked me to repeat my address. I heard my voice come out thin and unfamiliar. Behind me, people shifted and sighed. I wanted to turn around and disappear into the crowd, but my daughter was waiting at home. I opened the folder again, searching each pocket while the clerk watched the clock.

At the immigration office, Mateo stood between a mother with a sleeping baby and a man who kept checking his watch. The line bent around the hallway and vanished through a set of heavy doors. Mateo had rehearsed his answers on the bus, but now each one slipped away whenever an employee emerged and called a name. He pressed his appointment notice flat against his chest, smoothing the same crease again and again. When the ceiling speaker crackled, his shoulders jumped. The woman beside him offered a quiet smile; he tried to return it, but his mouth would not cooperate. His passport was safe in his inside pocket, yet he checked for it every few minutes. At last, the line moved forward by one place. Mateo took a shallow breath and followed.

I brought my father’s property papers to the county office, certain I had copied every page correctly. The line reached past the security desk, where a metal detector beeped whenever someone carried a belt buckle through. Each burst of noise made me grip my envelope harder. My appointment time had passed, and I kept imagining the clerk saying I would have to start over. When an elderly man ahead of me dropped his number ticket, I bent to retrieve it, grateful for a reason to look down. The pages inside my envelope had begun to stick together from my damp palms. I checked the deed once more, though I knew its blue seal was there. At the counter, I would have to explain why my father could no longer sign his name.

Nia had never visited the licensing office alone. At twenty-one, she expected the task to be simple: submit a form, take a number, wait. Instead, the line crept beneath fluorescent lights while a television showed weather reports with the sound turned off. A uniformed guard walked past, and she clamped her folder to her ribs. Her mother’s handwriting filled the emergency-contact section, but Nia had left the phone number blank. If the clerk noticed, would they send her away? She read the form from top to bottom, then started again, unable to absorb the words. Whenever someone reached the counter, the printer’s sharp whine made her flinch. The number display changed. Nia stood, sat, then stood once more, watching the doors as though they might close before she got through.

The line at the veterans’ records office moved so slowly that I began counting the tiles beneath my shoes. I had come to correct a mistake in my late husband’s service file, and the envelope on my lap held the only original document we had found. A child ran past the chairs, and I jerked the envelope against my chest before I could stop myself. My hands were cold despite the crowded room. When a clerk called the wrong surname, I rose halfway, then sank back down, heat rushing to my face. I kept rehearsing the first sentence I would say: the dates are wrong, and I can prove it. The words seemed too small for what depended on them. I pressed my thumbnail into the envelope flap until the paper began to tear.

Rashid waited at the tax office with a shoebox of receipts balanced on his knees. The line stretched through the lobby, past a poster explaining penalties in bold red letters. He had filed late after a hospital stay, and every time someone behind him mentioned an audit, his stomach tightened. A bead of sweat traveled down his neck although the air conditioner rattled overhead. He opened the box to check the receipts, then hurriedly shut it when one slid toward the floor. The guard glanced over, and Rashid lowered his eyes. His number was still several places away. He pictured the rent notice on his kitchen table and tried to calculate how much money remained in his account. When the display finally blinked, he rose with the box tucked firmly under one arm.

I stood in the passport office line with my son’s birth certificate folded inside my coat. Our flight was in four days, and the airline had already warned me that a damaged document could cause trouble. Each time the line lurched ahead, I reached inside to make sure the paper was still there. A man near the entrance argued with a clerk, and the sharp voices filled the high-ceilinged room. My son asked when we would leave. I told him soon, though the number board had not changed in twenty minutes. My tongue felt dry, and I kept swallowing without relief. At the service window, I laid the certificate down carefully, holding its corners so they would not curl. The clerk studied the seal in silence. I watched her face, waiting for the smallest sign.

Evelyn, a retired school custodian, sat in the city office line with a notice about her water bill folded into quarters. The amount was larger than anything she could spare, and she had brought a bank statement to show the charge was mistaken. Her fingers kept tracing the same crease in the notice. When the clerk behind the glass called another number, Evelyn’s breath caught; she had thought it was hers. The lobby smelled of wet coats, and rain tapped steadily at the windows. She checked her purse for the statement, then checked again, though it rested on her lap. A man nearby offered to let her go ahead, but she shook her head, unable to explain why speaking felt difficult. At last her number appeared. She rose slowly, gripping the purse strap until her knuckles paled.

I was the only person in the licensing office wearing a paint-splattered work jacket, and I could feel everyone noticing the red streak across my sleeve. The line curled past the photograph booth. My commercial permit had expired, and my supervisor had said there might be a fine if I missed another shift. I kept checking the time on my phone, although the screen was cracked and the minutes seemed to crawl. A clerk pushed open a side door, and I jolted hard enough to drop my ticket. It landed beneath a row of chairs. I crouched to reach it, hearing shoes shuffle around me, then wiped the dust from its edge. When I finally got to the counter, my prepared explanation vanished. I placed my papers down and waited for the clerk to speak first.

At the housing authority, Linh held a plastic sleeve of documents against her knees while the queue advanced in short, uneven bursts. She had brought her lease, pay stubs, and the letter requesting proof of income, but one envelope from her employer remained unopened. The possibility that it contained bad news made her leave it sealed. Around her, people whispered into phones or stared at the floor. Linh studied a crack in the tile and counted its branches until the announcement speaker sounded. Her shoulders rose toward her ears. When a staff member approached, she quickly tucked the envelope beneath the other papers, then felt ashamed of the gesture. The clerk called her number. Linh stood, nearly forgot her cane, and turned back to retrieve it before walking toward the window.

I went to the municipal office to register the small boat I had inherited, carrying a bill of sale that looked older than I was. The queue filled a narrow corridor, where every door bore a different department name. I worried I had chosen the wrong one. Whenever someone walked by in uniform, my grip tightened on the document tube. The paper inside had a pale brown stain, and I had spent the bus ride wondering whether that alone would make it unacceptable. A woman ahead of me was sent to another floor, and my stomach gave a hard twist. I considered leaving, but the boat was already tied at the marina, accumulating fees. When my turn came, I placed the bill of sale on the counter and kept both hands visible, as if sudden movements might make the whole matter worse.

Seventy-four-year-old George waited at the pension office with a letter he had received that morning. It said his monthly payment might stop unless he supplied a document he had never heard of. The line stretched from the lobby to the pavement outside, and the automatic door opened and shut behind him, letting in cold gusts. He read the letter again, though the print blurred whenever he reached the final paragraph. His breathing grew quick, so he counted backward from one hundred, losing his place at sixty-three. A young woman offered him a chair, but he declined and leaned against the wall instead. When an employee called his name, George looked around as if someone else might answer. Then he lifted the letter with both hands and stepped forward, careful not to let it tremble.

When the lights went out in our apartment building, I was halfway down the basement stairs with a basket of laundry. The darkness swallowed the landing, and my foot searched for a step that wasn’t there. I grabbed the rail so hard my knuckles hurt. Above me, doors opened and neighbors called to one another. I tried to answer, but my voice came out thin. Mrs. Alvarez from 2B appeared with a battery lantern, its small circle of light trembling across the walls. She offered to walk me upstairs. I said I could manage, then stayed close enough to brush her sleeve all the way up. In the lobby, residents gathered around a radio, listening for news from the utility company. I kept my laundry basket pressed against my stomach and watched the stairwell until every floor had someone waiting beside it.

At seventy-eight, Mr. Okafor had lived on Cedar Court long enough to know every sound his old house made. The sudden silence was worse. His oxygen machine had stopped, and its dark display reflected his face back at him. He reached for the emergency canister with shaking hands, but the latch stuck. Across the street, Lila noticed his porch light had vanished and hurried over with a flashlight. He tried to joke about the timing; the words snagged in his throat. Lila opened the canister and called the number on the medical label while he counted each breath under his breath. Soon two more neighbors arrived with charged batteries and a portable unit. Mr. Okafor sat between them, gripping the armrests as the machine began its steady hum again. He thanked everyone twice, then kept one hand on the power switch.

I was closing the bakery when the block went black, leaving only the oven’s orange pilot light. A crash sounded from the alley, followed by the scrape of something moving. I locked the front door, then immediately wished I hadn’t, because the shop felt smaller with the street outside invisible. My phone had twelve percent battery. Through the window, I saw neighbors gathering beneath the awning, each face briefly lit by a screen. I called out and asked them to stay together while I checked the back entrance. My knees felt loose as I crossed the kitchen, holding a rolling pin like it might help. The crash turned out to be a toppled recycling bin, its lid skittering in the wind. When I returned, everyone laughed, but I kept the rolling pin in my hand until the power came back.

Nia’s first night babysitting on Juniper Lane became memorable when the electricity failed during a thunderstorm. The child, Milo, slept upstairs, but the house’s electronic monitor went quiet. Nia stared at its blank screen and listened for any sound from his room. Rain tapped the windows; a branch scraped the siding. She carried a flashlight up the stairs, stopping whenever the floor creaked. At the bedroom door, she found Milo asleep, one hand curled around his stuffed fox. Relief loosened her shoulders, but she stayed beside the bed, counting his breaths while thunder rolled over the roof. A knock at the front door made her jump. It was the elderly neighbor, bringing a lantern and asking whether they needed anything. Nia accepted it with both hands and asked him to sit in the hallway until the storm passed.

The power failed in our row of townhouses just as I was heating dinner for my father. His wheelchair lift froze halfway up the ramp, and the sudden stop left him clutching the armrests. I ran outside, but the ramp’s metal rails were slick with rain. My hands kept slipping as I tried the manual release. Across the shared courtyard, the neighbors’ windows were dark too. I called for help, louder each time, and Mr. Chen came with a work lamp while the twins from next door held umbrellas over us. We read the lift’s instructions together, though the tiny print blurred whenever I blinked. At last the platform lowered with a grinding jerk. My father gave me a nod, but I remained crouched beside him, one palm pressed to the wet frame, until the building’s lights returned.

On Maple Street, the outage caught Reggie in the elevator between floors. He pressed the alarm button and heard only a faint click. The car’s emergency light flickered, then steadied at a dim red glow. He kept his hands flat against the wall, listening for footsteps beyond the doors. When someone called from the hallway, he answered too quickly and had to repeat himself. Neighbors gathered outside, including a retired electrician who explained that the elevator company was on its way. Reggie tried to follow the instructions to stay put, but his breathing came in short pulls. A teenager slid a bottle of water through the narrow gap and told him a story about her dog. By the time the rescue crew arrived, Reggie could manage a smile. He stepped out slowly, then stood with the group rather than walking home alone.

At the community garden, I was locking the tool shed when every porch and streetlamp blinked off at once. The path to my cottage crossed a patch of woods, and without the lights I could barely see the fence. I fumbled for my phone, but its battery was dead. A twig snapped somewhere near the compost bins. I froze with the keys biting into my palm. Then Mrs. Patel called my name from her greenhouse, where she had a camping lantern. I walked toward her voice, keeping my eyes on the bright square of the doorway. Three other gardeners were already there, sharing thermoses and checking the neighborhood message board on a radio. Nobody knew when power would return. I asked if I could wait with them, pretending to study the seed catalog while my fingers slowly stopped trembling.

Evelyn, a new arrival on Birch Row, had never met most of her neighbors before the outage. When the refrigerator stopped humming, she noticed how quiet the house had become. Then the smoke detector chirped once, and she stood motionless beneath it, staring at the ceiling. Her phone showed an emergency alert about a possible transformer fire nearby. She packed her cat into a carrier, but the animal’s claws caught her sleeve as she tried to close the door. On the sidewalk, people were gathering beneath the one working streetlamp at the corner. A man named Darnell offered to carry her groceries to his porch, where he had a battery radio. Evelyn kept glancing toward the dark block behind them. As neighbors traded updates and spare phone chargers, she sat near the open gate, ready to leave if the radio reported danger.

I was in the middle of a video call with my sister when the screen went black and the whole duplex fell silent. My dog began barking at the front window. I pulled the curtains aside just enough to see neighbors stepping into the street with flashlights. Across the road, a transformer gave a blue flash, and I dropped below the windowsill before I could think. My heart hammered against my ribs. I called to Mr. Lewis next door, asking whether he had heard anything. He waved me over to his porch, where several residents were gathered well back from the wires. We listened to a battery radio and waited for the fire crew. I kept my dog’s leash wrapped around my wrist, though he had stopped barking. When the truck arrived, I finally stood upright, but I stayed among the neighbors until the crew declared the block safe.

Farah was walking home from her late shift when the lights disappeared along Harbor Avenue. The crosswalk signals went dark, and traffic rolled unpredictably through the intersection. She stopped at the curb, gripping her work bag while headlights swept past in white bursts. A cyclist beside her muttered that the nearest signal had failed too. Farah wanted to hurry across before another car came, but her shoes stayed planted on the pavement. Then Mr. Bell, who lived above the corner shop, stepped into the road wearing a reflective vest and began guiding pedestrians in small groups. Farah followed close behind him, watching each approaching vehicle. On the far side, several neighbors offered her a place to wait until the buses resumed service. She accepted a paper cup of tea and held it between both palms, still listening for engines before taking each sip.

When the outage hit our apartment complex, I was alone in the laundry room with a dryer full of wet clothes. The machines stopped at once, and a heavy thud sounded from somewhere upstairs. I stood in the dark, unable to tell whether it had come from the stairwell or the ceiling. My fingers searched the wall for the doorframe. I called out, and my voice echoed back without an answer. After a moment, a flashlight beam appeared under the door. It belonged to Tanya from 5C, who had come down to check on everyone. She told me the thud was probably a dropped box, but she stayed while I unlocked the exit. Together we found three other residents in the lobby. I sat on the lowest step, still clutching a damp shirt, and watched the flashlight sweep across every corner.

On a quiet cul-de-sac, Tomas was feeding his newborn when the power cut out. The baby startled and began crying, while the bottle warmer’s display vanished. Tomas’s wife was still driving home, and the street outside had become a row of black shapes. He tried to soothe the child, but his arms felt stiff and his attention kept shifting toward the windows. A neighbor knocked, holding a lantern and a thermos of warm water. Tomas opened the door only a few inches at first, then recognized her voice and let her in. Together they warmed the bottle safely in a bowl and checked the utility company’s update on her phone. The baby quieted against his shoulder. Tomas kept the lantern beside the crib and called his wife to ask her to stay on the phone during the drive. Outside, neighbors began checking on one another.

At the laundromat, I opened the exam portal on my phone while my clothes thumped behind me. My thumb hovered over the blue button, and I kept checking the machine timer as if it might give me a reason to wait. When the page loaded, I pressed my lips together and read the score once, then again, though the numbers had not changed. A low mark would mean telling my father I might lose my scholarship. I slid down the plastic chair until my knees nearly touched my chest. A dryer buzzed, making me jump. The grade was better than I had expected, but I still couldn’t make myself call home. I typed, “Can we talk tonight?” and watched the message sit unsent.

Nadia, sixteen, sat at the back of the school bus with her laptop balanced on her knees. The exam portal kept spinning, and each pothole made the screen wobble beneath her hands. Her older brother had promised to help with college applications if she passed chemistry; she had promised herself she would not need to ask. When the grade finally appeared, she stopped breathing for a moment. The score was just below the cutoff. She folded the laptop shut, then opened it again to make sure she had read correctly. Around her, classmates traded jokes and snacks. Nadia pressed her palms against her jeans and rehearsed how she would explain the result without letting her voice crack.

I checked my grades from the staff room after closing the café, still wearing an apron dusted with flour. My exam in accounting decided whether I could keep my place in the evening program, and rent was due in four days. The login page rejected my password twice. I wiped my fingers on a towel, though they were already dry, and tried again. When the result appeared, my stomach tightened so sharply I leaned against the counter. I had passed, but only by two points. The kitchen’s refrigerator hummed while I stared at the screen, unable to celebrate. Then I saved a screenshot, printed it, and tucked the paper into my wallet as if it might vanish before morning.
