We attached the legs, pausing whenever the tool slipped from my fingers. The room smelled of cardboard and the coffee we had forgotten to drink. I heard someone practicing piano upstairs, beginning the same scale again whenever they reached the end. Luis tapped along with a bolt. I joined him with the wrench, and for a while the assembly had its own peculiar soundtrack.

At a lakeside cabin, Bethany and her wife, Mo, unpacked a compact wardrobe meant for their guest room. Bethany had expected a quick task before their friends arrived, but the panels seemed to multiply each time they opened the box. Mo studied the instructions under a lamp, while Bethany sat on the floor and pushed a loose screw back and forth with her thumbnail. Outside, a loon called across the water. Bethany answered with a soft imitation, then waited for a reply. Mo gave her the next bracket. She fitted it onto the frame, took it off, and checked the diagram again. “This is the exciting part,” Mo said, with mock ceremony. Bethany lifted the hammer as if presenting a prize, then tapped the back panel into place. Their finished wardrobe leaned slightly toward the wall until Mo adjusted one foot. Bethany opened the doors and placed a folded blanket inside, pleased to have something to do with the empty space.

I had read every notice on the platform twice, including the one warning about wet floors, and was tracing the cracks in my shoe with a thumbnail when the train began to pull away. My aunt’s scarf was still looped over my suitcase handle; she had waved from the carriage window, assuming I was already aboard. I snatched up the case and ran, its wheels rattling over the paving stones. The conductor leaned out and caught my sleeve just as the last door passed. He hauled me into the vestibule, where I stood panting beside a stack of parcels. My aunt laughed, then handed me a paper bag of oranges. I had spent the morning wishing something would interrupt the slow crawl of the minutes. Now the train lurched into the countryside, and I had to keep both hands on the bag to stop the oranges rolling away.

At sixteen, DeShawn had spent the station wait tapping a rhythm against his backpack and watching the clock hand creep between marks. His school trip group was already aboard the train to the science museum when he noticed his sketchbook still under the bench. He sprinted after the departing cars, sneakers slapping the platform, and waved the book overhead. A porter swung open the accessible carriage door and pulled him inside. DeShawn expected a lecture from his teacher, but she only pointed to the page fluttering open in his hands. His pencil drawing of the station had captured the porter mid-stride, one arm extended like a conductor’s baton. The man asked if he could keep a copy. For the rest of the ride, DeShawn had something to do: shading the porter’s grin and adding the train’s long shadow.

I had been sitting in the station café long enough to memorize the pattern on the sugar packets. The tea had gone cold, and I kept turning my phone over without checking it. When the whistle sounded, I saw my train edging away from the platform. My violin case was beside me, but my ticket was tucked into the coat I had left on the bench. I bolted back, grabbed the coat, and ran, the case thumping against my hip. A woman at the open carriage door reached out and caught the strap. I scrambled aboard with a breathless apology. Inside, a little boy stared at my violin case and asked whether I could play. I had planned to spend the ride staring out the window. Instead, I opened the case and gave him a quiet tune while the city slid out of sight.

Marta, a retired baker, had been watching the station clock as if she could hurry it by glaring. Her crossword was finished, the vending machine had swallowed her coin, and the same announcement had played three times. Then she spotted a small dog trotting after a train that had just started moving. Its leash was tangled around a luggage trolley, and its owner was still on the platform. Marta grabbed the loose end and ran alongside the carriage, calling for help. A railway worker opened a door and lifted the dog inside. Marta climbed aboard after it, leaving her shopping bag behind. The owner, a young man in a flour-dusted apron, was in the next carriage, searching frantically. When they reunited, he pressed a warm cinnamon bun into Marta’s hand. She smiled at the unexpected passenger and finally had a story worth telling at home.

I had been leaning on the platform rail, counting pigeons and watching them quarrel over a crust, when my train began to leave. My phone had no signal, my magazine was all advertisements, and the station clock seemed stuck. Then I saw my father’s old pocket watch lying on the bench where I had been sitting. I ran after the train, waving it in the air. The guard opened a door, and I hauled myself up while the wheels gathered speed. A stranger offered me a seat and asked if the watch still worked. I wound it; its tiny hand sprang forward. It had belonged to my father, who used to say every minute had a different sound. I held it to my ear as the carriage clicked over the rails, listening closely for the first time that day.

Nikhil had passed the time at the rural depot by arranging pebbles into neat rows, then scattering them and starting again. His train to the coast was finally departing, but he realized his thermos was still beneath the bench. He ran beside the carriage, one hand gripping his backpack, and a station attendant spotted him. The attendant pulled the door open just long enough for Nikhil to climb aboard. Inside, a woman was struggling to keep a basket of lemons from sliding across the floor. He set his thermos down and helped wedge the basket between two seats. One lemon rolled free and stopped against his shoe. The woman offered it to him, and he peeled it with his thumbnail, filling the compartment with a sharp citrus scent. The ride suddenly had a small, bright purpose: keeping the rest of the fruit from making a break for it.

I had been staring at the departure board until the letters blurred, then watching my reflection blink in the dark window. My train was supposed to take me to a job interview, though I had already practiced every answer so many times that the words felt worn out. When the doors chimed and the train began to slide away, I noticed my folder on the bench. I ran, clutching my scarf, and reached the carriage as a conductor held the door. My papers had spilled across the platform, but a teenager gathered them and ran after me, passing the folder through the opening. On the ride, I found a note tucked inside: “You’ll do great.” The handwriting was unfamiliar. I smoothed the paper and looked out at the passing rooftops, suddenly curious about the stranger who had taken the time to write it.

At the museum excursion’s station stop, Elsie had been flicking through the same three photos on her camera, waiting for the group to move. The train started off before she noticed that her grandfather’s knitted cap had slipped from her bag onto a bench. She sprinted after the carriage, calling to the teacher, and a conductor opened the door. Elsie climbed aboard, then spotted the cap outside, rolling toward the platform edge. A station cleaner scooped it up and tossed it through the open window. It landed in her lap, still warm from the sun. Her classmates laughed, and Elsie laughed too, turning the cap inside out to reveal a tiny stitched bird her grandfather had added. She had thought the trip would be a sequence of stops and instructions. Now she spent the ride inventing names for the villages they passed, while the others tried to guess them.

I was passing time at the station by counting the blue tiles along the wall and rubbing a crease in my ticket. My train to the harbor had just begun to pull away when I remembered the jar of sea glass on the bench. It was my mother’s, and I had promised to bring it to her new apartment. I ran hard enough to make my coat flap behind me, clutching the empty lid. A railway employee caught my arm and helped me onto the last carriage. The jar had been left with the ticket inspector, who carried it down the aisle and returned it without a word. I settled beside the window, where sunlight lit the green and cloudy pieces. At the next stop, I asked a child across from me to choose the prettiest one. We spent the rest of the journey debating what the glass might once have been.

Rafi, a traveling puppeteer, had entertained himself in the station by making his glove puppet nod at passing shoes. The trick stopped amusing even him after an hour. When his train started moving, he realized his wooden stage was still near the ticket kiosk. He ran alongside the carriages, puppet raised like a flag, and a conductor recognized the painted face from Rafi’s performance earlier. The door opened, and Rafi scrambled in. A little girl in the compartment immediately asked the puppet where it was going. Rafi answered in a solemn whisper: “Wherever the tracks take us.” The girl giggled and produced a paper crown from her backpack. Soon the puppet was wearing it, and the other passengers were suggesting adventures. Rafi had planned to rehearse alone during the ride. Instead, he improvised a whole tale about a royal mouse escaping a cheese castle.

I had spent my layover watching a janitor mop the same stretch of floor, stepping around the shining wet patch whenever I went to stretch my legs. Then the train began to depart, and I saw my grandfather’s tin lunchbox on the bench. I ran, my boots skidding at the edge of the puddle, and reached the carriage as the doors were closing. A passenger leaned out and hauled me in by the elbow. The lunchbox rattled open, revealing a stack of old postcards I had meant to mail. One showed my grandfather as a young man beside a locomotive, grinning at the camera. I turned it over and found his careful handwriting, addressed to someone whose name I didn’t recognize. Rather than put it away, I studied the faded picture and wondered about the person who had received the others. The ride passed quickly as I made up possible answers.

Amara had been rotating a paper cup between her palms, watching its cardboard seam slowly come unstuck, while the station announcement repeated the same departure times. When her train began to roll away, she realized her camera bag was beneath the seat. She ran after it, shouting to a conductor, who stopped the door from closing and pulled her aboard. The bag was safe, but the camera’s lens cap had fallen out. A little boy found it on the platform and held it up as the train moved. Amara waved, then noticed a bright red kite tangled in the station fence beyond him. She lifted her camera and photographed the boy, the cap, and the kite in one frame. The image was crooked and full of motion, yet she liked it better than the careful pictures she had taken all week. For once, the day had surprised her.

At dawn, I pushed my aluminum boat from the reeds and watched the lake turn from black to pewter. The fishing line slipped through my fingers, then hung still. I checked the bait twice, adjusted my cap, and checked it again. A heron crossed the water with more purpose than I could manage. I tapped the rod against my boot and counted the ripples spreading from the hull. When my phone showed no messages, I opened the weather app, though the sky was clear enough to read. At last, something tugged the line. I jerked upright, heart leaping, only to haul in a wet leaf. I laid it beside the tackle box and gave it a name: Captain. For the next hour, I introduced him to every passing cloud.

Mina had promised herself a peaceful morning on the lake, but by sunrise she had already rearranged the hooks in her tin twice. Her boat drifted past a low island while the rod rested across her knees. She rubbed a thumb over a chipped patch of paint, hummed three notes, then started again from the beginning. The first fish she caught was tiny, silver, and furious. Mina studied its whiskers as if it might offer useful advice, then slipped it back into the water. A loon called somewhere beyond the mist. She answered with a whistle, waited, and received no reply. When a floating branch bumped the boat, she saluted it solemnly and declared it the morning’s most reliable visitor.

I rowed out before the sun cleared the hills, carrying my grandfather’s old green tackle box. The lake barely moved. I cast toward a patch of reeds, then rested my chin on my palm and watched the float. It stayed upright. I shifted to the other side of the boat, as if that might improve its prospects. My knees cracked when I stood, and I folded and unfolded the map tucked beneath the seat. A pair of ducks paddled by in a neat line. I followed their progress until they vanished behind a point, then tried to whistle like them. The sound came out thin and squeaky. I laughed, cast again, and began inventing names for the clouds gathering over the far shore.

At five-thirty, Tomas steered his narrow skiff across the lake, hoping to catch perch before the marina opened. The water was smooth, the air cool, and his float had not twitched once. He leaned over to inspect it, sat back, then leaned over again. A thermos offered lukewarm coffee and no new ideas. He drummed his fingers on the gunwale in a rhythm that changed every few seconds. When a fish finally disturbed the surface, Tomas sprang up so quickly that his hat fell into the boat. The fish disappeared. He retrieved the hat, placed it on the empty seat, and told it to keep watch. After that, he spent more time coaching the hat than tending his line.

The first light was just touching the lake when I cast beside the old wooden pier. My grandfather used to say patience was part of fishing, but I had already untangled the same knot three times. I twisted the handle of my reel, stopped, and twisted it the other way. A misty ridge sat beyond the water, unchanged through every glance. I pulled a granola bar from my coat and crumbled it into tiny pieces, arranging them on the bench like a map. A fish splashed near the reeds. I grabbed my rod, missed the bite, and watched the rings spread out. Then I gave the crumbs imaginary boat names and launched them one by one into the lake.

Sana, a retired bus driver, brought a folding stool to the lake before dawn and settled near the cattails. She had packed three kinds of bait, a thermos, and a newspaper, but the newspaper was yesterday’s and she knew every headline. Her line rested in the water while she flipped through the pages without taking in a word. She traced the printed route map with one finger, following its blue lines from town to town. A kingfisher flashed past, and Sana sat up, alert for a moment. Nothing followed except a ripple. She checked her watch, then turned it face down. For amusement, she began assigning bus stops to the patches of fog drifting across the lake.

I took my kayak out at dawn because the lake is quiet before the anglers arrive. I tied a small bell to my rod, cast toward the far bank, and waited for the sound of a strike. The bell remained silent. I nudged it with a fingertip, then gave the rod a careful shake. The bell rang, and I grinned at the cleverness of my own trick. A flock of geese lifted from the water, leaving the cove empty again. I paddled in a slow circle, counting strokes until I lost track and began over. When my line snagged on a submerged branch, I spent ten minutes negotiating with it as though it were a stubborn neighbor. The branch won, but I made it to shore with a story.

At the edge of the lake, young Ibrahim watched the sky turn pale while his grandfather baited their hooks. Ibrahim cast his line and waited, shoulders slumped beneath his orange jacket. He scraped a thumbnail along the wooden handle, then studied the tiny bubbles rising near the boat. His grandfather nodded toward the float, but it had not moved. Ibrahim began making a list on the back of a receipt: birds, clouds, ripples, and the number of times he had checked the bait. By the time the sun appeared, the list had filled both sides. A sudden tug bent the rod. Ibrahim leaped up, and his grandfather laughed as a small bluegill splashed into the boat. The boy’s grin lasted all the way back to the dock.

Before sunrise, I eased my little motorboat away from the dock and let the engine idle near a rocky point. The fishing report had promised bass, but the water gave no sign of them. I opened my tackle case, lined the lures by color, and put them all back in a different order. My shoulders sagged as the minutes passed. A cabin light blinked on across the lake, then went dark again. I wondered whether its owner had made coffee yet. When the bobber drifted close to the boat, I nudged it outward with my paddle. It floated back. I nudged it once more, then began a quiet competition with it to see which of us could remain perfectly still.

Nellie, who repaired clocks in town, launched her rowboat while the dawn was still gray. She had chosen the lake because it offered nothing that needed fixing, yet her hands kept reaching for tasks. She wiped a clean seat, straightened the bait jar, and wound the line around her fingers before casting. The float bobbed gently in the open water. Nellie stared at it, then at her watch, then back at it. A breeze carried the smell of pine from shore. She counted the watch’s ticking in her head until the count slipped away. A fish surfaced near the bow, flashing once and vanishing. Nellie smiled, set down her watch, and began guessing what time the fish thought it was.

I reached the lake at dawn with a borrowed rod and a paper bag of sandwiches. The first cast landed too close to shore, so I reeled it in and tried again. My line stretched toward the middle, where a patch of fog hid the water. I shifted my weight from one foot to the other and kicked a pebble along the dock until it dropped between the boards. A fisherman farther out raised his arm; I waved back, though I could not tell whether he had caught anything. I opened a sandwich, took one bite, and wrapped it up again. Then I began sketching the shapes of distant trees on the bag. By the time a fish nibbled, the bag was covered in crooked forests.

At dawn, Pavel guided his flat-bottomed boat into a quiet cove, carrying a rod and a small radio. The station offered weather, then a long stretch of static. He turned the dial through several stations before switching it off. His line floated beside a fallen pine, untouched. Pavel rolled his shoulders, flexed his fingers, and counted the knots on the dock rope trailing behind him. A red leaf landed on his knee. He picked it up, examined both sides, and tucked it beneath the radio as a decoration. When a fish finally pulled the line, he grabbed the rod with sudden energy. The catch was a boot lace tangled around a twig. Pavel hung it from the branch like a flag and paddled on, looking for a more promising audience.

I had arranged the same six canvases three times before noon, nudging each frame a fraction to the left, then undoing the adjustment. The gallery’s white walls seemed to stretch farther whenever I glanced up from my level. My assistant asked whether I wanted music; I said no, then watched the dust drift through a sunbeam and counted the specks until she left. A stack of exhibition cards waited on the table. I shuffled them, aligned their corners, and shuffled them again. When a delivery van rattled outside, I followed its progress down the street through the window. At last, I peeled one card from the pile and wrote a note about the smallest painting, the one I had almost left out. Its crooked little doorway looked different from this angle. I carried it to the far wall, suddenly curious what it might reveal there.

At thirty, Darius had expected preparing his first gallery show to feel like a grand undertaking. Instead, he spent the morning smoothing labels that were already flat and checking the same wall hooks with his thumb. His phone offered a stream of messages; he opened each one, then set it facedown without answering. The gallery clock clicked above the reception desk. He began matching the clicks by tapping a paintbrush against his palm, stopping only when the curator glanced over. A crate of prints sat unopened near the door. Darius circled it twice, inspected a loose corner, and finally sliced the tape. Inside, a small etching showed a laundromat at midnight, its windows bright against the dark street. He leaned closer. The reflected lights made a pattern he had missed in the studio. He fetched a frame and cleared a place on the crowded display wall.

I was sure the exhibition would assemble itself if I kept staring at the floor plan. The little squares and arrows had begun to swim together, so I rolled my chair from one end of the studio to the other with a push of my heel. My tea had gone cold beside the stapler. I drank it anyway, then watched the second hand on the microwave make another lap. The gallery manager called to ask about the centerpiece. I answered with a list of dimensions, all delivered in the same flat voice. After we hung up, I wandered among the wrapped sculptures, lifting corners of cloth and lowering them again. One bundle rocked when I touched it. I unwrapped it and found the clay bird I had made during a rainy week years ago. Its beak pointed toward the window. I laughed softly, moved it to the packing table, and began clearing space for it.

Mina, a retired nurse who had taken up painting in her sixties, spent the afternoon preparing her first exhibition in a neighborhood café. She had already wiped the frames, checked the hanging wire, and reread the opening invitation until every sentence felt worn smooth. While the owner adjusted a lamp, Mina peeled the paper from a straw wrapper into thinner and thinner strips. She glanced at the clock, then at the silent espresso machine. Nothing about the room seemed ready to change. She carried a landscape from the back room and held it against a narrow wall, though she had planned to leave that spot empty. The painting showed a bus stop in winter, with one red mitten on the bench. Mina remembered finding it there after a long shift. She asked the owner to move a small table, making room for the picture. The work suddenly belonged to the room.

I had spent two hours deciding whether the silver frames looked better beside the blue ones or across the room from them. By the fourth rearrangement, I started lining up the screws on the counter by size. My gallery was still closed, and the street beyond the glass offered little more than a passing bicycle and a dog investigating a lamppost. I checked my watch, put it away, and checked it again almost at once. A painter friend messaged to ask if I was ready. I typed “nearly,” erased it, and sent a picture of the crooked label instead. Then I noticed the reflection in the front window: my own paintings appeared layered over the traffic outside. I tilted one frame until its painted river met the real gray street. The odd overlap made me step back. I moved the other works to follow that line, and the arrangement began to feel alive.

For the exhibition opening, eleven-year-old Sora had been trusted to help her aunt label a set of ceramic masks. She wrote each title carefully, then sat on a folding chair, swinging her legs until her sneakers brushed the wall. The gallery smelled of cardboard and fresh paint. Her aunt kept measuring the space between pedestals, repeating the same numbers under her breath. Sora traced a circle on a scrap of tape and stuck it to her sleeve. When her aunt went to answer the door, Sora wandered to the storage shelf and found a tiny mask with a chipped blue cheek. She turned it around, noticing a maker’s thumbprint on the back. Instead of hiding it in the crate, she placed it beside the largest mask, where visitors could see both. Her aunt returned, studied the pair, and asked Sora to write one more label.

I was preparing my photographs for a show in a converted train station, and the long room gave me too much time to hear my own footsteps. I walked the length of it, turned, and walked back, counting the floor tiles. The prints lay in neat piles on a bench, each one already checked for fingerprints. I picked up a sandwich, took one bite, and forgot it in my hand while watching a moth tap the high window. My curator asked whether the photographs needed more space. I shrugged, then moved a frame a few inches and moved it back. A train rumbled somewhere beyond the building, shaking the glass. One print slipped from the stack and landed faceup: a blurred platform with a woman running toward the edge of the frame. I pinned it at the entrance. The sudden motion gave the quiet images a beginning.

At twenty-two, Elias had imagined hanging his illustrations for the gallery show while friends admired them. Now he was alone with a toolbox, three ladders, and a row of wall labels that kept curling at the corners. He pressed them down with a ruler, then inspected the ruler for smudges. A radio played softly in the next room; he turned it off, then turned it back on. His shoulders rose each time the gallery door creaked, though no visitor ever appeared. To fill the time, he sorted the spare nails into little piles and counted them twice. One nail rolled beneath a radiator. Elias crouched to retrieve it and found an old pencil drawing wedged behind the pipe, a fox with a crooked tail. He had forgotten making it. He propped it beside the finished illustrations, where its rough lines looked braver than the polished work.

I had been preparing the exhibition since spring, but the final afternoon stretched like a corridor with no door at the end. I checked the lighting, walked outside for air, then returned to check the lighting once more. The gallery’s new white walls made every sound sharp: my keys, my shoes, the click of the thermostat. I opened my sketchbook to look busy and found a grocery list tucked between the pages. On the back, I had drawn a row of faces from the bus. Their expressions were more interesting than the carefully composed portraits on the walls. I pinned the page near the entrance, then shifted it lower so children could see it. The curator raised an eyebrow, but I asked her to leave it there. I spent the rest of the afternoon watching people pause at the page, trying to guess which face they would choose.

Nadia, a printmaker in a coastal town, prepared her gallery exhibition while rain stitched silver lines across the windows. She polished the glass on each frame, though her sleeve kept leaving new streaks. Her apprentice had gone to fetch more hooks, and Nadia found herself listening to the roof drip into a bucket. She tapped a pencil against her teeth, then drew tiny waves on the packing list. The same three seagulls circled the parking lot, disappearing behind the sign and reappearing moments later. She watched them until one landed on the sill. Its wet feathers clung close to its body. Nadia brought over a print she had nearly omitted: a storm cloud above an empty pier. The bird pecked at the window as she held it up. She laughed, shifted the artwork toward the light, and decided the rainy view belonged in the show.

I spent the morning preparing a gallery exhibition in a former bank, where the marble lobby echoed every sigh. My sculptures were already on their pedestals, and the labels had been straightened so often that their edges were beginning to fray. I leaned against the old teller counter and spun a coin across its surface, stopping it with my palm whenever it reached the edge. The building’s clock had stopped at 2:17. I checked my watch, then stared at the frozen clock again. A janitor came in pushing a bucket and asked whether I needed anything. I almost said a different room, but instead asked for a cloth. While he wiped the counter, I noticed a faint outline where a brass plate had once been. I placed my smallest sculpture there, a curled bronze leaf. The empty patch gave it a history the rest of the room lacked.

Gita was preparing a gallery show of quilts she had sewn during years of travel. She folded and unfolded the first one, aligning its corners with the edge of the table. The gallery assistant kept asking for decisions about spacing, and Gita answered with small nods that did not settle anything. Outside, a delivery cyclist locked and unlocked his bicycle while checking his phone. She watched him through the glass, then rubbed a thread between her fingers until it loosened. The room’s ceiling lights hummed above the silent quilts. Gita walked to the back wall and pressed her ear near one of the panels, as if it might make a sound. Instead, she noticed that the patchwork there repeated a pattern from her grandmother’s apron. She took the quilt down and hung it beside a newer one, letting the matching squares meet. At last, the wall told a story she wanted visitors to find.

I had counted every crack in the kitchen ceiling twice by the time Mr. Vale answered my call. The faucet kept up its thin, irregular drip, and I had started matching it with taps of my fingernail on the table. “The leak is still there,” I said, trying to sound brisk. “And the cabinet underneath is swelling.” He asked whether I had put a bowl beneath it. I looked at the three bowls already lined up like a tiny parade. “Yes. They’re taking turns.” There was a pause, so I described the damp wood and sent him another photograph. While he searched his calendar, I rolled a pea around my plate with a fork. He offered Thursday morning. I asked for a definite time, then wrote it on the back of an old envelope. When the call ended, the faucet dripped again, as if it had one more question.

Nadia kept her phone on speaker while she watched the washing machine shudder across the laundry nook. Its rinse cycle had ended an hour ago, but the lid remained locked and a wet sleeve showed through the glass. She had already sorted the buttons on her cardigan into color groups and rearranged the detergent bottles by height. When her landlord called back, she explained the machine’s clanking routine and the trapped laundry. “Could you send someone today?” she asked, flattening a crease in the same cushion again and again. He proposed next week. Nadia let out a long breath and asked whether a repair person could at least inspect it sooner. As they discussed access, she traced a slow circle on the tabletop. At last, he promised to come by that evening. She thanked him, then listened to the washer give one final, hollow knock.

I dragged my desk chair beneath the bedroom window and watched the loose latch rattle in the wind. A strip of masking tape I had stuck over the gap fluttered like a little flag. After checking the weather app several times, I phoned my landlord, Mr. Chen. I told him the window wouldn’t shut properly and that rain had begun finding its way onto the sill. He asked if I could describe the latch. I explained it, then took a photo, then explained it again while he opened the image. My thumb kept rubbing the corner of my phone case. “I can stop by Saturday,” he said. I asked if he could bring the replacement part, not just take a look. He laughed softly and agreed. I wrote Saturday on the calendar, though there was already a note there from last week saying the same thing.

At twenty-two, Malik had learned the exact route of every drip in his studio: from the bathroom ceiling to the towel, then from the towel to the tile. He stood with one sock on and one off while leaving a message for his landlord, describing the water stain that had spread above the shower. Afterward, he leaned against the doorframe and spun a key ring around his finger. When the landlord returned the call, Malik repeated the details, this time adding that the plaster had begun to bubble. The landlord suggested a plumber might come sometime Tuesday. “Morning or afternoon?” Malik asked. The answer was a shrug he could hear through the phone. He rubbed his forehead and requested a narrower window. They settled on noon to two. Malik put the time in his calendar, then watched the clock change by a single minute.

I was halfway through sorting my spice drawer by label color when the radiator gave its familiar metallic cough. It had done that all winter, but this afternoon it started leaking at the valve, so I called my landlord. I described the puddle and the steady hiss. He asked whether I could turn the knob. I tried, carefully, and told him it wouldn’t budge. While he considered the problem, I lined up the spice jars on the counter and nudged each one into place. “I can send a plumber tomorrow,” he said. I asked whether the person would need me to move the bookcase, then went quiet as he checked. He promised to text the details. The call ended, and I returned the jars to their drawer one by one, taking care not to put them back in the order I had just chosen.

Mrs. Alvarez had spent the afternoon moving a potted fern from one patch of sunlight to another when she noticed the living-room ceiling stain had darkened. She called her landlord and described the spreading ring above the bookcase. He asked whether there was water coming through. She stood beneath it, listening, then said she could hear a faint tick whenever the upstairs shower ran. While he made notes, she folded a grocery receipt into a small square, unfolded it, and smoothed it against her knee. He suggested waiting to see if the stain grew. “I have been watching it since lunch,” she replied, with a dry little laugh. She persuaded him to arrange an inspection the next morning. Afterward, she shifted the fern once more, although the light had not moved.

My bathroom fan had begun making a noise like a spoon trapped in a blender, and I finally called my landlord during a slow afternoon at home. I explained that it rattled whenever I switched it on and that the room stayed damp afterward. While he checked his repair list, I balanced a pencil on my upper lip and tried not to let it fall. “Could you send an electrician?” I asked. He said he would ask the building handyman to look first. I sighed, then described the fan’s strange wobble and offered to send a video. “That would help,” he said. I recorded ten seconds of the racket and sent it immediately. We agreed the handyman would come Friday. I put my phone down, picked it up again, and watched the delivery status change from sent to delivered.

Elliot had turned the kitchen light switch on and off so many times that he knew precisely how long it took to flicker. When it finally stayed dark, he called the woman who managed his building. He explained that the bulb was new and that the switch sparked once when he pressed it. She told him not to use it and promised to arrange an electrician. Elliot nodded, though she could not see him, and set the phone on the counter. As she searched for an appointment, he rolled an orange across the table, caught it, and rolled it back. “Thursday at three,” she said. He asked whether the electrician would call first. She promised they would. Elliot wrote the time on a sticky note and placed it beside the switch, where he immediately began straightening its edges.

I called my landlord from the front steps because the stairwell door had jammed again, leaving me to shove it with my shoulder every time I came home. I demonstrated the problem by pushing, waiting, and pushing once more, although no one was there to see it. Over the phone, I described the sticking hinge and the scrape along the floor. He said he would send a carpenter next week. I asked if the door could be adjusted sooner, since my grocery bags had nearly split during yesterday’s struggle. While he checked, I counted the bricks beside my shoe and then started over when a neighbor walked past. We settled on Monday afternoon. I thanked him and tested the handle again. It resisted, then gave way with a dramatic groan that seemed almost pleased with itself.

Priya discovered the kitchen drawer’s broken runner while searching for a teaspoon. It tilted forward, caught, and refused to close, so she pushed it back with two careful nudges and phoned her landlord. She described the crooked track and the drawer full of utensils now trapped behind it. He asked whether it had come completely off. Priya tried to explain without pulling it loose, drumming a spoon against her palm as she spoke. “I can send someone after work tomorrow,” he said. She asked him to bring the right hardware, not simply inspect the drawer. He agreed to check with the maintenance crew. Priya thanked him and set the spoon down. Then she opened the drawer a fraction, closed it, and opened it again, testing the same stubborn movement as if it might offer a new answer.

I noticed the hallway carpet lifting near my door when my slipper caught its edge for the third time that morning. I called the landlord, described the loose strip, and added that someone could easily trip over it. While he searched for a maintenance worker, I sat on the floor and pressed the carpet flat with my palm. It sprang up again. “Could they bring a tack strip?” I asked. He said they would inspect it first. I turned a loose thread around my finger, unwound it, and turned it again while we settled on an appointment for the next day. He asked me to keep the area clear. I moved my shoes to the opposite wall, lining them heel to toe. When the call ended, I nudged the carpet once more with my slipper. It lifted at the same corner.

At dusk, Theo stood beneath the porch light outside his rental house and watched it blink in uneven bursts. He called his landlord, explaining that the fixture had started flickering and sometimes went dark altogether. The landlord asked whether Theo had tried a different bulb. He had, and he said so, then described the brief crackling sound he heard when the light failed. His free hand kept smoothing the front of his jacket, though it was already neat. The landlord promised to send an electrician and asked him to leave the switch off. Theo agreed, then watched the dark porch while they chose a time for the visit. “Wednesday morning,” the landlord said. Theo repeated it aloud, as though testing the phrase. After the call, he walked to the end of the path and back, glancing up at the fixture each time.

I had stacked the tins of peaches three times, each row facing the same way, while the clock above the pantry crawled from ten past two to twelve past two. At the community food bank, the afternoon line had thinned, and my hands kept finding small jobs nobody had asked for. I tapped a pencil against the clipboard and watched dust drift through a stripe of sun. Then a boy near the door pointed at a dented can and asked whether it could be a spaceship. His grandmother laughed, and I told him the label looked more like a moon. Soon he was choosing ingredients for an imaginary crew, and I was setting aside crackers for their voyage. When they left, the room seemed quieter than before, but I kept the little paper rocket he had drawn beside the sign-in sheet.

Marta lined up cans of beans by expiration date, then rearranged them by label color just to give her fingers something to do. The community food bank’s back room smelled of cardboard and floor cleaner. A radio murmured weather updates nobody seemed to hear. She checked the wall clock, sighed, and began smoothing a torn flap on a box. A delivery driver arrived with a crate of unfamiliar vegetables, each one knobbly and streaked purple. Marta had never seen them before. She fetched the old cookbook from the staff shelf, and two other volunteers crowded around to identify the mystery roots. By the time they found a recipe, the room had filled with guesses and laughter. Marta wrote the cooking instructions on a card for visitors, pleased that the afternoon had finally offered something worth figuring out.

I kept switching the canned soup labels toward the aisle, though every one was already straight. The community food bank had been quiet for nearly an hour, and the fluorescent lights made the minutes feel especially long. I shifted my weight from heel to toe and traced the edge of my name badge with one thumb. Then a woman came in carrying a violin case and asked if she could leave a few jars of homemade apple butter. While I checked the donation rules, she opened the case and explained that she played at the bus station on weekends. A child waiting with his father recognized the tune she hummed. She gave a short performance between the shelves, and soon even the people sorting rice were keeping time with their hands. I forgot about the clock until the music ended.

At sixty-eight, Curtis volunteered at the neighborhood food bank every Thursday, where the usual task was folding paper bags and placing recipe cards inside. He folded one, then another, then glanced at the stack as if it might grow faster under inspection. His knee bounced beneath the table. When a new volunteer dropped a jar of cinnamon into the donation basket, its sharp scent spread through the room. Curtis remembered the peach cobbler his mother used to make and began describing it, measuring ingredients with gestures. A visitor waiting for groceries asked for the recipe, so Curtis wrote it down on the back of a spare card. Others gathered around, offering their own variations. Before long, the bags carried notes about cobbler, bread pudding, and spiced tea. Curtis tucked one recipe into his coat pocket to try at home.

I was counting packets of oatmeal into boxes at the community food bank, and my thoughts kept wandering to the train timetable folded in my jacket. The same ten packets went into every carton; I could do it without looking. I started estimating how many seconds each box took, then lost track and began again. A woman arrived with her teenage daughter, who was wearing a bright orange scarf and carrying a sketchbook. While they waited, the daughter drew quick portraits of the volunteers. She turned the page toward me: my hair stood up in dramatic spikes, and the oatmeal packet in my hand looked like a trophy. I laughed harder than I expected. She offered to draw the whole crew, so I gathered everyone near the loading door. The finished page now hangs above our packing table.

Nikhil took his place at the community food bank’s sorting table after finishing his college classes. The donated cans rolled past in steady batches, and he kept glancing at the window, where rain crept down the glass in crooked lines. He rotated a can of tomato soup, read the label, and rotated it again. Just as he considered asking for another task, a little girl arrived with her father and asked why some cans had pull tabs and others did not. Nikhil explained the difference, then showed her how volunteers checked dates and inspected dents. She wanted to help, so he gave her a marker and let her draw a small star on each box ready for delivery. Her serious concentration made him smile. Soon he was explaining the whole sorting system with the enthusiasm of a tour guide.

I had spent the morning at the community food bank attaching price-free labels to bags of lentils, and the repetitive peel-and-stick rhythm was making my shoulders sag. I glanced at the clock, then at the pile, which seemed unchanged. From the reception desk came the sound of someone practicing a trumpet, stopping after each uncertain note. I wandered over and found Leon, a retired music teacher, waiting for his grocery appointment. He said the instrument belonged to his grandson and he was trying to learn a birthday tune. I knew the melody from my childhood, so I hummed it while he searched for the right notes. A few volunteers joined in, clapping softly. The tune stumbled, recovered, and finally held together. When I returned to the lentils, I found myself peeling labels in time with the beat.

Yasmin, a high-school senior, volunteered at a community food bank while waiting for her evening shift at the cinema. Her job was to arrange donated toiletries in baskets, and she had already alphabetized the soap twice. She drummed her fingertips against the counter, watching the door for movement. A man came in with a box of handmade knitted hats, each one sporting a different animal face. He explained that his neighbors had made them for children picking up groceries. Yasmin tried on a fox hat, then a green frog one, while the man took photos for the knitting group. A young visitor chose a striped cat hat and wore it out proudly. The room brightened as volunteers modeled the remaining creations. Yasmin checked the clock later and realized her shift was almost over.

I was sorting donated books beside the food shelves, turning each volume over to check whether it was suitable for the community food bank’s little free-library cart. The room was still, and every page I opened seemed to contain another recipe for soup. I rolled a paperback between my palms and wondered whether the clock had stopped. Then I found a children’s book about a dragon who hoarded turnips. Its illustrations were ridiculous: the dragon wore spectacles and guarded a vegetable patch with a tiny umbrella. A father waiting for groceries leaned over to see the cover. His son recognized the story and began recounting the ending from memory. I asked him to read the first page aloud, and soon three children had gathered. Their dramatic dragon voices carried across the pantry. I set the book on top of the cart, ready for its next audience.

Otto, a former harbor mechanic, volunteered at a community food bank by checking the wheels on its delivery carts. He pushed each one down the corridor, listening for squeaks, and returned it to the same painted square. After the fourth cart, he leaned against the wall and watched rain bead on the windows. A new shipment arrived in a battered blue van, and one wheel kept wobbling. Otto examined the axle, then asked a volunteer to fetch a wrench. As he worked, a child nearby held the flashlight and offered increasingly elaborate advice. Otto played along, calling the child his chief engineer. They tightened the wheel together, and the cart rolled straight as a ruler. The child stamped an imaginary approval on Otto’s hand. He grinned and volunteered to inspect the rest of the fleet.

I stood at the community food bank’s welcome table, sliding appointment cards into neat stacks while the lobby remained nearly empty. The heater clicked on and off, and I had begun counting the ceiling tiles to occupy my mind. A delivery arrived in a van covered with hand-painted flowers. The driver, an older woman named Doreen, brought jars of honey from a local beekeeping club. She told me the bees had survived a particularly windy spring, then showed me a tiny photograph of the hives. I asked about the different shades of honey, and she explained how nearby flowers changed its flavor. The talk drew in two volunteers from the pantry, who asked questions while unloading the jars. I forgot the cards entirely. Before Doreen left, she promised to bring a sample for the staff tea kettle.

At the community food bank, sixteen-year-old Ezra was assigned to bundle fresh carrots with rubber bands. He worked through one crate, then stared at the next, his fingers flexing as if they were tired of the same motion. The coordinator noticed and asked him to help greet a group of elementary students visiting to learn about food donations. Ezra showed them the produce shelves and explained why volunteers sorted bruised vegetables separately. One student asked whether a carrot could grow crooked on purpose. Ezra admitted he did not know, so they examined a particularly twisted one together. The children invented names for its bends and decided it resembled a tiny antlered creature. By the end of the tour, Ezra was carrying their drawings back to the sorting room. He taped them above the carrot crates, where every volunteer could see them.

At nineteen, I arrived at the driving school with a paper cup of tea and the expectation that the lesson would crawl. Mr. Dube explained the mirrors while I watched a loose thread on my sleeve curl around my finger. At the first red light, I counted the cracks in the dashboard and let out a long breath. Then a delivery cyclist slipped between the car and curb, and Mr. Dube asked what I had noticed. I had seen him only at the last second. My hands tightened on the wheel. For the next blocks, I checked every mirror and tracked each person near the road. When the lesson ended, I was surprised to find my tea untouched and my shoulders aching from concentration.

Mara, a retired librarian, settled into the learner's seat with her gloves folded in her lap. Instructor Lee described the pedals, and she gave each explanation a small nod while gazing at a yellow leaf stuck to the windshield. At a quiet intersection, she began humming the same three notes under her breath. Lee asked her to pull over beside a community garden. A child there was trying to coax a runaway balloon away from the curb, and Mara watched the traffic before guiding the car around safely. Lee smiled and asked her to explain why she had waited. Mara sat straighter, studying the road ahead. She spent the remainder of the lesson asking about right-of-way, and the gloves stayed forgotten on the seat.

I was seventeen, and every practice session with Coach Alvarez seemed to begin with the same empty parking lot. While he adjusted his seat belt, I bounced my knee and traced circles on the fogged window. He asked me to steer between two rows of cones, but my mind kept drifting to the baseball game on the radio. Then a gust shoved a shopping cart across our path. I stamped the brake, and the car stopped just short of it. Coach Alvarez had me try the course again, this time watching farther ahead. I began spotting every cone before it reached the windshield. By the end, I was leaning forward, eager to see whether I could finish without touching one.

Nikhil had spent the morning folding shirts at his family's shop, and the evening lesson felt like another exercise in sitting still. His instructor, Jo, reviewed the dashboard lights as he clicked his pen against his knee. When they reached a narrow residential street, a dog darted from behind a parked van. Nikhil braked hard, then looked to Jo for approval. She asked him to describe what he could see beyond the next car. He began naming driveways, shadows, and children playing near a gate. The task gave his eyes somewhere useful to go. On the way back, he pointed out a ball rolling toward the roadway before Jo saw it. His pen remained in his pocket for the rest of the drive.

My first lesson took place in a small town where the roads were straight and the sky seemed to occupy most of the windshield. I was twenty-six and kept shifting my weight while Instructor Renee listed the steps for a three-point turn. A tractor appeared at the far end of the lane, moving at a pace that made me drum both thumbs on the steering wheel. Renee told me to practice judging distance, so I watched the tractor's approach and called out when it passed each mailbox. Then she had me turn around in a farm entrance. I needed three careful movements and one correction. When we returned, I asked if we could practice the maneuver again, even though the sun had nearly set.

Evelyn, a sixteen-year-old violinist, thought driving lessons would be another appointment to endure between school and rehearsal. Her instructor, Mr. Chen, talked through the controls while she rolled a guitar pick between her fingers. On the practice road, a sudden downpour blurred the lane markings. Mr. Chen asked her to slow down and locate the reflective markers at the edge of the pavement. Evelyn stopped fidgeting and leaned closer to the windshield. She followed each small glint, keeping the car centered until the rain eased. Afterward, she wanted to know how the headlights changed the markers' appearance. Mr. Chen answered while she examined the switch herself, then let her drive the final stretch through the wet streets.

I signed up for lessons at thirty-eight because the bus no longer reached the clinic where I had started working. During my first session, I kept rubbing the seam of my jacket while Instructor Pilar explained how to adjust the mirrors. The empty industrial road offered little to look at, and my eyelids grew heavy at a stop sign. Pilar asked me to find the nearest street number, then the next, then the one after that. Soon I was scanning shop fronts and calling out addresses before she could point. At a loading dock, a worker waved us around a stack of crates, and I navigated the detour without prompting. Pilar said I seemed more alert. I drove back to the school with both hands steady.

Leo, a seventeen-year-old from a mountain village, arrived for his lesson wearing headphones around his neck. Instructor Sana described the clutch, and he watched a moth circle the ceiling light inside the parked car. On the uphill road, the engine sputtered as he released the pedal too quickly. Sana told him to listen for the change in the motor's pitch. Leo tried again, concentrating on the sound rather than the view of the valley. The car rolled forward smoothly. They repeated the start at several steep driveways, each one different in slope and surface. By the last attempt, Leo was listening with his head tilted and his foot poised above the pedal. He asked Sana to choose the steepest route back.

My instructor, Dale, took me to a supermarket lot before opening time. I was twenty-two and kept checking my phone in the cup holder while he explained how to reverse into a space. The rows of painted lines looked identical, and I let out a sigh after my third attempt landed crooked. Dale set a paper cup on the ground behind the car and asked me to use it as a reference point. I watched it in the mirror, turning the wheel a little at a time. The next space came out straight. Then he moved the cup to a different corner, and I had to work out the angle again. When the store lights came on, I barely noticed; I was busy setting up one more attempt.

Sofia, a thirty-one-year-old baker, had flour on her cuffs when she climbed into the training car. She kept rubbing her thumb over a pale smudge while Instructor Martin explained lane changes. The broad boulevard ahead offered endless straight pavement, and her gaze wandered toward a billboard. Martin asked her to name a safe gap between the moving cars. Sofia blinked, then began tracking each vehicle's speed and distance. A bus pulled alongside them, briefly hiding the lane. She waited until it moved ahead before changing over smoothly. Martin asked what had made her pause, and she described the blind spot without hesitation. On the drive back, she watched the mirrors before he reminded her, her hands no longer fussing with the flour.

I was fifty-three and had postponed learning to drive for years, so I expected the lesson to feel like a long list of instructions. My instructor, Kim, demonstrated the turn signal while I peeled the paper label from my water bottle. We practiced on a quiet loop, and I began counting each lap under my breath. Then Kim asked me to navigate to the post office using only the street signs. I had to watch for names, remember the turns, and judge the traffic all at once. At a fork, I nearly chose the wrong road, but spotted the sign just in time. I arrived at the post office without help. On the return trip, I asked Kim to give me another destination.

Andre, a twenty-year-old exchange student, sat through the safety briefing with one heel tapping the floor mat. His instructor, Beth, took him to a quiet neighborhood and asked him to practice stopping smoothly. He watched the same hedges pass again and again, his chin sinking toward his chest. Then a street sweeper appeared ahead, leaving a narrow path between its brushes and parked cars. Andre had to judge the clearance and keep a careful distance. Beth guided him through it, then asked him to choose a wider route home. He scanned the blocks for alternate turns and called out each one before reaching the corner. His heel stayed still, and he kept glancing ahead as if the next decision might arrive at any moment.

For six weeks, my ankle had been wrapped in a brace, and the basketball court existed only beyond the gym’s glass doors. I finished every exercise my therapist assigned, then counted the ceiling tiles while the clock’s second hand clicked around. One afternoon, I began bouncing a foam ball off the wall from my chair, aiming for a laundry basket. The first shots missed by a mile. I adjusted my wrist, moved the basket, and kept score in the margin of my homework. When my therapist arrived, she found me grinning at a perfect swish. She cleared me to stand for a few minutes, so I took the ball to the court and made one careful shot. It rattled off the rim. I laughed, retrieved it, and tried again, already planning a better angle.

At twenty, Nia could identify every crack in the rehabilitation clinic’s pale blue ceiling. Her hamstring was healing, but the slow treadmill sessions seemed to stretch through entire afternoons. She rotated the resistance bands by color, rearranged the magazines, and asked the receptionist whether the wall clock had always ticked so loudly. Then a young patient arrived, nervous about beginning therapy. Nia showed him how to loop a band around his foot and make small, controlled pulls. His first attempt sent the band sliding across the room. They both laughed, and Nia retrieved it before he could reach. Helping him gave her a reason to pay attention to each repetition. By the time her own session ended, she had stopped watching the clock. Outside, she tested her repaired leg with a careful, steady step.

My shoulder was nearly strong again, according to the surgeon, but I still had to avoid serving in tennis. At home, I wandered from the kitchen to the window and back, opening cupboards without taking anything out. My racket leaned against the wall like an accusation. I finally carried it to the driveway and used it to tap a balloon upward with my good hand. Keeping the balloon aloft turned into a game; I shuffled carefully, laughed when it drifted onto the porch roof, and fetched a broom. The next week, my therapist approved gentle practice. At the club, I stood at the service line and tossed the ball without hitting it, feeling my shoulder stay calm. On the third toss, my coach said I could try a soft serve. The ball barely cleared the net, but I chased its bounce with a smile.

After fracturing his wrist, Tomas had become an expert at sitting through the afternoon baseball broadcasts without following a single inning. He peeled the labels off water bottles, folded a stack of flyers into tiny squares, and kept asking his sister what time it was. His cast came off on a bright Saturday, though the doctor warned that strength would return gradually. At the field, Tomas watched his teammates warm up, then offered to keep score. The pencil felt awkward between his fingers, so he practiced writing each player’s name in the margins. When the coach needed someone to toss soft balls for batting practice, Tomas volunteered. His first throw wobbled, and the batter swung too early. They adjusted their timing together. By sunset, Tomas’s wrist ached in the ordinary way of hard work, and he had filled the scorebook with neat, careful marks.

The ski lodge’s lounge had only three things to offer me: a humming radiator, a stack of old travel brochures, and a view of the slopes I couldn’t reach with my healing knee. I’d already read the same brochure about mountain trains twice. To stop myself from pacing, I drew little maps on its blank back pages, marking every run I hoped to try again. My physical therapist had approved a short walk, so I bundled up and followed the path beside the beginner hill. Children slid past on bright skis while I practiced bending and straightening my knee. A snowman wore one of my spare gloves by the trail sign. I added a paper map to its stick arm, then continued to the lodge entrance without leaning on the rail. The run could wait; making it that far felt like a new route.

Leila’s cycling accident had left her collarbone mending and her racing bike suspended from a hook in the garage. On rainy mornings, she lined up its tools by size, polished the helmet, and checked the weather app every few minutes. Her father suggested a puzzle, but she gave up after placing the same blue piece in the wrong spot three times. Her physiotherapist finally allowed her to use a stationary bike at the lowest setting. Leila clipped in and turned the pedals so slowly that the fan barely stirred her hair. She began naming each revolution after a street on her old training route. Soon she was tracing the whole route in her head, noticing the bakery corner and the steep bridge. When the timer rang, she asked for another minute. Her shoulder stayed comfortable, and she left the garage with a real ride to anticipate.

I was a goalie before a knee injury put me on the sideline, and watching practice from a folding chair made every whistle sound longer than it should. I tapped my fingers against my shin guards, rearranged the cones, and offered the coach increasingly useless observations about the clouds. One evening, our youngest player kept losing track of where to stand. I got up with my crutches and showed him how the goal looked from each corner of the box. He copied my stance, arms wide, and made a dramatic save against a rolling ball. I laughed hard enough to forget the ache for a moment. My doctor had just cleared me for balance drills, so I joined him for five careful shifts between cones. The team cheered when I stayed upright through the last one. I spent the ride home replaying that small victory.

Jun had been a competitive swimmer until a shoulder strain sent him to dry-land exercises and a poolside bench. He spent practice twisting a rubber band around his fingers, counting lane stripes, and reading the same three posters about hydration. His coach noticed him watching the novice group and asked if he would help demonstrate breathing rhythm. Jun hesitated, then showed the swimmers how to turn their heads without lifting their whole bodies. Their splashing soon became less chaotic. While they practiced, he followed the pattern with one hand, careful not to aggravate his shoulder. A week later, his therapist permitted easy laps with no hard pulls. Jun entered the water, pushed off gently, and glided across the first lane. The familiar coolness settled around him. He stopped at the wall, checked his shoulder, and asked the coach to time another lap.

My running injury had healed enough for short jogs, yet the doctor still banned hills. Around our flat neighborhood, I had memorized the sequence of mailboxes and could tell which lawns had been mowed that morning. One Tuesday, I ran out of things to count and began making up stories about the objects people left on their porches. A red boot belonged to a pirate, I decided; a cracked flowerpot was a moon crater. The game carried me past the usual turnaround point before I noticed. I walked the last block home, surprised by how quickly it had passed. At my next checkup, the doctor approved a gentle trail with no steep climbs. I took my sister along, narrating the strange history of every pinecone we found. She challenged my inventions, and we returned with muddy shoes and a route for next week.

Mara’s broken finger had healed, but the volleyball coach still kept her away from hard serves. She sat on the bleachers, flipping a coin across her knuckles and watching her teammates leap at the net. When practice ended, she offered to help sort the ball cart. Instead of stacking the balls immediately, she tested how each one bounced and marked the softest with a strip of tape. Her coach suggested using it for controlled passing drills. Mara joined a younger player, sending gentle underhand passes back and forth. The first few landed short, and she rolled her eyes at her own timing. Then the ball began meeting her forearms cleanly. She started calling out each target before sending it over. By the time the gym lights flickered, they had invented a three-point challenge. Mara’s finger felt fine, and she asked when she could try a real serve.

During recovery from a sprained wrist, I spent long hours in my grandmother’s apartment while my fencing club trained across town. I arranged the fruit bowl by color, sharpened pencils that were already sharp, and listened to the radiator knock. My coach sent a video of the team practicing footwork. I watched it once, then stood beside the sofa and copied the steps without holding a foil. At first my feet tangled; the carpet kept catching my socks. I moved to the hallway, where I could mark the advance and retreat with strips of masking tape. My grandmother timed each sequence with a kitchen timer, dramatically announcing every finish. When the therapist cleared me for light grip work, I practiced holding a wooden spoon like a foil and tracing small circles. The next club visit, I had new footwork to show, and my teammates asked to learn it.

Elias, a 67-year-old marathon walker, had torn a calf muscle during a charity event. His daughter brought him crossword books, but he filled them in quickly and then stared at the remaining blank squares as if they had offended him. The walking poles stood by the door, untouched. Once his physiotherapist approved short, level outings, Elias began visiting the neighborhood garden each morning. He moved slowly between the raised beds, asking gardeners what they were growing and offering to carry seed packets. A child showed him how a bean tendril curled around a stake. Elias returned the next day with a notebook and sketched its progress. Soon he had a routine: a measured walk, a page of observations, and a rest on the bench. By the time his calf was ready for longer distances, the gardeners had appointed him their unofficial record keeper.

I had arrived at the licensing office before sunrise, but the numbered display had barely moved since I took my ticket. Across the room, a child rolled a plastic bus along the grout lines, then began the route again. I counted ceiling tiles, lost my place, and started over. My phone showed three percent battery, so I put it away and watched a patch of sunlight crawl across my shoes. When the clerk called a number two digits higher than mine, I sat up, then sank back against the chair. I folded my appointment slip into a tiny boat, unfolded it, and smoothed the creases with my thumb. At last, the child’s bus bumped against my ankle. I pushed it back, grateful for the brief interruption.

Mina had brought a book to the municipal records office, convinced the wait would give her time to finish it. After reading the same paragraph four times, she let the book rest open on her lap. The line curved around a row of gray chairs, and the electronic sign blinked without changing its number. She watched a man peel the paper sleeve from his coffee cup, then studied the sleeve’s torn edge as if it might reveal a secret. Her heel tapped beneath the chair. When a clerk emerged with a stack of folders, Mina straightened, but the clerk disappeared through another door. She exhaled, tucked the bookmark into the book, and began sorting the loose threads on her scarf by color.

I was waiting at the immigration counter with a folder of carefully arranged papers and nowhere else to be. The line advanced whenever someone left, which seemed to happen about once every geological era. I traced the outline of my passport through my jacket pocket, checked my ticket, and checked it again. A wall clock made a small click with every second. Soon I was matching each click to the blinking lights on a vending machine across the room. A woman nearby sneezed, and several people looked up as if something dramatic had occurred. I almost laughed. When my number finally appeared, I sprang from the chair so quickly that my folder slid to the floor, scattering photocopies beneath the seats.

At the benefits office, Ravi had already memorized the faded poster about handwashing and the three chips missing from the blue counter. He shifted his weight from one foot to the other, then returned to the chair when the line stopped again. His appointment was for ten; the clock now showed nearly noon. He had eaten the last of his crackers, leaving only crumbs in the envelope, which he tipped into his palm and counted. A little girl nearby was making a crown from a receipt. Ravi offered her a spare paper clip, and she attached it like a jewel. For several minutes, he watched her design new decorations. When the clerk called his number, he needed a moment to remember why he had come.

I joined the queue at the tax office with a thermos, a newspaper, and an optimistic schedule. By eleven, the thermos was empty and the newspaper had been folded into smaller and smaller rectangles. I read the notices on the wall, including one warning about counterfeit stamps, then read them again from the other end of the room. The person ahead of me kept glancing at the screen, and I began copying the motion. Every few minutes we both lifted our heads, saw the same number, and looked down. I drew a map of the office on the back of my receipt, marking the water fountain and the exit. When my place finally came, I had added a tiny garden beside the photocopier.

Seventy-eight-year-old Lottie sat in the pension office line with her handbag firmly clasped between her knees. She had brought knitting, but after completing the same row twice, she discovered she had lost count. The fluorescent lights hummed overhead. She watched a security guard straighten a crooked sign, walk away, then return to straighten it again. Lottie’s fingers drummed on the handbag clasp, keeping time with the slow shuffle of shoes toward the counter. A young man beside her offered to check the number display. She thanked him, though she could see it perfectly well from her seat. To occupy her hands, she arranged her knitting needles parallel, crossed them, and arranged them parallel once more.

I was at the vehicle registration office, watching my place in line creep forward by inches. The man at the front had been searching his wallet for what felt like a complete season. I rubbed the ridges on my ticket until the paper softened, then tried to make the inked number appear darker by staring at it. A vending machine offered six kinds of chips and no sandwiches; I studied the labels as though selecting one required expert knowledge. My knee bounced beneath the chair. When the screen chimed, I stood, only to find that it had called someone from a different queue. I sat down again and arranged my keys from largest to smallest. Their neat little row was the most orderly thing in the building.

Niko, a delivery cyclist, had parked his helmet beside him at the passport office and kept checking the time on his wrist. The line barely shifted. He spun one bicycle key around his finger, caught it, and started again, stopping whenever a clerk opened a side door. Nobody came out. A toddler dropped a mitten, and Niko retrieved it before the parent noticed. He then examined the rubber tread on his gloves, rubbing each fingertip with his thumb. The office television showed a silent cooking program; he watched a chef chop onions, then watched the same segment replay. When his number finally appeared, he leaned forward with sudden energy, gathered his documents, and nearly left the helmet under the chair.

I took a ticket at the public housing office and found a seat beneath a poster about emergency exits. The poster had a tiny diagram, so I followed its arrows with my eyes until I could picture the route from every chair. Then I counted the people ahead of me. Someone left, someone else arrived, and my count became useless. I folded my hands, unfolded them, and inspected the faint ink stain on my palm. The wall clock had no second hand, which somehow made waiting feel even longer. A receptionist carried a stack of forms past us, and every head turned to follow her. My number was still far away. I began guessing what each person in line had brought in their folders.

At the county clerk’s office, Celeste balanced a carton of seedlings on her lap while waiting to file a name-change form. She had watered them that morning, but now she checked the leaves every few minutes, turning the carton to give each plant its share of the window light. The queue stretched past the drinking fountain and doubled back near the door. Celeste studied the pattern in the floor tiles, then tried to find pictures in the clouds visible through the high windows. A clerk called several numbers in quick succession, none hers. She sighed, lifted one seedling, and pinched away a dry leaf. When the line moved at last, she held the carton carefully against her chest and shuffled forward with the others.

I sat in the long queue at the unemployment office, listening to the ventilation fan click every time it turned. I had already read every message on my phone and deleted three photographs to make room for nothing in particular. Across from me, a man was turning a coin over his knuckles. I tried the same trick with my bus pass; it slipped between my fingers and skated under a chair. Retrieving it gave me a reason to stand, though the line had not moved. Back in my seat, I peeled the corner of a sticker from my folder, then pressed it down again. The display finally changed, and I checked my ticket twice before realizing my number was still several places away.

Priya had taken a morning off from her bakery to visit the licensing office, where the line stretched past a row of potted plants. She watched one leaf tremble whenever the door opened. Her phone battery had died, and the magazine on the table contained recipes she already knew by heart. She tapped the edge of her folder against her knee, then stopped when the papers inside began to slide out. A clerk called numbers in a brisk voice, and each time Priya lifted her head, expecting hers. She began identifying the different sounds in the room: the printer’s whirr, a cough near the entrance, a chair scraping the tile. When her turn arrived, she stood quickly, smoothing her apron before stepping toward the counter.

When the lights went out, I was halfway through sorting the junk drawer for the third time that month. The refrigerator stopped humming, and the apartment seemed to hold its breath. I checked my phone, then its battery, then the clock on the dark microwave, which was no help at all. Across the hall, Mr. Alvarez opened his door with a camping lantern in hand. I went over, mostly because the silence in my place had begun to feel enormous. He was trying to tune a battery radio, so I took a turn at the dial while he studied the antenna. Static gave way to a weather report, then a song neither of us recognized. We sat on the stairwell landing and tried to guess the singer. By the time the power returned, I had forgotten the drawer entirely.

Mina had already read every cereal box in her kitchen when the neighborhood went dark. She tapped the light switch twice, as if it might respond to persistence, then wandered to the window. On the sidewalk, a cluster of neighbors stood beneath the streetlamp, which was also out. Mina carried down a bowl of clementines and found a place beside a boy named Leon, who was trying to make shadow animals with his hands. His rabbit looked more like a lopsided duck, and Mina showed him how to angle his fingers. Soon the neighbors were taking turns inventing creatures against the glow of a lantern. Mina kept glancing at her watch, but the gathering grew louder and more elaborate. When the lamps finally flickered back on, Leon asked whether they could do it again sometime. Mina said she knew a few more animals.

I had spent the afternoon waiting for a delivery that never arrived, so when the power cut out, I was already pacing between my desk and the front window. The elevator stalled, and my neighbor Mrs. Okafor came up the stairs carrying a pan of bread dough. She needed somewhere warm for it to rise. I offered the last patch of sunlight on my kitchen counter, then followed her downstairs to check on the building’s older tenants. We knocked on doors with a flashlight, passing updates and a jar of jam along the way. In the lobby, a teenager produced a deck of cards, but nobody knew the rules to the game he suggested. I shuffled while everyone argued over them. The outage lasted two hours. By the end, I knew who made excellent bread and who cheated at cards with remarkable confidence.

At thirteen, Caleb had been told to stay inside during the outage, which left him leaning over the sill and watching neighbors move about with flashlights. His aunt was on a work call until the connection dropped, and his game console had gone quiet. He drummed his fingers on the glass, then noticed that the family across the courtyard was holding up handwritten signs. One said, “Anyone know the score?” Caleb grabbed a marker and a cereal carton. He made a sign offering the latest baseball results from memory, though he had to admit he might be a batter behind. Soon messages passed between windows: jokes, questions, and a request for more candles. His aunt joined in, spelling out a recipe suggestion. Caleb kept checking the windows for replies, and when the power came back, he was already planning what to write next.

The outage found me in the middle of repainting a chair, with one leg still its original brown. I set down the brush and listened to the sudden quiet. My phone had little charge, and the book beside me had a chapter I had already started twice. From the porch, I saw my neighbors gathered around a portable stove, attempting to heat soup. They waved me over, so I brought the uneven chair and a handful of clothespins. Someone suggested we turn it into a contest: decorate the chair using whatever was in our pockets. A bus driver contributed a bright route map; the twins next door offered stickers, and I tied on a blue shoelace. We judged the results with great seriousness. Mine won for “most likely to survive a move.” When the lights returned, I carried the chair home, still covered in its temporary finery.

Ravi had been staring at the same unfinished crossword clue for ten minutes when the power failed in his block. He walked downstairs with a flashlight and found two neighbors in the courtyard, each holding a nearly dead phone. Nobody could call the utility company, and the printed notice on the lobby door offered no useful estimate. Ravi pulled a pocket notebook from his jacket and began collecting guesses about when the electricity might return. The guesses turned into a competition: one neighbor predicted midnight, another said “before the kettle cools.” Ravi made a little chart and awarded points for confidence. When a child asked for a prize, he tore a page from the notebook and drew a gold medal. They spent the next half hour improving the medal design. At last the lights came on. Ravi looked at his crossword clue and found the answer immediately.

I was home between shifts, watching the minutes crawl across my watch, when the power vanished. My tea cooled on the table. I checked the hallway, where Mrs. Sato was holding a flashlight under her chin and making a ghost face for her cat. The cat was unimpressed; I laughed anyway.
