I flinched, then pressed my thumb against the watch through the cloth. A pair of ducks skimmed past, leaving neat V-shaped trails. I wished I could follow them somewhere without bills. Instead, I threaded on another worm and cast toward the reeds.

Lena set out on the lake before dawn with a borrowed rod and a list of names tucked inside her jacket. Her community kitchen had run out of food, and the delivery truck had broken down two towns away. She had promised the families they would still eat that night. The lake’s surface shivered beneath the first breeze. Lena cast again and again, scanning the water for movement while the bait dwindled. Her phone buzzed with messages she did not open. When a fish finally hooked itself, she hauled it in so quickly that it slapped against the boat floor. She held it there, chest rising, then wrapped it in a damp cloth. One fish would not feed everyone, but it was something she could carry back. She put fresh bait on the hook and began working the shoreline, searching every shadow beneath the trees.

I took my father’s old canoe onto the lake at dawn, though the weather radio had warned of wind. The search crew had called off the night’s effort for my younger brother, whose kayak had capsized somewhere beyond the north shore. I kept his bright orange lure tied to my line, hoping it might catch on something of his. The paddle blades shook in my grip. I called his name toward the empty coves and listened for an answer among the birds. Nothing came but the soft slap of water against the canoe. I checked the banks, then the reeds, then the small islands we used to race around as children. Each time I saw a patch of color, I lunged toward it. Once it was a leaf; once, a buoy. I kept moving until the sun showed above the ridge, refusing to turn back.

At dawn, Pavel pushed his fishing boat away from the dock with a sack of ice and a deadline from the power company folded in his pocket. The notice said service would be cut that afternoon. His wife was home with their infant, keeping the room warm with a small electric heater. Pavel started the motor, then listened as it sputtered and caught. He steered toward the lake’s deeper basin, where the morning catch was usually better. The first hour brought nothing but a torn net and a numb hand. He scraped the blood from his palm against his trousers and kept working. When the clouds brightened, he looked toward shore, gauging how long a run to the market would take. A weight shifted in the net. Pavel hauled steadily, lips moving as he counted each pull, and a cluster of fish flashed in the mesh.

I had three hours before the gallery doors opened, and the largest painting still leaned against my kitchen wall. The delivery van had failed to arrive; my phone showed a string of unanswered calls to the driver. I wrapped the canvas in a bedsheet and dragged it toward the stairwell, stopping whenever the frame caught on a corner. At the gallery, the curator was already arranging labels. “It’s coming,” I said, though I had no idea how. My hands shook as I borrowed a trolley from a nearby shop and pushed it through the rain. When I finally lifted the painting into place, one corner of the frame split. I pressed the crack together with both palms, holding it there while the curator searched for tape. The first guests were stepping inside when I let go.

At sixty-eight, Nadiya had never used a computer to prepare an exhibition, but the printer would not release the wall labels she needed by morning. She tapped the screen, tried another cable, then called her grandson, whose voicemail greeted her in cheerful tones. Around her, framed landscapes waited in neat rows, each one carrying the price of a week’s groceries. Nadiya copied the labels by hand, but her fingers cramped and the ink ran when a cup tipped over. She wiped the table with her sleeve, then began again on fresh paper. Near midnight, the gallery’s lights clicked off on a timer. She kept working by the glow of her phone, squinting at the names and dates. When the first volunteer arrived, Nadiya was still printing the final letter.

I had borrowed money for the frames, the van, even the clean shirt I planned to wear at the opening. Now the gallery manager was pointing at the empty stretch of wall where my photographs should have been. The courier had left them at the wrong address, and the building’s office was closed. I ran there anyway, knocking until a sleepy caretaker appeared behind the glass. “Please, just let me check the mailroom,” I said, pressing my forehead to the door. He let me in. I found the package beneath a stack of flyers, its corner crushed. Back at the gallery, I cut the wrapping with a key and inspected each print under the harsh ceiling lights. One was creased beyond repair. I hung the other eleven, then placed the damaged one on my lap and smoothed it with shaking hands.

Elias watched the gallery clock while his installation refused to balance. The suspended paper birds sagged toward the floor, their threads tangled around a ceiling hook. He climbed the ladder again, though his knees had begun to tremble, and tightened each knot with his teeth holding the loose ends. The curator had already warned him that the room must be cleared before the opening. A maintenance worker appeared with a toolbox, but Elias waved him away, then immediately called him back when another bird fell. “I need you to hold the ladder,” he said, his voice thinner than he intended. Together they lifted the sculpture, Elias directing every movement in quick bursts. At last, the flock hung level. He stepped down and looked at the pale marks the thread had left across his palms, then asked the worker to stay until the doors opened.

I had promised my father that his paintings would be shown together, but the gallery’s floor plan had changed overnight. The new wall was too short for all six canvases. I measured the space twice, then a third time, hoping the numbers would rearrange themselves. They did not. I called the director, who was driving and could barely hear me over traffic. While I waited for her to return, I shifted the smaller works, lifted one frame, put it down, and lifted it again. My father sat on a folding chair, pretending to study the exhibition leaflet. I could see his thumb worrying the paper’s edge. “We can make it work,” I told him, and pulled a canvas from its frame to gain an inch. The glass slipped, struck the floor, and shattered. I dropped beside it, gathering the pieces before he could stand.

Mina’s exhibition opened the next afternoon, but the paint on her newest canvas remained tacky. She had kept the studio windows shut against the winter air, and now the thick blue surface gleamed wet beneath the lamps. She waved a piece of cardboard over it, then aimed a hair dryer from the gallery office at the paint. The edges began to curl. Mina switched the dryer off and pressed the canvas flat with books, checking it every minute. Her assistant suggested replacing it with an older work. Mina stared at the empty wall, jaw tight, while guests’ names appeared on her phone screen. She carried the canvas into the corridor, found a draught from the stairwell, and stood there holding it upright until her arms ached. When the paint finally dulled, she lifted the books away one by one.

The gallery owner had given me one wall, and I had sold exactly one painting in three months. Still, I borrowed a ladder and began hanging the exhibition before anyone could change their mind. The nails kept bending. I straightened them with pliers, struck my thumb with the hammer, and wrapped it in the corner of my shirt. My rent notice sat folded in my pocket, its sharp edge rubbing my leg whenever I climbed. A visitor stepped in early and asked whether the paintings were for sale. I smiled too quickly and read out the prices, though I had rehearsed sounding casual. He studied a small charcoal drawing, then moved on without a word. I climbed back up and adjusted its frame until it sat perfectly level. By evening, I had checked the same nail so many times that the wall was dusted white.

Saira had spent a year preparing her first gallery show, but a burst pipe soaked the boxes containing her catalogue copies. She lifted each booklet from the water, pages sagging between her fingers, and laid them across the studio floor. The opening was the next morning. Her brother offered to print replacements, but the nearest shop closed in twenty minutes. Saira gathered the least-damaged pages and drove with them, gripping the steering wheel hard enough to whiten her knuckles. At the print counter, she explained the problem in a rush, then stopped when the clerk glanced at the long line behind her. “Please, even a small batch,” she said. The machine began to hum. Back at the gallery, she arranged the damp originals beneath the new copies, hiding the curled corners with a stack of pencils until the doors opened.

I was still labeling the sculptures when the gallery’s power cut out. The emergency lights made every bronze face look unfamiliar, and the opening reception was due to begin in forty minutes. I found the fuse box behind a locked service door, then searched my pockets for the key I had been given. My fingers came up with coins, tape, and a folded list, but no key. I called the manager twice; each time the phone rang out. The caterer was already bringing trays through the dark room. I ran outside and caught the building electrician as he was leaving. “I can’t open without the lights,” I blurted, holding up my marked hands. He followed me in and worked at the panel while I stood beside him, reading the labels aloud. When the lamps flashed on, I exhaled so sharply the nearest candle went out.

At twenty-two, Leo had borrowed his aunt’s van to bring his paintings to a gallery across town. Halfway there, the rear door sprang open at a stoplight. He heard a frame slide, jumped from the driver’s seat, and chased it into the intersection while cars leaned on their horns. A bus shelter stopped the canvas before it reached the curb. Leo carried it back, breath catching in his throat, and tied the door shut with a shoelace. At the gallery, the curator examined a long scrape along the frame. Leo offered to reduce the price, replace the frame, or take the work home—his words tumbling over one another. The curator only asked whether the painting itself was damaged. It was not. Leo leaned against the wall, eyes fixed on the scrape, while the curator helped him carry the remaining works inside.

I had spent the morning arranging my mother’s quilts for the exhibition, only to learn that the gallery would not allow them to touch the floor. The shortest display stands were still too tall, and the quilts’ stitched edges dragged whenever I lifted them. I folded one over my arm and searched the storeroom for clips, moving boxes with my hip. The curator checked the time twice. “I can make a new support,” I said, though I had never made one. I cut cardboard from a shipping carton and covered it with clean cotton, pinning the fabric in place with sewing needles from my kit. The first quilt sagged. I pulled it down and began again, fingers clumsy from the cold. When it finally held, I backed away only a step before reaching up to check every pin.

Farid’s exhibition depended on a projector that kept showing a blank screen. He had built the entire room around a sequence of home videos, and the gallery’s opening guests were already gathering outside. He unplugged the machine, reconnected it, and searched online for the model number with a thumb that slipped across the screen. The technician was not answering. Farid crawled beneath the table, tracing cables by touch, his shirt collecting dust. A volunteer asked whether they should delay the opening. He shook his head, then immediately asked her to hold the door while he ran to the next building for an adapter. He returned at a jog, breathless, and fitted it into place. The first image appeared: his family gathered around a dinner table. Farid stood beside the projector, hands pressed together, watching the picture remain steady.

Rain tapped through the ceiling into a saucepan, then a mixing bowl, then the last clean mug I owned. I carried the containers to Mr. Bell’s office before my night shift, my sleeves still damp. He glanced at the stain on my shoulder and said the roofer was booked for next month. I set my phone on his desk and played the recording of water dripping beside my daughter’s bed. She had slept on the kitchen floor for three nights, curled around her school backpack. My voice came out thin as I asked him to call someone, anyone, before the plaster gave way. He started explaining the lease. I slid a photograph of the sagging ceiling toward him. When he finally reached for his phone, I gripped the chair until my fingers hurt, watching his face for the first sign that he meant to act.

At sixty-eight, Darnell had learned to keep his voice level, but the broken lift made each trip to his fourth-floor flat a negotiation with his knees. He found the landlord beside the mailboxes and placed a paper bag of groceries at his feet. “The repair crew came twice,” she said, checking her messages. “They need a part.” Darnell took a folded sheet from his pocket: appointment times for his heart medication, missed because he could not manage the stairs with his cane and shopping. His hand trembled as he pointed to the date of the first report, six weeks earlier. A neighbor passed, pretending not to listen. Darnell lowered his voice and asked whether the landlord could carry the groceries up just once. Her expression shifted when he tried to lift the bag and had to stop halfway. She called the lift company while he waited, still gripping the mailbox ledge.

The refrigerator died on the hottest week of July, and every time I opened its warm door, the smell pushed me back. I called my landlord from the laundromat because my prepaid phone had only enough battery for one more conversation. “I’ll see what I can do,” he said, the same words he’d used on Monday. I told him about the insulin my mother kept in the freezer compartment, then read him the pharmacy’s warning label while a dryer thumped behind me. He asked if we could wait until payday. My mother was sitting at home beside a cooler packed with melting ice, fanning herself with an old bill. I pressed my thumbnail into my palm and asked him to repeat that suggestion slowly. There was a pause. Then I heard keys, a door, and his promise to send a repair technician before dinner.

When the bathroom pipe burst, Sana used every towel in the apartment to slow the water creeping toward the hallway. She called the landlord from the landing, where the signal was stronger, and described the stream pouring through the cabinet floor. He asked whether she had tried tightening the valve. Sana crouched beside the pipe, one knee soaking through her trousers, and told him the valve had snapped off in her hand. Her toddler cried inside the bedroom while she wedged a saucepan under the leak. She kept repeating the apartment number because her words were running ahead of her breath. The landlord finally said a plumber would come, though he could not give a time. Sana stared at the water line crossing the threshold and asked him to stay on the phone until the plumber arrived. He heard the child crying and stopped talking about the lease.

I had the landlord’s number written on the back of an envelope because my phone screen had gone black after the outlet sparked. The kitchen smelled sharp and smoky, and I stood outside the building holding my newborn while my sister watched the door. When the landlord answered, I tried to explain that the wiring had crackled again and the lights were flickering. He said he would send an electrician next week. I looked at the baby’s red face and at the dark windows above us. “Please don’t make me bring him back in there,” I said, then hated how my voice broke. I read aloud the dates of my earlier messages, one by one. He asked me to wait. I paced the pavement, counting each minute by the traffic light, until he called back to say an electrician was driving over.

The stairwell ceiling had been shedding grit for days, and Luis noticed a crack widening above the door to his flat. He met the landlord in the lobby carrying a bucket and a broom. “I’ve swept this up every morning,” he said, showing the dust caught in his cuffs. The landlord leaned back to inspect the ceiling but kept his hands in his coat pockets. Luis explained that his son had asthma and had begun coughing whenever they climbed the stairs. He had already moved the boy’s mattress into the kitchen, away from the bedroom wall. When the landlord suggested waiting for the building inspector, Luis placed the child’s inhaler on the reception counter. His jaw worked silently for a moment. Then he asked the landlord to look at the crack from upstairs, where a fresh line of plaster had dropped onto the pillow. The landlord followed without another delay.

For two weeks, the front door had refused to lock unless I lifted it with my shoulder. Tonight the latch broke while I was carrying my work bag and a bag of groceries, and the door swung open behind me. I called my landlord from the corridor, keeping one foot pressed against it. He said he could come tomorrow. I looked down the empty hallway and heard someone’s television click off. My hands were slick on the phone. I told him I had reported the sticking lock three times and that my little boy was asleep inside. He asked whether I could wedge a chair under the knob. I tried, but the chair slid across the floor. “I can’t leave him here with this open,” I said. After a long silence, the landlord told me to stay put and called a locksmith. I sat on the floor with my back against the door until the van arrived.

Mireya kept a notebook of every call about the heating, including the dates and the names of the people who had answered. In January, the radiators clicked but stayed cold, and frost feathered the inside of her bedroom window. She took the notebook to the landlord’s office, wearing two sweaters and fingerless gloves. He said the boiler had been inspected. Mireya turned to the page showing the technician’s canceled appointment and held it steady, though her knuckles were pale. Her father, recovering from surgery, sat at home under three blankets. She asked the landlord to come upstairs and feel the radiator himself. He began to object, then noticed her breath clouding in the office doorway. Mireya waited without sitting down. At last he called the maintenance company, gave them the address, and stayed on the line until someone agreed to come that afternoon.

A brown ring spread across the bedroom wall while I was getting ready for an interview. I called the landlord with my tie half-knotted and a suitcase open on the bed; the stain had reached the socket. He said the leak was probably from upstairs and told me to contact that tenant. I walked up, found no answer, then returned to the hallway and called again. My interview clothes were damp where I had brushed the wall. I asked him to shut off the water before the wiring caught. He sighed, and I heard myself apologize for calling, which made my stomach twist. The ceiling gave a soft pop overhead. I grabbed my documents and moved them into the corridor, then sent him a video of the dripping socket. He stopped speaking, told me not to touch the switch, and said he was coming over immediately.

At the end of her shift, Jo found the only toilet in her flat overflowing again. She shut the bathroom door and called the landlord from the kitchen, listening to water seep beneath it. He reminded her that a plumber had visited the previous month. Jo gripped the counter so hard her fingertips blanched. Her younger brother was due home from dialysis, and she had no working bathroom for him to use. She said this plainly, then repeated it when the landlord asked whether the problem could wait until morning. The phone slipped against her cheek as she dragged towels across the floor with her free hand. A neighbor knocked, asking if everything was all right. Jo looked at the swelling bathroom door and told the landlord she needed an answer, not another appointment window. He called a plumber while she stood barefoot in the spreading water.

I met my landlord in the courtyard with a jar of brown tap water. The kitchen faucet had been running rusty for three days, and the building notice said the water was safe without explaining the color. My grandmother refused to drink it, so I had been carrying bottles home from the corner shop, one trip at a time. My arms shook as I set the jar on the bench. The landlord said pipes sometimes cleared on their own. I unscrewed the lid and the metallic smell rose between us. “Would you give this to your child?” I asked. He looked at the jar, then at the stack of empty bottles beside my door. I had rehearsed a calmer speech, but the words vanished. He called the building manager and asked for a water test that day. I waited beside him, watching the phone in his hand as if it were the only faucet left.

Owen had been sleeping in the living room because the bedroom window would not shut, and winter wind kept lifting the curtain like a hand. He caught the landlord in the parking lot and showed him the strip of cardboard he had wedged into the frame. The landlord said replacement windows took time. Owen’s work uniform hung on a chair, damp from the condensation, and his pay envelope was nearly empty after buying space heaters. He asked whether the owner could at least send someone to seal the gap. When the landlord started toward his car, Owen stepped in front of the open door, then immediately moved aside, embarrassed by the gesture. He held up the tiny electric bill, marked with red ink, and explained that the heaters were tripping the circuit. The landlord studied the paper and called a glazier before driving away.

At six each morning, I unlocked the food bank beneath the Methodist church and arranged tins with their labels facing out. My own electricity notice sat folded in my coat pocket, its red date visible whenever I reached for a can. When a mother arrived with two children and asked whether we had anything they could eat without cooking, I filled a bag with fruit, bread, and peanut butter. Then I put my lunch apple on top. The pantry coordinator saw me checking the notice again and asked if I needed help. I said I was fine, too quickly, and began wiping a shelf that was already clean. She took the paper from my pocket, found the number for the local assistance office, and dialed while I stood beside her, twisting my volunteer badge between my fingers.

Ruben was seventy-two and volunteered at the food bank in the old railway depot, where the radiators clanked but never warmed the sorting room. His rent had risen, and the envelope from his landlord rested unopened beside his kettle at home. At the pantry, he carefully counted every bag of rice, then counted them again when the figures refused to settle in his head. A teenager asked if he could take an extra loaf for his grandmother. Ruben glanced toward the coordinator, expecting a reprimand, but she nodded. He slipped in two loaves and watched the boy hurry away. During the break, Ruben finally opened the envelope. His hands shook enough that he tore the edge crookedly. The coordinator sat nearby without asking questions, then showed him a list of senior housing counselors printed on the back of the pantry schedule.

I volunteer at the food bank on Thursdays because the shift fits around my nursing classes. This week, my car made a grinding sound in the parking lot, and the mechanic's estimate was more than I had in my account. I kept my face turned toward the crates while I sorted dented cans, pretending not to notice the phone buzzing with payment reminders. When an older man came in and said his fridge had stopped working, I found shelf-stable milk and tuna for him. He thanked me by name, reading it from my badge. That small kindness nearly undid me. I went into the supply closet and pressed both palms against the shelves until the tightness in my chest eased. Then I told the supervisor what had happened. She offered a ride to campus and wrote down the number of a repair fund.

Amina had moved to town three weeks earlier and volunteered at the neighborhood food bank while waiting for her work papers to clear. Each morning she checked her phone for a message from the agency, then tucked it away before the other volunteers arrived. Her daughter’s lunchbox was nearly empty at home, and Amina had started dividing one banana into pieces. At the pantry, she translated for a family who spoke the same language she did. The father kept apologizing for needing help. Amina told him the shelves existed for exactly that reason, though her voice caught on the last words. After the family left, she asked the manager whether volunteers could receive groceries too. He showed her the staff sign-up sheet and helped her choose food without requiring her to explain herself. She folded the list and held it close on the bus ride home.

I signed up to pack boxes at the food bank after my hours at the hotel were cut. I told everyone it was because I liked staying busy. In truth, the stack of overdue bills on my kitchen table had begun to seem taller each night. While I packed beans and oatmeal, I kept doing arithmetic in my head, subtracting rent from the small amount in my account and coming up short. A volunteer dropped a jar, and the sharp crash made me jump so hard I knocked over a carton of crackers. The coordinator brought me a chair and a glass of water. I stared at the floor, embarrassed by how badly my hands were trembling. She said the pantry had emergency grocery cards for volunteers as well as visitors. I accepted one, then asked if she knew anyone hiring for evening shifts.

Caleb arrived at the food bank with a split seam in his work trousers and a toolbox he had carried on the bus. He volunteered sorting produce because the hours kept him from sitting alone in his rented room. His plumbing business had lost its biggest client, and three unanswered calls sat on his screen. When a crate of bruised pears came in, he trimmed the soft spots and arranged the good fruit in paper bags. A woman collecting groceries asked whether he knew how to fix a leaking tap. Caleb almost laughed at the timing, then wrote his number on the back of a pantry flyer. By closing, she had sent him a photo of the pipe. He studied it under the fluorescent lights, shoulders hunched, and replied with a price she could afford. For the first time all day, he set his toolbox down gently.

I volunteer at the food bank in the community center where my father used to play dominoes. Since his stroke, I have been paying for his medicine and taking unpaid days to bring him to appointments. The pharmacy called during my shift to say the prescription was ready, and I watched the clock while stacking boxes of pasta. My thumb hovered over the call-back number; I could not make myself ask whether they would hold it. A woman at the pantry noticed me gripping the phone and offered to finish my row. I stepped outside, where rain tapped the awning, and called the clinic’s social worker instead. She found a prescription assistance program and stayed on the line while I wrote down each step. When I returned, the boxes were neatly stacked, and someone had left a mug of tea by my gloves.

Niko volunteered at a food bank in a converted fire station, where the red doors still bore faded lettering. He had been sleeping on his cousin’s couch since his restaurant closed, but he told people he was between apartments. One cold morning, he arrived early and checked the pantry’s delivery sheet three times, hoping a box of cooking oil would appear; his cousin’s stove worked, but their cupboard was bare. A delivery van pulled in with fewer crates than expected. Niko unloaded each one slowly, hiding the shake in his wrists by gripping the handles with both hands. When the coordinator offered him a grocery bag, he started to refuse. Then he pictured the children at his cousin’s table picking crumbs from an empty plate. He accepted the food and asked whether the shelter nearby needed evening volunteers. The coordinator wrote down an address and a bus route.

I had been volunteering at the food bank for months before my hours at the print shop vanished. I kept showing up, because the familiar work—checking dates, sealing bags, sweeping flour from the floor—gave the day a shape. At home, my landlord had left a note beneath the door, and I had read it so many times the paper was going soft. During a distribution, a little girl asked if the cereal was for her family. I smiled and said yes, then turned away to straighten a row of tins. My throat tightened; I counted to ten against the shelves. The shift leader found me there and asked what would make the next week easier. I showed her the note. She helped me call a tenant clinic, and together we arranged an appointment before the pantry doors closed.

Priya was a retired music teacher who volunteered at the food bank every Saturday. Since her partner died, the quiet apartment had grown difficult to enter, and the unpaid funeral bill waited in a drawer. She organized donated vegetables by size, making neat rows of carrots and potatoes. When the power company’s reminder appeared on her phone, she pressed the screen dark and continued working. A new volunteer spilled a box of onions and apologized repeatedly. Priya knelt to help gather them, but her knees protested and she had to grip the table edge. The volunteer fetched a chair and stayed beside her. Priya mentioned the bill, almost as if discussing the weather. The coordinator gave her a contact for a bereavement fund and offered to walk her through the application. Priya tucked the paper into her music folder, beside a melody she had not played in months.

I work the food bank’s evening shift after my delivery route, though lately there have been fewer packages and less pay. I keep my helmet on the counter while I sort donated soup, watching the rain blur the windows. My youngest needs new glasses, and the optician’s estimate is folded in my wallet beside a nearly empty bus card. When the pantry line thinned, I checked the estimate again, then rubbed the crease until the paper warmed under my thumb. A man asked if we had food that needed no stove; his room had only a kettle. I assembled a bag of instant oats, crackers, and fruit. The coordinator quietly offered me a grocery voucher too. I started to say no, then saw my wallet’s empty bill pocket. I took it, thanked her, and asked where I could find affordable eye care.

Elias volunteered in the food bank’s warehouse while his construction crew waited for a delayed contract. He had two children and a mortgage payment due on Monday; every message from the bank made his jaw lock. He lifted cartons onto the pallets with practiced ease, refusing help even when his shoulder began to throb. When a stack tilted, he lunged to catch it and sent cans rolling across the concrete. The noise brought everyone running. Elias stood frozen, breathing through his nose, staring at the scattered food as if one more mistake would settle everything. His supervisor guided him to a chair and handed him an ice pack. After a few minutes, Elias admitted he had missed a payment before. They called the lender together, then checked the food bank’s list of local job openings. He returned to the floor with the ice pack tucked beneath his shirt.

The clinic had called twice while I sat in the driver’s seat, gripping the wheel so hard my fingers tingled. My daughter’s fever was climbing, and the bus route to the children’s hospital had been suspended. “Again,” Mr. Alvarez said gently, as I stalled at the practice lot’s exit. I swallowed, turned the key, and tried to keep my eyes on the lane markings instead of the phone lighting up in my bag. We practiced a left turn, then a stop at the painted line. My foot trembled above the brake. When I finally pulled smoothly into traffic, Mr. Alvarez nodded and told me to breathe. I drove the loop without a single stall. At the lot, he signed my lesson card. I called the clinic with shaking hands and asked them to keep a room open while I arranged the next lesson.

At sixty-eight, Harlan had never needed a license; the fishing village’s buses had always been enough. Then his wife’s dialysis schedule changed, and the last bus home left before her treatment ended. He arrived at the driving school carrying a notebook filled with bus times and clinic addresses. During the first lesson, he stared at the pedals as if they might switch places when he blinked. His instructor, Jo, kept her voice even while he practiced starting and stopping along an empty industrial road. A truck rumbled past, and Harlan flinched, then checked both mirrors exactly as Jo had taught him. “I can’t keep asking my neighbor,” he muttered. At the end, he wrote down every correction. The following week, he returned before the doors opened, notebook tucked under one arm, ready to try the route to the clinic.

My passport appointment was across town, and the notice said there would be no second slot before my scholarship deadline. I had failed the road test once, so my brother paid for one more lesson and told me not to waste it. In the passenger seat, Ms. Reed watched me miss the first turn toward the test center. My mouth went dry. I kept seeing the rejection email in my mind, though it had not arrived. “Let’s reset,” she said, guiding me back to the intersection. I checked the signs, signaled, and made the turn correctly. For the next hour, she had me practice parallel parking between two battered cones. When the lesson ended, I had to ask her to repeat the appointment directions twice. I wrote them on my palm, then drove home with the window open and both hands fixed on the wheel.

Noura’s bakery had one delivery van, and its driver had broken his wrist the morning before the town’s spring festival. Orders were stacked in the kitchen, their pickup times circled in red. She booked a driving lesson during her lunch break, still wearing flour on her sleeves. Her instructor, Ben, began in the quiet school parking lot, where she practiced gentle turns around the painted arrows. Noura kept checking the clock whenever they stopped. “The bread won’t wait,” she said, rubbing a white streak from her cuff. Ben pointed out that rushing the clutch only made the engine stall. She tried again, listening for the engine’s rhythm, and pulled forward without a jerk. Before they finished, she drove along the back road behind the shops. At closing, she asked the bakery owner to save tomorrow’s first delivery route for her practice.

I had one month before my work permit expired, and the warehouse offered me a permanent shift only if I could get there before the first bus. My instructor, Mr. Cho, found me waiting outside the driving school at sunrise, tapping my shoes against the curb. I confessed that I kept mixing up the turn signal and the windshield wipers. He placed a small label beside the signal and sent me around a quiet block. Rain began streaking the glass; I hit the wipers by mistake and let out a breath through my teeth. Mr. Cho didn’t scold me. He asked me to pull over, identify each control, and start again. By the third circuit, I signaled before turning. I still had to pass the test, but when I got home, I filled out the shift application and pinned it beside my practice schedule.

After the storm washed out the footbridge, Mateo’s mother could no longer reach the neighboring town for her weekly insulin refill. His uncle’s car sat unused, but Mateo had never driven farther than a farm track. Instructor Lila met him at the village school and showed him how to adjust the mirrors before they pulled away. He kept glancing toward the dark clouds, then back at the road. At a narrow crossing, a tractor appeared around the bend. Mateo braked too hard, and a box of lesson materials slid off the back seat. “Look where you want the car to go,” Lila reminded him. He exhaled, steadied his hands, and eased forward when the road cleared. They practiced the route to the pharmacy twice. Before parting, Mateo copied the test office’s phone number onto the back of his hand.

The landlord’s notice was folded in my jacket pocket, its deadline only five days away. I had found a room in another district, but the early shift at my new job began before the trains ran. During my first lesson, I kept asking instructor Dana to repeat how far ahead to look. My eyes jumped from the speedometer to the curb, while my knee bounced beneath the dashboard. She directed me through a quiet neighborhood and had me stop beside a playground. “You’re trying to solve every mile at once,” she said. I rubbed my damp palms on my jeans and focused on the next corner. We practiced turning, parking, and pulling away until the movements felt less like a test. At home, I placed the notice beside my lesson receipt. The room was still available, but I called the owner that evening to ask how long she could hold it.

Seventeen-year-old Keisha needed to drive her younger brothers to their father’s apartment before the family’s temporary housing ended. Her aunt worked double shifts, and the boys’ school was a forty-minute walk away. Instructor Pavel started them in a nearly empty supermarket lot. Keisha’s shoulders rose toward her ears each time the car rolled forward. She watched Pavel’s face for signs that he might take the wheel. Instead, he asked her to narrate what she saw: the curb, the open lane, the parked truck. Naming each thing slowed her breathing. On the road, a horn blared behind them at a green light. Keisha’s hands tightened, but she moved through the intersection safely. Afterward, she called her aunt from the passenger seat and asked her to bring the boys to the next lesson. The instructor marked a new route on the map.

My father’s nursing home was two counties away, and the social worker said his room would be reassigned if I couldn’t visit and sign the papers by Friday. I hadn’t driven since college. Instructor Marisol met me in a rented sedan, and I apologized before I even adjusted the seat. My hands shook when the engine started. We spent the first lesson in an empty office park, circling broad lanes while I practiced braking smoothly. Whenever I looked at the clock, Marisol asked me to name the nearest road sign. It kept my eyes from darting to my phone. By the end, I could make a three-point turn without mounting the curb. I still didn’t know if I could manage the highway, so I called my cousin to ask for a ride to the next lesson and wrote the nursing home’s deadline on my calendar.

When the small coastal ferry canceled its winter crossing, Amos lost the only dependable link between his island home and the mainland dialysis center. His niece had offered her old car, but she could not stay long enough to teach him. Instructor Ruth found him waiting outside the community hall with a paper map folded into quarters. He had circled the clinic in blue ink. At first, he crept along the empty harbor road, peering over the steering wheel. Ruth adjusted his seat and showed him how to use the mirrors. A gull swooped low, and Amos jerked the wheel; she guided him to the shoulder until his breathing settled. They continued, practicing lane changes beside the seawall. At the lesson’s end, he traced the route with one finger and asked Ruth to schedule another session before the next clinic appointment.

The scholarship interview began at eight, and the only affordable room I’d found was beyond the last subway stop. I had no family nearby, so I enrolled in a driving lesson using the money I’d saved for meals. Instructor Greg took me to a quiet stretch of road and asked me to practice merging. Each time a car approached, my stomach clenched and I backed off too soon. “You have a gap,” he said, pointing toward the open lane. I signaled, checked the mirror, and moved over, though my voice caught when I told him what I was doing. We repeated it until I stopped braking at the sight of every passing vehicle. Afterward, I sat on a bench and calculated the bus fare to the test center. I called the interview office to ask whether arriving a few minutes late would end my chance.

Rafi had promised his grandmother he would take her to see the sea before her eyesight faded further. Her doctor had advised against the crowded coach, and no relative could leave work for the trip. At thirty-two, Rafi signed up for lessons, bringing his grandmother’s old photograph of the shoreline in his wallet. Instructor Helen began with basic controls in a quiet residential street. He stalled twice at a stop sign, then apologized to a row of empty houses. Helen asked him to focus on the car rather than an imagined audience. His jaw loosened a little as he practiced starting on a hill, though his hands stayed damp. They drove toward the edge of town, where the road opened between fields. Rafi asked whether the next lesson could include a short stretch of highway, then carefully tucked the photograph back into his wallet.

The doctor said six more weeks, and I stared at the crack in the clinic ceiling as if it might offer another answer. My right knee was wrapped beneath my jeans; every step to the bus stop reminded me how far the finish line had moved. The regional trials were in a month. At home, I propped my leg on a stack of library books and watched videos of runners exploding from the blocks. My little brother found me doing ankle circles at midnight and silently set a glass of water beside me. The next morning, I asked my coach to help me train everything that still worked. He brought resistance bands and a plan. I followed it until sweat ran down my back, then wrote each completed exercise on the calendar. The trial date stayed circled. So did the appointment when I could test a jog.

At thirty-eight, Dario had built his life around the climbing wall at the old mill. Then a falling hold twisted his wrist, and the surgeon pinned it in place. He sat in the gym lobby while younger climbers chalked their hands, turning his useless brace over and over. His rent depended on guiding summer groups, and the season had already started. When his sister suggested he take a quiet month, he tapped his fingers against his thigh until they hurt. Instead, he called the clinic and asked what he could safely do. Soon he was strengthening his legs, studying route maps, and teaching beginners from a chair. The first time he was cleared to climb, he chose the easiest wall. Halfway up, pain sparked through his wrist. He froze, breathed, and waited for it to settle before reaching for the next hold.

I heard the pop before I felt the pain, a sharp sound beneath the roar of the stadium. My ankle swelled inside my soccer sock, and the trainer shook her head at my pleading look. Scouts were watching the final, and my scholarship offer had no guarantee beyond that night. For days, I sat on the porch while my teammates practiced across the field, their whistles carrying through the screen door. I made a list of every exercise the physical therapist allowed and kept it folded in my pocket. Some mornings the list trembled in my hand. I still showed up at the field, first to observe, then to pass from a chair. Weeks later, I jogged one lap without stopping. My coach didn't clap; he just handed me the ball. I pressed it against my chest and blinked hard before taking my place in line.

Mei's shoulder surgery left her unable to lift a kettle, never mind the javelin she had thrown since high school. Her place at the national training center was under review, and each envelope from the federation made her stomach tighten. She kept them unopened on the kitchen table, beside the ice packs and exercise bands. Her grandfather, who ran a small noodle shop, began saving her a stool near the front window so she could watch the street instead of the clock. One afternoon, a child outside mimicked a throwing motion with a paper airplane. Mei laughed, then reached for the band. She worked through the therapist's slow sequence, stopping whenever her shoulder burned. Months passed before she could hold the javelin again. At the track, she made a short approach and released it. The throw barely cleared the grass, but she walked after it herself.

My bicycle lay twisted in the ditch, and my collarbone had a metal plate where the bone should have been. I was supposed to race across the state in June; now I couldn't pull a shirt over my head without help. My sponsor stopped returning calls, and I began checking my phone every few minutes anyway. At the rehab center, I asked the therapist how soon I could ride. She gave me a careful answer, so I asked what I could do today. We started with tiny shoulder movements and balance work. I kept a notebook, marking each repetition like a stage in a journey I couldn't yet see. When I finally rolled onto the indoor trainer, I lasted four minutes before tears blurred the display. I came back the next day and stayed for five. The road outside could wait, though I kept my helmet by the door.

Isaiah, a high-school swimmer in rural Louisiana, injured his back lifting a feed sack at his family's farm. The specialist forbade turns and hard kicking for months. With college coaches due to visit, he watched the team’s meet from the bleachers, one hand gripping the rail whenever the crowd cheered. His father offered to drive him to appointments before dawn, and Isaiah accepted without looking up. In therapy, he learned to brace his core and move without guarding every inch. He timed the exercises on his phone, then restarted whenever he lost count. His coach saved him a lane for gentle water work. The first session lasted six minutes. He emerged shivering, unable to tell whether the water or the waiting had made his hands shake. At home, he pinned the meet schedule above his desk and circled the next possible return date.

The cast made my left hand look like a clumsy stone mitten. I was a concert violinist, and the winter audition was the first chance I'd had at an orchestra job. When I fractured my fingers in a fall, I called the hall twice to ask whether the panel would postpone. They wouldn't. My teacher came over with a pencil and had me tap rhythms on the table using my good hand. I did it until my jaw ached, then asked to try again. Once the cast came off, each scale seemed to expose a new weakness. I pressed a warm cloth to my knuckles and repeated the passage slowly, measure by measure. On audition day, I could not play every note cleanly. Still, I stood beneath the lights, lifted the bow, and began. My fingers shook at first, then found the melody.

At sixty-two, Helena refused to let a torn calf muscle end her career as a race walker. The injury came during a charity event, where she had been leading a group of children through the park. Now she watched them practice from a bench, her walking poles crossed beside her. Her club had already chosen someone else to lead the spring team, and she kept rereading the message on her phone, searching for a sentence she could change. The physiotherapist taught her how to load the leg gradually. Helena followed every instruction, even when the smallest step left her breathing hard. She also volunteered to plan the route and mark safe crossings. On her first walk without support, she moved slowly around the park's outer path. A child fell into step beside her, matching her pace. Helena looked ahead and kept going.

I had one chance to qualify for the wheelchair basketball squad, and then my shoulder began grinding with every pass. The scan showed a tear; the surgeon said recovery would take most of the season. I sat in my apartment surrounded by unopened mail from the league, the envelope edges curling as the radiator warmed them. My teammate called each evening, but I kept saying I was fine until the words sounded ridiculous even to me. At therapy, I learned to stabilize the joint with small, controlled movements. I counted aloud because silence gave my thoughts too much room. When I was cleared to shoot, I wheeled into the empty gym before sunrise. The first ball struck the rim and bounced into the bleachers. I chased it, returned to the line, and shot again. The next one dropped through the net with a soft snap.

Bongani's sprinting career seemed to vanish when a hamstring tear pulled him from the national trials. He was twenty-two, working nights at a hotel, and had no sponsor to cover treatment. The clinic waiting room smelled of disinfectant; he sat hunched over his shoes, calculating bus fares and missed shifts. His aunt lent him money, though he promised to repay every coin. Recovery started with slow walks and careful stretches. On days when the muscle tightened, he gripped the counter and waited, face hot with frustration. His coach offered him work timing younger runners, but Bongani kept asking when he could return to the track. The answer changed from weeks to months. He learned to stop measuring each day against his old speed. When the doctor finally approved a short sprint, he crouched at the line, listened for the signal, and drove forward into the cool evening air.

The ski patrol carried me off the mountain after my wrist snapped beneath me. I had trained for the junior championship all year, and the event was only three weeks away. At home, I watched snow fall through the window while the plaster cast itched beneath my sleeve. My coach sent clips of the course, and I replayed them until my mother took the tablet away at dinner. The surgeon said I could keep my legs strong, so I pedaled a stationary bike with my cast balanced on a towel. Each morning, I asked whether the swelling looked smaller. Nobody gave me the answer I wanted. Once the cast came off, I practiced gripping a pole before I touched a slope. The first run was slow and shaky. At the bottom, I leaned against the fence, laughing and wiping my face with my sleeve.

Priya's handball season ended when a defender landed on her foot, fracturing two toes. Her club was fighting to qualify for the playoffs, and she watched the matches from the sideline with her shoe loose over the bandages. Every time the team fell behind, she leaned forward as if her body could cross the court without her. The doctor warned her not to rush; the coach needed her, but wouldn't risk making the injury worse. Priya followed the rehab schedule, balancing on one foot, then the other, beside her bedroom dresser. When she lost balance, she caught the wood and began again without checking the clock. Her teammates sent updates after practice, and she answered with questions about their formations. At last, she was cleared to train. She joined the warm-up carefully, then passed the ball across the court. The familiar sound steadied her.

I reached the county benefits office before sunrise, carrying the eviction notice folded inside my coat. By nine, the line had curled past the security desk and stopped beneath a clock whose minute hand seemed stuck. My phone showed three missed calls from the landlord. I pressed it to my ear anyway, though the battery warning had turned red. When the clerk announced that one window would close for lunch, people shifted forward, and I clutched my folder against my ribs. A form was missing my daughter’s school address; I wrote it on the back of a pharmacy receipt while balancing my papers on my knee. At the counter, my voice came out thin. The clerk slid a pen toward me. I signed where she pointed, watching her stamp the page, then held my breath as she reached for the next sheet.

At the passport office, Luis kept checking the departure board on his phone even though he knew the flight time by heart. His mother’s surgery had been moved up, and the airline would not hold his seat without a valid travel document. The queue advanced by inches. Each time the door opened, he stood, only to be waved back behind the yellow line. He had brought every certificate he owned, stacked by date in a plastic sleeve. When a child dropped a toy nearby, Luis retrieved it automatically, then glanced at the wall clock and rubbed the heel of his hand over his damp forehead. A guard said the office closed at four. Luis looked at the people still ahead of him, swallowed, and asked whether anyone had an urgent appointment. His fingers tightened around the sleeve until its corners bent.

I sat among the applicants at the licensing bureau with my work boots between my knees. The letter in my pocket said my commercial license would be suspended unless I corrected a clerical error by Friday. Friday was today. I had driven two buses to get here, and my supervisor’s last text asked whether I was coming back for the evening shift. Every time the line moved, I leaned forward, ready; every time it stopped, my stomach clenched again. A woman ahead of me began counting the numbered tickets aloud, so I counted with her under my breath. When the speaker called a number close to mine, I dropped my ticket. It skidded beneath a row of chairs. I crawled after it, retrieved it, and returned to my place with my palms gray from the floor.

Nadia had one week to prove she still lived at the address printed on her housing voucher. The government office required a document she had never received, and the help line had disconnected twice. She stood in the queue with a folder pressed to her chest, while her toddler slept against her shoulder. The child’s shoe slipped off; Nadia caught it before it hit the tile, then looked up to see that several people had moved ahead. Her lips parted, but no sound came. She asked the man behind her to save her place while she retied the tiny laces. He nodded, though the line kept inching forward. At the service window, Nadia spread out utility bills, a lease, and a handwritten note from her landlord. The clerk studied them without expression. Nadia watched the clock above the counter and tapped one finger against the folder.

I had been awake since my brother called from the county jail, asking me to bring proof that he lived with me. The records office was the only place that could print it, and the line reached almost to the entrance. I held his release paperwork in both hands so the pages would not shake. At the ticket machine, I pressed the wrong button and had to start again. A guard pointed me toward the back without looking up. I wanted to explain that the hearing was at noon, but my mouth felt packed with cotton. Instead, I showed him the court notice. He glanced at it and told me everyone had a deadline. I tucked the paper away, found a chair near the wall, and rehearsed my request silently. When my number finally appeared, I rose too quickly and had to steady myself on the seat.

At the immigration records office, Samuel watched the number display as if it might vanish when he blinked. His daughter’s school enrollment depended on a certificate that had been mailed to the wrong apartment. She waited across town with her backpack and a lunchbox, while he stood beneath fluorescent lights that made every face look pale. He had called the office during his break and been told to come in person, so he had traded shifts and borrowed bus fare. A clerk announced that the system was running slowly. Samuel folded and unfolded his appointment slip, smoothing its creases against his thigh. When an older man nearby began coughing, Samuel offered him water, then checked the screen again. His number was still several places away. He sent his daughter a message with one thumb: Stay with the teacher. I’m trying.

I joined the tax office queue with a cardboard box of receipts balanced against my hip. The notice said my refund could be withheld unless I corrected a mistake on the return, and that money was meant for the mechanic who had kept my car overnight. I had taken the morning off from the bakery, but my manager had already asked twice when I would be back. Each shuffle forward brought the counter closer and the deadline less forgiving. I sorted receipts by month, then discovered the one for the repair shop was missing. My hands went cold. I searched every pocket, opened my wallet, and checked the box again while people waited behind me. At last I found it stuck to the envelope lining. I held it up as though it might disappear, then stepped toward the window when my number was called.

Evelyn, a retired nurse, had spent the night beside her husband’s hospital bed before taking the bus to the pension office. A mistake in his benefit record had stopped the payment that covered their home aide. She brought the hospital bracelet, bank statements, and every letter she could find, arranged in a neat blue binder. The line barely moved. When she shifted her weight, pain ran through her knees, but she refused the empty chair near the exit in case someone thought she had left. A staff member called out that the computer network might go down again. Evelyn closed her eyes for one measured breath, then opened them and checked the binder clips. At the counter, she explained the situation in a voice polished by years of calming frightened patients. Her hand trembled only when she passed over the last document.

I stood in the municipal office line with a cracked tablet tucked under my arm. The grant for my repair shop would expire at closing, and one missing permit number was all that separated the application from approval. The city website had gone offline the night before, so I had no way to retrieve it. I kept refreshing the page anyway, watching a blank screen glow in my palm. Ahead of me, a man argued about a parking fine; each raised voice made my shoulders climb toward my ears. When the queue moved, I stepped forward and nearly left the tablet behind. I caught it against my chest, then looked at the time. My employee had sent a photo of the broken furnace, its metal casing peeled open. I typed, Hold on, and erased the message before sending it. At the window, I gave the clerk my application with both hands.

Ravi arrived at the unemployment office with a letter stating that his weekly payment had been paused because of an interview he never knew about. Rent was due the next morning, and his younger sister had left a grocery list on the kitchen table with three items crossed out. He kept his eyes on the queue’s numbered tickets, counting how many remained before his. His collar stuck to the back of his neck. When a chair opened, he started toward it, then saw the line advance and hurried back into place. A security guard reminded everyone to keep the aisle clear. Ravi apologized, though he had blocked nothing. At last his ticket appeared on the screen. He walked to the desk, laid out the letter, and asked the clerk to check the date. His voice cracked on the final word; he cleared his throat and tried again.

I carried my father’s death certificate to the veterans’ office because his final payment had gone to an account we could no longer access. The funeral home wanted its balance by Monday. I had promised my mother I would handle the paperwork, but the stack of forms looked taller every time I opened it. The line snaked around a partition, and the only seats were occupied by people holding folders like mine. I checked the certificate’s seal again, then again, as if the ink might have faded. When an employee passed through the lobby, I stood and asked whether I had the correct documents. She said she couldn’t tell until I reached a window. I sat down, took out my phone, and read my mother’s last message: Any news? My thumb hovered over the keyboard while the display showed another long stretch ahead.

Marta had brought her newborn to the public records office to request a birth certificate before the clinic would schedule a specialist visit. The baby fussed beneath a knitted blanket as the line gathered near the entrance. Marta rocked gently, one foot sliding forward and back, while she searched her bag for the appointment slip. She found it damp from a spilled bottle and tried to flatten it against her palm. The child’s breathing settled, but Marta’s eyes kept returning to the wall clock. A clerk announced that walk-ins might not be served after three. Marta looked at the people ahead, then at the small face tucked under her chin. She moved close enough to ask the woman in front how long she had been waiting. The answer made Marta close her eyes briefly. When her turn came, she lifted the baby and set the wrinkled slip on the counter.

When the lights failed, I was halfway through preparing my father’s oxygen concentrator for the night. The battery indicator blinked red, and my phone showed no signal. I ran next door in socks, pounding hard enough to hurt my knuckles. Mrs. Alvarez opened the door with a candle in one hand. I tried to explain, but the words tangled, so I held up the machine and pointed toward my father’s window. She called her nephew, who owned a generator, while I hurried back to check the portable tank. Every minute, I watched the gauge descend. The generator arrived on a handcart, rattling over the pavement. Together we dragged it to the porch, found an extension cord, and started it. When the concentrator hummed again, I sank onto the step, gripping the railing until my shaking eased.

Nia had promised to send her scholarship application before midnight, and the neighborhood outage swallowed the final hour. Her laptop showed a blank screen; the essay existed only on its dead drive, while the library’s website had closed. She carried her charger from house to house, asking whether anyone had power from a generator. At the corner, Mr. Bell’s garage glowed beneath a work lamp. He offered an outlet, but the modem was down. Nia paced between the car and the workbench, refreshing the page on her phone until its battery fell to twelve percent. Mr. Bell remembered that the community center had a backup connection. He drove her there in his old van. She uploaded the saved draft with three minutes left, then pressed both palms to her knees and let out a breath she had been holding.

I was watching my toddler when the apartment went black, and the refrigerator clicked silent behind us. The freezer held breast milk I had pumped for weeks; the next-door neighbors’ baby cried through the wall as if joining the alarm. I wrapped my daughter in a blanket and carried the cooler upstairs, knocking at every door. Nobody answered at first. Then a college student named Dev opened his, phone flashlight tucked under his chin. His family had a camping cooler and two frozen water bottles. We packed everything together, but the ice was already soft. I called the utility line, then my sister, then the pharmacy, my voice growing thinner each time. Across the courtyard, a neighbor’s car inverter was still running. We hurried the cooler there and took turns sitting beside it until the power returned.

At seventy-eight, Walter knew the stairwell by touch, but the outage had stopped the elevator on the ninth floor. His insulin was in the refrigerator, and the building manager’s number went straight to voicemail. He gripped the rail and climbed slowly, pausing on each landing while sweat gathered beneath his collar. On the sixth floor, a young couple came down carrying a battery lantern. They heard his uneven breathing and turned around without asking. One took his grocery bag; the other offered an arm. At his door, Walter fumbled twice with the key before getting it into the lock. The couple found a neighbor with a car and a cooler, then called the clinic for instructions. Walter kept checking his watch while they packed the medication. When the car finally pulled away, he pressed his forehead to the cool window and shut his eyes.

The outage hit just as our block’s flood siren began wailing. I had spent all afternoon helping my elderly neighbor, Mr. Sato, move boxes above the basement floor, but now the sump pump was silent. Rain hammered the windows, and water crept over my shoes. I ran outside with a flashlight, shouting for help. A family across the street brought extension cords; another neighbor wheeled over a portable generator that sputtered twice before catching. We hauled it beneath the porch roof, hands slipping on the wet casing. I kept staring at the waterline on the basement steps, measuring its rise against each breath. When the pump started, it coughed and shuddered, then began drawing water down. Mr. Sato sat on an overturned bucket, both hands locked around his cane. Nobody left until the rain eased.

Marisol’s bakery was full of cooling loaves when the power failed, and the electric oven had just begun a batch of wedding cakes. The couple would arrive at sunrise; the frosting was softening, and the shop’s backup battery powered only a small lamp. She hurried into the neighboring hardware store, where Mr. Cho was lowering the metal shutters by hand. He lent her a propane camp stove and several lanterns, while two apartment residents brought insulated blankets. Marisol shifted the cakes into carriers and walked them to a restaurant on the next block, knocking until the chef recognized her through the glass. Her hands trembled as she explained the schedule. He cleared space in his working refrigerator and let her finish the decorations under a battery light. Before dawn, she stood at the bakery door, flour on her sleeves, waiting for the first oven indicator to glow.

My little brother’s asthma inhaler was nearly empty when the lights went out, and the nebulizer stopped mid-treatment. I called emergency services, but the dispatcher said the road to our street was blocked by a fallen tree. I carried him downstairs, wrapped in his dinosaur blanket, while Mom searched every drawer for the spare battery. Our neighbors opened their doors, passing flashlights from hand to hand. Mr. Greene, who repaired boats, had a charged power pack in his truck. We ran a cable through the window and restarted the nebulizer. My brother’s breathing stayed rough, so I sat beside him, counting each inhale aloud and trying not to look at the clock. Mom called the clinic again while neighbors cleared branches from the road. When sirens finally sounded nearby, I held my brother’s hand so tightly he squeezed back.

At the laundromat, Keisha had one clean uniform left for her hospital shift, and the washer stopped with her clothes trapped inside. The neighboring apartments were dark too, their residents gathering on the sidewalk with candles and phones. She knocked on the laundromat’s side door, but the owner lived across town and could not reach the block. A mechanic from the corner garage brought a toolbox and removed the panel while Keisha held a flashlight steady. The lock resisted; she kept checking the time, then the bus schedule, then the uniform still sealed behind the machine’s glass. A retired electrician from upstairs joined them and found the manual release. The door popped open, water spilling over the tiles. Keisha wrung out the shirt and draped it across the garage radiator, standing beside it until the fabric stopped dripping. A neighbor drove her to work before the first bus arrived.

The blackout began during our tenants’ meeting, just as I was explaining that my landlord planned to sell the building. Then smoke drifted through the hallway from somewhere below. I grabbed the fire extinguisher, but the emergency lights were dead, and no one could tell which stairwell was clear. I shouted for everyone to stay together and used my phone screen to guide the residents toward the courtyard. Mrs. Lim was still upstairs with her cat, so I climbed back while the others called the fire department. My battery flashed its final warning as I found her crouched beside the bed. We came down slowly, her hand clamped around my sleeve. Outside, neighbors counted heads beneath the streetlamp on the next block. When firefighters arrived, I realized I had been holding the extinguisher pin in my fist so tightly it had marked my palm.

Rafi’s aquarium filter stopped when the neighborhood lost power, and the tank’s surface went still. His rare fish had survived a long shipment, and he had spent months keeping the water balanced. He carried a battery air pump from the basement, but its motor sputtered after a few minutes. Across the hall, a neighbor was charging a power station from a car. Rafi knocked, breath coming in short bursts, and explained what was happening. The neighbor lent it to him, then helped run a cord through the doorway. While the pump bubbled, Rafi called the aquarium shop and followed its instructions to keep the water moving by hand. He took turns stirring with a clean cup, watching the fish hover near the surface. At dawn, the utility crew restored service. Rafi sat on the floor beside the tank, too tired to move as the filter resumed its steady rush.

I had just opened the community fridge when the outage cut the lights, leaving dozens of donated meals behind a locked door. The temperature display vanished, and the nearest shelter was expecting dinner in an hour. I pounded on the adjoining apartment’s door until Omar answered with a headlamp. He knew the building caretaker, but the caretaker was out of town. We searched the basement for the manual key while other neighbors carried insulated bags from their kitchens. My phone battery dropped as I called the shelter and explained the delay. Omar found a ring of keys in the office, but none fit. A woman from the third floor remembered a spare tucked inside the mailbox panel. We opened the fridge and loaded the food into coolers, moving as quickly as we could without spilling. The shelter van arrived just as we sealed the last lid. I watched it pull away, hands still cold from the freezer.

Lena’s father was due home from surgery, but the apartment building’s power outage had disabled the entrance lift. He could barely stand, and the ambulance crew said they could not carry him up four flights without assistance. Lena rushed from door to door, asking neighbors to help clear the stairwell and find a sturdy chair. A delivery driver lent them a folding dolly; the retired firefighter downstairs showed everyone how to secure the straps. Lena held the stair rail, watching her father’s pale face as they lifted him one landing at a time. Each pause stretched while the crew checked his breathing. Neighbors formed a line to pass water and keep the hallway clear. At last, they reached his apartment. Lena unlocked the door with unsteady fingers, then knelt beside him, rubbing his hand while the crew connected a portable monitor. Outside, the block remained dark, but voices stayed close.

At the laundromat, I balanced my laptop on a plastic basket while the dryers thumped behind me. My nursing exam grade was due at midnight, and the hospital had given me until morning to prove I could stay in the program. The page kept refreshing without changing. I pressed my thumb into the trackpad, then stopped, afraid I would somehow break the screen. When the result finally appeared, I read the number twice, then a third time, mouthing each digit. It was two points below the cutoff. My hands went cold. I opened the appeal form, but the boxes blurred as I typed. A woman folding towels asked if I needed water. I nodded, though my eyes stayed fixed on the deadline clock and the empty field marked Explanation.

Tomas had borrowed his cousin’s phone because his own screen was cracked beyond use. On the bus home, he logged into the college portal and found his calculus grade waiting. His scholarship required a pass; without it, the rent money his mother had set aside would go toward tuition instead. He tapped the notification, then held the phone so tightly the case creaked. The grade was a D. He checked the course name, refreshed the page, and signed out before signing back in. Nothing changed. At his stop, he remained seated as the doors hissed shut. Then he hurried to the front, stumbling onto the pavement, and called his instructor. The automated message asked him to leave his name. He tried three times before he could get the words out.

I sat on the library floor between two shelves, where no one could see the screen over my shoulder. My final grade in organic chemistry would decide whether I could begin the research placement I had spent a year arranging. The portal asked for my birth date, and I entered it wrong twice. When the page opened, I scrolled past the other courses and stopped at the last line. A score of 68. I counted the points needed to reach the required 70, then opened every assignment in another tab, searching for a grading mistake. My knee bounced hard enough to knock a book loose. I caught it before it hit the floor, apologized to nobody, and wrote a careful email while the library’s closing announcement played overhead.

At seventeen, Nia had never logged in to the school portal from her father’s repair shop. She used the office computer after closing, with a stack of invoices beside the keyboard and a half-repaired radio humming softly. Her exam result would determine whether she could keep her place in the advanced program across town. The password box rejected her first attempt. She wiped her palms on her jeans and tried again, spelling each letter aloud under her breath. The grade appeared, lower than she needed. For several seconds she did not move. Then she opened the bus schedule, counted the minutes to the teacher’s office, and wrote down the route on the back of a receipt. Her father called from the workshop. She answered that she’d be right there, though she kept staring at the screen.

My apprenticeship depended on passing the licensing exam, and my supervisor had already asked twice whether the score was posted. I waited until the shared apartment was quiet, then opened the testing site on my tablet. The spinning icon seemed to take up the whole room. I refreshed once and immediately regretted it, convinced I might have erased something. When the result loaded, I leaned so close my nose nearly touched the glass. I had missed the mark by one question. The radiator clicked as I sat frozen, one sock half off my foot. I searched the site for a retake date, but the next available session was months away. I called the testing office, listened to the recorded options, and pressed zero until a person answered. My voice came out thin, but I asked about a score review.

Mateo checked his grades at the back of a crowded community center, where children were building towers from cardboard boxes. His engineering scholarship depended on keeping a certain average, and the semester’s final exam carried more weight than any other assignment. He refreshed the page, then refreshed it again, though the result had already appeared. One course sat just below the line he needed. He pulled a folded budget from his wallet and ran a finger down the column labeled tuition. The numbers blurred. When a child asked him to help with a tower, he straightened the crooked base and smiled. Then he returned to the portal and drafted a message to his professor, attaching the exam review he had saved. He checked every sentence twice before sending it.

I checked the online grade portal from the break room of the grocery store, still wearing my name badge and freezer jacket. I had taken the exam after night shifts, studying on my lunch breaks while the vending machine rattled beside me. Passing meant I could apply for the pharmacy technician position; failing meant another term of fees I had no way to cover. The page opened slowly. I clicked the grade, then gripped the edge of the table when the score appeared. It was below the required mark. My manager called my name from the aisle, but I could not make my legs move at first. I shut the laptop, opened it again, and searched the course page for instructions on review requests. A single typo in my email took five minutes to correct.

Leila sat in the back of a taxi with her infant asleep against her shoulder, refreshing the university page whenever traffic stopped. Her exam grade would determine whether she could return to clinical placement next month. She had arranged childcare, borrowed a uniform, and promised her mother that this final hurdle was manageable. The result appeared while the taxi waited at a red light. She read it once, then looked away and read it again. The score was short by three points. Her breath caught against the baby’s blanket. She asked the driver to pull over, then opened the instructor’s contact page with one shaking hand. The baby stirred as she typed a message asking to review the marked paper. Leila added her student number, erased the message, and began again.

My scholarship portal showed a warning banner before I even reached the exam results. I was sitting in a laundromat with a basket of uniforms at my feet, trying to keep my laptop balanced on one knee. The scholarship paid for my dorm room, and the grade I was about to see could decide whether I had a bed next term. I clicked the course tab. The score loaded, disappeared, and came back after I refreshed. It was lower than the minimum. My throat tightened, and I folded the laundry one shirt at a time, making each edge exact while I tried to think. Then I found the academic advising number and called. When the receptionist answered, I had to read my student ID from the screen because my hands would not stay still.

Sanjay opened the exam portal in the computer lab after everyone else had left. His parents believed he had passed the entrance course, and he had told them the result would be fine. The screen asked him to confirm his identity; he mistyped his address, then rubbed his eyes and started over. His grade appeared beside the course title, far below the score he needed to continue in the program. He stared at the number until the lab lights clicked off automatically. In the dimness, he found the retake policy and read it line by line. A deadline was less than a day away. He switched the lights back on, filled out the form, and attached a copy of his practice exams. Before submitting, he called home, listening to the phone ring with the application still open.

I was in the passenger seat outside my father’s dialysis clinic, refreshing the college portal while he finished his appointment. I had promised him I would keep my place in the biology program, because he had already taken extra shifts to help with my fees. The exam grade arrived between two notifications from the pharmacy. I opened it and felt my fingers go numb around the phone. The score was just under the cutoff. I checked the calculation, adding every assignment on a scrap of paper, then did it again in the margin. When my father came out, he asked how school was going. I said I was waiting on one answer. At home, I found the professor’s office hours and set an alarm, then kept the grade page open beside it all night.

At the hostel desk, Amara borrowed a charger and logged into the exam system on her laptop. Her visa renewal required proof that she remained enrolled, and a passing grade was necessary to keep her place in the course. The page took so long to load that the clerk asked whether the internet had failed. Amara shook her head, though her eyes stayed on the progress bar. When the result appeared, she read it aloud by mistake, then covered her mouth. She had missed the pass mark by a narrow margin. The clerk slid a glass of water across the counter.
