Luis looked at the rain and let his toolbox thump against the bench.

I was wearing my new white trainers because I had planned to walk into the office looking presentable. By the time I reached the bus stop, the rain had turned the pavement into a shallow, grimy stream. I stood beneath the shelter with one foot on the bench rail, trying to keep the shoes clean, while the arrival board scrolled through a series of apologies. A man beside me complained that nobody could run a schedule anymore. I gave him a tight nod, then checked the board again, as if staring harder might improve its manners. The bus came at last, full of passengers and fogged windows. It stopped, opened its doors, and announced that it was out of service. I lowered my foot into the puddle, looked at the spreading brown stain, and began searching for a taxi with one finger stabbing at my phone.

Nadia had just finished an overnight hospital shift when she reached the bus stop in the rain. Her scrubs were damp at the shoulders, and her eyelids felt heavy enough to pull her face down. The timetable claimed a bus every twelve minutes, but she had watched three intervals pass without seeing one. A man nearby kept pacing from the bench to the curb, stepping around the same puddle each time. Nadia checked the time, put her phone away, and rubbed the bridge of her nose. When a bus finally appeared, its destination sign showed the wrong route. She raised her hand anyway, hoping the driver might understand. It slowed, then continued past. Nadia stood very still for a moment, water dripping from her hair, before she kicked a pebble into the gutter and asked the gray morning what else it had planned.

I had promised my daughter I would be at her school assembly, and the bus stop was the last obstacle between me and the quickest route there. Rain soaked the sleeve holding my umbrella, while the other hand gripped her handmade paper medal. The bus app announced a delay, then cheerfully asked me to rate my journey. I tapped the screen harder than necessary and nearly dropped the medal. A cyclist swerved around a puddle and sprayed water across the timetable. I wiped it with my scarf, although the printed times had already blurred. When my daughter called to ask where I was, I told her I was coming, keeping my voice bright. Then I turned toward the empty road and whispered a string of complaints to the passing rain. The bus arrived at last, packed shoulder to shoulder.

Elliot stood at the stop outside the hardware store, holding a long wooden shelf under one arm. The rain kept sliding down the plastic wrapping, and the bus that could carry the awkward parcel was late. He had checked the route online, called the store, and read the posted schedule twice; none of it had changed the situation. A drop ran off the shelf and down his neck. Elliot shifted his grip, nearly clipped a passing umbrella, and apologized with a clipped little nod. The person under it moved away without replying. He watched the road, jaw set, while the digital sign restarted and displayed the same delay notice. At last the bus pulled in, but its front seats were crowded with luggage. Elliot looked at the shelf, then at the driver, and asked whether the next bus might have room for a passenger and half a tree.

I was waiting for the bus with a violin case tucked between my knees, trying to shield it from the slanting rain. My music lesson had ended late, and the next one began in less than an hour. Every few minutes I checked the road, then the clock, then the road again. A puddle expanded around the shelter post until it touched my shoes. I moved my case to the bench, but a gust blew rain straight beneath the roof. The arrival sign went blank. I pressed its button, and it came back showing “Service information unavailable.” My laugh startled a pigeon from the gutter. When a bus finally appeared, I waved both arms; it stopped, but the driver said this route was being rerouted and he could not take me there. I thanked him with exaggerated politeness, then sat down beside my damp case.

At dawn, Marta waited at a rural bus stop with a thermos tucked beneath her arm. Rain drummed on the shelter’s tin roof, drowning out the faint radio in the nearby shop. The bus was supposed to connect her to the train, and the train would take her to her first day at a new job. She had allowed plenty of time; the timetable had apparently allowed none. A tractor rolled by, showering the verge. Marta wiped mud from her cheek with the back of her hand and checked the road once more. The shopkeeper came out to say the bus sometimes skipped the stop when it was running late. Marta stared at him, then at the sign bearing the route number. She set her thermos down very carefully and asked, through clenched teeth, what the sign was for if not for the bus.

I signed the lease for a sunlit studio, which turned out to mean one narrow window facing a brick wall. By noon, three boxes had split, the elevator had stalled between floors, and my landlord was explaining that the water shutoff was “probably temporary.” I set a saucepan beneath the kitchen pipe and watched each drop land with the precision of a metronome. When the delivery crew called to say they were downstairs, I took the stairs, reached the lobby, and found them waiting beside a truck that had been ticketed. I pressed my lips together while the driver handed me the citation as if I had ordered it. Back upstairs, I unwrapped my only mug, filled it from a bottle, and sat on an unopened box. The wall outside my window offered no view at all, but at least it stayed quiet.

At sixty-eight, Marisol had moved into the apartment above a bakery, expecting the smell of bread to be a daily luxury. Instead, she discovered that the bedroom radiator clanked like a loose toolbox, and the building’s buzzer had no label for her unit. Her nephew carried in the final bookcase while she held the door open with one foot and called the superintendent for the fourth time. The call went to voicemail again. She stared at the phone, tapped the screen twice, then tucked it into her apron pocket with a sharp little motion. A delivery person rang every other apartment before guessing hers. Marisol welcomed the boxes, thanked him, and then spent twenty minutes searching for the screws packed in a carton marked “linens.” When the radiator began its nightly banging, she opened a cookbook and read aloud over it, as though the appliance might eventually learn some manners.

I had planned the move around my nursing shifts, so by the time I hauled my last suitcase into the new apartment, I had been awake for nearly a day. The key turned halfway and stopped. I leaned my shoulder into the door; it sprang open so suddenly that my suitcase rolled down the hall and struck a stack of mail. The apartment smelled of fresh paint, except the bathroom smelled unmistakably of wet socks. I called the property manager, who told me to “give it a few days.” My eyebrows climbed before I could stop them. I placed a towel under the sink, found a dead moth in the bathtub, and tried to assemble a chair with instructions printed in six languages, none of them useful. At midnight, I sat on the floor eating crackers from the box they came in. The chair remained in pieces, arranged like a small wooden accusation.

Darius had spent months saving for his first place, so the apartment’s crooked blinds seemed like a minor detail—until he tried to close them and the whole rail came down. He stood beneath the dangling slats, drill in hand, while his cousin waited with a box of kitchen supplies. The building manager had promised to send maintenance “sometime today,” a phrase Darius had now heard three times. He called again, listened to the hold music, and began sorting utensils with exaggerated care. When a neighbor knocked to ask if the hammering could stop, Darius looked at the half-mounted rail and then at the unopened tool case. He told her he was done for the evening, though he had not started. They both paused in the doorway, surrounded by cartons. After she left, he lowered the blinds gently onto the floor and hung a bedsheet over the window instead.

My new apartment was advertised as pet-friendly, a detail I had checked twice before bringing Juniper, my elderly cat. At the front desk, the building clerk insisted there was no record of my move-in appointment, though I had the email open in front of her. I held my phone out until the screen dimmed, then tapped it awake and held it up again. Juniper meowed from her carrier as a line formed behind me. At last, the clerk found the paperwork under the previous tenant’s name and handed me a key that opened the storage closet, not my door. I tested it once, then again, with a slow breath through my nose. Upstairs, I discovered the elevator had stopped on the lobby level. I carried Juniper and two bags up four flights, paused on each landing, and promised her that the new place would be calmer. She blinked at me as if she reserved judgment.

At twenty-two, Zola thought moving into a downtown apartment would make her feel grown-up. The first evening offered a different lesson: the kitchen cabinet doors hung crooked, the internet technician missed his appointment, and a neighbor’s bass line traveled through the wall with remarkable clarity. Zola arranged her plants on the windowsill, only to find that the radiator underneath ran hot enough to wilt the nearest leaves. She shifted each pot to the coffee table, then moved the table away from the only outlet. Her phone buzzed with a message from the landlord asking whether everything was satisfactory. She typed a reply, erased it, and finally sent a photo of the cabinet door resting on the counter. No answer came. Zola folded a blanket over a cardboard box and used it as a seat, listening to the music pulse through the wall while she ate noodles balanced on her knees.

I chose the apartment because it was close to the train station and had a little balcony for my herbs. On moving day, the train schedule changed, the balcony door jammed, and the delivery company left my mattress at the wrong building. I stood on the pavement with a basil plant under one arm, reading their confirmation email for the fifth time. The address was correct. Their driver had simply followed the map pin across the avenue. When I went upstairs to call, the stairwell light clicked off before I reached the landing. I climbed the last flight by phone glow, muttering the apartment number under my breath. The dispatcher apologized and promised a redelivery window that covered the entire afternoon. I put the basil on the kitchen counter, sat on the floor, and ate a sandwich from its wrapper. Outside, the balcony door refused to budge, guarding an empty little patch of concrete.

Eli had moved from a rural town to a crowded apartment block for a new job, and he expected the adjustment to take time. He did not expect the laundry room to require an app that rejected his payment card, or the elevator to announce every floor in a voice loud enough to wake the building. He stood beside his washer, phone held out, while the screen instructed him to “try again.” After the sixth attempt, he lowered the phone and stared at the machine as if it had personally chosen this arrangement. A woman carrying a basket showed him how to reset the app, then left before he could ask about the missing detergent shelf. In his apartment, he unpacked a box labeled “essentials” and found only a desk lamp and winter scarves. He placed the lamp on the floor, plugged it in, and ate cereal from a measuring cup beneath its bare bulb.

I moved into the apartment with my toddler, Niko, and a carefully labeled set of boxes. By lunchtime, the labels had become suggestions. The carton marked “bedroom” held mixing bowls, while the one marked “bathroom” contained every sock I owned. Niko discovered the doorstop, removed it, and watched the door swing shut on my fingers. I pressed my hand to my chest and counted slowly while he offered me a toy truck as an apology. Then the building’s fire alarm chirped every forty seconds. I called the office, where someone asked whether I had tried changing the battery. I looked at the ceiling, then at the ladder still folded in the hallway. “It’s a hardwired alarm,” I said, carefully and very clearly. There was a pause. Niko began pushing his truck across a box, making its wheels click in time with the chirp.

Priya arrived at her new apartment with two suitcases, a houseplant, and a plan to unpack before her evening shift. The front door opened onto a stack of someone else’s discarded furniture, and her key barely fit the lock. She called the leasing office; the agent cheerfully explained that the previous tenant had left “a few things.” Priya looked at the sagging armchair blocking half the entry and asked whether “a few” included a broken lamp, three paint cans, and a bag of mystery cables. The agent said maintenance could come tomorrow. Priya set her plant on the stair landing, rolled up her sleeves, and dragged the chair against the wall, stopping to wipe her palms on her jeans. Then she found that the refrigerator was unplugged and warm. She closed its door with two fingers, took a picture, and sent it to the office. Her unpacking plan became a list of phone calls.

I had pictured moving into my new apartment as a fresh start, preferably one involving coffee on the balcony. Instead, the balcony was locked, the coffee maker was buried, and the hallway smelled of varnish strong enough to make my eyes water. I found the maintenance number taped inside a cupboard and called it. A recorded message thanked me for my patience before asking me to leave a message. I hung up, called again, and listened to the same sentence with my jaw clenched. My neighbor lent me a mug and pointed out the shared laundry room, where a handwritten sign announced that the machines were “temporarily unavailable.” I thanked her, then carried my boxes back upstairs one at a time. In the kitchen, I found the coffee maker beneath a bundle of curtain rods. I made instant coffee instead and drank it beside the locked balcony door.

After years of traveling for work, Kenji finally rented an apartment near his daughter’s school. He arrived with a single vanload and assumed the move would take an hour. The loading zone was occupied by a delivery truck, the elevator was reserved for another tenant, and the building’s front entrance required a code nobody had sent him. He waited on the curb with a lamp balanced on his knee while the driver checked his phone. When the code finally arrived, it opened the garage gate but not the lobby door. Kenji tried it twice, then folded the paper with the number into a tiny square and tucked it into his pocket. His daughter came out of the van and asked if they could eat. He glanced at the towers of boxes visible through the glass. “Absolutely,” he said, then went to find the nearest restaurant, carrying the lamp like an oversized candle.

I had rehearsed my presentation on the water cycle so often that even the dog left the room when I began. At school, the projector refused to recognize my laptop, and my first slide appeared sideways. I rotated it; the next slide vanished. Behind me, someone tapped a pencil in a steady little rhythm. “Just speak without it,” Ms. Chen suggested, as if I had not spent three evenings making diagrams. I pinched the bridge of my nose, then pulled my notes from my folder. Half the pages were stuck together from the juice carton that had leaked in my bag. The bell rang before I reached condensation. I looked at the blank screen, took one long breath, and started drawing clouds on the board with a squeaky marker.

At twelve, Malik had built a model volcano from papier-mâché and painted its ridges with careful stripes. The morning of his presentation, the class pet hamster escaped and chose the volcano as a tunnel. Malik watched its nose poke through the crater while his classmates leaned closer. He scooped it up, set it safely in its cage, and tried to smooth the torn paper with one thumb. “It’s an active volcano now,” someone said. Malik’s jaw tightened. His cue cards slid from his desk, scattering beneath three pairs of shoes. He collected them without answering, then found his place by the red smudge on his palm. When he began explaining pressure and magma, he pointed at the chewed crater and used it as his opening example.

I practiced my presentation about my grandmother’s bakery in the kitchen, where the smell of cinnamon made every sentence easier. At school, the printer had cut off the bottom half of every photograph. I held up a page showing only the ceiling of her shop and heard a few snorts from the back row. “The pastries are just below the frame,” I said, too sharply. My teacher raised her eyebrows, so I pressed my lips together and shuffled to the next page. The clicker skipped three slides, then returned to the bakery sign. I could feel heat creeping up my neck. Instead of fighting the machine again, I put it down and described the ovens, the flour on Grandma’s sleeves, and how she let me shape the first loaf.

For her presentation on city birds, Priya had arranged photographs in neat order and labeled each one with its species. Then the classroom computer updated itself, freezing on a spinning circle while the clock hand crept toward her turn. She folded and unfolded the corner of her note card until it softened. “Technology is giving your birds a long migration,” her partner whispered. Priya gave him a look, then gathered her photographs from the desk. When the screen finally woke, the slideshow had scrambled the captions, placing “pigeon” beneath a hawk. She closed the laptop with a firm click. With the pictures held up by hand, she explained how to spot the difference by wing shape and flight. Her voice steadied as the class began asking questions.

I was ready to explain how bridges distribute weight, down to the last diagram. My model, made from craft sticks, had survived a week on my bedroom shelf and the bus ride to school. It collapsed when I set it on the presentation table. One leg skittered beneath the radiator. I stared at the loose sticks, then at the audience already waiting. “The bridge has demonstrated a design flaw,” I said, hearing the brittle edge in my own voice. I bent to retrieve the missing leg and bumped my head on the table. A couple of students laughed. My ears burned, but I stacked the pieces in front of me and used them to show where the load had shifted. The ruined model became the most convincing part of my talk.

At fourteen, Jun planned to present a family recipe from his father’s Korean restaurant. He had translated each ingredient and practiced saying the unfamiliar terms slowly. Just before class, a classmate spilled water across his handwritten cards. Jun lifted them one by one, watching the ink run into blue clouds. “You can use the slides,” his teacher said, pointing to the screen, but the slides contained only photographs. He rubbed his damp fingertips together and stared at the first image. The room’s chatter pressed against his ears. Jun set the ruined cards aside and described the recipe from memory, beginning with the sizzling garlic and ending with the rice his father always tasted twice. When he forgot a measurement, he admitted it and explained how cooks adjust by smell.

My presentation about the school garden was supposed to include a seedling I had grown at home. I carried it in a yogurt cup all morning, guarding it from elbows and backpack zippers. When my turn came, I lifted the cup and found the plant bent nearly flat. Someone had crushed the lid against it in my bag. I pinched the bridge of my nose and looked at the carefully printed chart behind me. “This is what happens when seedlings travel without proper protection,” I said, though my voice sounded like a snapped twig. The class leaned forward. I showed them the damaged stem and explained how we could build sturdier covers for the garden beds. By the end, three students were offering ideas, and I forgot to be angry at the cup.

Evelyn had prepared a presentation about the moon, complete with phases painted on black poster board. Her little brother had helped carry it to school, where the corner caught in the bus door and folded backward. She tried flattening it under a dictionary during homeroom, but the crease remained like a crooked horizon. When she stood before the class, the board kept sliding off the easel. Evelyn shoved it back into place and held it with one hand. “Gravity is making a guest appearance,” she muttered. A few classmates chuckled. She pointed to the painted phases with her free hand, explaining why the moon seemed to change shape. Each time the board tipped, she caught it without pausing. At the end, her teacher offered to mend the poster, but Evelyn asked to keep the crease as a reminder.

I spent Sunday recording interviews for my presentation on neighborhood history, and I had trimmed each clip to fit the time limit. At school, the speakers produced a loud buzz instead of my grandfather’s voice. I unplugged the cable, plugged it back in, and watched the same red light blink at me. My fingers drummed against the podium. “Maybe the microphone has a story of its own,” I said, not quite smiling. The teacher offered another cable, but the file still would not play. I looked at my notes and realized I remembered most of the interview. So I told the class how Grandpa described the old train station, imitating its whistle and the clatter of luggage. The broken speakers stayed silent while everyone listened.

Nadia’s presentation on recycling was organized into six bright slides, each with a statistic and a photograph. The classroom tablet, however, had been left at two percent battery. It shut down after the title appeared. She stared at the black screen, then held the power button until her thumb hurt. “That’s plenty,” she said when a classmate suggested borrowing a charger from the office. Her shoulders had climbed almost to her ears. Nadia took a marker and wrote three numbers on the whiteboard from memory. She explained what each figure meant, then asked the class to guess how long a plastic bottle lasted in a landfill. Hands rose across the room. By the time the tablet was plugged in, she had already made her point without a single slide.

I chose astronomy for my presentation because I loved explaining how stars were born. I also chose a glittery display board, which turned out to shed silver dust onto my sweater, my notes, and the classroom floor. When I tried to brush it away, the glitter spread farther, sparkling on my palms. My partner whispered that I looked like a comet. I gave him a narrow stare and moved to the front before I said something unhelpful. The projector displayed my star chart with half the labels cut off. I pointed to the bright dots and described their life cycles, pausing when a speck of glitter slid into my eye. The class waited while I blinked it clear. Then I carried on, using the accidental sparkle to explain how stars scatter elements.

At ten, Mateo was presenting a report on sea turtles when the classroom fish tank began gurgling loudly. His first sentence disappeared beneath the filter’s rattling, so he stopped and waited. The noise stopped too. He started again; the tank resumed its racket. Mateo’s hands curled around his note cards. “Could the fish have a turn after me?” he asked, his voice tight. The teacher switched off the filter, and the room fell quiet enough for everyone to hear the clock. Mateo glanced at his cards, which had the same opening sentence written twice because he had copied it by mistake. He crossed one out with a quick stroke and continued. He explained how turtles mistake floating plastic for food, then ended by asking the class to bring reusable bottles on the field trip.

I had planned to demonstrate how a simple electric circuit worked, using a battery, wires, and a tiny bulb. The bulb stayed dark no matter how carefully I connected the clips. I checked the battery, switched the wires, and pressed the clips so hard my fingertips turned white. Around the room, chairs creaked as everyone waited. “The electricity is taking a personal day,” I muttered. My teacher suggested that I explain the diagram instead. I nearly snapped that the diagram was not the point, but swallowed the words and turned the paper around. Then I spotted the loose wire, its metal end hidden beneath a strip of tape. I fixed it, and the bulb flashed on. A small cheer rose from the class, while I let my shoulders drop and began the explanation.

By ten o’clock, I had explained the difference between my chili oil and my sesame oil so many times that I began pointing instead of speaking. A customer tapped the same jar, asked what was in it, then frowned when I answered. Behind him, the queue stretched past the lantern seller, while my burner sputtered like it had a personal grudge. I turned the flame knob, wiped my hands on my apron, and found another order ticket stuck to my elbow. “One bowl, no noodles,” someone called, though noodles were the only thing I had left ready. I stared at the ticket, then at the customer, and let my ladle rest against the pot with a clank. My sister took over the serving window. I stepped out back, counted slowly to five, and returned before the broth boiled over.

Mina had arranged her dumplings in neat rows, each pleat facing the same way, until a gust flipped her handwritten menu onto the wet pavement. She retrieved it with two fingers, watched the ink blur, and set it beside the cash tin. A man leaned over the counter to ask whether the dumplings were steamed. She pointed to the cloud rising from the bamboo baskets. He asked again, louder, while a delivery scooter blocked her stall and its rider insisted he had the right address. Mina pressed her lips together and kept folding dough, though one dumpling came out shaped like a little boot. When the scooter finally moved, she pinned the soggy menu beneath a jar of pickled radish. The man ordered two portions. She gave him three, then made him pay for all three.

I have cooked fish cakes at this market every Friday for eleven years, and every Friday the power cord gets kicked loose by somebody carrying a crate. Tonight it happened while I was turning a full batch. The griddle went dark, the cakes sagged, and a customer asked whether they came that way. I crouched beneath the counter, bumped my head on the shelf, and found the plug tangled with my extension reel. When I stood, my knee nudged the sauce bottles into a wobbling row. “Nobody touch anything,” I said, louder than I meant to. A boy froze with his hand over the chili flakes. I plugged everything back in, scraped the ruined cakes into a bowl, and started again. Then I taped the cord to the ground with a strip of bright yellow tape, wide enough for even the most distracted feet to notice.

Arun’s stall sold sweet rice cakes, and he had spent the afternoon shaping them into crescents for the moon festival. A gust of smoke from the neighboring grill settled over the display, leaving every pale surface gray. He fanned the cakes with a menu, which only scattered flour across his cash box. A customer asked for the pink ones, although Arun had already explained that the color came from beetroot and not strawberry. He watched her point at the same tray again. “Pink,” she said. Arun picked up a cake, held it out, and waited while she reconsidered, then chose a yellow one. He set the pink cake down with care that made his knuckles stand out. At closing, he scrubbed the smoke from the trays while his cousin laughed at the floury coins. Arun handed him the brush and went to fetch fresh water.

I set up my noodle stall beside the market’s loudest drum troupe, which seemed like a good idea until the first performance began. Each time I called an order number, the drums swallowed it. Customers drifted away, then came back claiming they had been skipped. I held up bowls like signs and started writing numbers on paper plates, but the wind lifted them into the crowd. A woman waved a receipt at me while I was draining noodles, and the colander slipped, splashing hot water across my shoe. I bit down on the inside of my cheek, fetched a towel, and looked at the drummer nearest my counter. He grinned and struck a cymbal. “Could you move one stall over?” I asked. He pointed at the packed lane. I tied my order slips to a string across the counter and served whoever could find their number.

Leila ran a tiny stall selling stuffed peppers, with just enough room for one burner and a crate of ingredients. A group of tourists clustered around it, blocking the narrow lane while debating which pepper looked most photogenic. She reached for the tongs three times and found someone’s phone in the way each time. A pepper began to char. Leila snatched it from the pan, blew on her fingertips, and told the group that the food was for eating, not arranging. They asked her to hold the plate beneath a lantern for a picture. She set it down on the counter, then turned to the next customer without waiting for a reply. By the time the group moved aside, her apron was streaked with oil and the next batch needed turning. She took one deep breath, rotated every pepper at once, and kept her eyes on the pan.

I sell fried plantain from a cart with one wheel that always jams when the lane gets crowded. Tonight, the wheel locked just as a vendor carrying baskets came through. He sighed at me; I sighed back, and neither of us moved. My oil was hot, my queue was growing, and a child had begun chanting that he wanted the crispy pieces. I leaned into the cart until the wheel lurched free, sending my stack of paper trays sliding onto the ground. “Excellent,” I muttered, scooping them up one by one. The child stopped chanting long enough to ask if they were clean. I gave him a fresh tray and raised my eyebrows. Then I wedged a wooden chopstick beneath the stubborn wheel, tied the cart to a post, and served the remaining plantain without moving it an inch.

Sofia’s tiny stall served lentil fritters, and the batter had behaved perfectly until a customer asked for a dozen made without lentils. Sofia looked at the bowl, then at the man, as if a hidden alternative might appear. He repeated the request while she flipped a fritter. She laid down the spatula, wiped her palms on her apron, and explained that lentils were the main ingredient. He asked whether she could remove them after cooking. The line behind him shifted and someone’s shopping bag brushed her stack of napkins onto the floor. Sofia bent to retrieve them, stood, and found the man still waiting. She pointed to the sign that listed the ingredients in large letters. He finally ordered a portion. As she dropped the fritters into the paper cone, she folded the top twice and handed it over without another word.

I thought selling soup at a night market would be peaceful. Then the rain started, and my stall’s plastic roof collected water directly above the serving window. Every few minutes, a cold stream dumped onto my shoulder. I shifted the soup pot, moved the bowls, and finally propped a broom against the roof. A customer ducked under it and knocked the handle loose. Water poured over my menu, turning “pumpkin” into a brown blur. I pushed my wet hair back, pointed at the pot, and announced the choices from memory. Someone asked if I had chicken soup. “I have pumpkin,” I said, tapping the menu with one damp finger. My friend brought a tarp from her stall, but it was too short. We tied it to a lantern pole and accepted that one corner would keep dripping. I served soup with my shoulder tilted away from the leak.

Darius sold grilled corn from a stall at the far end of the market, where the crowd thinned whenever a parade passed. He had just loaded the grill when a parade marshal told him to shift his table two meters to the left. Darius lifted the table, the coal bucket, and his water jug in separate trips, only to learn the new spot was reserved for a fortune-teller who had not arrived. He set everything down carefully, then looked at the marshal’s clipboard. The marshal pointed to a different square. Darius rubbed the bridge of his nose and asked whether the market had a map showing where he was allowed to exist. Nobody answered. He pushed the table back to its first position, lit the coals, and began brushing butter over the corn. When the marshal returned, Darius handed him a cob and asked him to decide where the next bite should be cooked.

I serve tiny cups of ginger tea from a stall wedged between two music shops. A speaker from one shop played a song so loudly that I could not hear my kettle whistle. The first batch boiled dry while I was taking payment. I lifted the lid, saw the scorched ginger, and shut my eyes for one second. Then a customer asked if the tea was meant to smell burned. I poured it out and started over, measuring each slice as if the ginger might try to escape. The speaker’s owner leaned over to ask whether I could lower my voice when calling orders. I stared at him, then at the kettle, whose whistle was now shrill enough to cut through the music. “That’s the only thing either of us can hear,” I said. He turned the volume down. I poured fresh tea into paper cups and placed the scorched batch where he could smell it.

Nadia’s stall sold little savory pancakes, and her spatula had vanished just before the dinner rush. She checked beneath the counter, behind the gas canister, and inside the flour tub, finding only a damp receipt and a plastic fork. Customers waited while she tried turning pancakes with a serving spoon. The first folded in half; the second landed on the burner’s edge. Nadia stared at the pan, shoulders lifted toward her ears. A neighboring vendor offered a pair of tongs, but they were so large that they crushed the delicate batter. She returned them and used two chopsticks instead, working with painstaking care. When her missing spatula finally appeared in a customer’s tote bag—he had picked it up by mistake—Nadia held out her hand without smiling. He apologized. She accepted the tool, scraped the pan clean, and asked the next person in line what they wanted.

At 7:12, I peeled off my gloves and found the last discharge form still waiting beneath a paper cup of cold coffee. The printer blinked its familiar red light. I pressed the button once, then again, slower, as if the machine might respond to manners. Behind me, a call bell rang from a room that had just been checked. I shut my eyes for one breath. My feet throbbed inside my shoes, and the bridge of my nose bore the dent of my mask. When the printer finally spat out three blank pages, I let them drift to the floor. The day nurse stepped in, bright and brisk, asking whether anything needed attention. I handed over the chart, pointed to the bell, and said, “The printer has opinions.” Then I gathered my lunch bag and walked toward the exit before another task could appear.

Marisol had worked through a midnight admission, two confused patients, and a leak beneath the medication-room sink. At shift change, she tucked her stethoscope into her bag and discovered that the staff elevator had stopped between floors. The display showed a cheerful little arrow pointing nowhere. She pressed the call button. Nothing. A passing custodian suggested taking the stairs, though her locker was on the level below and her knees had begun to complain. Marisol stared at him until he stopped smiling. Then she took the stairs, one careful step at a time, carrying a thermos that sloshed against her hip. On the ground floor, the elevator doors opened as if nothing had happened. She gave it a flat glance, pushed through the exit, and let the cold morning air meet her face.

I was supposed to be home before sunrise, but the night seemed to stretch every time someone said, “Just one more thing.” At 6:50, a family member wanted the same update I had given twice, and the unit phone rang while I was explaining it. I held up one finger, answered, listened to a request for a number written on the wall, and pointed at the sign beside the phone. My jaw clicked when I finally unclenched it. The incoming nurse arrived with a notebook and a cheerful greeting. I began report, only to be interrupted by a missing chart. I tapped the empty counter with my pen, then stopped myself before the tapping became a drum solo. We found the chart under a stack of blankets. I gave the final details, signed out, and left without checking my phone.

Devon’s night had been mostly quiet until a delivery truck blocked the staff parking lot exit at dawn. He had finished his rounds, documented the final notes, and changed out of his hospital shoes, but the truck’s driver had vanished. Devon stood beside his small hatchback, still wearing his badge, and watched daylight brighten the windshield. He called security. They asked him to wait near the vehicle, then called back to ask which vehicle. He described it in three clipped sentences. A nurse from the next shift offered to drive him around the truck, but the narrow lane was crowded with carts. Devon set his bag down and rubbed the crease across his forehead. When the driver finally appeared carrying pastries, Devon accepted none. He backed out after the truck moved, waving once without turning his head.

My last hour included a bed alarm that sounded whenever its patient sneezed, a medication label printed sideways, and a supply cart stocked with everything except the gauze I needed. I checked the cart twice, then opened the cupboard and found gauze stacked directly in front of me. For a moment I just stood there, one hand on the door, listening to the alarm begin again. My shoulders had crept up near my ears. I lowered them and went back to the room. At handoff, I explained the patient’s plan, the odd alarm, and the missing-looking supplies. The next nurse asked whether I had tried switching the alarm off and on. I gave the control panel a long look. “Several times,” I said, keeping my voice level by sheer concentration. Then I hung my badge in my locker and stepped into the pale morning.

Ruth had spent the overnight shift caring for a restless toddler and his exhausted father in a crowded pediatric ward. As she prepared to leave, the unit printer produced a page listing every medication twice. She carried it to the desk, where someone suggested restarting the machine. Ruth turned it off, counted to ten, and turned it back on. The same page emerged. A new nurse leaned over her shoulder to offer a theory about the paper tray. Ruth folded the sheet into a neat square and placed it beside the keyboard. Her temples pulsed beneath her cap, and she could feel the seam of her socks against her toes. She completed the handoff, washed her hands, and collected her coat. Outside, a bus pulled away just as she reached the stop. She sat on the bench and watched the empty street.

When my shift ended, the locker-room faucet began spraying water sideways, soaking the sleeve of my clean shirt. I twisted the handle shut, but it squealed and kept dripping. After twelve hours of alarms, questions, and one very determined vending machine that had swallowed my coins, that little metallic squeak landed like a personal insult. I pulled the handle harder. A coworker called from the corridor that maintenance had been notified. “Wonderful,” I said, though nobody was close enough to hear the dry edge in my voice. I changed into my damp jacket, stuffed my uniform into a bag, and checked that I had my keys. At the entrance, the automatic doors opened halfway, paused, then shut. I stepped back, waited, and tried again with both hands visible, as if negotiating with a stubborn animal.

Elias finished his night shift at a rural clinic with a headache and a stack of unsigned forms. The fax machine had jammed during the final report, and the morning courier was already waiting at the front desk. He opened the tray, removed a curled page, and found the next sheet torn in half. The courier checked his watch. Elias looked at the clock, then at the machine, then at the courier’s polished shoes. “You can leave the envelope here,” he said, carefully smoothing the surviving pages. The courier asked whether the forms were complete. Elias set the pen down with deliberate precision and began checking each line again. When he finally signed the last one, he handed over the envelope and rubbed the pale band where his watch had been. His ride home was idling outside, and the driver had sent three messages.

I had promised myself I would leave on time, a modest ambition that lasted until a patient’s hearing aid disappeared beneath the bed. We searched with a flashlight, then moved the bed, then found it caught in the wheel. By then the incoming nurse was waiting for report while the patient wanted to know whether breakfast had arrived. I checked the clock and pressed my lips together. The breakfast cart was still on another floor. I explained this, finished the handoff, and reached the staff entrance with my coat over one arm. My phone showed a message from my sister asking if I could pick up her son. I typed that I was just leaving, deleted it, and typed it again. The screen dimmed before I could send. I stood there, thumb hovering, while the doors hummed open and closed.

Nadia’s overnight shift at the city hospital ended with a burst pipe in the staff washroom. Water crept toward the lockers in a shiny, determined line. She lifted her shoes onto a bench and called facilities, only to be asked whether the leak was near a sink. Nadia looked at the ceiling, where a dark patch was widening. “It is coming from above,” she said, slowly enough to make each word distinct. The person on the phone promised to send someone. Nadia gathered her things, stepped around the puddle, and found that her locker key had slipped into the water. She fished it out with a paper towel and wiped it clean. At the entrance, a colleague asked how the night had gone. Nadia held up the wet key. “The building wanted a handoff too,” she replied, and kept walking.

The unit was finally quiet when I sat down to finish my notes, but the computer demanded a password change. It rejected the new password, then rejected the old one, then locked me out for a minute. I watched the timer count down while my tea went cold beside the keyboard. Across the room, a monitor beeped once; the patient was asleep, and the reading settled immediately. I rolled my neck until it cracked. When the screen unlocked, I entered the notes with both hands poised above the keys, careful not to hit anything twice. At handoff, I told the day nurse where I had left the chart and which call light was temperamental. She asked if I could stay to help with a fresh admission. I looked at my empty coffee cup, then at the clock. “I’ve signed out,” I said, and picked up my coat.

Graham had spent the night in a rehabilitation ward, helping patients through restless hours and answering the same question about the morning schedule. At shift change, he discovered that someone had parked a wheelchair in front of his locker. He moved it aside and found a second chair behind it, then a laundry hamper blocking the narrow aisle. His lunch bag sat just beyond the obstacle course. He stared at the arrangement, one hand resting on the locker door, while the clock ticked toward eight. A cleaner appeared and asked whether the chairs belonged there. Graham pushed the hamper against the wall and said, “They seem to have settled in.” He retrieved his bag, changed his shoes, and checked that his badge was off. In the parking lot, his car was coated in fresh pollen. He wiped a small circle on the windshield and drove away.

I had labeled every box in the attic before we started: KEEP, DONATE, and TOSS, each in fat black marker. My brother Eli opened one and began reading every postcard aloud, including the ones from people neither of us remembered. I pressed the tape dispenser against my knee and waited. He held up a cracked mug. “This was Dad’s favorite.” Dad had owned six identical mugs, and this one had a chipped handle. I put it in TOSS. Eli slid it into KEEP while I was reaching for the next box. The label peeled off under my thumb. By the time we found the winter coats, my marker had dried out, the stairs were blocked, and Eli was trying to rescue a moth-eaten scarf. I set down the box, took the mug back out, and placed it carefully on top of the pile. “There,” I said. “You can dust it forever.”

Marisol climbed into the attic with a clipboard and a plan to finish before her lunch shift. Her younger brother Theo had brought no boxes, only a magnifying glass and a theory that every object might be valuable. He spent ten minutes inspecting a bent curtain rod while Marisol sorted a box of school papers. When she asked him to carry the papers downstairs, he picked up the wrong stack and scattered them across the floorboards. Marisol shut her eyes as dust drifted onto her eyelashes. “Could you follow one instruction without starting a museum exhibit?” she asked. Theo frowned at a report card. The attic fan squeaked overhead, repeating the same short shriek. Marisol gathered the papers into a grocery bag, then found Theo had labeled it “Important.” She peeled off the label, handed him the empty carton, and pointed firmly toward the stairs.

My sister Bea promised we’d be done by noon, which was bold considering she kept stopping to photograph everything. We were sorting the attic boxes at our aunt’s farmhouse, and every third object became a “memory worth documenting.” She aimed her phone at a tangled lamp cord while I balanced a box on my hip. A stack of old magazines slid off the shelf and landed around my boots. Bea lowered her phone. “Don’t move; this looks authentic.” I stared at her until she put the camera away. Then she asked whether we should keep a broken snow globe because it had a tiny horse inside. I pinched the bridge of my nose, set the box down, and swept the magazines into a pile with both arms. One page stuck to my sleeve. Bea finally took a carton downstairs, but returned with a sandwich and no empty box. I pointed at the stairs again.

At sixteen, Hassan had been assigned the attic because his older sister Nura claimed the boxes were “mostly his stuff.” He opened one and found a jumble of tangled holiday lights, cracked plastic toys, and a stack of his own notebooks. Nura sat nearby, carefully wrapping a porcelain bird she had found in another carton. Hassan asked where the packing paper was. She told him to check the closet, though he had already checked it twice. He stood, bumped his head on a beam, and held still with both hands gripping the box. “You know, if we keep everything, we’re not sorting anything,” he said. Nura added the bird to a carton marked KEEP, then asked him to find more tape. Hassan looked at the empty dispenser in his hand. He set it down beside her, lifted the entire carton, and carried it toward the stairs without another word.

I knew my brother was going to turn the attic into a guessing game as soon as he picked up the first box. “What do you think this is?” he asked, holding a dusty bundle that was obviously an old curtain. We had promised our landlord we’d clear the space by evening, and the hallway was already jammed with cartons. I pulled the bundle from his hands and dropped it into the donation pile. He rescued it, claiming the fabric could become a costume. Then he found a cracked plastic trumpet and started playing it. The note came out like a goose with a sore throat. I shoved cotton into my ears and pointed at the pile marked TRASH. He grinned, still gripping the trumpet. I took a deep breath, picked up the box beneath his chair, and discovered it contained nothing but loose buttons. “Excellent,” I said, tipping them into a jar and handing him the empty box.

Ruth had arranged the attic boxes by date, but her brother Cal kept moving them to make room for the folding table he wanted to use as a workbench. Each time Ruth turned around, a labeled carton had shifted several feet. She pressed a strip of tape onto one lid and wrote 1988 again, since Cal had covered the first label with a coffee ring. He was now trying to repair a cracked toy truck on top of a box marked FRAGILE. “That’s not a workbench,” Ruth said. Cal asked where else he was supposed to put it. She looked at the narrow attic, the piles of photographs, and the table blocking the only clear path. Her jaw tightened. She lifted the truck, set it on the floor, and pushed the table toward him until it bumped his knees. Cal finally moved it downstairs, leaving Ruth to restore the labels.

My twin brother and I were supposed to sort our grandparents’ attic before the movers arrived. I opened a box of kitchen linens, and he immediately wrapped a towel around his head like a turban. “You have to admit, this is a strong look,” he said. I held up a pair of stained oven mitts and waited for an answer about whether they were staying. He began humming a tune instead. The tape on my carton had stuck to my sleeve, and the attic was so hot that my hair clung to my forehead. I peeled the tape free, pressed it onto the box, and wrote DONATE in letters large enough for him to see. He tucked the mitts into KEEP. I took them out and placed them in the donation bag. When he started rummaging through the next carton for props, I handed him a marker and assigned him the labels.

At seventy-two, June had climbed the attic stairs with her grandson Mateo, expecting a tidy afternoon of sorting. Instead, he opened every box at once, convinced the one he wanted was hiding beneath the rest. Lids leaned against rafters, and tissue paper drifted across the floor. June asked him to close the cartons he wasn’t using. He nodded, then lifted a typewriter from one and set it on top of a stack of quilts. The stack sagged. June caught the typewriter before it slid off, her fingers gripping its cold metal edge. “One box at a time,” she said, slower than before. Mateo looked at the mess and began gathering paper. June handed him the lids, one after another, until the floor cleared enough to walk. When he reached for another carton, she placed a hand on top of it and passed him a broom instead.

I came to the attic with my sister Lila to find our father’s old record player, but she insisted we sort every box on the way. I pulled down one marked BOOKS and found only tangled extension cords. Lila checked the label twice as though the cords might turn into novels. Then she opened a carton marked CORDS and discovered a stack of cookbooks. I rubbed dust from the label with my sleeve; it only smeared the ink. “Maybe we should make a list,” she said, searching for paper. I pointed to the clipboard tucked under her arm. She blinked, then wrote down the contents of both boxes while I hauled them to the stairs. A loose button rolled beneath my shoe. I stopped, picked it up, and dropped it into a jar instead of asking which box it belonged to. Lila started another list. I took the jar downstairs.

Darius and his sister Quinn had inherited the attic contents along with the house, and they disagreed about nearly everything in it. Quinn wanted to keep the old science projects; Darius wanted enough floor space to reach the window. She held up a papier-mâché volcano while he tried to drag a carton past her. The carton caught on a nail, tearing a corner open. Plastic dinosaurs spilled across the boards. Quinn gasped as if he had knocked over a priceless display. Darius crouched, scooped the toys into a laundry basket, and shoved the damaged box aside. “We can decide later,” Quinn said, already rescuing a dinosaur with a missing tail. Darius straightened, rolling his shoulders. The sun was sinking, and they had cleared only one shelf. He carried the basket down himself, then returned with two empty bins and put them directly in front of Quinn.

My older sister Farah said sorting the attic would be simple, then spent half an hour looking for the key to a locked trunk. I held the flashlight while she tried hairpins, a butter knife, and finally the key ring that had been in her pocket all along. The trunk opened with a squeal. Inside were old costumes, a stack of programs, and a small box of tangled necklaces. Farah lifted each necklace to inspect it, laying them in a neat row across the dusty floor. I shifted my weight from one foot to the other until the flashlight beam wandered over the rafters. “Could we decide what we’re doing with these?” I asked. She said she needed to remember who had worn them. I lowered the flashlight onto the trunk and started carrying the costumes downstairs. When I came back, she had found a second box of jewelry and was sorting it by color.

Evelyn and her younger brother Kit were clearing the attic of their mother’s duplex when a storm warning appeared on his phone. Evelyn pointed out that rain was already tapping the skylight. Kit kept opening boxes, searching for a baseball glove he insisted had been packed away. He found a cracked lunchbox, three mismatched shoes, and a stack of old maps, but no glove. Evelyn held a tarp over the growing KEEP pile while he rummaged through another carton. A drop of water landed on the map in her hand. She folded it quickly and tucked it into a plastic bag. “We need to move the boxes away from the window,” she said. Kit answered that the glove might be near the back. Evelyn planted both hands on the largest carton and dragged it across the floor, scraping its bottom over the boards. Kit finally grabbed the other end and helped her carry it downstairs.

I had just straightened the last row of tomato stakes when the weather radio repeated its storm warning for the fourth time. The plants already leaned under a sky the color of wet slate, and the irrigation hose had chosen that morning to split beside the pump. I knelt in the mud, found the tear, and wrapped it with the only tape in my pocket, which promptly stuck to my glove instead of the hose. “Of course,” I muttered, peeling it free with my teeth. My dog watched from the truck bed while I checked the drainage ditch and found it packed with windblown leaves. I scooped them out by hand, glancing at the clouds between every shovel load. When the first drops struck my hat, I stood, planted both hands on my hips, and looked over the field as if it might finally cooperate.

Marta had spent the morning inspecting her barley, counting the patches flattened by hungry geese and the ones trampled by the delivery truck. Now thunder rolled over the ridge, and the sky promised to make the whole inventory irrelevant. She tugged her raincoat zipper; it snagged halfway, as it had all week. With a sharp breath, she abandoned it and hurried to the far gate to check the runoff channel. Someone had left a shovel across the opening. Marta lifted it, tossed it onto the grass, and watched muddy water begin to flow. Her nephew called from the barn that the tarp was missing. She shut her eyes for one long beat, then pointed him toward the tool shed without turning around. The first gust bent the barley in a single sweeping wave. Marta pinched the bridge of her nose, then went back to counting.

I drove the old tractor along the pumpkin rows, stopping every few yards to inspect the vines before the storm reached our valley. The forecast had shifted from evening to noon, then back to midafternoon, and I had planned around every version. At the north end, I found a broken trellis leaning across the path. I got down, lifted it, and felt the damp wood crumble between my fingers. My brother had promised to replace it last week. I looked toward the house, where his truck sat under the carport, and let out a breath through my nose. There was no time to argue. I dragged the pieces aside, checked the ditch for blockages, and found a plastic feed sack wedged in the culvert. Pulling it free soaked my sleeves. I wiped my hands on my jeans and muttered at the clouds, which were already swallowing the sun.

At sixty-eight, Juniper still walked her orchard rows faster than the hired crew, though the coming storm had made everyone scatter to finish early. She checked each young apple tree for loose ties, finding one knotted so tightly it cut into the bark. The worker who had done it was already driving away. Juniper stared after the truck, lips pressed thin, then fetched her pocketknife and freed the branch. A gust sent a crate tumbling downhill. She chased it, caught it against a fence, and found three bruised apples inside. “A fine day for quality control,” she said to nobody. Near the pump house, she noticed the drain was clogged with twigs and began pulling them out one by one. Rain speckled her glasses. She shoved them onto her head and kept working, muttering a running list of things that should have been finished yesterday.

I checked the rice seedlings at dawn, though the storm report said it might miss us entirely. The radio had been wrong twice this month, so I brought a coil of rope and walked the embankment myself. At the western corner, a section had slumped into the water. I crouched to press the mud back into place, and the whole edge gave way beneath my boot. I climbed out, dripping, and stared at the gap while my shirt clung to my shoulders. My daughter waved from the road, asking whether I wanted breakfast. I pointed at the embankment and shook my head. She brought me a spade instead, then realized she had left it at the house. I tapped my muddy foot against the bank and watched the clouds gather. Finally she returned with the tool, and I set to work without wasting breath on the obvious.

Calvin, a former city bus driver, had taken up farming expecting quiet mornings. His cabbage field offered little of it as he checked the leaves for pests beneath a sky darkening by the minute. The sprayer sputtered, coughed, and died just as he reached the far row. He gave the handle a brisk shake. Nothing. He opened the tank, discovered it was nearly empty, and looked toward the shed where the refill had been sitting since Tuesday. A crow called from the fence; Calvin waved it off with more force than necessary. He hurried back for the container, then found the shed door swollen shut from last night’s rain. After leaning his shoulder into it twice, he stopped and wiped his forehead with his sleeve. A low rumble crossed the fields. Calvin looked at his cabbages, then at the stubborn door, and tried the latch again.

I was checking the sweet corn when the wind began flipping the leaves inside out. The storm was still beyond the hills, but my phone kept buzzing with alerts, each one describing a different arrival time. I shoved it into my pocket and inspected the drainage furrows instead. One was blocked by a heap of cut weeds I had asked the crew to haul away. I kicked at the pile; it barely moved. Then I fetched a rake and dragged the mess clear, stopping every few minutes to brush sweat from my eyes. A loose sheet of plastic flapped against the greenhouse, slapping the frame like a hand clapping at a bad performance. I crossed the yard, tied it down, and found the knot had already come loose. My jaw tightened. I retied it with two firm pulls, tested it, and returned to the corn before the next alert could chime.

Nadia inspected her saffron plots with a clipboard tucked beneath one arm, trying to determine whether the flower beds could withstand the approaching downpour. Her irrigation timer had switched itself on overnight, leaving muddy channels between the rows. She stepped around them, marked the damage, and discovered the clipboard’s pen had stopped working. Nadia shook it, scribbled on the margin, then snapped the cap back on with a click. A farmhand shouted that the west gate was swinging loose. She turned to see it banging against its post in the rising wind. By the time she reached it, the latch had dropped into the weeds. She searched, found it beneath a flattened marigold, and brushed dirt from the metal with her thumb. “A little notice would be nice,” she said to the gate, fastening it shut. Then she returned to the plots, her pencil pressed hard enough to score the paper.

I had nearly finished checking the bean trellises when my neighbor called to ask whether I could lend him a ladder. The storm was coming, and my own ladder was already propping up the barn gutter, which had started sagging again. I told him that, then found the gutter had slipped farther since breakfast. I shoved the phone into my pocket and climbed onto a crate to reach the bracket. The crate wobbled. I stepped down, kicked it aside, and fetched the ladder from the shed, where a wheelbarrow blocked the door. After moving the wheelbarrow, I discovered the ladder’s feet were muddy and slick. I stood in the doorway, staring at the clutter as wind rattled the tin roof. Finally I carried everything out into the yard and set the ladder against the barn. The bean rows would have to wait another five minutes.

Elias, who had inherited the farm and its ancient machinery from his aunt, walked the potato field before the storm. A few plants had begun to wilt, and the water line he’d laid yesterday was kinked beneath a wheel track. He bent to pull it free, only to discover the coupling had cracked. His shoulders rose toward his ears. He carried the pipe to the shed, where three boxes labeled REPAIR PARTS contained nothing but screws and old receipts. Elias tipped one box onto the workbench and sorted through it, jaw working silently. A flash of lightning lit the windows. He found a usable coupling at the bottom of a coffee tin, fitted it, and hurried back outside. The line held. He stood over the potatoes, rain starting to tap his collar, and ran a hand through his hair before checking the next row.

I walked the strawberry beds with a basket on my arm, checking for ripe fruit before the storm could turn it mushy. The workers had left several crates under the open lean-to, though I’d asked them twice to move everything inside. I set down the basket and hauled the first crate toward the barn. Its bottom sagged, and berries slid into the dirt. I stared at the red mess, then picked up the salvageable ones with careful, pinched fingers. My watch said the rain was only minutes away. The second crate had a broken handle; I carried it against my chest, leaving a streak of juice on my shirt. At the barn, the door stuck on a stone. I nudged it with my boot, missed, and nudged it again. When it finally swung open, I entered without looking back at the scattered fruit.

Priya checked the sunflowers along the eastern field, testing each stake while gusts began to sweep dust over the rows. Several leaned at awkward angles, and one had snapped clean through. She fetched a bundle of replacements from the truck, but the tailgate jammed when she tried to lower it. Priya pulled the handle, pressed it, and tried again with both hands. Nothing moved. She gave the metal a flat look, then climbed into the bed and passed the stakes over the side one by one. A thunderclap made her duck, scattering two stakes across the gravel. She retrieved them, brushed grit from her palms, and set to bracing the tallest flowers. Her phone rang inside the cab. She let it ring while she tied the last stem, then climbed down and answered with a clipped, “I’m still in the field.”

I rolled my bicycle into the courtyard and found the rear tire flat again, though I had patched it only three days earlier. The repair kit kept slipping off the milk crate, and my pump’s handle squeaked with every useless stroke. When I pulled out the tube, a tiny shard of glass winked from the rubber. I dropped it into an empty jam jar, then watched it bounce straight back out. “Of course,” I muttered, crawling around to find it beneath the hedge. My neighbor offered a cup of tea; I pointed at the wheel with a greasy thumb and said I’d be finished in a minute. Forty minutes later, the tire held air, but the chain had fallen off. I stared at it, wiped both hands on my shirt, and laughed once without humor before reaching for the wrench.

At the edge of the schoolyard, twelve-year-old Nia turned her bicycle upside down and studied the bent pedal. Her father had promised the repair would take five minutes, but he was still on a work call, pacing beside the gate. Nia fetched the tool kit herself. The wrench slipped, scraped her knuckle, and landed in the gravel. She pressed her lips together, retrieved it, and tried again, while classmates streamed past toward the bus. The pedal finally loosened, only to reveal a stripped thread. Nia gave the crank a sharp spin; it clacked against the frame. “That’s not fixed,” she called. Her father covered the phone’s microphone and gave her a helpless shrug. She folded the tools into their case with brisk little snaps, then carried the bicycle home by its handlebars, its useless pedal knocking against the curb at every step.

I had borrowed the bicycle to ride to my shift, and its chain chose the one rainy morning I was already late. Under the station awning, I turned the bike upside down and tried to guide the chain back over the gears. It slid off as soon as I rotated the pedal. Grease streaked my cuff; a train announcement swallowed the curse I let out. A commuter stepped around me, then another. I took a breath through my nose and wedged a folded receipt behind the derailleur, hoping to hold it steady. The chain caught at last, but the wheel spun only halfway before locking. I checked the clock, then the wheel, then the clock again. Finally I wheeled the bicycle to a repair shop and watched the mechanic fix it in seconds. I nodded as if this had been my plan all along.

On the flat roof of her apartment building, Salma spread newspapers beneath the old bicycle and laid out every tool she owned. The back brake rubbed the rim, making a thin metallic chirp each time she turned the wheel. She adjusted the cable, tested it, and heard the same chirp. Her jaw shifted from side to side. A gust lifted the instruction sheet and sent it skittering toward the drain; she snatched it before it disappeared, pinning one corner under a flowerpot. The next adjustment made the brake stop working altogether. Salma lowered the wrench and looked across the rooftops, where evening lights were blinking on one by one. Then she rolled the bike in a circle, testing the lever with exaggerated care. The wheel stopped abruptly, and the chirp returned. She gathered the tools into a tin, each one clanging louder than necessary.

I bought the used bicycle because the seller swore it needed only a new inner tube. In my basement, I removed the wheel and discovered that the axle nut had been rounded off, the kind of detail nobody mentions in a cheerful online listing. I tried pliers, then a socket wrench, then a rubber band wrapped around the damaged nut. The rubber band snapped and flicked across my forehead. I sat back on the cold concrete, holding the wrench in both hands while the bicycle leaned against a laundry basket. My upstairs neighbor knocked to ask about the banging. I promised to keep it down, then tapped the stubborn axle once more with a hammer. It did not move. I studied the greasy wheel, sighed through my teeth, and typed a message to the seller asking whether he happened to own a miracle.

Mr. Hargrove’s bicycle had been making a clicking noise for weeks, and he finally decided to fix it before his Sunday ride. He set it on the porch and tightened the crank arm, following a video on his phone. The clicking stopped. He smiled, spun the pedals, and heard a rattle from the front wheel instead. He crouched to inspect it, bumping his head on the handlebar. His wife came outside with a basket of laundry and suggested taking the bike to the shop. “I’ve got it,” he said, though the video had moved on to a different model. He paused it, rewound, and tightened a bolt that was already tight. The wheel wobbled harder. Hargrove stood up slowly, flexed his fingers, and looked at the bicycle as if it had personally changed the rules. He carried it to the car without another word.

The bicycle’s front tire went soft halfway through my ride along the river path. I dragged it to a picnic table, where the shade was full of mosquitoes and my phone battery showed two percent. The patch kit had dried out. I rubbed the gummy cement between my fingers, then shook the tube as though that might improve it. A passing cyclist called out that a shop was just a mile away. I thanked him with a smile that felt pinned in place. The pump’s nozzle refused to seal, and every attempt to lock it down released another puff of air. I set the pump on the bench a little harder than necessary. After a moment, I folded the tube back into the tire and began pushing the bike along the path. Each rotation made the rim scrape the pavement, keeping time with my muttered complaints.

In the village garage, fifteen-year-old Tomas tried to repair his grandmother’s bicycle before she returned from market. The rear brake cable had snapped, and the spare cable was several centimeters too short. He pulled it taut, tied it in a knot, and squeezed the lever. Nothing happened. A jar of screws tipped from the workbench as he searched for something else to use. He scooped them up one by one, shoulders rising toward his ears. His grandmother arrived while he was threading a length of garden wire through the brake housing. She parked her groceries and watched him test it. The wire sprang loose, flicking the mudguard. Tomas dropped the pliers into the toolbox with a clang. “I can ride it slowly,” she said. He turned to her with wide eyes, then carefully pushed the bicycle toward the proper repair shop.

I found the bicycle abandoned behind the community theater and decided to make it rideable for the prop crew. The front wheel was twisted, the handlebars pointed at different angles, and one brake pad was missing. I fixed the bars first, tightening the stem until my forearms trembled. Then the wheel rubbed against the fork. I loosened it, centered it, and tightened it again; it still rubbed. The stage manager kept opening the door to ask whether the bicycle was ready for rehearsal. Each time, I held up one greasy finger and bent back over the axle. When the wheel finally turned freely, the chain slipped off with a clatter. I closed my eyes for a beat, took the chain in my palm, and started over. From inside came the sound of actors practicing their entrance. I answered with a wrench striking the floor.

Marta had promised her son that she would fix his bicycle before the neighborhood parade. The front basket sagged to one side, and the mounting bolt had vanished. She searched the kitchen drawer, the shed, and a tin of assorted fasteners, finding three screws that were almost right. The first was too short; the second bent when she tightened it. Her son stood nearby in his parade sash, shifting his weight from foot to foot. Marta kept her eyes on the basket and asked him to hold it level. He did, but the basket slipped just as she reached for the screwdriver. She let the tool clatter onto the path, then pinched the bridge of her nose. After a quiet moment, she secured the basket with two strips of wire. It tilted slightly, but held. Her son climbed on, and Marta walked beside him, watching every bump.

My bicycle started skipping gears on the steep hill behind the library, so I wheeled it into the parking lot and turned it upside down. The rear shifter cable had frayed, leaving a tiny nest of silver wires at the clamp. I trimmed them with nail scissors from my bag, tightened the bolt, and tried the gears. The chain jumped across two sprockets and wedged itself between them. I pulled, but it held fast. A delivery van idled nearby, its driver watching me in the mirror. My ears warmed as I wiped grit from my fingertips onto a napkin. I loosened the wheel, freed the chain, and reassembled everything in the wrong order. The wheel wouldn’t sit straight. I stared at the manual on my phone until the screen dimmed, then tapped it awake with a greasy knuckle and began from the first diagram.

At a campsite in the high desert, Leila discovered that her touring bicycle’s rear rack had cracked near the frame. The nearest town was miles away, and her panniers were packed with food and water. She unloaded everything onto the dust, then rummaged through her repair bag for a spare bolt. The only one she found was too long. She tried wrapping it in tape, but the tape softened in the sun and peeled away. A gust sent a map tumbling toward the road; Leila lunged after it, kicked a water bottle, and watched it roll beneath the picnic table. She retrieved it with a clipped breath, then used a metal tent peg to brace the rack. It held when she pressed down, though the frame creaked. She repacked the bags one at a time, testing each strap, and set off at a pace that made the loose rack barely rattle.

I had tuned the violin three times before the first chair in the community hall began clicking her pen. Each click landed exactly where my entrance should have been. I stopped, lowered the bow, and stared at the sheet music as if it had personally rearranged the notes. The accompanist tried the opening again, but the piano’s middle C sounded like a wooden door shutting. “One more time,” I said, rubbing the bridge of my nose. A child in the front row dropped a packet of crackers; the crinkle filled the pause. I tightened a peg, heard the string climb sharp, and let out a breath through my teeth. The concert was for twenty neighbors and their folding chairs, yet this rehearsal had acquired the grandeur of a siege. I began again, slower, while the pen clicked on.

At sixty-eight, Marisol had learned to ignore most inconveniences, but the church basement’s fluorescent light kept blinking in time with her clarinet scales. She paused and glared upward. The bulb steadied, only to have the drummer’s phone chirp from beneath a coat. “We’re rehearsing, not waiting for a dentist,” she muttered, then reset her reed. Her fingers knew the passage; the instrument kept answering with a thin, stubborn squeak. She swabbed it, checked the mouthpiece, and tried once more. On the other side of the room, two volunteers arranged paper cups for the small concert and whispered over the program. Marisol’s jaw tightened. She planted both feet, lifted the clarinet, and played the phrase cleanly at last. Nobody applauded. She gave them a look, and the drummer put his phone in a drawer.

The rehearsal room above the bakery smelled of burnt sugar and hot dust. I was supposed to play three gentle songs on my banjo at Friday’s café concert, but the new strap kept sliding toward my elbow. Every time I adjusted it, the instrument tilted and my pick skittered across the strings. “It’s a strap, not a pulley system,” I said, tugging the buckle hard enough to make it squeak. My bandmate offered a safety pin. I accepted it, then discovered the pin was bent. Downstairs, a mixer roared, drowning out my count-in. I shut my eyes, counted silently, and started the tune again. Halfway through, a string slipped out of tune. I stopped so abruptly my chair scraped backward. After a long breath, I tuned it by ear and carried on, refusing to let the room win.

Eli had brought his cello to the library meeting room early, hoping for twenty quiet minutes before the neighborhood arts showcase. Instead, the radiator knocked like someone trapped inside it, and a custodian pushed a cart past the door every few minutes. Eli pressed his lips together as the cart rattled by again. His bow caught on the same measure, producing a rasp that made his shoulders climb toward his ears. He checked the rosin, loosened the bow, then tightened it too far. “Perfect,” he murmured, staring at the horsehair. The accompanist suggested starting from the beginning. Eli looked at the clock, then at the crowded chairs waiting for the evening audience. He rolled his neck, set the bow carefully, and played the troublesome passage in tiny sections until it finally held together.

I was rehearsing my trumpet part in the laundromat’s back room because the apartment walls were too thin. The owner had promised the machines would be off for half an hour. They were not. A washer began thumping during my high entrance, and a dryer buzzer answered every rest. I lowered the horn and stared at the handwritten schedule taped to the wall. “Apparently, the spin cycle is our guest soloist,” I said. My mouth felt dry, and the mouthpiece had gone cold against my lips. I tried the passage again, forcing the notes through the noise, but a sock rolled under the door and landed beside my shoe. I picked it up, returned it to a basket, and started over. The small concert was tomorrow; I needed one clean run. I stood closer to the window and kept going.

Priya had organized the courtyard concert herself, so she was determined to make her sitar rehearsal work despite the gardeners’ leaf blower. The drone rattled the window panes while she tuned each string with a measured turn of the peg. A gust of dust slipped under the door. She stopped, covered the instrument, and watched the fine grit settle on her music stand. “Could we have five minutes without machinery?” she called. The gardener raised one hand but did not switch off the blower. Priya’s shoulders stiffened. She wiped the strings, adjusted the microphone, and began the raga again, only to hear feedback squeal from the speaker. She unplugged it with a sharp movement, then took a slow breath. The audience would be a dozen courtyard residents, not a royal court. Still, she wanted one rehearsal that did not fight back.

My accordion kept sticking on the same button, which was unfortunate because the button carried the melody everyone knew. In the senior center’s activity room, I pressed it harder, then softer, then gave the instrument a flat look. “You’ve had one job since 1942,” I told it. The small concert was meant to raise money for new garden benches, and the volunteers kept interrupting to ask whether I could play something livelier. I wiped my palms on my trousers and tried the tune from the top. The bellows snagged; a sour note burst out. Across the room, someone tested a microphone with a series of booming thumps. I set the accordion down before I could shove it beneath a chair. After checking the button with a fingernail, I lifted it again and played the melody slowly until the mechanism behaved.

At the marina pavilion, Tomas rehearsed his saxophone beside a stack of chairs for the sailing club’s summer concert. The wind kept turning his music pages, and each time he pinned one down, a gull swooped onto the railing and screamed over the melody. Tomas lowered the sax and watched the bird flap away. “You’ve made your point,” he called after it. His reeds were already damp from the sea air, and the notes came out breathy where he needed them bright. He switched reeds, blew a quick test, and began again. A page escaped and skated across the boards toward the water. He caught it with his shoe, pressed a hand over the rest, and continued from memory. By the last phrase, his neck was hot and his tie sat crooked, but he played it through without stopping.

I had practiced the guitar solo all week, yet every time I reached the final bend, the string buzzed against the fret. In the laundromat café where our trio would play, a blender started whenever I found the right note. I set the guitar in my lap and examined the neck, turning the tuning peg a fraction.
