I promised my daughter I’d bring home enough perch for supper, so I shoved off while the shoreline lamps were still glowing. The lake looked calm until I opened the bait bucket and found three worms missing and one crawling across my boot. I flicked it overboard, then discovered the tackle box latch had jammed. I pressed, twisted, and finally pried it open with a spoon from my lunch bag. Inside, every lure was tangled together in a bright metal knot. My jaw clenched as I picked them apart one barb at a time. A loon called somewhere beyond the mist; I answered with a sigh and a small, unnecessary splash from my paddle. When I finally cast, the line caught on the boat’s cleat. I stared at it, counted to five, and carefully freed the hook before it could find my thumb.

Ravi pushed his skiff into the lake at dawn, carrying a new electronic fish finder he had bought after weeks of saving. The screen flashed a warning before he had even untied the rope. He tapped the display, restarted it, and watched the same message return. “That’s useful,” he said to the empty boat. He tried another menu, then another, his thumb stabbing the buttons while the sun climbed above the pines. His older brother had insisted the device would make fishing effortless. Ravi glanced at the silent shoreline and pictured the lecture waiting at home. A sudden tug bent the rod beside him. He grabbed it, only for the line to snap against the rail. The fish finder chirped brightly. Ravi shut it off, tucked it beneath the seat, and picked up his hand-carved wooden lure instead.

I rowed out before dawn because the weather report promised a quiet morning. By the time I reached the middle of the lake, wind was pushing the boat sideways and my hat had blown under the seat. I leaned down to grab it, bumped my forehead on the bench, and sat up with a sharp hiss. The oarlocks squeaked each time I pulled. I tried oil from a tiny bottle in my kit, but the cap rolled overboard and disappeared. “Fine,” I told the squeaking boat. “You win.” Then my phone buzzed with a message from the fish market asking whether I had anything to sell. I typed a reply, deleted it, and tucked the phone away. The first cast landed neatly at last. A gust lifted the bait right off the hook, leaving me holding a bare line and an expression nobody on shore could mistake.

Marta left the harbor at first light, determined to reach her favorite fishing cove before the tour boats arrived. Halfway there, she noticed a plastic crate wedged beneath the bench, packed with someone else’s tangled nets. She tried shifting it with her foot, but it slid into the path of the steering handle. Marta stopped the motor and hauled the crate upright, grunting as the wet mesh snagged her watch. She freed it strand by strand, then found a handwritten label bearing the marina owner’s name. A gull landed on the bow and pecked at her sandwich. Marta shooed it away, wiped her hand on her trousers, and started the engine again. By the time she reached the cove, the first tour boat was already circling. She lowered her rod anyway, shoulders squared, and gave the distant guide a stare that needed no explanation.

I was halfway across the lake at dawn when the bell on my fishing rod began ringing, though there was nothing on the line. I reeled in and found a loop of weed wrapped around the hook. The bell kept chiming as I pulled it free. I removed the weed, reset the bait, and cast again. This time the line tangled around the handle of my coffee mug. My breakfast sloshed over the side, and I pressed my lips together until the urge to shout passed. The shoreline was only a gray blur behind me. I checked every knot, every guide, every connection, then made a third cast. The bell rang once more. A small fish had nibbled the bait and vanished, leaving the hook bare. I put the mug under the seat and switched to a quiet, stubborn sort of patience.

Seventy-four-year-old Oren eased his boat from the reeds as dawn spread over the lake. He had planned a peaceful morning, but the new outboard made a sound like a bucket of bolts. He killed the engine, lifted the cover, and found a loose cable. His fingers were stiff from the cold, and the tiny fastener kept slipping into the bilge. Oren retrieved it with a magnet, dropped it again, and stared at the water for a long moment. “You’d think machinery could manage one simple task,” he said. A nearby cabin door opened; someone called that the noise had woken them. Oren raised a hand in apology, then tightened the cable with his pocket wrench. The engine started smoothly. He guided the boat toward open water, but his fishing license had blown from the dashboard and was now drifting toward the stern.

I took my small boat out at dawn, hoping to beat the heat and the weekend crowd. A floating branch caught the propeller just beyond the launch. I cut the motor and leaned over with my pocketknife, trying to reach the wet wood without tipping myself in. The branch broke into three pieces, each one spinning away as if it had somewhere important to be. I restarted the engine. It sputtered, shuddered, and stopped. I sat very still, gripping the wheel until my knuckles paled. Then I pulled off my cap and fanned myself, though the air was cold. A kayaker glided past and asked if I needed help. “No, I’m enjoying the view,” I answered, too brightly. He pointed toward the shore, where the launch attendant was waving a long-handled rake. I let him tow me back, one slow inch at a time.

Nia pushed away from the dock in darkness, eager to fish before her shift at the bakery. She had packed her lunch carefully, but the paper bag had split along the bottom. An apple rolled beneath the seat, and two pastries slid into the tackle tray. She rescued them, brushed off the crumbs, and tied the bag shut with fishing line. The knot held until she reached for her rod. The bag tipped again. Nia stared at the damp pastry, then shut her eyes and counted to four. A motorboat roared past, rocking her skiff and sending the apple bobbing overboard. She watched it drift out of reach, wiped her palms on her apron, and set the remaining food aside. When a fish finally tugged, she jerked the rod too hard and lost it. Her mouth formed a silent word before she cast again.

I set out before sunrise with a borrowed boat and a carefully folded map. The lake had more coves than the map showed, and the marker I was looking for had apparently been moved. I turned in circles, comparing the shoreline to the faded drawing while my passenger, a sleepy terrier, whined at every change of direction. “I know,” I told him. “This is not where the blue line says it is.” I pulled out my phone for a compass, but the screen stayed black. After a minute of pressing the button, I laid it down with unusual care. The dog barked at a patch of mist. I followed the sound of water lapping against a rocky point and found a quiet inlet at last. My first cast snagged a branch. I loosened the line, scratched the dog behind the ears, and tried again.

Caleb had spent the night mending his nets, so when he finally launched at dawn, his eyes felt gritty and his back protested each movement. A passing barge had left rolling waves that knocked his boat against the dock. He pushed off again, only for a coil of rope to catch around his boot. Caleb stepped free, pulled the rope aboard, and coiled it properly while the boat drifted toward a cluster of reeds. By the time he reached his usual fishing ground, the sun was bright enough to warm the water. He lowered a net and waited. A floating bottle bumped the hull, followed by a second one. Caleb gathered both, wedged them beneath the bench, and looked toward the distant shore. There was no bin in sight. He rubbed the bridge of his nose, then went back to work, carefully setting the net where the fish might still be.

I had measured the gallery wall three times, yet the largest canvas still leaned like it was trying to escape. The installer blamed the old plaster, then disappeared to answer a call. I held the frame while my wrist trembled and watched the opening-night clock crawl forward. Across the room, my carefully printed labels curled at the corners in the damp air. I pressed them flat, only for one to peel up again. “Could we try the level?” I asked. The installer returned with a shrug and a hammer. I closed my eyes as he tapped the nail higher, then lower, then higher again. When the painting finally hung straight, a visitor’s coat brushed its edge. I caught the frame before it swung and stood there gripping it, jaw tight, while the room filled with cheerful chatter.

At sixty-eight, Marisol had prepared every painting herself, from the first coat of gesso to the final varnish. Now the gallery’s delivery van was late, the receptionist had misplaced the guest list, and someone had set a coffee cup on her stack of price cards. She picked up the soggy cards one by one, smoothing them against her skirt. “We open in forty minutes,” she said, each word clipped neatly apart. Her nephew offered to help, but kept asking where the tape was while standing beside the open supply drawer. Marisol inhaled through her nose and handed him the tape. When the van finally arrived, the driver had brought the wrong canvases. She stared at the familiar landscapes packed in foam, then looked at the empty walls. Without another word, she rolled up her sleeves and began rearranging the entire show.

I spent the morning arranging my photographs by color, then by subject, then by the order I had sworn I preferred. The gallery manager shifted one frame two inches and said the wall felt “more balanced.” I moved it back. A spot popped loose from the ceiling and landed on my best print, leaving a bright white circle across a stormy sea. I dabbed at it with a cloth, which only spread the mark. My teeth pressed together while the manager explained that the lighting crew would return after lunch. I asked whether they could return before lunch. He checked his phone as if the answer might be there. By opening time, I had rehung half the collection and invented a new caption for the damaged photograph: “Moon Over Harbor.” It was a poor joke, but at least the frame was straight.

Darius arrived at the gallery carrying six sculptures and a roll of bubble wrap under one arm. The staff had placed his plinths in a sunny window, though he had specified a dim corner for the delicate wax figures. He explained this once, then again, pointing to the email on his phone. The coordinator nodded while looking past him toward a delivery truck blocking the entrance. Darius set down a sculpture and rubbed the bridge of his nose. A volunteer began unwrapping the pieces with scissors. “Please use your hands,” he said, watching the blades approach a wax ear. She froze. He took the scissors from her and tucked them into his pocket. Together they moved each plinth across the room, stopping whenever someone needed to pass. When the last figure was in place, the coordinator asked if he could shift everything back for a sponsor’s banner.

My exhibition title was supposed to be painted in elegant gold letters above the entrance. Instead, the sign maker misspelled my surname, and the replacement arrived with the letters spaced so widely they looked like separate islands. I stood on a ladder, peeling off the vinyl while flakes clung to my sleeves. The gallery assistant kept saying it was “not noticeable,” although she had read the mistake aloud twice. I handed her the scraper and asked her to remove the remaining glue. She began in the center, where the sign was already clean. I took the tool back. Outside, guests gathered behind the glass, checking their invitations. I could hear the curator practicing my introduction. By the time I finished, my fingertips were sticky and the wall was bare. I wrote my name in marker on a strip of packing paper and taped it above the door.

Theo’s paintings were ready, but the gallery had installed a speaker directly beside the quietest one. A loop of cheerful piano music chimed through the room every twelve seconds. He asked the technician to lower it. The technician turned the volume down, then wandered off without checking whether the loop had stopped. Theo listened to the same bright notes repeat while placing labels beneath his canvases. One label was upside down; another belonged to a painting across the room. He flipped them over with sharp little motions, then stepped back and folded his arms. His partner offered to fetch coffee. Theo pointed silently at the speaker. The technician returned and said the sound was part of the atmosphere. Theo looked at the gray painting of an empty station, then at the smiling piano on the wall display. He unplugged the speaker. The room settled into silence, except for the technician’s sigh.

I had borrowed a cargo bicycle to bring my framed prints across town, because the gallery’s loading area was blocked by a food truck. Halfway there, rain began tapping the plastic covers. At the entrance, the door attendant told me the lift was out of order. I stared at the narrow stairwell, then at my stack of frames. “All of them?” I asked. He nodded and went back to his phone. I carried the prints upstairs one at a time, balancing each against my shoulder while the bicycle lock clinked in my pocket. On the fourth trip, a frame slipped and knocked the wall. I stopped, shut my eyes, and counted to five. The gallery manager appeared with a clipboard and asked whether I could move the display table. I set down the last print carefully and asked him to carry the table himself.

At twenty-two, Priya was the youngest artist in the group exhibition, and the gallery had given her a wall behind a tall potted palm. Every time she stepped back to assess her paintings, leaves blocked the central image. She asked the curator to move the plant. The curator suggested trimming it, then went to greet a donor. Priya shifted the pot herself, scraping its saucer across the floor. A leaf snapped off and landed on one of her labels. She brushed it away, leaving a green smear over the title. Her mouth tightened as she replaced the card with a clean copy. The palm still crowded the corner, so she turned the painting slightly to make space. A staff member immediately turned it back, explaining that all frames had to align. Priya looked at the row of identical angles, then carried the plant into the hallway.

I was finishing the final piece for my gallery exhibition when the printer jammed for the third time. The wall text was supposed to explain a series of maps I had drawn from memory, but the machine kept swallowing the last page. I opened its tray, removed a warm sheet, and found the text printed diagonally across the paper. My studio neighbor offered to print it at home, then discovered she had no ink. I pressed my palms against the table and stared at the neat pile of blank sheets. The gallery director called to ask whether everything was ready. “Nearly,” I said, looking at the clock. I rewrote the text by hand on cream paper, making each letter slow and deliberate. When I pinned it beside the maps, a thumbtack bent. I set the tack down, chose another, and tried again without looking at the clock.

Ruth had spent months assembling a gallery show from tiny embroidered portraits. On installation day, the hanging hooks were too far apart, and the smallest frames tilted whenever the door opened. She adjusted one, then another, while the curator discussed the wine order nearby. A draft lifted the corner of her artist statement. Ruth caught it before it hit the floor and weighted it with a catalog. “Can someone close that door?” she asked. Two people glanced over but kept talking. She crossed the room and shut it herself. When she returned, three frames had shifted again. Her hands hovered at her sides for a moment, fingers curled, before she began straightening them. A visitor asked whether the uneven arrangement was intentional. Ruth gave a tight smile and said she was still deciding. Then she moved the hooks, one by one, until every portrait held steady.

I arrived at the gallery with a crate of ceramic bowls, only to find the display shelves covered in dust and blue paint flecks. The cleaner said she had already finished, pointing to a spotless patch near the door. I took a cloth from my bag and began wiping each shelf myself. One bowl had a hairline crack from the trip, and I placed it aside, then noticed another piece was missing. The gallery manager checked the packing list and insisted the crate had arrived sealed. I looked at the loose tape dangling from its side. Nobody answered when I asked who had opened it. I lined up the remaining bowls, leaving a gap where the missing one belonged. Guests were due in half an hour. The manager suggested filling the space with a brochure. I folded the brochure into a stand and set it there, pressing its crease flat with my thumbnail.

Caleb’s exhibition was meant to open in a converted train depot, but the sound installation kept picking up announcements from the station next door. Each time he tested his recording, a distant voice cut across it. He unplugged the speakers, checked the cables, and plugged them back in. The gallery technician blamed the building’s wiring and offered to try again tomorrow. Caleb glanced at the invitations stacked by the entrance. “Tomorrow, the doors are open,” he said. He dragged the speakers away from the shared wall, shifting them until their cords stretched across the floor. A volunteer nearly tripped and asked him to move them back. Caleb held the cable aloft, eyebrows raised, while she stepped over it. At last he lowered the volume of the station feed and brought his own recording forward. The result was imperfect, but the room no longer sounded like a timetable.

I set the bucket beneath the ceiling drip before Mr. Vale arrived, though I had already moved it three times that morning. The landlord stepped around it and asked whether the stain had grown. I pointed to the fresh brown ring spreading above my kitchen table. He studied his phone, tapped the screen, and said he’d send someone when the maintenance schedule cleared. I took a breath through my nose and handed him the six messages I’d sent since Monday, printed out and clipped together. He blinked at the stack. “You brought receipts,” he said. “I brought a ceiling,” I replied, shifting the bucket as another drop struck the rim. He promised a roofer by Friday. I wrote the date on the top page and asked him to sign it. His smile thinned, but the pen finally came out.

At twenty-two, Nia had mastered the art of holding a conversation while watching water creep across her bathroom floor. She met the landlord by the mailboxes, where he announced that the toilet leak was probably just condensation. Nia lifted a damp towel from her tote and laid it on the counter between them. He glanced at it, then began explaining how old buildings behaved. Her fingers tightened around the strap of her bag. She recited the dates of her three repair requests without looking at her notes. When he suggested she submit another, she gave a small, flat laugh. “It’s already in your inbox.” He finally agreed to call a plumber, but asked her to be home all day. Nia stared at him until he offered a two-hour window instead.

I was halfway through a video call when the radiator began clanging like someone had dropped a wrench inside it. My landlord, Mrs. Chen, came over after I sent her a recording. She listened, nodded, and said the noise usually stopped on its own. As if summoned, the radiator went quiet. I kept my phone aimed at it, waiting. The moment she reached the door, it started banging again. I watched her shoulders jump. “Perhaps it has a schedule,” I said, with a smile that felt glued on. She promised to have it bled that afternoon. I asked whether the appointment could happen before my next client meeting, and she checked her calendar instead of telling me to be patient. The banging followed her down the hall.

Omar found the landlord in the courtyard watering geraniums while rain dripped through the cracked window frame upstairs. He described the draft, the swollen sill, and the puddle that had soaked his paperwork. Mr. Rusk suggested closing the curtains. Omar looked at the watering can, then at the clouds, and pressed his lips together. He had sealed the frame himself twice with removable strips, each attempt peeling loose by morning. Rather than repeat the whole history, he pulled a strip from his pocket and stuck it to the landlord’s sleeve. “This came off again.” The man brushed it away, startled. Omar held out a folder of photographs showing the damage after each storm. The landlord stopped smiling and agreed to bring a carpenter the next day.

I found the kitchen sink backed up again while packing lunch, so I called my landlord from beside the puddle. He said the plumber had already been there last month. I reminded him the plumber had snaked one drain, collected his fee, and left the other side bubbling. There was a pause long enough for me to hear the refrigerator hum. When the landlord asked if I could try boiling water, I set my lunch container down carefully, because I wanted both hands free to gesture. “I have tried everything you suggested,” I said, slower than necessary. “Now I need the repair you agreed to.” He sighed, but booked a visit for the afternoon. I wrote down the appointment time and asked him to confirm it by text. The sink burped loudly as he answered.

Maribel’s bedroom light flickered whenever the hallway fan switched on. She had replaced the bulb, tested the switch, and even borrowed a lamp from her neighbor. When she showed the landlord, he flipped the switch several times, as if the right rhythm might solve the wiring. Maribel folded her arms and watched the ceiling blink on and off. “Maybe the bulb is loose,” he said. She handed him the new bulb still in its package. His eyebrows rose. She listed the electrician’s number she had already found and asked whether he wanted to call or have her do it. He began to explain that tenants should not arrange contractors. Maribel tapped the package against her palm, once, twice, until he took out his phone and made the call himself.

I met Mr. Bell at the front steps with a photograph of the loose railing on my phone. He gripped it, gave it a testing shake, and said it seemed sturdy enough. I leaned on it gently. The whole post shifted toward the pavement. He jerked his hand away, then told me not to use the stairs until he could inspect it. I stared at him. “I have been using the stairs every day since I reported it two weeks ago.” My voice came out neat and clipped, which was better than what I had rehearsed. He glanced at the neighboring entrance and promised a carpenter by noon. I asked him to put that in writing. He did, while I stood beside the wobbling rail and watched him choose each word.

At the laundromat, Dev watched his landlord read the note about the broken washing-machine hookup in the basement. The leak had soaked a box of winter clothes and left a musty smell in the stairwell. The landlord said he thought the building’s caretaker had fixed it. Dev pointed to the water line still shining across the concrete. His jaw worked as he waited for an answer. When the landlord asked him to mop it, Dev handed him the mop leaning nearby. “I’ve done it twice this week.” The landlord looked at the handle, then at Dev’s damp shoes. He called the caretaker and arranged a replacement valve. Dev stayed until the call ended, making sure no one turned the water back on before the repair was scheduled.

I had placed a saucepan beneath the bathroom vent because rainwater was dripping through it again. When my landlord arrived, he asked why I hadn’t mentioned the problem sooner. I opened my email and scrolled to the message I’d sent three weeks earlier, then the one from last winter. He leaned toward the screen but didn’t read either. I let the saucepan fill until a drop splashed onto my wrist. “You can hear it,” I said. He looked up at the ceiling and finally stopped talking about the building’s age. I asked for a proper inspection, not another patch of sealant. He promised to call a roofer. I set a reminder on my phone while he was still standing there, and read the appointment date aloud before he left.

Yusuf’s front door had to be lifted and shoved before the lock would catch. His landlord called it a minor adjustment, though Yusuf had missed work twice waiting for a locksmith who never came. During their meeting in the hallway, the landlord turned the key and shrugged when it stuck. Yusuf offered him the bent key he’d been using, then held the door as it swung open by itself. A neighbor’s dog trotted past. The landlord stepped aside, embarrassed, while Yusuf retrieved the dog and returned it to its owner. “Can we deal with the lock now?” Yusuf asked. He kept his hand on the door so it could not drift shut. The landlord agreed to replace the cylinder that day and called a locksmith from the landing.

I was trying to prepare dinner when the kitchen outlet sparked beneath my kettle. I unplugged everything and called the landlord, who asked whether I might have overloaded the circuit. I stared at the dark socket and counted to five before answering. The kettle was the only thing plugged in. He said he could stop by in the morning. I told him I would not use the outlet overnight, but I needed an electrician sooner. He started listing other tenants’ requests. I pulled the kettle farther from the wall and said, “This one is sparking.” The sentence came out so level that he went quiet. He arranged an emergency visit and asked me to send a picture. I did, then waited in the living room with the kitchen lights off.

When the elevator stalled between floors for the second time that month, Lorna took the stairs up to meet her landlord, carrying her grocery bags and a log of the outages. He skimmed the dates and said the repair company had been notified. Lorna pointed out that the notice on the elevator had been there for nine days. He replied that parts could take time. Her fingers dug into the paper handles of the bags. She set them down, flattened the log against the lobby table, and asked him to give residents a realistic update. He started to say he couldn’t control the vendor. Lorna looked at the dark elevator doors, then back at him. He agreed to call the company while she waited. She stayed until he spoke to a person, not voicemail.

I arrived at the food bank before sunrise, ready to sort the donated cans before my shift at the clinic. The label printer jammed on the first sheet, then spat out a strip of crooked stickers that clung to my sleeve. I tapped the machine’s lid with two fingers and watched it blink the same red light. When a delivery driver asked where to leave six crates of pears, I pointed to the marked pallet; he set them beside the doorway instead. I moved them myself, one crate at a time, while the printer made a grinding noise behind me. “We have a system,” I said, more sharply than I meant to. A volunteer offered to help, but I handed her the labels and took a long breath by the sink. The pears were bruised, the stickers were upside down, and the doors would open in four minutes.

At the Eastside pantry, Lionel kept checking the wall clock as a line of clients curled past the coat rack. He had spent the morning assembling grocery bags according to the new dietary chart, only to learn that the chart had been replaced overnight. The coordinator was on the phone, repeating the same instructions to someone who could not hear her. Lionel pressed his lips together and slid a bag of beans back onto the shelf. Then a child knocked over a basket of apples, and two rolled beneath the folding table. He retrieved them, stood, and found that someone had moved the cart he had just organized. “If the signs change again, please tell me before I fill forty bags,” he said, rubbing the bridge of his nose. He stayed to help, but arranged each item with tight, deliberate movements.

I volunteered at the church food cupboard because I knew what it meant to stretch a grocery budget. Today, every box seemed to arrive with a surprise. The canned soup was stacked on top of the flour, the rice bags had split, and someone had put frozen chicken in the pantry cupboard. I fetched a broom, then a mop, then another broom after the first one shed bristles across the floor. A regular volunteer kept asking where things belonged, though I had taped labels to every shelf. I answered with a smile that felt pinned in place. When the donation van arrived early, I set down the mop and looked at the driver’s full cart. “Could we get one quiet minute to finish the mess we already have?” I asked. Nobody answered. I rolled up my sleeves, sorted the boxes, and muttered the shelf numbers under my breath.

Mei had arranged the food bank’s produce table by color, with sturdy vegetables at the front for people using walkers. A late shipment arrived in a jumble of damp cartons, and the delivery form listed twice as many carrots as the van contained. She counted the bundles once, then again, hoping the numbers might improve. They did not. Across the room, a volunteer had placed the sign for free bread beside the cereal, sending three visitors to the wrong table. Mei walked over, turned the sign around, and returned to find that someone had moved her carefully stacked squash. Her shoulders rose toward her ears. “Please leave the labels where they are,” she said, flattening one with her palm. A client thanked her for the fresh pears, and Mei’s expression softened for a moment. Then the office phone rang, and the clipboard slid off the counter.

I signed up at the neighborhood food bank after retiring, expecting quiet work and decent company. Instead, the donation spreadsheet crashed just as I entered the week’s inventory. I restarted the computer, waited through its wheezing, and watched the same blank screen return. Behind me, a volunteer asked whether pasta counted as a grain, while another had set a carton of eggs beneath a leaking pipe. I moved the eggs, found a bucket, and tried not to look at the growing puddle around my shoes. When the supervisor suggested I print the list again, I held up the useless screen. “With what printer?” I asked. The printer was open on the table, its paper tray balanced on a stack of cereal. I closed my eyes for three seconds, then began writing the counts by hand. My pen ran dry halfway through the beans.

Darnell worked the Saturday shift at a food bank inside a converted library. He liked greeting families and knowing which shelves needed restocking, but today the volunteer schedule had been altered without warning. Two people were assigned to unload trucks, while the front desk stood empty. He carried boxes until his palms grew slick, then returned to find the hand truck parked behind a locked closet. The key was on a hook across the room, under a handwritten note that said not to move it. Darnell stared at the note, then at the boxes blocking the fire exit. He fetched the key. A new volunteer asked if he could take a break, and Darnell gave him a look that made the question disappear. “Someone should tell the schedule it has to meet the actual work,” he said, shoving the closet door shut with his heel.

My first shift at the mobile food pantry began with a flat tire on the delivery van. I helped unload the crates onto the pavement while our driver called for roadside assistance. Rain spotted the paper bags, so I carried them under a bus shelter, then discovered that we had brought the wrong size of boxes for the produce. A man waiting nearby offered to hold an umbrella, but the wind turned it inside out. I stared at its bent spokes and let out a laugh with no humor in it. The coordinator called to ask whether we could still open on time. I glanced at the slow-moving traffic, the damp labels, and the bananas warming in their carton. “Sure, if the weather agrees to read our schedule,” I said. Then I began handing out groceries from the shelter, balancing the clipboard on my knee as rain ran down my collar.

At the campus food bank, Priya was responsible for checking expiration dates before the evening rush. A donation arrived in mixed boxes, each sealed with tape that tore into thin, useless strands. She opened one box with a key, another with scissors, and the third by pulling until the cardboard gave way. Half the cans lacked readable dates. Meanwhile, the volunteer beside her kept stacking them on the cleared table before she could inspect them. Priya moved the cans back into the sorting area, and he stacked them again. She set down her marker and pressed both hands against the table edge. “Please wait until I’ve checked them,” she said, slowly and clearly. He apologized, then asked where the marker had gone. Priya picked it up from beside his elbow and resumed the task, writing dates on a fresh sheet while the waiting line grew longer.

I volunteer at a rural food bank where the shelves are narrow and every delivery has to be carried in by hand. This morning, the truck brought twelve cases of peaches after we had already cleared space for potatoes. I shifted the potatoes, then discovered the peaches were leaking syrup through their cardboard bottoms. One case collapsed while I was lifting it, and cans rolled beneath the shelving. Our newest helper fetched a dustpan but returned with a broom too wide to fit between the racks. I took it from him, tried once, and heard the handle scrape every can in reach. “That’s a fine tool for a very different room,” I said. My neck felt stiff as I crouched and collected the cans one by one. By the time the shelves were rearranged, the lunch bell rang, and I realized I had left my sandwich in the truck.

Gloria, a retired bus driver, volunteered at a community food bank near the depot. She knew how to keep a queue moving, but the new check-in tablets froze whenever two families arrived together. Each time the screen stalled, the greeter called Gloria over to reset it. She had already explained the same steps three times, pointing to the green button and the paper backup list. On the fourth call, she wiped her hands on her apron and walked across the room without answering. A stack of donated bread sat unattended by the entrance, and the automatic door kept opening in the cold. Gloria restarted the tablet, then placed the paper forms beside it. “We can use both systems instead of pretending this one works,” she said. She tucked her chin into her scarf and began checking names by hand, tapping the table whenever the device chimed.

I took a volunteer shift at the food bank’s after-school program, where kids helped pack weekend meal kits. The labels said nut-free, but the cartons of snack bars had been mixed with the regular donations. I sorted every box, then watched someone wheel the unverified snacks straight back to the packing station. My jaw tightened as I stopped the cart and explained the difference again. A child asked if she could decorate the bags, and I handed her the markers before I could answer the volunteer. At least the children listened: they drew bright stars while I checked ingredients. Then the marker caps went missing, the tape dispenser vanished, and the packing list turned up under a pile of drawings. “The supplies are playing hide-and-seek today,” I said, looking beneath the table. I found the list stuck to my shoe and finished the kits with a pen borrowed from the sign-in desk.

When Tomas arrived at the food bank, he found a handwritten note saying the freezer was full. He had spent the previous evening negotiating for a donation of frozen vegetables, and the truck was already backing toward the loading door. He opened the freezer and saw a single box of ice packs taking up the bottom shelf. The regular freezer volunteer had gone home, leaving no explanation. Tomas shifted the ice packs into a cooler, made room for the vegetables, and wiped frost from his sleeves. Then the loading team brought in three more boxes than the invoice listed. He checked the paper twice, his finger tracking each line, while the driver waited with the engine running. “We need a list that matches what actually shows up,” Tomas said, setting the clipboard down harder than necessary. He signed for the extra boxes and went back inside to find the cooler lid had come loose.

I had practiced the clutch’s biting point in my head all morning, but the car still lurched forward and stalled at the quietest intersection in town. My instructor, Mr. Bell, calmly asked me to try again. A cyclist waited behind us, then a delivery van, while the light changed twice. I gripped the wheel until my fingers ached and made the engine cough once more. “You’re releasing it too quickly,” he said, as if the pedal had not been discussed for the last forty minutes. I stared at the dashboard, counted to five, and started over. On the next attempt, we rolled smoothly across the line. Mr. Bell praised the turn. I nodded, then pointedly asked whether we could practice somewhere without an audience.

At sixty-eight, Mabel had expected the lesson to involve a few careful laps around the block, not a lecture on mirrors that seemed to have multiplied overnight. Her instructor, Tasha, adjusted the seat for the third time while Mabel’s scarf slipped toward the gearshift. “Check your blind spot,” Tasha reminded her. Mabel twisted around so sharply that her hat slid over one eye. She pulled it back into place and let out a long breath through her nose. When the car rolled over the painted line, Tasha reached for the wheel. Mabel pressed her lips together and parked neatly at the curb. She asked for a moment, then rearranged every mirror herself, one by one. The next time Tasha said “blind spot,” Mabel checked it without turning her whole body.

The lesson was supposed to end before my shift at the bakery, but rain had turned the practice lot into a maze of puddles and orange cones. My instructor, Dev, kept asking me to reverse into the same narrow space. I straightened the wheel, backed up, and clipped a cone with the bumper. He moved it back into place without comment. I tapped the steering wheel with both thumbs while water blurred the windows. “Try using the side mirror,” he said. I did, and the car ended up crooked enough to straddle the line. My apron was folded on the passenger seat, and I could practically smell the bread cooling without me. I asked Dev to demonstrate once, then copied his slow movements. The car landed squarely between the lines. I grabbed my apron and headed inside.

Jonah’s first highway lesson began with a chorus of horns behind the learner car. His instructor, Petra, directed him toward the entrance ramp, where traffic streamed past in bright, impatient ribbons. Jonah checked the mirror, checked it again, and waited until the opening disappeared. Petra said they could go on the next gap. He flexed his hands on the wheel, then adjusted his grip, then asked whether the next gap might arrive before sunset. Petra gave him a level look and pointed to a space opening ahead. Jonah pressed the accelerator. The car joined the traffic with room to spare. His shoulders stayed high as they settled into the lane, and he kept glancing at the speedometer. When Petra praised his merge, he answered by asking how many more exits they had to practice.

My instructor, Luis, had promised an easy lesson in the suburbs, but every street seemed to contain a stop sign hidden behind a tree. I braked at one, rolled forward, and stopped again when Luis reminded me to look both ways. “I did look,” I said, turning my head toward him for emphasis. He pointed toward the cross street I had missed. I pressed my tongue against my teeth and scanned the road once more. A dog walker waited on the sidewalk while I completed the turn at a speed usually reserved for parades. At the next corner, I called out each sign before Luis could mention it. He folded his arms and let me lead. I made the turn cleanly, then asked if he could find a route with fewer leafy obstacles.

Nia’s instructor had chosen a hill for the day’s practice, though the street was lined with parked cars and impatient delivery drivers. Each time Nia stopped, the car rolled backward an inch before she found the gas. Omar explained the handbrake again, patiently drawing a diagram on the lesson sheet. Nia stared at the diagram until the pencil point tore the paper. A van behind them gave a brief honk. She set the brake, checked the mirror, and tried the hill start once more. This time the car held steady, then climbed. Omar smiled and said she had it. Nia eased into a side street and parked. She handed him the torn sheet, wiped her palms on her trousers, and asked to spend the rest of the lesson on flat ground.

I had thought parallel parking was mostly a matter of turning the wheel at the right moment. My instructor, Hana, had me repeat the maneuver beside a row of empty spaces until the curb looked like it was following us. On attempt four, I mounted it. On attempt five, I stopped several feet from it. Hana’s quiet “a little closer” made me stare at the dashboard as if it might offer another option. I repositioned the car, checked the mirror, and began again, counting each turn aloud. A bus slowed behind us, and I heard its air brakes sigh. My face warmed. Somehow, the car slid into the space with a clean little pause. Hana marked the lesson sheet. I asked her to write down that the curb had been unusually difficult.

After three weeks of lessons, Bram still mixed up the turn signal and the windshield wipers. His instructor, Elise, watched rain begin to bead across the glass as the wipers swept back and forth beneath a clear patch of sky. Bram switched them off, found the signal, and turned into the school parking lot. Elise asked him to stop by the painted arrows. He stopped beside the arrows, not on them. She pointed to the correct space, and he guided the car forward with exaggerated care. When the tires finally lined up, Elise said, “There you go.” Bram looked at the wiper switch, then at the signal stalk, and rubbed his forehead with the heel of his hand. He asked for five minutes to label both controls with removable tape before they went back onto the road.

My instructor, Farah, said the downtown route would be useful practice, which sounded less convincing after I met a tangle of buses, cyclists, and a taxi nosing into my lane. I tried to follow her directions while a pedestrian waved me on and the navigation voice announced a turn too late. Farah repeated the instruction, slower this time. I raised one finger to ask her to wait, then concentrated on the street signs until the right one appeared. We circled the block because I missed the turn. The second time, I caught it, signaled early, and eased into the correct lane. Farah praised my awareness. I gave the navigation screen a long look and asked if it could learn to speak before the turn instead of after it.

Priya’s lesson took place on a country road where the pavement narrowed without warning and sheep gathered behind a stone wall. Her instructor, Malcolm, asked her to keep a steady speed. Then he asked her to slow for a bend, then accelerate once it straightened. Priya followed each direction, but the speed kept drifting a few miles above or below the target. Malcolm tapped the speedometer with one finger. She loosened her jaw and began reciting the numbers on the roadside markers. At the next bend, she braked smoothly and kept the car well within its lane. A sheep watched from the wall as they passed. Priya glanced at Malcolm, who was writing on his clipboard, and asked whether the sheep had been assigned to grade her steering.

The driving school’s compact car smelled of lemon cleaner and old coffee, and my instructor, Kenji, had me practice three-point turns on a narrow residential street. I turned the wheel, reversed, and discovered a recycling bin directly behind us. Kenji had me stop before we touched it. I looked at the bin, then at the tiny space between our bumper and the curb. “We’ll reset,” he said. I reached for the wheel, paused, and shook out my cramped hand. The second attempt took so long that a neighbor came outside to collect the bin. I thanked her through the open window and started again. This time, the car turned around cleanly. Kenji made a note on his clipboard. I asked if the bin could receive its own lesson credit.

At the airport road, Mateo’s instructor, June, wanted him to practice following directions through several lanes of traffic. The lesson began well, until a sign announced a temporary detour and the route changed twice in a minute. June pointed left; the marked lane seemed to point right. Mateo blinked at the arrows, then looked at June, who was studying her map. He eased the car into a safe turnout. “Let’s figure it out before we move,” he said, with careful politeness and both hands resting flat on the wheel. June traced the route and found that the detour had changed again. Mateo waited while a line of cars streamed by, drumming one fingertip against his knee. When they finally set off, he followed the signs instead of the map and asked June to keep the directions brief.

I’d been cleared to jog for exactly six minutes, which felt less like training and more like being allowed to borrow my own legs. At the park, I set my watch, took three careful strides, and stopped when the repaired tendon tugged. My physiotherapist had warned me not to test it, so I walked a lap while two teenagers sprinted past, laughing. The watch beeped before I’d reached the far bench. I slapped its button harder than necessary and sat down. A gust flipped the rehab sheet from my pocket into a puddle. I fished it out, wiped mud from the little diagrams, and read the instructions again, as if they might have changed. They hadn’t. At home, I iced my ankle, then lined up my shoes for tomorrow’s six minutes. I wanted to throw them into the cupboard. Instead, I loosened the laces and set the timer.

Nia had expected the rowing machine to welcome her back with a satisfying pull. Instead, her shoulder tightened halfway through the first set, and the coach waved her to a stop. She lowered the handle with a clatter, then stared at the screen: barely three hundred meters. The team’s boats hissed over the water outside, each stroke flashing past the boathouse windows. Nia rolled her shoulder and asked whether the machine was set too low. The coach checked it, then suggested she follow the recovery plan. She gave a short nod and tugged at the tape around her wrist until one corner peeled loose. After practice, she carried the oars to storage, though she’d been told to leave them. Their smooth shafts pressed against her injured side. At the doorway, she paused, returned them to the rack, and walked back to the therapy room with her hands jammed into her jacket pockets.

My first day back on the basketball court began with a whistle and ended with me counting wall passes. The surgeon had repaired my knee; the trainer had forbidden jumping. Each bounce sounded louder than it should, especially when I watched the rest of the squad run drills. I passed to the wall, caught the ball, and passed again. On the ninth repetition, it rolled beneath the bleachers. I limped after it, then stopped when the knee pinched. A teammate fetched the ball without comment, which somehow made the moment worse. I snapped, “I can get it,” though he was already holding it out. He shrugged and returned to practice. I took a breath, checked the brace straps, and resumed my passes. By the time the gym lights clicked off, the ball had left a red mark on my palms. I kept it tucked under my arm all the way home.

At forty-two, Mateo was the oldest runner in his neighborhood club, but nobody had told his fractured foot that. The bone had healed, and his doctor had approved short walks. On the first outing, Mateo found the group waiting at the corner, shoes bright and laces snug. He tried to keep pace, but the others moved ahead while he measured each block. A delivery van parked across the curb cut, forcing him to detour around a stack of crates. He muttered at the obstacle and tapped his cane against the pavement. One runner slowed to accompany him. Mateo waved him onward, then regretted the gesture when the group vanished around the bend. He stopped beneath a streetlamp, checked the swelling, and read the clinic’s exercise card. The walk was still progress, the card said. He folded it into his pocket with a sharp crease and chose the longer route home.

The pool smelled exactly as it had before my shoulder surgery, which seemed unfair. I stood at the lane’s edge while the swim coach demonstrated the gentle stroke I was allowed to try. My arm entered the water awkwardly, and the first lap took longer than the warm-up used to. At the wall, I looked up at the clock, then down at my hand, as though either had caused the delay. The next swimmer touched the tiles behind me. I pressed myself into the corner and let him pass, jaw clenched around a mouthful of chlorinated water. “Take your time,” the coach called. I nodded, but my fingers squeezed the lane rope until it bit into my skin. After five laps, I climbed out and dried off. My towel caught on the locker handle; I yanked it free, folded it carefully, and scheduled another session.

Luz had spent six months rehabilitating the wrist she broke during a climbing competition. When she finally returned to the gym, the easiest route was marked with bright green tape. She chalked her hands, grabbed the first hold, and stopped almost immediately. Her wrist wobbled. From the mat, her younger brother offered a suggestion about foot placement. Luz climbed down without answering, then adjusted the tape on her brace even though it was already straight. The route setter passed by and said the holds could be changed if she needed. She looked at the wall, where every grip seemed smaller than she remembered. “I’m fine,” she said, too quickly. Then she picked a lower traverse and completed it one careful move at a time. At the last hold, she dropped onto the mat, shook out her hand, and asked the setter to leave the green route up for next week.

I had imagined my return to tennis as a cinematic moment: serve, ace, applause. Instead, the first ball I hit after my calf strain sailed into the fence and stuck in a patch of ivy. My coach told me to practice short steps, not chase it. I stood with my racket hanging from one hand, watching the ball twitch in the leaves whenever the wind moved. “Can we use another?” I asked. He tossed one over. It bounced at my feet while I was still staring at the fence. I kicked it back, then winced at the sudden pull in my leg. The coach lowered his basket and reminded me why we were keeping the session easy. I tightened the strings on my grip, loosened them again, and began the footwork drill. Afterward, I drove home in silence, the abandoned ball still visible through the court gate.

Dev’s ankle had finally healed enough for him to rejoin the cricket club, but the captain assigned him to scorekeeping. The scoreboard numbers seemed to crawl while the others ran between wickets. Dev sat beneath the pavilion awning, pencil tapping against the book. When a batter glanced over and asked for the score, Dev answered without looking up. Then he discovered he had recorded a run twice and had to cross out the neat column. The pencil snapped in his fingers. He stared at the broken halves, set them down, and borrowed another from the tea table. During the next break, he asked the captain whether he could bowl a few gentle deliveries. The captain pointed to Dev’s support brace and said they would review it next week. Dev shut the scorebook, opened it again, and carefully corrected the total before the players returned to the field.

My ski coach had promised that the beginner slope would be quiet on a weekday. It was, except for the lift stopping every few minutes and a child who kept dropping a mitten in the loading area. I was recovering from a torn ligament, so my first runs had to be slow and controlled. Each time I reached the bottom, I unclipped my skis and waited while the line shuffled forward. My repaired knee felt sturdy; my patience did not. When the lift paused again, I planted my poles in the snow and watched the empty chair swing above me. A worker asked if I wanted to rest. I said I’d just gotten started, though the hill had been holding me for nearly an hour. At the top, I took the marked route, turned carefully, and finished without falling. I brushed snow from my gloves and joined the queue once more.

At the baseball field, Jonah returned after surgery on his throwing elbow and discovered his old position belonged to a rookie. The coach handed him a bucket of practice balls and asked him to toss them underhand. Jonah’s first throw bounced before the plate. He collected it, walked back, and threw again, slower this time. From the dugout came the crack of a bat and a burst of cheers. Jonah’s shoulders rose toward his ears. He lined the remaining balls in a row, then kicked one out of place with his cleat. The coach reminded him that rebuilding strength took time. Jonah wiped his palm on his pants and asked how much time, exactly. There was no answer he liked. He finished the bucket, gathering every ball before heading to the bench. On the way, he stopped to watch the rookie’s next pitch, arms folded tight across his chest.

I’d been out of cycling for months after a collision left my collarbone plated, and now my first ride was a loop around the neighborhood. My sister came along, insisting we keep the pace gentle. At every hill, I shifted gears so early that the chain clanked. On the third climb, a loose dog barked from behind a fence, and I braked hard enough to wobble. My sister called to check on me. “I know how to ride,” I said, though I was gripping the handlebars until my knuckles paled. We stopped at a corner store. I peeled off one glove, rubbed the scar beneath my jersey, and stared at the bikes locked outside. The ride home was slower still. When my computer announced we had covered only four miles, I pressed the button until the display went blank. Then I leaned my bike against the wall and charged its lights.

Sandeep had been training for a fencing tournament when a hamstring tear forced him off the piste. Now, cleared for light footwork, he returned to the club and found the younger athletes practicing fast advances. His own steps were small and deliberate. The coach placed a strip of tape on the floor for him to follow. Sandeep missed it twice, then lifted his mask and looked at the clock. Practice had barely begun. He shook out his leg, tugged his jacket straight, and asked if he could try the sequence again. The coach said yes, but reminded him to stop if the muscle pulled. Sandeep completed the pattern at half speed. When another fencer crossed behind him, he halted and let out a breath through his nose. He gathered his equipment, returned the mask to its hook, and wrote the next therapy appointment on his phone before leaving.

I arrived at the licensing office before sunrise, carrying every form listed on its website in a folder sorted by color. By nine, the line had advanced exactly three floor tiles. A child kept kicking the back of my shoe, and the ticket display blinked the same number as if it were proud of itself. When I reached the counter, the clerk pointed to a box I had left blank. I filled it in on the ledge, pressing so hard the pen nearly tore the paper, then returned to the end of the line. My phone battery dropped to four percent. I called my supervisor and explained that I would be late, while watching another window close for lunch. At last, a guard announced that the printer was down. I folded my folder shut with a sharp snap and stared at the ceiling.

At the county benefits office, Marisol stood beneath a clock that had stopped at 10:17. She had brought her toddler, a bottle, two snacks, and a stack of documents sealed against the rain. Whenever the queue shuffled forward, she lifted the stroller over a strip of cracked flooring, then maneuvered it back when someone squeezed past. A clerk called a number three ahead of hers, disappeared, and left the window empty. Marisol rubbed the bridge of her nose and checked the same appointment slip for the fifth time. Her son dropped a cracker; she picked it up, gave him the last clean one, and watched the line swell behind them. When the clerk finally returned, he asked for a photocopy she had been told was unnecessary. Marisol set her jaw, gathered the papers, and asked where the nearest copy machine was.

I took a day off work to replace my damaged passport, only to find the government office packed clear to the entrance. The number machine was out of tickets, so a security guard handed me a handwritten scrap with 86 on it. A man behind me insisted he had arrived first; we compared watches like detectives, while the line curled around a rack of old pamphlets. My knees began to ache. Each time the display chimed, it showed a number nowhere near ours. I asked at the information desk whether appointments had a separate queue, and the clerk pointed vaguely toward the same crowd. When my turn finally came, I slid my forms across the counter. The clerk noticed a missing signature and pushed them back. I uncapped my pen, signed with a cramped hand, and took one slow breath before joining the line again.

Gideon had driven two hours to the regional tax office, where a notice on the door promised quick service. Inside, he found one open window and a line stretching past the water fountain. He balanced a metal lunch tin on his knees while a television played a silent weather forecast. Every few minutes, someone asked whether the queue was for payments or appeals, and the attendant repeated the same answer without looking up. Gideon’s coffee went cold. When a woman slipped ahead claiming she only needed to ask a question, he tapped the numbered ticket in his palm and pointed toward the back. She sighed loudly; he answered with a clipped, “We’re all waiting.” After nearly three hours, his number appeared. The clerk informed him that the payment system had gone offline, and Gideon folded the notice into a tiny square, then unfolded it again.

I needed a residency certificate before my lease renewal, so I joined the line at city hall with a folder and a carefully rehearsed explanation. The queue moved in bursts: three people at once, then nothing for twenty minutes. A wall fan clicked with every turn, stirring the smell of wet coats and old carpet. I leaned against a pillar until a guard told me that spot was reserved for wheelchair access. I moved, apologized, and shifted my weight from one foot to the other. When a family near the front began sorting documents across the chairs, I watched the empty seats vanish. My number was finally called, but I had misheard it over the fan and missed the window. The clerk waved me back to the ticket machine. I pressed its button harder than necessary, caught the new slip before it fell, and returned to the line.

Ravi brought his mother to the immigration office for a records update, arriving with a thermos and a cushion for her chair. The queue barely fit inside the building, and the afternoon sun turned the glass doors into a bright wall. He asked the receptionist how long the wait might be; she glanced at the crowd and said she could not predict it. His mother’s appointment paper softened in her hand as she fanned herself with it. Ravi checked the online portal, which still listed them as not checked in, although they had been there since morning. When he returned to the desk, the receptionist asked him to repeat the case number. He recited it slowly, syllable by syllable, while his fingers drummed against the thermos. A new sign appeared: “Service temporarily delayed.” Ravi read it twice, then carefully folded the paper before helping his mother stand.

I went to the municipal records office to correct one letter in my birth certificate. The line seemed to orbit the room without ever reaching the counter. A fluorescent tube above me flickered, and a man nearby kept narrating every movement of the queue as if calling a race. When the ticket display froze, several people stood up at once. I stayed seated, gripping my number until its corners bent. At the window, the clerk asked for proof of the spelling I had been using my whole life. I showed her an old school record, then an expired library card, then the original certificate with the error. She pushed each item back and asked for something else. I looked at the clock and heard my parking meter ticking in my imagination. Finally, she wrote down a website address. I copied it neatly, though my pen scratched through the paper.

Nadine had taken the bus across town to renew her food vendor permit, hauling a cooler of samples she could not leave unattended. The licensing office line passed a row of numbered chairs, all occupied by people holding envelopes. She stood near the wall, keeping one hand on the cooler handle while the other checked the time. A man at the desk said the forms had changed last month, though the old version was still stacked beside him. Nadine picked up a fresh packet and found the same questions in a different order. She pinched the bridge of her nose, then asked whether she could complete it while waiting. “If you can write standing up,” the clerk replied. She filled in the pages against the cooler lid, correcting a smudge with her sleeve. When a chair opened, someone else claimed it. Nadine tucked the forms under her arm and kept standing.

I had promised my daughter I would collect her school records before the afternoon pickup, but the education department’s service hall had only two working windows. I joined the line behind a man carrying a birdcage, its occupant chirping whenever the number display beeped. The air smelled of damp wool and printer toner. I watched the minute hand crawl, then checked my phone and saw three messages from the school. Each time a clerk called a number, someone searched a pocket or bag while the rest of us waited. At the counter, I explained that I needed a sealed transcript. The clerk asked for a form available only at another desk, where a second queue had formed. I let out a breath through my teeth, walked over, and took a fresh ticket. The paper crumpled in my fist before I smoothed it against my knee.

Otto, a retired carpenter, carried a neat stack of pension documents to the district office. He had written each appointment detail in a pocket notebook, yet the receptionist told him his booking was for the previous Tuesday. Otto turned the page toward her and pointed to the date. She shrugged and directed him to the walk-in queue, where the last chair was missing a leg. He stood with both hands resting on his cane, listening to a printer jam and a phone ring unanswered. A young man offered to let him go ahead, but the attendant said everyone had to follow ticket order. Otto nodded, though his mouth tightened. After two hours, the clerk asked for a document already clipped to the top of the stack. Otto unclipped it, placed it squarely on the counter, and said, “Here it is, just where I showed you.”

I came to the public housing office with a folder of rent receipts and a stomach that had been empty since breakfast. The line reached the stairwell, where a hand-lettered sign warned us not to block the exit. I shifted against the railing whenever someone passed, keeping my place with one shoe on the landing. A baby cried below me; upstairs, a copier coughed out blank sheets. My caseworker had told me the review would take ten minutes, but the clock showed I had already spent two hours waiting. When I reached the reception window, the clerk said my file was in another building. I asked whether anyone had called ahead, and she repeated that I should wait for a supervisor. My jaw ached from holding it still. I sat on the floor beside my folder and arranged the receipts by date, one more time.

Selene arrived at the vehicle registration office with a borrowed car and a deadline printed in red ink. The queue snaked between plastic stanchions, while a ceiling speaker announced numbers in a voice that crackled at the end of every sentence. She had brought the title, insurance card, emissions report, and proof of address, each tucked into a labeled sleeve. A clerk inspected the stack, then asked for a second proof of address. Selene opened her bag and produced a utility bill, though her fingers struggled with the zipper. The clerk said the bill was too old by three days. Selene stared at the date, then at the sign listing accepted documents. “That sign doesn’t say that,” she said, keeping her voice level. The clerk reached for the next ticket. Selene gathered her papers slowly, as if any sudden movement might scatter the whole day across the floor.

When the lights went out, I was halfway through making soup for the block’s potluck, with three neighbors already waiting in my kitchen. I tried the breaker, then the flashlight app, then the breaker again, as if repetition might persuade it. “The building’s gone dark,” said Mr. Alvarez from the hallway, holding a candle that dripped onto his sleeve. I set the pot on the cold stove and took a breath through my nose. The soup could wait; the elevator could not, because Mrs. Kim was upstairs with a walker and a grocery bag. I climbed six flights, stopping twice to untangle my phone cord from my pocket. By the time I reached her, she had packed the groceries into a laundry basket and was ready to descend. We carried it together, while my abandoned pot sat below, steadily cooling into a very expensive vegetable arrangement.

Darnell had just settled his toddler for a nap when the power cut out, waking the child with the sudden silence. He checked the fuse box, then the utility company’s map, which showed his street cheerfully lit in green. Outside, every porch was dark. His neighbor called from across the walk to ask if he had a spare extension cord, and Darnell stared at the cord in his hand, useless without electricity. He pressed his lips together and set it down carefully. The toddler began crying again. Darnell paced the living room, testing the light switch twice before remembering what had happened. When Mrs. Patel knocked with a battery lantern, he opened the door so quickly it banged against the wall. They gathered the children in her cooler basement, where the air was calm and the grown-ups could compare outage reports. Darnell kept refreshing his phone, though no new information appeared.

I had planned to finish hemming a client’s wedding dress before dinner, but the outage turned my sewing room into a dim box full of unfinished seams. My neighbor, Len, came over carrying a camping lantern and asked whether I knew why his freezer was humming no longer. I explained that none of us knew, then heard myself give the explanation again when he asked if the power company had called. I tugged the measuring tape straight, though it had not twisted, and moved the dress toward the window. A delivery truck crawled past without stopping; the driver had brought the replacement batteries I’d ordered. I stood on the porch and waved until he backed up. Len held the lantern while I worked by the gray afternoon light, and we traded updates with the other houses. At last, the machine beeped back to life, right as I snipped a thread too short.

At seventy-eight, Ruth had learned to keep a kettle ready, but the outage arrived just before her weekly tea with the neighbors. The electric kettle clicked uselessly, and her small radio faded into static. She pressed its buttons one after another, then placed it on the counter with deliberate care. Across the courtyard, young Mateo was waving a phone with a bright screen. Ruth went out to ask whether the utility crew had given an estimate. He had none, only a map that spun around whenever he tried to zoom in. Ruth looked at the screen, then at the dark windows above them. “That map seems to be enjoying itself,” she said. The neighbors brought chairs into the shared garden, and she found a thermos of hot water from the morning. She poured tea for everyone, including Mateo, who finally stopped tapping his phone long enough to sit down.

The outage began while I was leading a remote pottery class, my hands thick with clay and six students waiting for instructions on their frozen screens. I wiped my fingers on my apron and called my neighbor, who had a generator for his workshop. He was using it to keep a fish tank running, so there went my plan to power the router. I stared at the blank laptop, then at the half-formed bowl collapsing on the wheel. Outside, people were gathering near the mailboxes, each holding a phone at a different angle, searching for a signal. I carried my clay to the porch and gave the class from there, shouting directions whenever someone’s connection flickered back. A child across the street asked if we were making “darkness pots.” I nearly laughed, but instead pressed the clay back into shape. The students finished their pieces by lantern light, and none of us pretended the lesson had gone as planned.

Nadia was carrying a birthday cake through the apartment lobby when the power failed, leaving the elevator stalled between floors. Her neighbor’s son was inside, calling through the doors that he was fine but wanted out immediately. Nadia set the cake on the mail table and took out her phone to call building maintenance. The line placed her on hold with cheerful music, which she silenced after four bars. She checked the emergency instructions posted beside the elevator, then read them again while the boy rattled the doors. “Please don’t try to pry them,” she called, keeping her voice level. A superintendent arrived with a key and released him safely. Nadia retrieved the cake, now slightly tilted from its journey, and carried it upstairs by the stairwell. On each landing another neighbor asked what had happened. By the time she reached the party, the candles were in her pocket and the frosting had slid against one side.

I was halfway through an online exam when the lights snapped off and my laptop began counting down its battery. The apartment’s backup lamp blinked once, then died. I took my notes and ran next door, where my neighbor Sora had a power bank, but its cable fit neither my computer nor my stubborn little adapter. I turned the plugs around, checked them, and tried once more. Sora offered to drive me to the library, which had a generator, but the street was already filling with cars and confused residents. I packed everything into my bag, including the adapter that had accomplished nothing. On the walk, we passed a man trying to charge his phone from a parked car while holding the door open with his foot. The library’s lights were bright enough to hurt. I sat down, opened the exam page, and discovered the timer had expired during the outage.

Harold had promised the people in his duplex that he would repair the shared porch light before the evening walk. Then the neighborhood lost power, and the porch vanished into darkness along with the rest of the block. He took his toolbox outside and found three neighbors standing around the dead fixture, each offering a different theory. Harold listened, nodded, and climbed the short ladder anyway. The bulb was fine; the whole circuit was out. He lowered the ladder with a long scrape and rubbed the bridge of his nose. One neighbor asked whether he could fix the streetlight too. Harold looked down the black road, where a cyclist was carefully steering around a recycling bin. Instead of answering, he fetched a battery lantern and set it on the porch rail. The neighbors arranged more lanterns along the walkway, turning the job into a small chain of lights. Harold’s toolbox stayed shut for once.

The power failed just as I had started a video call with my sister, who lives three time zones away and had finally found a free evening. My screen went black, and the router’s lights disappeared one by one. I walked to the window, lifted my phone high, and got one bar before it vanished. My neighbor came into the hallway carrying a portable radio, but its weather report was about a county two hundred miles away. I asked him to try another station; he turned the dial so slowly that the static seemed to grow in stages. With my coat still on, I went outside and found several residents comparing outage notices. None explained why our building was dark while the supermarket across the avenue glowed. I left my sister a voice message, then another when the first failed to send. She called back an hour later, and I answered from the stairwell where the signal finally held.

Mei was baking bread for the community pantry when the oven shut off, leaving two loaves pale and heavy in their tins. She checked the wall clock, though its hands had stopped, and then opened the oven door as if the heat might have returned while she blinked. Across the hall, her neighbor Jamal was trying to keep his aquarium aerated with a hand pump. Mei carried the dough and tins to the building’s courtyard, where residents had gathered around a portable grill. The grill was too small for bread, but Jamal’s cousin had brought a camp stove, and everyone began proposing ways to finish the loaves. Mei listened, then pointed out that the dough still needed warmth, not another committee. She set the tins near the stove and wrapped them in towels. The bread rose unevenly, but by nightfall the neighbors had enough to share, and Mei finally sat down.

I had just brought home a week’s groceries when the outage took the lights and the elevator at once. Two bags split on the lobby floor, sending oranges rolling beneath the mailboxes. My neighbor, a teenager named Eli, helped me chase them while I checked whether the elevator had stopped between floors. It had. Someone inside pressed the alarm button repeatedly, producing a tiny metallic chirp that seemed to echo through the whole building. I called the superintendent, got voicemail, and left a message so clipped I had to call back and repeat the apartment number. Eli carried the remaining bags upstairs while I stayed by the elevator and spoke to the trapped passenger through the doors. Maintenance arrived twenty minutes later. When the doors opened, the passenger stepped out holding a potted fern and asked if anyone had seen a grocery bag. I pointed to the oranges still rolling near the stairs.

Salma’s corner store lost power during the evening rush, just as a line of customers formed at the register. The card reader went blank, the refrigerator fans stopped, and the automatic door froze halfway open. She switched on a flashlight and asked everyone to wait while she checked the breaker. Her neighbor, Mr. Boyd, appeared with a folding chair and began directing people away from the narrow entrance. Salma tried to explain that she could not accept cards offline, then repeated it when a customer held out a phone as though that might change the machine’s mind. She kept her voice polite, but her jaw tightened as she counted cash by flashlight. Mr. Boyd wrote prices on a scrap of cardboard and helped her keep track of purchases. When the lights came back, the register rebooted with a loud chime. Salma looked at the queue, picked up the cardboard, and started the totals again.

I refreshed the grades page so many times that the little wheel seemed to be laughing at me. My biology score finally appeared, but the page listed a blank beside the lab section that I had submitted weeks ago. I opened the course portal, found the receipt, and sent it to my instructor with a careful note. While I waited, my tea went cold and the laundry buzzer sounded twice. The reply arrived: the score had been entered under the wrong student. I stared at the corrected grade, then at the message asking me to confirm it. My fingers hovered over the keyboard. I typed “Confirmed,” deleted it, and typed it again. At least the number was right now. I closed the laptop with both hands, as if it might otherwise spring open and offer one more surprise.

Marisol checked her chemistry grade between customers at the bakery, balancing her phone beside a tray of cooling conchas. The page took ages to load, then showed a score far below what she expected. She tapped the details. One answer had been marked wrong because the system rejected a minus sign typed in a different font. Her jaw tightened. She sent a screenshot to the teaching assistant, wiped flour from her hands, and served three customers before a reply came. “The software is picky,” the message said, with no promise to change anything. Marisol let out a breath through her nose and opened the course handbook, searching for the grading policy. When she found the relevant line, she forwarded it with a neat explanation. The bakery oven chimed behind her. She slid in another batch, then watched her inbox instead of the timer.

I logged in from the bus, expecting to see my history exam result before my stop. The portal demanded a password reset, then rejected the new password for containing a word it had never warned me about. A man beside me shifted as I muttered at the screen. At last, the grade appeared: a number that did not match the rubric notes my professor had given me. I scrolled through the comments, finding praise for my essay and a deduction for a missing page that was plainly attached. The bus lurched, and my thumb hit the wrong button, sending me back to the login screen. I squeezed the phone until its case creaked. At the next stop, I stepped onto the sidewalk, opened the attachment on my laptop, and drafted a message with every detail listed in order. The bus pulled away before I finished.

Devon had just finished a night shift at the hospital when he checked his calculus grade in the staff lounge. The screen showed a zero for an online quiz he remembered completing during his break. He rubbed the bridge of his nose and searched his email for the submission receipt. There it was, timestamped precisely before the deadline. The course site, however, claimed he had started but never pressed submit. Devon forwarded the receipt to his professor, then refreshed the page, though he knew that would change nothing. A coworker asked whether he was all right. “Apparently my answers vanished into the academic void,” he said, too sharply, and immediately apologized. He packed his lunch container, found the professor’s office hours, and added them to his calendar. Before leaving, he checked the portal once more. The zero sat there, perfectly unmoved.

I checked my economics grade in the laundromat while my clothes circled behind me. The site showed “pending” for nearly a minute, then flashed a score with no explanation. I knew I had answered the final question correctly; I had even written out the calculation in the margin. The posted solution used a different rounding rule, one never mentioned in class. I read the question again, then read it a third time, my damp sock forgotten in my hand. The spin cycle rattled like a small engine. I drafted a message asking where the rule came from, deleted the sentence that sounded too sharp, and tried again. My washer stopped. I moved the clothes to a dryer, returned to my phone, and saw the same number waiting. I folded one shirt with unnecessary precision before sending the note.
