I set the cup on a ledge and tried to wipe the stain with a napkin, but the paper tore into damp scraps. A station employee told me the delay would be ten minutes. I nodded, though I had heard her clearly the first time. I checked the machine’s receipt, folded it into smaller and smaller squares, and watched the clock advance.

When the train began to leave, Anika ran with her camera bouncing against her chest. She had spent the afternoon photographing an old neighborhood before it was demolished, and her memory card held the final images. The train was supposed to take her to the exhibition opening, where the pictures were due that evening. She reached the platform too late and sprinted beside the carriage, one hand raised, the other clamped around the camera strap. The last window slid past. Anika stopped beneath a departure sign and opened her camera to check the card, although she had checked it moments earlier. Every photograph was still there; the problem was the clock. She let out a breath through her nose and tightened the strap until it bit her shoulder. A taxi pulled up outside the station. She gathered her equipment and hurried toward it, muttering the address as she went.

I pushed the aluminum boat off the gravel before sunrise, certain the new depth finder would finally show where the trout gathered. Instead, its screen blinked and went black. I tapped the casing, checked the battery, then checked it again, harder each time, while the lake turned silver around me. My line tangled in the rod holder as I reached for the spare fuse. A loon called from the reeds, and I answered with a sharp breath through my nose. At the launch, my brother had promised the device was ready. I pictured his confident grin and muttered something I would not repeat at supper. The fish were surely down there, beyond the reach of guesswork. I lowered the anchor, watched it drag across the bottom, and hauled it back with both hands. By the time the screen flickered on, the best light had already slipped behind a bank of clouds.

At sixty-eight, Beatrice knew every bend of the lake’s eastern shore, but the new motor refused to start when she eased away from the dock at dawn. She pulled the cord once, then again, each time leaning farther over the stern. The engine coughed and died. Her thermos rolled under the bench, spilling coffee across a folded map. Beatrice pressed her lips together and wiped the mess with her sleeve, though the stain only spread. A pair of early kayakers glided past without looking over. She tried the choke, counted to three, and yanked the cord so fiercely that her shoulder twinged. At last the motor caught, sputtering like a stubborn old stove. She steered toward her favorite cove, shoulders still tight, and found a floating branch lodged against the propeller. Beatrice shut off the engine and stared at the pale sky before reaching for her gloves.

I left the cabin at four-thirty with my grandfather’s cedar rod wrapped in a towel. The lake lay quiet beneath the first strip of pink, and I had promised myself one clean cast before work. My lure snagged on the dock railing. I tugged gently, then jerked it free so abruptly that it shot into the water without its hook. For a moment I stood holding the bare line, jaw clenched, while the reel clicked uselessly. I rummaged through my tackle tin and found three kinds of bait but no spare hooks. The wind nudged the boat against its mooring, knocking the hull against the pier in a steady, hollow rhythm. I kicked the dock post, regretted it when my toe hurt, and sat down to tie a knot with cold fingers. A fish rolled beyond casting distance. I watched the rings widen, then narrowed my eyes at the empty line.

Ravi had driven two hours to fish the lake before dawn, bringing a carefully packed breakfast and a weather forecast that promised calm water. By the time he launched, gusts were already pushing the boat sideways. He rowed toward the sheltered inlet, grunting whenever the oars slipped from their locks. Each time he settled into a rhythm, a gust turned the bow again. His cap blew off and landed near the reeds; he snatched it back with a wet sleeve and shoved it beneath the seat. The first cast tangled around a branch. Ravi reeled in, unwound the line, and glanced at his watch. The minutes seemed to be vanishing in plain sight. When he finally dropped the lure into open water, a wave slapped the side and soaked his breakfast bag. He pressed the soggy bread flat, set it aside, and rowed on, refusing to head back before he had tried the far cove.

I had saved for months to bring my daughter to the lake at dawn, but she woke with a fever and my neighbor canceled at the last minute. I went alone anyway, carrying the bright orange tackle box she had packed for me. The latch stuck. I worked at it with a thumbnail until it snapped open and sent bobbers skittering across the boat floor. One rolled into the bilge. I reached for it, bumped my elbow, and knocked the thermos over. The coffee spread beneath the seat while the shoreline brightened without a sound. I set the box upright and arranged the lures in the careful order she had chosen. Then I cast toward the reeds. The line caught on something almost at once. I pulled, paused, and pulled again, keeping my teeth together as the rod bowed. When the line broke, I stared at the empty water and began tying on another lure.

Marta launched her small skiff before sunrise, hoping to catch perch for the café she ran in town. The lake was smooth, but her old outboard coughed whenever she slowed to troll. She adjusted the throttle by a hair, and the engine roared loud enough to scatter birds from the marsh. Her hands tightened around the tiller. A customer’s note, tucked in her pocket, listed an order for fresh fish by noon; she could almost hear him asking whether she had managed it. Marta shut off the motor and drifted, counting breaths while a row of bubbles rose beside the hull. Then she restarted it, eased the throttle forward, and watched the needle jump. She slapped the dashboard with an open palm. The sound startled her more than the engine did. When a perch finally took the bait, she hauled it aboard too quickly and dropped it between her boots. She bent down, retrieved it, and wiped her hands on her apron.

My first morning fishing alone began with a promise from the rental shop that the lake would be easy to navigate. At dawn, fog erased the far shore, and the map on my phone spun in circles. I held the device high, turned around twice, and watched the blue dot wander somewhere behind me. The battery warning appeared just as I tried to zoom in. I set the phone in a dry bag, then had to fish it out again when the zipper jammed. A sharp crease formed between my eyebrows. Somewhere ahead, a bell buoy rang, but the sound seemed to move as the mist shifted. I rowed toward it, stopped, and rowed back toward the reeds, refusing to admit I had lost the launch. My paddle scraped stone. I let it rest across my knees and listened until I heard traffic from the road. Then I followed the faint engine noise home, the bait untouched.

Hector reached the lake while the sky was still dark, carrying a hand-built rod he had spent the winter repairing. He tied on a lure, made one practice cast, and watched the line whip around the tip. His knot had slipped. He cut away the tangled section and started over, fingers stiff in the chilly air. A neighboring fisherman offered a suggestion from his boat. Hector nodded without looking up, then tried the knot again, pulling it tight with his teeth. The line snapped. He dropped the clippers onto the floor and rubbed his thumb where the braid had bitten into it. Pale light spread along the water, and the morning seemed to be moving on without him. He could have borrowed a spare rig, but pride kept his hands busy. On the fourth attempt, the knot held. Hector cast toward the reeds; the lure landed short, splashing beside his own boat.

I took my grandfather’s battered rowboat onto the lake at dawn, eager to prove I could manage it without his help. The left oar kept slipping from its lock. I tightened the wing nut, tested it, and heard the same clack a few strokes later. Each time it dropped, the boat turned in a slow circle. I muttered at the oar as if it had chosen this morning to misbehave. Across the water, the old fishing pier stood straight and steady, looking almost smug. I tied a strip of cloth around the lock, pulled the knot hard, and tried again. The oar stayed put for half a dozen strokes, then popped free and splashed into the lake. I leaned over, grabbed it by the handle, and hauled it aboard. My sleeve dripped onto the seat. After a long stare at the shoreline, I set the oar back in place and rowed on with smaller, careful strokes.

Niko, a retired bus driver, arrived at the reservoir before dawn with a bait bucket that had a hairline crack. He noticed the leak only after the worms were swimming in a puddle at his feet. He moved the bucket onto the bench, then folded an old newspaper beneath it. The paper darkened at once. Niko pressed a thumb over the crack, but the water found a way around it. He looked at the clock on the dashboard and gave a short, dry laugh. The bait shop would not open for another hour, and the fish were already rising beyond the dock. He picked out the worms that remained, arranging them in a tin cup he used for sinkers. One wriggled across his palm and dropped into the boat. Niko pinched it up with two fingers, carefully, then set his jaw and launched. He cast with what he had, glancing now and then at the growing puddle.

The lake looked inviting when I backed the trailer down the ramp in the blue-gray dawn. Then the boat’s bow slid off the rollers crooked, and the trailer tire sank into the soft edge of the launch. I put the truck in reverse, eased forward, and tried again. The wheel spun, flinging mud across the tailgate. My fishing partner was late, and my phone had no signal, so I stood with both hands on my hips, breathing through my mouth. A man loading his canoe watched from the parking lot but did not offer to help. I reached for a board in the truck bed, slipped in the muck, and came up with one muddy knee. After I wedged the board beneath the tire, the truck climbed free. The boat floated at last, but my tackle bag had tipped over and scattered hooks across the ramp. I crouched to gather them while the sun cleared the trees.

Lena had promised her son a fish for breakfast, so she guided the canoe onto the lake before the dawn mist lifted. She had packed the wrong hook size and realized it only after baiting the line. Every cast sent the worm spinning in a wide, useless arc. Her son sat at the bow, swinging his feet and asking how long fish took to wake up. Lena smiled, but her shoulders crept toward her ears. She searched the tackle pouch twice, turning out swivels, weights, and a broken pair of pliers. At last she found one small hook in the bottom seam. As she tied it on, the canoe drifted into a patch of reeds. She shoved them aside with the paddle, careful not to splash her son. The line went out again. A tug came almost immediately, followed by a sudden slackness. Lena reeled in an empty hook and looked toward the brightening shore before quietly beginning another cast.

I had arranged the paintings by color three times before the gallery lights came on, and each time the blue landscape looked wrong beside the red portrait. My assistant kept offering suggestions from the doorway while I moved the frames a fraction of an inch, then moved them back. A label printer jammed, swallowing the names of two pieces, and the ladder wobbled when I climbed up to fix a crooked hook. I climbed down hard enough to make the tools rattle. The opening was an hour away. I pressed my palms against the worktable and counted its scratches until my breathing slowed. Then I took every painting off the wall and began again, refusing to look toward the clock.

At sixty-eight, Marisol had spent months preparing her first solo exhibition in the converted train station. On installation morning, the delivery crew brought the sculptures in the wrong order, and one crate blocked the narrow passage to the main room. She pointed to the floor plan, then tapped the penciled labels with a fingernail. The crew leader shrugged and said they could return later. Marisol’s jaw tightened. She carried the smallest piece herself, though its plinth scraped the polished floor, leaving a pale streak. When a volunteer hurried over with a cloth, she waved him away, then stood very still beside the mark. After a long breath, she fetched the repair kit and redrew the layout on the wall in thick charcoal.

I am used to painting outdoors, where the weather gets a vote, but the gallery’s temperature controls had dried my newest canvases before the varnish settled. Their surfaces caught the spotlights in blunt, shiny patches. I called the technician, who promised to come after lunch, and watched the guests arrive for the preview. One woman leaned close to a painting and asked whether the streaks were intentional. I smiled without showing my teeth. In the storage room, I rolled a paintbrush between my fingers until its handle creaked. Then I returned to the gallery and shifted the lamps, one by one, testing each angle. The shine softened. I left the canvases where they were and silently rehearsed a better answer.

Theo, a self-taught sculptor from a fishing village, had built the centerpiece from driftwood collected over several winters. The gallery’s freight elevator stopped between floors with the sculpture inside, its tallest branch pressed against the ceiling. He stood in the lobby, staring at the service panel while the curator called maintenance. A printed schedule fluttered off the desk and slid beneath a bench. Theo retrieved it, flattened it against his thigh, and found his opening time circled in red. When the doors finally parted, the sculpture had lost one delicate twig. He held the broken piece in his palm, then examined the remaining branches. Instead of demanding an explanation, he fetched wire and made the repair visible, twisting the join into a small, deliberate knot.

I spent the morning writing wall labels, trimming each sentence until the descriptions fit the gallery’s narrow cards. At noon, I discovered that the printer had substituted a different font, shrinking the text until it looked like ants marching across the paper. I slapped the stack onto the table. My partner asked if I wanted help, and I said, “Unless you know how to persuade a printer, no.” The words came out sharper than I meant. I pinched the bridge of my nose, then opened the file again. The exhibition began in three hours, and there were twenty-seven labels to redo. I enlarged the type, printed one test sheet, and watched it emerge correctly. The next stack came out crooked, but at least it was readable.

Nikhil had borrowed a van to bring his photographs to a neighborhood arts center, only to find the loading entrance locked. He knocked, waited, and knocked again while rain stippled the cardboard corners of the frames. Inside, the curator waved through the glass and searched for a key. Nikhil set down the heaviest frame; its edge landed in a puddle. He wiped it with his sleeve, then paced the curb, hands buried in his coat pockets. A bus hissed past and splashed his shoes. When the door finally opened, he entered without greeting anyone and began checking every frame for water damage. One print had a cloudy corner. He took a cloth from his bag and worked at it carefully, muttering each time the mark spread.

My exhibition was supposed to open in a quiet room, but the café next door had booked a band for the same evening. Their bass thudded through the wall, rattling the glass in my framed collages. I asked the manager if the music could be lowered. He said the musicians had already started their set. I walked back and forth between the doorway and my largest piece, measuring the vibration with my fingertips against its frame. Then I dragged a padded bench across the floor, making a long squeal that drew every eye. The curator winced. I stopped, wiped my hands on my trousers, and moved the bench more carefully. We placed it along the shared wall, and its weight dulled the worst of the noise.

At twenty-two, Celeste was preparing an exhibition of hand-dyed fabrics in a university gallery. The ceiling hooks were too low, so her hanging panels pooled on the floor despite the careful measurements she had made at home. She climbed the stepladder, adjusted one clip, and watched the cloth sag again. Her lips pressed into a thin line. A classmate suggested cutting the hems, which made Celeste turn away before answering. She crouched beside the longest panel, smoothing its folds with both hands. Then she noticed a row of unused rails along the opposite wall. With the curator’s permission, she rehung the work there, threading each panel through the rails in a continuous sweep. The new arrangement took longer, but the colors finally moved freely.

I arrived at the gallery before sunrise with a box of ceramic birds and found the display tables covered in someone else’s event flyers. The cleaner said the room had been reserved for a workshop, though my booking email was pinned to the door. I stacked the flyers, then watched another pile appear when a staff member entered carrying more. My fingers curled around the cardboard box until one corner buckled. I could have raised my voice; instead, I asked for the manager and read the booking confirmation aloud, slowly. She checked the calendar and apologized. The tables were cleared, but a strip of tape left sticky tracks across the wood. I scrubbed at them with a damp cloth, pausing whenever the residue gathered under my nails.

Boris, a retired postal worker, had painted every canvas in his exhibition during the long months after his wife died. On the morning of the opening, a ceiling leak left a dark blotch above the series of garden scenes. The gallery director brought a bucket, which caught only half the drops. Boris watched the water bead on the floor, then picked up the nearest painting and carried it to safety. His knuckles whitened around the frame. He asked for plastic sheeting and received a roll too narrow to cover the wall. For several seconds he stared at it, lips moving without sound. Then he cut the roll into strips and layered them across the ceiling corner, checking each seam before he rehung the paintings.

I had planned a neat row of tiny ink drawings, but the gallery’s white walls swallowed them whole. From across the room, they looked like dust specks. I tried stronger bulbs, then darker mats, then a different spacing. Each change made the whole display feel less like mine. The curator said the room was elegant, which was not the same as saying anyone could see the work. I rubbed a thumb over a smudge on the nearest frame and left a gray streak. After cleaning it, I pulled a folding screen from storage and set it behind the drawings. Its muted green surface gave the ink somewhere to land. I stepped back, arms crossed, and waited until my shoulders dropped before deciding the arrangement could stay.

Linh had made a series of intricate paper maps for an exhibition about migration, each one folded and stitched by hand. A delivery cart struck the display case as the installers maneuvered it through the doorway. Several maps slid to the floor, and one corner tore across a stitched border. Linh knelt among the scattered pieces, gathering them with careful, quick movements. The installer kept apologizing, but she did not look up. She set the torn map on her lap and picked at the loose paper fibers. For a moment, she pressed both hands flat against the floor. Then she asked for a needle, thread, and a sheet of archival backing. The repair would remain visible, she decided, a route interrupted and mended.

I set the dripping kitchen tap on the counter between us, wrapped in a dish towel, and asked Mr. Bell for the third time when someone would come. He glanced at his watch while water ticked onto the linoleum from the sink. “The plumber has a full schedule,” he said. I slid my notebook toward him, open to the dates I’d called and the times I’d stayed home waiting. My jaw ached from holding it still. He promised Friday, and I asked him to write that down. When he reached for the notebook, I kept one finger on the page until he looked at me. Then I carried the tap back upstairs, stepping around the bucket that had filled again. At least now I had his promise in ink, though I knew I’d be checking the clock all morning Friday.

When the ceiling began shedding flakes into her cereal, Nia photographed the stain and walked downstairs to the landlord’s office. She had already moved her table twice to keep it clear of the spreading brown patch. Mr. Crane studied the picture, then asked whether she might have left a window open. Nia pressed her lips together and showed him the forecast on her phone: rain all week, with the window shut. He offered to send a handyman “when there’s a gap.” Her fingers tightened around the phone. “The gap is in my ceiling,” she said, in a level voice that made the receptionist stop typing. She requested a date, not another estimate, and waited while he called the repair company. By the time she went back upstairs, she had an appointment for the next morning—and a fresh cereal bowl ready beneath the stain.

I met my landlord beside the lobby mailboxes because he kept missing my calls about the broken heater. The cold had made my hands stiff, and I had to restart my phone twice before the video of the clicking thermostat would play. He watched a few seconds, shrugged, and said old systems made noises. I let the clip run until the heater gave its sharp metallic knock again. “It does this all night,” I said. My scarf was still wrapped around my neck indoors. He suggested I use a space heater, so I asked whether he’d bring one over himself and stay until morning. His smile vanished. After a pause, he called a technician. I took down the appointment time carefully, then held the lobby door for him with a politeness that felt like work.

Rafael found the bathroom floor slick again and laid a towel over the loose tile before calling his landlord. The leak had been reported two weeks earlier; now a dark line had crept along the baseboard. He met Ms. Dunn in the hall, where she said she thought the plumber had already fixed it. Rafael opened his phone and scrolled through the unanswered messages, stopping at the one with a photograph of the first puddle. His thumb hovered over the screen. “This is the same leak,” he said, holding the phone out until she actually looked. She began explaining that the building had many units. Rafael took a slow breath and asked her to repeat the repair date. When she gave none, he requested the plumber’s number and wrote it down himself, pressing so hard the pen nearly tore the paper.

I carried the cracked window latch to the property manager’s desk in a small paper bag, as if presenting evidence in court. The wind had been pushing the sash open every night, and my toddler’s room was the coldest in the apartment. Ms. Holt said maintenance would get to it after the weekend. I looked past her at the neat row of labeled folders and asked which one held my request. She blinked, then searched the computer. The original work order had been marked complete, though nobody had visited. I felt heat rise behind my ears. “Please reopen it while I’m standing here,” I said. She did, and I asked for the confirmation number. On the way upstairs, I stopped at the office door to read the posted emergency procedure twice, memorizing every name and extension.

At twenty-two, Priya had never asked anyone to fix anything on her behalf. But the apartment’s front door scraped so badly that she had to shoulder it shut, and the lock no longer caught. She found her landlord in the courtyard and demonstrated the problem. The door bounced open behind her. He said he would inspect it next week. Priya stared at the gap, then at the keys already clenched in her palm. “I can’t secure the apartment tonight,” she said. He began talking about the building’s budget. She cut in, more sharply than she intended, and asked him to call a locksmith while they stood there. When he hesitated, she started writing the date and time in her notes. He made the call before she finished. Priya tested the repaired lock herself, turning the key several times before handing it back.

I brought a jar of the brown water from my kitchen pipes to Mr. Lewis’s office. He leaned away from it and told me the water company sometimes flushed the lines. I had heard that explanation twice already, but this time I had also saved a video of the tap running orange for nearly a minute. I played it without speaking. The little jar sat between us, sediment settling at the bottom. He reached for a pen and promised to ask maintenance to check the pipes. I asked when. He said he’d find out, and I tapped the jar once with my fingernail. “Before I have to fill another one?” He looked up, then called the building supervisor. I left with a date for an inspection, carrying the jar carefully so it wouldn’t spill on the stairs.

Marlene’s elevator had been out of service for four days, and each trip to her sixth-floor apartment left her knee throbbing. She caught the landlord near the loading entrance and asked when repairs would be finished. He pointed to a notice promising an update soon. Marlene unfolded the notice she had brought from the lobby; it was the same one, now creased at the corners. She had written the dates of every missed grocery delivery on its blank back. “I need a real answer,” she said, keeping her voice steady while her shopping bag dug into her fingers. He said the parts were delayed. She asked him to arrange help carrying necessities upstairs until they arrived. He started to object, then noticed her cane. By evening, a building porter had brought her groceries up, though she still planned to call again in the morning.

I called my landlord from the laundromat, where I’d been washing clothes by hand because the apartment washer flooded the kitchen every cycle. He said he hadn’t received my maintenance request. I pulled up the email and read him the timestamp, then the confirmation that he had replied, “We’ll look into it.” The washing machine thumped behind me, and I raised my voice over it. He said he’d send someone when he could. I watched suds creep across the laundromat floor and asked whether he considered a week a reasonable wait for a working appliance. Silence stretched over the line. Then he offered a visit the next afternoon. I repeated the time back to him, slowly, and sent a follow-up message while we were still speaking. The laundromat attendant handed me a mop without asking why.

After a pipe burst beneath the kitchen sink, Omar placed a mixing bowl under the drip and called his landlord before work. The landlord suggested tightening a valve himself. Omar had already tried; the wrench marks showed on the metal, and his sleeve was wet to the elbow. He sent a photograph, then waited through two rings of silence. “I’m not a plumber,” he said when the landlord offered another do-it-yourself tip. His train was due in twelve minutes. He stood in the kitchen with his coat on, watching each drop strike the bowl. Finally, he asked the landlord to contact an emergency repair service and text him the details. The landlord agreed. Omar left a key with the upstairs neighbor and took the train at a run, checking his phone at every stop for confirmation.

I met the landlord in the courtyard with a loose radiator knob in my coat pocket. It had fallen off during the night, leaving the bedroom cold enough that I could see my breath near the window. He looked at the knob and said it was probably cosmetic. I turned it over in my palm, showing him the stripped threads. “The radiator won’t turn on,” I said. He checked the time and told me maintenance was busy with a larger job. My shoulders crept toward my ears. I asked whether he could at least provide a temporary heater, then waited without filling the silence for him. He finally agreed to bring one that evening. I wrote the promise on the back of my grocery receipt and handed him a copy, keeping the original in my pocket.

At the end of a long shift, Bethany returned to find the ceiling fan still wobbling above her bed. She had reported it after a blade came loose, and the landlord’s reply had been that someone would stop by. Nobody had. She called him and placed the phone on speaker while the fan clicked overhead. He said he couldn’t hear the noise. Bethany moved beneath it, holding the phone up until the clicking filled the call. “I’m not sleeping under this,” she said. He suggested she turn it off, and she replied that the room had no other ventilation. Her hand was shaking, so she set the phone on the dresser and read the work-order number from her email. He agreed to send a repairer first thing. She slept on the sofa and left the fan switched off.

I had arranged the canned vegetables by label, then by size, then by the date stamped on each tin. Every time I finished, someone moved a box to reach the rice behind it. By noon, the shelves looked like a puzzle assembled by a storm. I pressed my lips together and began again, slower this time, while the volunteer coordinator called for help at the registration desk. A family was waiting, and the printer had jammed halfway through their forms. I tugged at the paper, but it tore into a narrow strip. “Of course,” I muttered, then caught the father watching me and softened my face. I found a pencil and wrote their information by hand. When they left with groceries, I returned to the shelves. The labels were still crooked. I put the tins away without sorting them again.

Nia arrived at the community food bank before opening, hoping to finish packing produce bags before the queue formed. The scale kept blinking between pounds and ounces, and the apples rolled off the table whenever she reached for the cabbage. She wiped her hands on her apron and tapped the display twice. Nothing changed. Behind her, a volunteer asked where the bread belonged, then asked again while she was reading the scale manual. Nia inhaled through her nose, held the breath, and pointed toward the blue crates. A delivery driver appeared with three boxes of bruised pears, though the order listed potatoes. She stared at the manifest, rubbed the bridge of her nose, and called the supplier. When the line began to gather, she abandoned the scale and divided the fruit by eye. The bags were uneven, but everyone got some.

I volunteered at the food bank because I knew what it meant to stretch a meal. Today, though, the donation spreadsheet refused to save, and every click produced the same spinning circle. I had entered the figures twice already. My jaw tightened as I watched the clock creep toward closing time. At the sorting table, someone had mixed soap packets into a box of cereal, so I carried the whole thing back and separated it item by item. “We need a better system,” I said, louder than I meant to. The new volunteer went quiet. I lowered my voice and showed her the color-coded bins, then returned to the computer. The screen finally refreshed, but half the entries were missing. I shut my eyes for a moment, opened a fresh page, and began typing again, one careful number at a time.

At the East Harbor pantry, Tomas was assigned to assemble family meal boxes. The printed checklist called for pasta, sauce, beans, and cereal, but the cereal shipment had not arrived. He crossed it out, wrote “oatmeal,” then discovered the oatmeal was stored in a locked cabinet whose key had vanished. The line outside pressed closer to the doorway. Tomas turned the key ring over in his palm, each metal tooth clicking against the next. A coworker suggested checking the office, where he had already searched twice. He walked there anyway, shoulders high, and found the key beneath a stack of flyers. Back at the packing station, he added oatmeal to every box and revised the checklist once more. When a child asked if the boxes were ready, Tomas gave a quick nod and slid one across the table.

I was supposed to load the van with the bakery donation, but the driver had parked across the alley and blocked the pantry entrance. I carried trays around the building, one at a time, while rain tapped against the cardboard covers. Then a wheel on the handcart snapped. I stood in the puddle, holding a tray against my chest, and stared at the useless cart. My sleeves were soaked to the elbows. “This is taking forever,” I said, though nobody had asked. A shop owner poked her head out and offered a spare dolly. I thanked her, loaded the bread, and pushed it toward the storage room. The van was still blocking the doorway when I returned. I set the last tray down, wiped rain from my eyelashes, and asked the driver if he could move six feet forward.

Maribel had planned a smooth shift at the neighborhood food bank, with volunteers taking turns at the welcome desk and the packing tables. Two people called in sick, and a delivery arrived early, leaving her to cover every gap. She tried to answer a visitor’s question while counting cans, but lost her place at seventeen. The stack leaned. She caught it against her hip and glanced at the growing queue. A man asked whether the pantry had gluten-free food; Maribel checked the shelf, then checked the storage room, where the box was buried behind sacks of rice. She pulled it free, breathing sharply as dust clung to her sleeves. “I’ll get you sorted,” she said, keeping her voice level. Once he had his bag, she returned to the cans and placed them in smaller stacks that would not topple.

I came to the food bank after my shift at the bus depot, still wearing my uniform shirt. The online system had assigned me to inventory, but the tablet kept freezing whenever I scanned a barcode. I tried the scanner from three angles, then wiped its glass with my sleeve. The same error flashed again. A box of donated soup sat open beside me, and someone had written the wrong count on the lid. I ran my thumb along the cardboard crease, resisting the urge to toss the tablet onto the table. Instead, I counted the cans by hand and made a note on a scrap of paper. When the coordinator asked for the updated total, I handed it over without looking up. Then I unplugged the scanner, waited five seconds, and plugged it back in. The screen returned to the login page.

At the food bank’s Saturday shift, Gideon sorted donated coats and pantry goods in a crowded church basement. A box labeled “winter supplies” held tangled extension cords, plastic cups, and one lonely mitten. He read the label twice, then looked toward the crowded doorway, where more boxes were arriving. The tape dispenser had disappeared, so he held a carton shut with one hand while searching the table with the other. A volunteer asked if he had seen the labels for the rice bags. Gideon looked at the pile of loose stickers, then dragged a hand over his close-cropped hair. He found the labels stuck to the bottom of a clipboard. “There they are,” he said, with a short laugh that held no amusement. He relabeled the carton, stacked it beside the right shelf, and carried the cords to the donation-reject bin.

I was organizing the food bank’s freezers when the temperature alarm began chirping. I checked the display, opened the door, and saw a mound of frozen meals packed right against the vent. We had been told not to stack anything there, but the delivery crew had left before I arrived. I shifted cartons into the cooler, then called the building manager. The alarm kept chirping in the background while the call went to voicemail. My fingers felt clumsy in the cold, and I kept pressing the wrong button on the keypad. “Please, just stop,” I whispered at the panel. It did not. I wrote the temperature on a clipboard, moved the remaining meals to a backup freezer, and taped a handwritten warning across the door. The chirping followed me down the hall until another volunteer finally found the mute switch.

Lena volunteered at a rural food bank where the pantry shared space with a library meeting room. She had arranged the shelves so visitors could reach staples without asking for help, but someone had moved the flour to make room for donated books. A mother came in looking for it, and Lena searched three cupboards before finding the bags behind a box of dictionaries. She returned them to the pantry shelf, only to have a librarian ask her to clear the aisle again. Lena folded her arms, then unfolded them when she noticed the mother waiting. She carried the books to a corner table and shifted the flour back into view. A chair scraped loudly across the floor. She paused, pressed her fingertips to her temple, and continued arranging the room. By closing, both the books and groceries had their own clearly marked spaces.

I was checking expiration dates when I found a whole case of donated yogurt that would be out of date tomorrow. The cooler was already full, and the food bank had no room for another shelf. I called two nearby shelters, but both had enough dairy for the day. While I waited for someone to call back, volunteers kept setting more boxes beside me. I stacked them neatly, then watched the pile lean toward the doorway. My shoulders crept up near my ears. “We can’t keep putting things here,” I said, pointing at the narrow passage. The coordinator brought a rolling rack from the office, but one caster wobbled. We loaded the yogurt anyway and wheeled it to the front, where families could take it home. I checked each lid, marked the date in thick ink, and moved the remaining boxes away from the doorway.

When Malik took his first shift at the community food bank, he expected to pack bags, not troubleshoot the label printer. The machine printed each address halfway down the page, leaving the rest blank. He opened the tray, removed the paper, and tried again. A crooked sheet jammed inside. The queue at the desk grew, and the receptionist kept asking whether he could print one more label. Malik’s fingers drummed against the counter as the machine whirred without producing anything. He crouched, found a scrap caught beneath the roller, and pulled it free. The next page came out clean. He handed it over, then tested three more sheets before calling the receptionist back. She thanked him and hurried to the waiting visitors. Malik watched the printer for another moment, then taped a note to it: “Feed paper slowly.”

At thirty-eight, I had expected learning to drive to feel like a practical skill, not a weekly argument with a clutch. My instructor, Mr. Velez, sat calmly beside me while I stalled at the same stop sign for the fourth time. A cyclist rolled past, and my ears burned. “Try again, slowly,” he said. I pressed the pedal too hard, then jerked forward. My hands tightened around the wheel until my knuckles paled. At the next red light, I let out a long breath and stared at the dashboard. Mr. Velez suggested we practice in an empty lot instead. I wanted to tell him I knew that already, but swallowed the words. We circled the lot until the car finally moved smoothly. I smiled, though my jaw still ached.

Nina, a seventeen-year-old drummer, tapped an impatient rhythm against her thigh as her instructor explained parallel parking. The first attempt ended with the rear tire kissing the curb. The second left the car crooked across the marked space. Her instructor, Daryl, calmly asked her to reset. Nina stared through the windshield, lips pressed together, then backed out with a sharp turn that made him reach for the dashboard handle. “I can do this,” she said, her voice higher than she intended. Daryl pointed out a mailbox ahead and asked her to use it as a reference. She tried again, adjusting the wheel in small increments. The car slid neatly between the cones. Nina’s shoulders dropped, but she still muttered at the curb as they drove away.

I was thirty-two and had driven farm equipment for years, so I thought the lesson would be easy. Then Ms. Okafor asked me to merge onto a busy road, and every car seemed to arrive at once. I slowed at the ramp, then sped up, then slowed again. A horn sounded behind us. My palms slipped on the steering wheel, and I wiped them on my jeans at the next turnout. “You have room,” Ms. Okafor said, pointing to a gap. I nodded, but my foot hovered over the brake. She had me pull over and practice judging the traffic from a stop. On the next try, I checked the mirror, signaled, and merged. I kept my eyes forward, though my teeth were clenched.

At sixty-four, Mr. Chen signed up for lessons after moving to a town where the bus came only twice a day. His instructor, Beth, asked him to make a left turn at a quiet intersection. He waited through two green lights, watching oncoming cars pass. Beth repeated the directions, and he gripped the wheel harder. “I heard you,” he said, more sharply than he meant to. She suggested they talk through the steps: signal, check, turn when clear. On the next green, he followed the sequence but turned too wide, bumping over the painted line. He slapped the steering wheel once, then apologized. Beth guided him back to the training route. By the time they returned to the intersection, his breathing had steadied enough for another attempt.

My instructor said the hill-start exercise would take ten minutes. Forty minutes later, I was still rolling backward toward the orange cone. I’m Leila, twenty-six, and I’d come straight from a bakery shift with flour dust on my sleeves. Each time the car slipped, I made a small noise through my teeth and reset the brake. Mr. Hsu kept his voice even, which somehow made me more aware of every mistake. “Hold the clutch point,” he said. I stared at my foot as if I could command it by glaring. On the next try, the engine caught and the car climbed without sliding. I let out a laugh that sounded nearly like a sob. Mr. Hsu handed me a tissue, and I brushed flour from the gearshift.

Omar, a twenty-year-old exchange student, kept confusing the wipers and turn signal during his first rainy lesson. Each time he meant to indicate a turn, the blades swept across the windshield with a squeak. His instructor, Gwen, waited patiently while he tried to correct them. “These controls are in the wrong place,” Omar grumbled, then immediately apologized. At a junction, he reached for the signal again and turned on the rear defroster. A line of cars gathered behind them. He rubbed his forehead while Gwen directed him into a side street. They parked beneath a plane tree and reviewed the dashboard controls. Omar practiced the signal lever without starting the car, repeating the motion until he could find it by touch. When they set off again, the wipers stayed still until he needed them.

I brought my mother’s old hatchback to the lesson because it was the car I’d eventually have to drive. The clutch made a dry shudder whenever I started, and my instructor, Sal, said the car was fine. I, Mateo, twenty-three, kept restarting at the curb while neighbors watched from their porches. One woman lifted her eyebrows after my third stall. I stared straight ahead and tried again, pressing the pedal with careful patience that lasted about five seconds. “Don’t fight it,” Sal said. I wanted to argue that the machine had started the fight, but my shoulders were already up around my ears. He asked me to listen for the engine instead of watching the tachometer. The next start was smooth. I drove off without looking at the porches.

Priya, forty-five, needed a license for her new nursing job, but the lesson began badly when she missed a turn and entered a one-way street. Her instructor, Mr. Bell, calmly told her to continue to the next block. Priya’s cheeks warmed as a delivery van honked behind them. “I saw the sign,” she said, though she had not. At the next safe corner, they pulled over. She pressed both hands against her thighs and stared at the map on the dashboard. Mr. Bell asked her to trace the route with her finger before they moved again. She did, tapping each turn with clipped little motions. When they restarted, she checked every street sign and made the correct turn. The route took longer, but she reached the practice lot without another wrong turn.

I had watched driving videos for months, so I was certain I understood a three-point turn. Then my instructor, Ana, asked me to do one on a narrow residential street, and the car ended up angled toward a hedge. I’m Rob, twenty-nine, and I could feel heat crawling up my neck as I reversed, corrected, and reversed again. A dog barked from behind a fence. “Take your time,” Ana said. I answered with a tight nod and turned the wheel too far. She asked me to pause and notice where the front tires were pointing. I exhaled through my nose, checked the mirrors, and made smaller adjustments. The car completed the turn at last. I glanced at the hedge, then drove on, keeping my hands at ten and two.

At eighteen, Junie had no trouble steering on empty roads, but her instructor, Luis, insisted she practice roundabouts during the afternoon rush. Cars flowed around the circle while she waited at the entrance, one hand tapping the wheel. Luis reminded her to yield to traffic already inside. Junie nodded, then missed her opening and circled around again. On the second lap, she muttered at a driver who left a large gap but gave no signal. Luis asked her to focus on the next safe opportunity. Her shoulders rose as she watched the passing cars. Finally, she entered, chose the correct exit, and pulled into a nearby lot. She sat with both hands still on the wheel. Luis praised her timing. Junie answered with a brief “Okay,” then flexed her fingers.

My instructor, Mrs. Alvarez, had me practice backing into a parking space behind the community center. I’m Darnell, fifty-one, and the painted lines seemed to shift every time I checked the mirrors. On my first try, I stopped across two spaces. On my second, I ended up too close to a shopping cart. I pressed my lips together while Mrs. Alvarez explained which mirror to watch. A teenager walked by and glanced at the car; I pretended not to notice. “Let’s reset,” she said. I pulled forward, counted slowly, and turned the wheel only when the rear bumper reached the marker. The car settled between the lines. I checked both sides twice, then looked at her. “That’s the one,” she said. I rubbed the heel of my hand against my forehead.

Sofia, twenty-four, had practiced on quiet streets, but her first lesson on a freeway left her gripping the wheel as if it might escape. Her instructor, Ken, asked her to maintain speed and leave space ahead. A truck merged in front of them, and Sofia lifted her foot from the accelerator. The car behind flashed its headlights. “I’m doing what you said,” she snapped, then glanced at Ken. He pointed out the growing gap and coached her to ease back up to speed. She followed, jaw tight, eyes flicking between the mirrors and road. At the next exit, Ken took them to a rest area. Sofia leaned her forehead against the headrest and let her hands fall open. After a drink of water, she agreed to try the on-ramp once more.

I used to know exactly how the last hill on the cycling route would feel. After my collarbone healed, even the gentle slope behind our apartment made my shoulder throb and my legs turn clumsy. Coach said to keep the ride easy, so I pedaled slowly while my training partner vanished around the bend. At the top, I stopped and stared at my watch, where the numbers looked embarrassingly small. I pressed the button too hard and nearly dropped it. “You’re rebuilding,” my sister reminded me when I got home. I answered with a grunt, then sat on the floor, unable to take off my helmet because my arm wouldn’t lift far enough. The next morning, I taped a paper calendar above my desk. Each ride earned one mark. The marks didn’t make me faster, but they gave the days somewhere to go.

At sixteen, Mateo had expected to be back in goal before the soccer season ended. Instead, his repaired ankle puffed up after ten minutes of drills, and the assistant coach sent him to the bench again. He tugged at the elastic wrap until the trainer told him to leave it alone. Across the field, the younger keeper made a clumsy save, then grinned as teammates slapped his shoulders. Mateo kicked a pebble beneath the bench. It skittered into a puddle, splashing his clean socks. His father arrived with a paper bag of sandwiches and asked how practice went. “Great,” Mateo said, staring at the wet ground. The next afternoon, he asked to join the goalkeeper drills, even if he could only handle throws. He dropped the first three balls. On the fourth, he caught it against his chest and held on while everyone else moved to the next station.

The surgeon cleared me to swim again, but the pool felt twice as long as it had before my shoulder injury. I made it to the far wall, turned, and watched two teenagers glide past with lazy, perfect strokes. My arm dragged through the water like a loose rope. I slapped the surface, swallowed a mouthful, and grabbed the lane divider. The lifeguard asked if I needed help. “I need the clock to stop staring at me,” I said, though he couldn’t hear over the vents. I climbed out and sat dripping beside my towel, jaw tight. For a minute I considered going home. Then I pulled on the kickboard and tried a few lengths using only my legs. When I finished, my hands were shaking, but I wrote the distance in my notebook. The page had plenty of blank space left; I left it open anyway.

Nadia’s wrist had healed enough for her to return to the climbing gym, but every hold seemed designed to expose what she could no longer do. She tested a familiar route, reached for the overhang, and slipped before her fingers settled. A boy waiting below offered advice about foot placement. Nadia gave him a smile that lasted only until he turned away, then shook out her hand as if the wall had personally offended her. The physical therapist had warned her not to force it. She remembered that warning while chalking up for another attempt, pressing powder into her palms with unnecessary care. This time she chose an easier route with broad holds. Halfway up, she paused, breathing hard, and watched the other climbers pass on the wall beside her. She finished without falling. At the mat, she studied the harder route again and asked the desk worker when the gym was least crowded.

My first tennis lesson after knee surgery lasted twelve minutes before I started counting every mistake. The ball kept landing just beyond my racket, and each quick step sent a warning pinch through the joint. I could hear the coach calling, “Take your time,” which made me swing harder. A ball clipped the net and rolled beneath the bench. I bent to retrieve it, then froze halfway down, one hand braced on my thigh. My old tournament photos were still on the club wall, bright and smug above the courts. I turned my racket in my grip until the tape creaked. After the lesson, I sat in the car with the engine off, watching people cross the parking lot. The next week, I asked the coach to feed balls without making me chase them. We worked on clean contact. When I finally hit one deep, I let out a breath I hadn’t realized I was holding.

Leon had spent months recovering from a torn hamstring, and the track’s painted lanes now seemed to mock his cautious jog. He started with the junior group, though he was twenty-eight and once ran faster than any of them. When a teenager passed him during a warm-up, Leon’s hands clenched at his sides. He surged forward, felt a sharp pull, and stopped so abruptly that his shoes scraped the track. The coach walked over without scolding. Leon looked away, cheeks hot, while the rest of the group circled the field. “I know what the plan says,” he muttered. “I also know I used to be better.” The coach handed him a water bottle and waited. Leon took a long drink, then walked one lap instead of leaving. On the next practice day, he brought a stopwatch but left it in his bag. He measured the session by how steadily he finished.

I broke two fingers in a skateboarding fall, and by the time the doctor let me return, the new park had opened across town. My friends were learning tricks on the big ramp while I practiced rolling over a painted line. Every time my board wobbled, I stomped it flat and glanced toward the ramp. “That’s not even skating,” I said, though nobody had asked. My right hand still felt stiff when I gripped the rail, and the brace made my sleeve bunch at the wrist. I tried a small turn, caught an edge, and sat down hard on the concrete. For a few seconds, I just stared at my scraped shoe. Then I checked my fingers, took a breath, and climbed back onto the board. My friend rolled over and offered to practice beside me. We spent the rest of the afternoon tracing circles around the same cracked patch of pavement.

Inés, a marathon runner from Bogotá, had returned to training after a stress fracture with strict instructions to increase her mileage slowly. On the first group run, she watched the others disappear down the road while she followed the coach at a walk-jog pace. Her watch beeped at each interval, and she silenced it with a sharp tap. When a bus splashed gutter water onto her shoes, she muttered at the driver and kept moving. At the café afterward, teammates traded stories about their best races. Inés stirred her coffee long after the sugar dissolved, then opened a race website on her phone. She closed it before registering. That evening, she laid out her shoes for the next morning instead. The planned route was only two kilometers. She wrote the distance on a sticky note and stuck it to the door, where she would have to see it before heading outside.

The surgeon said my elbow was ready for archery practice, but the bowstring seemed heavier than I remembered. At the range, I drew it back, felt a tremor in my arm, and let go too soon. The arrow struck the target frame with a hollow clank. A couple of people glanced over. I lowered my bow and rubbed the scar beneath my sleeve, wishing the lane were empty. My instructor suggested a lighter bow. I shook my head, then immediately regretted it when my next shot landed wide. “Maybe I’m done for today,” I said, stacking arrows with more force than necessary. The instructor didn’t argue. He simply asked me to try one shot from closer range. I moved forward, planted my feet, and drew slowly. The arrow landed in the outer ring. I wanted the center, but I stayed at the line and nocked another arrow before the feeling in my arm faded.

Priya’s ankle had healed, yet the volleyball team kept her out of the starting lineup. During drills, she fed balls to the other hitters and watched them attempt the approach she had practiced since childhood. When the coach praised a freshman’s powerful spike, Priya slapped the ball cart with her palm. The noise turned a few heads. She mumbled an apology and tightened the laces on her brace. After practice, she stayed to serve. Her first ball clipped the net; the next sailed long. She retrieved each one without looking toward the scoreboard. By the time the gym lights flickered, her shoulder was sore and the ball had begun to feel slick in her hands. She asked the custodian for five more minutes. Her final serve cleared the net and landed just inside the back line. Priya gathered the balls slowly, then asked the coach what she should improve before Monday.

I returned to rowing after a rib injury, expecting the familiar rhythm to carry me through. Instead, the first pull made my side seize, and I lost pace almost immediately. The coach’s launch followed nearby, its motor buzzing over the river. I gripped the handle until my knuckles blanched and tried to match the crew ahead. They moved together while I lagged, blade catching at the wrong angle. “Easy pressure,” the coach called. I stared at the boat’s wake and pushed too hard again. At the dock, I climbed out carefully, then kicked my shoe against a post when nobody was looking. The coach suggested shortening the session. I nearly argued, but the ache in my ribs answered first. We switched to technique drills on land. I went through each movement with an empty handle, counting the beats under my breath until my shoulders loosened. The river kept moving without me, but I stayed until the crew returned.

After a concussion kept him from competitive fencing, twelve-year-old Ellis returned to the salle wearing a padded mask and strict limits from his doctor. He wanted to spar, but the coach assigned him footwork beside the mirror. Ellis stamped forward and back, faster each time, until his trainer told him to slow down. He stopped with his hands on his hips, watching older students cross blades and salute. Their metallic clacks made his stomach tighten. At home, he tossed his practice jacket onto a chair and left it there for days. His grandmother found him tracing fencing steps across the kitchen tiles. She didn’t ask about the jacket; she marked a strip of floor with tape and challenged him to stay inside it. Ellis scowled at the narrow lane, then began again, careful not to cross the lines. By the end of the week, he could complete the sequence without losing his balance. He asked his coach to watch.

I had taken the morning off to renew my license, but the line at the county office barely moved. The digital sign kept changing from 38 to 39, then back again, as if it were teasing us. My lunch sat untouched in my bag while a toddler kicked the chair behind me. When the clerk called a number higher than mine, I stood up so quickly my folder slid to the floor. “Excuse me, I’ve been here since eight,” I said, keeping my voice level by pressing my tongue against my teeth. She pointed to a notice about a second queue and returned to her screen. I gathered my papers, squared their edges, and checked the number again. At noon, a man arrived, pulled a ticket, and was served before me. I folded my appointment slip into a tiny square and unfolded it again.

At seventy-two, Ruth had learned to bring a book everywhere, but the government office was making even the mystery novel feel impossible. She read the same paragraph four times while the line inched past the ticket machine. Each time someone approached the counter to ask a question, the clerk sent them to the back, then paused to answer a phone call. Ruth tapped her cane against the tile, stopped, and tucked it between her knees. Her application for a heating rebate lay open on her lap, every box carefully filled. When the man ahead of her discovered he had brought the wrong proof of address, he groaned and stepped aside. Ruth’s shoulders rose toward her ears. She looked at the clock, then at the number in her hand, and let out a slow breath through pursed lips. The book remained open to the same page.

I’d brought my daughter’s birth certificate, school letter, and every form listed on the website. At the immigration services office, a line curled around the lobby and past a vending machine that hummed louder than the announcements. I shifted my sleeping baby from one arm to the other, then tried to keep the folder from slipping under the stroller. The screen called numbers in a calm, bright voice, always from a row ahead of mine. When I finally reached the desk, the clerk said one page needed a signature in blue ink. The only pen I had was black. I stared at it for a beat, then asked where I could find a blue one. “You’ll have to wait again,” she said. I put the cap back on with a sharp click and pushed the stroller toward the far wall, careful not to wake the baby.

Malik had arranged his delivery route around the appointment, promising his supervisor he would be back by lunch. The municipal office’s queue had other plans. He stood between a man clutching a shoebox of tax receipts and a woman whose phone played the same ringtone every few minutes. Malik checked the time, then checked it again, though the display had not changed. His parking meter was running outside, and his van held a stack of packages that needed signatures. When the clerk announced a system outage, people began asking how long it would last. Malik rubbed the bridge of his nose and looked at the exit. A security guard told everyone to remain in line. He folded his appointment card along its printed border, pressing the crease until it was nearly white, then called his supervisor and explained that the route would have to wait.

I needed a replacement benefits card before my next shift, so I left the restaurant kitchen with flour still caught in the seam of my sleeve. At the state office, a taped sign said the ticket machine was out of order; a second sign directed everyone to a different counter, where the queue already filled the hallway. I asked whether the form I’d downloaded was still current. The guard shrugged without looking up. My phone battery dwindled while I watched people go in and out of a door marked STAFF ONLY. When a clerk finally called my name, she said I had brought the old version. I blinked at the form, then at the website open on my screen. “That’s the one your site gave me,” I said, louder than I meant to. I smoothed the paper against my knee and asked for the correct address before the line swallowed another hour.

At the licensing bureau, eleven-year-old Becca sat beside her grandfather while he waited to renew his permit. He had brought a thermos and a stack of crossword puzzles, but his pencil had snapped and the coffee was cooling. The queue advanced in fits: three numbers at once, then none for nearly half an hour. When a clerk called an elderly couple who had just entered, Granddad stood and pointed at his ticket. The clerk apologized and said the display had skipped. He sat down with a stiff little nod, then pressed both hands over his knees. Becca offered him her colored pencil. He tried to smile, but his jaw kept working as he stared toward the counter. By the time their number appeared, the office was closing for a staff meeting. He packed the thermos with deliberate care, one item at a time, while Becca watched the clock.

I came to the courthouse annex to correct a clerical error on my voter registration. The line snaked past a poster about civic participation, which felt like a joke after the fourth time the ticket display froze. I had printed the confirmation email and highlighted the case number, but the man at the information desk kept telling me to wait for my turn. Behind me, someone sighed every few seconds. I looked at my watch and counted the minutes until my bus home. When the screen finally changed, it called a number from the previous hour. I stepped toward the desk, then stopped when the clerk raised one finger without turning around. The paper in my hand developed a ragged corner from all my picking. I tucked it into my pocket, rolled my shoulders back, and rehearsed the question I would ask when I was finally allowed to speak.

Pavel had driven forty miles to the regional records office for a marriage certificate, only to find the waiting room packed with people holding folders. The air conditioner rattled but did little against the afternoon heat. He stood beneath a clock whose minute hand seemed pinned in place, shifting his weight from one boot to the other. When he asked whether walk-ins were being served, the receptionist said, “Eventually,” without looking up. Pavel swallowed a reply and examined the checklist taped to the wall. One item contradicted the instructions he had received by phone. He took a photo of both notices, then returned to his spot as a new family joined the line ahead of him. His fingers drummed on the folder until a child turned to stare. Pavel folded his hands together and fixed his gaze on the counter, lips moving silently as he counted the numbers called.

I was there to register a small food stall, and the form required details I’d already entered online. The government office smelled of wet coats and printer toner. I stood in line with a cardboard tube of plans tucked under my arm, careful not to bump the man in front of me. Every few minutes, an employee walked through the lobby carrying a stack of files, and everyone straightened as if our turn had come. It never had. When my number was skipped, I went to the desk and asked about it. The clerk said I must have missed the call. I looked around at the silent room and felt my ears grow hot. “Could you check once more?” I asked, clipping each word short. She searched the screen, found my place, and pointed to a bench. I sat down without taking my coat off.

Nia brought her father’s power-of-attorney papers to the county office, keeping them in a plastic sleeve against the rain. The line began outside the entrance and doubled back through the lobby. Her father sat on a bench near the door, conserving his strength, while she stood with their ticket and watched the display. When a family argued about whose turn it was, the queue stopped moving entirely. Nia glanced at her father, who had begun rubbing his hands together for warmth. She went to the information window and asked if people with mobility needs could wait somewhere inside. The clerk gestured toward the same crowded benches. Nia returned, mouth set, and draped her scarf over her father’s shoulders. Each announcement seemed to take longer than the last. She held the papers tight enough to bend one corner, then carefully flattened it with her thumb.

I had promised my landlord I’d bring proof of my address that afternoon, so I joined the line at the housing authority before opening time. The lobby filled quickly, and the ticket dispenser ran out of paper before I reached it. An employee refilled it, then told everyone to take a new number because the first batch had printed incorrectly. My hands closed around the useless slip. I asked whether the office could honor the number I’d been given. He repeated the instruction and moved on. I leaned against the wall, then pushed away when a security guard told me not to block the corridor. The address document in my folder was damp from the rain. I spread it carefully across my knees, checking that the ink hadn’t run, and listened as the numbers advanced at a pace that made my deadline feel less real by the minute.

Evelyn, a retired bus driver, was waiting at the tax office to dispute a charge she could not afford. She had organized her receipts by month and clipped each bundle in order. Across the room, a printer jammed, and the clerk called for help twice before anyone came. Evelyn’s ticket was only four numbers away, but the desk closed for a scheduled break. She stood, gathered her papers, and asked how long the pause would last. “Twenty minutes,” the clerk replied, already turning away. Evelyn’s mouth tightened. She sat again, placed the receipts in a neat stack, and aligned their edges with the bench. A young man offered her his place near the window, but she shook her head and thanked him. She kept her eyes on the empty counter, one hand resting on her folder as if guarding it from another delay.

When the apartment block went dark, I was halfway through submitting my nursing-school application. My laptop screen vanished, taking the essay with it, and the printer in the hallway gave one final click. I pressed the power button twice, as if the building might reconsider. Across the landing, Mr. Alvarez opened his door with a flashlight between his teeth. I asked whether anyone knew how long the outage would last; he shrugged and said the utility had no estimate. My jaw tightened. I carried my laptop downstairs, hoping the lobby emergency lights might somehow help, then remembered the battery was nearly empty. Neighbors gathered around the glass entrance, checking phones and trading guesses. A child kept spinning the dark elevator’s call button. I finally sat on the stairs and began rewriting my essay by hand on the back of a grocery receipt, pressing so hard the pencil snapped.

Darnell had promised the neighbors he would cook for the courtyard potluck, and the stew was almost ready when the power cut. The electric stove went cold; the vent fan died, leaving the room thick with onion steam. He turned the burner knobs back and forth, though he knew they could not help. From the next unit, Mei called through the open window to ask if anyone had a camping stove. Darnell answered that he did, then found it buried beneath a stack of storage boxes. A folding chair collapsed under his knee as he dragged it out. By the time he lit the stove outside, three neighbors were offering different advice at once. He set the pot down, wiped his forehead with his sleeve, and counted to five before replying. The stew survived, but the rice stayed uncooked, and Darnell served everyone crackers with an apologetic lift of his eyebrows.

The outage caught me during my online tutoring session, just as my student was finally solving fractions without help. My router blinked out, then the whole street disappeared into darkness. I stood in the kitchen holding my phone above my head, searching for a signal, while the lesson timer kept running on the dead laptop. Mrs. Cho from next door knocked with a candle and asked whether I knew what had happened. I gave her the utility number, but the recording looped through the same options without connecting us to a person. I paced from the window to the front step, refreshing the service page until my thumb hurt. When my student’s mother texted that they would try again tomorrow, I stared at the unfinished worksheet. Then I printed nothing, charged nothing, and could do nothing but tape a note to the door promising a replacement lesson.

At sixty-eight, Ruth knew the building’s old elevator made a peculiar shudder before each stop. With the power gone, it froze between floors, carrying her neighbor Leon and two grocery bags somewhere above the lobby. She hurried to the stairwell and called up, but his answer came faintly through the shaft. The manager was away, and the emergency phone produced only a hollow buzz. Ruth marched back to the front desk, searching drawers for the maintenance list, while her cane tapped sharply against the tile. Other residents gathered, each suggesting a different number to call. She took their phones and wrote the names down in careful block letters, then called the fire department. When help arrived, Leon was safe, though his ice cream had melted into the bags. Ruth folded the useless list, tucked it into her purse, and muttered that the building could at least keep its phone charged.

I was halfway through assembling a bookshelf for the new neighbors when the lights blinked out. The cordless drill stopped with a screw only partway in, and the instruction sheet slipped beneath the couch. I fetched my headlamp, but its beam landed on a pile of mismatched boards that all looked alike. In the hallway, Imani from upstairs offered to hold a flashlight. Her light wobbled every time she tried to read the tiny diagrams, while I kept turning the same plank around. I could hear rain striking the windows and the neighbors’ children asking if the bookcase would be ready tonight. I set the drill down more firmly than necessary. After a long breath, I suggested we switch to sorting the hardware by hand. We finished one shelf by candlelight, though the back panel went on upside down, and I left the hammer resting on top like a warning.

Noor’s bakery shared a wall with three small apartments, so when the neighborhood lost power, everyone appeared at her back door to ask what was happening. She had a birthday cake in the refrigerator and a dozen orders due at dawn. The display case went dark, the cooling fans stopped, and the backup generator refused to start. She yanked the starter cord until her palm reddened, then kicked a tire and apologized to it. Her neighbor Pavel brought a toolbox; a teenager arrived with a phone flashlight. They crowded around the machine, offering theories while Noor checked the clock again and again. At last, she borrowed a cooler from the fish shop down the block and packed the cake in ice. The neighbors carried boxes together, but when someone suggested she relax, Noor pointed to the silent generator and asked if they planned to frost the orders by candlelight.

I had just put my toddler down when the power failed, and the white-noise machine stopped mid-hum. A minute later, Tessa began crying in her crib. I tried rocking her by the window, where the streetlamps usually made a soft glow, but the whole block was black. My partner went to ask the neighbors if anyone had spare batteries. I kept checking the monitor, though its screen was blank, and shushing louder than the baby. From downstairs came the clatter of a flashlight dropped on the stairs, followed by someone’s cheerful offer of candles. I wanted to explain that candles would not soothe a one-year-old, but I only rubbed my temples and asked for batteries again. When the neighbor returned with a lantern, I set it safely out of reach and began singing the same lullaby from the beginning, slower each time.

Mateo was carrying a tray of dumplings to the community center when the power outage stopped the traffic lights and darkened the whole intersection. He waited at the curb while neighbors argued about whose turn it was to cross. One driver leaned on a horn, then crawled forward without looking. Mateo tightened his grip on the tray and called for everyone to stay back. A woman from the corner apartment came out with a reflective vest and began directing cars, though nobody had asked her to. Mateo joined her, waving the tray like a signal flag until another resident found a battery lantern. The dumplings cooled as they stood there, and a cyclist complained that the crossing was taking too long. Mateo looked at the scattered traffic, shut his eyes for a moment, then pointed the cyclist toward the safer side street. Only after the intersection cleared did he notice sauce dripping onto his shoe.

The outage arrived while I was hosting a video call with my book club. My screen froze on six faces, all mid-sentence, and the router’s lights vanished. I rebooted it, unplugged it, and plugged it back in, then stared at the dark box as though it had personally interrupted me. Across the hall, the Kims were already in the corridor with a portable radio. I asked if they had heard anything useful; the broadcast was mostly static and an announcer repeating the same notice. We carried chairs to the courtyard, where neighbors compared phone batteries and predicted when service would return. Someone suggested discussing the book from memory. I opened my notes app, only to see my phone at three percent. Instead of making another attempt to reconnect, I put the phone face down on my knee and told the group I had forgotten the ending. The radio crackled in reply.

At the laundromat, Elaine watched the machines stop with her sheets still soaked inside. The outage had also darkened the neighboring apartments, whose residents soon came down carrying baskets and questions. The owner searched beneath the counter for a flashlight while Elaine tried every washer door, then pressed each button in a brisk little sequence. Nothing changed. A boy asked whether the dryer could run on batteries, and she answered with a tight smile that it could not. The owner found a hand-cranked radio, but it reported only that crews were investigating. Elaine pulled a wet sheet from one machine and folded it over her arm, leaving a dark trail across the tile. When a neighbor offered to help wring out the rest, she handed him a corner without a word. Together they twisted the fabric until water streamed into a bucket.

I was practicing for my driving test in the apartment courtyard when the power went out across the neighborhood. The gate’s automatic arm stopped halfway across the driveway, trapping my car inside and blocking a delivery van outside. I got out and tried lifting the arm, but it barely shifted. My neighbor, Mrs. Okafor, arrived with a flashlight and held it on the control box while I searched for a manual release. The van driver kept checking his watch and tapping the steering wheel. I found three levers, none labeled, and pulled the wrong one; the gate dropped with a clank. Mrs. Okafor raised an eyebrow as I pushed it back into place. We finally wedged it open with a wooden crate. The van rolled through, and I climbed back into my car, gripping the wheel while my instructor’s reminder about staying calm replayed in my head.

Linh had prepared a neighborhood presentation about rising rent, complete with slides, printed charts, and a projector borrowed from the library. Ten minutes before the meeting, the outage blacked out the recreation room. Residents arrived anyway, carrying candles and folding chairs, while the building supervisor searched for an extension cord that could not possibly help. Linh tapped the blank projector screen with her pointer, then set the pointer down with a sharp click. A neighbor suggested postponing; another wanted to debate the issue from memory. Linh took the printed charts from her folder and passed them around, explaining the figures by the light of several phones. Whenever someone interrupted, she paused, pressed her lips together, and resumed from the exact sentence she had lost. The meeting ran long, but every resident signed the petition. Linh stacked the unused slides carefully, as if they had failed an important test.

I checked my biology grade on the bus, wedged between a grocery bag and a stranger’s damp umbrella. The page took so long to load that I refreshed it twice, then stared at the score: lower than the practice tests I had finished in half the time. I scrolled through the comments, hoping for a note about a missed page. Nothing. At home, I spread my notes across the kitchen table and found the exact diagram I had labeled correctly in my study guide. My jaw tightened as I compared it with the marked answer. I opened the course forum, typed a question, erased it, then typed it again with fewer exclamation marks. Mom asked if I wanted dinner. “In a minute,” I said, though the food had already gone cold. I started a list of questions for office hours, pressing hard enough to leave grooves in the paper.

When the exam portal opened, Darnell was in the back room of his family’s barbershop, waiting for his next appointment. He clicked the grade beside his history course and let out a sharp breath. The score was far below what he expected after staying up to review primary sources. He checked the date, then the course name, then signed out and back in, as if the numbers might rearrange themselves. His little cousin asked whether he had passed. Darnell turned the laptop so the screen faced away and said, “I’m checking the rubric.” He printed the feedback at the shop’s old printer; the paper emerged crooked, with a black streak through the comments. He flattened it with his palm and circled two deductions. Between haircuts, he drafted a polite email to the instructor, revising the first sentence until it sounded less like an accusation.

I refreshed the grade page in the laundromat while my clothes tumbled behind me. The score appeared beside a neat green check mark, which seemed almost rude.
