The wheel gave a grudging quarter turn. I loosened the cable, pulled it through, and tightened the clamp, but the brake still dragged. Flour from my work apron dusted the tire as I leaned closer. A delivery scooter buzzed past; I checked my watch and clicked my tongue. Then I noticed the wheel itself sat crooked in the frame. I loosened the axle nuts, nudged the wheel into place, and tightened them in quick alternating turns. The rim spun freely at last. I wiped my hands on the apron and pedaled off, standing on the first few strokes.

Malik had promised his grandson a ride along the canal, but the bicycle’s seat post had sunk so low that his knees nearly touched his chest. He found an adjustable wrench in the garage and loosened the clamp. The post would not rise. He pulled, twisted, and knocked it with the heel of his hand. The clock above the freezer ticked loudly between attempts. A neighbor passing the open door suggested penetrating oil. Malik fetched it, sprayed the joint, and paced the length of the driveway while it worked. After a few minutes, the post turned with a dry squeak. He raised it to the mark, tightened the clamp, and tested it with a firm push. His grandson was already waiting at the gate.

I found the bicycle outside the train station with its chain jammed between the gears. Rain dotted my glasses, and the departure board changed while I crouched beside the wheel. I pulled the chain backward; it pinched my thumb. I shook my hand, wiped it on my coat, and tried from another angle. The links stayed wedged. A woman with an umbrella stepped around me as I muttered at the gears. I used a pen from my pocket to pry the chain free, careful not to bend the derailleur. It sprang loose and slapped the frame. I checked the links for damage, then turned the pedals by hand. They moved smoothly. I folded the pen away and jogged toward the platform, leaving a black smear on my sleeve.

In the coastal repair shed, Beatriz worked on a bicycle whose front wheel kept rubbing the fork. The group ride would depart in half an hour, and she had already missed the first briefing. She loosened the quick-release, centered the wheel, and snapped it closed. The tire still brushed one side. Beatriz stood, paced around the work stand, then crouched again to inspect the fork. A pebble was wedged near the brake pad. She picked it out with tweezers, spun the wheel, and heard the same faint scrape. Her shoulders rose. She adjusted the brake pads by tiny increments, testing after each turn of the screw. At last the wheel spun without a whisper. She grabbed her helmet and hurried to catch the group.

I needed the bicycle ready before the neighborhood parade, but the bell had fallen apart in my hands. Its spring rolled beneath the porch steps. I dropped to my knees and reached into the dark, brushing away leaves and a spiderweb. My phone timer counted down the minutes until the parade passed our street. I found the spring, then misplaced the tiny screw. After sweeping the boards with my palm, I spotted it caught in a crack. I balanced the bell pieces on one knee and tried to fit them together. The spring popped free twice. On the third attempt I held it with a clothespin while tightening the screw. The bell rang, bright and clear. I tested it four times, then rolled the bicycle toward the curb.

At the mountain lodge, Edwin noticed that his bicycle’s gear shifter had gone slack just as the clouds gathered over the ridge. He set his pack down and opened the tool roll, pulling out each tool in turn. The cable end had slipped from its anchor. Edwin tried threading it back with cold fingers, but the strand kept fraying. He blew on his hands, pinched the cable with pliers, and tugged until it seated. The shifter clicked through the gears, then skipped past the smallest cog. Edwin gave the barrel adjuster a sharp twist, tested again, and frowned at the wheel. A lodge cook called that the rain was starting. Edwin ignored the first drops, made one careful adjustment, and watched the chain settle into gear.

I had tuned the mandolin twice before the café owner finished arranging the chairs. The concert was meant to begin at seven, but the clock above the espresso machine still showed 6:22. I ran the opening reel again, then stopped halfway through to ask whether the microphone had been tested. It had. I checked it myself anyway, tapping the head until the owner gave me a look. My heel kept striking the stage boards, making the tea glasses tremble. When a couple entered early, I stood so quickly that my music slid off the stool. They smiled and took seats. I gathered the pages, shuffled them into order, and asked if they wanted to hear a tune. They said they were waiting for friends. I sat down, tightened a string that was already tight, and began the reel once more, this time watching the door between every phrase.

At the community hall, Darius practiced his trumpet while volunteers taped paper stars to the walls. His small concert was scheduled for the end of the evening, after the children’s choir. He finished one scale and glanced at the clock, then started it again faster. A loose valve made a soft click, and he took the horn apart with brisk, careful fingers. When the coordinator asked him to keep the volume down, Darius nodded, lowered the bell, and blew a silent fingering exercise instead. His knee bounced against a folding chair. He asked twice whether the choir had arrived, then offered to carry their music stands from the lobby. No one had called for help. Back at his seat, he polished the trumpet though its surface already shone, lined up his sheet music, and peered through the open doorway as if the next sound might be his cue.

I set my cello beside the bookstore’s front window and began the passage that always tangled near the end. The chairs were empty except for one man reading a travel guide, and the bookseller was still placing candles on the counter. I played the troublesome bars, stopped, and began again before the final note had faded. My bow hand felt damp inside its grip. “How much longer?” I asked, though I knew the concert started at eight. The bookseller pointed to the clock. I wiped the cello strings with a cloth, adjusted the endpin, and moved my chair three inches to the left. Then I moved it back. The traveler turned a page with exquisite slowness. I lifted my bow, ready to launch into the piece, but a delivery cart rattled outside. I lowered the bow, watched the minute hand crawl, and tapped the rhythm against my knee.

Nina’s accordion rehearsal had taken over the narrow back room of a seaside bakery. Her little audience would be the evening’s customers, once the ovens cooled and the tables were cleared. She played the waltz from the beginning, then cut herself off to ask whether the baker had chosen a tablecloth. He pointed toward a stack of blue ones. Nina folded and unfolded the bellows, testing their resistance, while her gaze kept returning to the kitchen clock. Each time a tray clanged, she looked up, expecting someone to announce that the doors were open. Instead, the baker dusted flour from his sleeves. Nina tightened a strap, loosened it, and tightened it again. She ran through the ending at double speed, frowned at the result, and started over at the proper tempo. A customer wandered in for a loaf, and she straightened at once, accordion poised across her lap.

I was the only person in the church basement who could hear the radiator knocking in time with my guitar. The neighborhood concert was set for seven, and my watch insisted it was only 6:10. I practiced the quiet introduction, then struck the strings harder when the radiator drowned it out. My sister, who had come to help with the chairs, asked me to save my voice for later. I answered with a nod and checked the sound cable again. It was secure. I coiled it, uncoiled it, and plugged it in once more. The first audience members were supposed to be arriving soon; nobody had appeared. I stood, sat, and stood again, brushing invisible dust from my trousers. When footsteps sounded in the hallway, I rushed to the doorway. It was only the caretaker carrying a bucket. I returned to the bench and began the introduction from the first chord.

At a neighborhood garden club, Mei arranged her flute music on a folding stand while a handful of guests chatted among the potted geraniums. Her brief recital would follow the club’s announcements. She had rehearsed the opening so often that her fingers moved without hesitation, yet she kept looking toward the lectern. The club president was still describing a planned rose sale. Mei lowered her flute and rolled her shoulders, then raised it again when the speaker paused to drink water. The pause stretched. She tested a high note, soft enough not to interrupt, and watched several people turn around. A leaf clung to her sleeve; she plucked it off and placed it carefully on the stand. When the president began another announcement, Mei’s jaw tightened. She arranged the pages in a perfect stack and silently counted the beats until her name was finally called.

I brought my banjo to the laundromat because the owner had offered me a corner for a tiny evening concert. The dryers thumped behind me while I practiced a bright tune for the few regulars who might stay. My fingers kept racing ahead of the melody. I stopped, shook out my hands, and checked the clock above the detergent shelves. The owner was still folding towels behind the counter. “You said after the last load,” I reminded him. He held up a damp sheet and shrugged. I retuned the banjo, though its pitch was fine, then tried the chorus at a slower pace. A dryer buzzer sounded, and I sprang up to see whether the room was ready. Two customers were still sorting socks. I sat back down, lining up my picks along the edge of the chair, and began the tune again with one eye on the spinning machines.

Elias practiced his violin in the lobby of a small retirement residence, where six residents had gathered for the promised concert. The activities director was delayed bringing the piano bench, and Elias kept glancing at the empty space beside his music stand. He played a few bars, then stopped to tighten a bow screw that needed no adjustment. One resident asked whether the music would start soon. Elias gave a quick smile and said he was nearly ready, though his fingers were already set on the strings. He paced to the water cooler, drank half a cup, and returned before the others had settled. A clock ticked above the reception desk. He shifted his weight from foot to foot, then tested the opening note at barely more than a whisper. At last, the director appeared with the bench. Elias lifted his violin before it was fully in place.

I had borrowed the museum’s little atrium for a clarinet performance, and the guard had promised to unlock the side doors at six. At 5:43, I was already dressed and playing the same phrase into the empty room. Its echo returned a fraction late, throwing off my timing. I shortened the phrase, tried it again, and glanced toward the locked entrance. My reed felt dry, so I wet it, tested it, and wet it once more. A school group shuffled past behind a rope barrier, their guide speaking in a low voice. I stood straight whenever someone looked my way, hoping they were early listeners. They continued toward the dinosaur gallery. I adjusted my music stand, raised it, lowered it, then placed my case squarely beneath it. When the guard finally turned the key, I was halfway through another run and nearly missed the new footsteps.

Tessa had set up her small drum kit in the back room of a neighborhood diner, where she would play during the lull between dinner and closing. The cook still had onions sizzling, and every hiss seemed to interrupt her practice. She tapped the snare softly, checked the clock, and asked the waitress whether the last table had ordered dessert. The waitress pointed to a family sharing pie. Tessa spun one drumstick between her fingers, dropped it, and retrieved it with a sharp exhale. She ran the bridge again, this time rushing the fills, then shook her head and counted herself in more slowly. The cook called for another plate, and she glanced toward the kitchen pass-through. Her cymbals quivered from a passing truck outside. She tightened one stand, straightened the rug beneath the kit, and kept her sticks poised until the clatter in the kitchen finally stopped.

I was rehearsing my harmonica set in the back room of a barber shop, where a few customers had agreed to stay after closing. The barber was finishing a trim in the front chair, and every snip of his scissors seemed to mark another wasted second. I practiced the opening melody, lowered the instrument, and checked the wall clock. It had barely moved. I wiped my palms on my jeans and slid the harmonica into a different pocket, then pulled it right back out. When the barber swept hair into a neat pile, I leaned into the doorway. He raised one finger: not yet. I returned to my stool and played the final passage under my breath. A customer stood to inspect his haircut, and I took that as a sign. I straightened, drew a breath, and waited through one more careful adjustment of the mirror.

At the village library, Owen rehearsed a short marimba piece for a concert with only a dozen chairs set out. He had arrived early enough to arrange the mallets by size, but now he kept swapping their positions. The librarian was still helping a patron print a form at the desk. Owen played the opening pattern, stopped after four notes, and began again, striking each bar a little harder. A child peeked around the shelves, and he gave her a hopeful grin. She disappeared without a word. Owen checked his phone, put it away, then checked it again. He nudged the instrument stand, although it stood level, and counted the empty seats. When the printer finally whirred to a halt, he lifted both mallets. The librarian thanked the patron, closed the drawer, and turned toward him. Owen was already poised over the first note.

The train doors sighed open, and I stepped into a station whose signs seemed designed to send me in circles. My phone showed a map, but the blue dot spun uselessly while I stood beneath a clock that had stopped at 4:10. I checked my watch, tapped the screen, then asked a porter where the airport bus left. He began explaining the history of the station. I nodded at the first sentence and glanced past him toward the exits. When he finally pointed, I hurried down the stairs, hauling my suitcase so fast that its wheels rattled over every edge. Outside, a bus pulled away just as I reached the curb. I slapped the timetable with my palm, then paced between the shelter and the street, counting the minutes until the next one appeared.

At twenty, Kiana had crossed three time zones to reach Bellport, and the taxi queue barely moved. She shifted her backpack from shoulder to shoulder, watched each cab collect someone ahead of her, and opened the ride app again though the price had not changed. A man at the front struggled with a stack of boxes. Kiana exhaled sharply and checked the time for the fourth time in a minute. When her turn came, the driver asked whether she preferred the scenic route. She answered with the hotel address and a quick shake of her head. The car crawled through streets crowded with festival traffic. Kiana leaned forward at every green light, as if her gaze could push the vehicle onward. By the time they reached the hotel, she had rehearsed her complaint about the fare twice.

I arrived in Marrowick with a presentation due at noon and a suitcase whose handle kept collapsing. The station café had one cashier, who was carefully explaining the ingredients in a pastry to a customer. I drummed my fingers against the counter, then leaned sideways to see whether another till was open. Nothing. When my turn finally came, I ordered coffee and asked for the quickest route to the convention center. The cashier started drawing a map on a napkin. I thanked her, tucked it away without looking, and strode outside. At the crossing, I pressed the walk button twice and watched the red figure remain fixed. My foot bounced against the pavement. A cyclist rolled past and told me the light took forever. I took off down the block, coffee sloshing over the lid, determined to find a faster way.

After a night bus delivered him to unfamiliar Dunwich, Mateo found that the hotel would not release his room until afternoon. He stood beside the lobby desk while the clerk searched through a ledger, then looked toward the elevators, the windows, and the clock in quick succession. His duffel slid from his shoulder and thumped onto the floor. The clerk offered to store it and suggested a nearby museum. Mateo gave a tight smile, asked how long the walk took, and left before hearing the whole answer. Outside, he marched past the museum entrance and hailed a cab for the harbor instead. Traffic stopped beside a delivery truck. Mateo tapped the door handle, craned his neck to see around the truck, and asked the driver if there was another street. The driver shrugged. Mateo paid at the next corner and continued on foot.

The first thing I learned about Vela was that its tram map had no street names. I had an interview across town, and every minute spent squinting at colored lines made my jaw tighten. A woman waiting nearby offered help, but she was trying to comfort a crying toddler while explaining the transfers. I kept shifting my briefcase and peering down the tracks. When the tram finally arrived, I climbed aboard before the doors had fully opened. At the next stop, I realized I had boarded in the wrong direction. I groaned, jumped down, and started walking along the rails, checking my watch at every corner. A bakery smelled wonderful, but I barely noticed it. By the time I found the correct platform, my shirt clung to my back, and I was muttering the interviewer's name under my breath.

Noura reached the mountain city of Velin with a stiff neck and a list of errands from her brother. The rental counter attendant needed to reboot the computer, so she paced between the desk and the glass doors, dragging her suitcase in a short, squeaking loop. Each time the screen flickered, she stopped and leaned over the counter. The attendant said it would only take another moment. Noura pressed her lips together and pointed at the clock. Once she had the keys, she hurried to the parking lot, where a shuttle driver was loading bags one at a time. She offered to lift her own case, then did so without waiting for his reply. On the ride downtown, she watched the road signs flash by and asked twice whether they were close. At the hotel, she set off toward the entrance before the shuttle had fully stopped.

I stepped off the ferry in Port Ansel just as rain began needling the pavement. The map kiosk kept flashing a message that it was unavailable, and I struck the side of it with the heel of my hand. A shopkeeper pointed me toward the old quarter, but her directions included three lanes with nearly identical names. I thanked her, then hurried off before she could add more. At the first intersection, I chose wrong and ended up beside a fish market. My suitcase bumped into a crate, and a vendor shouted after me. I raised one hand in apology without stopping. The hotel was supposedly ten minutes away; after half an hour, I asked a courier for help. He unfolded a paper map at a leisurely pace while I bounced on my toes and stared at the rain dripping from his helmet.

At sixty-three, Peter was used to managing his own travel, but the buses in Lydon displayed their destinations only after they pulled away from the curb. He stood with his ticket in hand, watching vehicle after vehicle depart while he tried to decipher the route board. A student offered to help, and Peter pointed at the address on his phone. The student searched slowly through a transit app. Peter cleared his throat, stepped closer, and suggested a taxi instead. At the taxi stand, a driver was finishing a long phone call. Peter opened the rear door, shut it again, then checked the meter before getting in. The route crossed a bridge crowded with roadworks. He drummed a rhythm on his knee and asked the driver to turn at a side street. When they stopped at a light, Peter was already reaching for the door latch.

My first morning in Caldor began with a broken coffee machine and a landlord who said the repair person was on the way. I had only one day to find the archive where my grandmother's letters were stored. While the landlord called again, I stood in the narrow hallway, tying and untying my scarf. He kept saying the technician was nearby. I nodded, took my bag, and left without coffee. On the street, I asked a passerby for the archive. She paused to consider, then pulled out a paper directory. I glanced toward the corner, checked my phone, and asked if she could simply point me in the right direction. She did, and I set off at a brisk clip. At the archive desk, a clerk began explaining the registration forms. I gathered them up before she finished and filled in every blank at once.

Yusuf arrived in Orsini with a violin case and a concert audition scheduled for late afternoon. The station's information booth had a handwritten note saying the attendant would return soon. He circled the booth twice, then found a cleaner and asked for the quickest route to the music school. The cleaner began describing a neighborhood landmark. Yusuf nodded rapidly, adjusted the case strap, and set off before he had the whole route. At a plaza, he stopped three people in succession, each giving slightly different directions. His heel kept lifting from the stones while they spoke. When a delivery van blocked the narrow lane, he squeezed past it, nearly knocking his bow against the wall. He reached the school with minutes to spare, hair damp at his temples. The receptionist asked him to wait for the director, and Yusuf's fingers drummed against the violin case.

I landed in Sable City before dawn and discovered that the train into town was suspended for track repairs. The replacement bus sat across the terminal, but its driver was helping an elderly passenger climb aboard. I shifted my backpack, looked at the queue, and checked the departure board although it still showed the same delay. When I finally got on, every seat was taken. I stood in the aisle, gripping a pole, while the bus crawled through sleepy streets. At each stop I leaned toward the doors, ready to jump out if it looked closer to my hostel. A passenger told me the central square was only two stops away. I pressed the button immediately and ended up stepping off at the wrong one. I unfolded my map, folded it again, and started walking, my stride growing longer with every block.

Seventeen-year-old Elsie had never visited Brackenport, and the coach left her at a terminal miles from the youth hostel. She asked the information clerk for directions, but a school group had gathered around the desk with questions of their own. Elsie rocked from heel to toe, tugging at the strap of her overnight bag. When the clerk finally looked up, she gave Elsie a bus number and pointed toward the stop. Elsie sprinted across the terminal, arriving just as the bus doors folded shut. She slapped the side lightly and watched it pull away, then marched to the posted schedule. The next one was due in twenty-five minutes. She paced the painted curb, scrolled through every taxi listing, and kept glancing down the road. When a bus appeared from the far end, Elsie raised her arm before she could read its destination.

The message arrived at 9:07: Please come to my office when you have a moment. I had a shipment of ceramic tiles waiting at the loading bay and a driver who kept checking his watch. I tapped my pencil against the desk, then stood, sat, and stood again while the printer crawled through a stack of invoices. At last I went down the hall. My manager was on a call, so I hovered beside the door, shifting my weight and glancing at the clock above her cabinet. When she finally waved me in, she asked whether I could cover Saturday. I looked at the shipment schedule already clutched in my hand. “If this is all, I need to get those tiles moving,” I said, too quickly. She blinked, then nodded. I apologized, tucked the schedule under my arm, and reached the loading bay before the driver started his engine.

At sixty-two, Marisol had learned to keep three clocks in view: the wall clock, the oven timer on her phone, and the tiny display on the label printer. When her supervisor called her into the office, she glanced at all three. The bakery’s holiday orders were backing up, and a rack of cooling rolls needed wrapping before the afternoon courier arrived. In the office, her supervisor searched through a drawer for a form, stopping twice to answer messages. Marisol’s fingers drummed against her apron. She leaned toward the desk, then straightened when the supervisor looked up. “Could we get to the reason you sent for me?” she asked. The supervisor explained that a customer had praised her new cardamom loaf and wanted the recipe. Marisol’s shoulders lowered. She gave the measurements, then hurried back to the ovens, where the timer had begun its sharp, insistent beeping.

I was halfway through repairing the museum’s ticket scanner when my team lead’s message popped up: Office. Now, please. I wiped grease from my fingers and crossed the building, rehearsing possible disasters. In the office, he was arranging colored sticky notes into neat rows. I watched him move one, pause, and move it back. My knee bounced under the chair. “Is the scanner down again?” I asked. He said no, then explained that the museum director wanted me to demonstrate the repair at a staff meeting next week. I glanced through the open doorway toward the queue forming at the entrance. “Could we settle the time today? I have people waiting on that machine.” He checked his calendar, asked me to repeat the available slots, and finally chose one. I was out the door before he finished describing the meeting room, already reaching for my screwdriver.

Nico’s lunch break had been reduced to a granola bar when the manager summoned him upstairs. He had a delivery route to map, two new couriers waiting for instructions, and a phone that kept lighting up with questions. In the office, the manager began with a long account of a client’s latest request, circling the subject without landing on it. Nico’s foot tapped against the chair leg. He folded and unfolded the corner of his route sheet until the paper softened. “What do you need me to do?” he asked, his voice brisk. The manager finally handed him a revised schedule and asked him to train the new drivers. Nico scanned the pages, pointed out that one address was missing, and asked for the corrected version before the couriers left. His manager made the change. Nico took the sheet and headed downstairs, biting into the granola bar on the way.

My shift at the aquarium ended in twenty minutes, and the penguin enclosure still needed its evening checks. Then the office phone rang, and my supervisor asked me to come upstairs. I wiped my hands on my uniform and jogged along the corridor, expecting an emergency. She was studying a spreadsheet, clicking through tabs without speaking. I stood by the door, watching the seconds change on the digital clock. “Is something wrong with the water readings?” I asked. She shook her head and said she wanted to offer me a weekend position leading the school tours. I looked at the stack of checklists in my pocket and asked when she needed an answer. “Before you leave,” she said. I pressed my lips together while she described the pay and schedule, then agreed to try it for a month. Downstairs, I finished the checks with enough time to wave goodnight to the penguins.

Evelyn had spent the morning untangling a mistake in the payroll system when her manager called her into his office. She brought the error report, expecting him to approve the fix. Instead, he asked about a new software course, then searched his inbox for the enrollment link. Evelyn watched the cursor crawl through message after message. Her hands rested flat on the desk, but one thumb kept rubbing the edge of the report. “Can we handle the payroll correction first?” she said. “The deadline is in an hour.” He looked up, surprised, and opened the document she had brought. They corrected the figures in minutes. He then forwarded the course link, which had been sitting near the top of his inbox all along. Evelyn thanked him, took the printout, and returned to her desk. The payroll team was waiting for her confirmation, and she sent it before the printer had finished warming up.

I was loading paint cans into the van when our store manager called from the office. “Can you come here?” he asked, leaving out why. I parked the hand truck and hurried inside, shoes squeaking on the polished floor. He was on the phone, pointing to a chair. I sat for a few seconds, stood to look through the window at the customers gathering by the checkout, then sat again. When he ended the call, he started telling me about a display he’d seen in another branch. I cut in and asked whether the van could leave first; the delivery crew had been waiting since dawn. He glanced at the clock and immediately signed the dispatch form. Then he asked if I could build the display tomorrow. “Send me the measurements today,” I said, already backing toward the door. The hand truck’s handle was warm under my palm when I reached it.

At twenty-four, Darius was the newest analyst in a busy insurance office, and he had been waiting all morning for approval to send a report. His manager finally called him in, but began by asking about the weekend football match. Darius gave a short answer and glanced at the folder on the desk between them. The manager turned to a second topic, then shuffled through a pile of mail. Darius’s fingers pinched the folder’s edge; his shoe traced a quick rhythm against the carpet. “The client needs the report before noon,” he said. “Could you review the final page now?” The manager opened it, spotted a missing signature, and signed. Darius thanked him, gathered the pages, and was halfway back to his workstation before the manager added a question about the match. He called back a polite answer over his shoulder and pressed Send as soon as he sat down.

The call from my manager came while I was helping a customer choose a wheelchair ramp. She said she needed me in her office, and I asked if I should bring anything. “Just yourself,” she replied. I finished explaining the ramp’s measurements, then walked to her office with my catalog tucked under one arm. She was arranging a bouquet on the filing cabinet, turning each stem until it sat just so. I shifted the catalog from hand to hand and checked the clock above her desk. “What did you need?” I asked. She smiled and told me the company had approved a small budget for accessibility training. She wanted me to lead it. I asked when the money would be available and whether the sessions could happen during scheduled work hours. She opened the budget sheet, and we settled both points. I returned to the showroom with the dates written in thick marker across my notepad.

Priya was repairing a torn costume seam when the theater’s production manager called her upstairs. The dress had to be back on the performer before rehearsal, and the needle kept catching in the heavy fabric. In the office, the manager was describing a new storage plan, pausing to search for a diagram on his computer. Priya stood beside the desk, turning the pincushion around her wrist. “Can you show me the plan?” she asked. He clicked through folders while she watched the rehearsal clock through the glass wall. At last the diagram appeared. The new shelves would clear space in the costume room, but they would arrive next week. Priya asked him to approve temporary racks for today. He signed the request, and she hurried back downstairs. The performer was waiting in the doorway, one sleeve half on, as Priya threaded her needle again.

My manager sent for me just as I was closing the month-end books. I left the figures open on my screen and hurried into her office, carrying a notebook in case she needed details. She was composing an email and asked me to wait. I sat, then stood to stretch, then leaned against the filing cabinet, eyes flicking between her hands and the clock. When she finally turned around, she asked whether I could explain the new expense categories to the interns. I told her I could, but the closing figures had to be submitted first. “How long will that take?” she asked. I pointed to the unfinished line on my notebook and gave her a time. She moved the intern session to the afternoon. I went back to my desk, completed the final check, and sent the report with two minutes to spare.

Wesley had a pot of soup simmering in the staff kitchen when the hotel manager asked him to come by the office. He dried his hands on a towel and checked the stove dial before leaving. The manager was reading a guest review aloud, stopping to comment on every sentence. Wesley’s gaze kept darting toward the kitchen doorway, where steam was beginning to cloud the glass. He shifted from heel to toe and finally said, “Would you like me to answer the review, or is there another task?” The manager set the tablet down and asked him to prepare a complimentary meal for the guest. Wesley suggested a dish that could be made quickly and checked whether the kitchen had the ingredients. It did. He returned downstairs, lowered the heat, and started chopping vegetables while the manager sent the guest an apology.

I had already read every poster in the clinic hallway, including the one about handwashing that had a cartoon bear on it. My blood test was supposed to be ready by ten, and the clock above reception now showed 10:17. I tapped my shoe against the chair leg, stopped when a woman glanced over, then started again more quietly. Each time the door opened, I sat straighter, only to watch someone else get called. My phone had no new messages, so I checked it again, then opened the clinic app and refreshed the blank results page. The receptionist was helping a family with forms; I knew she was busy, but I leaned toward the desk anyway. When she finally looked up, I asked whether the lab had sent anything. She checked the screen and promised to find out. I folded my appointment card into a tiny square while I waited for her answer.

At seventy-two, Mr. Okafor had brought a newspaper to the clinic, but he had not turned a page in half an hour. His knee bounced beneath the chair, making the folded paper tremble in his hands. The doctor had said the scan results would be discussed after the radiologist reviewed them. Every time a nurse crossed the waiting room, Okafor lifted his chin and studied her face for a clue. He asked the receptionist how long the review usually took, then apologized when she explained that it varied. His daughter offered him a cup of water. He drank it in three swallows and immediately checked the hallway again. To keep himself occupied, he counted the blue tiles along the opposite wall, lost his place, and began over. When the physician finally appeared, Okafor stood so quickly that his newspaper slid to the floor.

The clinic’s fish tank had one orange fish that kept swimming the same loop. I followed it with my eyes, then checked the digital clock: 2:06. The nurse had said my allergy panel should be back shortly, but “shortly” had stretched across two episodes of a cooking show on the waiting-room television. I slid my jacket on, took it off, and tucked my hands under my thighs so I would stop drumming my fingers. A child across from me was building a tower from paper cups; I watched each cup wobble as if it were a countdown. When the phone in my pocket vibrated, I nearly dropped it, but it was only a delivery notice. I went to the desk and asked whether I could step outside without missing my name. The receptionist said she would call me. I chose a seat beside the door and kept my eyes on it.

Mina had arrived before sunrise for her clinic appointment, carrying a thermos of ginger tea and a notebook filled with questions. By late morning, the tea was cold and the notebook had been opened to the same page so many times that its corner had softened. The technician had promised to send her test results to the physician, who would come speak with her. Mina watched staff badges pass the doorway and tried to match each face to the person she expected. She paced from the window to the vending machine, then returned to her chair when another patient entered. A receptionist said the doctor was reviewing a complicated case. Mina nodded, but her fingers tightened around the notebook’s spine. She rehearsed a calm way to ask for an update, discarded it, and tried again. At last, the physician called her name. Mina rose before the final syllable had left his mouth.

I was meant to pick up my twins from school at three, and the clinic had told me my results would be ready well before then. At 2:35, I had checked the clock often enough to know its second hand made a faint click at the top. My phone sat open on my lap, showing the school’s number, though nobody had called. I asked the nurse whether the lab had reported back. She said she was checking, and I stood beside the reception desk instead of returning to my seat. A man with a cane needed help filling out a form, so I moved aside and held the door for him. Once he was settled, I looked at the clock again. My foot traced quick circles on the floor. When the nurse returned with an update, I stopped moving long enough to hear every word.

Darius, a college drummer, kept a pair of sticks in his backpack, and the clinic’s vinyl chair seemed to invite him to practice. He tapped a silent pattern against his jeans, sped it up, then caught himself when the woman beside him frowned. His bloodwork was routine, the nurse had said, and the results would appear in the patient portal that afternoon. He refreshed the page so often that the screen dimmed between attempts. At reception, he asked if the lab had an estimated time. The clerk gave him a kind smile and no definite answer. Darius walked to the water cooler, filled a paper cup, and drank without tasting it. He tried calling his bandmate, but the unanswered call left him staring at the portal again. When the result finally appeared, he read it once, then hurried to find the nurse who could explain the unfamiliar numbers.

I had promised myself I would not watch the hallway, so I focused on the little cracks in the floor. There were three near my shoes and one shaped like a crooked branch. Then a nurse pushed open the door, and my head snapped up before I could stop it. My test results were due before the clinic closed, and the afternoon seemed to be thinning away. I asked for the time, though the clock was directly above the receptionist. She told me there was no news yet. I thanked her, returned to my chair, and folded the paper sleeve from my coffee into smaller and smaller strips. My sister texted to ask if I had heard anything. I typed, “Not yet,” erased it, and sent the same words again. When footsteps approached, I stood, then sat back down after they passed. The next time the door opened, I stayed on my feet.

At twenty-four, Noa had never spent this long in a medical waiting room. She was there for a thyroid test, and the clinician had said the results might be ready before her lunch break ended. Now the break was nearly over. Noa arranged the magazines by size, then returned them when the receptionist gave her a puzzled look. She opened a message from her manager, read it twice, and typed that she would be late returning to work. Her heel knocked a brisk rhythm against the chair. When another patient was called, Noa leaned forward, expecting her own name to follow, but the hallway door closed again. She walked to the desk and asked if the lab had sent her numbers. The receptionist offered to check. Noa took a slow breath, then another, while watching the computer screen from across the counter. A printer started, and she was already standing when the page emerged.

The clinic’s waiting room was decorated with framed landscape photographs, and I had memorized every mountain and river before my test results arrived. The doctor had said the blood panel might take an hour; it had been nearly two. I kept my coat on even though the room was warm, then peeled it off and draped it across my knees. My hands moved from my pockets to my phone and back again. A receptionist answered a call, and I listened for any mention of the lab, though she was speaking to someone else. I asked whether I could get an estimate. She said she would look into it, and I nodded too quickly. While she searched, I walked to the window and back, counting each step. The clinic door opened to a gust of rain. I checked the time once more, then went to the desk to ask if the doctor had seen the report.

Rosa had traveled two buses from her bakery job to get a follow-up test, and she had to return before the evening rush. The clinic staff had told her the results could be reviewed while she waited. She kept smoothing the flour dust from her sleeves, though there was hardly any left. Each time the receptionist picked up the phone, Rosa paused mid-motion and listened. She checked the bus schedule on her phone, closed it, and opened it again three minutes later. A nurse said the physician was finishing with another patient. Rosa asked whether she could at least learn if the report had arrived. The nurse promised to check. Rosa stood by the doorway, shifting her weight from one foot to the other, then sat when a new patient needed the chair. At the sound of her name, she grabbed her bag and nearly left her umbrella behind.

I was trying to finish a crossword while I waited for the clinic to call me in with my test results. The clues seemed easy until I noticed I had written the same answer in three boxes and ruined the whole corner. I rubbed it out hard enough to tear the page. The nurse had said the lab was running behind, but the clock kept moving at its ordinary pace, which felt personal. I asked the front desk whether my report had arrived. They had not heard back, so I returned to my chair and crossed my arms. My phone rang with a number I did not recognize; I answered before the second ring, only to hear a recorded offer for insurance. I hung up and stared at the clinic entrance. When the nurse finally appeared, I rose with the crossword still crumpled in my fist.

At the rural clinic, Tomas sat beneath a calendar from last year because it was the only open seat near the nurse’s station. He had driven in from his farm to learn whether his infection test had cleared, and he needed to be back before the afternoon animals were fed. The receptionist said the clinician would speak with him as soon as the lab fax came through. Tomas watched the machine across the room, its tray empty, then asked whether it had been checked. He walked to the water fountain, took a sip, and returned before the stream had stopped dripping. His boot scraped the floor in short strokes. When the receptionist answered another call, he leaned forward, ready to ask again, but held back. At last, the fax machine whirred. Tomas stood beside his chair, hands clasped, as the first sheet curled into the tray.

At seven, I had already watched three older kids leap from the pool’s edge while Dad was still explaining how to blow bubbles. I kicked the water, splashing his shirt. “Can we get to the real swimming now?” I asked, staring at the blue lane rope beyond us. Dad put a hand beneath my belly and told me to float. I lifted my head every few seconds to check whether he was still holding me, and each time my legs sank. He showed me again, slow as a clock hand. My fingers curled around his wrist. Finally, he let go for one breath. I moved my arms in a clumsy circle and reached the steps by myself. Dad grinned, but I was already pointing toward the deep end, asking how soon we could try that.

Mara, nine, had packed her goggles the night before and wore them on her forehead through breakfast. At the community pool, her mother started with the steps: sit, kick, count to five. Mara counted loudly, then asked if five could mean five fast numbers. Her heels drummed against the water while her mother demonstrated a slow flutter kick. When the lesson moved to holding the wall, Mara glanced at the diving board and sighed so sharply that a lifeguard looked over. Her mother asked her to practice one push-off. Mara shoved away, stretched her arms, and glided farther than before. She surfaced with wet hair across her face, blinking in surprise. “Again,” she said, before her mother could praise her. This time, she remembered to keep her chin down and made it to the next marker.

I was ten and convinced that the lake had been waiting long enough. My uncle had tied a bright float around my waist and was teaching me to paddle beside the dock. Each time he stopped to correct my hands, I slapped the surface and asked whether we could swim to the buoy yet. The sun warmed my shoulders; the buoy bobbed just beyond easy reach. Uncle Reza kept his voice calm and had me practice turning onto my back. I rolled over, swallowed a mouthful of water, and grabbed for his arm. He steadied me without a lecture, then showed me how to breathe out slowly. I wanted to try the buoy again before my cough had finished. But when he asked me to float for ten full seconds, I managed it, watching clouds drift overhead instead of checking the distance.

In the hotel pool, six-year-old Theo kept asking his father when they would leave the shallow ledge. His father had promised to teach him to swim before dinner, and Theo treated every pause as a delay in the schedule. He wriggled out of the kickboard straps, then had to put them back on. “I know how already,” he said, though he still clung to the rail. His father asked him to practice blowing a trail of bubbles from one tile to the next. Theo puffed once, popped up, and demanded a longer distance. They tried again. Halfway across, Theo’s feet began to paddle without being told. He reached the father’s waiting hands and immediately asked to repeat the trip without the board. His father nodded, and Theo pushed off before the answer was fully finished.

At the YMCA, I watched the clock above the lifeguard’s chair while Mom taught me to float. I was twelve, old enough to hate being watched and young enough to need her hand beneath my back. Every time she said, “Relax your shoulders,” I stiffened them harder. The lesson seemed to consist mostly of stopping, breathing, and trying again. I scraped my toes along the pool floor and asked if we could skip ahead to laps. Mom didn’t argue; she simply moved her hand a little farther away. When I noticed, I kept my arms spread and let the water hold me. A quiet minute passed. Then I tipped forward and swam three strokes toward her. My lungs burned, but I reached her without grabbing the wall. I asked if we could do five strokes next, already standing on my toes.

Nico’s grandmother had brought him to the indoor pool before the morning crowd arrived. At five, he wanted to race the floating ducks she had placed in the shallow end, but she began by showing him how to hold the rail and kick. He kicked so hard that one duck spun away. “That’s enough practicing,” he declared, reaching for it. Grandma retrieved the toy and asked him to try a gentler motion. He twisted his mouth, then copied the small, quick kicks she demonstrated. The duck drifted back within reach. She guided him away from the wall, supporting his chest as he paddled toward it. Nico kept looking over her shoulder at the toy, which now floated near the steps. When his feet found the floor, he hurried over, then turned around and demanded another trip, this time without her hand on his shirt.

I had brought my son to the beach because he kept saying the ocean looked easy. Now the tide tugged at our ankles, and he was asking for the fourth time when we could go past the breaking waves. I showed him how to float on his back in the calm shallows, one palm beneath his shoulder blades. He kicked up spray and complained that lying still was not swimming. A cold wave rolled in, and he clutched my neck. I held him until his breathing eased, then pointed to the foam line and asked him to paddle with me only as far as that. He glanced toward the distant surfers, jaw tight, but followed my arms through the water. At the foam line, he turned onto his back and stayed afloat for several breaths. “Next time, farther,” he said, already pulling at my hand.

Priya’s father had cleared the backyard pool for her first swimming lesson, but she kept checking the clock on the patio table. She was eight and had planned to invite a friend over afterward; the lesson was eating into her afternoon. Her father showed her how to hold a kickboard and move from one side to the other. Priya drove her feet through the water, reached the steps, and asked whether that counted as learning. He pointed out that she had lifted her head and forgotten to breathe. She groaned, pushed wet hair from her eyes, and climbed back in. On the next crossing, she kept her face low and turned to the side for air. When she arrived, she looked first at the clock, then at her father. He smiled and handed her the board. “One more,” she said, already backing away.

My father taught me in the apartment building’s narrow pool, where every lap seemed to end almost as soon as it began. I was eleven and kept asking him to remove the foam belt. He said I should first learn to kick without staring at my feet. I rolled my eyes and launched myself forward, but my knees bent and I barely moved. The belt bobbed while I hauled myself back to the wall. Dad demonstrated again, making small movements from his hips. I copied him, counting each kick under my breath and glancing at the far end after every few. At last, I crossed the pool without scraping my toes along the floor. Dad reached for the belt buckle. I stepped away, eager to find out what it felt like without the foam, though my fingers were already gripping the wall.

At the campground pond, Eli wanted his father to teach him the stroke he had seen in a swimming video. His father began with safe entry and practiced floating beside the dock. Eli groaned when they spent several minutes learning how to reach the ladder, then pointed toward the open water. A dragonfly skimmed the surface, and Eli tracked it instead of listening. His father asked him to swim from the dock to a bright orange marker just a few feet away. Eli took off with splashing strokes, lifted his head too high, and stopped halfway. His father stayed close, guiding him back to a steady kick. On the second try, Eli made it to the marker and tapped it with one finger. He turned around at once, ready to go again, while his father reminded him to wait until they had both caught their breath.

I was nine when Aunt Laila took me to the public pool and said we would learn to swim before my cousins arrived. I wanted to show them something impressive, not spend the morning gripping the gutter while she explained how to breathe. I asked the same question whenever she paused: “Can I go now?” She answered by having me practice pushing off and gliding. My first try lasted about a second before I grabbed the wall again. I pressed my lips together and tried harder, shooting forward with my arms locked. The water carried me past a painted star on the bottom. I popped up, startled by how far I had gone. Aunt Laila laughed softly and told me to remember that feeling. I nodded, but my feet were already braced against the wall for another launch.

Mika’s mother taught swimming at a small hotel pool in Kyoto, and Mika expected the lesson to take less time than unpacking their bags. He was seven and had spotted a shelf of colorful kickboards across the deck. His mother asked him to practice putting his face in the water and blowing bubbles. Mika dipped his chin, rose instantly, and asked if he could choose a board now. She set a timer for one minute and challenged him to make bubbles until it rang. He watched the digits crawl, puffing out air in short bursts and bouncing on his heels between them. When the alarm sounded, he snatched a yellow board and kicked toward his mother. He reached her with a crooked path but stayed afloat. Rather than climb out, he handed her the board and pointed back to the starting wall.

At 4:12, my van was still trapped behind a street sweeper moving at the speed of a slow parade. The bakery box beside me held a wedding cake, and the couple had already called twice. I drummed the steering wheel, checked the clock, then checked it again as if the numbers might have changed out of courtesy. When the sweeper finally pulled aside, I took the next turn too quickly and had to circle a block around a road crew. At the venue, I carried the cake up three flights, breathing through my teeth. The bride reached for it with trembling hands. I managed a smile, but my foot kept tapping against the tile while she inspected the frosting.

Nadia’s last parcel was a crate of replacement violin strings, due at a music academy before its afternoon rehearsal. A stalled bus blocked the narrow avenue, and the navigation screen kept drawing a bright blue route through the unmoving traffic. She leaned forward over the wheel, jaw set, and clicked her turn signal on and off. At the next opening, she slipped down an alley, only to meet a delivery truck backing out of a loading dock. Nadia exhaled sharply and checked the time on her dashboard. When she reached the academy, a student was waiting at the curb. She handed over the crate without a word, then watched the student sprint inside as she hurried back to her van.

I had promised the clinic that the insulated bag would arrive before the afternoon dose, but a freight train had other plans. Its cars crawled past the crossing one by one, each rattling by like a fresh insult. I tapped my badge against the steering wheel and called dispatch, then hung up before the hold music finished. A cyclist rolled past and gave me a cheerful wave. I stared after him, fingers drumming on the window. When the barrier rose, I accelerated toward the clinic, stopped at a red light, and pressed my lips together. The nurse met me at the entrance. I passed her the bag, then paced beside the door while she checked its seal.

For Luis, the apartment tower’s elevator seemed to stop on every floor except the one he needed. His delivery cart carried twelve boxes of printer paper, and the office manager had sent three messages asking where they were. He jabbed the call button again, although its light was already glowing. A resident stepped out, thanked him for holding the door, and began searching through a purse. Luis shifted his weight from heel to heel, eyes fixed on the rising numbers above the lift. When it finally opened, he pushed the cart inside and rode upward with both hands gripping the handle. At the office, he stacked the boxes neatly, then glanced at his watch before the manager could thank him.

The seafood order was meant to reach the restaurant before the lunch rush, and I was already twenty minutes behind when a flock of geese occupied the road. They wandered between my wheels, honking as if I were the one blocking traffic. I drummed my fingers on the gearshift and muttered at the windshield. A farmer came out carrying a bucket, but the birds took their time following him. I checked the temperature display on the cooler twice. Once the road cleared, I drove carefully, though every red light felt personal. The chef was waiting at the back entrance. He took the fish, inspected the ice, and nodded. I was already halfway to my van before he finished speaking.

Marlene had six grocery deliveries left when a sudden downpour flooded the underpass. Her route app rerouted her through a school zone just as the final bell rang. A stream of children crossed the street, and she gripped the wheel while her knee bounced beneath it. One child dropped a mitten; Marlene waited as a teacher retrieved it, watching the minutes slide away on the dashboard clock. At the next stop, an elderly customer opened the door slowly and asked her to bring the bags inside. Marlene’s shoulders rose, then lowered. She carried each sack to the kitchen, set them by the counter, and checked her phone before the customer could offer her tea.

I was carrying a bundle of legal documents to the courthouse, where a clerk had warned me about the filing deadline. Then the drawbridge lifted for a sailboat that seemed to be inching along for the scenery. I bounced my heel against the floor mat and watched the clock crawl past the minute mark. My phone buzzed with another message from the law office. I typed, “Still coming,” deleted it, and sent only my location. When traffic finally rolled, I took the waterfront road and got stuck behind a tour bus stopping at every corner. I arrived with the envelope held flat beneath my jacket. The clerk stamped it without looking up. I let out a breath and rubbed the crease my fingers had made.

Theo’s delivery van was late to the community theater, and the prop sword inside was needed for the evening’s opening scene. A parade had closed the main street, so he steered through residential blocks, turning wherever a gap appeared. At one corner, a dog walker paused to untangle two leashes. Theo’s hands tightened around the wheel; he watched the clock, then the leashes, then the clock again. The theater’s stage manager called while he was still parking. Theo carried the long package through the lobby and up a narrow staircase, taking the steps two at a time. A performer grabbed the sword and dashed backstage. Theo stayed by the doorway, shifting his weight as the distant curtain bell rang.

I was supposed to deliver a replacement hearing aid to a retired teacher before her daughter left for work. My scooter’s rear tire had picked up a nail, and the repair shop said ten minutes, then twenty. I stood beside the counter, checking the time on my phone until the screen dimmed. The mechanic worked steadily, which somehow made every turn of his wrench seem louder. When he handed back the keys, I thanked him too quickly and rode across town, avoiding the roughest streets. The teacher’s daughter was waiting on the porch, coat on and keys in hand. I gave her the small case. She thanked me, and I nodded, already backing toward the steps.

Priya’s final stop was a greenhouse on the edge of town, where a box of seedlings needed to arrive before the afternoon heat. A tractor had slowed the country road to a crawl, trailing dust across the windshield. She drummed her thumb on the steering wheel and leaned toward the window, looking for a chance to pass. There was none. At last the tractor turned into a field, and Priya picked up speed, only to find a herd of sheep scattered across the next lane. She pressed her lips together as the farmer guided them aside. At the greenhouse, she carried the box straight to the shade house. The gardener checked the labels while Priya stood with one hand on her hip, foot tapping.

The costume shop had packed a child’s astronaut suit for a school presentation, and I was due there before the students went onstage. A fallen branch blocked the road, so I followed a detour that wound through a maze of one-way streets. I kept glancing at the parcel on the passenger seat, as though it could reassure me. At a stop sign, I drummed both hands on the wheel before remembering to move. The school’s front doors were locked, and I had to circle to the gym entrance. A teacher met me there, holding a clipboard and looking toward the curtain. I handed over the suit. When the child appeared in the doorway wearing it, my shoulders finally dropped.

Rafael’s van was running late with a box of fresh pastries for a hotel breakfast meeting. A water main repair had turned the hotel’s street into a trench of cones and machinery. He parked two blocks away and carried the box beneath one arm, weaving around workers and puddles. Each time someone stopped to inspect a map or answer a call, Rafael’s steps faltered and his fingers tightened around the cardboard. At the hotel entrance, a guest held the door while balancing a stack of luggage tags. Rafael gave a clipped thanks and hurried to the ballroom. The meeting organizer took the pastries, checked the time, and began arranging them. Rafael remained beside the cart, watching the clock above the reception desk.

At sixty-eight, I traded my accounting desk for a narrow strip of backyard and a packet of tomato seeds. The instructions said to keep the soil warm, so I stood over the bed with a thermometer, checking it every few minutes. By noon I had moved the pots into sunlight, then shifted them again when a cloud crossed. My wife suggested I make tea; I carried the mug outside and forgot to drink it. Each morning I pressed a finger into the earth, searching for a green hook that had not appeared. On the fifth day, I dug carefully beside one seed, convinced it might have gone wrong. The tiny white root I uncovered looked healthy, but I covered it at once, cheeks hot. After that, I set a chair beside the bed and practiced letting the earth do its work.

Marlene, newly retired from the city library, planted radishes in a raised bed behind her bungalow. The packet promised a quick harvest, and she took that as a personal schedule. Every afternoon she crouched to inspect the rows, brushing soil aside with a teaspoon. When her neighbor waved from the fence, Marlene answered without looking up. She watered twice in one morning, then consulted a gardening book to learn whether she had overdone it. The book offered no forecast for the particular patch of dirt under her nose. On the ninth day, she tugged at a leaf and pulled up a radish no bigger than a marble. She set it on the kitchen windowsill, resisting the urge to pull the others. By the weekend, several had filled out, and she sliced them into a salad, still counting the days until the next batch.

I was seventy-two when I planted beans along the fence, determined to have something climbing before my sister visited in June. The canes leaned at odd angles, and I kept straightening them, though the wind nudged them crooked again. Each time I passed the bed, I lifted a leaf to see whether a tendril had appeared. Nothing. I tapped the packet against my palm and reread the growing chart, as if the dates might have changed. One afternoon, I carried a watering can outside, noticed the surface was damp, and poured anyway. The next morning the soil had pooled around the seeds. I fetched a trowel to make little channels, then stopped myself before turning the whole bed over. A week later, green shoots looped around the canes. I called my sister to report their progress, then went back out to check that they were still there.

After retiring from the railway, Dev planted spinach in a sunny corner of his allotment. He had imagined tidy rows, but the ground was lumpy and his first furrow wandered like a railway line on a bad map. He kept glancing at his watch, although there was nowhere he needed to be. When the seeds disappeared beneath the soil, he swept his hands clean and returned ten minutes later to examine the bed. A passing gardener advised him to give the seedlings time. Dev nodded, then asked how much time, exactly. He searched online for growth photographs and compared them with the bare patch. At dawn, he found two green points and hurried inside to fetch his reading glasses. The shoots were still there when he returned. He marked their place with wooden labels and spent the afternoon repairing a gate instead of hovering over them.

I planted zucchini after leaving my job as a school custodian, choosing the biggest seeds because they looked as if they meant business. The garden plot behind my apartment building was small, but I pictured baskets of squash arriving by midsummer. Every evening I checked the soil, poked a knuckle into it, and stared at the spot where I had planted. When nothing showed, I blamed the chilly nights, then the seed company, then my own watering. I nearly planted another batch on top. Instead, I paced the path between the beds, counting steps until my knees complained. A retired nurse from upstairs saw me circling and handed me a folding chair. I sat for perhaps three minutes before leaning forward again. The first leaves finally opened, broad and crinkled. I took a photograph, sent it to my children, and began calculating how many squash one plant could possibly produce.

Nora, sixty-five and newly finished with a career in catering, sowed carrots in the sandy soil beside her cottage. She had always worked to a clock, so waiting for seeds to sprout felt like being assigned a shift with no tasks. She checked the weather app before breakfast and the bed before lunch. If a bird landed nearby, she hurried out to shoo it away, waving a dish towel. Her husband offered to help, but she snatched the watering can from him, certain he would flood the rows. On the tenth day, she loosened the crusted surface with a fork, then froze when she saw how close the seeds were. That evening she left the bed alone, though she kept looking through the window during the news. A fine green fringe appeared two mornings later. Nora smiled, fetched a ruler, and measured the tallest sprout twice.

When I retired at sixty-nine, I turned the sunny patch beside my garage into a garden for peppers. The catalog showed glossy red fruit, and I wanted those colors before summer faded. I planted seedlings and then read that peppers take their time. The phrase lodged in my head while I carried out a stool, checked the leaves, and counted the unopened buds. One afternoon I pinched a bud between my fingers, trying to decide whether it was large enough to become a pepper. My daughter caught me and told me to stop touching the plant. I crossed my arms and watched from the kitchen instead. A week passed with no visible change, and I began moving the pots to chase the sun. Then one pale blossom opened. I called my daughter over as if the plant had performed a trick, and we stood beside it until a bee arrived.

At seventy-four, Luis left his plumbing business and planted lettuce in a community garden near the harbor. He liked the neat rows, but the seedlings seemed to take forever to form proper leaves. He visited before breakfast, after lunch, and again on his way home from the pharmacy. Each time, he bent low, lips pursed, and compared the plants with a picture on the seed packet. A gull’s shadow crossed the plot, and Luis chased it off with a rake held like a flag. His plot neighbor laughed and said the birds were not interested in lettuce. Luis replied that he preferred not to test the theory. When a cold evening slowed the new growth, he covered the bed with cloth and checked beneath it twice before midnight. By the following week, the leaves had broadened. He cut only a few, then returned the next morning to see whether the rest had caught up.

I planted cucumbers in a barrel on my balcony after retiring from forty years of driving a bus. I was used to watching the clock and reaching every stop on time, but the vine refused to follow a timetable. I tied it to a trellis, loosened the knot, tightened it again, and checked the leaves for signs of progress. A flower appeared, and I leaned over the railing to see whether a cucumber might be hiding beneath it. The balcony chair stayed empty; I preferred standing where I could inspect the plant. My granddaughter told me that pollination mattered, so I carried a small brush outside and dabbed every blossom. The neighbors in the next building watched from their windows. Days later, a tiny cucumber emerged. I fetched a tape measure, then laughed at myself when it barely reached an inch. I measured it anyway, recording the date in my old route log.

Beatrice had retired from nursing at sixty-seven and wanted a vegetable garden that would supply her Sunday table. She chose peas, built a tidy support, and marked each row with painted stones. The first shoots came up unevenly, which bothered her more than she expected. She knelt to check the gaps, then carried extra seeds from the shed, ready to fill them. Her brother reminded her that some sprouts might simply be late. Beatrice frowned at the bare patches and consulted three different gardening guides. None agreed on the ideal spacing. She decided to wait one more day, but spent the evening looking out at the rows between television programs. In the morning, two new shoots had appeared. She moved the stones to make room, then stood back with her hands on her hips. The peas eventually covered their support, and she served the first bowl with a careful count of the pods.

I was sixty-six when I planted potatoes in sacks on the patio, certain I could manage them without bending over a full garden bed. After covering the first shoots, I checked the sacks every morning to see whether the plants had pushed upward. Nothing happened for days. I tapped the sides, lifted the rims, and worried that I had buried the seed potatoes too deep. My son recommended leaving them alone. I said I was leaving them alone while I stood beside them with a trowel. One afternoon, I started to dig down and stopped when I remembered how easily I could damage a growing shoot. I went inside and assembled a bookshelf instead, though I kept glancing at the patio door. The leaves finally broke through in a cluster. I hurried out in slippers, then resisted the urge to uncover the rest. The sacks grew taller, and so did my patience, a little at a time.

After retiring from teaching, Hakeem began a garden behind his duplex, setting out eggplant seedlings in a carefully measured bed. He had taught children to wait their turn for years, yet he found himself checking the plants before sunrise. Their leaves drooped after transplanting, and he circled them with a watering hose, adjusting the spray every few seconds. He searched for recovery in each stem and sighed when the afternoon heat made them sag again. His neighbor offered shade cloth, but Hakeem wanted to see whether the plants could manage on their own. He sat on the porch with a notebook, recording leaf color and soil dampness. On the fourth day, one plant stood upright. He drew a star beside its entry and moved the notebook closer to the door. By late summer, purple fruit hung beneath the leaves. He brought one to his former classroom, where the students asked how long it had taken.

I checked the station clock again, though its hands had barely shifted since the last time. My train was due in eight minutes, and the platform display still said DELAYED without offering a reason. I tapped my boot against the concrete, stopped when a child copied me, then began drumming my fingers on my suitcase handle instead. A gust pushed a newspaper against my ankle. I kicked it free and watched it tumble under a bench. When the ticket clerk called my name, I spun around so quickly my bag tipped over. She held out a cream envelope addressed in my late father's careful handwriting. I opened it standing beside the timetable. Inside was a note asking me to visit the old orchard before selling it. The train announcement crackled overhead, but I read the page twice, suddenly willing to let it leave without me.

At the bakery, Nia kept glancing at the oven timer as if her stare could hurry it along. The wedding cake had to be boxed before noon, and every minute seemed to bring another request from the bride's family. Nia wiped flour from her hands, checked the timer, and shifted the cake stand an inch to the left, then back again. The postman arrived with a large envelope while she was reaching for the piping bag. It bore the logo of an art school she had applied to months earlier. She tore it open, leaving a small streak of frosting on the paper. The letter offered her a place in the evening program, with a scholarship attached. For a moment she forgot the cake entirely. Then the timer rang, and Nia hurried to the oven smiling, no longer looking at the clock every few seconds.

I had refreshed the application page so many times that the library computer briefly froze. My scholarship decision was supposed to arrive by email, but the librarian pointed out a thick envelope waiting at the front desk. I walked there fast, then had to wait while someone searched through a stack of parcels. My knee bounced against the counter. When the envelope finally appeared, the return address belonged to a farm in Montana, not the university. My aunt had died the previous winter, and I expected only paperwork. Instead, her letter said she had left me a small cabin and included a key taped to the last page. She wanted me to spend one summer there before deciding what to do with it. I read the instructions twice, then set my phone aside. The scholarship could wait until I found out what she had seen in that place.

During the city council meeting, Omar kept checking the clock above the exit. The public comment period was running late, and he had promised to pick up his daughter before her dance class ended. He rearranged his notes, uncapped and recapped his pen, and leaned toward the microphone whenever another speaker paused. Just as the chair called a short recess, a staff member handed him a letter that had been delivered to the wrong office. The return address was a neighborhood print shop he had visited that morning. Inside was a proof of the mural design he had submitted months ago, along with a note saying the owners wanted him to paint their courtyard wall. Omar's eyes moved over the vivid sketch. He had assumed the project was forgotten. When the meeting resumed, he tucked the letter into his jacket and raised his hand to speak, suddenly ready to stay.

I was halfway through packing my apartment when the mail slot clattered. I dropped a roll of tape and strode to the door, hoping the delivery notice was for the replacement laptop I needed before Monday. The envelope on the mat was handwritten, its stamp from a town where I had lived as a child. My old neighbor, Mr. Bell, had sent it. I tore the flap with my thumb and found a photograph of a tiny brass compass, plus a note saying he had discovered it behind a loose board in the treehouse we built. He wondered if I wanted it back. I sat among the boxes and turned the picture toward the light. The compass had belonged to my mother. I had been rushing all morning, but now I searched for a pen, wrote his address on a card, and promised to come by for it myself.

Sofia paced the greenhouse aisle while the printer spat out shipping labels one at a time. A customer had ordered rare seedlings for a festival, and the courier was already circling the block. She nudged a tray into place, checked the clock, then leaned over the printer as though that might improve its pace. A volunteer came in carrying a sealed letter addressed to Sofia from the botanical garden where she had once interned. She opened it with a pair of pruning scissors. The director invited her to lead a new seed-saving project, beginning the following month. Sofia read the page, then glanced at the rows of plants she had grown herself. Until that moment, she had thought of the greenhouse as a temporary job. She asked the volunteer to finish the labels, pulled a chair to the desk, and began drafting her reply before the courier arrived.

I stared at the empty loading dock while the ferry crew unloaded crates one by one. My brother's fishing boat was meant to be among them, and nobody at the harbor office could tell me why it was late. I kept asking whether they had checked the far pier, then the storage shed, then the list again. A clerk finally offered me a letter that had been left at the office that morning. It was from my brother, written before his boat disappeared from the tracking screen. He said he had taken shelter on a small island after the engine failed and would return with the next tide. He had mailed the letter from a passing cargo ship. I read it with my hands still clenched around the dock railing. The crew's laughter carried across the water. I found a bench and waited, this time watching the horizon instead of the clock.

At the courthouse, Glenn kept shuffling the papers for his father's estate. His appointment was running behind, and he had a bus to catch across town for his night shift. He checked his watch, tapped the folder against his palm, and stood whenever footsteps approached the hallway. A messenger arrived with a letter addressed to him, forwarded from a boarding school he had attended decades earlier. The seal came from the headmaster's office. Glenn opened it beside the drinking fountain. The letter explained that an old classmate had left him a small collection of letters and wanted him to choose whether the school should preserve them. One contained a note of apology for a quarrel Glenn had barely remembered. He read the name again, then sat down. When the clerk called him at last, Glenn asked for a few minutes to make a phone call first.

I had been waiting outside the recording studio for nearly an hour, watching the red light above the door switch on and off. My bandmates were inside mixing our demo, and I kept composing messages to ask whether they had heard back from the label. Before I could send one, the receptionist brought me an envelope that had arrived by courier. The logo belonged to a music magazine I had written to years ago, asking how to become a reviewer. Inside was an invitation to interview a famous singer on tour. They needed an answer by that evening. I read the offer, then looked through the studio window at my friends arguing over a guitar track. I had expected one kind of news and received another. My foot was still bouncing, but now I was pacing for a reason. I called the editor, accepted, and ran back to tell the band.

Leila stood at the pharmacy counter while the technician searched for her prescription. She had already checked the time twice and shifted her shopping bag from one arm to the other. A courier entered carrying a flat envelope with her name printed across it. The return address belonged to a museum in Cairo, where she had submitted photographs of her grandmother's embroidery for an exhibit. Leila opened it before the technician returned. The curator wanted to display the photographs alongside the original garments and asked her to record her grandmother's stories for visitors. She reread the invitation, then gripped the counter to steady her hands. The prescription was ready, but she barely noticed when it was placed beside her. On the walk home, she called her grandmother and asked which dress held the most memories. For once, Leila let the traffic lights dictate the pace.

I was lining up dominoes across the kitchen floor when the doorbell rang. My daughter had promised to help finish the pattern after her shift, but she was late, and I kept glancing at the clock instead of watching the pieces. The visitor was our mail carrier with a registered letter requiring my signature. It came from a small theater in the next county. I had sent them a play years ago and forgotten about it after hearing nothing. Their artistic director had found the manuscript in an old submission box and wanted to stage it that winter.
