When the front door opened, Tomas was still holding the spare screws. He counted them twice before smiling at the finished tables.

I checked the station clock for the sixth time, then checked my phone in case its clock disagreed. The minute hand had barely moved. My train was already humming at the platform, doors open, while a family blocked the ticket gate to rearrange three backpacks. I shifted from foot to foot and tried to edge around them without knocking over a child’s juice. When the gate finally cleared, I sprinted, my scarf streaming behind me. The conductor raised one hand as if to signal that boarding was over. I waved my ticket above my head, then hurried up the steps two at a time. Just as I reached the carriage, the doors beeped. I slipped through sideways, breathing hard, and landed beside a passenger who calmly resumed reading. My knee bounced all the way to the next stop.

At the rural platform, Nia watched the red lights at the rear of the train blink against the dusk. Her bus had arrived late, and the station agent was still explaining something to a man with a folded map. She tapped the toe of her boot against the bench leg, then abandoned her suitcase and ran. Gravel skittered beneath her shoes. The train began to roll just as she reached the platform edge, so she shouted and waved both arms. A conductor leaned from the last open doorway and caught the handle of her bag. Nia hauled herself aboard, cheeks burning, then stood in the vestibule while the countryside slid past. She kept glancing at the watch on her wrist, although the next connection was nearly an hour away. When the conductor smiled, she only gave a quick nod and started sorting through her pockets for her ticket.

I had rehearsed my opening sentence for the interview during the entire walk to the station. Then the ticket machine froze, its screen showing a spinning blue circle. I jabbed the help button twice, watched the train pull in, and grabbed a paper ticket from the kiosk instead. The doors chimed while I bolted down the stairs, one hand gripping my portfolio and the other holding my coat shut. At the platform, a cyclist rolled between me and the nearest carriage. I swerved around him, nearly lost a shoe, and made it aboard as the doors began closing. Nobody looked up. I stood over my portfolio, forcing my breath into an even rhythm. At the next station, I checked the interview address again, then checked it once more. My practiced sentence had vanished, replaced by the sound of the wheels rattling beneath me.

Yusuf had promised his daughter he would be in the front row for her school play, and the promise sat heavily in his mind as the platform display changed to FINAL CALL. His delivery van was parked three blocks away, but traffic had swallowed the time he thought he had. He ran with his lunch tin clanging against his hip, weaving around commuters who stood still beneath the departure board. The train was already moving when he reached it. He raced alongside the last carriage, waving his arm until a railway worker pointed toward a door still open near the middle. Yusuf lunged aboard and caught the rail with both hands. Once inside, he leaned against the wall, mouth open, while his phone lit with a message from the school. He typed that he was on his way, erased it, and began again with shaking thumbs.

I stood behind a slow-moving queue at the bakery, staring through the station windows as my train waited at the platform. The woman ahead of me debated pastry fillings with the cashier. I drummed my fingers on the counter, then left my coffee untouched and hurried out. My backpack snagged on the door handle; I yanked it free and ran down the steps, taking them two at a time. The whistle sounded before I reached the platform. I sprinted past a row of people with rolling cases, calling apologies as I squeezed through. A porter held the carriage door while I scrambled aboard, my receipt fluttering loose behind me. I found an empty seat and pressed my palms to my knees until they stopped trembling. The coffee had spilled inside my bag, but I kept checking the window for the station clock as we pulled away.

Marta had spent ten minutes trying to print a shipping label at the station kiosk, each new screen asking for another confirmation. When the printer finally whirred, her train’s departure announcement echoed overhead. She snatched the label, shoved it into her coat, and ran toward the platform with a parcel tucked under one arm. The parcel slipped; she caught it against her ribs without slowing. Ahead, the doors were closing on a carriage full of seated passengers. Marta called to the conductor, who reopened them just enough for her to squeeze through. Her hat fell onto the platform, and she watched it disappear behind the glass. She sat down across from a child who was peeling an orange, then glanced repeatedly at the route map. At every stop, she leaned toward the window before the train had fully slowed, as if the next sign might have changed.

I saw the train across the concourse just as the station announcement began listing its stops. My suitcase wheels rattled over every seam in the floor, and the crowd kept folding across my path. I pulled the case behind me, then abandoned it when one wheel caught in a crack. With my coat flapping open, I ran for the stairs and took the escalator steps two at a time. At the platform, a guard pointed toward the last carriage. I raced along the yellow line, heard the doors chime, and threw myself through the nearest opening. My suitcase arrived a moment later, bumping into my ankle. I muttered an apology to the passenger I had startled and checked my watch again. The train had not even left the station, but I was already counting the stops and tapping my thumb against the window latch.

At eighty-two, Mr. Bell refused to let his grandson carry the small suitcase. He had packed the violin himself and wanted to deliver it before the afternoon rehearsal, but the taxi had dropped him at the wrong entrance. He hurried through the station, one hand gripping the case, the other lifting his hat against the draft. A departure bell rang. Bell broke into a run, his polished shoes clicking unevenly on the tile. The train began to move as he reached the platform. A young attendant took the suitcase and helped him step aboard, while Bell clutched the rail and pulled himself up. He thanked her, then immediately asked how many minutes remained before the next stop. When she answered, he looked at his watch and shook it once, though it was keeping perfect time. His grandson’s message glowed unanswered on the phone in his pocket.

I had chosen the station café because it was beside my platform, but the espresso machine chose that morning to sputter and stop. I stared at the barista, who was taking the casing apart with a tiny screwdriver, then at the train beyond the glass. My fingers drummed on the counter. I left coins beside the cup and bolted through the exit, still carrying my coat over one arm. The platform stretched farther than it had looked from inside. I ran past the departure sign and reached the train just as the doors began to slide together. A passenger held one side while I slipped into the carriage. My cup sloshed onto my sleeve. I wiped it with a napkin, then checked the station board through the window, watching the letters change as we pulled away. I had not even tasted the coffee.

Ravi’s phone showed a new message from the clinic: his mother’s appointment had been moved earlier. He was already at the station, but on the wrong platform, and the connecting passage seemed to stretch beneath the tracks forever. He hurried down the stairs, took the tunnel at a near run, and charged up the opposite steps as the train gave its warning chime. A railway employee began to close the gate. Ravi raised his ticket and called out, his voice cracking. The employee paused; Ravi slipped through and ran beside the carriage until he found an open door. He climbed aboard and stood clutching the rail, breathing in short pulls. Once the train moved, he dialed the clinic, ended the call before it connected, then tried again. His heel kept striking the floor while the phone rang.

Leonie had promised to bring the signed contract to the publisher before the train reached the city. The envelope was tucked beneath her arm as she hurried through the station, muttering the platform number under her breath. A vending machine had swallowed her coins, and she had spent too long pressing its refund button. Now the train was pulling out. She ran along the platform, boots striking the concrete, and waved the envelope at a conductor near the rear door. He leaned out and caught her wrist, steadying her as she stepped aboard. Leonie thanked him in a rush, then checked the envelope for creases. She sat only after finding her carriage, and even then she kept looking toward the doors whenever someone passed. At the first stop, she stood before the train had fully settled, clutching the contract against her chest.

I shoved the thermos under the seat and checked my watch for the fourth time. Dawn had barely lifted the dark from Lake Mercer, but I’d been awake since three, picturing the trout striking. My uncle’s old motor coughed while I pulled the starter cord again. It caught, then sputtered out. I slapped the casing with my palm and muttered at it as if the engine had chosen this morning to spite me. A loon called somewhere beyond the reeds. I leaned over the gunwale, scanning the water for movement, though we hadn’t even reached the fishing grounds. When the motor finally held, I pushed the throttle too far and sent a sheet of cold spray across my knees. I barely noticed. The shoreline slipped away, and I gripped the rod before the boat had stopped rocking, already twitching its tip to test the line.

Nessa had packed her tackle box the night before, then unpacked it twice to be certain the hooks were there. At dawn she rowed across the lake, each stroke landing harder than the last. A thin veil of mist clung to the water, and the far bank seemed to move no closer. She glanced at the bundled clouds, then at the empty line trailing behind the boat. “Come on,” she said, though there was nothing to hurry but the morning itself. Near a patch of lily pads, she dropped anchor and baited her hook with quick, clumsy fingers. The knot slipped. Nessa hissed, cut the line, and started over, tugging each loop tight enough to redden her fingertips. When a fish finally nudged the bait, she jerked the rod so sharply that the hook flew back and caught her hat. She stared at it, then laughed once and began tying again.

My daughter said the lake would look different before sunrise, so I agreed to take her out. I had expected quiet; instead, the waiting made my shoulders climb toward my ears. The old skiff rocked beside the dock while I fussed with the fuel cap and tapped my boot against a post. Across the water, the eastern clouds brightened by degrees. “It’s almost time,” I said, for the third time. Mina kept watching a heron stalk the shallows. I wanted to tell her we needed to get moving, but her stillness made my own restless motions look ridiculous. At last, we pushed away from shore. I pulled the starter cord, then yanked it again before the engine had finished turning. It roared awake, and I grinned as if I’d won something. Mina pointed to the water, where the heron had just lifted a silver fish. For a moment, I forgot my rod.

At sixty-eight, Rafi still raced the sunrise to Lake Juniper. He parked before the first birds stirred and loaded his little boat in the dark, dropping a wrench twice because his hands were moving faster than his eyes. The launch ramp was slick with dew. He kept looking over his shoulder at the brightening sky, as though dawn might leave without him. Once afloat, he shoved off before his tackle bag was secure. It slid across the floorboards, scattering sinkers beneath the bench. Rafi let out a sharp breath and reached for them, then stopped when the boat drifted toward open water. He grabbed an oar and corrected course with several fierce strokes. A patch of ripples appeared near the reeds. He cast before he had chosen the right lure, watched the line fall short, and reeled it in immediately. On his next try, he paused long enough to notice a kingfisher diving beside him.

The forecast promised a calm morning, but the lake kept slapping the hull while I tried to thread my line. I had taken the first boat out from the marina, eager to reach the rocky point before other anglers claimed it. My fingers fumbled with the tiny swivel. I pulled it tight, saw the knot unravel, and bit back a curse. The sun was only a pale strip behind the hills, yet I was already squinting at the water for signs of fish. When I glanced at my phone, it showed no signal and no new messages. I tucked it away, then immediately dug it out again, as if the screen might have changed. A wake from a passing duck rocked the boat, sending my tackle tin skidding. I caught it with my foot and finally tied the knot. My first cast sailed well past the point. I reeled in at once, determined to get another chance.

Before dawn, thirteen-year-old Felix convinced his grandmother to let him steer their aluminum boat. He sat stiff-backed at the tiller, glancing from the compass to the pale horizon every few seconds. The lake’s surface was smooth enough to mirror the clouds, but he kept nudging the throttle forward. “We’re going plenty fast,” his grandmother reminded him. Felix answered with a quick nod and leaned toward the bow, searching for the cove she had described. When they reached it, he shut off the motor too late; the boat glided past the best spot and bumped softly into a screen of reeds. He pushed the branches away with an oar, face warm beneath his cap. His grandmother calmly baited her hook while Felix clipped on a lure, dropped it, and had to retrieve it from the floor. Then he cast. The line landed close to the reeds at last, and he held perfectly still, eyes fixed on the bobber.

I’d promised myself I wouldn’t check the time, but my wrist kept turning toward my face as I steered out onto Lake Alder. The coffee in my travel mug had gone cold, and I swallowed it anyway while the boat crept through a narrow channel. Reeds brushed the sides with a papery hiss. I wanted to be beyond them, where the deeper water began, but the fog hid every familiar marker. I squeezed the throttle, eased it back, then squeezed again. My brother had warned me that visibility would be poor, and I could hear his caution in my head, which only made me scowl. A buoy emerged beside the bow, close enough to make me jerk the wheel. The boat swung wide, and my tackle bag toppled over. I gathered the scattered hooks one by one. By the time I reached open water, the sky had turned peach, and I finally let the engine idle.

Luz had driven from the city for the opening morning of the season, arriving at the lake with a stiff neck and a cooler full of sandwiches. She launched her kayak beneath a sky just beginning to pale. Each paddle stroke sent her farther from shore, yet she kept checking the map on her phone, tapping it whenever the screen lagged. The fishing cove was only a short distance away, according to the marker. She turned the phone off, then back on, then tucked it into a dry bag with an annoyed little shove. A beaver surfaced beside her and vanished before she could get her camera. Luz spun around, searching the water for its wake, while her kayak drifted sideways. By the time she faced forward, she had passed the cove. She dug her paddle into the water with several brisk strokes and circled back. Once there, she baited her hook carefully, forcing herself to slow down as the bobber settled.

I heard the alarm and got out of bed so quickly that I knocked a book from the nightstand. By the time I reached the lake, the horizon was still dark blue. I launched my borrowed rowboat alone, though its oarlocks squeaked with every pull. My plan was to reach the old bridge before the fish began feeding. Halfway there, a loose seat shifted beneath me. I wedged it back into place, then rowed harder, splashing water over my sleeves. The bridge appeared slowly through the mist. I gripped the handles, jaw tight, and counted strokes as if numbers could shorten the distance. At the far side, I dropped anchor and reached for my bait. It wasn’t in the box. I searched the pockets of my jacket, then the floorboards, patting each spot with increasing force. At last I found the worm tin beneath my hat. I opened it, breathed out, and cast toward the bridge.

I had a new rod, new boots, and a handwritten map from a man at the bait shop, but the lake refused to match the map. At dawn I motored along the northern shore, searching for a small inlet marked with a red circle. Every point of land looked like the next. I leaned over the console to peer at the paper, then craned around the windshield for landmarks. My knee bounced against the seat. When I spotted a narrow gap between two pines, I cut the engine and paddled toward it. The gap opened onto a muddy pocket with no sign of fish. I slapped the map flat and studied it again, leaving a wet thumbprint across the ink. A ripple spread near the reeds. I cast there quickly, but the lure landed in a low branch. After freeing it, I shut my eyes for a breath, opened them, and looked farther down the shore.

I had arranged the paintings by noon, but the labels were still somewhere in the printer’s queue. Every few minutes I leaned over the machine to check its tiny screen, then tapped the paper tray as if it might hurry things along. The gallery clock clicked with theatrical precision. I straightened a frame, stepped back, and straightened it again, though it had not moved. When the intern asked whether we should wait for the labels before hanging the last canvas, I said, “We can do both,” too sharply. I carried the canvas to the wall myself and held it there while he searched for a level. Outside, visitors had begun gathering behind the locked glass doors. I could see their faces turned toward the empty space. The printer finally whirred, and I snatched the first warm label before it had fully emerged.

Mina had promised herself she would spend the afternoon calmly arranging her ceramic birds. Instead, she kept glancing at the gallery entrance, where the delivery van had yet to appear. She moved one plinth three inches left, then shoved it back to its original mark. A pencil rolled from her pocket; she kicked it beneath a bench and continued measuring. Her assistant suggested they unpack the smaller pieces first. Mina gave a brisk nod, then checked her phone again before lifting a single box. The opening was less than an hour away, and the empty shelves seemed to multiply whenever she looked at them. When the van finally stopped outside, she was already at the door, hand on the latch. The driver had barely lowered the tailgate before she began calling out which crate to bring in first.

I was still painting the exhibition map when the gallery manager announced that the doors would open in twenty minutes. My brush hovered over the paper while I stared at the blank square where my largest installation belonged. The work was stuck in traffic across town. I checked the street through the front window, returned to the map, and drew the square anyway, pressing so hard the pen nearly tore through. Then I paced between the entrance and the storage room, stopping each time a vehicle slowed outside. “Could we shift the opening?” I asked, though I knew the answer. The manager shook her head and began arranging programs on the table. I squared the stacks, scattered them, and squared them again. When a phone buzzed with the driver’s update, I grabbed my coat before reading the whole message.

At sixty-eight, Leon had learned to let paint dry at its own pace, but the gallery’s freshly painted walls tested that wisdom. He walked from one end of the room to the other, touching each patch with the back of a finger. The curator reminded him that the hooks could not go in until the surface set. Leon studied the clock, then picked up a hammer and tapped the first hook into place. A flake of paint curled away. He muttered, pulled the hook out, and began smoothing the mark with a rag. While he worked, he asked three times whether the walls looked dry yet. The curator kept answering with patient little shrugs. At last, Leon put the hammer down and folded his arms. A moment later he picked it up again, testing the next section with one quick fingertip.

The gallery’s new lighting system blinked on and off while I tried to photograph my paintings for the exhibition catalog. Each time I framed a shot, one spotlight went dark, turning the reds muddy and the blues nearly black. I adjusted the tripod, twisted a bulb, and watched the ceiling as though it had personally offended me. The electrician was due at three; my watch said three-oh-seven. I sent a message, deleted it, then sent another with only a question mark. My sister told me to sit down before I knocked over the camera. I crouched to inspect the cables instead, pulling one loose and making every light vanish. In the sudden dimness, I heard my own breath catch. When the bulbs returned, I was already holding the camera up, ready to try again.

Rafi’s exhibition consisted of tiny ink drawings that needed careful spacing, but the wall-mounted measuring tape kept slipping loose. He pressed its end against the corner with one thumb and marked the wall with the other hand. The tape snapped back, stinging his wrist. He swore under his breath, fetched blue painter’s tape, and made a crooked guide. His friend offered to take over; Rafi waved him off and began marking again at double speed. Each new mark seemed to land a little farther from the measurements on his sketch. He rubbed one away with his sleeve, leaving a gray smudge, then scrubbed at that too. The first guests were due soon, and the drawings still lay in their crates. When his friend silently held the tape steady, Rafi let out a long breath and handed over the pencil.

I had planned to write a thoughtful note beside every photograph, but the gallery printer produced one page at a time, pausing between each with a mechanical sigh. I stood beside it, arms folded, counting the seconds. After the third page, I started pressing the button again before the machine had finished. It beeped angrily and displayed an error. I opened the tray, shut it, and opened it once more, hoping the paper might have changed its mind. The curator called from the main room to ask if the captions were ready. “Almost,” I answered, though half the images still lacked text. I typed faster, leaving out a sentence I had revised all week. When the next sheet finally slid out, I grabbed it by the corner and hurried toward the wall, smoothing it flat with both palms.

Nessa, a sculptor from Accra, arrived early to arrange the small stone figures in her exhibition. The plinths were not yet in the room, and the delivery crew had stopped for breakfast. She called the gallery twice, then paced around the crates stacked by the door. A loose pebble clicked beneath her shoe. She picked it up, turned it over, and set it carefully on the nearest box. Every few moments, she checked the street through the tall windows. Her assistant suggested using temporary tables, but Nessa shook her head and began clearing a path to the center of the room. She moved packing foam, folded cardboard, and shifted a crate that was far too heavy for one person. When the crew finally arrived, she was waiting with a hand truck and a list of exact positions.

I put on my best shirt for the exhibition preview, then noticed a smear of cobalt paint across one cuff. The cleaner had promised to bring the garment steamer, but the hallway remained empty. I dabbed the stain with a damp cloth, made it larger, and rolled the cuff twice to hide it. The gallery clock seemed to jump forward whenever I looked away. I checked my phone, refreshed my messages, and called the cleaner; the call went straight to voicemail. My paintings were ready, the wine was chilled, and I was still trying to look like someone who had not spent the morning hauling frames. I grabbed a black marker and colored over the stain. It looked worse. When the doorbell rang, I pulled on my jacket, tucked the cuff out of sight, and went to greet the first guests.

Jun was arranging a sound installation in a narrow gallery, but the speakers arrived without the cables he needed. He opened each box, searched the packing paper, and checked beneath the van’s seats. Then he called the supplier, walking tight circles around a coil of wire while it rang. His collaborator tried to explain that another cable shop might have the right connectors. Jun interrupted to ask for the address, then rushed out before she finished giving it. At the shop, he tapped his fingers against the counter while the clerk searched a drawer. Back at the gallery, he plugged everything in so quickly that one speaker crackled and went silent. He froze, jaw clenched, then traced the connections with more care. The test tone filled the room just as the first visitors reached the door.

I kept changing the order of the paintings because the exhibition looked wrong from every angle. The curator had already approved the arrangement, but I took one canvas down and placed it beside the entrance. Then I carried it back, leaving a pale rectangle on the wall where it had hung. My hands smelled of metal hooks, and my shoulders were beginning to ache. I walked to the far corner, squinted, and marched back to move another painting half a handspan. “You said the layout was finished,” the curator reminded me. I said I was checking the sightline, though I had checked it many times. A delivery cart rattled outside, and I looked toward the door again. Finally, I stood still in the center of the room. The paintings seemed to settle into place when I stopped touching them.

At twenty-two, Beatriz was preparing her first gallery exhibition and had made a list for every task. The list was complete, but the wall text had not arrived from the translator. She checked her inbox, refreshed it, and checked again while pacing between the reception desk and her largest canvas. Her grandfather, who had come to help, offered to read the artist statement aloud from her draft. Beatriz interrupted him twice to ask whether the translation had come through. She picked at a loose thread on her sleeve until it came free, then began folding it into smaller and smaller pieces. The opening guests were expected in forty minutes. When the file finally appeared, she printed it, cut the pages apart, and carried them to the wall before the ink had dried. Her grandfather followed with the tape and a quiet smile.

I set the saucepan beneath the leak and watched another drop strike the bottom with a metallic ping. Mr. Bell had promised to come by after lunch, and it was nearly four. I called his office, then paced the kitchen while the recorded greeting explained how much my patience mattered to them. When he finally answered, I spoke so quickly that he asked me to start again. I described the swollen cabinet door, the damp patch spreading above it, and the three messages I had already left. He said the plumber was running late. I glanced at the water climbing the side of the saucepan and told him I could meet the plumber at the door, but I could not keep rearranging my shifts around a maybe. There was a pause. Then Mr. Bell gave me an exact arrival time and said he would stay on the line until the plumber confirmed.

Nadia had carried the broken stair rail in her mind for two weeks, gripping the wall whenever she climbed to her apartment. At the building office, she found the landlord sorting mail and placed a printed photo beside his coffee. He said he had forwarded her request to maintenance. Nadia tapped the date on the image, then the date on her phone. Her jaw tightened as she listed the neighbors who had nearly slipped and asked whether forwarding a message counted as fixing anything. The landlord began to explain the contractor’s schedule. She cut in, voice crisp, and asked him to call the contractor while she waited. A minute later, he did. Nadia remained by the desk, arms folded, until they agreed the rail would be secured that afternoon. She tested it herself before heading upstairs, pressing her full weight against the metal.

I had planned to spend Saturday painting, but the radiator clanked like a toolbox tumbling down stairs. I found my landlord, Luis, in the courtyard and asked when someone could look at it. He said he would check the maintenance calendar. I watched him unlock his phone, scroll, and stop to answer a text. The noise from my apartment seemed to follow me outside. “Could we do this now?” I asked, already pulling up the video I had recorded at dawn. Luis listened, eyebrows rising at each bang, then said the heating technician might come Monday. I rubbed my thumb over a paint stain and told him Monday was no good if the pipe burst before then. He called the technician on speaker. While it rang, I circled the courtyard path twice, checking my screen after every few steps. The technician agreed to stop by that evening, and I finally let my shoulders drop.

At sixty-eight, Walter had learned that a loose bathroom tile could turn an ordinary morning into a balancing act. He cornered his landlord, Priya, near the mailboxes and showed her the tile rocking under his shoe. She promised to submit a work order. Walter glanced toward the office computer, then asked whether she could submit it while he stood there. Priya began to say she had other tenants to call. He nodded, but his fingers drummed a quick rhythm against his cane. “I’ve been stepping around this since Tuesday,” he said, looking directly at her. “Give me a number, not another form.” The firmness in his voice surprised them both. Priya opened the maintenance portal and entered the request. Walter waited beside the desk, leaning forward as each field appeared on screen. When she read out the contractor’s visit time, he wrote it on the back of his grocery receipt.

The kitchen window had jammed open during a rainstorm, and I’d spent the morning shoving towels along the sill. My landlord, Simone, said she could send someone sometime next week. I stood in the doorway with wet sleeves and a list of every call I had made since Monday. As she explained that the usual carpenter was booked, I kept shifting my weight and checking the puddle beneath the radiator. “I need a date before we finish this conversation,” I said. Simone’s mouth tightened, and she asked whether I could let her check another supplier. I followed her to the office, still holding the list. She called two repair shops; the first declined, but the second had an opening the next morning. I asked her to text me the appointment details while I watched. When my phone buzzed, I read the message twice, then finally set the towels in the laundry basket.

Ravi’s bathroom fan had stopped working, leaving the mirror clouded long after every shower. He called his landlord, Beth, during a break at the print shop and explained that the damp ceiling had begun to spot. She said she would ask the building’s electrician. Ravi heard papers shuffling at her end and looked at the minutes slipping away on the wall clock. He offered to wait while she called. Beth sounded surprised, then put him on speaker as she tried the electrician’s number. Ravi paced between the paper cutter and the supply shelves, answering customer questions with a raised finger while the phone rang. When the electrician picked up, Beth arranged a visit for that afternoon. Ravi thanked her, but added that he would call back if nobody arrived by five. He wrote the appointment time across his palm, not trusting himself to wait for a later reminder.

I emailed my landlord, Dean, about the refrigerator making a hot, sour smell. He replied that he would send a repair person, but no one showed up on the day he named. The next morning, I found him in the lobby and held out the spoiled groceries I had packed into a grocery bag. He looked uncomfortable and started describing a mix-up with the service company. I cut through the explanation to ask what he was doing now. My heel bounced against the tile while he searched his contacts. “I’m not leaving until we have a time,” I said, louder than I intended. He called the company and managed to book a technician for that afternoon. I asked him to repeat the time, then sent myself a message so I would have it in writing. On my way upstairs, I dropped the groceries in the bin and checked my phone once more.

Keiko’s bedroom ceiling developed a brown ring after a storm, and each day the mark crept closer to her bookcase. Her landlord, Martin, said a roofer would inspect it when the weather cleared. Keiko met him at the entrance, holding a ruler against a photograph she had taken the night before. She pointed out that the stain had grown nearly an inch. Martin rubbed his forehead and said he was still waiting for the roofer to call back. Keiko asked him to try again while she stood there. He started to suggest she email instead, but she had already opened her calendar and blocked off the afternoon. “Please don’t send me away with another promise,” she said, her voice thin and steady. Martin phoned the roofer and arranged a visit for the next morning. Keiko photographed the ceiling again before leaving, adding the new image to her record.

The front door lock stuck so badly that I had to shoulder it every time I came home with groceries. I caught my landlord, Omar, as he was carrying a box into the building and showed him how the key turned without moving the bolt. He said he would ask the locksmith to fit me in. I tried the key again, harder, and it scraped uselessly. “Can you call while we’re standing here?” I asked. Omar glanced at his watch, then at the residents gathering behind us. I could feel my ears warming as I explained that I had already been locked out twice. He took out his phone. The locksmith promised to arrive before dinner, but Omar began to mention a possible delay. I held up my hand and asked him to get confirmation by text. A moment later, the message came through. I tested the key once more, then handed Omar the groceries that had started slipping from my arms.

Milo, a graduate student, had been washing dishes in the bathtub because the kitchen sink drained only a teaspoon at a time. His landlord, Elaine, listened to the problem and suggested trying a bottle of drain cleaner. Milo’s eyebrows climbed. He explained that he had already used one, twice, and showed her the receipt tucked into his phone case. Elaine started to say that a plumber could be costly. Milo was shifting from foot to foot in the hallway, glancing toward the overflowing dish tub behind him. “I’m not asking for a renovation,” he said. “I need a working sink.” Elaine stopped sorting her keys and called the plumbing company. Their dispatcher could come the following morning. Milo asked her to confirm the appointment by email before he left for class. He hurried upstairs, put the dishes back beside the sink, and set an alarm to check that the plumber arrived.

I noticed the living-room outlet sparking when I plugged in my reading lamp. My landlord, Graham, told me not to use it and said an electrician would be contacted. I unplugged the lamp, but the little flash stayed in my mind through dinner. The next day I went to his office and asked whether the electrician had been called. Graham began searching his inbox. I watched his cursor crawl through old messages, then let out a breath through my teeth. “Could you phone them instead?” I asked, tapping the counter with two fingers. He started to explain that email created a paper trail. “Fine, but please do it now,” I said. The electrician’s office answered and offered a visit between one and three. Graham wrote the slot on a card and gave it to me. I took a photo of the card before returning upstairs, where I kept the lamp unplugged and waited near my phone.

At a corner apartment above a bakery, Estelle woke to water dripping through the light fixture. She called her landlord, Darius, and described the steady patter. He said he would contact the upstairs tenant and investigate. Estelle looked at the bowl already filling on her table and asked when he planned to arrive. He said he was finishing an errand across town. She began moving her chairs and books, then stopped to call him again ten minutes later. When Darius answered, she spoke in clipped bursts, naming the expanding stain and the electrical fixture directly below it. “I’m coming now,” he said. Estelle stayed on the line until she heard his car pull up outside. He shut off the power and found a split hose upstairs. While he arranged an emergency plumber, Estelle stood with a dish towel twisted in her hands, watching each drop land in the bowl.

I arrived at the Harbor Street food bank before the doors opened, carrying a box of donated apples and checking my watch every few minutes. The line outside barely moved as staff arranged crates inside. I shifted my weight, tapped the box against my knee, and asked whether we could start handing out bags before the forms were ready. When a new volunteer struggled with the folding table, I grabbed one end and snapped, “We’ve got people waiting.” She glanced at me, then kept working. A little girl near the entrance dropped a mitten, so I picked it up and held it out. Her mother thanked me while I watched the clock again. The doors finally swung wide, and I hurried to my station, already reaching for the next bag.

At the church basement pantry, Tomas lined up cans by label while volunteers prepared grocery bags. He kept looking toward the entrance, where a delivery van had been expected twenty minutes earlier. Each time tires sounded on the street, he set down his marker and went to the window. When the coordinator asked him to sort dented tins, he pushed the crate aside. “We could be serving people instead of rearranging cans,” he said, drumming his fingers on the counter. A senior volunteer calmly showed him how to check each lid. Tomas sighed and worked faster, stacking the safe ones in neat rows. When the van finally backed into the alley, he was already outside, waving the driver toward the loading door.

I volunteered at the campus food cupboard because my scholarship covered tuition but not every meal. On Thursday, I was assigned to enter delivery numbers into a spreadsheet while the others unpacked boxes. The computer froze at the first page. I clicked, waited, clicked again, and pressed my lips into a thin line. “Can’t we just count the bags by hand?” I asked. The supervisor pointed out that the records helped the pantry order enough food for next week. I folded my arms, then noticed a stack of rice sacks leaning dangerously near the doorway. I went to steady them, muttering at the slow computer as I worked. By the time the screen returned, I had moved the sacks and found a better outlet for the charger.

Mina had taken the early shift at the neighborhood food bank, hoping to finish before her afternoon nursing class. The volunteer coordinator was explaining a new check-in system when Mina began rubbing the edge of her badge with her thumb. She glanced at the wall clock, then at the long row of empty carts. When the explanation paused for questions, she blurted, “Could we learn this while people are being served?” Her voice carried across the room. A father at the doorway looked over, and Mina lowered her eyes. She took a cart and started helping sort produce, moving each crate with brisk, clipped motions. Soon she was showing another volunteer where the apples belonged, though she still checked the clock between customers.

At the food bank in our old railway station, I was supposed to wait for the coordinator to assign me a task. Ten minutes passed. Then another five. I paced between the donation shelves, straightened a crooked sign, and asked twice whether anyone needed help. A volunteer sorting bread finally pointed me toward the freezer, where boxes had to be counted before lunch. I hauled the door open and began reading labels aloud, faster each time I reached a number. When I lost my place, I slapped the clipboard against my palm. Then an older man wheeled in a cart with one stuck wheel. I stopped counting, crouched to fix it, and returned to the freezer with grease on my sleeve and a steadier hand.

At a rural food bank, Calvin was responsible for directing cars through the pickup lane. A rain shower had slowed everything, and the line of vehicles curled past the post office. He waved one car forward, then leaned toward the next driver before the first had cleared the turn. “Keep it moving, please,” he called, his jaw tight beneath his hood. The coordinator reminded him to leave space for pedestrians. Calvin threw one hand toward the stalled cars but stepped back. A child crossing with her grandmother slipped on the wet curb; he hurried over and offered his arm. After they reached the covered walkway, he returned to the lane and began guiding each car with deliberate signals, watching every gap.

I was sorting donated coats beside the food pantry when I heard that the bread truck had taken a wrong turn. The grocery pickup was supposed to begin soon, and people were already waiting outside. I checked my phone, shoved it into my pocket, and asked the dispatcher for an update. No answer. I pulled open the front door, looked down the street, and came back inside. “We can’t hand out empty shelves,” I said, though nobody had suggested we could. To keep busy, I carried boxes from the storeroom and arranged them by size. A neighbor arrived with two loaves she had baked that morning. I set them on the table carefully, then stayed near the doorway, scanning the street.

At the downtown community pantry, Beatrice volunteered at the sign-in desk after retiring from a career in accounting. One morning, the printer jammed just as a crowd gathered. She opened the tray, pulled out a crumpled page, and tapped the machine’s side with two sharp knuckles. “It worked yesterday,” she said, although the printer made no reply. The line behind the desk lengthened, and she began writing names by hand, pressing hard enough to score the paper beneath. A teenager offered to help, but Beatrice waved him toward the food shelves. Then she noticed his careful handwriting and handed him the clipboard. Together they recorded the arrivals while she kept one eye on the stubborn printer.

I signed up to stock the food bank’s market shelves, where guests could choose their own groceries. The delivery arrived late, and the boxes were stacked so high that I couldn’t reach the canned soup. I fetched a step stool, climbed it, and started unloading faster than the labels could be read. A can slipped from my hand and rolled under the table. I crouched to retrieve it, bumping my head on the frame. “This is taking forever,” I muttered, then heard a child laugh from the next aisle. His mother was choosing pasta with him, comparing shapes as if there were no clock at all. I slowed down enough to sort the soup by type, though I kept glancing toward the empty shelves.

Nadia, a high school senior, volunteered at a food bank that operated out of a converted laundromat. She had an exam review session across town and had promised to leave by noon. At eleven forty-five, the coordinator was still explaining how to pack allergy-safe bags. Nadia’s foot bounced under the folding table. She asked whether the instructions were written down, then began reading them before the answer came. When a guest mentioned a peanut allergy, Nadia stopped mid-sentence and checked every label herself. The packing took longer than she expected, but she double-checked each bag and marked it clearly. At the door, she looked at her phone, grabbed her backpack, and hurried toward the bus stop with a flour smudge on her sleeve.

I volunteered at a seaside food bank where most deliveries arrived by van, except when a local fishing boat brought fresh catch. The boat was late, and I kept stepping outside to peer at the harbor. Inside, the freezer hummed while volunteers packed canned goods for the afternoon distribution. I rearranged the same stack of boxes three times, then asked the coordinator if we should call the crew. She was already doing that. I took a deep breath, but my fingers kept drumming on the counter. A woman waiting for groceries asked where the tea was, so I walked her to the shelf and helped choose a tin. When I returned, the boat’s horn sounded beyond the windows, and I was halfway to the loading ramp.

Leon worked the evening shift at a food bank in an apartment complex community room. A plumbing leak had forced the volunteers to move the produce table, delaying the start of distribution. He carried crates to the far wall, then paced back to see whether the folding tables were ready. When one leg refused to lock, he gave it a hard shove. “We’re losing the whole evening,” he said. The building custodian brought a wrench and showed him a bent hinge. Leon held the table steady while the repair was made, his fingers gripping the edge. Soon the produce was arranged and the room opened. He greeted each arriving neighbor with a quick nod, passing out bags while glancing at the repaired table as if it might fail again.

At twenty-nine, I had already checked the dashboard clock four times before Ms. Alvarez finished adjusting my mirrors. The empty training lot stretched ahead, bright with morning sun, and I kept tapping my heel against the floor mat. “Can we get onto the road now?” I asked, gripping the wheel before she had buckled in. She pointed to the seat belt and asked me to name each control. I rattled them off, then started the engine while she was still explaining the brake. Her hand settled calmly over the key. We began again, one step at a time. When I finally eased the car around the painted cones without clipping one, I glanced at her for the next challenge. She smiled and told me to park between two lines. I breathed out, loosened my shoulders, and tried the maneuver properly.

Nia, a twenty-year-old nursing student, arrived for her lesson with a bus timetable folded in her pocket and a shift beginning at noon. Her instructor, Mr. Bell, asked her to practice a slow turn in the community college lot. She completed it, then pointed toward the exit. “I can do the street now,” she said, already reaching for the gear selector. He reminded her to check both mirrors and scan for pedestrians. Nia pressed her lips together as a delivery van rolled past at walking speed. At the next turn, she braked too late and stopped beyond the painted line. Mr. Bell asked her to reset and try again. She drummed her fingers against her thigh, then carefully repeated the checks. This time she stopped cleanly. The clock still mattered, but she listened as he mapped a route that would get her back in time.

I was forty-six and used to making decisions quickly in the kitchen, so crawling around a quiet industrial park felt like being made to stir soup one grain at a time. My instructor, Darnell, had me practice starting and stopping. Each time the car rolled a few feet, I asked what came next. He kept his eyes on the road and said, “The same thing again, until it feels steady.” I let out a sharp breath when a cyclist passed us and we waited. My fingers drummed on the steering wheel. Then Darnell asked me to pull over beside a loading dock and explain what I had noticed. I named the cyclist, a puddle, and a truck backing from a bay. He nodded. The next stretch felt less like a delay and more like a test I could actually pass.

On his seventeenth birthday, Mateo expected his driving lesson to include the wide boulevard near his house. Instead, his instructor, Priya, directed him to a small school lot and asked him to practice smooth stops. A row of orange cones seemed to multiply while he waited for his turn to circle them. He looked at the clock on the console and asked twice when they would leave the lot. Priya said they would go once he could steer without staring at his hands. Mateo’s jaw tightened. He made another circuit, clipped a cone, and threw up his palms. Priya simply reset it. On the next lap he watched the open space ahead and guided the car cleanly around every marker. She led him to a neighborhood street. Mateo sat taller, checking each mirror before the car moved.

I had driven tractors on my aunt’s farm since I was twelve, and at thirty-one I thought the lesson would be a formality. My instructor, Gwen, disagreed when I rolled through a stop sign in the quiet suburb. She made me circle the block and approach it again. I stared at the empty cross street, then at the clock, while my foot hovered over the brake. “There’s nothing coming,” I said. Gwen asked what the sign required, not what the road happened to contain. I halted, counted, checked both directions, and pulled away. At the next corner, I started to ask whether we could practice parking instead. She raised an eyebrow. I swallowed the question and completed the full stop. By the end of the block, I was noticing signs sooner—and no longer treating every pause as wasted time.

At sixty-three, Salma had spent months arranging lessons around her tailoring shop, and every canceled appointment felt like another week added to the wait. On this clear Tuesday, instructor Owen began with parallel parking between two plastic barrels. Salma watched the empty road beyond the lot and asked whether they might practice driving through town instead. Owen handed her a diagram showing the parking steps. Her mouth flattened as she studied it. She backed up too quickly, straightened, and had to begin again. A pair of students crossed behind the car, and she waited, fingers curled around the wheel. On her fourth attempt, the car settled neatly between the barrels. Owen praised her spacing and offered a route through town. Salma gave a brisk nod, then adjusted her mirrors before setting off.

I was new to the country, and every day I spent learning road signs seemed to add another obstacle between me and a job interview across town. During my first lesson, Mr. Sato took me to a quiet lane and asked me to identify the signs aloud. I pointed to one and said we should turn, though the arrow meant the road narrowed. He corrected me gently. I pressed my thumbnail into my palm and asked if we could just drive the route. He explained that the route would be safer once I understood what the signs were saying. So I read each one as we passed: school crossing, yield, no parking. When a cyclist appeared near the curb, I slowed without being told. Mr. Sato gave me the map for the next lesson. I folded it carefully and asked him to start there next time.

Jules, a twenty-four-year-old drummer, had a gig that evening and wanted to borrow his brother’s car without depending on a ride. Instructor Lila began in an empty shopping-center lot, teaching him to reverse into a marked space. Jules backed in crookedly, pulled forward, and checked the time on his phone. “Can’t we do the useful part now?” he asked. Lila pointed out that leaving a space safely was useful, too. He rubbed his forehead while she explained how to line up the mirrors. On the next attempt, he turned the wheel too far and ended up across the lines. A cart rattled by in the wind as he reset. This time he moved slowly, glanced over his shoulder, and parked within the markings. Lila directed him toward the lot exit. Jules put his phone away and checked for traffic.

My instructor, Rosa, had me drive around a residential block while the rain blurred the windshield. I was twenty-six, and I had been saving for lessons since my bakery job changed to an early shift. Every stoplight seemed to hold us for an extra minute. When Rosa asked me to leave more space behind the car ahead, I muttered that the gap was wide enough already. She asked me to notice how the wet road changed stopping distance. I gripped the wheel, then eased off the accelerator. At a green light, the car in front hesitated, and I stopped well short of its bumper. The wipers swept back and forth. Rosa nodded toward a side street and asked me to turn when it was clear. I checked twice, waited for a passing van, and made the turn without jerking the wheel.

Before dawn, Arun, a thirty-eight-year-old wildlife photographer, met his instructor at a nearly empty park-and-ride. He wanted a license before the spring field season, when the distant blinds and trails would be easier to reach by car. His instructor, Beth, began with the seat, mirrors, and a slow loop around the lot. Arun kept glancing at the gate, where the road beyond disappeared into blue morning mist. He asked if they could take the highway today. Beth suggested practicing a smooth lane change first. He tapped the indicator twice before she finished speaking, then caught himself and waited for her signal. On the road, a bus pulled alongside. Arun’s shoulders rose, but he checked the mirror, signaled, and changed lanes when the space opened. Beth said nothing for a moment. He looked over, ready for the next instruction.

I had promised my grandmother I would drive her to the seaside market, and at fifty-two I was tired of asking cousins to take me. My instructor, Celeste, chose a hilly street for our lesson. We stopped at the bottom of a slope to practice starting without rolling backward. The first attempt lurched, and a car behind us gave a short horn blast. Heat climbed into my face. I asked Celeste to let me try again before the driver could honk a second time. She reminded me to find the clutch’s biting point and hold it. I did, but released too fast. We reset. On the third try, the car moved uphill steadily. At the next intersection, I waited for a clear gap instead of forcing one. Celeste pointed toward the market road, and I followed the signs with both hands steady.

Sixteen-year-old Harper had been looking forward to driving since her older sister got a license, but her first lesson began in a cemetery parking lot because the roads nearby were busy. Instructor Dev asked her to practice turning in broad circles. Harper completed one and immediately asked to try the public road. He reminded her to keep her eyes far ahead rather than fixating on the hood. She rolled her eyes, then followed his instruction through another circle. A groundskeeper crossed in front of them, pushing a cart, and Harper braked smoothly. Dev asked what she had seen. “The cart, the stop sign, and that car entering,” she answered, pointing. He said they were ready to leave the lot. Harper sat back, tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear, and checked the mirrors before easing toward the exit.

The clinic had told me to give my ankle another week, but the track was already drying beneath the spring sun. I sat on the bench, lacing my running shoes over the brace, then unlaced them when the swelling showed above the strap. My coach’s message said, “Easy walk only.” I walked three laps around the infield, checking my watch after every turn as if the seconds might have changed their minds. When a teammate sprinted past, I pushed off after him and made it six steps before the joint pinched. I stopped, jaw clenched, and pretended to study a loose shoelace. At home, I set my rehabilitation exercises beside the front door, ready for morning. The calendar still showed seven empty squares before my next appointment. I crossed off today’s square anyway, pressing the pen so hard it tore the paper.

At seventeen, Malik had learned every crack in the pool tiles during his shoulder recovery. His therapist wanted another month before he returned to butterfly, but the regional trials were only three weeks away. He arrived early, goggles already on his forehead, and asked the lifeguard whether he could “just test one lap.” The answer was no. Malik slapped the water with his good hand, then tried to hide the sting in his face by adjusting his cap. During band exercises, he snapped through each repetition and kept glancing toward the lanes where his friends practiced starts. When the therapist corrected his posture, he exhaled sharply and started again, slower this time. That evening, he watched a video of his old race, pausing it at the finish. His shoulder throbbed, but he opened the exercise sheet and set a timer for the next session.

The cast came off on Tuesday, and I expected the mountain bike to be waiting like a loyal dog. Instead, Dr. Chen handed me a list of small wrist movements and said the trails were still out of reach. I nodded, then rode my bike around the parking lot with one hand barely touching the handlebar. A bump sent pain up my arm. I circled back, annoyed at the gravel, the doctor, and my own wrist for taking so long. At home, I opened the trail map and traced the steep descent with my finger. My helmet sat on the table beside the rehab putty. I squeezed the putty so hard it slipped from my palm, then picked it up and tried again. The next morning, I returned to the clinic before my appointment, hoping the swelling would have vanished overnight.

Rosa’s fractured foot had healed enough for the boot to come off, but her dance instructor still barred her from rehearsals. The spring showcase poster covered the studio window, each dancer’s name printed in gold. Rosa stood outside after class, tapping the toe of her shoe against the pavement while music leaked through the door. At home, she practiced arm movements in front of the mirror, turning too sharply and catching herself against the dresser. Her brother reminded her that the doctor had said no jumps. She answered with a clipped “I know” and sat down, rubbing the tender arch. The following day, she arrived at physical therapy ten minutes early and asked whether the balance tests could be skipped. When the therapist said they mattered, Rosa rolled her eyes, then steadied herself on the foam pad. She wanted the stage, but she stayed until every repetition was finished.

I had broken my collarbone in a cycling crash, and the sling made every ordinary task feel like a slow parade. My friends were planning a charity ride through the hills, while I was learning to lift a paper cup without grimacing. Each morning I checked the calendar and counted the days until my follow-up. At the café, I watched cyclists stream past the window and drummed my fingers against the table. The surgeon said the bone was knitting well but warned me against grabbing the handlebars. So I took my bike apart in the garage instead, cleaning the chain and arranging the tools in neat rows. When my younger cousin asked if I could race again soon, I started to say yes, then looked at the sling. I swallowed the promise and practiced the shoulder stretches. They were tiny movements, but I marked each one on the calendar.

Elias was a goalkeeper with a sprained thumb, and the team’s playoff match was approaching fast. The trainer had taped the joint and ordered him to avoid catching hard shots for several days. Elias paced beside the practice field, bouncing a ball against his thigh and watching the reserve keeper take his place. When a stray kick rolled toward him, he scooped it up with both hands before anyone could object. A sharp ache made him wince. He tossed the ball back and muttered that it had been an easy save. At home, his father found him tightening the tape for the third time that evening. Elias loosened it, then followed the trainer’s instructions for gentle mobility work. He asked twice whether the swelling looked smaller. By bedtime, he had packed his gloves beside the door, though the match remained days away.

My hamstring pulled halfway through a rugby match, and the team physio said I should spend two weeks building strength before sprinting again. Two weeks sounded like an entire season. I tried jogging on the third morning, telling myself the grass felt soft enough to be harmless. The muscle tugged, and I stopped so abruptly that my teammate nearly ran into me. For the rest of practice, I stood near the touchline, folding and unfolding the paper rehab plan. At home, I set my alarm earlier, convinced that extra minutes would somehow speed the process. The exercises were dull: bridges, careful stretches, slow steps up the stairs. I rushed through them until my leg trembled, then had to begin the set again. On Friday, I asked the physio whether I could join warm-ups. He said I could walk beside the team. I showed up before everyone.

At fifty-two, Nia had returned to masters tennis after surgery on her knee, but her surgeon limited her to short, controlled rallies. She hated watching balls land just beyond her reach. Between points, she spun her racket and stared at the court clock, while her partner reminded her to keep the steps small. One morning, Nia lunged for a wide shot and felt the knee tighten. She stopped, gripping the net post until the flash of discomfort passed. “That one doesn’t count,” she said, though the point was already over. Her physical therapist later showed her a video of the lunge and pointed out how quickly she had twisted. Nia watched it twice, lips pressed together. She returned to the court the next day and asked for slower feeds. Every time she resisted chasing a ball, she marked the choice as a win.

The fracture in my finger was small, the doctor said, but the splint made climbing impossible. I spent evenings at the bouldering gym, watching other people move over the walls while I held my water bottle in my left hand. My coach told me not to test the grip yet. I kept taking the splint off to see whether the finger looked less swollen, then putting it back on when it stiffened. One night, I reached for a low hold with my good hand and tried to pull myself up. Pain snapped through the injured finger, and I dropped onto the mat, cheeks burning even though nobody had seen. The next morning, I followed the prescribed mobility drills at the kitchen table. I moved the finger carefully, counting each bend aloud. The wall was still there; I just had to wait until my hand could meet it safely.

Jun’s ankle injury had sidelined him from his university rowing crew just as the team began preparing for nationals. He hated the sound of oars striking water without him. From the dock, he shouted corrections before the coach asked, then checked his phone for updates from the sports clinic. His rehabilitation required balance work, which seemed laughably slow compared with the crew’s long sessions. He hurried through the heel raises and nearly tipped into a stack of life jackets. The therapist made him start the set over. Jun’s ears turned red, but he planted his feet and tried again, holding each rise for the full count. Later, he sat in the boat shed and polished his oar, though he would not be using it yet. When the next practice began, he watched quietly, hands clasped tight around the warm-up band.

I tore a muscle in my calf during a basketball tournament, and the doctor banned me from jumping until the follow-up scan. The gym’s squeaking sneakers made my foot bounce under the chair while I watched practice from the sideline. My teammates ran drills, and I kept picturing myself cutting toward the basket. At home, I tried a few toe raises before dinner. The calf tightened, so I sat down hard and stared at the ceiling, furious with the empty room. My sister brought over the rehabilitation sheet and pointed to the pace printed at the top. I followed it, though I wanted to race through every movement. After each set, I checked the clock and asked whether enough time had passed to do another. By the end of the week, I could walk without limping. I told the coach, then waited for the scan before asking about practice.

Sandeep, a trail runner who had moved to Colorado from Mumbai, developed a stress fracture and had to trade mountain paths for a walking boot. He kept his race bib pinned to a corkboard above the desk, even after the event passed. Every afternoon, he walked to the window when he heard runners on the road, then returned to the exercise mat with a scowl. His doctor had prescribed upper-body work and short, careful walks. Sandeep tried to double the distance one Saturday, turning back only when his shin began to throb. At the clinic, he admitted what he had done before the therapist could ask. She adjusted his plan but did not scold him. He studied the new schedule, tapping the page with one finger. That evening, he set out his walking shoes and followed the exact route, stopping at the marked bench.

I had taken a number before sunrise, yet the display still showed 18 while my ticket said 63. The office smelled of wet coats and warm printer toner. I tapped my shoe against the chair leg, stopped when an old man glanced over, then began drumming my fingers on my folder. My appointment was for renewing my taxi permit, and the meter outside was earning nothing. When a clerk disappeared through a side door carrying a stack of files, I leaned toward the counter. “Could you tell me how long?” I asked. She pointed to a sign explaining that estimates were unavailable. I checked my phone, though I already knew the time, and stood to stretch my back. The number changed to 19. I sat again, gripping the ticket so tightly its corner curled.

At seventy-four, Noreen had learned to bring a cushion to the licensing office, but it did little against the hard plastic chair or the hours crawling past. Her number remained frozen on the screen. She watched people arrive after her, collect tickets, and somehow get called first for different counters. Each time the door opened, she lifted her head, then let it drop when another clerk emerged with no explanation. Her bus home left at four, and she had already pictured the driver pulling away while she stood beneath the office clock. Noreen checked her documents for the fifth time, aligning their edges with sharp little taps. When a child began swinging his legs beside her, she smiled politely, then turned toward the display again. A new number blinked. Not hers.

I was missing a shift at the bakery, and the smell of cinnamon on my sleeves made the government office seem even less suited to my morning. My number was 204. The screen had reached 177, then stopped because somebody’s file could not be found. I bounced one knee until the chair squeaked. A woman at the counter explained the same form to a visitor for what felt like the tenth time, each sentence slower than the last. I opened my folder, shut it, and checked that my birth certificate was still there. It was. I knew it was. When the clerk finally called 178, I stood too quickly and nearly dropped my papers. “That’s not me,” I muttered, though no one had asked. I paced to the water cooler and back, counting each step.

Mateo had promised his daughter he would collect her after school, but the passport office line had barely moved since lunch. His ticket was folded into a tiny square between his fingers. He kept glancing at the clock, then at the row of closed service windows, as if one might open through sheer attention. A man behind him asked whether the queue was for all applications, and Mateo answered with a clipped nod. When the display skipped from 41 to 43, he stood and approached the attendant. She checked the list and said number 42 had been called twice. Mateo looked at his ticket, then at the people around him. The missing number was his. He let out a breath, gathered his papers, and hurried toward the counter, already rehearsing what he would tell his daughter.

I had arranged childcare, taken two buses, and brought every document listed online. Now I was watching a government clerk eat a sandwich behind the glass while my number sat seventeen places away. My heel clicked against the floor in a steady rhythm. When it annoyed the woman beside me, I tucked my foot under the chair, but my fingers kept turning the ticket over and over. The application was for a housing benefit, and each week of delay meant another bill I could not cover. I went to the information desk and asked whether the line might speed up after lunch. The attendant gave me a printed leaflet instead of an answer. Back in my seat, I read the same paragraph three times. Then the display chimed, and I sprang upright before realizing it was someone else’s turn.

Ravi’s number had been called while he was in the restroom, and now the screen showed a figure far beyond his own. He approached the counter, explaining that he had only stepped away for a minute. The clerk told him to take another ticket. He stared at the dispenser, jaw set, while the line behind him folded around a pillar. He needed a permit to sell vegetables at the market, and the opening date was two days away. Returning to his chair, he checked the clock, then the paper slip, then the clock again. A security guard wheeled a bin past at an unhurried pace. Ravi’s shoulders rose toward his ears. When another number appeared, he leaned forward so abruptly that his cap slid to the floor. He snatched it up and watched the display without blinking.

I brought knitting to the benefits office, believing it would make the wait manageable. After an hour, I had unraveled the same row twice and stabbed my thumb with the needle. My number was still nowhere near the screen. Rain crawled down the windows, and the radiator clicked like it was keeping count. I went to ask the receptionist whether my appointment had been recorded. She searched her computer, frowned, and said the system was running behind. “How far behind?” I asked, hearing the edge in my own voice. She could not say. I returned to my chair and folded the knitting into my bag. The person beside me offered a mint. I thanked him, but kept my eyes fixed on the display, lifting my chin at every beep.

At twenty-two, Zola had never needed a paper residence card before, and the government office seemed designed to punish anyone who had not learned its rituals. She had arrived with the correct form, only to discover that she needed a photocopy of a document she was already holding. After buying one from the kiosk, she rejoined the long queue. Her backpack slid down one shoulder; she hauled it up and checked her phone. The battery was at nine percent. Every time the line advanced, she took two quick steps, then stopped short as the person ahead inspected a stack of papers. A clerk called for the next applicant, and Zola was sure it was her turn. It belonged to someone at another window. She pressed her lips together and began counting the tiles under her shoes.

I had come to the municipal office to correct a mistake on my mother’s property record. The queue bent around the lobby, past a vending machine that had swallowed someone’s coins and a poster curling away from the wall. I kept shifting my weight from one foot to the other. My folder was damp where my palm had been gripping it. When an employee walked by, I asked if there was a separate desk for corrections. He said the same line served everyone, then vanished through a door. I looked at the clock: twenty minutes had passed since the last number changed. My mother called to ask whether I was nearly finished. “Almost,” I said, though I was nowhere close. A baby cried behind me. I rubbed my forehead and edged forward whenever the person ahead moved, even an inch.

Clive had taken the morning off to replace his lost identification card, expecting a quick stop before his afternoon delivery route. Now he sat beneath a flickering fluorescent tube, watching the government office’s ticket display skip from 86 to 88. His ticket showed 87. He rose and waved it toward the attendant, who said the missing applicant might have been called already. Clive’s mouth tightened. He had been listening carefully; no one had called his number. His van was parked in a two-hour space, and the meter outside would not pause for paperwork. He walked to the window, then back to his chair, then checked the time on his watch. At last he asked the person beside him to listen for his number while he ran downstairs to move the van. He took the stairs two at a time.

I was trying to register my newborn, and every minute in the crowded office seemed to stretch across the whole morning. The baby slept against my chest while I stood behind a man sorting receipts into neat piles. My feet hurt, and my shoulders burned under the carrier straps. I checked the queue screen, then checked it again before it could possibly change. When someone stepped out to take a phone call, I shifted closer to the counter, hoping the gap might count as progress. A staff member told us to remain in order. I apologized, though I had not said anything. The baby stirred, and I bounced gently while scanning the room for a clock. At the next chime, I straightened so fast that the folder under my arm slid to the floor.

Beatrice had come to the government office to dispute a fine, carrying photographs, receipts, and a handwritten timeline in a bright yellow envelope. Her number was separated from the display by a long stretch of digits. She sat for five minutes, stood for two, then sat again, unable to settle. A clerk called out that the system was delayed, prompting several people to groan. Beatrice’s fingers tightened around the envelope. She had already paid for parking and could not afford another ticket while attending to this one. When the line moved, she followed the person ahead so closely that he glanced back. She stepped away at once, cheeks warm, and studied the wall notice as if it contained new information. The clock’s minute hand advanced. Beatrice gathered her papers and went to ask for an estimate.

When the lights died, I was halfway through frosting a cake for the block’s welcome party. The neighbors gathered in my kitchen, holding phone flashlights while I jabbed the dead oven buttons as if they might answer. “The bakery closes in twenty minutes,” I said, checking my watch again. Mrs. Alvarez suggested we carry the cake next door and finish it there, where her gas stove still worked. I had already wrapped the layers, but the frosting bowl sat uncovered, softening in the heat. I tapped my sneaker against the cabinet and kept asking whether anyone had called the utility company. Then a boy from upstairs arrived with a hand-cranked mixer he’d found in his grandmother’s cupboard. I took it from him, turned the handle too fast, and sent a curl of frosting over the counter. Everyone laughed. I wiped it up, slowed my arm, and let the neighbors take turns.

At seventy-two, Lenora had learned to wait for many things, but the dark elevator had stopped her on the sixth floor with a basket of groceries cutting into her hands. She set it down, pressed the call button, then pressed it again. From the stairwell came the shuffle of neighbors carrying candles and offering guesses about when the power would return. Lenora kept glancing at her watch. Her insulin needed refrigeration, and she had promised to bring soup to the man downstairs. When a teenager offered to carry the basket, she waved him on and took the stairs herself, one landing at a time. On the third floor she stopped to catch her breath. The neighbors had gathered there around a battery lantern, sharing cold food before it spoiled. Lenora handed over the milk and asked someone to hold the soup pot while she checked the building’s emergency freezer.

I had queued up the championship match just as our street went black. My neighbors drifted into the courtyard, and I marched out with my tablet raised, hunting for a signal. The game was already underway somewhere beyond the dark windows. “Does anyone have a radio?” I asked, too loudly, then checked the screen for the fifth time. Mr. Okafor brought out an old transistor set, but it needed batteries. Three people rummaged through kitchen drawers while I paced between the benches, calculating how much of the first half we’d missed. A girl from the next building found a pair in a toy flashlight. The radio crackled to life, and the announcer’s voice spilled over the courtyard. I sat on the low wall, still bouncing one heel. By halftime, I had stopped checking my tablet and was explaining the rules to the children gathered beside me.

Marek had promised the neighbors he would repair the community garden gate before the weekend market, and the outage had shut off the workshop lights. He clicked his headlamp twice, though its beam had already gone dim, then hurried from shed to shed asking for a charged battery. Each answer came with a story about a freezer, a phone, or a child afraid of the dark. Marek’s jaw tightened as he looked at the bent hinge. He set his tools on the ground and began sorting them by touch, muttering the names of screws under his breath. Mrs. Bell arrived with a camping lantern and held it steady while he worked. When the replacement bolt slipped into the gravel, Marek swept his hand across the stones, searching with quick, sharp movements. A neighbor found it near his boot. Marek exhaled, thanked him, and finished the repair by lantern light.

My laundry was trapped in the building’s basement washer when the power cut out, and I had an early shift at the clinic. I ran downstairs, pushed every button on the machine, then leaned close as though I might hear it restart. It stayed silent. Two neighbors were already there, their baskets balanced on their hips. “The laundromat’s probably open,” one said. I looked at the soaked clothes and groaned, then started wringing out a sleeve by hand. The others joined in, turning the basement into a row of people twisting shirts over a mop bucket. A retired tailor from the fourth floor showed us how to roll each garment inside a towel and press out the water. I kept checking my phone’s dead screen, although I knew it wouldn’t help. By the time we finished, the clothes were merely damp, and someone had found a line of spare hangers.

Priya was waiting for a remote job interview when the power failed, and her laptop battery showed four percent. She ran to the hallway, asking whether any neighbor had a charged hotspot or a working outlet. Doors opened along the corridor; people emerged with flashlights, phone cables, and conflicting advice. Priya paced in front of the stairwell, tapping her fingers against the laptop lid. The interview began in twelve minutes. Mr. Dorsey from next door remembered that the building’s lobby had a backup generator, so they hurried downstairs together. It powered the emergency lights but not the outlets. Priya shut every open program and lowered the screen brightness. A neighbor offered to hold a phone near the window where its signal was strongest. She joined the call with seconds to spare, perched on the lobby’s radiator cover while the other residents kept watch over her battery bar.

I was supposed to meet my sister at the train station, but the neighborhood outage had stopped the traffic lights and left my car charging in the garage. I went door to door, asking if anyone knew whether the station was still operating. Every answer began with “I think,” which made me grip my keys harder. My neighbor Salma suggested we walk to the main road together and look for a bus. I kept striding ahead, then doubling back when I realized she was carrying a toddler.
