Their grandmother had taught both of them to sew on it. He tried lifting the box, but his arms shook and the weight barely moved. Zofia wedged a broom beneath one edge while Marek pushed with his shoulder. The box shifted, then tipped away. They inspected the damage together, finding the machine’s metal body intact beneath the splintered casing. Marek swallowed, blinking hard, and asked if they could build a new cover. Zofia nodded and began measuring the broken pieces.

My sister June and I were sorting attic boxes in the cottage we had rented for the summer. We planned to look for old games, but I found a nest of wasps tucked behind a suitcase. One flew past my ear. I dropped the lid and bolted toward the stairs, only to find June blocking the narrow passage with a box of board games. “Move!” I yelled, backing away as another insect circled the lamp. My lungs seemed to forget their usual rhythm. June shoved the games against the wall, and we squeezed through together, knocking over a stack of hats. Downstairs, I slammed the attic door and pressed both hands against it. June went to fetch the caretaker. I kept watching the ceiling, certain I could hear wings above us, until she returned with a sealed spray can and a calm voice.

At seventy-two, Osvaldo climbed the attic stairs with his granddaughter Pilar to sort the boxes before his house was sold. He wanted her to keep the family photographs, but he could not remember which carton held them. A row of labels blurred together as he searched. When Pilar opened a box of old bills, Osvaldo’s breathing turned shallow. He had promised his late wife he would protect the albums from careless hands. He began lifting cartons down too quickly, stacking them near the ladder until Pilar caught his elbow. “Grandpa, stop. We’ll do one at a time.” He looked at the narrow stairwell and the unstable pile, then gripped the railing. His fingertips had gone numb. Pilar found the albums in a hatbox beneath a quilt and carried them to a clear patch of floor. Osvaldo sat beside her, smoothing each cover with his palm while the boxes remained untouched.

My brother Simon and I sorted the attic boxes after our parents announced they were moving abroad. I had told everyone I was excited, but the packed suitcases downstairs made the house feel as if it were already empty. I dug through our childhood toys, searching for the wooden music box we used to wind before bed. Simon found it first, but its lid was stuck. I twisted the key until it bent, then tried to pry the hinge with a screwdriver. “You’re going to break it,” he said. My jaw tightened; my hands would not stay still. The music box finally sprang open, playing a few slow notes before stopping. I sat back against a crate, suddenly unable to speak. Simon set the toy between us and offered me the bent key. Together we wound it gently, listening until the melody finished.

Tessa and her younger brother Milo sorted their attic while a crew repaired the ceiling below. Their father had asked them to keep the old quilts dry, but a stain was widening across the plaster above the largest stack. Tessa climbed onto a chair to move the quilts, and Milo passed them up one by one. A drop struck his cheek. Then another landed on the box marked FAMILY RECORDS. Tessa’s hands flew, pulling at the wet cardboard, but the bottom split and papers slid toward the leak. Milo shoved a plastic storage bin beneath the drip while she scooped documents into it. Their voices overlapped, each asking where to put things. When the repair crew called that the pipe was fixed, Tessa remained crouched on the floor, clutching a damp folder against her chest. Milo placed a dry towel over her shoulders and started sorting the rescued papers.

I was halfway down the bean rows when the western sky turned the color of a bruise. My phone showed the storm arriving in twenty minutes, though the weather radio had promised an hour. I ran back for the tarp, caught my boot in a vine, and landed hard enough to knock the breath from me. The beans were still low, but the drainage ditch had already begun to fill. I tried calling my sister for help; my fingers struck the wrong numbers twice. Then I saw the gate hanging open where the creek crossed the lower field. If water poured through there, it would sweep away the seedlings. I grabbed a shovel and sprinted toward it, glancing over my shoulder at each flash of light. The first drops struck my neck as I reached the gate, and I could hear the creek rising before I could see it.

At seventy-two, Arturo could judge rain by the ache in his left knee, but the clouds above his cornfield moved faster than any forecast he had heard. He walked the rows with a clipboard tucked under one arm, marking stalks bent by the afternoon wind. When thunder cracked, the pencil snapped between his fingers. He hurried toward the irrigation pump, then stopped, unable to remember whether he had shut the fuel valve. His breath came in short pulls. He checked his pockets, dropped the keys, and scrambled after them in the dirt. The pump was still running, sending water into furrows that would soon overflow. Arturo twisted the valve closed and hurried to the shed for sandbags. As the rain began, he kept counting them aloud, losing his place whenever lightning whitened the field.

I had promised my grandfather I would check the peach orchard before the storm, so I drove out even though the wind shoved the truck from lane to lane. The fruit was nearly ripe, and hail could turn a year’s work into bruised pulp. I hurried between the trees, lifting branches and checking the nets, but one corner had torn loose. My hands fumbled at the knots. A gust sent the ladder skidding, and I chased it until it struck a fence post. I kept thinking of the repair bill, then of my grandfather’s quiet face if I came home with no answer. I tied the net with baling twine, pulled until my palms stung, and tested it twice. The sky flashed beyond the ridge. I ran for the truck, then doubled back because I could not remember whether I had latched the orchard gate.

Nia had only been managing the farm for six weeks when the storm warning arrived. She checked the tomato beds, then the young pepper plants, moving so quickly that she forgot the tool basket beside the greenhouse. A sheet of plastic snapped overhead. She ducked, covered her head, and rushed to secure its loose edge, but the ladder wobbled beneath her. Her phone buzzed with a message from the farm owner asking whether the drainage channel was clear. Nia stared at the screen, thumb hovering, while thunder rolled over the valley. She had not checked it. She ran through the rows, slipping in wet soil, and found a wheelbarrow blocking the channel. The water was already spilling around its tires. She shoved it aside with both hands, then stood listening as the first heavy drops drummed on the greenhouse roof.

I spotted the storm shelf from the tractor seat and shut off the engine so abruptly that the cultivator jolted behind me. The barley was still standing, but the low corner of the field had a habit of flooding. I climbed down, leaving the cab door open, and jogged toward the ditch. My chest beat hard enough to make my shirt jump. A plastic feed sack had clogged the culvert, and muddy water was gathering on the uphill side. I pulled at it once, slipped, and landed on my knees. The sack would not budge. I found a branch and worked it under the plastic, muttering at it as if it could hear me. When the blockage finally came free, water rushed through with a roar. I stumbled back, wiped my face with my sleeve, and hurried to start the tractor before the rain reached the barley.

Before the storm, Malcolm walked the apple trees with a canvas bag of fallen fruit bumping against his leg. The forecast had changed twice, and he no longer trusted the pale patch of sky above the barn. He checked each row for broken limbs, looking back at the clouds after every few steps. Near the far fence, he found a young tree leaning sharply where a rabbit guard had slipped. He tried to straighten it, but the soil shifted under his boots. His phone slid from his pocket into the grass. He snatched it up, wiped the screen on his jacket, and called his neighbor. The call rang without an answer. Malcolm began tying the trunk to a stake, pulling the cord too tight, then loosening it and starting again. A gust rattled the leaves overhead, and he worked faster, jaw clenched, while the first drops darkened the path.

I was checking the rice paddies when the wind sent a ripple across the water, all moving in one direction toward the breached bank. The storm was still beyond the hills, but the clouds were swallowing the afternoon light. I ran to the sluice gate and found its handle jammed with weeds. My cousin had gone to fetch the tractor, and I could not reach him over the crackling radio. I twisted the handle until my shoulders burned, then wedged a length of wood beneath it. The water kept climbing against the bank. My thoughts jumped from the seedlings to the house, to my mother waiting there with the windows open. I ran for sandbags, dropped one, and chased it as it rolled toward the ditch. When I got back, the wooden brace was bending. I shoved another board against it and shouted for help into the empty field.

At fourteen, Beatriz knew every shortcut through her family’s squash patch, but that evening she kept taking the long way around, checking the sky between rows. Her father was away delivering produce, and the storm warning on the radio said hail was possible. She found a split in the greenhouse cover and hurried to fetch the repair tape. The roll was on a shelf above her reach, and she knocked down a jar while stretching for it. Glass scattered across the floor. She froze, then swept the pieces aside with a cardboard box and ran outside. The tape stuck to her wet fingers as she patched the tear. A gust lifted one edge before she could smooth it down. She pressed both palms against the plastic, shoulders trembling, and called her father again. This time, she left a message in a rush, then ran to secure the greenhouse door.

I had just finished checking the pumpkin vines when the radio crackled with a warning to shelter before the storm arrived. The biggest pumpkins sat in the lowest patch, where runoff from the road crossed our land. I grabbed the wheelbarrow and started moving them uphill, but its left wheel kept sinking into the mud. Each trip took longer than the last. I looked toward the farmhouse, where my partner was bringing in the dog, and tried to shout, but wind stole my words. One pumpkin rolled off the barrow and came to rest against a shallow ditch. I lunged after it, scraped my arm on a fence wire, and pushed it back with my shoulder. The first thunder shook the windows. I loaded two smaller pumpkins, abandoned the rest, and ran for the house, looking over my shoulder at the water beginning to stream across the patch.

Hassan was inspecting the grape trellises when the storm warning flashed across the farm office computer. He had planned to finish before supper, yet the vines still needed their loose wires tightened. He hurried down the slope, carrying pliers in one hand and a coil of wire in the other. A gust whipped his hat into the rows. He chased it, retrieved it, and found that the coil had unwound behind him like a silver trail. His breathing grew shallow as he gathered it back up. At the final trellis, one post leaned toward the road. He braced it with his shoulder and tried to hammer a stake into the hard ground. The hammer slipped, striking his thumb. He sucked in air, shook his hand, and drove the stake again. When the wind bent the vines, he dropped the tools and sprinted toward the barn.

I was checking the young cotton when I noticed the clouds turning greenish over the county road. The forecast had mentioned a chance of wind, not the wall of weather coming toward us now. I hurried to the equipment shed for stakes, but the padlock stuck, and I fumbled with the key until it finally turned. Back in the field, I drove stakes beside the most exposed seedlings, missing twice and striking stones. My hands shook so badly that I had to grip the mallet with both of them. Then I heard the barn door bang open behind me. I ran there, latched it, and remembered the south field was still unchecked. For a moment I stood with my hand on the latch, unable to choose. Another gust rattled the roof. I grabbed the truck keys and drove toward the cotton, tires spitting gravel, while the sky darkened in the mirror.

Lorna, a retired schoolteacher who had taken up farming after moving to the coast, checked her potato rows as the storm siren began to pulse. She had never heard that sound outside a test. The plants looked healthy, but water was already seeping through the lower boundary. She hurried to the shed for a spade and knocked a stack of seed trays onto the floor. Instead of leaving them, she picked them up one by one, then glanced at the doorway and hurried out again. Her boots slipped on the wet path. At the field’s edge, she dug a shallow channel toward the drainage pond, stopping whenever thunder rolled close overhead. The trench filled almost as fast as she cleared it. Lorna kept working, hair plastered to her forehead, until a neighbor pulled up in a pickup and waved her toward shelter. She dropped the spade and climbed aboard without looking back.

The chain slipped off just as I reached the station, and the clock above the platform showed four minutes until my train. I dropped my bag, crouched beside the bicycle, and tried to push the chain back with my bare fingers. Grease streaked my sleeve. My hands kept skidding, and each announcement from the loudspeaker made me look up. “Could you hold the wheel?” I called to a passing guard, though my voice came out thin. He turned the bike upside down while I guided the chain onto the smallest gear. It caught, then clattered loose again. I swallowed hard, took one slow breath, and noticed the rear wheel was crooked. A quick adjustment to the axle straightened it. The chain settled into place. I pedaled toward the platform, bag bouncing against my hip, as the train doors began to close.

At the edge of the desert road, Mateo heard a sharp crack and felt his bicycle lurch beneath him. The front tire sagged against the gravel. He stared at the distant gas station, then at the darkening sky, and hurried to unpack his repair kit. His fingers fumbled with the tiny levers; one flew into the dust. He crawled after it, breathing through his teeth, while a truck’s headlights swept across the road. The inner tube had split near the valve. Mateo patched it, pressing the rubber hard with both thumbs, but the glue tube was nearly empty. He shook it, squeezed, and watched one last bead emerge. After waiting only a few seconds, he fitted the tire back on. The wheel held air. He climbed aboard and pedaled toward the station, glancing behind him until the lights vanished.

I was halfway through leading the children’s bike tour when the pedal on my old bicycle suddenly spun free. Twelve small faces turned toward me. “Everyone stay by the fountain,” I said, smiling so tightly my cheeks hurt. My toolkit was in the pannier, but the crank bolt had worked loose and bounced somewhere along the path. I knelt in the grass and swept both hands through clover, checking the same patch twice. One child offered a shiny marble. I almost laughed, then spotted the bolt caught in the chain guard. My wrench slipped on the first attempt. I braced the crank with my shoe and tightened until my wrist ached. The pedal turned smoothly. I tested it once, then again, before announcing we could continue. Behind me, the children were already lining up.

In the basement of the apartment block, Lila found her bicycle locked beneath a leaking pipe. The rear wheel would not turn, and her phone showed a message from her sister: the baby had arrived early. She set the phone on a paint can and bent over the bike. A bent fender was wedged against the tire. Lila tugged at it, then grabbed pliers from the shelf, knocking a jar of screws onto the concrete. Metal pieces scattered under the laundry machines. She pressed her lips together and forced the fender away from the rubber. The wheel spun once, then stopped with a scrape. She checked the brake cable and loosened it a fraction. This time the tire moved freely. Lila snatched up her phone, called a cab, and carried the bicycle upstairs, still breathing in short bursts.

My delivery bag was packed with cooling soup when the bicycle’s chain jammed in an alley. The restaurant owner had warned me the customer was waiting downstairs, and the order timer flashed red on my phone. I flipped the bike over, but the chain was twisted around the gear teeth. A car rolled slowly toward the alley mouth, its headlights filling the brick walls. I tried to pull the chain free with a napkin, which tore at once. My thumb slipped between two links; I jerked it back and shook out my hand. Then I found the small screwdriver in my bag and eased the chain backward, one tooth at a time. It dropped into place with a metallic click. I wiped my fingers on my apron, tested the pedals, and pushed off hard, keeping the soup level as I raced away.

At a quiet campground, Noor discovered that her bicycle’s handlebars had gone loose while she was loading it for the morning ride. The campsite map showed the nearest repair shop twenty miles away. She tightened the stem bolt with a multitool, but the bars still shifted whenever she leaned on them. Her little brother watched from the picnic table, asking whether they would miss the ferry. Noor answered too quickly and dropped the tool into the dirt. She brushed grit from its handle, then examined the clamp closely. One bolt was missing; the other had backed out almost completely. A spare from her water-bottle cage fit the empty hole. She secured both sides evenly, gripping the bars and testing them with short, forceful turns. They held steady. Noor packed the map, checked the ferry schedule again, and started down the campground lane.

I was riding to my first job interview when the bicycle’s rear brake seized at the bottom of a hill. I dragged it onto the sidewalk, shoes scraping, and stared at the wheel that refused to spin. My appointment was in fifteen minutes. The brake cable had slipped out of its housing, so I crouched beside the bike and tried to guide it back with a key. My fingers trembled enough to make the metal tip chatter against the frame. A woman walking her dog asked if I needed help. I nodded, unable to form a proper sentence. She held the cable taut while I loosened the pinch bolt and reseated it. I tightened the bolt with both hands, then spun the wheel. It turned cleanly. I thanked her, straightened my tie in a shop window, and hurried toward the office with grease on one cuff.

During a sudden downpour, Victor’s bicycle began making a grinding noise beneath the awning of a closed bakery. Water streamed along the curb, and his sketchbook sat unsecured in the front basket. He pulled the bike under cover and examined the gears, blinking rain from his eyelashes. A small twig was jammed between the chain and derailleur. He tried to remove it with his fingers, but the branch snapped and wedged deeper. His jaw tightened as he rummaged through his backpack, shifting pencils and papers onto the wet pavement. At last he found a pair of tweezers in his drawing kit. He eased the broken pieces out, then turned the pedals by hand. The gears clicked but worked. Victor wrapped the sketchbook in his jacket, mounted the bicycle, and rode carefully through the shining streets, listening for any return of the grinding.

The bicycle was the only way I could get to my grandmother’s house before her nurse left, and its tire went flat in the middle of a park. I pulled over beside a bench, my phone showing a nearly empty battery. The pump was in my basket, but the tube had split near the rim. I kept looking toward the park gate, as if a repair shop might appear there. Instead, a jogger slowed and pointed out a patch kit clipped beneath my seat. I tore open the packet with my teeth, spilled the patches, then gathered them from the path. Following the printed steps, I roughened the rubber and pressed a patch over the hole. The adhesive needed time, but I counted seconds under my breath and fitted the tube back. It held. I pedaled away, checking the tire after every few turns.

At the schoolyard, Inez found her daughter’s bicycle with a chain hanging slack beside the rear wheel. The class was about to end, and the child waited by the gate in a paper crown, watching her mother work. Inez set down her groceries and knelt on the pavement. The chain had slipped off the front ring, but the derailleur was bent inward. She tried to straighten it with a wrench, glancing repeatedly at the clock above the entrance. The tool slipped and struck the frame with a loud tap. Her daughter stepped closer; Inez asked her to stay behind the painted line, speaking more sharply than she meant to. She loosened the derailleur bolt, nudged the part outward, then retightened it. The chain finally seated. She spun the pedal twice, lifted the groceries, and hurried with her daughter toward the bus stop.

I heard the bicycle’s front wheel wobble while crossing the covered bridge, and the wooden boards rattled under every step. I stopped beside the railing, where the river rushed far below, and squeezed the front brake. The wheel scraped against one brake pad. My toolbox was back at the campsite, so I searched my pockets and found only a small coin and a folded receipt. I loosened the quick-release lever with the coin’s edge, trying to center the wheel. It shifted too far left. My palms dampened against the handlebars, and I had to start again. This time I held the fork steady and tightened the lever in short turns. The rim cleared both pads. I pushed the bicycle across the remaining boards rather than riding, then checked the wheel once more on solid ground before continuing.

Sanjay had promised to arrive at the community theater with a box of costumes, but his bicycle’s rack had snapped halfway there. The box tilted toward the spinning spokes. He grabbed it before the fabric caught, then stood under a streetlamp, staring at the broken metal strut. His phone buzzed with a message asking where he was. He typed a reply, erased it, and shoved the phone into his pocket. From his repair pouch he took a sturdy cable tie and looped it around the rack and frame. The tie slipped twice, so he threaded it through a narrower gap and pulled until the plastic creaked. He tested the rack with a tug; it held the box clear of the wheel. Sanjay walked the bicycle the final blocks, one hand steadying the costumes, and reached the theater just as the stage lights came on.

I had twenty minutes before the neighborhood concert, and the clarinet kept making a dry, cracked note where the high passage should have bloomed. My fingers were slick enough to lose their grip on the keys. I took the instrument apart, wiped it, put it together again, then checked the reed as if it might have changed while I blinked. In the hall, folding chairs scraped into place and someone tested the microphone with a thump. I tried the passage slower, but my breath ran out halfway through. The conductor appeared in the doorway, smiling, and asked whether I was ready. I nodded too quickly. Then I noticed the reed case on the piano bench: empty. The good reed was still in my coat pocket, downstairs in the dressing room. I snatched up my instrument and ran, counting every stair as though the missing minutes might be found there.

At sixty-eight, Marisol had played the accordion at weddings for decades, but tonight’s library concert held only thirty seats and somehow felt more perilous than a ballroom. She kept checking the buttons, pressing each one twice, while her heel tapped an uneven beat beneath the music stand. The first tune began in four minutes. A child in the front row leaned close to inspect the bellows, and Marisol’s hands paused midair. She could no longer remember whether she had packed the spare strap. Without it, the instrument might slide from her shoulder during the fast section. She searched her bag, spilling mints and sheet music onto the floor. The librarian started to announce her name. Marisol’s face warmed as she spotted the strap looped around the chair behind her. She fastened it with trembling fingers, drew one careful breath, and stepped toward the little platform.

The basement studio smelled of dust and hot cables, and my trumpet seemed determined to announce every mistake to the whole building. My small concert was upstairs in the café, where twelve people were already finding seats. I ran the opening bars again, but the notes came out pinched. When I reached for my mute, it wasn’t in its usual pocket. I emptied the case onto the amp, checking beneath the cloth and inside the side compartment, though I had just looked there. My watch showed six minutes. My mouth had gone dry; even swallowing felt like work. A knock sounded on the door, followed by the café owner calling that they were ready. I stared at the trumpet, then at the stack of laundry beside the stairs. The mute had slipped into my jacket pocket when I changed. I found it, fitted it in place, and hurried up, still rubbing my damp palms on my trousers.

Niko had promised his grandfather he would perform the old folk song on violin without stopping. Now, in the community garden shed, the bow shook against the strings and produced a thin squeal. Beyond the open door, neighbors carried lanterns toward the tiny concert area. Niko’s phone displayed a message from the accompanist: stuck in traffic. He read it again, hoping the words might rearrange themselves. His jaw tightened. He tried the first phrase alone, lost his place, and flipped through the pages so quickly they fanned onto the floor. His grandfather was already sitting in the front row, hands folded over his cane. Niko bent to gather the sheets, but his fingers kept missing their edges. Then he remembered the melody had been taught to him by ear long before there was any music to read. He set the pages aside, lifted the violin, and began humming the tune softly.

I was supposed to sing three songs at the bookstore’s after-hours concert, but the first lyric vanished the instant I saw the audience through the curtain. The room held perhaps twenty people, all close enough to notice the small stage, the water glass, and me gripping the microphone stand. My throat felt lined with paper. I whispered the opening verse, then whispered it again, each time losing a different word. The pianist asked if I wanted to run the chorus. I said yes, though my voice came out as a squeak. On the table, my lyric cards were stacked in the wrong order. I scattered them and tried to rebuild the sequence while the host introduced the event. The cards fluttered to the floor. One had a blue corner, just like the first song’s cue card. I found it beside my shoe, pressed the stack together, and walked out before I could begin another search.

Asha’s flute case would not close. One clasp had bent, and the silver instrument lay exposed while she sat in the hallway outside the retirement home’s music room. Her quartet was meant to play a gentle set for residents, but the start time was approaching and the other musicians were already tuning inside. She pushed the clasp, released it, and pushed again. Each attempt made the metal click louder. A resident passing with a walker stopped to watch. Asha’s shoulders drew up; her breathing became shallow. She pictured the flute rolling out when she carried it and striking the tile. Rather than force the case, she wrapped the instrument in its velvet cloth and tucked it safely beneath her arm. When the quartet leader opened the door, she apologized in a rush. He handed her a spare case from the storage closet, and she joined the warm-up with the new clasp firmly shut.

My first solo gig was in a boat club, where the little audience gathered beside a wall of framed fishing photographs. I had rehearsed the guitar piece for weeks, but backstage I could not make my fingers form the opening chord. They hovered over the strings, stiff and damp. Through the door came laughter, then the organizer’s voice announcing that the performer would be ready shortly. I checked the tuning, although every string already sounded right. Then I checked it again. The strap buckle had twisted, and I kept turning it without fixing anything. My stomach clenched when I heard someone ask how long the changeover would take. I set the guitar down, straightened the buckle slowly, and planted both shoes flat on the floor. A spot on the wood caught my eye; I followed its grain to the edge of the stage. When my name came, I carried the guitar out and played the first chord before looking up.

At the school’s tiny spring concert, Darius had one job: keep the cajón steady beneath a violin duet. He sat on the edge of the stage, tapping the wooden box with fingertips that felt numb at their ends. The other players were still arranging chairs, and the audience’s low chatter seemed to swell each time he missed a beat. His music stand wobbled. He tightened its screw, but the sheet slid sideways and nearly fell. Darius caught it against his knee, knocking the cajón with a loud, hollow thud. Several heads turned. He stared at the page, unable to find the marked entrance. The music teacher whispered that they could start whenever he was ready. He nodded, then rubbed his palms against his jeans. One small pencil mark showed where the first beat began. Darius drew the stand close, placed his hands on the box, and counted four silent beats before the violinists lifted their bows.

I had spent the afternoon rehearsing a piano set in my apartment, but at the café the keyboard’s middle C sounded strangely thin. The room was barely large enough for the instrument and three rows of chairs, yet the audience’s arrival made the walls seem to inch closer. I pressed the key again, then leaned beneath the stand to inspect the cable. My knee struck the pedal, and a low note rumbled through the speakers. The café owner looked over from the counter. I smiled as though the noise had been planned, then searched the floor for a loose connection. My hands were shaking enough to make the cable ends click together. The first piece was printed on a page that had slipped behind the keyboard. I tugged it free, nearly tearing the corner, and set it on the stand. A borrowed adapter lay beside the bench. I plugged it in, tested the note once, and sat upright as the host approached.

Priya’s small concert was scheduled in the greenhouse, with potted lemon trees standing behind her music stand. She had practiced the cello suite for months, but the warm air softened the rosin and her bow began to slide. She wiped it, tested a phrase, and heard the notes blur. Guests were filing through the glass doors, carrying paper cups of lemonade. Priya’s gaze darted from the bow to the clock and back again. Her fingers pressed too hard on the strings, leaving pale dents that disappeared as soon as she lifted them. She asked the volunteer for a cloth, then dropped the cloth while reaching for it. The volunteer quietly offered a fresh cake of rosin from the supply box. Priya drew the bow across the strings, testing its grip in short strokes. The sound steadied. She adjusted the chair, rested the cello between her knees, and began the opening measure as the last guests settled.

I was rehearsing a saxophone piece in the church side room when I realized my printed solo had only two pages. The final page was missing, and the concert upstairs would begin in ten minutes. I searched the folder, the case, and the pocket of my jacket, turning each place inside out. A radiator hissed beneath the window. My shirt clung between my shoulder blades, and I kept wetting my lips, though they dried at once. I tried to remember the ending from practice, but the notes scrambled whenever I reached the last phrase. The pianist tapped gently on the door and asked if I had the music. I answered that I was looking. A copy machine stood in the choir office; perhaps the page had been left there. I hurried down the corridor, nearly passing the open door. The missing sheet sat face down on the copier. I grabbed it, returned at a fast walk, and laid it on the stand just as the introduction began.

Elliot had built a set around a homemade banjo, and the small concert in the makerspace was meant to be casual. Still, the instrument’s fifth string had snapped during the final rehearsal, leaving its end curled near the tuning peg. He stared at it, then glanced toward the open room where people were gathering around worktables. His hands fumbled through a tin of spare strings, spilling picks across the floor. The repair needed a tiny wrench, but he had no idea which drawer held one. Someone tested a drill nearby, making him jerk and drop the new string. He crouched to find it, breathing through parted lips while the host started welcoming everyone. A fellow maker knelt beside him and offered a wrench from her apron. Elliot fixed the string, turned the peg until the note held, and plucked a simple chord. The banjo rang bright and clean. He wiped his palms on his shirt and carried it into the circle.

The train doors shut behind me, and I stared at the station map as if the colored lines might rearrange themselves into English. My phone showed one percent battery. I had no idea which exit led to the hotel, and the crowd streamed past on both sides, carrying me toward a staircase I hadn't meant to take. My fingers kept slipping on the screen while I tried to enlarge the address. A man in a bright vest asked if I needed help; I nodded too quickly and thrust the phone at him. He pointed to a kiosk, but I heard only fragments over the station announcements. When my battery warning flashed, I swallowed hard and copied the hotel name onto my ticket with a shaking pen. Then I followed the signs one at a time, counting each turn aloud under my breath.

At twenty, Malik had crossed an ocean for a music audition, but the bus dropped him beside a market where every street seemed to bend away from the others. He checked the paper address, then checked it again, though the ink had not changed. A brass band burst into a tune nearby, and the sudden noise made him jerk so sharply that his suitcase toppled. People stepped around him. His chest worked in short, shallow pulls while he searched for a familiar landmark among awnings and balconies. He asked a fruit seller for directions, but his voice came out thin and clipped. The seller drew a route on a napkin and gave him a bottle of water. Malik gripped both, repeating the street name silently as he set off, careful to keep the napkin visible in his hand.

I arrived in Veyra after midnight, expecting the airport shuttle to stop near my hostel. Instead, the driver left me outside a closed tram depot and rattled away before I could ask anything. Rain slid down my collar. I hauled my bag beneath a narrow awning and opened the booking email, but the map refused to load. A taxi rolled past without slowing. My pulse hammered against my throat as I tried the emergency number, then hung up before it connected, afraid I wouldn't understand whoever answered. Across the street, a bakery worker was stacking chairs. I crossed too quickly, nearly stepping into a puddle deep enough to soak my shoes, and held out my reservation. She studied it, then used her own phone to call the hostel. While she spoke, I pressed both hands against the counter to keep them still.

Dr. Sato had presented research on three continents, yet the maze of terminals at Ordan Airport reduced her to clutching her suitcase handle with both hands. Her connecting train was due to leave in twelve minutes. The electronic signs switched languages before she could finish reading them, and each corridor opened onto another bank of departures. She hurried toward a uniformed attendant, then stopped when she realized she had left her passport on a bench. Her face drained of color. She spun around, weaving against the current of travelers, and found the bench empty. A child pointed beneath it, where the passport had slid against a radiator. Sato snatched it up, checked every page, and ran back to the attendant. This time she spoke slowly, showing the ticket and asking for the platform number. The answer came with a printed map.

The taxi dropped me in front of a hotel with the same name as the one I had booked, except this one stood across town. I realized it when the clerk asked for a reservation number and the confirmation screen showed a different address. My stomach tightened. I backed away from the desk, bumping a brass luggage cart, and fumbled for the map saved on my phone. The driver had already vanished into traffic. I tried to explain to the clerk, but my words tangled, and I kept glancing at the revolving door as if the correct building might appear outside. He offered to call the other hotel. I nodded, unable to sit still, and paced between a potted palm and the window. When he finally gave me the new address, I repeated it twice and wrote it on my sleeve in pen.

At seventy-three, Beatrice was used to traveling alone, but the sudden cancellation of her ferry left her stranded in a harbor city she had never visited. The ticket office shuttered while she was still reading the notice. She pressed her itinerary to the glass, then turned in a slow circle, searching for someone who looked as though they might know what came next. Buses hissed past, their destination boards glowing in unfamiliar abbreviations. Her handbag clasp clicked open and shut beneath her thumb. She tried calling her daughter, but the connection broke after one ring. A young porter noticed her standing by the curb and brought a folded local transit map. Beatrice traced the routes with a fingernail, pausing whenever the lines crossed. She thanked him, tucked the map into her coat, and asked him to point out the stop nearest a working hotel.

I stepped off the overnight coach in Bellport and found my backpack missing from the luggage hold. The other passengers dispersed, leaving me beside the curb with a paper ticket and a small canvas tote. I rushed back to the driver, but he was already pulling away. My hands went cold as I searched the pavement for a claim tag, then patted every pocket, although I knew I had put it inside the bag. The station's announcements echoed over my head. I tried to tell a nearby attendant what had happened, but I spoke so fast he asked me to start again. I forced myself to show him the ticket instead. He called the coach company and pointed me toward their office two blocks away. I set off at a stiff, quick walk, repeating the coach number so I wouldn't lose it.

Nico arrived in the mountain city of Luro with a cello case, a scholarship letter, and no working data connection. The conservatory shuttle had left ten minutes earlier. He stood under the station clock while the minute hand advanced with a sharp click, staring at the address written in his notebook. A crowd surged around him, and someone knocked his shoulder; he clamped both arms around the instrument. His breath snagged as he tried to remember the route from the email. He approached a woman selling roasted chestnuts and showed her the letter. She spoke little of his language but recognized the conservatory crest. Together they found a streetcar stop, where she helped him match the letter's address to a route number. Nico climbed aboard just before the doors closed, keeping the paper pinched between trembling fingers.

I left the station in Marseille and walked straight into a protest that had filled the square. My hotel was supposed to be two blocks away, but barriers cut off every street shown on my map. Sirens sounded somewhere beyond the crowd. I turned left, then right, only to reach another row of fencing, and my suitcase wheels caught in the paving stones. My mouth had gone dry. I tried asking a police officer for a way through, but the words came out in a rush, mixed with the little French I remembered from school. He pointed toward a side alley and told me to keep moving. I pulled the suitcase over a curb, nearly dropping my passport, then checked it was still in my pocket. At the alley's end, a café owner let me use his phone to call the hotel.

Priya had planned every detail of her first solo trip to the capital, except for the construction that closed the metro entrance beside her guesthouse. With two bags and a dead phone, she stood at the barricade while commuters streamed around her. The address on her reservation seemed suddenly useless. She opened her wallet, counted the remaining cash, then counted it again. Her shoulders crept toward her ears, and she kept looking back at the station as though the barriers might move. A delivery cyclist stopped when she waved both arms. Priya showed him the printed booking slip. He recognized the neighborhood and sketched a route on the back of a receipt, marking a bus stop and a distinctive blue church. She folded the receipt carefully, thanked him, and walked toward the stop, repeating the church's name until it felt fixed in her mind.

The rain in Hoshima was so heavy that the street signs blurred before I could read them. I had arrived for a job interview and realized my folder of documents was still on the airport train. My hands shook as I searched my pockets for the rail office number. A shopkeeper let me stand inside, but the wet jacket clung to my arms, and I kept pacing between the door and a display of umbrellas. I called the office and stumbled through the details: train line, time, carriage, folder color. The clerk asked me to wait while someone checked. Each passing minute stretched as I watched water gather along the curb. At last, a station worker called back to say the folder had been found. I wrote the station name on my palm, thanked the shopkeeper, and hurried there with my collar pulled tight.

Elias arrived in a desert city just as a sandstorm warning sent shutters clattering across the bus terminal. He had promised his brother he could find the family apartment without help, but the address was written in a script he could barely decipher. Dust slipped through the doors, and his eyes watered as he tried to unfold the street map. The paper tore at one corner. He grabbed it against his chest and searched for a taxi, but the queue had vanished indoors. His breathing turned uneven; he kept checking the time, then the address, then the time again. A terminal cleaner noticed and guided him to a public phone. Elias called his brother, but the line crackled. He read the street names aloud, one by one, until his brother recognized a nearby landmark and gave him a route through the covered arcade.

When the message arrived, I was labeling jars in the bakery’s walk-in fridge. My manager wanted me upstairs immediately. The marker slipped from my hand and rolled beneath a shelf. I left the labels crooked, wiped my damp palms on my apron, and climbed the stairs too quickly, catching my toe on the last one. In her office, a folder lay open beside a printout of yesterday’s orders. I tried to ask what was wrong, but my voice came out thin. She pointed to a delivery marked incomplete. I stared at the figures until they blurred, certain I had sent the wrong cake to a wedding. Then she said the customer had called to praise the frosting and ask for the recipe. My shoulders dropped so sharply they hurt. I let out a breath I hadn’t noticed I was holding, and laughed once, louder than the moment seemed to require.

Darius kept checking the time on the microwave display, though it hadn’t changed in the few seconds since his last glance. His supervisor had asked him to come to the office after the shift, without explaining why. He replayed every conversation from the week as he walked there, rubbing his thumb over the frayed edge of his badge. The office door stood open. A stack of forms waited on the desk, and his supervisor’s expression gave nothing away. Darius sat on the chair’s edge, knees bouncing, and began listing the mistakes he might have made. The supervisor raised a hand to stop him. A customer had left a wallet at the register, and Darius was the only employee who had seen which taxi took them. The wallet was safe in a drawer. Darius blinked, pressed both feet flat to the floor, and finally unclenched his jaw.

I was halfway through cleaning a hotel room when the front desk called and said the manager needed me in her office. My cart blocked the corridor, towels hung from one hand, and my thoughts sprinted ahead to the guest complaint I’d received that morning. I set everything down and hurried toward the elevators, then had to turn back for my keys. In the office, a maintenance worker stood beside a cracked lamp. My stomach tightened as the manager asked whether I had noticed it. I explained that I’d reported the loose base two days earlier, but the work order was still open. She checked her computer, found the report, and thanked me for documenting it. The lamp had fallen after the room was empty. I nodded too many times, then noticed I’d been gripping my key ring hard enough to leave marks in my palm. She offered me water, and I took it with both hands.

At the aquarium gift shop, Mei was counting cash when the intercom requested her in the manager’s office. She dropped a stack of coins, and they scattered under the counter. Her coworker offered to gather them, but Mei was already wiping her hands on her trousers and hurrying away. She had taken a long lunch to call her son’s school; perhaps someone had complained. In the office, the manager closed the door and asked her to sit. Mei perched on the chair, eyes fixed on a tiny crack in the desk. The manager opened a package containing a handmade paper fish. A child had mailed it to thank Mei for helping him find his lost grandfather during a busy visit. The manager wanted to put it on display. Mei’s breath came in a shaky rush; she pressed her fingers to her collarbone, then smiled as the room settled around her.

The email said, “Please come see me before you leave.” I read it three times, then stood so fast my chair scraped across the floor. I was working at a small architecture firm, and a client’s revised measurements had gone out under my name that morning. On the walk to my manager’s office, every doorway looked like a possible escape route. My mouth felt dry. I kept rehearsing an apology, changing the words each time I reached the end of the hall. My manager was waiting with two cups of tea and a rolled blueprint. She wanted me to explain a clever adjustment I’d made to fit a wheelchair ramp into a narrow entrance. I had assumed the client would object; instead, they had approved it. The cup rattled against its saucer as I picked it up. I covered the sound with a cough and let myself sit back in the chair.

Before the morning rush, Luis received a note telling him to report to the manager’s office. He had worked at the hardware store for only three weeks, and the request made him forget the customer standing at the paint counter. He apologized, fetched another employee, and walked to the back room with his hands pressed against his sides. His thoughts jumped from the missing box cutter to the display he had arranged incorrectly. The manager was speaking on the phone, so Luis waited beside a filing cabinet, shifting his weight from foot to foot. When the call ended, she turned a monitor toward him. A shopper had praised his patience while helping an elderly couple choose a heater. The store wanted him to train new staff. Luis stared at the screen, eyebrows raised, then asked whether she was sure it was him. His ears warmed, and he had to read the message twice before replying.

I heard my name over the factory speaker and nearly dropped the metal bracket I was holding. The manager wanted me in her office. I placed the bracket in its tray, but my hands shook enough to make it clatter against the others. Had the batch failed inspection? I wiped my palms on my work shirt and walked past the humming machines, counting each step as if that might steady me. In the office, a safety report lay on the desk. My manager asked whether I had noticed the loose guard on press three. I had reported it the previous afternoon, but the repair crew hadn’t arrived. For a second I could only stare at the paper. She thanked me for stopping the line and said no one had been hurt. My knees softened, and I gripped the chair before sitting. When I finally spoke, my voice sounded as if it belonged to someone across the room.

Nia was sorting donation envelopes at the community theater when the director asked her to come to his office. She slipped the envelopes into a drawer, then immediately worried she’d put them in the wrong one. On the way down the corridor, she twisted the ring on her finger until it pinched. The director’s office was crowded with costume boxes, and he stood beside a small table covered in handwritten notes. Nia apologized before he had said anything. He looked puzzled, then explained that the lead actor had lost her voice and the evening performance needed a replacement. Nia had once mentioned that she studied stage lighting and knew the script by heart, but she had never acted in front of an audience. Her lips parted without sound. She glanced toward the exit, then at the clock. The director offered to stand backstage with her. Nia’s hands fluttered over the notes before she picked one up and began reading.

My manager’s assistant called just as I was sealing a shipment at the bike-parts warehouse. I had to come upstairs now. The tape dispenser slipped from my fingers, and I ripped the label while trying to peel it free. I started over, but the numbers on the screen seemed to rearrange themselves. Had I entered the wrong destination for the expensive order? The elevator took forever. In the office, my manager held a printed spreadsheet and asked me to look at one line. I felt heat spread up my neck. Then he pointed to a savings figure: my new inventory system had cut wasted packaging by a third. He wanted me to present it to the regional team. I gripped the edge of the desk while he explained the travel dates, hearing only pieces at first. When I understood, a laugh escaped me, small and breathless. I asked him to repeat the dates, buying a few seconds to make my hands behave.

At the city library, Gordon was returning a cart of books when the branch manager asked to see him privately. He stopped so abruptly that the cart bumped his hip. For several minutes he had been trying to remember whether he had locked the back entrance after taking out recycling. Now every detail of the shift lined up in his mind, each one seeming less reliable than the last. He followed the manager into her office, rubbing a damp patch on his sleeve. She had found a wallet in the reading room and wanted Gordon to identify its owner from the security log. He searched the screen with a fingertip that kept missing the right row. When the owner’s name appeared, he recognized the person who had come back asking for it. The wallet was still safe. Gordon’s shoulders lowered, but his knees remained unsteady. He asked if he could sit, then took a long drink from the glass of water she offered.

I was balancing plates at the seaside restaurant when the head manager asked me to step into her office. She didn’t say why. A fork slid against a plate as I set the tray down, and I apologized to the diners even though nothing had spilled. All afternoon I’d been covering for a coworker, and I couldn’t remember whether I’d entered one table’s allergy note correctly. I walked to the office with my fingers pressed against my apron pocket, searching for the order pad that wasn’t there. The manager turned her laptop toward me. A customer had written that I’d caught a dangerous ingredient before the meal reached the table. I remembered the moment: the kitchen had substituted a sauce, and I’d checked twice. The manager wanted to thank me and offer a shift-lead role. I stared at the screen, then looked down at my trembling fingertips. When I answered, I asked her to give me a minute before I chose.

Rafi was replacing price tags at an electronics shop when his manager called him into the office. He checked his shirt for dust, then checked it again, certain there must be a reason for such a sudden request. In the narrow hallway, the buzzing ceiling light seemed unusually loud. He had accidentally left a tablet display unlocked the day before and spent the night imagining the consequences. Now he stood beside the manager’s desk, hands clasped behind his back to hide their movement. She held up a customer review describing an employee who had patiently recovered family photos from an old phone. Rafi recognized the customer and the cracked device. The manager wanted to nominate him for a service award. He stared at her, waiting for the rest of the news, while his breath caught high in his chest. Then she smiled. Rafi’s clasped hands opened, and he asked to see the review again, reading every line slowly.

The clinic’s wall clock clicked louder than it should have. I kept checking the number on my ticket, though it had not changed, and rubbed the corner until the paper softened. A nurse had said the blood test results would be ready soon. Soon had stretched past forty minutes. My phone slipped from my damp fingers, and I nearly dropped it while trying to call my sister. When a door opened, I stood so quickly my chair scraped backward. It was only a delivery worker. I sat down again, forcing air through my nose, then read every poster in the room without taking in a word. At last, the nurse appeared with a folder. I pressed both feet flat against the floor and waited for her to say my name.

Marlon sat beneath a framed photograph of a mountain lake, his coat still buttoned although the clinic was warm. The doctor had ordered a scan after finding a shadow on his routine image, and now a receptionist had promised to bring the report when it arrived. He refreshed the clinic’s patient portal until the screen dimmed, then tapped it awake with a trembling thumb. Each time footsteps approached, his shoulders lifted. A child nearby rolled a toy truck along the tiles; Marlon watched it bump against his shoe and could not remember how to smile. He rehearsed questions silently, lost his place, and started again. When the receptionist finally came through the door, he rose before she reached the desk, gripping his appointment card as if it might keep him upright.

I counted the blue squares in the waiting-room carpet, lost count at thirty-seven, and began again. The clinic had taken a sample from my throat that morning, and the clinician said someone would explain the result before I left. My bus pass bent between my fingers. I checked the time, then checked it again almost immediately, as though the clock might have skipped ahead. A receptionist called another patient’s name, and my stomach clenched so hard I leaned forward with my elbows on my knees. I tried to read a travel magazine, but every page seemed to contain the same blurry photograph. When my name finally came, I stood, sat back down, and stood once more. The nurse waited patiently while I gathered my bag and followed her.

At sixty-eight, Beatriz had learned to bring knitting to appointments, but the red scarf in her lap remained only three stitches longer than when she arrived. Her clinic had called her back after a routine chest image, and the specialist was reviewing the results. She tugged the yarn tight, then loosened it, watching the needles quiver. A man at the front desk laughed at something on his phone. Beatriz flinched at the sudden sound and dropped a needle beneath her chair. She searched for it with one hand while keeping her eyes fixed on the consultation-room door. Her daughter had offered to come, but Beatriz had insisted she could manage alone. Now she wished she could hear her daughter’s steady voice. The door opened, and the doctor stepped into the hall.

I had promised myself I would stay calm until the lab called, but the clinic’s waiting area made every minute feel exposed. The test was for a condition that ran in my family, and I had spent the morning pretending the appointment was ordinary. I turned my paper cup around and around, spilling a little water onto my sleeve. The receptionist noticed and offered a tissue. I thanked her too quickly, then stared at the floor while my knee bounced beneath the chair. My brother sent a message asking whether I had heard anything; I typed “not yet,” erased it, and typed it again. When a nurse came out carrying a clipboard, I forgot to breathe for a moment. She glanced at the page and called me over.

Darius paced from the clinic window to the vending machine and back, taking exactly twelve steps each way. His daughter was asleep in a stroller beside the chair, one mitten dangling from her hand. He had brought her along because the childcare arrangement fell through, and now he kept checking that the stroller’s brake was on. The doctor had said the bloodwork might explain his sudden spells of weakness; the results were being reviewed upstairs. Darius tried to read a message from work, but the words scattered whenever the elevator chimed. He pressed his palms against his thighs and counted slowly, stopping whenever someone entered the corridor. Finally, a medical assistant appeared with his chart. Darius scooped up the loose mitten, tucked it into his pocket, and followed her down the hall.

The clinic smelled of lemon cleaner, and I could taste it even though I had not touched the sanitizer. My biopsy results were supposed to be discussed that afternoon. I sat beside a window overlooking the parking lot and watched cars pull in, unload people, and leave again. A nurse had told me to wait, then disappeared behind a door. I held my phone so tightly its case creaked. My partner texted a heart, and I pressed the screen against my chest before answering with a thumbs-up. The gesture looked cheerful, which was useful because my mouth had gone dry. When a cart rattled past, my whole body jerked. I apologized to no one in particular, smoothed my trousers, and fixed my eyes on the doorway where the clinician would appear.

Nia’s appointment was meant to be a quick review, but the clinic staff had asked her to remain while a technician checked the results. She sat with her backpack on her knees, its zipper held between both hands. At twenty-two, she had expected to feel grown-up enough to handle a follow-up alone. Instead, she kept glancing toward the reception desk, where a printer fed out forms one at a time. Each sheet made her shoulders tighten. She opened a music app, chose a song, then stopped it before the first note. Her roommate had offered to wait outside, but Nia had waved her away with a confident grin. Now she wished she could take that grin back. When the physician called her name, Nia’s backpack slid to the floor as she hurried to stand.

I watched the second hand sweep around the clock while my test results sat somewhere beyond the clinic’s closed doors. The doctor had ordered the scan after I began losing my balance, and I had come straight from my shift at the bakery. Flour still dusted one cuff. I rubbed it away, then rubbed the same spot again until the fabric darkened. A receptionist said the specialist was finishing with another patient. I nodded, though my jaw had locked so firmly it hurt. My phone buzzed in my pocket, and I jumped hard enough to draw a glance from the woman beside me. It was only an advertisement. I silenced it, placed both hands on my knees, and tried to keep them still. A moment later, the inner door opened, and the doctor beckoned.

Evelyn stood at the clinic’s water cooler, filled a paper cup, and left it untouched on the counter. She had come for results from a screening test and had been told the clinician would speak with her before closing. The waiting room was nearly empty now. She folded her appointment slip into a narrow strip, unfolded it, and smoothed it against her palm. A janitor pushed a mop bucket past the doorway, and Evelyn moved aside though there was plenty of room. She thought about calling her son, but did not want him to hear the thinness in her voice. The receptionist glanced up and said the clinician was on the way. Evelyn nodded, then gripped the edge of the counter when her knees seemed to soften. The cup tipped over, sending water across the floor.

I tried to make a list of errands for after the appointment, but every line turned into the same question: what would the results say? The clinic had tested my thyroid after months of sleepless nights, and the nurse had said the doctor would review the numbers today. I pressed my thumbnail into the seam of my coat, counting each stitch. Across the room, a television showed a cooking program with the sound off. The cheerful captions changed too quickly for me to follow. I stood to stretch, sat again, then stood when a staff member opened the hallway door. She was looking for someone else. My breath came in short catches, and I covered them with a cough. Finally, the doctor appeared at reception and asked me to come in. I forgot my coat on the chair.

At the rural clinic, Theo could hear the rain ticking against the metal awning and the receptionist’s keyboard tapping behind the glass. He had driven forty miles for a follow-up after an unusual result, bringing a thermos that had gone cold. His work boots rested side by side beneath his chair, but one heel kept lifting and lowering. He checked the road through the window, as if the doctor might arrive by car even though the office was already open. A nurse walked past carrying a stack of folders; Theo rose, then sat when she continued down the corridor. He wiped his palms on his jeans and uncapped the thermos, only to screw the lid back on without drinking. When the physician finally called him, Theo left the thermos behind and stepped into the examination room.

When Dad led me down the pool steps, the water climbed past my waist and my breath snagged. I grabbed his wrist so hard he winced. “I can’t,” I said, though I had not tried yet. The blue tiles seemed to tilt beneath me, and every splash from the next lane made me jerk. Dad crouched until we were eye to eye and asked me to hold the wall while he stayed beside me. My fingers clung to the gutter. He showed me how to blow bubbles, slowly, then waited while I tried. The first breath came out in a burst. I surfaced coughing, cheeks hot, and reached for him again. He didn’t pull me forward. He only kept one hand near my shoulder as I practiced letting go for a single second.

At the lake’s roped-off shallows, Marisol watched her son Leo stare at the dark water beyond his knees. His sandals scraped the sandy bottom as he backed toward her. “It’s moving,” he whispered, though the surface barely stirred. His shoulders had climbed to his ears, and he kept wiping wet palms on his shirt. Marisol sat on the dock and invited him to hold her fingers while she floated on her back. When a small wave rocked her, Leo yelped and tightened his grip. She turned over, steadying herself, then showed him how to kick while standing where he could touch bottom. He copied her in quick, uneven bursts. By the time a loon called across the lake, he had moved three strokes away, then hurried back to press against her side.

My daughter Nia was eight, and I had promised her that the community center pool would be easy. Then the instructor’s whistle shrilled, and she froze at the edge, eyes fixed on the deep end. I crouched beside her, still wearing my work badge, and asked her to put one toe in. She did, then snatched it back as if the water had bitten. “What if I sink?” she asked. Her voice came thin, and her hands twisted the hem of her rash guard. I told her we would stay by the steps and that I would keep hold of her. We practiced exhaling into the water together. Each time she lifted her face, she searched mine. Eventually she let me support her belly while her legs fluttered, stiff at first, then looser.

On a humid afternoon in Baton Rouge, Calvin brought his nephew Andre to the apartment complex pool for his first lesson. Andre wore goggles pushed up on his forehead and kept asking how deep the water was, even though he stood on the shallow step. When Calvin suggested floating, Andre’s knees locked. He seized the metal rail and stared at the ripples as if they were opening beneath him. Calvin didn’t hurry him. He demonstrated a back float with one hand under his own neck, explaining where Andre could feel support. Andre lowered himself inch by inch, mouth tight, then jerked upright at the first splash. His breathing came in small, rapid pulls. Calvin offered the rail again. After a while Andre tried once more, this time letting his ears touch the surface before grabbing for his uncle’s forearm.

The ocean looked nothing like the diagrams in my swim book. My son, Finn, stood ankle-deep beside me, watching foam race around his feet. When a wave rolled higher than the last, he stumbled backward and clamped both arms around my leg. His chin trembled, and he kept saying the water was coming back. I had planned to teach him to paddle, but instead I sat with him where the sand stayed firm. We watched three waves arrive and fade. I held his hand and showed him how to step forward when the water slid away, then retreat as it returned. He copied me, eyes fixed on the tide. Later, with me holding his waist, he kicked in a calm patch between waves. A gull cried overhead; Finn flinched, then laughed when I did too.

Before sunrise, Hana took her daughter Yuki to the indoor pool, hoping the quiet would make lessons easier. The echo of a single splash proved otherwise. Yuki gripped the ladder, knuckles pale, and refused to look away from the waterline. “Please don’t let go,” she said. Hana promised she wouldn’t, then asked Yuki to lean forward and feel the water support her arms. Yuki’s mouth opened, but no sound came. Her heels tapped the step in quick succession. Hana guided her through a gentle kick while keeping one hand beneath her chest. When a swimmer crossed nearby, the wake nudged Yuki’s shoulder; she scrambled upright and clung to her mother’s sleeve. They paused at the edge, sharing a towel around their shoulders. After a few minutes, Yuki asked to try the kick again, but only beside the wall.

I took my grandson Mateo to the YMCA pool because he had been asking to learn all summer. The moment the water reached his ribs, he grabbed my shirt and twisted it into a rope. His eyes darted from the lane ropes to the lifeguard chair, and his words tumbled over one another: “What if my feet can’t find the floor?” I told him we would stay where they could. We practiced holding the gutter, then blowing bubbles with our noses close to the surface. Mateo made one tiny bubble and immediately wiped his face. I showed him again, keeping my palm under his stomach as he tried to float. His legs kicked stiffly, splashing my glasses. I pretended the drops were rain, and he managed a quick smile before asking me to keep both hands on him.

At a summer camp in the foothills, Priya was teaching her son Dev to swim in the shallow end of a clear quarry pool. Dev had learned to ride a bicycle without help, but here he stood rigid, arms pressed to his sides. A child’s cannonball sent water slapping against the ledge. Dev grabbed Priya’s elbow and blurted, “We should go.” His face had gone pale beneath his freckles. Priya suggested they sit on the submerged step and count the stones visible below. They named each one, slowly, until his shoulders dropped a little. Then she showed him how to push off the step and glide into her waiting hands. He tried, stopped halfway, and reached for her. She steadied him without pulling him out. On his next attempt, he traveled farther before touching her palms.

My father had brought a bright orange kickboard, but when I stepped into the hotel pool, I forgot everything he had explained in the room. The water lapped at my chest. I grabbed the board against myself and could not make my fingers loosen. “I’m okay,” I insisted, while my knees knocked together. Dad stayed close and asked me to place the board on the water instead of clutching it. I watched it bob, then copied him by resting my hands on top. He held the back of my swimsuit while I kicked toward the tiled wall, only a few feet away. The splashes sounded enormous. Halfway there, I stopped and looked over my shoulder; Dad nodded, still beside me. My feet found the wall, and I pressed my forehead against the cool tile until my breath settled.

In a neighborhood pool in Phoenix, Omar promised his daughter Salma that she could learn at her own pace. Salma nodded, then stood so still that the water barely moved around her legs. She kept glancing toward the gate and rubbing her thumb over a small scratch on her wrist. Omar offered a floating noodle, but she held it close to her chest instead of lying on it. When he suggested she rest her arms across it, she whispered, “Stay right there.” Omar moved only a step away and kept his hands ready. Salma leaned forward, eyes wide, and let the noodle carry her for a moment. A splash from the next lane made her sit up sharply. She scrambled to the wall, breathing fast. Omar waited with her. Soon she asked if they could try again, this time facing the steps.

My mother chose the river’s calm inlet because she said it would be gentler than the public pool. I stood on a flat rock, toes curled over its edge, while water slid past my ankles. My little brother had already splashed in, but I could not follow. Each time the current brushed my legs, my stomach tightened and I snatched at Mom’s hand. She led me to a sandy patch where the water stayed below my waist. We practiced bending our knees and pushing off the bottom, with her holding my hands. I swallowed a mouthful when I tried to blow bubbles, then coughed against her shoulder. She waited while I wiped my eyes. On the next try, I managed three bubbles and a short kick. The current tugged at my swimsuit, but Mom’s steady grip gave me somewhere to look.

During a rainy week in Glasgow, Ewan took his son Callum to the school pool for lessons. The roof drummed overhead, and Callum watched the windows instead of listening. At the edge, he clutched his father’s fingers and repeated, “Not yet,” each time Ewan mentioned getting in. His shoulders rose with every breath, and his lips had lost their color. Ewan sat on the lowest step and invited him to join without letting go. Callum lowered one foot, then paused long enough for a whistle to echo across the pool. He jerked backward, nearly bumping into the wall. Ewan wrapped a towel around him and spoke quietly until his hands stopped shaking. They tried again, with Callum holding the rail and Ewan beside him. The boy practiced floating his hands on the surface, then asked to stay just one minute longer.

The bakery boxes slid against the passenger seat as I took the hill too fast, then tapped the brake and watched the clock change to 8:17. The wedding cake was due at eight. My phone showed the venue only six blocks away, but every street seemed to have a delivery truck parked in the worst possible place. I called the bride, got voicemail, and left a message that came out in a breathless jumble. At the next light, I drummed both hands on the steering wheel until a cyclist glanced over. When traffic finally moved, I turned down an alley marked no entry and found a gate across it. I backed out, scraped a hedge, and kept going. At the venue, a server rushed toward my van. I carried the cake inside with both arms locked tight, praying the icing had survived.

Nia had promised the pharmacy that the insulin would reach Mr. Alvarez before his evening dose. A bridge closure had turned her usual route into a crawl, and the delivery app kept adding minutes in bright red numbers. She leaned toward the windshield as if that might make the line of cars part. Her fingers slipped on the steering wheel; she wiped them on her trousers, then checked the insulated bag again. The phone rang from the dashboard. The pharmacist asked where she was, and Nia answered with a street name she wasn’t even sure of. At a red light, she tapped the map, missed the button, and nearly dropped the phone beneath the seat. When she reached the apartment, she took the stairs two at a time. Mr. Alvarez opened the door, and she finally let out the breath she had been holding.

I was already twenty minutes late when the school called to say the science kits had to be in the gym before the buses arrived. A flat tire had eaten up my morning, and now rain blurred every sign along the route. I kept glancing at the boxes stacked behind me, each labeled with a classroom number. At a roundabout, I missed my exit and circled back, muttering the directions aloud. My shirt stuck between my shoulder blades. When I pulled up at the school, the main entrance was locked, so I hauled two cartons to the side door and banged on it with my elbow. A custodian appeared, startled by my wet hair and crooked cap. I tried to explain, but the words tangled together. He waved me inside. I set the kits down just as the first bus hissed at the curb.

Caleb’s refrigerated van was supposed to bring fresh seafood to the restaurant by four, but a collision had shut down the highway. The digital temperature display blinked steadily while his phone buzzed with messages from the chef. He pulled into a service station, searched for another route, then stared at the map until the blue line seemed to swim. His jaw worked as he called dispatch. They suggested a country road, though the directions were patchy. Caleb gripped the wheel and followed them past fields, checking the clock at every bend. A tractor appeared ahead, moving at a walking pace. He slapped the steering wheel once, then immediately lowered his hand when the driver looked back. By the time Caleb reached the kitchen entrance, the chef stood waiting with folded arms. Caleb lifted the cooler out carefully, his shoulders still drawn high.

The florist’s van smelled of lilies and damp cardboard, and I could feel the minutes shrinking as I followed the detour signs. The bouquet for the memorial service had to arrive before the family entered the chapel. My phone had no signal, so I drove on with the printed address crumpled in my fist at the next stop sign. I read it again, though I knew every line by heart. My pulse thudded in my throat. A tractor blocked the narrow lane ahead, and I leaned on the horn before catching myself. The farmer waved me around through a muddy field entrance. I eased the van over the ruts, one hand clenched around the wheel. At the chapel, I carried the flowers in and nearly stumbled on the step. The director took the arrangement from me and nodded toward the empty front table.

At sixty-eight, Lourdes knew the neighborhood better than the navigation system, but today every shortcut seemed to end at construction barriers. Her grocery delivery was late, and one customer had already called twice because a birthday dinner depended on the missing ingredients. Lourdes read the new route at a stoplight, then looked up to find the light green and cars waiting behind her. She pulled forward with a sharp apology. The paper bags rustled on the passenger seat whenever she turned. At the apartment building, the elevator was out, and the customer lived on the fifth floor. Lourdes stared at the stairs, pressed a hand to her chest, then gathered two bags in each arm. She climbed slowly, stopping on the third landing to catch her breath. The birthday host opened the door before she knocked. Lourdes handed over the bags and explained the detour in a rush.

I had three medical supply stops left, and the last clinic closed its receiving desk at noon. A train crossing held me for what felt like an entire season. When it finally cleared, my dashboard clock read 11:38. I called the clinic, but the line kept ringing. I bit the inside of my cheek and sped up until a pothole sent a box lurching against the cargo wall. I pulled over, checked the packaging, then checked the clock again. The route offered a narrow street through a market, crowded with carts and people carrying umbrellas. I eased through with both hands tight on the wheel, murmuring apologies through the open window. At the clinic, the loading door was closing. I jumped out, grabbed the container, and ran the last few steps. The receptionist caught the door with her foot as I reached it.

Marek’s bread delivery to the mountain lodge was running late after a fallen branch blocked the pass. The lodge manager had warned that the kitchen needed the loaves before lunch service, and the van’s clock showed eleven minutes left. Marek stepped out, moved the branch with a passing hiker, and returned to find the engine turning over weakly. He tried again, eyes fixed on the dashboard. The engine caught. He drove on, shoulders rigid, one thumb rubbing the steering wheel seam. The road narrowed beside a steep drop, and fog softened the edges of the trees. When the lodge finally came into view, Marek let out a noise halfway between a laugh and a gasp. He backed toward the kitchen entrance, then hurried to unload the baskets. The cook checked the warm loaves and gave him a quick thumbs-up. Marek rested both palms on the van’s hood.

I was delivering costumes to a community theater when the van’s navigation sent me to the wrong entrance. Opening night was less than an hour away, and the director had already texted a row of question marks. I circled the block, looking for a loading dock, while costume bags swung from their hooks behind me. My mouth had gone dry. I called the theater and got a volunteer who sounded equally unsure, then followed her directions into a one-way lane. A bus blocked the turn. I reversed carefully as cars gathered behind me, their horns beginning one after another. The bags toppled when I finally reached the alley. I rushed inside, dragging them over the threshold, and found an actor waiting in one sock. He seized the right garment and ran. I stayed by the door, trying to slow my breathing before carrying in the rest.

Tessa was bringing a replacement laptop to a law office before a remote hearing began. A sudden downpour had flooded the underpass, and the detour added nearly half an hour. She watched water crawl across the road and backed away, hands trembling against the wheel. Her phone rang; the office administrator asked if she was close. Tessa said yes, then looked at the map and felt her stomach tighten at the distance still ahead. She took a side street, dodged a road crew, and missed the turn because her windshield fogged over. At the next curb, she wiped a clear patch with her sleeve and entered the address again. When she reached the office, the hearing had started. She hurried through reception, clutching the laptop box to her chest. The administrator met her at the conference room door and gestured for her to come in.

My last package was a jar of rare honey bound for a tasting event, and I had promised to arrive before the guests.
