I was sixty-one, a postal worker who had trained for half-marathons on weekends. On my first morning back, I wore two watches and checked both after every few steps. My neighbor Len jogged beside me, talking about the weather. I barely heard him. A pebble shifted under my shoe, and I lurched sideways, grabbing his sleeve. He asked if I wanted to stop. I shook my head too fast, then walked in circles, pressing my thumb into the watch button until the screen changed. My calf quivered. Len suggested we count lamp posts instead of minutes. We reached the fourth, then the fifth. I tried a slow jog between them, listening to each footfall. Nothing hurt. At the gate, I leaned forward with my hands on my thighs, surprised by how loudly I was breathing.

Noura, a twenty-four-year-old fencer, had repaired her knee with months of careful exercises. At her first club session, she stood just outside the strip, watching blades flash and masks turn toward one another. The familiar metallic taps made her fingers twitch around the grip. Her instructor offered a practice bout at half speed. Noura agreed, then asked to see the floor surface and knee brace again. She adjusted the strap until the skin beneath it reddened. When her partner advanced, Noura retreated too quickly and nearly collided with the wall. She pulled off her mask, cheeks flushed, and said she needed a minute. The instructor moved a chair nearby without making a spectacle of it. Noura sat, counted the tiles beneath her shoes, and drank water. Afterward, she returned to the strip. She completed three cautious exchanges, stepping forward once instead of backing away. The session ended with the instructor walking beside her to the locker room.

I had broken two fingers catching a line drive, and the baseball season seemed to continue without me. At thirty, I came back to the batting cage with a padded glove and a head full of worst-case pictures. The pitching machine clicked into motion. I stood in the box, shoulders tight, and asked my brother to turn it off. He did, then waited while I loosened my grip. The first ball rolled past the plate. I ducked anyway. Heat crept up my neck as I heard someone laugh from another cage, though they were probably laughing at something else. My brother lowered the speed and tossed me a soft ball by hand. I swung late and missed. He retrieved it without comment. On the next toss, the bat connected with a hollow crack. The ball traveled only a few feet, but I stared after it as if it had crossed the whole field. I asked for another.

Seventy-year-old Arturo had played pétanque for decades before surgery on his hip kept him away from the neighborhood court. His friends had saved him a place, but the familiar circle of players felt daunting when he arrived with a cane. He watched the metal boules roll across the gravel, shifting his weight from foot to foot. When his turn came, he reached for a boule and then set it down, rubbing his hip through his trousers. “Maybe next round,” he said. His voice sounded thin to him. One friend offered a lighter boule, while another moved a chair close to the throwing line. Arturo sat, planted both feet, and took several measured breaths. He stood again and tossed. The boule landed short, barely past the marker. Nobody groaned; one friend simply returned it. Arturo adjusted his stance and tried once more. The throw traveled farther. He smiled, though his hand kept trembling as he took the cane back.

I had been in the licensing office line for nearly two hours when the clerk announced that the building would close in twenty minutes. My renewal papers were still missing a signature from the back of the packet, and the person ahead of me had spread a dozen forms across the counter. I dug through my folder so quickly that my photographs slipped onto the floor. A woman behind me picked them up, but I could barely thank her; my throat had tightened, and the numbers on the wall clock seemed to jump forward each time I looked away. I called my sister, whispering that she needed to find the signed page in my kitchen drawer. When the line moved, I clutched the folder against my chest and rehearsed what I would say if they refused to help. The clerk finally waved me forward, and I laid out every page with shaking hands.

At the county benefits office, Malik watched the digital queue display skip from 184 to 186. His ticket said 185. He stood, sat, then stood again, scanning the room for someone who might explain the missing number. His phone showed a message from the landlord asking when rent would arrive, and his thumb hovered over the reply without pressing anything. The line curled past rows of plastic chairs, while a toddler cried near the entrance and a printer coughed out forms. Malik checked his ticket so often its corner softened beneath his fingers. When a clerk called another number, he hurried to the desk before realizing it belonged to a different window. Heat climbed up his neck. He returned to his chair, opened the folder containing his income records, and counted the pages again, certain one had vanished. At last, a staff member noticed him and beckoned him over.

The passport office smelled of wet coats and toner, and I had brought the wrong birth certificate. I realized it after joining the line, when I opened my envelope to check the appointment notice. My hands went cold. The correct document was at my apartment, forty minutes away, while my appointment time was already passing on the wall clock. I stepped out to call my brother, but his voicemail answered. Behind me, the queue kept advancing without me, shoulder by shoulder. I tried the online document portal on my phone, mistyped my password twice, and watched the screen lock me out. A security guard asked whether I needed help. I nodded too fast and explained everything in a rush, then stopped because I had run out of breath. He directed me to a service desk that could check a digital copy. I hurried there, holding my envelope so tightly its flap tore.

Seventy-year-old Beatrice had taken two buses to the tax office, carrying her late husband’s records in a shopping bag. The line snaked beyond the numbered posts, and the appointment slip in her pocket had grown damp against her palm. She searched the bag for the folder she needed, pulling out receipts, a knitted scarf, and a tin of peppermints. Each time someone passed toward the counter, she leaned forward, afraid she had missed her turn. Her breathing became shallow, and she kept asking the young man beside her whether the numbers were being called aloud. He showed her the display and offered his seat. Beatrice refused, then immediately wished she had accepted. When her number appeared, she rose so quickly that the bag tipped over. Papers scattered beneath the chairs. Two strangers helped gather them while she repeated the counter number under her breath.

I joined the immigration records line with my daughter’s school enrollment deadline written across the top of my folder. The clerk needed a stamped copy, but the notice said the office might stop taking applications at noon. It was 11:47. A man in front of me kept arguing about a fee, and every raised word made my shoulders climb closer to my ears. I refreshed the office website, hoping for a rule that would save us, but the page would not load. My daughter tugged my sleeve and asked if we could still go to the library afterward. I told her yes, though my mouth had gone dry. Then I noticed the stamp request form was blank. I bent over the clipboard, missed the first line, and started again with my fingers trembling. A clerk came down the queue and spotted the empty form. She handed me a pen and pointed to the fields I needed.

Eli, a nursing student, reached the municipal office with a folder of scholarship residency documents and found a queue wrapped around the lobby. His train back to campus left in an hour. He checked the departure time, then the ticket in his hand, then the departure time again. Sweat gathered beneath his collar despite the air conditioner. When the line moved, he stepped forward and discovered that one shoelace had come undone; he stared at it, unable to decide whether tying it would cost him his place. A woman behind him offered to hold his folder while he fixed it. He thanked her, but the words came out clipped. At the counter, the clerk asked for proof of address. Eli opened the folder and found only a photocopy, not the original he had promised himself he packed. His face drained as he searched every pocket. The clerk suggested a nearby copy center and wrote down its address.

I was fourth in line at the veterans’ records office when my phone buzzed with a message from the hospital: my father’s procedure had been moved earlier. They needed a copy of his service record before admitting him. The office queue had barely shifted in half an hour, and the woman at the front was asking detailed questions about a decades-old form. I called the hospital, but the signal dropped halfway through my explanation. My heel tapped against the tile, faster and faster, while I gripped my phone with both hands. I considered leaving, then pictured the empty chair beside my father’s bed and stayed. When a clerk stepped out to refill a water jug, I hurried over and explained the deadline. My voice cracked on the date. She studied the paperwork, asked for his authorization, and pointed to a separate expedited desk. I ran there, nearly leaving the folder behind.

Nadia had promised her café staff that she would be back before the lunch rush, but the permit office line had not moved since she arrived. A delivery driver kept calling to ask where to leave the flour, and each ring made her jump. She silenced the phone, then turned it faceup, then silenced it again. Her permit application was folded into a pocket beside a receipt covered in coffee stains. When she finally checked the pages, the signature box was empty. Nadia stared at it while the room’s conversations blurred into a low hum. She pressed her palms against her thighs to keep them still and asked the clerk stationed near the door whether she could borrow a pen. The clerk handed her one and pointed to a counter where forms could be corrected. Nadia filled the box in a cramped scrawl, then hurried back toward the queue, unsure whether anyone would let her reclaim her place.

I sat in the social security office with my mother’s appointment card pinched between my fingers. She had sent me to ask about a benefit review, but the folder contained three versions of the same letter and no photo identification. I checked every pocket twice, though I knew the missing card was probably on her dresser at home. The queue stretched toward the entrance, and my bus back would leave in thirty-five minutes. I called her, but she was at a clinic and did not answer. A man nearby offered to let me use his phone charger; I declined, then realized my own battery was at one percent. My knee bounced hard enough to shake the chair. When the display flashed our number, I stood and walked to the wrong window. The clerk redirected me without looking up. I apologized, gathered the papers that had slipped from my folder, and asked whether a scanned identification card would be accepted.

At the city clerk’s office, twelve-year-old Tomas sat beside his grandmother while she waited to replace a lost identity card. She had asked him to hold the queue ticket, and he kept turning it over to make sure the number had not changed. The lobby clock clicked loudly above them. When a clerk called a number close to theirs, Tomas grabbed his grandmother’s sleeve, then realized it belonged to someone else. She squeezed his hand, but her fingers were cool and damp. Their ride home was due to meet them outside in twenty minutes, and the driver had said he could not wait. Tomas tried to read the forms, but the letters swam whenever he looked down. He asked a guard how long the line might take. The guard could not say. Tomas began counting the chairs between them and the counter, losing track at nine. When their number finally appeared, he guided his grandmother forward with the ticket held high.

I reached the unemployment office with a notice saying my appeal had to be filed that day. The line moved in short bursts, then stopped, and I began checking the date on the notice every few minutes. What if I had read the deadline wrong? What if the clerk rejected the envelope because I used the wrong form? I had spent the bus ride rehearsing answers, but now each sentence vanished as I tried to recall it. My shirt clung to my back. I opened my backpack, searched for the appeal copy, and found only a grocery list and a tangled pair of headphones. The folder was in my other bag, left at my cousin’s apartment. I called him and heard the office noise swallow my words. He agreed to send a photograph of the pages. When the clerk called me, I presented the image on my phone and asked, too quickly, if it would count.

Rosa, a retired school custodian, waited at the housing authority office to submit paperwork for a rent adjustment. She had brought every bill requested, arranged by month, but could not find the envelope containing her bank statement. The line behind her lengthened as people arrived from the rain. She pressed her thumb against the seam of her handbag and searched it again, feeling each zipper pull with stiff fingers. Her hearing aid gave a brief whistle, and she flinched, certain someone had called her name. A security officer announced that the office would close its intake window in fifteen minutes. Rosa’s lips moved as she counted the documents she did have. She considered stepping outside to call her daughter, but the thought of losing her place kept her rooted to the floor. A young man offered to look through the bag. Together they found the envelope caught beneath the lining, and Rosa let out a long breath before advancing to the desk.

When the apartment lights died, I was halfway through warming my daughter’s bottle. The refrigerator clicked silent, and the baby began crying from the bedroom. I fumbled for my phone, dropped it, then crawled under the table where its screen had skidded. Across the hall, Mrs. Alvarez opened her door with a candle in one hand. I asked whether she had a flashlight, though I could barely get the words out. She lent me a lantern and came along while I checked the baby. My daughter was safe, just hungry, but the bottle sat cold in the dark kitchen. Mrs. Alvarez offered her gas stove, and together we heated water while I kept glancing at the black windows, expecting the power to return with every passing second.

At the corner house, Darnell heard the freezer alarm chirp once and then stop. His hands began sorting through drawers at a frantic pace, though he had no idea what he was searching for. The outage had also shut down the stairwell lights, and his elderly neighbor, Mr. Cho, was somewhere upstairs with a walker. Darnell snatched a camping lantern and climbed, calling the man’s name at every landing. A door opened on the third floor. Mr. Cho stood inside, steady but embarrassed, holding a bag of melting groceries. Darnell let out a sharp breath he had been holding and offered to carry everything down to his own cooler. Soon several neighbors were gathered around it, passing ice packs from hand to hand as the building settled into darkness.

I was setting out folding chairs for our block’s evening potluck when every porch lamp went dark. The string lights sagged overhead, and someone’s grill timer started beeping in the sudden quiet. I checked my phone: no service. My fingers kept slipping as I tried the emergency radio, while my mind raced through the list of neighbors who used medical equipment. Then I remembered Mrs. Bell’s oxygen concentrator next door. I knocked hard enough to make the screen door rattle. Her grandson answered, already holding a battery pack, but it was nearly empty. We hurried down the street to the community center, where a generator was running. By the time we returned, two other residents had joined us with spare batteries, and the potluck had become an improvised supply station.

Mina was alone in the laundromat when the washers stopped mid-cycle. The fluorescent tubes blinked out, leaving the damp room lit only by a red exit sign. She heard a child crying behind the folding counter and hurried over, knocking a basket of socks onto the floor. A neighbor, Mr. Patel, emerged from the back room with his toddler clutched to his chest. The front door’s electric lock would not release. Mina’s throat tightened as she tugged at it, then she remembered the manual lever beneath the register. Her hands shook so badly that Mr. Patel had to guide them. The door gave way. Outside, other shopkeepers were checking on one another, and a passing bus driver let the family wait in the illuminated vehicle until the streetlights came back.

The blackout began while I was watching my neighbor’s twins in her kitchen. Their cartoon vanished, and both children started shouting at once. I reached for the drawer where I thought she kept candles, but instead found a jumble of batteries and takeout menus. Their voices climbed higher. I crouched between them and tried to sound cheerful, although my chest had become tight and my breath kept catching. Mr. Okafor from downstairs tapped at the window with a flashlight. He had brought a battery lantern and knew where the building’s backup lights were supposed to switch on. They never did. We moved the twins to the shared courtyard, where other residents had gathered, and I let them help arrange glow sticks while I called their mother from a neighbor’s working landline.

When the power failed in the small rural duplex, Ezra’s insulin fridge went quiet. He stared at its dark display, then checked it again as if the numbers might reappear. His phone showed one bar, then none. He paced from window to window, rubbing his palms against his jeans, while his neighbor Tasha searched a drawer for the utility company’s number. She found a handwritten note instead: the volunteer fire station kept a generator for emergencies. Ezra grabbed his cooler, but his keys were missing. Tasha spotted them in the lock and drove him herself, talking steadily while he sat rigid in the passenger seat. At the station, volunteers packed the medication in a chilled container and helped him contact his clinic. On the way home, he finally unclenched his jaw.

I had just finished a late shift and was climbing the apartment stairs when the lights disappeared. My shoe caught the edge of a step, and I grabbed the railing so hard my wrist hurt. Somewhere above me, a door slammed. I called out, but the echo made the hallway feel even emptier. My neighbor Lila answered from the landing, carrying a candle and a paper grocery bag. She had been bringing soup to the retired couple on the fifth floor. I offered to go with her, though my knees still felt unreliable. We climbed together, counting steps aloud so no one would stumble. The couple were fine but had no working phone. Lila shared her mobile hotspot long enough for them to message their daughter, and I stayed until their battery lantern was set up.

Rafi was repairing a bicycle in the shared garage when the overhead door froze halfway down. The workbench lamp blinked off, and the motor made a dead, metallic click. He bolted toward the wall switch, then stopped when he heard his neighbor’s little dog barking outside the trapped door. His breathing came fast as he searched for the manual release, knocking tools from their hooks. Mrs. Keene appeared with a flashlight, calmly pointing to the red cord above the motor. Rafi dragged over a ladder, but his fingers skated on the rung. She held it steady while he pulled. The door lifted a few inches, enough for the dog to scramble under. A few other residents arrived with headlamps, and together they raised it by hand, then walked the dog upstairs.

The power went out during our neighborhood council meeting, right as I was presenting the budget. In the dark, chairs scraped and several people spoke at once. I gripped my notes, unable to find the next line, and felt heat rise under my collar. My neighbor Pavel switched on a small rechargeable lamp, but its beam landed on the ceiling. I tried to continue and heard my voice wobble. Then Mrs. James, who lived two houses away, began reading the figures from her printed copy. Others found phone lights and passed them around the table. I stepped outside for air and saw the whole block dark beneath a clear sky. When I returned, the group had arranged itself in a circle on the porch, and I managed to finish the discussion without looking at the silent projector.

Tess was rinsing paintbrushes at the kitchen sink when the lights blinked out. Her ceramics kiln had been firing in the studio next door, and the power loss left her uncertain whether the batch would crack. She pressed the kiln’s dead buttons, then hurried to the window to see if the whole street had gone dark. Her neighbor Jun was already outside with a headlamp, asking whether anyone had a generator. Tess’s fingers fluttered uselessly over her phone before she remembered the kiln’s manual instructions. She fetched them from a shelf and read by Jun’s beam while he checked the breaker panel. Nothing could restart the firing until service returned. Together they called the utility company and warned the other artists in the shared studio, then carried finished pieces away from the dark kiln.

I was giving my elderly neighbor, Ruth, a ride home when the traffic signals vanished. Cars crept toward the intersection from every direction, and a horn blared behind us. My foot hovered over the brake as I tried to work out who had the right of way. Ruth gripped the dashboard and began naming the streets, her voice thin but precise. I rolled down my window and waved to the driver beside us. He waved back and let us cross. At Ruth’s building, the elevator was stopped between floors, so we took the stairs slowly. She insisted on carrying her own bag, though it kept slipping from her hand. I stayed beside her until we reached her door, then called the building manager from my car to report the trapped elevator.

Nikhil was hosting a dinner for the neighbors when the kitchen went black. A pot began hissing on the gas burner, and the smoke alarm chirped as the fan stopped. He reached for the knob, missed, and knocked a spoon onto the floor. Across the table, Mrs. Foster switched on her phone light and aimed it at the stove while he shut off the gas. The guests crowded into the hallway, talking over one another. Nikhil kept checking the dead oven clock, his shoulders lifted nearly to his ears. Their neighbor, a nurse named Celeste, suggested moving everyone to the courtyard, where fresh air and space would help. Someone brought battery lamps; someone else carried out the food. By the time the utility crew arrived, the dinner had become a candlelit picnic.

I refreshed the grade portal so many times that the little wheel seemed to be turning behind my eyes. My chemistry score finally appeared, but the number was blurred by the water gathering in my eyes. I wiped my face on my sleeve and leaned closer, counting the digits one by one. The library clock clicked toward closing. Around me, students packed their bags, while I sat rigidly with my phone clenched in both hands. I tapped the instructor’s name, then backed out before the message form opened. What could I say? My breathing came in short pulls. At last I took a screenshot, tucked the phone into my coat, and walked to the desk to ask when office hours began.

When the grades went live, Mateo was waiting for a bus outside the community college. He opened the portal, saw his calculus result, and nearly dropped his phone into a puddle. His thumb hovered over the screen while the bus pulled up with a hiss. He let it leave without him. The score was lower than the number he had promised his scholarship adviser, and every passing car seemed to splash the same cold thought across his mind. Mateo stood beneath the shelter, reading the feedback twice, then a third time. He called his older sister, but when she answered, his voice came out thin. He asked her to stay on the line while he found the page explaining retakes.

The grade page loaded while I was wedged between two suitcases at the airport. My history exam mark sat beneath a red banner, and I stopped hearing the announcements overhead. I pinched the bridge of my nose, then checked that I was looking at the right course. The same number remained. My boarding group was called. I shoved my laptop into its sleeve, missed the zipper twice, and hurried toward the gate with my passport open in my hand. At the desk, the attendant asked me to step aside. I nodded, although my mind was still fixed on the feedback box. Before boarding, I typed a message to my professor, deleted it, and finally sent a simple request to meet.

Nia checked her biology grade in the back room of the bakery where she worked evenings. A tray timer began shrilling just as the portal displayed her result. She stared at it, then opened the page again, convinced she had clicked the wrong semester. Her hands shook enough to make the phone rattle against the counter. Flour dusted her apron as she reached for the timer, but she forgot which oven held the rolls. The manager called her name from the front. Nia swallowed, answered that she was coming, and saved the grade page before the screen could lock. On her break, she found the course policy and traced the appeal deadline with one finger, whispering the date to herself.

I was in the school gym, waiting for my younger brother’s basketball game to start, when the exam portal sent its notification. I opened it beneath the bleachers. My statistics grade flashed up, and the crowd’s cheers turned into a distant rumble. I pressed my sneaker into the floor until my toes hurt. The score was far below what I needed for the program application due Monday. My brother waved from the court, and I forced my arm up in reply. Then I slipped into the hallway and called the advising office. The automated menu asked me to choose a department, so I listened to it twice, forgetting each option as soon as it was spoken. I wrote the numbers down on my palm.

At a crowded noodle shop, Haruto refreshed the exam portal between bites. His physics grade appeared while steam fogged his glasses. He wiped them with a napkin, checked the score again, and felt his chopsticks slip from his fingers. The table beside him erupted in laughter, but he could not join in when his roommate asked how the exam went. Haruto searched the course page for a grading breakdown, tapping through links with an unsteady hand. His bowl cooled untouched. When he found that one lab score had not been entered, he leaned toward the screen so closely his hair brushed the table. He took a careful breath, opened a draft email, and began listing the dates of his lab submissions.

I checked my literature exam grade in the laundromat, where the dryers thumped like heavy doors closing. The portal took long enough to load that I stood up, sat down, and stood again. When the result appeared, I gripped the edge of the plastic chair. My scholarship required a certain average, and I could not remember whether this score kept me above it. A dryer buzzed; I jumped and knocked my detergent bottle onto the floor. I gathered the spilled packets while trying to calculate my term average on my phone. The numbers would not stay straight. I called my academic adviser, listened to the ring, and nearly hung up. When she answered, I asked her to walk me through the calculation.

Evelyn checked her anatomy exam result on a tablet in the hospital cafeteria during her nursing placement. The grade appeared just as a nurse called for help carrying a stack of charts. Evelyn locked the screen, stood too quickly, and had to grip the table until the room steadied. She helped with the charts, but the result kept replaying in her head whenever someone spoke. At the end of her shift, she found a quiet stairwell and logged in again. The score had not changed. Her fingers hovered above the course coordinator’s contact details. She typed a question about extra review sessions, erased three versions, then sent one that simply asked when she could come by. She stayed on the landing until her hands stopped trembling.

My economics grade arrived while I was riding the elevator to my grandmother’s apartment. I opened the portal, saw the mark, and pressed the wrong floor button. The doors opened on an empty corridor, and I stepped out before realizing where I was. My stomach tightened as I checked the grade again under the fluorescent lights. I had told my family the exam felt easy. Now I rehearsed how to explain the number without making it sound final. The elevator doors began to close, and I darted back inside, catching them with my elbow. At Grandma’s door, I put my phone in my pocket and tried to smile. She took one look at me and asked whether I wanted tea before we talked.

During a rainstorm, Yusuf opened his engineering grades on a computer at the public library. The result appeared, and he read the line so many times that the librarian glanced over. His jacket dripped onto the carpet. He pulled a notebook from his bag and began calculating what the score meant for his final average, but the page filled with crossed-out sums. When the library announced it would close in ten minutes, Yusuf packed nothing. He searched the instructor’s page for a regrade policy, clicking through tabs until a small link appeared. He copied the deadline onto his wrist with a pen, then saved the policy to his phone. At closing, he thanked the librarian twice and hurried into the wet evening.

I checked my exam grades in the parking lot before a shift at the animal shelter. The portal showed my psychology score, and the keys in my hand began to clatter against each other. I opened the grade details, expecting to find a missed page or a calculation error. Nothing changed. A dog barked from the building, and I flinched so hard that my phone slipped onto the passenger seat. I sat with both hands flat on the steering wheel, trying to remember the questions I had left blank. My shift started in five minutes. I went inside, greeted the dogs, and followed the feeding chart carefully, checking every name twice. During my break, I wrote to my professor asking to review the exam.

At the rural train station, Priya used the weak signal on her phone to check her exam grade. The portal stalled, then loaded the result while she stood under a leaking roof. She pressed her lips together and stared at the number as water tapped her shoulder. Her train was due in three minutes, but she could not make herself put the phone away. She searched for the grading rubric, losing the page whenever the connection dropped. When the train lights appeared, Priya took a screenshot and shoved the phone into her bag. She boarded at the last moment, breathing through her mouth as she found a seat. Once the doors shut, she opened her notes and wrote down three questions for her professor.

I had planned the lamb to the minute, which was why the smoke alarm began shrieking ten minutes before my partner’s parents arrived. I stood on a chair, waving a dish towel beneath it, while the roast blackened in the oven and my phone slid off the counter into a bowl of gravy. When the doorbell rang, I climbed down too fast and knocked over the carefully arranged glasses. “Everything’s under control,” I called, though nobody had asked. My partner’s mother stepped inside and looked from the smoke to my flour-covered shirt. I tried to laugh, but my throat made a dry click. Then I remembered the spare lasagna in the freezer. I shoved it into the microwave, punched buttons without checking them, and watched the plate rotate. My hands kept trembling as I poured water into glasses, filling one so high it spilled over the rim.

At sixty-eight, Doreen had hosted countless suppers, but never one for the parents of her new partner, Elias. She checked the roast, then the clock, then the front window, repeating the circuit until the potatoes began to collapse in their pot. A text from Elias said they were already outside, though the driveway was empty. She wiped her palms on her apron and hurried to unlock the door anyway. The guests arrived five minutes later carrying a pie. Doreen greeted them with the wrong names, corrected herself, then offered to hang their coats while still holding the oven mitts. When Elias’s father asked where he might sit, she pointed toward the pantry. Her cheeks burned. She moved a chair into place, but its leg caught on the rug, sending a fork skittering under the table. Nobody complained; that made her listen even harder for every small sound.

I thought serving dinner in my tiny studio would feel charming. Then my partner, Ren, texted that her parents were bringing an aunt, too. I counted plates, counted chairs, and counted the remaining minutes, as if one of those numbers might improve. The soup boiled over while I was dragging a desk against the wall to make room. I shoved laundry into the shower and covered the heap with a curtain. When the buzzer sounded, I pressed the intercom button and said nothing. Ren called from the hallway, “It’s us,” and I finally let them in. Her father noticed the desk wedged beneath my bed and kindly pretended not to. I ladled soup with a spoon that clanged against the pot, spilling a stripe across the tablecloth. My smile stayed fixed while I searched each face for a sign that the room, the meal, or I had failed.

Malik had promised his partner’s parents a traditional Sunday dinner, then discovered that his grandmother’s handwritten recipe used measurements like “a good handful.” He stood in his apartment kitchen with the card in one hand and a phone full of conflicting instructions in the other. The onions browned too quickly. He scraped them into a bowl and started again, checking the hallway every few seconds for footsteps. When the guests arrived, he opened the door with a wooden spoon still in his fist. His partner, Celia, introduced everyone, but Malik heard only the ticking kitchen timer. He hurried back to stir the stew, bumped the counter, and sent a stack of clean napkins sliding onto the floor. Celia’s mother bent to help. Malik blurted, “Please don’t,” then softened his voice and gathered them himself, fingers fumbling over the corners.

My partner’s parents were coming to my house in rural Vermont, and the only road was slick with fresh snow. I kept glancing at the weather app while the pie crust split beneath my rolling pin. “They’ll be fine,” Jo said, but I could hear the tightness in my own reply when I asked whether she had checked the road report again. I put the pie in the oven, forgot to set the timer, and went outside to sweep the porch before anyone had arrived. Inside, the stew simmered unattended. When headlights finally appeared, I rushed in, slipped on the mat, and caught myself against the refrigerator. Jo’s parents came through the door smiling, bringing snow on their boots. I greeted them too loudly, then offered tea before taking their coats. The kettle whistled behind me while I stood frozen beside the table, trying to remember which dish I had meant to serve first.

At twenty-three, Priya had never cooked for anyone’s parents, much less the two people who had raised her boyfriend, Daniel. She arranged the dining table with careful symmetry, then shifted every plate half an inch and started again. The curry smelled right, but the rice cooker’s display blinked an unfamiliar code. She unplugged it, plugged it back in, and pressed buttons until the lid clicked open on a mound of uncooked grains. When the doorbell rang, she wiped her hands on her jeans and left a streak of turmeric across one thigh. Daniel’s father asked if he could help. Priya handed him a serving spoon, then immediately took it back, apologizing twice. The rice began to hiss from the cooker, and she reached for the switch with unsteady fingers. At the table, she kept her eyes on everyone’s plates, ready to refill them before anyone had to ask.

I was determined to impress Marisol’s parents with a meal from my hometown, so I made tamales the way my uncle taught me. By the time the first guests knocked, half the husks had split and the kitchen counter looked like a flour storm. I wiped it, then noticed masa on the sleeve of my good shirt. Marisol whispered that I could change, but I couldn’t make my legs move toward the bedroom. Her mother stepped in and complimented the smell. I nodded too many times, trying to answer while listening for the steamer’s sputter. A sharp hiss came from the stove. I spun around, bumped the ladle, and sent sauce across the backsplash. “Just a little decoration,” I said. My laugh came out thin. During dinner I kept lifting the pot lid, although the tamales were already done, and each time I sat down my knees bounced beneath the table.

Before his partner’s parents arrived, Graham hid the broken dining chair in the garage and set out folding chairs instead. Then the garage door jammed halfway shut, trapping the chair just inside. He tried the remote, the wall button, and finally the manual release, growing more disheveled with each attempt. A saucepan boiled over behind him. The smell of scorched onions filled the kitchen, but he kept tugging the cord until his partner, Noa, came to find him. “They’re here,” she said. Graham stared at the dangling release handle as if it might explain what to do next. He rushed back indoors, wiped his hands on a dish towel, and opened the front door with one sleeve still wet. Noa’s parents were gracious, but Graham kept checking the garage window. When they asked about the meal, he answered with a list of ingredients, then forgot to offer anyone a drink.

I had invited Sumi’s parents for dinner at the community garden, thinking the picnic tables would make everything easy. Then the wind lifted the tablecloth, scattered the paper napkins, and sent a bowl of chopped herbs rolling beneath a bench. I chased the bowl while holding a tray of grilled vegetables against my chest. Sumi’s mother arrived carrying a beautiful glass dish. I was still crouched in the dirt, trying to retrieve a napkin tangled around a tomato plant. “Welcome,” I said, standing so quickly that the tray tilted. Sumi caught it before anything fell. I kept checking the sky, even though the clouds had already passed. At the table, I served everyone else before remembering my own plate. My fork scraped against the paper one, and I apologized for the noise. Her father asked me about the garden; I answered with the watering schedule, unable to recall the names of any flowers.

Bea’s partner, Victor, had said his parents were relaxed, but Bea still changed the menu three times before settling on roast chicken. At the grocery store, she realized she had forgotten the lemons and hurried back inside, leaving the car door open. By the time she reached home, the chicken was in the oven and her phone was vibrating beneath a pile of dish towels. Victor called from the porch that his parents had arrived early. Bea rushed to the door with one oven mitt on and one bare hand, then ushered them toward the living room while mentally inventorying everything unfinished. The salad remained unwilted in the sink, the table lacked forks, and the dog had stolen a dinner roll. She spoke quickly about traffic and weather, offering the same question twice. When Victor’s mother asked where she could put her coat, Bea pointed toward the refrigerator before correcting herself.

My partner’s parents were visiting from another country, and I wanted dinner to show that I had learned their family’s favorite dishes. I printed recipes, labeled ingredients, and taped instructions to cupboard doors. Then I mixed up the sugar and salt, tasted the sauce, and dropped the spoon with a clatter. “We can order food,” Amir said. I shook my head and started over, although my fingers had gone cold. When his parents knocked, I was still stirring a new pot, watching the sauce for any sign that I had made another mistake. I welcomed them with a practiced greeting, then forgot the next sentence I had rehearsed. Amir’s mother smiled and asked to see the kitchen. I stepped aside so abruptly that I knocked a measuring cup to the floor. At dinner, I waited after every bite, studying their expressions before I let myself reach for my own glass.

Rafael was hosting his partner’s parents in a rented cabin, where the oven ran hot and the smoke detector hung directly above it. He had set a timer, but the cabin clock was twenty minutes slow, and the vegetables emerged dark at the edges. He scraped them onto a platter, hiding the worst side against the wall, then tried to fan away the smell with a magazine. The front door opened before he had put the magazine down. His partner, Mae, introduced her parents, while Rafael stood beside the counter with a streak of ash on his cheek. He offered them cider, knocked over a stack of coasters, and caught one against his shoe. Mae’s father asked about the cabin’s trail map. Rafael began explaining, stopped mid-sentence, and glanced at the stove. The timer was ringing again, though the oven was empty. He silenced it, pressed both palms to the counter, and drew a careful breath before returning to the table.

When the water stain spread across the kitchen ceiling, I called Darius before I called the landlord. He was a carpenter who made cabinets to fit impossible corners, and I needed one built around the pipe that had started dripping behind the old pantry. He arrived with a tape measure and found me pacing between the sink and the back door, checking my phone every few seconds. The plumber was due in an hour; the landlord kept sending messages asking whether the leak was “minor.” Darius sketched a narrow cabinet with a removable back panel, but I barely followed his pencil. I kept wiping the same dry patch of counter. Then he showed me how the new cabinet would leave the shutoff valve reachable. I finally stopped moving long enough to hold the flashlight while he measured. The ceiling still dripped, but at least there was a plan with dimensions.

At the museum, Inez was given until closing to replace the display cabinet shattered during a school tour. The curator stood nearby, repeatedly asking whether the ancient mask could be returned before the donors arrived. Inez, a carpenter with silver hair and a habit of humming, began designing a custom case from the surviving measurements. Her assistant, Malik, noticed that she kept dropping the pencil and wiping her palms on her apron. Each time a door opened, she looked up sharply. The glass supplier had not confirmed delivery, and the clock above the loading bay seemed louder than usual. Inez drew a cabinet with a temporary acrylic front, then crossed it out, then drew it again. At last she called a nearby workshop and arranged to borrow a panel. Her shoulders lowered a fraction as Malik began cutting the frame. The mask would have a secure place by evening.

I had promised my sister the cabinet would be ready before her bakery opened, but the wall measurements were wrong by nearly two inches. The carpenter, Tomas, studied my notes while I stood beside the half-built cupboard, twisting a receipt into a thin rope. A delivery van idled outside with the replacement boards, and the driver was tapping his steering wheel. My sister kept calling from the shop to ask whether she should cancel the morning orders. I pressed my thumb against the edge of the workbench until it hurt, then asked Tomas to check the measurements once more. He found that the plaster bowed near the floor. Instead of forcing the cabinet into place, he proposed a tapered side panel and marked the cut. I watched every movement of the saw, holding my breath whenever the blade touched wood. When the panel fitted snugly, I called my sister with the first good news of the day.

Nadia had spent months saving for a custom cabinet to hold her father’s radio collection. Now the moving truck was parked outside, the apartment lease ended at noon, and the carpenter had discovered that the largest radio would not pass through the cabinet’s central opening. Nadia stared at the narrow gap, her keys clenched so tightly their teeth pressed into her palm. She kept looking from the radio to the clock and back again. The carpenter, Owen, suggested a removable divider and wider doors, but she asked him to repeat the plan twice. Her voice came out thinner each time. Owen loosened the hinges while Nadia wrapped the radios in towels, one by one, though the movers were waiting. The divider slid free, and the largest set finally fit. Nadia exhaled against the cabinet’s polished side, then hurried to sign the moving papers before the driver could leave.

The storm siren sounded just as I was choosing hardware for the custom cabinet in my new workshop. My carpenter, Bea, kept working, but I dropped a brass handle and couldn’t find it beneath the bench. The radio announced a flood warning for the riverside blocks, including mine. I checked the door, then the windows, then my phone, where my partner’s last message was still unanswered. Bea asked me to hold a shelf steady. My fingers slipped twice, and I apologized so many times that she finally put a hand over the board and told me to sit down. I tried calling home; the line rang without answer. Bea secured the unfinished cabinet against the wall, packed her tools, and offered to drive me uphill. I grabbed my coat but left one sleeve inside out. We reached the car as water began sliding along the curb, and I kept watching the phone screen all the way to higher ground.

At the coastal clinic, Dr. Sato needed a custom cabinet for medicines before the inspection team arrived at dawn. The carpenter, Leila, had drawn a compact design with lockable drawers and a shelf for temperature-sensitive supplies. As staff members carried boxes through the room, Dr. Sato kept checking the labels against a clipboard, then checking them again. A pen rolled from her fingers and vanished beneath a chair. She bent to retrieve it, bumped her head, and immediately began sorting the same labels from the beginning. Leila asked which drawer should hold emergency kits. Dr. Sato gave one answer, then changed it when a delivery nurse called from the corridor. The inspection was only hours away, and half the medicines still sat in cartons. Leila marked the drawers clearly and built the cabinet’s frame while Dr. Sato moved supplies in small, careful batches. By midnight, every box had a place.

I heard that my landlord was coming to inspect the apartment, and the cabinet I had built into the hallway still had no doors. My carpenter, Luis, arrived to finish them while I rushed around hiding paint cans and loose screws. The inspection notice had been taped to my door that morning, though I had somehow read the date wrong. I kept asking Luis how long each hinge would take, then walking to the entrance to listen for footsteps. He laid out three door styles, and I couldn’t choose between them. My mouth felt dry; I swallowed and pointed at the plainest option. When the first door hung crooked, I nearly pulled it off myself. Luis adjusted the top hinge by a fraction and showed me the even gap. A knock sounded from the neighboring apartment, and I flinched so hard the screwdriver fell. The landlord was still downstairs, but the cabinet finally closed cleanly.

Mina, a carpenter who usually worked on boats, was building a custom cabinet for a community theater’s cramped prop room. The opening night was that evening, and the director had just discovered that the lead actor’s oversized puppet could not fit through the finished doors. He paced between the cabinet and the stage, clutching his headset cord. Every few moments he asked whether the doors could be widened without damaging the frame. Mina studied the hinges, then measured the puppet again while the director watched the tape as if it might change. His instructions tumbled together: save the paint, keep the shelves, leave room for costumes. Mina took a breath, removed the doors, and proposed a pair of sliding panels. The director stopped pacing long enough to hold one end of a board. Together they cleared the opening, and the puppet settled inside with inches to spare. From the stage, the first cue sounded.

My grandmother’s handwritten recipe cards were scattered across the dining room after a pipe burst, and I needed a cabinet built before the restoration crew arrived. I called Amara, a carpenter from the next block, while I gathered the cards in damp handfuls. She designed a shallow cabinet with sealed drawers, but I kept interrupting to ask whether the wood would warp or the cards would fade. The restoration crew had given me a narrow window before they removed the floorboards. My phone buzzed against the table, and I jumped each time it did. Amara calmly explained that the cabinet could be mounted above the wet area. I nodded, then realized I had been holding a card upside down and reading the blank back. She handed me a dry towel and asked me to sort the recipes by color. The simple task steadied my hands enough to continue. By afternoon, the cards were safe in labeled drawers.

When the school’s old trophy case broke, sixteen-year-old Eli volunteered to help carpenter Mr. Bell build a replacement for the hallway. The principal wanted it finished before parents arrived for the science fair, and Eli had never used a table saw. He kept staring at the spinning blade even when it was switched off, rubbing his palms against his jeans. A box of trophies waited on a cart, and the janitor was asking where to move it. Mr. Bell gave Eli the safer job of sanding the cabinet doors, but the boy’s strokes grew shorter and faster until he barely touched the wood. He glanced at the clock after every few passes. Mr. Bell set a steady rhythm by tapping the workbench and asked him to match it. Eli’s shoulders eased as the rough edges smoothed. Together they installed the glass panels, then arranged the trophies behind them before the first families came through the entrance.

The custom cabinet for my photography studio was supposed to hide cables, lenses, and the printer, but the carpenter called to say his van had broken down. The opening reception began in three hours. I carried boxes from one side of the room to the other, making each pile less orderly, while my phone remained pressed to my ear. When Priya finally arrived with a borrowed trailer, I was standing on a chair trying to measure the alcove myself. My tape measure snapped back and struck my knuckles. I kept apologizing, although she had said nothing was ruined. She examined the space and sketched a cabinet with a temporary open shelf, promising to add doors later. I asked how many minutes it would take, then asked again before she had finished answering. We worked until the room filled with guests. The cabinet wasn’t perfect, but every lens was tucked away, and I could greet people without turning toward the clutter.

Rafael was building a cabinet for his food truck when a city inspector moved the visit forward by two days. The carpenter, June, had already cut the panels, but Rafael needed a locked compartment for cash and permits before the truck could reopen. He kept wiping grease from his hands onto a rag, leaving dark fingerprints across the drawings. His employee called from the street to ask whether to cancel the lunch orders. Rafael looked at the empty truck, then at the clock above the garage door, and started listing tasks so quickly that June asked him to slow down. She fitted a narrow lockbox into the cabinet’s side and reinforced the shelf with a steel bracket. Rafael hovered beside the drill, shifting his weight each time June reached for a tool. When the lock clicked shut, he tested it three times. Then he phoned his employee and said to keep the orders. The inspector would find the permits in their proper place.

I watched the red numbers on the dashboard clock change while the cars ahead stayed locked in place. My nursing interview began in twenty minutes, and my clean shirt was already sticking between my shoulder blades. I tapped the steering wheel, then gripped it so tightly my knuckles blanched. The navigation screen offered a new route, but every side street it suggested was shaded crimson. I called the clinic and got voicemail; my greeting came out in a thin rush before I hung up without leaving a message. A siren sounded somewhere behind us, then faded beneath the steady horns. I checked my portfolio on the passenger seat, though I knew the papers were still there. When traffic moved half a car length, I lurched forward, brake squealing, and whispered the clinic’s address as if repeating it might make the road open.

At forty-seven, Hassan had learned to keep his bakery deliveries orderly, but the jam on the ring road had turned the van into a hot, flour-dusted box. A wedding cake stood strapped behind him, its icing flowers trembling whenever a driver leaned on a horn. The venue coordinator kept calling. Hassan’s thumb slipped across the phone screen twice before he managed to answer through the hands-free system. He promised he was close, then stared at the unmoving line of trucks ahead. Sweat gathered beneath his cap. He checked the clock, checked the cake in the mirror, and checked the clock again. A motorcyclist squeezed between lanes, vanishing toward an exit. Hassan shifted into park, then drive, then park once more, his foot bouncing against the pedal while the cake’s delicate tiers waited in the sweltering silence.

The traffic had stopped beneath an overpass, and I could no longer see the airport signs. My daughter’s first flight was boarding soon; she was alone in the terminal with a violin case and a phone battery nearly dead. I pressed the call button, listened to three rings, and ended it before voicemail picked up. The heater was off, yet my palms felt slick on the wheel. I leaned toward the windshield, searching between buses for any hint of movement. A delivery truck’s brake lights glowed inches from my bumper. “Come on,” I said, then louder, though nobody could hear me. I opened the map, closed it, and opened it again. When my phone buzzed with her message—At gate now—I fumbled it onto the passenger seat, then reached for it with both hands before remembering I was still driving.

Mara, a city bus driver nearing retirement, had a full load of commuters and a wheelchair ramp that needed to be deployed at the next stop. The avenue was a solid chain of cars, and the schedule display showed her falling further behind every minute. A passenger at the front asked whether they would make the train connection. Mara answered with a practiced smile, but her fingers kept returning to the radio microphone. Dispatch crackled, then dissolved into static. She swallowed, adjusted the mirror, and counted the passengers visible in its reflection. The bus in front edged forward, stopped, and edged forward again. Mara eased her vehicle into the gap, careful not to jolt anyone, while her heel tapped against the floor. Somewhere behind her, a baby began to cry, and the sound made her glance once more at the stalled intersection.

I had promised to meet my brother outside the courthouse before his hearing, and now the freeway was barely crawling. My phone showed his last message: Here. Don’t leave me waiting. I tried to call, but the connection dropped as soon as I heard his voice. My stomach tightened. I kept looking from the phone to the clock, although neither could change the line of brake lights stretching ahead. The driver beside me rolled down his window and shouted at someone; I flinched and knocked my water bottle over. It rolled beneath the seat, leaving a dark streak across the floor mat. I reached for it, missed, and sat upright again, breathing through my teeth. When a gap appeared, I moved into it, then worried I had cut someone off and checked the mirror three times.

Eli, a seventeen-year-old apprentice electrician, was late to his first solo job across town. His supervisor had handed him the address that morning and told him not to be late; the tool bag on the passenger seat seemed to grow heavier with each minute. Traffic crowded the bridge, boxed in by concrete barriers on both sides. Eli wiped his hands on his jeans and watched the temperature needle climb. He tapped the hazard button by mistake, then fumbled to switch it off as a car behind him honked. His breathing turned shallow. He opened the window, but exhaust rolled in with the humid air. The map insisted he would arrive in six minutes. He glanced at the unmoving cars, then at the screen, and muttered the estimate back to himself, as if challenging it to be true.

The doctor had said my father needed his medication before noon, and the pharmacy was on the far side of the city. Now my cab sat trapped between a cement mixer and a row of taxis, with the clock on the console creeping past eleven-thirty. I called the pharmacy, but the words tumbled out too quickly for the clerk to understand. After she asked me to repeat myself, I gripped the edge of the seat and tried again. Outside, a cyclist slid between bumpers, his bell ringing sharply. I jumped at the sound and dropped my purse. Receipts and mints scattered across the floor. The driver suggested a side street, but the map showed another red ribbon of traffic. I kept checking my father’s last text, though it had not changed: Please don’t forget.

Nadia was driving her borrowed hatchback to a scholarship audition when the boulevard filled with stalled vehicles. Her cello rested across the back seat, secured with a belt, and every horn seemed to vibrate through its case. The audition office had already called once. Nadia set the phone on speaker and heard a receptionist say they could hold her place for only a few minutes. She answered that she was coming, then pressed her lips together until they hurt. A bus blocked the view of the next intersection; beyond it, nothing moved. She drummed both thumbs against the steering wheel, stopped, and started again. When rain began speckling the glass, she switched on the wipers too fast. They swept back and forth as she stared at the clock and tried to keep her hands from shaking.

I was bringing the signed lease to my new landlord, and the envelope was on the seat beside me, curling in the afternoon heat. The appointment was at four. The dashboard said 3:42, and the traffic report had just added another delay. I called my partner, but as soon as they answered I blurted out that I might lose the apartment. They reminded me the landlord knew about the roadworks; I nodded, even though they couldn’t see. A truck changed lanes in front of me, and I hit the brake hard enough to send the envelope sliding onto the floor. I reached down, stopped myself, and stared at it until the car behind me honked. My mouth had gone dry. I took a sip from my bottle, missed the opening, and spilled water down my sleeve.

Leon, a retired carpenter, was taking his grandson to a school play across town. The boy wore a paper crown and kept asking whether they would arrive before his scene. Cars clogged every lane, and a road crew’s flashing arrow directed traffic into an even slower queue. Leon’s grip tightened on the wheel. He promised they would make it, then checked the clock and said nothing more. His grandson began reciting his lines in the back seat. Leon smiled at the rearview mirror, but his jaw worked from side to side. He tried a side road and found a delivery truck blocking the entrance. Reversing out took several careful maneuvers while drivers waited behind him. Back on the main road, he tapped the steering wheel in a quick, uneven rhythm, watching for any opening between the long rows of cars.

I had one hour to get to the animal shelter before they closed, and the kitten I wanted to adopt was being held only until then. Traffic had stalled beneath a railway crossing. The barrier was down, though no train had appeared, and the cars ahead formed a motionless tunnel. I checked the shelter’s closing time, then called to say I was on my way. My voice cracked on the last word. A car behind me honked, and I jolted hard enough to knock my sunglasses from the dashboard. They landed near the pedals. I left them there and stared at the crossing lights. The map showed a detour, but its estimated arrival kept jumping later. I pressed my fingertips against my lips, then lowered them and began counting the cars ahead, losing track before I reached ten.

Jun, a traveling translator, was on the way to a live conference where he was scheduled to interpret the opening remarks. His laptop bag sat buckled beside him, and the printed speech lay open on his lap at a red light that never seemed to change. The avenue was gridlocked, with buses, delivery vans, and impatient drivers hemmed between construction fences. Jun tried reviewing the first paragraph, but the lines blurred whenever he glanced at the clock. He called the event organizer and got no answer. His collar felt tight, so he loosened it, then tightened it again when a horn blared behind him. The car ahead rolled forward a few feet. Jun followed, whispering the opening sentence under his breath, then stopped abruptly as brake lights flared across the entire intersection.

I slid the loan application across the bakery counter, then pulled it back to check the figures again. Flour clung to my sleeves as I tapped the calculator, though I had already done the math three times. The oven timer shrilled, and I flinched so hard that my pencil rolled beneath the refrigerator. Rent was due Friday; the new mixer had stopped working yesterday, leaving me kneading every batch by hand. At the bank, the officer asked for my projected revenue. My throat tightened. I opened the folder, but the pages stuck together under my damp fingers. “I have the invoices,” I said, too quickly, and began sorting them in the wrong order. Behind me, the line shifted and someone sighed. I found the right sheet at last, but the numbers swam until I pressed both feet firmly against the floor.

At sixty-eight, Rosa had run her shoe-repair shop long enough to recognize trouble by its sound: the compressor sputtering, then falling silent. She filled out a small-business loan application at the kitchen table, with her granddaughter’s school drawings pushed aside. Each time the phone buzzed, she reached for it before it finished vibrating. The bank’s online form rejected her password twice. Rosa wiped her palms on her apron and wrote the password on an envelope, then stared at the screen as if it might change its mind. When the loan officer called, she stood so abruptly that her chair scraped backward. She answered with a bright greeting, but her voice cracked on the word “equipment.” A pile of unrepaired boots waited by the shop door, and the compressor’s dead hush seemed to fill the whole house.

I had forty minutes before the lender closed, and my food truck was parked outside with its generator coughing like an old engine. The loan application sat open on my laptop while I tried to upload the repair estimate. The progress bar stopped at ninety-nine percent. I clicked again, then again, until the page went blank. Heat crawled up my neck. In the truck, a customer tapped on the window, but I couldn’t make myself look over. The new loan would cover the generator and keep me serving lunch at the hospital, where my regulars depended on the route. I called the bank, pacing between the sink and the cash drawer. When someone answered, I read my account number from a receipt and dropped it twice. “Please stay with me,” I said, gripping the counter until my knuckles paled.

Malik’s bicycle shop had a waiting list for repairs, but the landlord had posted a notice about the building’s rising rent. He applied for a loan to buy a small storefront, then discovered the bank needed a tax document his accountant had not sent. He refreshed his inbox so often that the page began to lag. His knee bounced beneath the desk, rattling a tin of spare screws. When the accountant finally called, Malik spoke over the first sentence, asking whether the file was ready. He apologized and tried again, but his breath came in short pulls. Across the room, a customer waited beside a bicycle with a bent wheel. Malik looked at the loan portal, then at the clock. He typed the accountant’s email address into the lender’s message box, erased it, and typed it once more, carefully checking every letter.

I own a tiny translation agency above a laundromat, and the loan application was supposed to be the straightforward part. Then the bank asked for a personal guarantee. I read the clause while the dryers thumped through the floorboards, each heavy tumble seeming to shake another thought loose. My cursor hovered over the signature box. If I signed, my apartment could be at risk; if I didn’t, I might lose the contract that would let me hire two translators. I reached for water and knocked the glass against the desk. It tipped, and I snatched up the papers before the spill reached them. The loan officer called just then. I tried to ask one clear question, but three came out together. She paused. I pressed my thumb into the edge of the desk and asked her to explain the guarantee again, slowly.

Nina’s flower shop had booked several weddings, but the cooler was failing during the hottest week of the year. She submitted a loan request for a replacement and sat beside the phone, watching the screen light up with every notification. None came from the bank. A bucket of lilies leaned against the counter, their heads beginning to droop. Nina checked the temperature display, opened the application portal, and checked it again. When a lender called, she rushed to answer and bumped a vase with her elbow. Water spread across the counter as she listened to questions about monthly sales. Her answers were accurate, but she kept losing her place in the spreadsheet. She folded a paper towel into smaller and smaller squares beneath one hand while the other held the phone tight against her ear.

I make custom fishing nets from a workshop behind my house, and a large harbor order could keep me busy all winter. The materials supplier wanted payment upfront, so I applied for a business loan. At the bank, I carried a folder thick with invoices, but the loan officer asked about a deposit I couldn’t find. My stomach seemed to drop below the chair. I emptied the folder onto the table, sorting papers by date while the officer waited. A receipt slid under her shoe. I bent for it, struck my head on the table, and apologized before I even stood upright. My hands kept fumbling the paper clips. I knew the deposit was there; I had entered it in the ledger myself. When I found the receipt, I held it out with both hands, as if a sudden movement might make it disappear again.

At twenty-six, Jo had turned a spare bedroom into a screen-printing studio and built a loyal following among local bands. A loan would let her rent proper workspace, but the application required a forecast for the next three years. She stared at the blank cells until the digits on her calculator seemed to run together. Her phone rang; she silenced it, then immediately checked whether the caller had left a message. The lender’s deadline was that afternoon. Jo opened a spreadsheet, entered a figure, deleted it, and began again. Her foot knocked a stack of sample shirts to the floor. When her roommate asked if she wanted lunch, Jo said she wasn’t hungry, then took a bite of a cold granola bar without tasting it. She attached the forecast and hovered over “submit,” breathing through pursed lips before clicking.

I run a small seafood stall at the market, and my ice machine gave out just before the weekend rush. I applied for a loan to replace it, then learned the lender wanted proof that my stall had been profitable for six months. The records were in a box at home, beneath old menus and utility bills. I drove there, returned, and realized I had brought the wrong box. At the market, the fish tubs were packed in fresh ice, but it wouldn’t last all day. I called my brother to search the cupboard while I refreshed the bank’s message page. Every passing minute made me check the ice again. When he read out a date from a receipt, I shouted for him to repeat it, then lowered my voice and apologized. My fingers had curled so tightly around the phone that they ached.

Evelyn, who had spent decades tailoring costumes for community theater, needed a loan to replace two industrial sewing machines. The application asked for collateral, and she listed the equipment she hoped to buy before noticing the mistake. Her face went still. She called the bank, put the phone on speaker, then snatched it up when the hold music began. The studio was crowded with half-finished costumes, and a director was due to collect them that evening. Evelyn tried to work while she waited, but threaded the needle backward twice. When the loan officer returned, she spoke so fast that he asked her to repeat the account number. She folded a measuring tape into her palm, squeezed it, and explained the error. The officer said it could be corrected online. Evelyn opened her laptop with shaking hands and searched for the right page.

My neighborhood repair café grew out of a folding table and a drawer full of screwdrivers. Now I needed a loan to lease a storefront, and the application asked for a business plan I had promised to finish by Monday. On Sunday night, the printer jammed with the only complete copy inside it. I pulled at the paper, heard it tear, and froze with a strip in each hand. The laptop battery warning blinked in the dark. I plugged it in, but the cord barely reached the table. My thoughts kept jumping from rent to insurance to the committee meeting at nine. I called my friend to ask for a spare printer, then couldn’t remember the street number. Once the new copy emerged, I checked every page twice, stacked them neatly, and still carried the folder to bed beside me.

Farid had built a thriving mobile pet-grooming service, but his van’s lift mechanism was failing, making it hard to serve older dogs safely. He applied for a business loan and arranged a meeting with a credit union near the depot. Before he left, he printed the repair estimate and packed it into his jacket. At the meeting, the lender asked for the company’s registration number. Farid searched his phone, then his wallet, then the folder he had already checked. His breath caught as the minutes passed. He called his bookkeeper, listening to the rings while his free hand drummed against the table. A dog barked outside, and he jerked around. The bookkeeper answered and read the number aloud. Farid repeated it under his breath, entered it carefully, and asked the lender to confirm each digit before moving on.

My granddaughter’s school auditorium had three doors, and every one seemed to lead somewhere different. I had promised Lila I would sit in the front row, but now the lights were dimming and I was still in the corridor, holding a paper program upside down. A teacher hurried past with a box of cardboard stars. “The stage is through there,” she said, pointing behind me. I turned too quickly and bumped a display of painted planets. One wobbled on its string. My fingers fumbled with the buttons on my coat, though I was already sweating beneath it. From inside came a piano note, then another. Lila was supposed to be the moon in the opening scene. I followed the sound, took the wrong turn, and found myself beside the cafeteria. A custodian saw my face, walked me straight to the auditorium, and slipped me into a seat just as the curtain began to rise.

Nia had rehearsed the route to the school play twice, yet the bus dropped her on the opposite side of the campus. Her grandson Mateo would be looking for her in the audience; he had drawn her a seat with a bright green star on its program. She hurried across the courtyard, clutching the gift bag so tightly its handles cut into her palm. The building doors were locked. Through the glass, she saw families moving down a hallway, then vanish around a corner. Nia pressed the buzzer, but her voice came out thin when someone answered. “The theater entrance is around back,” the secretary told her. She ran, her shoes slipping on damp leaves, and reached the stage door as a student in a cardboard crown emerged. A volunteer recognized Mateo’s name and guided her inside. She found the green-star seat during the first line of his scene.

I was halfway through fastening my grandson’s costume at home when I realized I had taken the wrong jacket from the closet. The school play started in twenty minutes, and the other jacket held the parking pass in its pocket. I patted every pocket anyway, then checked the kitchen counter, the laundry basket, and the car, moving faster while remembering less. At the school, cars crowded the curb and the entrance sign pointed toward a gymnasium that looked exactly like the one across town. I called my daughter, but the call went to voicemail. Inside, a child dressed as a fox ran past carrying a lantern. I followed the stream of parents, stopped at a door marked MUSIC ROOM, and heard the audience applauding somewhere beyond it. My hands shook as I tugged the handle. A stagehand opened it from within and waved me toward the back row, where my grandson was already scanning faces.

When the auditorium lights blinked twice, Mr. Bell’s cane caught in the strap of the tote bag on his lap. His granddaughter Orla was playing a village baker, and he had promised not to miss her entrance. The school’s new seating arrangement made little sense to him: rows were numbered on the floor, but the paper ticket in his hand had a letter instead. He squinted, turned it over, then asked a passing usher. The usher pointed toward the balcony. Mr. Bell climbed the stairs one careful step at a time, hearing the play’s opening music grow louder. At the top, a door led to a dark storage closet. He backed out, knocking his cane against the frame. A student volunteer spotted him and checked the ticket. “You’re on the other side, sir.” His jaw tightened. Together they crossed the lobby and reached the right section as Orla lifted a flour-dusted tray.

My grandson had told me to look for the red banner above the school theater, but the whole building seemed draped in red banners. I walked past the library, the gym, and a corridor lined with paper fish, asking no one because I was sure the next sign would settle it. Then the bell rang, and students poured around me like a current. I clutched the bouquet I had brought for Emmett, its stems crackling under my grip. A door swung shut just as I reached it. Behind it, I heard a crowd laughing. Was that his play? I tried the handle, then another, while the bouquet brushed against the wall. At last a girl carrying a cardboard submarine asked whom I was visiting. When I said Emmett’s name, she pointed to a small auditorium downstairs. I took the stairs too fast, caught the railing, and arrived with my breath coming in sharp bursts just as the sailors began their song.

Salma had driven three hours to see her grandson’s performance, but the school’s address led her to a fenced construction site. She checked the message on her phone; the map’s blue dot spun without settling. The first note of a violin floated from somewhere nearby. Salma gripped the steering wheel, then called her daughter, listening to each ring while watching the clock advance. A groundskeeper finally came through the gate and explained that the play was at the old elementary building two streets away. She parked crookedly, grabbed her scarf, and hurried to the next entrance. Inside, the lobby was empty except for a row of paper pumpkins. A muffled voice announced the cast. Salma pushed open the nearest door and found a classroom, not a theater. Her cheeks burned. A custodian heard her explain and escorted her to the auditorium. She entered quietly, but her grandson Yusuf saw her and gave a small, relieved wave from the stage.

The program said my granddaughter’s scene was near the end, so I thought there was plenty of time to find a seat. Then a teacher announced that the show would begin early because the next class needed the stage. I had just reached the school when my phone slipped from my hand and skidded beneath a parked car. I knelt, scraped my knuckles retrieving it, and saw three missed calls from my son. Inside, the lobby smelled of wet wool and tempera paint. I followed a cluster of parents through a doorway and found myself in the band room, where trumpets rested on chairs. A student pointed down another corridor. I could hear children reciting lines now, each voice clearer than the last. My breath snagged as I hurried past the trophy case. At the theater entrance, an usher took my coat and whispered that Maribel was waiting in the wings. I found a seat just before her cue.

At eighty-one, George had learned to ignore most school notices, but his grandson’s handwritten invitation had been pinned to the refrigerator for weeks. The night of the play, he arrived with a small wooden airplane he had carved for the boy. The main entrance was crowded, and a banner directed visitors to check in at the office. George joined the line, then noticed the lobby clock had stopped. His fingers tightened around the airplane. When he reached the desk, the secretary said the audience had already been seated and sent him toward the side doors. He chose one, opened it, and faced a stairwell descending into darkness. The applause inside grew louder. George shut the door and tried the next one. A parent emerging from the theater recognized the cast list in his hand and escorted him to the proper entrance. He lowered himself into an aisle seat, carefully protecting the little airplane in his coat.

I had promised Suki I would clap loudest when she appeared as a tree, which seemed easy until I reached the school and found the play listed under a different title. The office secretary searched the computer while I stood tapping my ticket against my leg. “It’s in the black-box theater,” she said, pointing toward a hall I had never seen. I set off, passed a staircase, doubled back, and nearly walked into a group of children wearing leafy costumes. One of them said the black box was downstairs. The stairwell echoed with footsteps, and I gripped the handrail all the way down. At the bottom, a door was propped open by a bucket. Inside, folding chairs filled a room no bigger than my living room. I scanned the audience, found no empty seat, and felt my mouth go dry. Then a teacher spotted my ticket and brought over a chair just as Suki’s scene began.

Ruben reached the school just as rain began battering the windows. His granddaughter Elena was performing in a play about explorers, and she had asked him to bring the old compass he used on camping trips. Now the compass was missing. He searched his pockets, the car seat, and the damp paper bag where he had packed it. Parents streamed through the lobby, shedding umbrellas. Ruben kept stepping aside, then darting forward whenever he saw a student in costume. A small boy carrying a painted map told him the cast was gathering backstage.
