Bea calmly directed me into the nearer lane, and we continued without incident. At the next intersection, I leaned forward to read every sign twice. “You don’t have to solve the whole road at once,” she said. I nodded, watching the painted arrows slide beneath the hood.

Sixteen-year-old Tessa arrived at the driving school with a notebook full of diagrams. Her instructor, Mr. Bell, praised her careful notes, then asked her to merge onto a broad avenue. Tessa checked the mirror and saw a car approaching, but its distance refused to settle in her mind. She looked again, then once more, while Mr. Bell waited. “Is it far enough?” she asked. He asked her to judge the speed instead of the space. Tessa studied the moving car, tightened her grip, and gave an uncertain nod. With his calm guidance, she accelerated into the lane. Nothing dramatic happened; traffic flowed around them. Still, at the next merge, she began counting the seconds between cars under her breath, then stopped when she realized she had lost track.

My instructor, Diego, chose an empty supermarket lot for my first lesson, which seemed sensible until he asked me to park between two painted lines. I was fifty-two, and I could back a trailer into a narrow shed, yet the little hatchback made the task feel oddly delicate. I turned the wheel left, but the rear seemed to swing the wrong way. Diego drew a simple diagram on a receipt. I followed it, then watched the car drift toward the line again. “I’m doing what the picture says,” I murmured. He asked me to pause and look at the mirrors one at a time. Their reflections showed different angles, and I kept shifting my gaze to reconcile them. After a few tries, the car settled between the stripes. I climbed out to check, surprised by how much space remained.

Amina had never driven outside her village, where the roads were narrow and familiar. In the city, instructor Jules guided her toward a roundabout with four exits and a fountain in the middle. “Take the second exit,” he said. Amina counted the openings as they approached, but one was partly hidden by a bus. She glanced at Jules, then at the circling traffic. Her hands moved higher on the wheel. “Is this the first?” she asked, though they had not entered yet. Jules described the entry point and asked her to count from there. Amina repeated the sequence softly as she joined the flow. She passed one exit, then another, and left smoothly. A block later, she looked back toward the fountain and wondered aloud why the painted arrows had seemed to point in different directions.

I enrolled in lessons at sixty-three because my new job required visits to farms beyond the bus route. Instructor Nia took me onto a quiet road and asked me to follow the speed limit. The sign showed thirty, but the dashboard needle wavered between twenty-eight and thirty-two. I kept easing off the accelerator, then pressing it again, unable to decide whether the needle was settling or climbing. Nia asked what I noticed about the road. “That it keeps changing,” I said, watching the hedges blur. She explained that small movement was normal and encouraged me to hold a steady pressure. I tried, but the engine note rose whenever the road sloped upward. At the next sign, I checked the speedometer, then the sign, then the speedometer again. Nia smiled and asked me to trust one reading at a time.

Ravi’s instructor took him to a hilly neighborhood, explaining that the lesson would cover starting on an incline. Ravi understood the words, but when the car stopped on a slope, the street seemed to tilt more sharply than before. Mr. Chen told him to release the brake gradually and add a little gas. Ravi did both, then felt the car roll backward. He pressed the brake hard. A cyclist waited behind them, watching with patient interest. Ravi’s ears warmed as he asked which action should happen first. Mr. Chen demonstrated the sequence and reassured him that the car had plenty of room. On the next attempt, Ravi held the brake, found the biting point, and moved forward. At the top of the hill, he looked down at the pedals as if they had quietly changed their arrangement.

The instructor handed me the keys outside a rural library and asked me to adjust the mirrors. I moved each one until I could see mostly the road, but then the rear window disappeared from the center mirror. “Is that right?” I asked. Mrs. Alvarez told me there was no single perfect view, only a useful one. I changed the mirrors again, trying to balance the three scenes. Each adjustment made one angle clearer and another less familiar. When we finally pulled away, a tractor appeared in the side mirror and seemed to be beside us already. I glanced over my shoulder, then back at the glass. Mrs. Alvarez guided me through the check calmly. By the time we stopped, I had learned the routine, though I still wondered how drivers could keep all those separate views straight.

At nineteen, Noor was confident on a bicycle and expected the car to respond with the same directness. Instructor Pete asked her to make a gentle turn around a row of barrels. Noor began steering early, then corrected sharply when the car did not change direction at once. The tires crossed the painted boundary. Pete asked what she had expected the car to do. Noor rubbed her thumb along the wheel seam. “Turn when I turn it,” she said, sounding less certain than she intended. He explained that the car needed a moment to follow her hands. They tried again at a slower pace. Noor watched the barrels approach, then made a small movement and waited. The car curved around them neatly. She looked at Pete as if hoping he could confirm that waiting was truly part of the maneuver.

My first lesson took place in a coastal town during a sudden drizzle. Instructor Lottie had me use the wipers, but I turned the knob and watched them sweep once, pause, then sweep again. I tried another setting; now they moved continuously, faster than seemed necessary. “Which one clears the glass without racing?” I asked. Lottie showed me the intermittent control, though the symbols were tiny and crowded together. I leaned close at a red light to inspect them, then realized I was blocking the view of the road. My shoulders rose toward my ears. Lottie suggested I learn the controls while parked. We pulled into a safe lay-by, and I tested each setting. When we continued, rain beaded across the windshield, and I kept one eye on the road while my fingers rested near the switch.

Eighty-year-old Emmett had delayed learning to drive because he preferred walking, until his sister moved beyond the town bus line. His instructor, Yasmin, began with a calm route through empty streets. At a four-way stop, Emmett watched another car arrive from the left and then a second from across the intersection. Yasmin explained who should go first, but Emmett kept looking from one driver to the other, waiting for some signal. A hand lifted, then vanished behind a windshield glare. “Now?” he asked. Yasmin guided him through the rule, and he proceeded slowly. Afterward, he pressed his lips together and replayed the scene aloud, listing each arrival in order. Yasmin praised his careful attention and asked him to focus on the next block. Emmett gave a small nod, still checking the intersection in the mirror.

When the sports doctor cleared me to jog, I expected my ankle to feel like it used to. Instead, it held steady for three laps, then trembled whenever I stepped onto the track’s painted lines. I asked whether the stripes were somehow changing my stride. Dr. Chen checked my shoes, then watched me run again without them. Nothing explained it. At home, I lined up my old race medals beside the new exercise sheet, as if one might offer a clue. My sister said recovery rarely follows a straight route, but I kept circling the same question: why did the ankle behave differently on a track I had known for years? The next morning, I tried a grassy field. There, every step felt ordinary, which only made the painted lines harder to account for.

I broke my wrist during a regional climbing final, and six months later I was back at the gym, gripping holds with both hands. The therapist had warned me that strength would return gradually, but I hadn’t expected the easy routes to be the hardest. On a steep wall, I trusted my repaired wrist and moved smoothly. On a beginner’s slab, I froze before a broad, rounded hold. I tested it with one finger, then another, while my climbing partner waited below. The grip was solid. My wrist didn’t hurt. Still, my fingers hovered as if the hold might shift. I tried a different route, then returned to the same spot after everyone left. By closing time, I had climbed harder walls but could not explain why that harmless hold kept stopping me.

Nia’s knee had healed enough for her to resume fencing, though she still wore a light brace beneath her uniform. At practice, she lunged cleanly toward the coach’s target, then hesitated whenever her opponent advanced. Her feet seemed to forget a sequence she had performed thousands of times. She asked the coach to call the moves aloud; the instructions made her slower, not faster. Between bouts, she traced the court’s boundary with her shoe and looked toward the door, as if a missing piece of equipment might be there. The knee felt firm, and the physician’s tests had been reassuring. Nia finally requested one more bout, then stepped back when the starting signal came. She could not point to pain or weakness, only to a blank beat between hearing the signal and moving.

I was a marathon runner before a stress fracture forced me to spend eight weeks on a bicycle. When my doctor let me run again, I chose the riverside path where I had trained for years. My legs felt strong, but every time I passed the old mile marker, I checked my watch twice. The numbers showed the same pace; the distance signs said the same thing. I stopped to inspect the marker’s bolts, then jogged back to it from the other direction. Nothing had changed. My running group waited farther down the path, waving me onward, while I stood there rubbing the healed spot on my shin. I finished the workout, but afterward I drew the route on a napkin and circled the marker, still unable to say why that point had unsettled my stride.

Amir, a wheelchair basketball player, had injured two fingers in a collision and spent weeks rebuilding his grip. His doctor cleared him for light drills, so he joined the team in the school gym. The ball felt secure in his hands, and his passes reached their targets. But whenever he approached the free-throw line, he rotated his chair a few inches, then corrected it, then checked the floor markings. His teammates asked if the fingers were hurting. Amir flexed them and shrugged. The line looked straight, the basket sat in its usual place, and the gym had not been rearranged. Still, his chair never seemed quite aligned. After practice, he measured the distance with the wheels and found no problem. He left the tape measure on the court, staring at the ordinary white stripe.

After surgery on my elbow, I returned to softball in a town where everyone knew my throwing motion. The first practice went well until our coach asked me to toss a ball gently to first base. I could throw hard without trouble, yet the soft toss kept sailing high. I adjusted my stance, changed my grip, and asked my catcher to stand closer. Each attempt landed somewhere unexpected. My elbow felt fine, and the physical therapist had watched me throw the day before without concern. I began wondering whether the ball itself felt lighter than usual, so I weighed it beside another from the equipment bag. They matched. The team packed up while I stayed to make one more gentle throw. It landed perfectly, but I couldn’t identify what I had done differently.

Greta, a competitive cyclist from a farming village, was eager to ride outside after recovering from a collarbone fracture. Her first training loop passed familiar barns and windbreaks, but she kept slowing near a wooden bridge she had crossed since childhood. The bridge was unchanged, and the repaired bone caused no pain. Still, each time she reached its entrance, she squeezed the brakes and looked over the railing. Her coach rode back to ask whether she needed a rest. Greta pointed to the boards, then stopped speaking, unable to name anything wrong with them. She crossed at walking speed and completed the ride. That evening, she spread a map on the kitchen table and marked the bridge with a pencil. The route made sense; her sudden caution did not.

I’m a sprinter, and a torn hamstring kept me away from competition for nearly a year. When I finally returned, my coach placed me in lane four, the lane I’d always preferred. At the blocks, I kept turning to check lane five, where nobody was warming up. I adjusted my starting position, asked for the lane assignment again, and looked at the numbers painted on the track. They were clear. My leg felt powerful during practice starts, but I could not settle into the familiar routine. The coach suggested I switch lanes. In lane two, I launched cleanly, then asked to go back to four. We tried both twice. The results were nearly identical, leaving me with no reason for the extra glances that had delayed every start.

After a broken thumb healed, fourteen-year-old Lila returned to archery at the county range. She could draw the bow smoothly and release without discomfort, but her arrows began landing low. Her father checked the sight, tightened a screw, and asked her to try again. The next arrows struck the same place. Lila examined the target, then the bowstring, then her bandaged thumb, which was no longer bandaged. She asked whether the target might have been moved, though its stand was planted in the usual ground. The coach measured the distance and found it correct. Lila shot a final arrow; it landed near the center. Instead of smiling, she looked down at her hand and rotated it, trying to discover what had changed between that shot and all the others.

I play professional rugby, and a shoulder dislocation made tackling the first skill I had to rebuild. Months later, I passed every strength test and returned to full practice. During drills, though, I kept asking teammates to explain where they planned to meet me, even when the play had been rehearsed. I could see the formation, hear the calls, and move without pain. Yet at the moment of contact, my feet slowed. The coach replayed the drill on video. My shoulder stayed tucked safely, and my timing looked sound. I watched the clip again, searching for a gap in the instructions or a signal I had missed. There was none. After practice, I stayed on the field, marking the drill’s starting points with cones, then moving them back where they belonged.

Yusuf, a trail runner who had moved from Morocco to Norway, was recovering from a badly sprained knee. When his physiotherapist approved an easy forest route, he set off beneath a canopy of dark pines. His knee held up on roots and slopes, yet he stopped repeatedly at wooden trail signs. The arrows pointed in familiar directions, but Yusuf kept turning his map sideways and comparing it with the trees. He had run these paths before the injury. Nothing about the markings had changed. A pair of hikers passed and asked if he was lost; he said no, then watched them disappear around the bend. He reached the cabin on schedule, with steady legs and a clean route on his watch. Back at the trailhead, he studied the sign once more, unable to explain why it had seemed unreliable.

I had been waiting at the licensing office long enough to memorize the pattern of cracks in the tile when the clerk handed me a blue slip. “Take this to window twelve,” she said, though the room had only eight windows. I looked behind me, then at the directory, where the numbers skipped from ten to fourteen. The people around me kept their eyes on their forms. I carried the slip to the security guard, who tapped its corner and pointed toward the elevators. Upstairs, a janitor was polishing an empty corridor. He examined the slip and said, “They moved twelve downstairs.” I returned to the same line, where my number had already passed. When I asked the clerk what to do, she glanced at the blue paper as if it had just appeared in my hand. I folded it carefully and joined the back of the queue.

At the county records office, Devika held her place in a line that curled around a pillar and ended beside a vending machine. She had come to replace a missing birth certificate, but the notice in her folder listed three different fees, each beside a different form. At the counter, an employee had told her to wait until her number appeared; the display showed letters instead. Devika watched a man with the same paperwork step forward, only to be sent back for a document nobody had mentioned. She opened her folder, sorted the pages, then sorted them again. When the screen chimed, it displayed “C-6,” though her ticket was “G-6.” She approached the desk with one finger raised, lowered it, and returned to the line. The vending machine swallowed her coin without dispensing anything.

I stood in the immigration office with my coat folded over one arm and a packet of papers balanced on the other. The line barely moved. Above the counters, a screen flashed symbols that looked like bus routes, while the ticket in my hand had a number and no letter. I asked the woman ahead of me whether I should join the queue marked “appointments.” She studied my ticket, then shrugged and pointed to the opposite side of the room. A clerk there waved me back without looking up. I returned to my original spot, where the line had shifted around a row of chairs. My packet slid open, spilling translated copies onto the floor. As I gathered them, I noticed everyone else holding a yellow card. Mine was white. I turned it over twice, searching for instructions, while the screen quietly changed to a language I could not read.

Malcolm, a retired electrician, arrived at the benefits office carrying a letter that instructed him to bring the letter itself. After an hour in line, he reached a desk where the clerk asked for a case number. He pointed to the only number printed on the page. She typed it in, frowned at her monitor, and asked whether he had another one. Malcolm removed his glasses, cleaned them on his sleeve, and inspected every corner of the letter. Behind him, the queue shuffled forward. The clerk gave him a small card bearing a different number and told him to wait again. He sat beneath a wall clock that had stopped at 2:17, though the office announcement said it was nearly four. He checked his watch, then the clock, then the announcement speaker, as if one might explain the others.

I had been in the passport office line since breakfast when a teenager in a staff badge came by collecting forms. She took mine, glanced at the photo, and returned it with a sticky note attached. The note said “Room B.” I could see Room B across the lobby, but a rope blocked the entrance and a sign said “Staff only.” I asked the teenager if I could go through. She said to wait for my number. The display had no numbers, only a blinking dash. I watched people walk into the room carrying folders, then emerge empty-handed and take fresh tickets. My palms grew damp around the paper. When I finally reached the counter, the clerk asked why my form had a note on it. I pointed at the badge-wearing teenager, but she had vanished behind a stack of boxes.

Linh sat beneath a notice at the municipal office that promised service in four languages. The notice itself was printed in two. She had come to register a food cart and brought a carefully labeled folder, but the first clerk directed her to the tax line, while the tax clerk sent her to permits. Each counter displayed the same sign: “Begin here.” Linh followed the arrows painted on the floor, which formed a loop around the waiting area. At each turn, she checked the folder tabs and pressed her lips together. A man beside her said he had been sent around twice already. Linh offered him a mint, then compared their forms; his was green, hers was cream. When her ticket number appeared, the screen showed a symbol like a tiny umbrella. She stood, sat down, and watched it disappear.

I took a number at the city housing office and settled into a line that stretched past the water fountain. The paper ticket said 41, but the display was calling numbers in the 200s. I checked the machine and found a second ticket tucked under my sleeve: 214. I had no memory of taking it. A guard said the machine sometimes printed two copies, then directed me to a different queue. There, people were holding green slips, while mine was white. I asked the woman at the front whether colors mattered. She looked at my ticket, then at the sign behind her, and told me to ask at reception. Reception was now closed for lunch. I stood with both tickets in my hands, aligning their edges, trying to decide which one had brought me there and which one I was meant to keep.

Esteban had driven from a farm outside town to renew his water-use permit, only to discover that the government office had moved its line indoors. He joined a crowd beneath a ceiling fan that clicked at every turn. A wall map showed the permit desk on the second floor; a handwritten arrow sent applicants downstairs. Esteban asked a clerk which instruction was current. She pointed to the map, then to the arrow, and hurried away when another visitor called her name. He studied the two directions, scratching his cheek with the corner of his application. The queue advanced, but nobody seemed to reach a counter. At last a door opened and a voice called “field permits.” Esteban stepped forward, then noticed the people ahead carried folders marked “building.” He stopped with one boot over the floor line and let them pass.

I was waiting at the courthouse records office when the clerk asked whether I wanted a certified copy or an original copy. I said I needed the document my grandmother had filed, and she handed me a form with boxes for both. The line behind me pressed close, so I stepped aside and read the instructions. One sentence said originals could not be issued; another listed the original-copy fee. I returned to the queue and asked the man behind me what he had selected. He tapped a box on his form, then covered it with his thumb. At the counter, I tried to explain that the choices seemed to overlap. The clerk nodded, slid me a pen, and pointed to the same two boxes. I held the pen above the page while the people behind me shifted their weight and stared at the ceiling.

Priya had come to the tax office to correct a spelling error, a small task that had somehow earned her a ticket, a stamped envelope, and a place in a slow-moving line. The form asked for her former surname, though she had never changed it. She showed this to an attendant, who circled a blank field and sent her back to the chairs. Priya sat, rose again, and compared the form with the sample posted on the wall. The sample included a box that her form did not have. She took a photograph of both pages, then worried that phones were forbidden and slipped hers into her bag. When her turn came, the clerk studied the paperwork and asked why she had left a section empty. Priya pointed to the missing box. The clerk turned the page over, searching for it too.

I joined the line at the vehicle registration office with a folder of receipts and a little model car my son had slipped into my pocket. A sign said “renewals to the left,” but the left side held two queues, one beside a window and one beside a door. I chose the shorter line. After forty minutes, a clerk announced that this queue was for commercial vehicles only. I looked down at my ordinary sedan paperwork, then at the people ahead of me, who were holding nearly identical folders. Nobody moved. When I asked the clerk where personal renewals belonged, she pointed across the room to a line that seemed to begin behind a vending machine. My ticket had softened from being handled. I tucked the toy car back into my pocket and followed the pointing finger, though it stopped at a blank wall.

Nora, a music teacher in her seventies, waited at the public assistance office with a paper bag of documents resting on her knees. The ticket machine had given her a number, then announced that she needed a number from the information desk. At the desk, a worker asked for the first number and stamped it with a purple mark. Nora returned to the queue, where an electronic voice called the unstamped number. She rose halfway, sat again, and looked around for someone who had heard the same thing. A young father offered to read the stamp, but the ink had smeared into a dark oval. Nora unfolded each document, checking whether another page explained the procedure. Her papers fluttered in the air from the vent. At last, she placed both tickets side by side on her lap and waited for the machine to tell her which one belonged to her.

When the lights went out on our block, I was halfway through kneading dough in my apartment. I wiped flour from my hands and went downstairs, where three neighbors stood around the open fuse cabinet as if it might offer instructions. Mr. Bell insisted the outage was only in our building, though every window across the street had gone dark too. I pointed this out, and he peered through his glasses, then asked whether the streetlights were usually so dim. Nobody answered. We tried the utility’s phone line, but the recording gave a restoration estimate for a town two counties away. I read it aloud twice, listening for some clue we had missed. Then the little girl from 2B brought out a battery lantern, and we gathered on the steps to share it. My dough could wait; I kept glancing from the silent wires to the far-off glow of the highway.

At seventy-four, Lidia knew her apartment building’s sounds: the elevator’s groan, the radiator’s ping, the upstairs twins racing down the hall. When the power failed, all of them vanished at once. She opened her door and found Omar from across the hall holding a flashlight under his chin. He said the outage had begun while he was heating soup, but the stove was gas, so the soup was fine. Lidia tapped the wall switch several times, then examined the dark hallway as though the bulbs might have changed places. Outside, a crew truck rolled past without stopping. Omar suggested the transformer near the corner, although neither of them could see it from the lobby. They carried folding chairs to the entrance and waited with other residents, comparing the different times their clocks had stopped. Lidia’s watch still ticked; she held it to her ear, then looked toward the blank elevator display.

I was closing the laundromat when the machines stopped together, leaving six neighbors staring at wet clothes trapped behind glass. The emergency lights made everyone look green. A teenager named Kaleb said the whole avenue had lost power, but Mrs. Wu pointed toward the pharmacy sign, still glowing across the intersection. I went outside to check. The pharmacy was dark too; what we had seen was a reflection from a passing bus. Back inside, we tried the breaker panel, though the labels were faded and one switch had no number at all. I asked if anyone knew which circuit served the dryers. Three people offered three different answers. We moved the damp laundry into baskets and set them by the front window, where the evening air could reach it. While we waited, I kept pressing the wall button for the sign, then stopped when Kaleb gently reminded me that it ran on the same dead circuit.

Ravi was assembling a model airplane at his kitchen table when the lamps blinked out. He stepped onto the balcony and saw neighbors gathering below, each carrying a different theory. One blamed construction; another said a squirrel had probably reached the wires. Ravi checked his phone, but the map showed no outage near their street. He refreshed it, turned the screen toward the others, and asked why the map seemed to disagree with the dark buildings around them. A woman from the next entrance suggested the report might be delayed. They went door to door, making sure older residents had candles and working phones. At Mr. Dorsey’s unit, the television still played from a battery backup, showing a weather report from yesterday. Ravi stared at the date in its corner, then at the silent clock on the wall. He left his unfinished airplane on the table and helped carry a thermos downstairs.

Our row of houses lost electricity during the neighborhood potluck, just as I was bringing out a tray of roasted vegetables. The porch bulbs died, and someone’s speaker fell silent in the middle of a song. I set the tray down and asked whether the community hall had a backup generator. Nobody seemed sure; the hall’s caretaker had gone home. Mr. Alvarez walked to the curb to inspect the utility pole, while I held my phone up for a signal that kept appearing and disappearing. A child said she could see lights on the next street, so we followed her pointing finger and found only reflections in a row of parked cars. We moved the food to the one gas grill that still worked and shared what we could cook. As neighbors talked, I kept counting the dark windows, then recounting them because I couldn’t remember whether the corner house had been lit before the outage.

Nadine had just returned from night shift when the power cut out in her apartment building. She sat on the stair landing with her shoes still on, listening for the elevator to restart. It did not. A neighbor came up carrying a box of candles, but each candle had a different size and none fit the holders they found in the lobby. Nadine used her phone’s flashlight to read the building notice, which listed a maintenance number that rang endlessly. She called the utility instead and got a recorded message about a scheduled interruption on a street with a similar name. The neighbors compared addresses, tracing the wording with their fingers. Their street was not listed. Nadine walked to the entrance and checked the notice again, then looked at the blank call box. Someone proposed a walk to the corner store for batteries. She joined them, still turning the paper over as if another explanation might be printed on the back.

I was teaching my next-door neighbors how to make dumplings when the kitchen lights disappeared. The gas burner kept hissing, so I shut it off and opened the back door. Mrs. Park brought a lantern from her pantry, but its batteries were installed backward. We fixed that, then tried to work out whether the outage affected just our row or the entire district. From my window, the bakery’s sign was dark, yet the traffic signals at the main road still changed colors. My neighbor Theo went to look and returned saying one signal had gone blank while the others worked. We stood around the table, pointing in different directions and comparing what each person had seen. I checked the stove clock, pressed its button, and watched it flash twelve. Instead of finishing the meal, we carried the dumplings to the courtyard and asked everyone to bring a dish that needed no cooking.

Miriam was counting coins at the corner shop when the lights went out and the register stopped mid-sale. Through the front window, she saw residents emerge from their homes with phones raised like tiny beacons. The shopkeeper opened the door and asked whether anyone knew if the outage was planned. A retired electrician began naming possible causes, then paused because the street transformer looked intact. Miriam checked the time on her wristwatch and compared it with the clock above the counter, which had frozen at 8:17. She asked the shopkeeper if it had been running fast before, and he shrugged. They put handwritten prices beside the cash box and continued selling bread by lantern light. When a customer brought in a radio, its announcer reported a fault several miles away, but gave no neighborhood names. Miriam listened closely, then asked the same question once more, hoping she had missed an address.

I live above a bicycle repair shop, and the outage began while I was trying to assemble a shelf. The drill stopped with one screw still half driven, and every apartment door opened within seconds. Our landlord said he had reported the problem, though he could not say to whom. I looked at the breaker panel in the hall and found one switch sitting between on and off. I nudged it, but the lights stayed dead. Downstairs, the repair shop’s bell rang when the door swung in the breeze, although no one was entering. My neighbor Salma thought the power might return if we unplugged our appliances. We did, one by one, and waited for a change. Nothing happened. I wrote the time on a scrap of cardboard and taped it beside the panel, then added a question mark. A few minutes later, I erased the mark and drew it again, larger.

At the edge of the subdivision, Hector’s house went dark along with the rest of the block. He took a flashlight outside and found two neighbors examining a utility cabinet, careful not to touch it. One had already called the city; the other had called his brother, who worked for a cable company. Neither call had produced a useful answer. Hector noticed that the houses across the drainage ditch still had porch lights, although they belonged to the same development. He walked to the footbridge to get a better view and saw that only one side of the road was dark. Back at the cabinet, he studied the labels, then asked why the street seemed divided so neatly. The neighbors checked their addresses against a paper map in his garage. It showed an old boundary line that no longer matched the street layout. They marked the dark houses with a pencil and called the utility again.

The power failed during our building’s weekly board-game night, just as I was explaining the rules to a new neighbor. We switched on a camping lantern, but its battery gave out after a few minutes. Someone brought a candle, someone else a bag of glow sticks, and soon the table looked like a strange little festival. I could not remember whether the game pieces had been on the board before the lights went out, so I asked each person what they had seen. Their accounts differed, and we began reconstructing the last turn from scraps of memory. A neighbor from upstairs came down to say her hallway lights still worked, which sent us all to check the stairwell. They were dark too. We abandoned the game and sat by the open entrance, where the night breeze cooled the room. I kept the instruction booklet open on my knees, though nobody had asked me to read it.

Juniper, who had recently moved into the neighborhood, was preparing for an online job interview when the outage struck. Her laptop screen went black, and the small ring light vanished with it. She hurried downstairs to ask the building manager whether the shared generator powered any outlets. He pointed toward a wall socket and said it usually did, though he had never tested it. Juniper plugged in her charger; nothing happened. In the lobby, neighbors were debating whether the outage began before or after a distant flash of lightning. The sky was clear, and nobody could agree on the time. Juniper checked her phone’s weather history, then compared it with the timestamp on a message from her recruiter. She paced between the dark elevator and the front windows, rehearsing an explanation for the missed call. When the recruiter finally texted that the interview would be rescheduled, she leaned against the wall and looked again at the dead socket.

At the laundromat, I balanced my laptop on a detergent box and opened the university grade portal. My statistics score had appeared, but the page showed a blue bar at 82 and a letter grade of C-minus. I refreshed it twice, then clicked the tiny rubric icon. The rubric added up to 82, while the syllabus said that anything above 80 earned a B. A dryer thumped behind me as I compared the two screens, tracing the numbers with my finger. I typed a message to Professor Lin, deleted it, and checked whether I had selected the right course. I had. When my sister called, I told her the score looked respectable but the letter had taken an unexpected detour. She asked what I planned to do. I took a screenshot, attached the syllabus, and wrote a polite question, still staring at the stubborn C.

Tariq logged in from the back seat of his father's van, parked outside a grocery store. His chemistry grade was listed as 91, yet the portal marked the class as incomplete. He tapped the status label, which opened a blank box, then signed out and tried again with the same result. His father returned with a paper bag, and Tariq turned the screen toward him. They checked the course calendar: every lab had a check mark, including the final one. Tariq rubbed the edge of his phone case and scrolled through his submissions, finding the lab report stamped received. He began typing to the instructor, stopped to reread the notice, and wondered if a second page hid below it. The van's turn signal clicked steadily while he searched. At last, he saved a screenshot and sent a short message asking what the incomplete status meant.

I checked my exam grade during a break at the community theater, still wearing a paint-splattered apron. The portal showed 76 out of 100, but beside it sat a note: “adjusted score: 68.” I opened the exam review, expecting to find a deduction, and saw no comments at all. The questions were visible, each answer marked with a green check. I leaned against a stack of folding chairs and counted them one by one; the points seemed to total 76. Perhaps the adjustment referred to something else, but the page offered no explanation. I called my classmate Nia, who said her grade had no note. My thumb hovered over the instructor’s contact link while the stage manager called for help moving a ladder. I took one last look, copied the message into a draft, and went back to work with the number turning over in my mind.

At the public library, Mei opened her exam results on a desktop computer and found a score of zero beside a comment saying “submitted late.” She remembered uploading the file the night before the deadline, from her grandmother’s kitchen, and had received an automated receipt. She searched her email, then the portal’s submission history. The timestamp on the receipt was 11:42 p.m.; the course page listed a deadline of midnight. On the grade page, however, the submission appeared under the following morning. Mei adjusted her glasses, checked the date settings, and wrote both times on the back of a library receipt. A student waiting nearby shifted from foot to foot as she compared the records again. Mei printed the page, folded it carefully, and drafted a note to the teaching assistant asking whether the system might have recorded a different time zone.

I was on a ferry when I checked the online grade for my history exam. The score was 88, which seemed fine, until I noticed that the comments praised an answer about the French Revolution. My exam had been about maritime trade, and I had written nothing about France. I refreshed the page, hoping the screen had loaded the wrong details, but the same feedback returned. The wind rattled the windows as I opened the course roster and confirmed my student number. Then I examined the other comments: one mentioned a map, another a quotation I did not recognize. I started a message to the professor, but the boat lurched and I deleted half of it by mistake. After a long breath, I took screenshots of the score and feedback, attached them to a calmer note, and watched the message send while the shoreline slid past.

Brianna checked her biology grade while waiting for a bus after her shift at a bakery. The page showed 84 percent, but the exam was labeled “not yet graded.” She tapped the score, expecting a breakdown, and found a blank chart with a spinning circle. The bus arrived, so she climbed aboard and tried the portal on cellular data. The chart vanished; the label stayed. Brianna opened the class announcements, where the instructor had written that grades were final. She glanced between that announcement and her own screen, lips pressed together, then signed out and back in. Nothing changed. Her friend beside her asked whether she had passed. Brianna answered that the number looked like a pass, though the label seemed to belong to another version of the page. She saved a screenshot and decided to ask the instructor before celebrating.

I opened my exam result in the greenhouse behind the school, where I volunteer after classes. The portal displayed 45 out of 50, followed by a red warning that said I had failed to meet the minimum score. I checked the course outline on my phone: the passing mark was 60 percent. Forty-five out of fifty was much higher than that. Maybe the warning belonged to an earlier attempt, but the page showed only one exam entry. I pressed the small arrow beside the warning; it led to a help page about attendance, not scores. Beside me, a sprinkler ticked across the seedlings. I read the result aloud, then laughed once without feeling amused. Before leaving, I copied the screen and sent my instructor a message asking whether the warning had been attached to the wrong record.

Dmitri checked his calculus grade in a crowded airport lounge, balancing his tablet on a backpack. The exam score read 72, while the course dashboard showed that same exam as worth 30 percent of the final grade. Yet the total displayed beside his name had dropped by twelve points overnight. He opened the grade calculator and entered the numbers from the syllabus. His result differed from the portal’s total by several points. He checked whether a missing assignment might account for the change, but every other row had a score. A boarding announcement interrupted him just as he reached the grade history. He saved the page and hurried to his gate, glancing back at the figures whenever the line paused. On the plane, he began a message to the registrar, including his calculation and a screenshot, and reread it carefully before sending.

I checked the exam portal from the pottery studio, my hands still dusty with clay. My literature essay had earned 93, but the feedback panel displayed comments about a physics formula and a diagram. I wondered whether the instructor had clicked the wrong file. The assignment title was correct, as was my student number, so I downloaded the feedback document and opened it separately. It belonged to someone named Elena, whose answers discussed gravity and mass. I closed it quickly, then returned to my own result. The score remained 93, without any comments about the essay I had submitted. My classmates were cleaning their tools, but I stayed by the sink, scrolling through the page for a way to report a privacy mistake. I found a contact link, described the mismatch without naming the other student, and sent the instructor a screenshot of the strange pairing.

At the neighborhood clinic, where he was waiting for his little brother’s appointment, Leon checked his economics exam grade. A bright green badge said “graded,” but the score field contained two dashes. He tapped the badge, opened the feedback tab, and found a note saying, “See attached rubric.” No attachment appeared. Leon pulled his laptop from his bag and signed in there, thinking the phone view might be incomplete. The same dashes waited on the larger screen. He checked the assignment list: his exam was the only item with a grade status but no number. The receptionist called his brother’s name, and Leon closed the laptop halfway, then opened it again before following. In the hallway, he drafted a message asking whether the score had been withheld intentionally or had failed to display, and checked the sent folder twice to make sure it had gone through.

I was visiting my aunt in a mountain town when I checked the exam site on her kitchen computer. My geography score appeared as 107 out of 100. I looked over my answers, trying to recall whether there had been bonus questions, but the exam instructions mentioned none. The grade history showed a previous entry of 71, then the new total, with no explanation between them. I reloaded the page and watched the number return unchanged. My aunt leaned over my shoulder and asked if I had discovered a secret extra-credit section. I shook my head and opened the rubric, where the listed points added up to exactly 100. I took a screenshot before the site could change its mind, then wrote to my instructor. I thanked them for the result but asked how the total had passed the exam’s maximum.

Nora checked her online exam grade during a quiet moment at the aquarium gift shop, where she worked weekends. The portal gave her 64 points, but the class average beside it was 18. She read the figures again, certain she had swapped the columns, then turned her phone sideways and enlarged the page. The labels stayed in place: “your score” and “class mean.” She opened the detailed results, which showed correct answers marked in blue and blank spaces where feedback might have appeared. A message on the course forum said several students were seeing unusual statistics, but no one explained what the numbers meant. Nora started a reply, erased it, and instead emailed her instructor with a screenshot. When a customer asked for a receipt, she tucked the phone away, yet kept returning to the posted grade whenever the counter was empty.

I set the table with the good blue plates, then moved one of them twice because my partner’s mother had said she preferred “the usual place.” At our apartment, every chair seemed usual to me. When her parents arrived, his father went straight to the kitchen and opened the cupboard beneath the sink. “Still here,” he said, smiling at a bottle of lemon oil. I glanced at Theo, who was already pouring drinks. During dinner, his mother passed the potatoes to an empty chair, then caught herself and set them down. Nobody explained. I watched their hands and waited for a clue in their faces. After dessert, I asked Theo about the cupboard. He kissed my cheek and said his parents used to live in this building. I looked at the sink again, wondering what else in our home belonged to a story I hadn’t heard.

Malik had planned a Moroccan dinner for his partner’s parents, even grinding the cumin by hand. When they arrived, Marjorie studied the spread and asked whether he had made the stew without onions. He had used three. Her husband, Len, leaned over the pot, sniffed, and announced that it smelled exactly right. Marjorie took a spoonful, then looked at Len as if he’d changed a rule mid-game. Malik glanced between them, holding the serving spoon in midair. The couple began discussing a recipe from their first apartment, each correcting the other’s measurements. Malik lowered the spoon, then raised it again when they both reached for the same bowl. At last Marjorie laughed and admitted she had meant garlic. Malik nodded, though his eyes flicked toward the chopped onion still visible beside her plate.

I chose a quiet Italian restaurant for dinner at home, which meant borrowing my neighbor’s folding chairs and asking my partner’s parents to arrive early. My partner, Jules, said her father liked surprises. He arrived carrying a paper bag and set a tiny brass bell beside my candles. “For the toast,” he told me. I waited for Jules to explain, but she was busy greeting her mother. After the first course, he rang the bell once. Everyone fell silent except me; I had just swallowed a mouthful of pasta. Her father looked at me expectantly. I lifted my glass, and he nodded, satisfied. Later, Jules said the bell was a family signal for whoever had cooked to speak. I stared at the small object in my hand. No one had mentioned that the cook was supposed to give a speech.

At twenty-four, Priya had never hosted anyone’s parents, so she wrote the evening’s schedule on the back of a grocery receipt. Her partner’s mother arrived with a cake, while his father carried a toolbox. He inspected the dining-room light, which had been flickering for weeks, and asked for a screwdriver before taking off his coat. Priya set out the soup, listening to the faint click above them each time the lamp blinked. Her partner, Owen, kept smiling as if this were ordinary. When the father finally sat down, he placed the repaired switch on the table beside the bread. Priya picked it up, then put it down again. “You always fix something when you visit?” she asked. His mother said he’d been an electrician for forty years. Owen quietly added that the light had been bothering him, and Priya’s spoon paused halfway to her mouth.

I had spent the afternoon making dumplings when my partner’s parents arrived with a jar of bright red sauce. His mother placed it beside my carefully arranged dipping bowls and asked if I remembered the “proper one.” I didn’t, though I smiled as if I might. At the table, everyone tasted my sauce first. His father chewed thoughtfully, then reached for the jar. His mother watched him, her fingertips tightening around her napkin. I held my chopsticks still while they whispered about a restaurant that had closed before I met their son. Then his father dipped a dumpling in the red sauce and grinned. “There it is,” he said. I looked from the jar to my own bowls, trying to identify what had just been found. My partner explained that his parents had searched for years to recreate a flavor from their first date.

Elliot hosted his partner’s parents in a small house outside Glasgow, where the dining room doubled as his painting studio. He had moved the canvases, but one unfinished portrait leaned behind the curtains. During dinner, his partner’s mother kept glancing toward that corner. Her husband asked about the empty frame above the mantel. Elliot said he hadn’t chosen what to put there. The mother smiled at her daughter, who was carefully separating peas from the roast. Their glances passed around the table without landing on Elliot. He set down his fork. “Is there something I’ve missed?” he asked, then immediately regretted how sharp it sounded. His partner finally said the portrait was meant to be a surprise: her parents had commissioned a painting of their old cottage. Elliot looked toward the hidden canvas, then at the blank frame, unsure which secret had been intended for him.

I was serving dinner when my partner’s father asked for the salt, though it sat beside his elbow. I passed it over, and he thanked me with an elaborate bow. His wife gave him a look that seemed to carry a whole conversation. I glanced at Lena, but she was arranging roasted carrots on her plate. The same thing happened with the pepper, then the butter. Each time, I handed over an object already within reach. When I finally asked if the table was too crowded, the father patted his jacket pocket. He had forgotten his reading glasses and was pretending the labels were too small to see. His wife laughed, and Lena admitted she’d known since the first request. I looked at the salt shaker, then at the man who had just asked me to read the label on a jar of jam.

At her first dinner with her partner’s parents, Leila made a careful list of dietary restrictions and taped it inside a cupboard door. The parents arrived bearing a loaf of bread and a bottle of wine. Her partner, Max, carried both to the kitchen, where his mother immediately began slicing the loaf with Leila’s serrated knife. Leila watched the crumbs scatter across the counter. “That one’s for the tomatoes,” she said, pointing to the knife. Max’s father lifted the bottle and asked whether it was the wine they had brought. Leila checked the label: it was a bottle she’d bought weeks ago, identical to theirs. The two men studied the matching labels as if comparing evidence. Max’s mother served bread, then said she had used that knife for everything in her own kitchen for thirty years. Leila quietly moved the tomatoes.

I made a seafood stew for my partner’s parents, who had driven in from a fishing town on the coast. His mother tasted it and asked whether I had added saffron. I shook my head. She nodded, then took another spoonful and asked again. My partner, Sam, busied himself with the wine. His father was watching the steam rise from the pot, one eyebrow lifted. I checked the recipe on my phone beneath the table, although I had followed it exactly. Then his mother asked if I’d used the blue bowl. I had. Everyone exchanged a look, and Sam finally explained that his grandmother served the stew in that bowl whenever she was announcing good news. I looked down at the plain ceramic rim. His parents had driven three hours, and now they were waiting for me to say something I had no idea I was supposed to announce.

Nina hosted her partner’s parents on the balcony of her high-rise apartment, hoping the city lights would make the simple meal feel special. His father stood near the railing and kept checking his watch. His mother asked how long the building had been there, then leaned over to inspect the planter boxes. Nina served grilled corn and waited for them to sit. Instead, both parents began counting the windows across the courtyard. Her partner, Luis, followed their gaze but offered no explanation. When a light came on in one particular apartment, his mother clapped once. His father looked relieved and finally joined them at the table. Nina held a platter against her hip, watching their faces brighten at a stranger’s window. Luis explained that his parents had lived across the courtyard years earlier, and the apartment belonged to an old friend. Nina glanced back at the lit windows, then at the untouched corn.

I hosted my partner’s parents in my new flat, where the oven had a habit of switching itself off. The roast was nearly ready when I opened the door and found the display blank. My partner’s mother said not to worry, then asked where I kept the matches. I pointed to a drawer. She and her husband exchanged a look before he went to the hallway and flicked a switch beside the coat rack. The oven came back on. I stood holding a carving fork while they resumed talking about the weather. At dinner, his father asked whether the kitchen had always been on that circuit. My partner stared at his plate. I followed their attention to the wall, where a small patch of paint was a shade lighter. They eventually explained that the flat had belonged to his aunt, who had wired the kitchen herself. I set down the fork and looked at the switch.

Darius invited his partner’s parents over for dinner in his home in New Orleans, serving red beans with rice and a crisp salad. His partner’s mother inspected the table, then asked where the extra plate was. Darius had set four. She looked at her husband, who shook his head, and then at the empty space beside their son. Darius carried another plate from the cupboard. Nobody used it. Throughout dinner, the parents occasionally glanced toward that place, while his partner kept telling stories about work. Darius adjusted the unused fork twice. After the meal, his partner’s father thanked him for setting the extra place, though he didn’t explain why. His mother wrapped a portion of rice in foil and tucked it into her bag. Only when they were leaving did his partner say the family always saved a seat for his late grandmother. Darius watched them walk away, the fourth plate still clean.

When Inez asked me to build a cabinet that would fit beneath her bakery’s sloping stairwell, she brought no measurements, only a brass key and a sketch of three crooked rectangles. I measured the space twice, then held the key against the drawing. “It opens something,” she said, and tucked it away before I could ask what. I made a cabinet with a narrow hidden compartment, though I had no reason to think the key would fit. On delivery day, Inez tried it in every lock on the cabinet, then stared at the blank wall behind it. She tapped the brass with one fingernail, lips moving as if counting. At last she put the key in the flour tin and smiled at the cabinet’s shelves. I went back to my shop turning over the sketch, still unsure whether I had built what she wanted or merely what she could describe.

Ravi, a retired bus driver, came to the workshop carrying a jar of buttons and a precise list of cabinet dimensions. He wanted a place to store his late wife’s sewing things, but kept changing the height of the shelves. Each time carpenter Moira asked what would go there, Ravi sorted the buttons by color, then gathered them back into the jar. “The blue ones used to be on top,” he said, though the jar had no compartments. Moira built adjustable shelves and left the pegs loose enough to move. When Ravi saw the finished cabinet, he opened every door, shut them, and opened the smallest one again. His fingers rested on the empty shelf. He asked whether a shelf could be made to remember where something belonged. Moira showed him the movable pegs. He nodded slowly, watching them as if they might answer a question he had not managed to ask.

I was hired to make a cabinet for a lighthouse keeper who insisted it needed a window. The requested cabinet would stand in his kitchen, nowhere near the lantern room, and he could not say what the window should look out on. I drew several designs while he paced beside my bench, stopping each time to inspect the grain of a different board. Finally, I built a small glass panel into one door. When I delivered it, he stood in front of the cabinet and leaned close to the pane. It reflected his face and the harbor behind him. He turned the cabinet toward the wall, then back toward the stove. “Not quite,” he murmured. I asked what he had expected to see. He rubbed the bridge of his nose and looked through the glass again. I left him with the cabinet and a set of curtains he had never requested.

At the community center, Lila asked carpenter Ben to build a cabinet for board games, but she brought a shoebox full of oddly shaped wooden pieces instead of a list. She arranged them across his worktable, then shifted them into a circle, then put them back in the box. Ben asked whether they belonged to one game. Lila studied a red piece with a tiny brass hinge and shrugged. The cabinet he made had broad shelves, deep drawers, and one small compartment with a latch. When it arrived, the center’s children crowded around it. Lila placed the pieces inside, one at a time, pausing before each choice. She opened the latched compartment, peered in, and closed it again. “That seems right,” she said, though her eyebrows stayed knitted. Ben asked if she wanted anything changed. She looked at the empty tabletop, then at the cabinet, as if expecting a missing clue to appear.

My client, Tomas, wanted a cabinet for his apartment’s narrow entryway, but he brought me a photograph of a room I didn’t recognize. In it, a small wooden door stood behind a chair. He asked me to copy the door’s proportions, then kept turning the photograph upside down. I asked if he knew what was behind it. “That’s the part I can’t tell,” he said, and pressed his thumb against the chair in the image. I built the cabinet with a miniature door on its front, fitted with a working brass knob. When I installed it, Tomas crouched to peer through the little opening. Inside was only a shallow shelf, exactly as planned. He blinked, closed the door, then opened it again. The photograph remained on his counter, now face down. He thanked me, but spent the evening moving the cabinet an inch in either direction.

Nora, a marine biologist, commissioned a cabinet for jars of shells in her coastal field station. She arrived with a notebook full of tide charts, yet none of the jars had labels. When carpenter Ellis asked where each should go, she rotated them until the shells inside shifted with a soft rattle. One jar held a single pale spiral; another seemed empty until sunlight caught a sliver near its base. Ellis built shelves of different depths and added a strip of blue glass across the top. Nora studied the finished cabinet, then rearranged every jar by height. She stopped at the apparently empty one and tilted it toward the light. “I thought there were two,” she said. Ellis checked the shelf and found no second jar. Nora opened her notebook, turned several pages, and traced a tide line with her finger. She asked him to leave one shelf bare, just in case.

I made custom cabinets for a train station café, where the owner, Ewan, wanted one drawer that would not open. He couldn’t explain why; he only pointed to a faded mark on the floor and said the old counter had stood there. I asked if something had been stored in that drawer. Ewan rubbed his palms on his apron and watched the rain crawl down the window. I built the cabinet with a false-front drawer, fixed securely in place. When I brought it in, he tried the handle once, then walked around to inspect the back. He tapped the wood at several spots, listening for a hollow sound. Nothing answered. “Maybe it was on the other side,” he said. I showed him the plans, but he frowned at the measurements as though the numbers had rearranged themselves. The cabinet fit perfectly, yet he kept glancing at the empty patch of floor beside it.

At her greenhouse, Marisol wanted a cabinet for seed packets, gardening tools, and one chipped teacup. Carpenter Jules offered a design with labeled drawers, but Marisol crossed out every label and drew a small moon on the sketch instead. She could not say whether the moon belonged on the door or inside. Jules carved it into both places. When the cabinet was finished, Marisol opened each drawer in a different order, then laid the teacup on the top shelf. She turned it so its handle faced the wall, reconsidered, and rotated it toward the aisle. “It used to sit somewhere,” she said, touching the rim. Jules asked whether she meant in the old shed. Marisol looked around the bright greenhouse, where seedlings leaned toward the glass. She picked up the cup and carried it to the potting bench, leaving the cabinet doors open behind her.

I was building a cabinet for a village archive when Arun, its new caretaker, brought me three keys and said only one belonged to the cabinet. He had no old cabinet to show me, just a paper tag marked with a date from forty years earlier. I cut three different locks into a sample board, and he tried the keys without looking at the tag. None turned. He tucked them into his pocket, then asked me to make the cabinet without a lock after all. I fitted simple brass pulls and delivered it the next week. Arun stood in front of it, holding the keys in his palm. He tested one against a drawer pull, then another against the hinge. “Perhaps it’s not for this,” he said. The archive room smelled of dust and wet wool. He opened the cabinet and placed the tag on an empty shelf, where he could see it whenever he walked past.

Delia, who repaired violins, wanted a cabinet for scraps of wood too small to use in instruments. She brought a bundle of pieces wrapped in a scarf and laid them out according to no pattern the carpenter, Oskar, could follow. A few were pale maple; others were dark and scorched at the edges. Delia shifted them whenever he reached for his pencil. “This one came from the first,” she said, pointing to a strip that looked like all the others. Oskar built shallow drawers so the pieces could lie flat, then added a broad work surface. Delia slid each scrap into a drawer, withdrew it, and tried another place. Her shoulders lifted each time two pieces nearly matched in color. At last she set one dark strip on the countertop. She asked Oskar whether the cabinet might have a drawer just for things that did not fit anywhere else. He added one beneath the others.

My neighbor Celso ordered a cabinet for the porch of his old farmhouse and insisted it needed to face the road. The porch had no road view, only a brick wall and a plum tree. I asked whether he planned to move it later. He shook his head, then unfolded a map with several roads drawn in pencil, none labeled. I built a sturdy cabinet with a pair of doors that opened outward. When I set it in place, Celso stood behind it, checking the view through the gaps between the slats. He moved one chair, then another, and asked me to turn the cabinet a few degrees. The doors now faced the tree. He stepped back, squinting at the branches. “That’s nearer,” he said, although nothing about the view had changed. I left him studying the map on the porch table, one finger resting on a road that ended at the edge of the paper.

At a small theater, costume designer Petra asked carpenter Lin to build a cabinet with exactly seven compartments. She had six masks to store and a bundle of feathers she would not put away. Lin measured everything twice and made the seventh compartment narrow enough for the feathers. Petra examined the cabinet, counting the openings under her breath. Then she counted again, touching each edge with one fingertip. She placed five masks inside and carried the sixth to the dressing room. When she returned, she had no feathers. She opened the narrow compartment, stared at its clean wooden interior, and shut it carefully. “I thought there were seven,” she said. Lin pointed to the compartments. Petra counted once more, starting from the bottom this time. After a pause, she laughed without much sound and asked him to leave the smallest space empty. The cabinet stood beneath the stage lights, its open doors casting long, uneven shadows.

I had been inching along Route 9 for twenty minutes when every car ahead turned on its hazard lights, though nothing blocked the road. A man in a delivery van leaned out and pointed toward the sky. I followed his finger, saw only a clear blue afternoon, then checked the traffic app; it showed a red warning shaped like a spoon. I tapped it, but the notice vanished. The radio host was discussing a missing parade balloon, which seemed unrelated until a silver elephant drifted above the overpass. Drivers began waving at it. I lowered my window and asked the woman beside me what was happening. She shrugged, then pointed to a street sign that had been turned backward. I read it twice, unable to make the letters settle into any familiar name. The line of cars stayed motionless while the balloon sailed on.

At the same intersection, Nia sat in her rideshare with a paper bag of pastries balanced on her knees. Traffic had stopped beneath a green light, and no one seemed willing to cross the painted line. A cyclist rolled up beside her window and silently held out a tiny plastic crown. Nia glanced at the driver, who shook his head as if the crown explained something. Then a school bus behind them played a tune that sounded like the first notes of “Happy Birthday,” stopping at exactly the same point each time. She checked the date on her phone; it was Tuesday, nowhere near anyone’s birthday. When the light changed, the cars ahead remained still. Nia twisted around to see whether an emergency vehicle was coming, but the street behind them was empty. The cyclist placed the crown on his helmet and pedaled away.

My train was delayed, so I had borrowed my sister’s car and joined the crawl on the beltway. A flock of geese occupied the lane ahead, walking in a neat line between bumpers. I expected them to move toward the verge, but they kept circling one parked hatchback. Its trunk was open, and a bright red umbrella stood upright inside, though there was no rain. The driver was nowhere in sight. I rolled forward a few feet, then stopped when the geese turned as one and stared at me. My phone’s map insisted I was driving through a lake. I refreshed it; the blue patch remained, complete with a little boat icon. I looked through the windshield at the dry asphalt, then down at the map again. A horn sounded behind me, but I could not tell which direction the suggested detour was supposed to go.

Darius, a night-shift baker, was trapped on the bridge with a tray of cooling rolls in the passenger seat. The traffic had not moved since sunset. Ahead, a road worker in a reflective vest stood beside a cone, repeatedly turning it around. Each time its hollow opening faced west, the brake lights dimmed for a moment; when he turned it east, they glowed red again. Darius watched the pattern, then leaned toward the windshield to make sure he had not imagined it. A woman in the next car lowered her window and asked the worker a question. He answered by pointing at the moon, which was still hidden behind clouds. Darius checked his dashboard clock, then the moon’s faint reflection in the side mirror. The worker set the cone down and walked away. The traffic stayed frozen, and the rolls gave off a warm, sweet smell.

I was driving home from a ceramics class when the expressway packed tight around a small green car. Its driver had put a handwritten sign in the rear window: PLEASE KEEP LEFT. There was no lane to the left, only a concrete divider. I read the words again at the next pause, wondering whether they were meant for us or for someone inside the car. A child in the back seat held up a paper drawing of a red door. The car’s turn signal blinked steadily, though it was parked in the middle lane. I checked the overhead signs; one announced a tunnel, the next promised an airport, and the third displayed a picture of a fish. My navigation voice kept saying, “Continue straight,” in a tone that sounded less certain each time. I gripped the steering wheel and watched the green car’s driver point toward the divider.

When the freeway slowed to a standstill, Omar noticed a woman in the next lane holding a bouquet of bananas. She was dressed for a formal dinner, complete with a silver necklace, and kept looking from the fruit to the clock on her dashboard. A minute later, a man on the shoulder waved a white handkerchief at the cars. Nobody responded, so he folded it into a paper airplane and sent it gliding over the roofs. It landed inside Omar’s open sunroof. He picked it up; a tiny map had been drawn on it, with a star marked where the traffic jam currently stood. Omar glanced at his navigation screen, which showed no roads at all, just a blinking star. The woman with the bananas began clapping slowly. He lowered his window to ask what she knew, but she pointed at the bouquet and mouthed a word he could not make out.

I was on my way to a job interview when the cars stopped beneath an enormous billboard advertising invisible paint. The picture showed a blank white wall and the words LOOK CLOSER. I leaned toward the glass, but the wall remained blank. Then the billboard’s digital clock began counting upward instead of down, jumping from 4:12 to 19:03 and then to a string of symbols. The truck ahead had a ladder tied to its roof; a single red mitten hung from one rung. I checked the time on my phone, and it was exactly the same as the billboard’s first number. My interview address appeared in my calendar, then changed to “near the water.” I had no idea which water it meant. A horn blared behind me. I looked in the mirror, then back at the sign, hoping one of them would offer a usable clue.

Sofia had just finished a long shift at the aquarium when the traffic on Harbor Avenue stopped outside a dry-cleaning shop. In the shop window, a goldfish swam through a glass bowl, but the bowl sat on a shelf with no water in it. She blinked and looked again. The fish was still there, flicking its tail as if it were perfectly comfortable. A taxi driver beside her rolled down his window and asked whether she could see it too. Before she answered, the pedestrian signal began showing a white hand holding a tiny umbrella. The rain had ended hours earlier. Sofia searched the cross street for a parade, a film crew, or some explanation, but found only a man carrying an empty birdcage. The lights changed twice. No cars moved, and the fish turned in a slow circle.

I was driving my father’s old pickup through downtown when a traffic jam formed around a bus stop with no bus shelter. Three people there were holding identical cardboard boxes, each marked with a different weekday. One said MONDAY, another THURSDAY, and the third had a calendar square with no number. They took turns setting the boxes on the curb, then lifting them again whenever a car honked. I checked my own calendar at a red light: Friday. The navigation system announced that I had arrived, even though I was still surrounded by bumpers and had not entered any street number. I looked at the address on the envelope in my passenger seat; it was written in my father’s handwriting, but the final digit had been rubbed away. The person with the blank calendar square pointed at my truck. I opened my mouth to ask why, then the line lurched forward.

Evelyn, a retired violinist, sat in the passenger seat while her grandson steered through heavy traffic. Every car ahead had its windshield wipers moving, despite the dry weather. The wipers beat in different rhythms until, one by one, they matched the tune Evelyn used to play before concerts. She recognized the melody but could not recall its name. Her grandson turned off their wipers; the cars around them continued tapping out the notes. A motorcycle courier pulled alongside and handed her a yellow envelope through the open window. It was addressed to “the person who remembers the ending.” Evelyn examined the blank back, then looked at the stopped traffic stretching toward the horizon. She asked her grandson whether he had ordered anything. He shook his head. The courier had already vanished between lanes. She held the envelope to the light, searching for writing that would tell her what ending it meant.

I was late for a dentist appointment when the avenue became a slow-moving parade of cars, though there were no floats or marching bands. A small dog in a raincoat trotted between the lanes carrying a feather twice its size. Drivers lowered their windows to watch it. The dog stopped beside my car and dropped the feather on my hood. I waited for its owner to call, but no one came forward. A billboard overhead displayed my car’s color, then changed to a picture of a door with a number I recognized from the appointment reminder. I checked the reminder again; the clinic was three miles away, not above the road. My dashboard compass spun in a full circle and settled pointing at the dog. I reached for the feather, then hesitated. The dog sat, tilted its head, and barked once. Behind me, several horns answered in different pitches.

Keon was driving his mother to the airport when a jam stopped them beside a construction site. A crane held a steel beam perfectly still in midair, while its operator leaned from the cab and studied a sandwich. The beam’s shadow moved across the road in the shape of a clock hand, pointing first at the airport, then at Keon’s dashboard. His mother checked her watch; it had stopped at 2:17. Keon’s phone showed 2:17 too, though the minute had passed several times on the car radio. He asked the driver in front whether he knew what was going on. The man lifted a newspaper with its pages turned to a blank sheet. A worker in a hard hat walked over and tapped their hood twice, then pointed toward an exit sign that seemed to lead into the construction site itself. Keon looked at his mother, waiting for her to make sense of it.

I had run my bicycle-repair shop for six years before applying for a loan to add a second workbench. The bank’s website asked for “seasonal operating figures,” though my income barely changed from month to month. I entered the same totals in two boxes, then erased one when a warning appeared. At the branch, the loan officer tapped a page with her pen and asked whether I had included “noncash adjustments.” I looked at the neat columns I had prepared and turned them sideways, as if another angle might reveal what I had missed. “Is that the equipment depreciation?” I asked. She nodded, then pointed to a different line. I rubbed the bridge of my nose and checked my folder again. The figures matched my accountant’s report, yet the form seemed to be asking for a story the numbers weren’t telling. I left with a checklist and no new workbench.

At forty-eight, Soraya had built a thriving bakery in a converted laundromat, and she wanted a loan for a delivery van. The application asked for collateral, so she listed her ovens, mixer, and refrigerated display case. A clerk called the next day to say the bank preferred “liquid assets.” Soraya opened her books on the counter and studied the phrase, her flour-dusted finger hovering over the page. She had cash in the business account, but it was earmarked for payroll and butter orders. When she explained this, the clerk said the money still counted, then mailed a form asking for the account’s “available balance.” Soraya set the phone down and read the two pages side by side. Her eyebrows drew together. She phoned her bookkeeper, who was also unsure what the bank meant by available. That afternoon, Soraya drove to the branch with both forms and asked someone to point to the exact number.

I run a tiny kayaking outfitter on the Oregon coast, and I applied for a loan to replace our aging trailer. The online form wanted a monthly rent figure, but my shop sits on land leased by the harbor, with fees that shift according to the season. I tried averaging them, then the site rejected my entry because it contained a decimal. At the credit union, a staff member told me to use the “base occupancy cost.” I wrote that down on the back of a receipt and stared at it while gulls wheeled above the parking lot. Was the dock fee part of it? What about the storage shed? I could explain every charge to a customer, yet here I kept opening my ledger to the same two pages. The loan officer waited kindly as I sorted my papers into little piles. Finally, I asked her to show me a completed example.

Milan, a former school librarian, wanted a loan to expand his neighborhood bookshop into the empty unit next door. The bank’s estimate of his monthly payments differed from the calculator on its own website by nearly eighty dollars. He printed both figures and carried them to the appointment in a blue folder. The loan officer glanced at the pages and said one included a “rate adjustment.” Milan traced the figures with a capped pen, stopping at each column as though the discrepancy might be hiding between them. “Does that happen every year?” he asked. The officer began describing an index, then paused to draw a small chart. Milan nodded at the right moments but kept turning the paper toward the window, where the numbers looked sharper. He didn’t want to sign until he could explain the payment to his partner. Before leaving, he asked for the calculation in writing and tucked it carefully beside the application.

I make custom dance costumes in a room above a florist, and I applied for a small loan to buy a better sewing machine. The application asked how many employees I had. I work alone most days, but two dressmakers help me during festival season. I entered zero, then changed it to two, then hovered over the help icon. It defined an employee as someone paid through payroll. My helpers invoice me, so I put zero again. At the branch, the adviser asked about “contract labor” and pointed to a different section. I held my reading glasses in one hand and my pencil in the other, flipping between the pages until the corners bent. “So I’m not counting them here?” I asked. She said that depended on the question.
