When footsteps approached, he stopped it and folded his hands; the steps passed by. He looked at the clock, then at the door, then at the clock again. A poster about teamwork hung slightly crooked, and he used its angle to focus his eyes while drawing a slow breath. The receptionist appeared to say the director had been called to another ward. Darnell thanked her, voice even, and asked whether there was anything else he could prepare. After she left, he turned his résumé face down so he would stop reading it.

I waited in the back room of a bike shop, surrounded by frames hanging from the ceiling. The manager had asked me to come early for a mechanic position, and I had taken that as a sign to arrive forty minutes ahead. Grease darkened the cuffs of my work shirt, though I had washed my hands twice. I rubbed my palms on my thighs, noticed the marks, and stopped. A clock above the tool bench had no second hand, which somehow made the silence worse. I reviewed the repair challenge I had completed for them, then worried I had tightened one bolt too firmly. The shop bell rang out front. I stood, sat, and stood again before a customer wandered into the room asking for a pump. I helped him find one, grateful for a task. When the manager came through the curtain, I was holding the pump like a shield.

At the airport hotel, Elise waited outside a ballroom where the interview panel had gathered. Her suitcase stood beside her because she had flown in that morning, and its handle kept slipping down whenever she leaned on it. She checked the pocket containing her printed references, then checked it again with a quick pat. Voices drifted through the double doors, followed by a burst of laughter. Elise tried to decide whether they were discussing work or a story from lunch. Her mouth had gone dry, so she took a sip from the bottle in her tote and nearly missed the opening. A staff member passed carrying a stack of name cards. Elise asked whether the panel was running behind, and the question came out thinner than she intended. The staff member said only a few minutes. Elise nodded, straightened her jacket, and silently counted five breaths before looking at the doors again.

I sat in the public library’s glass study room, waiting for a video interview with a software company. My laptop showed my own face in a small preview window, and I kept adjusting the angle until the books behind me looked straight. The internet icon flickered once. I leaned closer to the screen, then forced myself back into the chair. A librarian wheeled a cart past the door; each squeak made me glance up. My notes were arranged beside the keyboard, but I had written the same three project names at the top of two pages. I turned one sheet over and pressed its corner flat. The meeting link said the interviewer would join shortly. I tested my microphone again, though the meter had already responded. When the connection chime sounded, I inhaled too sharply, clicked the camera on, and greeted the empty screen before the other person appeared.

Tomas waited in a converted warehouse office with exposed brick and a large metal clock. He had applied to manage the building’s community programs, and the interview was due to start at ten. At ten past, he asked the receptionist if he had misunderstood the room number. She checked her screen and assured him the panel was finishing another meeting. Tomas thanked her, then stood beside the window and watched buses pull away from the curb. He had planned to mention his work with neighborhood teenagers, but now he kept replaying one awkward answer from a practice session. His fingers curled around the edge of his résumé until the paper bent. He eased his grip and smoothed it against his knee. A door opened at the far end of the hall. Tomas squared his shoulders, but it was a courier with a package. He gave a small laugh at himself, then returned to his chair.

I waited in a greenhouse office for the head gardener to interview me about a seasonal position. Damp air clung to my sleeves, and every leaf seemed to shine under the glass roof. I had brought a notebook, but my pen kept slipping between my fingers. A watering system clicked on nearby, sending a fine spray against the panes. I read the job description again and reached the line about weekend shifts, though I already knew it by heart. My knee moved beneath the chair. I pressed both shoes flat to the tile and listened to the rain outside, trying to separate it from the water pattering overhead. When a woman in muddy boots appeared, I sprang up and knocked my notebook onto the floor. She caught it before I could. “You must be the candidate,” she said. I thanked her, cheeks warm, and followed her between the rows of seedlings.

Mina sat in the reception area of a radio station while a producer finished an interview in the studio. Through the glass, she could see a microphone and a red recording light, but not the person speaking. She had prepared a pitch for a reporting role and mouthed its first line without sound. Her reflection in the dark window moved with her, lips shaping the words a beat later. She stopped and folded her hands together. The receptionist offered a magazine, but Mina declined, then immediately wished she had something to look at. A burst of laughter came from the studio speakers. She checked the time on her phone, opened a message from her brother, and typed “all good” before deleting it. The studio door finally opened. Mina rose, tucked her phone away, and found that the strap of her bag had twisted around her wrist. She freed it as the producer called her name.

I waited for the interview in a small room above a hardware store, where the heating rattled every few minutes. The company sold custom cabinets, and I had applied to draw plans for customers. My sample sketches lay on the table, aligned with the edge, then realigned after I noticed one corner drifting. I could hear someone downstairs testing a drill. Each sudden burst made my shoulders jump before I could stop them. The office assistant said the owner would come up soon and went back to her desk. I practiced describing a kitchen project under my breath, but the words sounded too fast, so I started over. A framed photograph of a finished cabinet hung opposite me; I stared at its tiny brass handles and counted them. When footsteps climbed the stairs, I stood and clipped my portfolio shut. The owner appeared carrying two coffees, and I had to remind myself to accept one.

At the university’s marine science building, June waited outside a professor’s office for an interview about a research assistant position. Her backpack rested between her shoes, zipped and zipped again after she noticed the pull tab was crooked. A tank in the corridor held a slow-moving octopus. June watched one arm curl around a rock, then realized she had been holding her breath. She let it out carefully and checked the notes on her phone. The professor had asked applicants to discuss fieldwork, and June’s best example involved a boat engine that had failed miles from shore. She wondered if the story made her sound careless, despite the team’s safe return. A student hurried past carrying wet boots, leaving small prints on the floor. June wiped one mark with her sleeve, then stopped when the office door opened. She picked up her backpack and greeted the professor with a smile that took effort to hold.

The dispatch crackled while I was tightening a bootlace: smoke reported behind a row of shops, with people possibly upstairs. My fingers fumbled the knot twice. At the station, I checked my mask, then checked it again, though Mateo had already tapped the green gauge. The engine lurched through wet streets, and I counted each traffic light under my breath. Behind the shops, a baker waved us toward a narrow stairwell, flour whitening his sleeves. I climbed with the hose, keeping my breaths measured as heat pressed through the door above. A child sat on the landing, clutching a toy rabbit, while smoke curled from a laundry room. I passed the child to my partner and helped smother a scorched dryer. Outside, the baker kept thanking us. I nodded, unable to make my hands stop trembling until I had packed the hose.

At fifty-eight, Darnell had learned to read a room before stepping into it, but the radio call gave him little to work with: a vehicle in a ditch, driver not seen. He left his coffee untouched and climbed aboard, rubbing a thumb over the seam of his glove. Snow swept across the highway when the crew arrived. Darnell crouched beside the car, calling through the broken window while his gaze flicked between the dark interior and the passing trucks. No answer. He signaled for the jaws of life, then changed the plan when he spotted a boot beneath a blanket in the back seat. The driver was conscious, wedged against the door. Darnell kept his voice low and steady as they freed her. After the ambulance pulled away, he stared at the tire tracks until his captain asked him twice to come back to the engine.

I was halfway through helping my daughter with her science project when the pager announced an apartment fire. The glue on my fingertips caught on my turnout coat, and I had to pull free before running outside. At the address, residents crowded the sidewalk in slippers, each asking whether someone had checked the top floor. I followed the crew up the stairwell, repeating the apartment number so I wouldn’t lose it among the alarms. A kitchen pan had flared, filling the unit with smoke, and an elderly tenant was coughing beside the open window. We guided her out, then checked every room. On the ride back, I noticed a streak of glitter from the project across my sleeve. My daughter had planned to make a model volcano. I pressed my palms flat on my knees and watched the station lights approach, already trying to remember which supplies we still needed.

Sana was driving the brush truck when the call came from a campground on the ridge. A wind-driven grass fire had crossed the access road, and several campers were unaccounted for. She gripped the wheel hard enough to pale her knuckles, then loosened one hand to point out the safest route. Dust and pine needles battered the windshield. At the campsite, she assigned two crew members to the cabins and carried a hose toward a picnic shelter where an older man stood frozen beside a cooler. Sana asked him to walk with her, one step at a time. He kept looking back for his dog, so she sent a firefighter to search the nearby tent. They found the animal under a table. Once everyone was beyond the road, Sana checked the map again, tracing the route with a finger that would not stay still.

My first call as acting captain was a report of smoke in a school auditorium during a weekend dance recital. Parents poured toward the doors while a teacher insisted every child had been counted. I asked her to count again as the crew entered, and the numbers kept slipping from my head whenever the alarm blared. We found a haze near the lighting booth, where a cable had begun to burn. The crew cut power and put out the small fire. I walked the rows with the teacher, touching each seatback as we checked beneath them. Everyone was outside, though one little boy had hidden behind a curtain because he thought the alarms meant he was in trouble. I crouched until he came with me. Later, I wrote the incident report three times, crossing out the same sentence whenever the pen dug through the paper.

Eli, a volunteer firefighter who worked days at a fish market, was rinsing scales from his hands when the call came: a boat fire at the marina. He arrived still smelling of salt and lemon soap. Flames flickered inside a cabin, and a woman on the dock kept pointing toward a neighboring vessel tied close by. Eli helped stretch a line across the slick planks, glancing down each time his boots shifted. The owner said his medication was aboard, then changed which compartment he meant. Eli asked him to stay behind the tape while another firefighter searched the boat after the flames were contained. When they found the bag, the owner began laughing and crying at once. Eli carried it over carefully. Back at the market, he scrubbed his hands longer than necessary, watching the water circle the drain.

The call sent us to a house where a smoke alarm had been sounding for nearly an hour. I expected an empty place, but a teenager opened the door, holding a wet towel over her mouth. She said her grandfather was asleep in the back room. I moved quickly, then caught myself rushing ahead of the hose team and stepped aside. Smoke leaked from a pot left on the stove; the grandfather was awake but confused by the noise. We guided him out while my partner handled the burner. On the porch, the girl kept apologizing for calling, twisting the towel into a rope. I told her she had done the right thing, then checked the address on my tablet though I already knew it. The engine ride back seemed unusually loud. I folded and refolded the same glove, trying to get its fingers to lie flat.

Marlene had promised her brother she would make his retirement dinner, but the dispatch tone sent her toward a warehouse instead. A worker had fallen from a loading platform, and a forklift blocked the nearest entrance. Marlene directed the crew around the building, her jaw working as she listened to overlapping radio reports. Inside, the injured man was awake, pinned beneath a pallet. She knelt beside him and asked about his breathing while the team stabilized the load. His jokes came too quickly, and Marlene matched them with a calm voice, though she kept wiping her palms on her trousers. They lifted the pallet enough to slide him onto a board. At the hospital entrance, he thanked her by name. She checked the clock, then called her brother to say dinner would be late. In the background, the engine radio crackled with another address.

I had just settled into the station bunk after a double shift when a call came in for a carbon monoxide alarm at a small motel. I sat up so fast my shoulder struck the wall. The hallway smelled of detergent and old carpet; the guests stood outside in coats over pajamas, asking whether they could go back in. I checked the meter at each doorway, calling out the readings while my partner opened windows. One room showed a dangerous level near a faulty heater. A family had been sleeping there, including a baby who was quiet in its mother’s arms. We moved them to the ambulance for evaluation. I wrote down the room number on my glove, then copied it onto the report because the first note had blurred. At dawn, I washed my face in the station sink and watched the water run over the same spot twice.

At the dispatch center, Noor heard a report of smoke coming from a church basement during a winter food drive. She passed the address to the crew and rode along, gripping the clipboard against her knees. Volunteers had left pots warming on a stove while they carried groceries upstairs. A scorched towel smoldered near one burner, and smoke had settled beneath the low ceiling. Noor helped guide the volunteers out, pausing to make sure an older man with a cane had both feet on the steps. He kept asking about the soup. Once the crew extinguished the towel and checked the kitchen, Noor returned for the donation list, which had been left beside the sink. She read every line twice before handing it to the coordinator. Outside, flakes of snow stuck to her eyelashes as she waited for the radio to confirm the building was clear.

When the call came, I was repairing a bicycle chain in the station bay. A small fire had started in a greenhouse, and the owner feared the neighboring homes would catch. My grease-blackened fingers slipped on the helmet buckle, so I wiped them on a rag and tried again. At the property, rows of glass panes reflected the orange glow from a heater surrounded by dry cardboard. We pulled a line around the side rather than crossing the brittle walkway. The owner kept offering directions, then interrupting himself to point at different doors. I asked him to stand with the police officer while we worked. The flames went out quickly, but we checked the soil beds and storage shed for hidden heat. During cleanup, I found the bicycle chain still lying on the concrete. I picked it up, put it in my pocket, and forgot it was there until it clinked against my keys at home.

Jasper had been counting the minutes until his shift ended when dispatch sent the crew to a remote cabin. A caller reported a chimney fire, and the access road was barely wide enough for the engine. Jasper watched the tree branches scrape along the mirrors, then checked the map for a turn they had already passed. At the cabin, an exhausted couple stood outside in socks, their dog circling their legs. Smoke rose from the chimney, but the roof was still intact. Jasper climbed the ladder with a hose while his partner entered to inspect the stove. The couple asked the same question several times: would the house be safe? He answered plainly each time, keeping his eyes on the roofline. Once the chimney was clear, Jasper helped the dog into the truck cab. He returned to the station and found his shift had ended forty minutes earlier.

I was nine when I brought my blue plastic rocket to Willow Bend Park, tucked under my arm like a precious delivery. Dad had said we could stay only until the clouds reached the water tower, and I kept checking them while trying to climb the rope net. When I reached the top, the rocket was gone. I searched my jacket, then the ground, then every rung I had just crossed. My fingers kept catching on the rough rope, and my voice came out too loud when I asked the other children. I pictured my little brother waiting at home to borrow it. A groundskeeper spotted it beside the drinking fountain, where a toddler had set it down. I clutched it all the way to the gate, barely hearing Dad say we could stay a little longer.

At six, Mateo carried a knitted fox everywhere, including the neighborhood park where his aunt met friends after work. He noticed it missing when the swings had already begun to slow. His shoulders rose toward his ears as he checked the bench, the slide, and the patch of clover where he had eaten crackers. Each time someone crossed the path, he turned quickly, hoping to see the fox in their hands. His aunt offered to retrace their route, but Mateo shook his head and started searching again, faster now. A girl near the sandbox held up one orange paw; the fox had snagged beneath her bucket. Mateo took it carefully and pressed its soft nose to his cheek. On the walk home, he kept one hand wrapped around its tail.

I was twelve, and the park basketball court was crowded enough that I had to leave my sketchbook beside the picnic table. My favorite toy, a tiny wind-up penguin, sat on top of it, ready for my cousin to see. After a game, the table was empty. I checked underneath, then hurried along the path, scanning every pair of shoes and every stroller. My jaw hurt from clenching it. I tried to remember whether I had carried the penguin toward the drinking fountain, but the game replayed in my head in scattered flashes. A boy waved from the tennis fence: he had found it near a drain. One flipper was bent, but it still waddled when I wound the key. I slipped it into my pocket and walked back slowly, counting each step.

Nia, who was eight, brought a small green dinosaur to the park while her grandmother practiced tai chi nearby. She placed it on the low stone wall before joining a game of tag. When she returned, only a pale square of dust remained. Nia stopped mid-step. Her hands opened and closed at her sides as she searched beneath the wall and around the bushes. She asked the children nearby, but the words came out in a thin rush, one question tumbling into another. Her grandmother calmly suggested they look toward the pond. Nia followed, watching the reeds move in the breeze. The dinosaur was perched on a duck-feeding sign, its tail caught in a crack. She lifted it free and wiped its feet against her shirt, then stayed close to her grandmother for the rest of the afternoon.

I had just turned five when I took my yellow toy bus to the park near our apartment. I liked rolling it along the painted lines while my mother pushed my baby sister. Then a dog barked beside the climbing frame, and I dropped the bus as I covered my ears. When the noise stopped, the bus was nowhere beside me. I tugged at my mother's sleeve so hard she nearly lost her grip on the stroller. We looked behind the slide and around the benches. My throat felt tight, and I kept saying, “It was right here,” even when we were already checking somewhere else. A boy in a red cap found it lodged in the sandbox tunnel. I held it against my chest and let my mother carry me to the path.

Fourteen-year-old Ellis rarely brought toys outside, but a wooden yo-yo carved by his grandfather traveled in his coat pocket. At the park, he showed a younger neighbor how to make it climb the string. Later, while helping set up a picnic, he realized the pocket was empty. He searched the grass in widening circles, brushing leaves aside with both hands. His breathing turned quick, and he kept glancing toward the street as if the toy might have rolled there. The neighbor retraced their steps and found it beneath the bench where they had practiced. A small chip marked the painted side. Ellis rubbed it with his thumb, then tied the string securely around his finger. He thanked the child twice, though the first time his voice barely carried over the park fountain.

I was seven and had brought my stuffed rabbit to the park because its ear needed sunshine after a wash. I set it beside me on the picnic blanket while I chased soap bubbles with my cousins. When we packed up, the rabbit was missing. I ran back and forth between the blanket spot and the play structure, breathing through my mouth and forgetting which way I had already checked. My cousin asked me to slow down, but my feet kept moving. I imagined telling my father I had lost the toy he had sewn for me, and my eyes prickled. Then I noticed a corner of faded cloth beneath the blanket folded in the stroller basket. I pulled the rabbit out, dusty but whole, and held it under my chin. We left together, my hand gripping its paw.

Rafi, age ten, had a miniature red submarine that he liked to launch down the smooth park slide. He set it on the bench while he went to fill his water bottle. On returning, he found a family had gathered around the spot, and the submarine had vanished. Rafi asked each person, trying to keep his voice even, but his words came clipped at the ends. He crouched to inspect the ground, then checked the nearby trash bin and the edge of the pond. His ears felt hot beneath his cap. A toddler eventually emerged from behind the slide, holding the toy and making engine sounds. Rafi knelt and explained that it belonged to him. The toddler's father handed it over with an apology. Rafi nodded, wiped the red hull on his shorts, and put it deep in his backpack.

I was eleven, and the park was where I went when the apartment upstairs got too loud. My little wind-up mouse usually made me laugh, so I brought it along and set it by the chess tables. A sudden gust scattered my papers. I gathered them, but when I looked back, the mouse was gone. I checked under every table, moving so quickly that a man had to step aside. My stomach seemed to twist tighter each time I came up empty. I kept replaying the gust, trying to see whether the toy had rolled away with my notes. A woman who had been feeding pigeons pointed toward a flower bed. The mouse had stopped against a stone border. I picked it up, wound the key, and watched it scurry across my palm before slipping it safely into my pocket.

At three, Lottie carried a plush moon in a canvas tote to the park where her older brother played soccer. While their father watched the match, she took the moon out and sat beneath a maple. Later, she climbed onto the low playground bridge, leaving the tote behind. The moon was gone when she returned. Lottie pressed her lips together and stared at the empty bag, then tugged at her father's sleeve without speaking. He walked her along the path, asking where she had stopped. She pointed in several directions, each gesture smaller than the last. Near the soccer goal, a player had noticed the toy and placed it on the scoreboard ledge. Lottie reached up with help, then held the moon over her head as if checking that it was still there. Her father carried the tote for the walk home.

I was thirteen when my aunt took me to a lakeside park before my first week at a new school. I had brought a little brass compass toy from my old desk, though its needle barely worked. I sat on the pier to show it to her, then joined a group tossing stones. When I returned, the compass had disappeared. I searched the boards one by one, kneeling until my jeans darkened with lake spray. My thoughts kept jumping to the bus ride home, the new classrooms, and the things I had not packed. Aunt Salma asked me to breathe with her, but I still scanned the water between breaths. A park worker had found the compass beside a post and kept it at the information kiosk. I thanked him, closed my fist around it, and let my aunt choose the route back.

Six-year-old Juniper brought a felt owl to the park's community garden, where her father volunteered on Saturdays. She set it on a crate while helping water the seedlings. Afterward, the crate was empty. Juniper went still, then began checking every planter, lifting leaves with careful fingers that soon started to tremble. She called for her father, but her voice was swallowed by the hose and nearby chatter. He shut off the water and asked what the owl looked like. Juniper described its mismatched button eyes, repeating the details as they searched. A volunteer found it nestled inside a watering can, where someone had placed it to keep it from the mud. Juniper held the owl close and examined its buttons. Her father offered to finish the watering. She stayed beside him, watching the can from then on.

At 11:40 p.m., I watched the release countdown shrink beside the build button. One test had turned red, though it had passed all afternoon. I rubbed the heel of my hand over my eyes, then ran it again. The same failure appeared. My tea had gone cold; I drank it anyway while tracing the log line by line. When my sister called to ask whether I was still coming to breakfast, I said, “Probably,” and muted the phone before she could answer. A tiny change in the payment module fixed the test, but the full suite would take twenty minutes. I paced between my desk and the dark kitchen, checking the progress bar whenever I passed. At the final green check, I let out a breath I had been holding and clicked publish. The confirmation took three seconds to arrive.

Niko had promised the museum director that the new audio-guide app would be ready before the doors opened. At dawn, a crash appeared on the oldest borrowed tablet, the exact model the school groups used. He crouched beside the charger cart, plugging and unplugging the device while his laptop balanced on a folded coat. Each restart showed a different percentage, and his fingers tapped the floor in a quick, uneven rhythm. The director appeared in the doorway with a box of brochures. Niko smiled too broadly and said the final check was underway. He found the culprit in a sound file with an extra space in its name. After correcting it, he watched the test finish without blinking. The app loaded, the guide spoke, and Niko finally sat back against the wall as the first visitors entered.

I had one hour before the launch of my neighborhood weather app, and the map kept placing the river on the wrong side of town. My laptop fan whined while I compared coordinates with a paper atlas spread across the café table. A barista set down my sandwich; I moved it without looking, nearly sweeping it onto the floor. The launch page was already public, and three friends had sent screenshots of the crooked map. I typed an apology, deleted it, then reopened the data file. The mistake came from an old sample dataset I had forgotten to replace. I corrected it and pushed a new build, but the upload stalled at ninety-eight percent. My knee bounced against the table leg as I watched. When the map refreshed correctly, I texted the friends a link and took one careful bite of the untouched sandwich.

At a coworking space above a bakery, Amara was trying to ship a language-learning update before the morning announcement. The release checklist lay open beside her keyboard, every item crossed out except one: verify offline lessons. The building's Wi-Fi blinked out just as she began. She pressed her lips together, tethered her laptop to her phone, and watched the battery icon drop. Her colleague offered to take over, but Amara answered with a sharp “I’ve got it,” then softened her voice and thanked him. The offline files opened on her test device, yet one lesson displayed blank illustrations. She searched the asset folder, hands moving faster than her eyes, until she found a mismatched filename. Once fixed, the package passed. She submitted it, then stood at the window, flexing her fingers while the bakery downstairs rolled up its shutters.

The launch was scheduled for noon, and I was still trying to make my budgeting tool export a clean spreadsheet. My father had asked me to build it for his repair shop, so the blank cells felt personal. I ran the export, saw the same broken column, and dragged both hands through my hair. A delivery cart rattled past my apartment door; I flinched, then laughed at myself. I opened a copy of the file and tested each field separately, whispering the names as if they might behave better that way. The date format was slipping whenever a customer had no phone number. I patched the condition and ran the report again. At 11:56, the columns lined up. I sent Dad the download link and watched the message sit unread. Then I refreshed the launch page twice, though nothing there could change.

Ravi, a retired teacher turned software developer, had never shipped anything to thousands of people at once. His reading app was due to launch at the start of the library's summer program, and the final build refused to install on an older phone. He kept a handwritten list of each attempt, but the page now held arrows, crossed-out numbers, and a coffee ring. His shoulders crept toward his ears as he compared the system logs. When his grandson asked if the app was ready, Ravi replied, “Almost,” without lifting his eyes. The error came from a permission the newer phones granted automatically. He added a clear prompt, rebuilt the package, and tested it on the old device. The screen filled with book covers. Ravi smoothed the crumpled checklist flat, then called the librarian to say the download was available.

I was releasing a tiny game I had made between shifts at the aquarium, and the launch window began in fifteen minutes. Just before upload, the final level froze when a player collected a pearl. I leaned close to the screen until my nose nearly touched it, then backed away and read the code aloud. My roommate asked whether I wanted dinner; I answered, “In a minute,” though the microwave clock had already changed twice. The bug came from a counter that kept running after the level ended. I added a stop condition and started the build. While it compiled, I sorted pens by color, then immediately scattered them looking for the blue one. The test level ran cleanly. I uploaded the game with two minutes to spare and watched the download page load on my phone, thumb hovering over refresh.

Elise's coastal mapping project was set to launch during a public science fair, where visitors would use it to report beach litter. On the morning of the event, the location pin landed miles inland. She pulled a folding chair close to the laptop and examined the newest changes, jaw working as she scrolled. The volunteer coordinator kept glancing at the clock and arranging the same stack of flyers. Elise asked for five quiet minutes, then turned off the location cache and tested again. A warning appeared, followed by another. She pressed her fingertips against her temples, read each message, and corrected the outdated permission setting. The pin settled on the beach. A volunteer tried the form and submitted a report about a bottle beside the pier. Elise nodded, saved the release, and stepped outside to help set up the first display.

My clinic appointment app was supposed to go live before the small practice opened, and the printer beside my desk kept spitting out test pages. A nurse had found that cancellations vanished from the schedule, so I replayed the steps on a spare account. The clock's second hand seemed louder than the computer. I kept clicking my pen until the tip snapped, then gathered the little pieces from the keyboard. The bug appeared only when a patient changed the appointment twice. I followed the records through the database and found an old value overwriting the newer one. After the fix, I tried the sequence again, then asked the nurse to check it on her tablet. She gave me a thumbs-up. I pushed the release, wiped the ink from my fingers, and finally noticed the printer had run out of paper.

In the back room of a bicycle shop, Mateo was preparing a repair-tracking app for its first customers. The launch email was ready, but the barcode scanner stopped recognizing frames with a certain prefix. He moved his stool closer to the router, though the signal bars stayed stubbornly low. His heel drummed against a box of inner tubes while he switched between the scanner and his code editor. The shop owner asked if the system could wait until tomorrow. Mateo said it could, then immediately reopened the test logs. A leading zero was being stripped before the lookup ran. He changed the parser and scanned a dozen labels, one after another. Each result appeared correctly. When the owner tested a customer’s bike, Mateo watched the screen over his shoulder, hands clasped so tightly his knuckles paled. The record appeared, and the owner grinned.

I promised the farmers' market that my ordering site would open at sunrise. At 5:20, the basket total doubled whenever someone changed a quantity, and the first vendor was already texting me screenshots. I sat on the kitchen floor with the laptop plugged into the wall, surrounded by charging cables. My toast cooled beside me while I replayed the checkout. I muttered the numbers under my breath, then checked them on a scrap of paper. A stale value was being added instead of replaced. I corrected the calculation and tested several baskets, including one with a single jar of honey. The total finally stayed put. My phone buzzed again; I turned it face down and ran the whole purchase once more. When the site opened, the first order arrived from a stall selling tomatoes. I saved the receipt and let my shoulders drop.

Hana's indie publishing platform was scheduled for release at the end of a community writing workshop. The final screen showed authors a preview of their books, but it cropped every image on smaller laptops. She folded her arms, unfolded them, and leaned over the monitor as workshop participants gathered outside the meeting room. Her cofounder offered to postpone the launch. Hana glanced at the clock, then asked him to keep the group occupied for ten minutes. She found a fixed-width rule in the preview layout and replaced it with a responsive setting. The page shifted, briefly showing a jumble of covers before settling into place. Hana tested three screen sizes, tapping each corner of the trackpad as the pages loaded. The preview held. She released the update and opened the door. When the first writer saw her book cover displayed properly, Hana’s tight smile became genuine.

I spread the wardrobe pieces across our bedroom floor, matching each board to the tiny diagrams while the clock clicked toward my remote-work deadline. My partner, Niko, kept asking where the dowels were, though I had arranged them in labeled cups. I answered too quickly, then heard the sharpness in my own voice. A screw rolled beneath the bed. I dropped to my knees and reached for it, banging my forehead on the frame. For a moment I stayed there with my cheek against the dusty floor, breathing through my teeth. Niko crouched beside me and offered the flashlight without a joke. We found the screw, but one panel was backward. I pressed my palms to my eyes, then let them fall. “Let’s take that one apart,” I said, more quietly. The deadline still waited upstairs on my laptop, but we turned the board around together.

At twenty-two, Safiya had never owned a table that required an Allen key. She and her girlfriend, June, sat cross-legged among the cartons in their first apartment, with rain tapping the bare windows. Safiya checked the instructions for the fourth time, tracing a diagram with one finger while her phone lit up with messages from her new supervisor. Each buzz made her shoulders jump. When June fitted a leg into the wrong corner, Safiya snatched the wrench and corrected it, then froze at June’s raised eyebrows. Her stomach felt cinched like a knot. She set the tool down and rubbed a pale crescent into her palm. June turned the phone facedown and asked her to hold the tabletop steady. Safiya did. The table wobbled once, then settled as they tightened the last bolts. She left the unanswered messages for the length of one shared cup of tea.

I had promised my father I would finish the crib before he arrived, even though the baby was still six weeks away and the nursery looked like a shipping depot. My husband, Mateo, read the instructions aloud while I sorted hardware on a folded towel. The tiny metal brackets kept slipping between my fingers. I checked the wall clock, then the doorway, then the clock again. When Mateo said we could stop for dinner, I told him the crib would collapse if we paused. He blinked at me, and I heard how thin my voice had become. A hot pulse beat behind my ears. I sat on the carpet and lined every screw into a precise row. Mateo lowered himself beside me without a word. We started again, one step at a time, and discovered I had been holding the side rails upside down. Once they clicked into place, I laughed, though my hands still trembled.

Ruben had spent all day translating medical forms at the clinic, and the bookcase box waiting in his kitchen seemed to contain more pieces than the label promised. His partner, Leah, spread a blanket over the tile so the shelves would not scratch. Ruben kept glancing at his watch; his mother was due to call about her appointment, and he feared missing her. He tightened one bolt until the cheap wrench bent slightly. Leah touched his wrist, and he pulled away before he could think. The room went quiet except for a neighbor’s television through the wall. Ruben stared at the warped tool, jaw working. Then he apologized and fetched pliers from a drawer. Leah held the shelf while he eased the bolt loose. They assembled the remaining frame slowly, leaving the top shelf empty for now. When his mother called, Leah answered and carried the phone over, her free hand steadying the bookcase.

The secondhand dresser had arrived with no instructions, three mismatched screws, and a drawer that smelled faintly of cedar. I was already running late for my evening shift when my boyfriend, Ellis, spread the pieces across the living-room rug. My phone kept lighting up with reminders from the rent app. I picked up a side panel, put it down, then picked up the same panel again, unable to decide which way it faced. Ellis hummed while testing the drawer runners. The tune scraped against my nerves, and I asked him to stop. He did, looking puzzled. My throat had gone dry; I swallowed and looked at the clock. Instead of rushing, I took a photo of the assembled frame and compared it with the hardware marks. We found the correct orientation. Ellis held the panel upright while I drove in the screws, and the drawer slid smoothly at last. I left for work with the rent notice still unanswered.

Marlene’s hands smelled of printer ink after a week of covering extra shifts at the library. At home, she and her wife, Petra, were assembling a narrow desk for their son’s room. The manual showed a left-facing drawer, but the parts seemed designed for a right-facing one. Marlene flipped the page back and forth until the paper tore at the fold. She pressed the torn edge flat, then smoothed it again and again. Petra suggested checking the manufacturer’s website. Marlene snapped that the desk would be crooked no matter what they did. The words hung between them. She swallowed, cheeks warming, and began gathering the scattered screws into a saucer. Petra sat down beside her and opened the online diagram. The pieces were correct; the printed sheet was not. Marlene let out a breath she had been holding and rested her forehead against Petra’s shoulder. They finished the desk after midnight, leaving the final drawer handle for morning.

I was sure assembling the patio chairs would be an easy Saturday project, which was why I had invited my partner, Andre, over between errands. Then the first bolt refused to catch, and the second chair came with a cracked armrest. My grocery list fluttered across the balcony whenever the wind lifted. I chased it, came back, and found Andre had sorted the bolts by length. “Can we just make one chair usable?” I asked, though the question came out almost like a challenge. A muscle jumped in my cheek. Andre laid the damaged piece aside and handed me the sturdier frame. We worked in silence, passing tools without looking up. When a neighbor’s dog barked, I dropped the wrench and stared at it on the concrete. Andre nudged it toward me with his shoe. I picked it up, and together we tightened the last joint. One chair stood firm; we carried it inside before the wind could topple it.

After a delayed train and a tense call with her landlord, Priya arrived at the new flat to find her boyfriend, Tom, wrestling a flat-pack sofa frame alone. A maze of cardboard covered the hallway, blocking the front door. Priya put down her bag and immediately began counting the bolts, losing track whenever Tom asked which piece he needed. Her fingers tapped against her thigh. When he fitted a rail backward, she shut her eyes and pinched the bridge of her nose. Tom stopped moving. Priya opened her eyes, saw his tight expression, and said she was sorry. They shifted the cardboard into the kitchen and cleared a path to the door. With room to move, the frame went together more easily. Priya still checked each connection twice, but she let Tom read the steps aloud. When they lowered the cushions onto the finished base, she sat down heavily and kept both feet planted on the floor.

I had been awake since dawn waiting for news about my sister’s surgery when the wardrobe kit arrived. My wife, Celeste, insisted we build it before the delivery crew returned for the empty boxes. The bedroom was narrow, and every time I shifted a panel, its corner caught the curtains. I checked my phone so often that the screen dimmed between glances. Celeste asked me to hold a side upright; my arms began to quiver, and I said I had it when I clearly didn’t. The board slid, thumping against the wall. I stood very still, listening for a message tone. Nothing. Celeste took the panel’s weight and guided it down safely. Then she brought me a glass of water and waited while I drank. We finished the frame with the phone beside us on the floor. When it finally rang, I answered before the last screw was tight.

Eighteen-year-old Darius and his boyfriend, Micah, were putting together a gaming desk in Darius’s aunt’s garage. The instructions were smudged from a drizzle, and a basketball rolled beneath the workbench whenever the door rattled in the wind. Darius had a college application due at midnight; the unfinished essay glowed on his phone beside the screwdriver. He kept switching between the assembly steps and the blank document, his knee bouncing hard enough to shake a bag of washers. Micah asked him to hold the metal crossbar level. Darius grabbed it too high, then adjusted it three times. “I can’t keep doing both,” he muttered. Micah turned the phone facedown and promised to handle the remaining steps while Darius worked on the essay. The choice seemed to loosen his clenched jaw. They secured the desk frame, then sat on overturned buckets as Darius typed a rough first sentence.

The kitchen clock had stopped, but I kept glancing at it while my partner, Noor, and I assembled a pantry rack. My restaurant’s opening inspection was scheduled for the next morning, and my mind kept returning to the checklist I had left at work. I drove a screw into the wrong hole, backed it out, and tried again. The screwdriver slipped, leaving a red mark across my thumb. Noor offered a bandage. I said I didn’t need one, then held my hand under the tap when the sting sharpened. Water drummed against the steel sink. Noor placed the next shelf beside me and waited instead of rushing. I found the correct hole by matching the small marks in the metal. We attached each level, checking that none tilted. Once the rack stood straight, I wrapped my thumb and finally looked at Noor. “Can you read the inspection list with me?” I asked. We moved the checklist onto the counter together.

Evelyn had promised her girlfriend, Rosa, that the nursery rocking chair would be ready before the adoption home visit. The final approval call was expected any day, and the living room had become a jumble of curved rails, washers, and packing foam. Evelyn read each direction aloud, but her voice kept catching whenever her phone vibrated. She checked the caller screen even when it was only a delivery alert. Rosa fitted a rocker backward, and Evelyn took the piece from her too abruptly. Rosa lowered her hands. Evelyn stared at the floor, rubbing her thumb over a rough splinter in the wood. “I keep thinking we’ll miss something,” she said. Rosa brought over a small bowl for the loose hardware and asked Evelyn to check the joints while she tightened them. The task gave Evelyn somewhere useful to put her attention. When the chair rocked smoothly, they sat side by side and let it sway once, listening for the phone.

I saw the doors begin to fold shut just as I reached the platform stairs. My laptop bag thumped against my hip while I took the steps two at a time, gripping the rail with a damp hand. The train slid forward, and I ran beside it, waving at the conductor through the glass. He glanced toward me but kept moving. At the far end, a woman in a green coat pressed the door button from inside. The doors opened for a breath, and I stumbled aboard, knocking my shoulder against the frame. My phone buzzed with three messages from the client waiting at the other end of the line. I straightened my shirt, tried to slow my breathing, and typed that I was on my way. My fingers hit the wrong keys twice.

At sixty-eight, Bernard had promised his granddaughter he would make the school recital, and the departing train was already humming at the platform. He hurried past a kiosk, one hand clamped around the paper ticket and the other holding his hat against the wind. His knee caught on the final step. He swallowed a sharp sound, pushed upright, and waved his cane toward the nearest carriage. A porter spotted him and slapped the door release. Bernard climbed aboard just before it shut, then stood in the aisle, chest lifting beneath his coat. The recital program had softened in his pocket from the pressure of his fist. When the train pulled away, he unfolded it carefully, smoothing the creases with his thumb as if the little names printed there might disappear.

I heard the departure chime while the bakery’s back door was still swinging behind me. Flour dust clung to my sleeves, and my shoes squeaked over the station tiles as I sprinted for the train. My brother’s handmade cake sat level in its box, balanced in both arms; I couldn’t risk dropping it, so I ran with short, stiff steps. The last carriage began to roll. A station worker lifted the barrier, and I darted through just as the doors parted. Inside, a child stared at the frosting smeared across one corner. I pressed the lid down and checked my watch again. There was no time to start over, and my brother had been waiting weeks for this birthday. I kept the cake steady on my knees, counting each bump in the track.

Nia had two minutes to reach the train carrying the only replacement part her repair shop could not make locally. The station clock clicked over as she burst through the entrance, a canvas tool roll slapping against her back. She ran, scanning the platform signs, then veered toward the wrong track and had to double back around a pillar. The train gave its warning beep. Her breath snagged, and she clenched her jaw as she raced alongside the carriage, calling out to the conductor. A passenger pulled the door lever from within. Nia hauled herself aboard and stood bent over her knees, listening to the wheels gather speed. The parcel was still tucked under her arm. She checked its label three times before letting herself sit.

The doors were closing when I reached the platform, and my son’s blue mitten was clenched in my fist. He had left it at my apartment, and the train was taking him to his father’s for the weekend. I ran along the yellow line, calling his name, though the glass swallowed my voice. A guard pointed to the next door, where a passenger held it open. I jumped aboard, nearly losing the mitten, then found my son staring from his seat with his backpack still on. He looked surprised, then gave a small wave. I pressed the mitten into his hand and tried to say something cheerful. The train moved. My mouth went dry, and I kept one palm against the window until the platform slipped away.

Ravi was halfway through a call with the hospital when the train began to leave. His mother’s appointment card was folded in his wallet, its time circled in red. He ran across the platform, phone pinned between his ear and shoulder, repeating the clinic address over the thunder of wheels. His briefcase swung open, scattering two folders. He snatched them up without checking which was which and lunged for the last carriage. A conductor caught his sleeve and pulled him inside. Ravi thanked him too quickly, then stood gripping the overhead rail while the doctor’s office asked him to confirm a date. He looked down at the crumpled papers in his hand. The digits blurred until he stopped moving his lips and read them again.

I spotted the train through the station windows as I came off the bus, already rolling away from the platform. My violin case knocked against my back while I ran, my shoes slipping on the rain-dark pavement. The audition began in forty minutes; the printed directions were folded in my pocket, but the address seemed to have vanished from my mind. I chased the carriage to the far end and found a door still open. A stranger caught the case as I stumbled aboard. I thanked her, then checked each zipper, touching the latch twice before sitting down. The bow was safe. My hands were not steady enough to tune, so I rested them flat on my knees and watched the station lights stream past.

When the final boarding call sounded, Elaine pushed her cart away from the café counter and ran for the train. Her father’s old camera was wrapped in a scarf inside her tote, and she had promised to bring it to his memorial before the family gathered. One wheel of the cart had left a red mark across her palm. She abandoned it beside a bench, then sprinted down the platform, glancing at the numbered signs as if they might change. The train started moving. A conductor leaned out and pointed to a door, and Elaine reached it with a sharp gasp. Once inside, she hugged the tote against her ribs. The scarf had loosened; she tucked it back around the camera, folding each corner with deliberate care.

I had rehearsed the speech on the walk to the station, but the words scattered when I heard the train’s warning tone. My manager’s message was still open on my phone: the investors wanted me there before the presentation began. I ran, nearly clipping a man with a suitcase, and kept apologizing without stopping. The carriage doors slid shut ahead of me. I slapped the glass once, then saw a passenger point toward a door farther down. I sprinted again and made it aboard, lungs burning. In the vestibule, I read my notes from the top, though I had memorized them yesterday. Every sentence looked unfamiliar. I locked the phone, unlocked it, and checked the meeting time once more.

The train carrying the championship team was easing out when Mateo reached the platform. His younger sister’s cleats were looped over one shoulder, and he had promised to deliver them before the match. He sprinted past the waiting crowd, weaving between suitcases, his heel striking the floor hard enough to sting. The coach appeared in a window and shook his head, but a teammate opened the door from inside. Mateo jumped aboard and nearly collided with the equipment bags. He handed over the cleats, then searched the faces for his sister. She was already seated, pale beneath her team cap. He sat across from her and checked the departure board through the glass, though the train was moving too quickly for the numbers to hold still.

I heard the engine pull away just as my presentation boards slid from my hands. One corner bent on the platform, and I stared at the crease for half a second before grabbing everything and running. The train was my only route to the community center, where the council vote would decide whether our garden stayed open. My scarf came loose and trailed behind me. I gathered it without breaking stride, then waved the boards at the conductor. He opened the door, and I squeezed in sideways, careful not to crush the paper. A woman offered me a seat. I shook my head, smoothing the damaged corner with my palm while the carriage rattled toward the meeting.

At the station, June watched the train begin to depart with her passport still in her coat pocket and her boarding document in her hand. She had spent the morning checking both, yet now she could not remember which pocket held what. She ran along the platform, shouting for the attendant as her suitcase bounced behind her. The wheels caught on a seam, and she dragged it free with a jerk that pulled her shoulder. A passenger held the nearest door open. June climbed inside, face hot, and immediately searched her pockets. Passport, ticket, wallet: each appeared in turn. She lined them up on the seat beside her, then counted them again as the train gathered speed.

I pushed the skiff from shore before the sun cleared the ridge, though I had checked the weather three times and packed the same thermos twice. The engine coughed, and my fingers tightened around the tiller until my knuckles paled. At home, the overdue rent notice sat beneath a chipped mug; out here, I could almost pretend it was beyond the water. My phone buzzed in my pocket. I let it buzz again, then pulled it out and saw my sister’s name. The boat drifted toward a stand of reeds while I stared at the screen. Finally, I answered. She told me Dad had forgotten his morning pills, and I shut my eyes for one long breath. The lake was brightening around me. I turned the boat toward the dock, already counting the minutes and the things I would need to remember.

At fifty-eight, Miriam knew every shallow shelf in the lake, but that morning she steered past her usual fishing spot without noticing. Her tackle box rattled with each small wave. She kept glancing at the paper folded in her coat pocket: the clinic’s estimate for her husband’s treatment, covered in figures she had added and crossed out until the creases softened. A fish struck near the boat, and she jerked the rod upright, nearly upsetting the coffee beside her boot. She muttered an apology to the empty water. The line slackened. Miriam rested her forehead against the cold handle and listened to the motor idle. When a loon called from the far shore, she looked up. The sound did not solve anything, but it gave her one clear moment in which to choose a direction. She cast again, slower this time.

By dawn I had already spilled bait in the truck, missed a call from my foreman, and driven back home for the thermos I’d left on the counter. I’m twenty-six, new to the night shift at the mill, and my eyes felt gritty as I guided the aluminum boat across the lake. A list of unfinished repairs kept arranging itself in my head: the leaky roof, the loose step, the truck’s warning light. I tied a knot, pulled it tight, then tugged it twice more. When the hook snagged a submerged branch, a sharp breath escaped me. I yanked until the line snapped, and the rod tip sprang back against my wrist. For a moment I sat motionless, listening to the tiny waves slap the hull. Then I opened the tackle tin, found another hook, and made myself work through the steps one at a time.

Luis had promised his daughter he would bring home a fish for breakfast, and the promise followed him onto the lake like another passenger. The dawn air silvered his beard as he rowed beyond the cove. Each time the phone in his jacket vibrated, his shoulders jumped. He had left his restaurant kitchen in the care of a new cook, and three messages were waiting before he reached the fishing grounds. He read none of them, though his thumb hovered over the screen. The bobber dipped. Luis grabbed the rod too quickly, and the fish slipped free. He whispered a curse, then looked toward the dim shoreline where his daughter was probably waking. He set the phone beneath the seat and baited the hook again. This time he waited until the float sank fully before lifting the rod, his breathing gradually falling into the rhythm of the water.

The lake was still dark when I launched my little boat, and the cabin windows along the shore looked like watchful eyes. I had spent the night rehearsing what to say at my hearing, each version worse than the last. Out on the water, I tried to count casts instead of arguments. My hands moved too fast; I dropped the lure, then fumbled with the knot while the boat drifted sideways. A gull cried overhead, and I flinched hard enough to bump my elbow on the gunwale. I rubbed the spot and stared at the ripples spreading from the hull. The hearing would begin at nine, and I had less than an hour to get back. I checked the motor, then checked it again. At last, I stowed the rod and turned toward the landing, keeping my eyes on the pale strip of sky ahead.

Nora brought her late brother’s fishing pole to the lake because sorting his apartment had filled every room with decisions she could not finish. She was seventy-two and usually moved with deliberate care, but that morning she kept searching her pockets for keys already in her hand. The first cast landed short. She reeled in, jaw set, and tried again while mist curled over the water. A message from the estate office waited on her phone, demanding an answer about the old boat. Nora turned the device face down on the bench. When a fish tugged at the line, she gripped the rod with both hands and leaned back too sharply. The catch escaped, leaving the hook bare. She sat with the pole across her knees, then wiped her eyes with the heel of one hand and began threading fresh bait, carefully, as her brother had taught her.

I was supposed to be fishing, but I kept checking the fuel gauge as if the needle might change through sheer attention. The boat carried my father’s old outboard, which had stalled twice on the way across the lake. At home, my toddler had a fever, and my partner was managing alone while I tried to meet a deadline for my carpentry job. The two obligations pulled at me from opposite shores. I set the rod down and listened to the motor’s uneven sputter. A quick gust pushed the bow around, making my stomach clench. I grabbed the rope, tied it to the cleat, and tested the knot with a hard pull. Then I called home. My partner said the fever had eased, and the rush in my chest softened a notch. I stayed close to shore, casting into the reeds while keeping the landing in view.

Eli, a nursing student, left the dock before sunrise because the exam schedule on his kitchen wall had begun to look like a row of locked doors. He packed flash cards beside the bait and tried reciting definitions while the boat hummed over the lake. Halfway to the island, he lost his place and slapped the cards against his knee. Their corners fluttered away in the breeze. He watched one land near his boot and pinned it there with a shaking finger. The fishing line went slack, unnoticed, until the rod slid toward the water. Eli snatched it up just in time, then sat with his elbows braced on his thighs. He could hear his own rushed breathing over the motor. After tying on a fresh lure, he put the cards in a dry box and cast. For several minutes, he let himself attend only to the float.

At dawn I rowed out with my work boots still damp from the bakery floor. The owner had changed the delivery route without telling me, and I had spent the night replaying every mistake I might make at the new address. On the lake, the oars squeaked with each stroke, matching the tight little rhythm in my chest. I tried to fish, but my hands kept arranging the bait tin, the net, and the folded map into perfect rows. A dark cloud gathered over the hills. I glanced at it, then at my watch, then back at the cloud. When the first drops struck my cap, I fumbled the oar and spun the boat in a slow circle. I stopped, pressed both palms against the bench, and counted the ripples around me. Then I chose the shortest route to the landing and began rowing steadily.

Grace had recently retired from the school office, but her mornings still began with the sensation that she was late for something. She carried that feeling into the boat as the lake turned from charcoal to blue. Her son had called the previous night about another argument with his landlord, and she had offered advice he had not wanted. Now she kept composing a better reply in her head while her fishing line floated unattended. When the wind nudged the boat toward a rocky point, she jerked the oars into the water and pulled hard. The sudden effort made her breath catch. Grace anchored well away from the rocks and opened her thermos, though the coffee had gone lukewarm. She listened to the lid click shut, then sent her son a simple message asking whether he had eaten. Afterward, she watched the bobber instead of her phone.

I took the boat out because the apartment walls seemed to hold every unfinished task in place: the broken heater, the unopened bills, the email from my supervisor waiting for an answer. The lake offered no better plan, but at least it had room to look at. I was thirty-nine, a paramedic on leave after a rough month, and my hands still moved as if someone might call for help at any second. I baited the hook, dropped it, and scraped mud from my palm with my thumbnail. When a distant motor started, I turned toward it before realizing it was only another fisherman. My shoulders stayed lifted near my ears. I lowered them deliberately and let the rod rest across my lap. A small fish tapped the line. I reeled it in without hurry, released it, and watched it disappear beneath the brightening surface.

At sixty-four, Pavel had learned to mend nets quickly, but he could not make the message from his landlord disappear. He had read it on the dock before pushing off, then folded the phone into his jacket as if that settled anything. Dawn laid a pale path across the lake. He steered toward his favorite inlet and found another boat already anchored there, its occupants speaking in low voices. Pavel circled once, too close, then turned away with his mouth pressed thin. His line tangled around the reel. He pulled at it, stopped, and began again when the knot only tightened. A passing ripple rocked the boat, and he grabbed the rail. After a moment, he set the reel in his lap and patiently unwound each loop. The inlet was still there when he returned, and this time he eased into the quiet without looking at his phone.

By noon, I had measured the west wall six times and still kept the tape measure looped around my wrist. The gallery owner wanted the paintings hung before the donors arrived, and one frame leaned a fraction lower than its neighbor. I climbed the ladder, shifted it, climbed down, and saw the gap had changed on the other side. My coffee sat untouched beside a stack of labels. When a delivery cart rattled in the hall, I dropped the pencil and watched it roll under the radiator. My assistant asked whether we should open the doors. “Give me five minutes,” I said, though the clock above the desk had already passed the hour. Then I noticed the paintings looked balanced from the entrance, where everyone would see them. I folded the tape measure and let my hands hang at my sides.

At sixty-eight, Farida had never used a digital projector, but the gallery insisted her charcoal studies needed one for the opening. She clicked through menus while her nephew waited with a tray of tea, each wrong button bringing up another window. A strand of hair stuck to her damp cheek. She checked the printed schedule, then the projector, then the schedule again, lips moving over the minutes. The first guests were due in forty minutes. When the image finally appeared, it stretched across the wall and swallowed the small drawing beneath it. Farida pressed her palms to her skirt and stared at the blank patch where the work should be. Her nephew suggested turning the machine off. She gave him a quick nod, then carefully repositioned the drawing herself, testing the distance with two fingers held up like a frame.

I spread the exhibition checklist across my studio floor, where it covered a curl of copper wire and three half-eaten crackers. The courier had called to say the crate might arrive after the opening, and the piece inside was the one I had promised the curator. I refreshed my email until the screen dimmed, then tapped it awake and did it again. A staple caught in my sleeve as I packed the smaller works. My phone buzzed; I flinched hard enough to knock over a jar of brushes. It was only a weather alert. I wiped the paint water from the table and tried to write a new wall label, but my handwriting narrowed into a tangle. Finally I drew a simple map showing where the missing work would go. The empty space on the gallery plan looked less like a mistake when I gave it a border.

Mateo had borrowed his sister’s van to carry six ceramic sculptures to the gallery, and now the engine would not turn over. He sat behind the wheel with both hands fixed at ten and two, watching the dashboard lights blink. The opening began at seven; the clock on his phone said six twelve. He called roadside assistance, hung up before the recorded menu ended, and called again. In the cargo area, the sculptures were wedged between blankets, each one labeled in his careful block letters. A passerby knocked on the window to ask if he needed help. Mateo tried to answer, but his mouth felt dry, so he only pointed toward the hood. When the tow truck arrived, he climbed out and checked every blanket before letting the driver attach the cable. At the gallery, his sister was already waiting with a handcart.

I had painted the gallery walls a warm gray, but beneath the track lights they looked almost lavender. The curator said it was fine; I heard myself ask if she was certain, then asked again while she carried in a box of brochures. I backed into a stack of empty frames and caught them before they hit the floor. For a moment I stood holding all three, elbows locked, listening to the ventilation hum. My own paintings were still wrapped, and the opening was less than a day away. I peeled tape from a corner, checked the color, and folded it back down. Then I made myself drink water, though the paper cup trembled against my teeth. One canvas at a time, I unwrapped the work and leaned it against the wall. The gray seemed quieter once the paintings were in place.

Nia’s exhibition included a sound installation made from recordings of the city’s underground trains. On opening morning, the speakers produced a thin hiss instead of the deep rumble she had tested in her apartment. She crouched behind the plinth, tracing cables with one finger while the electrician waited beside the fuse box. Her knees pressed into the concrete. Each time someone entered the gallery, Nia sprang upright and asked them to use the other door. The technician said the file might be corrupted. She stared at the laptop, then at the empty room, and rubbed the bridge of her nose until it reddened. A backup drive was in her tote, which she had left on the bus. She called the transit lost-and-found, speaking too quickly at first. When the driver answered, she repeated the route number slowly and wrote it on her palm.

I carried the framed photographs into the gallery myself because the hired movers were delayed. By the fourth trip, my shoulder had begun to twitch, and I kept checking the doorway as if another person might appear to take over. The labels were printed, but one name had an accent missing. I set down the frame and searched the artist’s website with a finger that kept hitting the wrong keys. The opening guests would arrive in an hour. I asked the receptionist for scissors, then forgot why I had asked and stood beside her desk holding the frame. She handed me a glass of water without comment. I drank it in three quick swallows, corrected the label, and taped it straight beneath the photograph. Before lifting the next frame, I rolled my shoulder once and counted to four.

At thirty, Pavel was the youngest artist in the group exhibition, and he had spent the night arranging his paper sculptures in the gallery’s narrowest room. The air conditioner kept stirring their delicate folds, so he turned it off; within minutes, the room grew close and warm. He checked each piece, then checked the door to see whether the curator had noticed the shutdown. A custodian wheeled a bin past, making one sculpture shiver. Pavel held his breath until it settled. He had brought spare paper, but the folds looked wrong under the bright lights. When the curator arrived, he launched into an explanation of the temperature, the vents, and the hanging plan without pausing. She listened, then suggested moving the smallest pieces farther from the vent. Pavel nodded and fetched his step stool. His fingers were still unsteady as he adjusted the final pin.

My exhibition was supposed to open at six, and at five thirty the gallery still had no working card reader. I had promised to sell small prints at the entrance, so I arranged them in neat piles, then rearranged them by color, then by price. A line of visitors had begun forming outside. I wiped my palms on my trousers and tested the device again. The screen flashed an error message. My friend offered to take cash, but I could not remember where I had put the change tin. I searched under the table, behind the brochures, and inside the box of mailing envelopes. It was in my coat pocket, where I had placed it myself. I laughed once, a thin sound, and set it beside the prints. Then I wrote “cash welcome” on a scrap of card and propped it against the reader.

Luzia had spent months making a series of portraits from memory, but on installation day she could not decide which one should greet visitors. She stood at the entrance with two canvases held against her chest, glancing from one to the other. The gallery manager was waiting to lock the final layout, and the printer kept spitting out revised labels in the office. Luzia tucked a loose thread behind her ear, then pulled it out again. She asked a passing technician which portrait he preferred. He pointed to the one with the red scarf, and she immediately wondered whether he had chosen it just to be kind. A cart squeaked in the hallway. She carried both canvases to the wall and placed them side by side. Their different expressions seemed to make a stronger opening than either could alone, so she marked the hooks without asking anyone else.

I had arranged the gallery exhibition around a single glass case, and now the case would not fit through the doorway. The delivery crew had measured it, I had measured the doorway, and somehow the numbers had failed to meet. I watched the crew tilt the case one way, then another, while my thumbnail pressed a white crescent into my palm. The opening was tomorrow. My small sculptures sat wrapped in tissue on the floor, waiting for their display. I walked to the far end of the hall and back, counting the ceiling tiles to keep from interrupting. The crew leader suggested removing the door. I fetched a screwdriver, dropped it, and heard it skitter under a radiator. Once the hinges came off, the case slid through with a soft scrape. I let out a breath I had been holding and began unwrapping the sculptures.

Juniper, a retired marine engineer, had built a wall of tiny painted boats for her first gallery exhibition. On the morning of the opening, one section had come loose and leaned away from the wall like a sail catching wind. She fetched a level, a drill, and a box of screws, then laid everything out in a precise row. The gallery assistant asked if she wanted help. Juniper said she had it, though she checked the assistant’s face for signs of doubt. Her hand slipped on the drill trigger, and the bit chewed a small mark into the plaster. She set the tool down and pressed both palms against the wall until her fingers stopped buzzing. The assistant held the panel steady while Juniper fitted a new anchor. When the boats sat straight again, she stepped back, examined the line, and quietly asked for a cloth to wipe away the dust.

I set the bucket beneath the kitchen ceiling before calling Mr. Bell, though the rain had stopped an hour earlier. A brown ring had spread above the stove, and each time a drop landed in the bucket, I lost my place in the notes I had prepared. When he answered, I read the list too quickly: ceiling, loose cabinet hinge, outlet that sparked. He asked whether I could send photographs. My phone slid in my damp hand, and I took three blurry shots before trying again. “I need someone to come this week,” I said, hearing my voice rise at the end. He promised to check the schedule. After we hung up, I stood listening to the quiet kitchen, counting the seconds between drips. Then I moved the bucket away from the stove and made another list, this time with dates beside every call.

At seventy-two, Eulalia had repaired plenty of things herself, but the stair rail in her rental had begun pulling away from the wall. She called her landlord from the landing, gripping the rail with one hand while the phone pressed against her ear. He suggested she avoid using the stairs until he could look at it. “I live upstairs,” she replied, each word clipped. Her grocery bag rested on the floor, oranges rolling toward the steps. He said he would send a carpenter the next morning, then asked her to text a photograph. Eulalia took the picture with her free hand, missed the loose bracket, and tried again. When she finally went inside, she set the bag down without unpacking it. She called her neighbor to carry the groceries up and left the landlord’s message open on her screen, checking it whenever the phone lit.

I had an online interview in twenty minutes when the radiator began knocking hard enough to rattle the desk. My landlord, Dev, answered while I was pinning my hair with one hand and holding the phone with the other. I explained that the heat had vanished overnight and the pipes were making a sound like someone tapping a spoon against a pan. He asked me to turn a valve in the basement. I looked at my clean blouse, then at the damp towel I had wrapped around my shoulders. “Could you send a technician instead?” I asked. The pause on the line stretched. I wrote down his appointment window on the back of an envelope, underlined it twice, and put it beside my laptop. During the interview, every knock from the radiator made me glance toward the hallway, though the camera showed only my face.

Mateo had just finished a night shift when he found water creeping beneath the bathroom door. He called his landlord, who answered over the noise of a bus. Mateo explained that the toilet had overflowed twice and that towels were already soaked through. His words came out in short bursts; he kept rubbing a wet thumb over the phone case. The landlord told him to shut off the valve and said a plumber might arrive after lunch. Mateo crouched beside the toilet, turning the handle carefully while his work boots left muddy marks on the tile. “Please call me when you know,” he said, then repeated the number although it was saved in the landlord’s phone. He sat on the bathtub edge, elbows on his knees, watching the puddle spread toward the hall. When the plumber’s van finally pulled up, Mateo was still holding the wrench.

I was carrying my baby against my shoulder when the bedroom window refused to close. Cold air slipped through the gap, stirring the curtains and lifting the corner of the crib blanket. I called Mrs. Ortiz, my landlord, and tried to keep my voice low because the baby had just settled. She asked whether I had tried lifting the sash. I did, but the frame jerked and my wrist hurt. “I can’t keep holding it shut all night,” I said. A pause followed, then she offered to send her maintenance person the next day. I thanked her, though the appointment was nearly twenty-four hours away. After hanging up, I wedged a folded towel along the sill and tested it with the back of my hand. The baby’s breathing stayed even. I remained beside the window, listening for the latch to slip again.

Nadine kept her bakery uniform on while she spoke with her landlord in the courtyard. A leak above the shop’s small kitchen had soaked the flour sacks, and the morning delivery was due in less than an hour. She showed him a video of water threading down the wall, then pointed to the ceiling stain spreading toward the mixer. He said the upstairs tenant would need to be home before repairs could begin. Nadine’s jaw tightened. She pressed her fingernails into the phone case and asked whether someone could at least inspect the pipe today. The landlord called the upstairs unit, but no one answered. Nadine looked through the open kitchen door at the ruined flour and wiped her palms on her apron. She began shifting equipment away from the leak, pausing each time another drop struck the metal bowl.

I called the landlord from the laundromat because the bathroom sink had stopped draining and my apartment smelled of old water. While he searched for a plumber, I folded the same shirt three times, then unfolded it to check whether it was still damp. He asked if I had tried a drain cleaner. I said I had, twice, and read the bottle instructions aloud because my mind kept skipping lines. He promised to come by after work to look at the pipes. “Please don’t forget,” I said, then immediately wished I had said it differently. The machines thumped around me, shaking the plastic chair beneath my knees. I set an alarm on my phone for the promised time and watched the minutes change.
