The young man claimed he liked the music, but his gaze kept dropping to the open instrument case, where Niko’s earnings from the week sat beneath a folded cloth. Niko moved the coins into his coat pocket and watched the nephew’s smile falter. Later, a string on the violin loosened although Niko had tightened it minutes earlier. He inspected the peg, then the case, finding flour dust on the clasp. At sound check, he asked the baker to keep the courtyard gate shut. The nephew protested that guests needed room to enter. Niko handed him a stack of chairs to carry instead. All evening, Niko kept his violin in hand, even between pieces.

I had one hour before my small concert at the museum, so I rehearsed beside the marble statues while the caretaker polished the gallery. He passed behind me three times, each time pausing at the same bar in my score. I turned a page; he stopped polishing. I began again; the cloth moved. “Do you need something?” I asked. He said he was checking the floor, though his shoes never crossed the damp section he claimed to be watching. My viola rested on a chair while I adjusted the music stand. When I looked back, the score had been turned to a page I had not marked. I checked the margins for a note or a tear, then slipped the sheets into my folder. The caretaker offered to carry my instrument to the stage. I thanked him and held the case myself, keeping my thumb over the latch until the audience arrived.

At the harbor café, Sanaa rehearsed a set of old sea songs on her qanun before a dozen customers arrived for the evening performance. The owner had promised her a quiet corner, but two men at a table kept asking which songs she planned to play. Their questions sounded casual until one requested the piece she had just told the owner she had removed from the program. Sanaa smiled, retuned a string, and changed the order of her pages. One man leaned closer whenever she opened the instrument’s padded cover. She began to keep it closed between songs. When the owner brought her a glass of water, she asked whether he had seen anyone near her case. He looked offended and said the staff were busy. Sanaa placed the glass on the floor and finished rehearsal without drinking. At the concert, she chose a different opening tune and watched the two men throughout the first verse.

I rehearsed my clarinet in a rented dance studio before a small concert at the veterans’ club. The instructor had left a note saying the back entrance would stay unlocked for deliveries, but I found the door bolted from inside. A minute later, someone tried the handle from the other side. I stopped playing. No one answered when I called out. The handle shifted again, then went still. I packed my mouthpiece and checked the studio mirror for movement behind me, although the room was empty. When the instructor finally came in, he said the delivery driver had probably made a mistake. I asked why there was a fresh scrape near the lock. He bent to inspect it, then changed the subject to my concert clothes. I kept my case beside my chair through the rest of rehearsal. Every time the hallway creaked, my fingers tightened around the clarinet before I could make them relax.

Elliot, sixteen, practiced drums in the basement of his aunt’s row house before a tiny neighborhood concert. His cousin had offered to help set up microphones, but kept unplugging the recorder Elliot used to check his timing. Each time, she said the cable was in her way. He moved it farther from her feet; the plug came loose again. Elliot began recording with his phone hidden beneath a towel on the shelf. When his cousin went upstairs, he found the recorder’s settings had been changed and a file deleted. He called after her, but she answered that she had not touched anything. Instead of arguing, he restored the file from backup and asked his aunt to watch the equipment during the show. His cousin rolled her eyes and left the room. Elliot drummed through the final set, but left the microphone off until he could test every cable himself.

I was tuning my harp in the hotel lounge where I would play a short set after dinner. The manager had placed a vase beside my music stand, though there was plenty of space on the table. Its water kept trembling whenever I plucked the lowest strings. I moved the vase, and the ripples continued. Then I noticed a small black device tucked beneath the table edge, its wire trailing toward the office door. When I asked the manager about it, he said it was part of the sound system. I requested a look at the wiring diagram; he told me not to fuss over details. My fingers hovered above the strings. I packed the harp’s tuning key and asked a waiter to stay while I rehearsed. The device disappeared before the guests arrived. I played the concert anyway, but chose pieces that needed no spoken introduction, and kept my eyes on the manager’s hands.

Luz practiced her flute in an elementary-school music room before a small concert for parents. The substitute teacher had borrowed her pencil to mark the program, then returned it with the eraser chewed and a new note written on her sheet music: skip the final measure. Luz asked who had added it. The teacher said it must have been her own reminder, but Luz had never used that handwriting. She erased the note and placed her pencil inside her case. While rehearsing, she heard a drawer close behind her. The teacher stood by the piano, though he had been near the door moments before. Luz checked the drawer and found her concert program inside, folded around a key she did not recognize. She said nothing, copied the music onto a clean page, and asked the school secretary to lock the room during the performance. Her flute stayed in her hands until the audience was seated.

I brought my electric bass to the rooftop room above a laundromat, where I was rehearsing for a small concert at the tenants’ meeting. The building superintendent had promised to check the amplifier, but the volume knob was turned down every time I stepped away. I marked its position with a strip of tape. When I returned from getting water, the tape had been peeled off and stuck to the windowsill. The superintendent said the vibration bothered the tenants, although the machine downstairs was louder than my practice. I unplugged the amp and played acoustically. A message appeared on my phone from an unknown number: Don’t play the last song. I looked toward the stairwell, where the light had just gone out. I packed my bass and went downstairs instead of finishing the set. Before the concert, I asked the tenants’ organizer to check the rooftop door and confirm who had access.

Ravi rehearsed a short marimba program in the basement of a town hall before the monthly concert. The caretaker had laid a clean cloth over the instrument’s bars, saying it would protect them from dust. Ravi lifted it and found a pale streak across the wood, as though someone had dragged a metal tool along the row. He asked who else had been in the room. The caretaker named three people, then changed the list when Ravi mentioned the fresh footprints near the storage closet. Ravi inspected each bar and tested the notes, listening for cracks. One tone rang dull, though it had sounded clear the day before. The caretaker blamed the room’s damp air. Ravi set up a second instrument and asked the organizer to witness the sound check. During the concert, he used the spare marimba and kept the marked one locked away, with the cloth folded separately in his bag.

The taxi left me beside a fountain whose water had gone green, and the driver refused to say why every shop on the square was shut before dusk. He pointed toward a narrow hotel, then watched until I crossed the street. Inside, the clerk greeted me by a name I had not given. I kept my suitcase between us while he searched the ledger. The room key was already on the counter, its brass tag marked with my train number. I asked how he knew it. He smiled and said the station sent guests ahead. From the stairs, I could see him lift the telephone as soon as I entered the hall. I didn’t unlock my door. Instead, I carried my bag back downstairs and asked for a room facing the street. His smile vanished, and he slid the key toward me without meeting my eyes.

At thirty-eight, Devika had crossed three borders for a conference, yet the driver’s offer to carry her case made her pause. He knew the name of her hotel, though she had only said the district. She thanked him and held the handle herself. On the tram, a man in a tan coat boarded at the same stop and stood beside the door, looking at her reflection in the glass. Devika changed cars at the next station. He changed too. She stepped onto the platform and walked quickly toward a staffed kiosk, pretending to read its map. When she glanced back, the man had stopped near a pillar, speaking into his cuff. Devika called the conference organizer and asked someone to meet her at the station. The man moved away before her colleague arrived, leaving behind a paper ticket folded into a tight square.

I arrived in Bellmere with a violin case and no working phone. At the station, a cheerful woman in a red scarf offered to show me the musicians’ quarter. She knew the name of my old conservatory, though I had not mentioned it. I told her I preferred to walk alone. Three blocks later, she appeared in a bakery window behind me, stirring coffee without drinking it. I took a different route, doubling back through an arcade crowded with schoolchildren. A boy bumped my shoulder and whispered that the woman had asked where I was staying. I ducked into a crowded bookstore and watched through the front glass. The red scarf paused across the street, then lifted as if to signal someone. I left through the rear entrance and spent the afternoon practicing in a public square, where there were plenty of witnesses.

Niko, a retired ferry mechanic, arrived in the mountain city carrying a tin box of family photographs. At his guesthouse, the owner insisted on keeping the box in a locked office while Niko went to supper. He declined and set it beneath his chair. The owner’s eyes lingered on the brass latch. Later, Niko found a fresh scrape beside the keyhole of his room. He tested the window, checked the wardrobe, then placed a strand of gray thread across the door’s lower edge. In the morning, it lay snapped on the floor. Nothing appeared missing, but one photograph had been turned face down. Niko packed the tin box and asked a café worker about a different lodging house. When the owner appeared in the doorway, Niko was already walking toward the market with the box held tight against his ribs.

By the time my bus reached Orska, the snow had covered the street signs. A porter at the terminal insisted there was no public taxi stand, though I could see one through the glass. He offered to take my bags to a car waiting around the corner. I asked him to repeat the hotel’s address. He gave me a different street name than the one on my reservation. I kept my gloves on and went to the taxi stand myself. The driver there examined my booking, then glanced toward the terminal doors. The porter was watching us from inside. I gave the driver the address and asked him to take the main road, not the shortcut he suggested. At the hotel, I checked the room number with the receptionist before handing over my passport, then wedged a chair under the door handle for the night.

Mara, a twenty-year-old architecture student, stepped off the night train in a city where every building seemed to lean over the alleys. A local guide offered to lead her to the hostel and pointed out a shortcut through an empty courtyard. She noticed he kept checking the brass watch on her wrist. She said she needed cash first and walked into a brightly lit pharmacy. Through the window, she saw him wait at the courtyard entrance, then circle to the far side. Mara asked the pharmacist to call a licensed cab. The guide followed the cab for two turns on a motorbike before disappearing into traffic. At the hostel, Mara asked the receptionist to confirm that no one had requested her room. She placed the watch inside her sock before sleeping, and kept the bedside lamp on until dawn.

I had barely reached the harbor when a boy in a school uniform ran up with a message supposedly from my sister. He said she was waiting at a café across the canal. My sister lived in another country and had no idea I was in Veyra. I asked who had sent him. He stared at my suitcase wheels and shrugged. I walked toward the police kiosk instead of the café. The boy darted into the crowd. At the kiosk, the officer listened, then asked me to describe the message. It was written in my sister’s handwriting, down to the tiny star she used instead of a dot. I turned the paper over and found a phone number. I didn’t call it. I asked the officer to walk me to my hotel, keeping the note folded inside my passport.

When Sandeep arrived in the desert city, a hotel clerk welcomed him as though they had spoken before. She mentioned his late flight and offered a room facing the alley, saying the street side was being repaired. Sandeep looked at the guest register; his own name was written several lines below a blank entry. He asked to see the room first. The clerk’s hand tightened around the key ring. Upstairs, the window latch had fresh scratches, and a second cup sat beside the sink. Sandeep went back down and requested a room near the lobby. The clerk said there were none. He left his bags by the desk and walked to a brightly lit restaurant across the street. From his table, he watched the hotel entrance until a uniformed employee emerged and carried his suitcase upstairs.

I came to Marrowgate to deliver a package to the university archive. At the station, a woman with a clipboard asked whether I was the courier from Leeds. I had not told anyone which train I’d taken. When I said she had the wrong person, she checked my coat pocket with her eyes and stepped aside. I crossed the concourse, then doubled back behind a row of vending machines. She was speaking to a man in a maintenance vest, pointing toward the exit I’d used. I tucked the package beneath my jacket and joined a tour group heading toward the museum. At the archive, the guard examined my identification twice and called the recipient down in person. Only after the handover did I notice a tiny slit in the envelope’s seal. I asked the archivist to record it before either of us touched the contents.

Eleven-year-old Laleh arrived with her uncle in a city of glass towers, but he disappeared while buying bus tickets. A woman at the counter said she could help and reached for Laleh’s backpack. Laleh stepped behind a metal post and asked her to name her uncle. The woman paused, then guessed a name that belonged to Laleh’s teacher. Laleh pressed the emergency button on her watch. The woman’s smile tightened as a transit worker came over. She claimed she had only been offering directions, yet she left before the worker finished asking questions. Laleh stayed beside the information desk, where a family waited nearby, and called her uncle from the number saved in her watch. When he arrived, she made him show his ticket and say their agreed meeting phrase before she went anywhere with him.

The city’s old quarter smelled of rain and coal smoke, and I was glad to find a room above a bakery. Then the baker asked whether I still carried the blue envelope. I had told no one about it. I moved my hand to my coat pocket and felt the envelope’s stiff edge. He laughed, saying he meant a different traveler, but his gaze kept dropping to the same pocket. I paid for one night and went upstairs. Through the floorboards, I heard him speaking to someone in the kitchen, followed by the scrape of a chair toward the back door. I packed without turning on the lamp, left through the front entrance, and checked the pavement for anyone trailing me. At the railway station, I bought a ticket under my middle name and kept the envelope pressed flat beneath my shirt.

Rosa, a seventy-two-year-old botanist, arrived in the coastal city to identify a rare plant in the municipal garden. The man who met her at the station introduced himself as the curator, but his badge named a different institution. He knew which specimen she had come to examine and suggested they go directly to a private greenhouse. Rosa asked to see his appointment letter. He said it was in the car, then reached for her field bag. She stepped behind a pillar and called the garden’s published number. While she waited, he walked toward the taxi rank, looking back twice. The real curator arrived ten minutes later, carrying an official letter and a familiar face from their email exchange. Rosa showed him the badge description and asked that the gate staff be alerted before she entered the garden.

When my manager’s message arrived, it said only, “Come by at two.” I reread it until the words seemed to shift. At two, I carried a folder I didn’t need and paused outside her office, listening. A printer hummed; someone laughed in the corridor. Inside, she pointed to the chair and closed the door. I noticed a second mug on her desk, still warm, and a spreadsheet turned facedown beneath her hand. “How’s the new inventory system?” she asked. I answered carefully, wondering why she hadn’t mentioned the project in weeks. Then she slid over a form asking me to train the incoming team. I searched her face for a catch, but she was already explaining the schedule. Even after she smiled and thanked me, I left with my folder clutched to my chest, trying to work out who else had been asked.

Nia arrived at the manager’s office with a notebook open to a clean page. The calendar invitation had come from an unfamiliar assistant, and its subject line was simply “Quick chat.” She’d spent the morning replaying yesterday’s meeting, searching for a sentence that might have landed badly. In the doorway, she saw her manager turn a phone screen facedown. “You wanted to see me?” Nia asked, keeping her voice even. He gestured toward a chair and asked whether she knew who had moved the late shift assignments. Nia glanced at the printed roster between them. Her name appeared beside several changes she hadn’t made. She explained that the scheduling software had been glitching, then watched him read her expression instead of the page. He finally said he’d found the error log. Nia nodded, but kept her hands folded until he turned the monitor around.

I was halfway through repairing a display case when the office phone rang. My supervisor asked me to come upstairs, though the day’s work was nearly done. In the stairwell, I counted each step and wondered why he hadn’t used the radio. His office door stood ajar. A paper cup sat beside my time sheet, and the top page had a yellow mark next to Tuesday. “Have a seat, Omar,” he said, too brightly. I stayed standing until he explained that a customer had praised my repair and wanted me to lead a restoration project. The praise sounded real; the marked time sheet did not. I asked whether there was a problem with my hours. He blinked, then laughed and admitted payroll had queried everyone’s entries. I accepted the project, but on the way out I checked the hallway for anyone waiting to ask about Tuesday.

At the bakery, Mei had learned that unexpected meetings usually meant a broken oven or an unhappy customer. So when the manager summoned her just before closing, she wiped flour from her palms twice before entering. A chair had been pulled away from the desk, while a sealed envelope lay near the keyboard. Her manager asked about the delivery van, then about a box of pastries that had gone missing. Mei’s gaze darted to the envelope. She had signed for the box, but left it in the loading area while helping a customer. “I didn’t take anything,” she said, faster than she intended. The manager looked surprised and opened the envelope: it held an offer for a paid baking course. The missing pastries had been found in the driver’s cab. Mei smiled at the news, though she kept glancing at the envelope as if another page might appear.

My manager sent a calendar request with no description, then called me into her office ten minutes before lunch. I brought my access badge and left my coffee untouched on the desk. She had the blinds half closed, which made the room feel smaller than usual. “You’ve been looking at the archive?” she asked. My stomach tightened. I had opened three old case files to answer a client’s question, and the system had shown a warning banner. I asked which files she meant, trying to keep my face still. She turned her laptop toward me. The list showed every document I’d viewed, including two I didn’t recognize. Instead of accusing me, she asked if I could help test a new search tool. I agreed, but pointed out the unfamiliar entries. She checked the audit log and found they belonged to an automated preview. I returned to my desk and read the calendar request again.

Rafael was called into the manager’s office while the warehouse crew watched from behind their carts. He wiped his hands on his uniform and asked the dispatcher whether anyone had mentioned a damaged shipment. Nobody answered. Inside, his manager had placed a small metal tag on the desk, its stamped number matching a crate Rafael had inspected that morning. “Do you know how this ended up in the returns bin?” she asked. Rafael described the cracked seal and the photos he had taken. He noticed she kept the door open, as though expecting someone else to join them. When she asked for his phone, he hesitated before unlocking it. The photos were still there, time-stamped and clear. She studied them, then called the supplier to verify the shipment history. The tag turned out to be from an older crate. Rafael handed back his phone, but waited until she ended the call before relaxing his grip on it.

The call came while I was helping a customer compare paint samples. My manager’s assistant said he needed to see me “right away,” then hung up before I could ask why. I walked to the office with a color chart still in my hand. My manager sat beside the window, and a woman I didn’t know stood near the filing cabinet. I looked from her to the locked drawer behind the desk. “This is Dana from the new branch,” he said. “We’d like your advice on opening displays.” I thanked him, but my attention kept returning to the stranger’s badge, which had no company logo. Dana explained that she was a consultant and asked how we tracked returned paint. I answered, then asked whether the visit was connected to last week’s stock count. My manager said it wasn’t. Only when Dana showed me her project brief did I set down the chart and pull up a chair.

The manager’s message reached Leon during a video call: Please come to my office afterward. He finished the meeting without hearing much of the final presentation. On the walk upstairs, he noticed two coworkers stop talking as he passed. The office door was shut, and a folder with his department’s name sat on the chair. His manager asked whether he had changed the shared drive permissions. Leon said he had restored access for the night crew, as requested, and offered to show the ticket. She tapped a pen against the folder while he opened the system history. The change appeared under an unfamiliar account. Leon watched her eyes move to his badge, then to the timestamp. He asked whether someone else had used his login. She paused before answering and said the review was routine. He left after giving her the ticket number, still wondering why she had asked him first and checked the records second.

I was called into the manager’s office after a customer complained that someone had opened a package in the returns room. My manager didn’t say who had reported it. A half-eaten granola bar sat beside the incident form, and the camera monitor had been turned away from me. I asked whether I should bring a representative. She raised her eyebrows and said she only wanted to understand the room’s key log. I explained that I had borrowed the key to fetch packing tape, then returned it immediately. While I spoke, I watched her write down the exact time. She asked me to repeat it. I gave her the time again and offered to show the note I’d made on my shift sheet. That seemed to change the conversation. She checked the camera footage, then apologized: the package had been opened by a courier. I thanked her, but kept my own copy of the log.

At the museum, Priya was halfway through cataloguing donated maps when the director asked her to come upstairs. The request came through a new staff member who wouldn’t meet her eye. Priya took the stairs slowly, trying to remember whether she had left any records incomplete. In the office, the director had set out two chairs and a sealed envelope. “We found this in the conservation room,” he said. The envelope bore Priya’s handwriting, though she didn’t recognize it. She asked where it had been discovered. He said it was tucked inside a ledger she had checked out. Priya kept her hands in her pockets while he opened it. Inside was a note about a map’s hidden inscription, written years earlier by another curator. The director wanted her to investigate. Priya leaned closer, but first asked him to photograph the envelope and record exactly where it had been found.

My manager asked me to stop by after the morning briefing, and I spent the next hour noticing every whisper near my desk. In her office, she had a stack of printed emails and a bowl of wrapped candies. One candy wrapper was already open. She asked whether I had sent a message to the regional team about the new pricing table. I said I had, after getting approval, and asked if the numbers were wrong. She didn’t answer immediately. Instead, she turned one page over and studied the blank side. I began listing who had reviewed the table, careful not to leave anyone out. Then she told me the regional director had praised the clear explanation and wanted me to present it at the next meeting. I laughed, though it came out thin. On my way back, I checked my sent mail again, making sure the approval thread was still attached.

When Victor was summoned to the manager’s office, he carried a stack of invoices as a shield. The manager had asked for him by name, but the receptionist wouldn’t say what the meeting concerned. Inside, a desk lamp pointed at a single invoice from a supplier Victor had never used. His manager asked whether he recognized the signature at the bottom. Victor leaned in, then stepped back without touching the page. The handwriting resembled his, but the date fell on a day he had worked from home. He asked who had submitted it. His manager said it had arrived through the normal system and watched him closely while he answered. Victor opened his calendar and pulled up the work log, then offered to contact the supplier with her present. The manager agreed. The company had entered the wrong employee code, and the signature belonged to a contractor. Victor set down his invoices only after they corrected the record.

I sat beneath the clinic’s clock, watching the receptionist slide a folder beneath her desk whenever I looked up. She had told me my blood results would take twenty minutes; now the minute hand had crossed the hour. When a nurse came through the door, I asked whether the lab had sent anything. “Not yet,” she said, though a corner of paper stuck out of her clipboard, marked with my birth date. I pretended to read a magazine and listened as she whispered to the receptionist. Both glanced my way. My palms dampened around the paper cup. Perhaps they were discussing another patient, but I had heard my surname. I stood and asked for the clinic manager. The nurse’s smile tightened. Then she handed me the page: the lab had called, but they had mixed up my sample with someone else’s.

At seventy-two, Ruthie knew exactly how long a receptionist could take to answer a simple question. She watched the woman tap at her keyboard, then turn the monitor a few inches away. The clinic had promised results before lunch, yet the waiting room was nearly empty and no one had called her name. Ruthie folded her hands over her purse and kept her eyes on the hallway. A man in a white coat came out carrying a tray; the receptionist stopped him with a murmured word. He looked toward Ruthie, then went back inside. She rose before anyone could tell her to sit down. “My sample has my label, doesn’t it?” she asked. The doctor blinked, checked the chart, and admitted the lab had entered the wrong date of birth. Ruthie asked to watch him correct it.

I brought a crossword to the walk-in clinic, but I couldn’t fill in a single square. A technician had said my throat swab results would be ready shortly. When I asked the desk clerk for an update, she covered the phone receiver and told me to wait. Then she carried a sealed envelope toward the back, passing my chair without looking at me. I noticed my initials on its edge. My knee bounced hard enough to rattle the chair legs. I followed at a distance, stopping when she entered a room marked STAFF ONLY. A few minutes later, a doctor came out holding the same envelope. “You’ve been waiting on this?” he asked. I nodded. He explained that the clerk had mistaken my chart for another patient’s and apologized for the delay. The result itself was negative.

Mateo, a night-shift cook, checked his phone every thirty seconds while waiting for a clinic to call him in with his test results. The nurse who had taken his sample had asked twice whether he had recently traveled, then exchanged a look with another staff member. Now, at the desk, the receptionist said the doctor was reviewing the report. Mateo leaned forward to see what she was typing, but she lowered the screen. He rubbed the seam of his work jacket and asked if the lab had found something unusual. “We can’t discuss it here,” she replied. That answer followed him down the corridor. When the doctor finally opened the door, Mateo had already rehearsed three explanations. It turned out the sample container had arrived without a barcode; they needed to collect another one, and no one had told him.

I kept my coat on even though the clinic room was warm. The nurse said my scan report was being checked, then left without saying by whom. Through the half-open door, I heard a printer start and stop. A receptionist passed with a sheet tucked against her chest; when she saw me, she turned it over. I watched her disappear around the corner, then asked the nurse at the station whether my name was on that page. She frowned and said she couldn’t tell. My fingers pressed little crescents into my palm. The physician finally came in carrying a tablet and apologized for keeping me. The report was clear, he said, but the first file he’d received belonged to a different patient with the same last name. I asked him to show me the corrected record before I left.

Nadia had driven two hours to the rural clinic and did not appreciate being told that her results had been delayed by a computer problem. The receptionist had said the system was down, yet she kept taking calls and printing forms. Nadia watched the printer feed out a page, then saw the clerk slide it under a stack when she approached. “Is that my report?” Nadia asked. The clerk said no too quickly. Nadia’s jaw set as she sat again, eyes fixed on the desk. When a doctor came out, she asked him to confirm that her sample had not been sent to the wrong hospital. He checked the screen, then went quiet. The courier had delivered it to a neighboring town’s clinic by mistake. Nadia requested the tracking number and waited while he arranged a fresh delivery.

I sat near the fish tank, counting bubbles while the clinic searched for my blood test. A nurse had taken the vial an hour ago, but now the receptionist said it wasn’t in the system. I asked her to check the paper log. She glanced at the nurse, who shook her head slightly. That tiny gesture made my stomach clench. I remembered the nurse labeling the vial after she had drawn it, not before. Had she put someone else’s name on mine? I walked to the counter and asked to speak with whoever handled specimens. The receptionist started to object, then called the lab. A technician returned with a clipboard and confirmed the label had peeled off in transit. They would need another sample. I rolled up my sleeve without taking my eyes off the vial tray.

Elliot, a retired bus driver, sat with his hat balanced on both knees as the clinic staff reviewed his heart test. The physician had said the results were straightforward, yet two nurses came in separately to ask his age and the date of his appointment. Each wrote something down without explaining why. Elliot watched them leave, then inspected the wristband they had given him. One digit in his birthday was wrong. He went to the desk and pointed it out. The receptionist said it didn’t matter, but he kept his finger on the printed number until she checked his file. A second patient with a similar name had been booked that morning. The doctor returned, confirmed Elliot’s own test was normal, and thanked him for catching the mix-up before the report was filed.

I heard my name called, then watched the nurse look past me toward a woman at the far end of the waiting room. She called it again, this time with a different first name attached. I raised my hand. “I’m here for the results of my skin test,” I said. The nurse studied the chart, then asked me to confirm my address. I answered and saw her mouth tighten. The other woman was gone, but the nurse kept glancing at the empty seat she had occupied. I asked whether my results had been placed in the wrong chart. She said she would check. The pause stretched while she typed. Finally, she explained that the two of us shared a surname and the receptionist had opened the wrong file. My result was ready, but I asked her to verify every page.

At the neighborhood clinic, Juniper waited for a phone call about her allergy panel while sitting beside a window that faced the staff parking lot. She saw the doctor arrive, carry a paper bag inside, and leave again without coming to the waiting room. The receptionist had promised he would discuss her results in person. Juniper asked whether the doctor had reviewed them; the receptionist said yes, then looked down at her hands. Juniper’s throat felt dry. She called her partner and quietly described what she had seen. When the doctor returned, she asked why he had left. He seemed surprised, then explained he had only dropped off lunch and had not yet opened her file. The panel showed one mild allergy. Juniper asked him to read the numbers aloud as she followed along on the printed sheet.

I had been waiting forty minutes when a man in a lab coat walked through the clinic lobby carrying a folder with my name on it. He didn’t stop at the desk; he went straight outside. I followed him to the glass doors and watched him put the folder in his car. When I asked the receptionist, she said the doctor had taken my results to review them elsewhere. That made no sense to me. I asked for the office manager and kept my voice low, though my cheeks burned. The man came back a few minutes later, empty-handed and apologetic. He was a courier, he explained, and the folder was meant for another branch. Mine was still being processed. I stayed at the counter until the staff confirmed my sample was safely in the clinic lab.

Marlene, a young violinist, waited in a crowded clinic lobby for the results of a routine test. A staff member had told her the doctor would call her name, but when the door opened, the physician spoke quietly to the receptionist and both glanced at Marlene’s chart. She crossed her ankles and studied their faces. The receptionist then called a name that sounded almost like hers. Marlene stood, but the nurse said it was someone else. “Then why are you holding my file?” Marlene asked. The receptionist looked down at the folder in her hands. A new patient had been entered under Marlene’s phone number by mistake, so the clinic had attached the wrong appointment to her record. They untangled the entries while Marlene waited beside the desk, checking the information on each form before signing.

Dad said the community pool was empty, but three wet footprints crossed the tiles before we reached the gate. I stopped while he unlocked it. He glanced at the prints, then said the cleaner must have made them, though the building had been closed all morning. I kept my towel wrapped tight and watched him test the water with his hand. “Come on, Mina,” he said, holding out the kickboard. His smile stayed fixed when I asked who had been here. I stepped in only after he climbed down beside me. He showed me how to float, one palm beneath my shoulders, and told me to breathe slowly. When a locker clanged in the hallway, I grabbed his wrist. He looked toward the door, too. After a moment, he called out, and a sleepy lifeguard emerged from the office carrying a mop. Only then did I let my legs drift free.

At the lake, Tomas brought a new life vest for his daughter, Leni, though she already owned one. He said the old buckle was unreliable, then tucked it into his bag before she could inspect it. Leni studied the replacement label, still stiff and bright, and asked why it had been cut off. Tomas answered that it had snagged on the car door. She pinched the straps between her fingers and made him pull each one hard. He laughed, but his eyes kept darting toward the deep-water marker. For her first lesson, he stayed close, guiding her hands through the water and showing her how to kick. When a passing boat sent waves against the dock, Leni clutched the ladder. Tomas steadied her, then pointed to the vest’s hidden safety tag inside the lining. Its serial number matched the receipt in his pocket. She loosened her grip and tried again.

My mother chose a quiet hotel pool for my first swimming lesson and insisted we use the far end, away from the windows. She had brought goggles, a cap, and a laminated diagram of the pool’s depths. I asked why she kept checking the ceiling camera. “Habit,” she said, though her jaw tightened each time its red light blinked. She knelt beside me and demonstrated a gentle flutter kick. I copied her from the steps, keeping one hand on the rail. Then a staff member appeared with a clipboard and asked whether we had reserved the lane. Mom’s shoulders lifted. She showed him our booking email, but I watched his badge instead of his face. He explained that a swim class had been moved to another pool. When he left, Mom finally let out her breath. She stayed beside me while I practiced floating, and I counted the camera’s flashes until the water felt less strange.

Rafi had promised his son, Devon, a lesson in the apartment complex pool, but he arrived carrying two towels and no goggles. Devon noticed the missing gear and asked whether they had stopped at the shop. Rafi said he had packed everything. He rummaged through the bag twice, producing a hairbrush, a sandwich, and a folded newspaper. Devon sat on the edge, watching his father’s hands. Rafi finally admitted he had left the goggles at home, then offered to teach without them. Devon made him check the bag once more. A small plastic key slid out from under the newspaper, stamped with the pool’s maintenance-room number. Rafi’s face changed; he said the manager had asked him to return it. Devon waited until he had placed it on the front desk. Then they began the lesson. Rafi showed him how to blow bubbles, and Devon practiced while keeping one eye on the key behind the glass.

I signed up for swim lessons with my aunt because she said the river beach was safe in summer. Before we went in, she made me stand beside a yellow sign and read every line aloud. I thought it was an odd game. She kept glancing toward a man in a red cap who had been sitting by the launch ramp since we arrived. When he stood, Aunt Jo shifted between us and the water. “Let’s practice in the shallows first,” she said, speaking more brightly than usual. She taught me to kick while holding her shoulders, but her gaze kept returning to the ramp. The man finally walked over, holding a small dog’s leash. He had lost the dog’s tag and wanted help reading the sign’s number for beach staff. Aunt Jo pointed him to the lifeguard station. After he left, she showed me how to float on my back. Her hand stayed firm beneath me, and mine unclenched around her sleeve.

At the indoor recreation center, twelve-year-old Niko had agreed to teach his little sister, Bea, to swim while their father watched from the bleachers. Their father kept checking his phone and turning the screen facedown whenever Bea looked over. Niko noticed, too. He asked why Dad had brought a second set of car keys and placed them under his towel. Dad said he was expecting a call from work. Bea refused to leave the steps until he put the phone away. He sighed, then joined them in the shallow lane. He showed her how to glide, hands stretched forward, and promised not to let go. Bea kept looking toward the bleachers. At last Dad retrieved the keys and revealed a paper wristband beneath them: he had arranged a surprise visit from their cousin, who was waiting in the lobby. Bea checked the name on it herself before she pushed off. Niko caught her after a short, wobbly glide.

My father took me to the public beach before sunrise, saying the calm water would make learning easier. He had brought a thermos but no bathing suit for himself, which seemed strange if he planned to stay beside me. I kept checking the empty lifeguard tower and the dark line of rocks. Dad said he had spoken with a ranger, yet when I asked the ranger’s name, he rubbed the back of his neck and changed the subject. He waded in wearing rolled-up jeans and showed me how to kick while holding the shore rope. Each time a wave moved the rope, he pulled me closer. I asked whether it was anchored. He tested the knot and discovered it had loosened from its post. We stepped out and found a beach worker, who secured it properly. Dad apologized for rushing. Afterward, with the rope firm and the sky brightening, I practiced floating while he stood close enough to catch me.

Mei’s mother brought her to a hotel pool during a business trip and said they could use it before breakfast. Mei noticed a handwritten notice taped beside the entrance, though her mother walked past without reading it. She stopped and asked what it said. Her mother claimed it was only about towels, then tried the locked gate. Mei stayed behind the painted line. A cleaner emerged carrying a bucket and explained that the pool was closed for testing. Mother nodded too quickly and asked when it would reopen. Mei watched her carefully as she folded the towel back into her bag. They found a public pool two blocks away, where her mother checked the posted hours and spoke with the attendant before paying. During the lesson, she showed Mei how to push off the wall and glide. Mei made her demonstrate the depth with a measuring pole first. Her mother did so without complaint, and Mei finally let her feet leave the tiles.

Grandpa said the old quarry pond was shallow near the shore, but he kept steering me away from a patch of reeds. I asked what was behind them. He said nothing, then looked toward the parking lot as if expecting someone. He had brought a rope and tied one end around a tree, telling me it would help me feel secure while I kicked. I tugged the knot twice. It slid a little. Grandpa frowned and replaced it with a stronger loop, explaining that he had used the wrong branch. I didn’t get in until he tested it with his full weight. He stood in the water and held my hands while I practiced moving my legs. A rustle came from the reeds, and I climbed out fast. A turtle crawled onto a rock, followed by a second one. Grandpa laughed softly, but I watched the water for another minute before trying again. This time, he stayed right beside me.

At a small YMCA pool, Saira’s father offered to teach her after the instructor canceled. He kept insisting they use the lane nearest the supply closet, even though a whistle lay unattended at the far end. Saira asked why he wanted that lane. He said it was quieter, then examined the door’s narrow window. She stood with her arms folded while he tested the water and explained how to hold the wall. A custodian entered the closet, and her father immediately stepped in front of her. The custodian emerged carrying a stack of kickboards and apologized for leaving the door ajar. Saira asked her father whether he knew the custodian. He said no, but his fingers had tightened around the whistle. They moved to a lane where the lifeguard could see them clearly. Her father demonstrated a front float, and Saira copied him, pausing whenever the closet door opened until the lesson was nearly over.

My mother said she had found a private swimming cove, but the directions on her phone led us to a fenced resort beach. She claimed the map had changed. I watched her try the gate, then read the sign about guest access. She told me to wait while she spoke to the guard. I stayed close enough to hear her give our name, then watched the guard shake his head. Mom returned, cheeks pink, and admitted she had mistaken the cove entrance. We walked around to a public beach, where she asked a lifeguard about the safest area for a beginner. He pointed to a flagged shallow section. I made her read the flag colors with me before we went in. She taught me to breathe out underwater, counting on her fingers. When a group arrived carrying bright boards, I backed toward shore. Mom checked with the lifeguard that the area was still open, then showed me how to float while we kept to the marked boundary.

Elias brought his eight-year-old son, Kit, to a farm pond and promised to teach him to swim. Kit noticed that his father had placed a flat stone over a small wooden box near the bank. When he asked what it was, Elias said it held fishing hooks. Kit asked why it was there instead of in the tackle bag. His father paused, then admitted he had hidden Kit’s birthday present so it would stay dry. Kit wouldn’t enter until they opened the box together. Inside was a model sailboat wrapped in cloth. Elias let him hold it while they waded into the shallows. He explained how to blow bubbles and kick, keeping one hand beneath Kit’s chest. Kit asked him to show that the water never went above his own waist. Elias walked back and forth to prove it, then returned. Once Kit had seen the pond’s bottom clearly and watched his father test every step, he practiced floating with the sailboat waiting safely on shore.

I was forty minutes behind when I reached the blue house on Alder Street, where the porch light blinked though the afternoon was bright. The customer had asked for the parcel to be left beside the side gate, not at the front door. As I carried it around, I noticed fresh footprints in the damp flower bed, all pointing toward the house and none leading back. The gate stood open by a finger’s width. I set the box down without stepping through and checked the delivery notes again. They had been edited twice, the last change made while I was already on the road. A curtain shifted upstairs. I called dispatch and asked them to confirm the address. Through the phone, my supervisor said the customer was still on the line, insisting I hurry. I backed toward the van before answering.

At 6:20, Darnell was still three stops behind, and the apartment buzzer at his next address kept clicking by itself. He pressed the unit number listed on the label. A man’s voice told him to leave the package in the lobby, then immediately asked whether Darnell had seen anyone enter the building. Darnell glanced at the glass doors; the street beyond was empty except for a parked sedan with its headlights on. The voice repeated the question, slower this time. Darnell looked down at the parcel. Its shipping label had been peeled and stuck back on crookedly, with another name visible beneath the corner. He carried it back to his cart and told the caller he needed a signature. The buzzer went silent. As he rolled toward the lobby exit, the sedan’s engine started.

I had promised my daughter I’d be home before her recital, but a flat tire put me an hour behind. At the final stop, an old man waved me toward a barn instead of the farmhouse printed on the label. He said the owners were away and he’d take the parcel inside. His coat was dry, though rain streamed off the barn roof, and he kept glancing at my van’s open cargo door. I asked him to sign the handheld screen. He made a mark that looked nothing like the name on the delivery. When I mentioned the mismatch, his smile held while his eyes moved to the road behind me. A second vehicle had turned in without headlights. I picked up the box again, told him dispatch required a photo at the listed address, and walked back to my van with my keys between my fingers.

Mei’s route had slipped badly after a bridge closure, so she reached the hotel supply entrance near midnight. The man waiting there wore a staff badge, but he kept it tucked beneath his jacket and asked her to bring the cartons through a door marked EMPLOYEES ONLY. Her scanner showed the delivery belonged at the front desk. He said the desk clerk was new and had been told not to log the shipment. Mei studied the badge’s blurred photograph, then the fresh scrape around the lock. From inside came a thump, followed by a muffled voice. The man moved closer and held out his hand for the scanner. Mei turned the screen toward herself and pretended to call her dispatcher. When she read out the hotel address, he stepped away from the door. She left the cartons by the public entrance and waited beside the lit lobby until security arrived.

I was running late because the expressway had been shut for a parade, and the bakery box in my passenger seat was beginning to tilt. The delivery instructions said to knock twice at the rear entrance. A woman opened the door before my second knock, though I hadn’t made the first. She knew the order number and said the owner was expecting me, but the address on my screen belonged to a house across the lane. I asked her to confirm the recipient’s name. She gave me a different one, then laughed and said everyone was tired. Behind her, a hallway mirror reflected a figure standing where no one was visible. I took a step back and said I’d need the owner to verify the change through the app. Her hand tightened around the door edge. I returned to the van and called the number attached to the order.

With evening traffic crawling, Lionel arrived late at a rural mailbox cluster and found a child standing beside it, holding a phone that rang in Lionel’s pocket. The package label showed an adult recipient several miles away. The child said the recipient had asked for the parcel and pointed toward a gravel lane. Lionel checked the app; the delivery location dot sat on the main road, not down that lane. A fresh set of tire tracks crossed the mud and disappeared between the trees. When Lionel asked the child to call the named customer, the phone went quiet. The child stared at his van’s license plate and recited the last three digits. Lionel lowered the box onto the passenger seat and locked the doors. He drove to the nearest gas station, then reported the encounter and waited for an address confirmation before continuing.

My last delivery was already late when the customer messaged, “Come around back, don’t use the bell.” I was in a crowded market district, with scooters threading between parked cars and my route timer flashing red. The alley behind the building smelled of wet cardboard. A man stood beside a loading door, holding a clipboard with my company logo printed upside down. He called me by my first name before I introduced myself. I asked for the order code. He gave a number that matched, but the screen showed the package required a handoff to the named recipient. He said she was upstairs and pointed to a narrow stairwell. A second person stepped into the alley behind me. I kept the parcel in my arms and asked them to have the customer meet me at the front. Neither moved. I walked back toward the market, speaking loudly into my phone as if dispatch were listening.

Nadia’s delivery van was nearly an hour late after a burst water main rerouted the entire district. At the listed address, a man in a spotless suit waited beneath a bare porch bulb and said the parcel was for his neighbor. The label plainly showed his own house number. He asked Nadia to scan it as delivered, then claimed he would take it across himself. When she declined, he began describing the contents: a small brass instrument packed in foam. Nadia had not mentioned what she was carrying. She tilted the scanner so he couldn’t see the screen and asked him to show identification. Instead, he reached toward the van’s side door, saying the real box might still be inside. Nadia slid the lock shut with her hip. A dog barked from the neighboring yard, and the man’s gaze snapped toward it. She used the moment to call her supervisor.

I was behind schedule on a mountain route when I reached the cabin marked for a signature. The porch was empty, but a kettle whistled inside and the front door stood open. I called out the customer’s name. A voice from the woods answered, telling me to leave the package under the mat. The mat was folded back, exposing a rectangle of clean wood amid the dust. I checked the label again; the parcel was addressed to a medical clinic, not a cabin. The route app had sent me here only after a sudden update. My phone showed no signal, yet a new message appeared on the screen: “Don’t go back the way you came.” I put the box on the porch, took a photo from the road, and climbed into the van. In the mirror, someone emerged from the trees carrying a second, identical parcel.

After a crash slowed the ring road, Pavel reached the office tower well past the promised delivery window. The receptionist took one look at the envelope and said the recipient had already gone home. A security guard behind her asked Pavel to leave it with him, though the envelope was marked for personal hand delivery. The guard knew the sender’s name and the exact color of the sealed folder inside. Pavel asked to see his badge. The guard covered it with his palm and said the elevators were down. Yet one elevator opened behind him, empty and lit. Pavel glanced at the visitor log; the last page had been torn out. He told them company policy required a failed-attempt scan and carried the envelope back to the loading bay. On the way, he called the sender from the number on the label, keeping his eyes on the tower’s glass entrance.

I was an hour late to the marina after getting trapped behind roadwork, and the parcel’s recipient was waiting beside a row of dark boats. He said he’d been watching the road for me. The shipping address listed a house inland, so I asked why he’d chosen the marina as the handoff point. He shrugged and said the package was fragile. Then he recited the delivery code before I’d opened the app. My thumb hovered above the screen. On the dock, a coil of rope had been cut cleanly, its loose end trailing into the water. The man asked me to step aboard so he could sign. I told him the scanner needed a signal and took two paces toward the parking lot. He followed, still smiling, and asked whether I’d noticed a second van. I hadn’t. I looked over my shoulder and saw one idling with its lights off.

Rosa was late to the final stop after a snowplow blocked the neighborhood entrance. A teenager opened the door and said his parents were asleep, then asked whether the package contained a phone. The label identified it as a box of replacement printer parts. Rosa held it close and asked for an adult’s signature. The teenager glanced past her toward the van, where a man stood behind the frosted window, though Rosa had arrived alone. She looked again; the seat was empty. The boy insisted she had already delivered to this house last week and described the color of her gloves. Rosa had never been on this street before. She marked the attempt incomplete and started back toward the road. The porch light switched off behind her. Before she reached the van, her route app refreshed, moving her next stop to an address across town.

When I retired from the county bus depot, I claimed the sunny strip behind my bungalow for tomatoes and beans. On the second morning, a neat row of seed packets sat beside my tools, though I had left them locked in the shed. My neighbor, Mr. Pike, waved from his porch and said he’d been “helping out.” I thanked him, then counted the packets twice. One was missing, and a damp footprint crossed the soil toward the fence. I moved my trowel indoors and set a folding chair where I could see the beds from the kitchen. The next afternoon, a sprinkler clicked on while its hose was still coiled. I shut it off and found a fresh hole beneath the tomato cage. Whatever was happening, I decided, would have to happen while I was watching.

At seventy-one, Noreen had traded her pharmacy counter for six raised beds behind a cottage in coastal Maine. She planted kale, carrots, and peas, then found small stones arranged in a circle around each seedling. Her son said the pattern looked like a child’s game. Noreen studied the stones, then checked the garden gate, whose latch had a new scratch. She began keeping a notebook of watering times and harvest counts. When a stranger at the market asked which bed held her rare purple beans, she smiled without answering. That evening she tucked the seed tin beneath a loose floorboard. In the morning, the stones had been moved into a line pointing toward the shed. Noreen stood very still, listening to the gulls and the quiet scrape of something shifting behind the wooden door.

I spent thirty years repairing radios, so I notice when a signal changes. My new garden in the Arizona retirement complex seemed simple enough: peppers, squash, a few herbs. Then the building manager started appearing whenever I watered, asking how deep I’d dug and whether the soil came from elsewhere. I gave him cheerful answers, but after he left, I checked the little stakes marking my rows. Two had been turned around. A week later, a resident I barely knew offered to “take care” of my plot while I visited my sister. I declined and brought my hand tools into my apartment. That night, I heard footsteps stop outside my door. In the morning, my watering can was full, though I’d stored it empty. I set it back exactly where it had been and watched the hallway from behind the curtain.

Gideon, a retired lighthouse keeper, planted vegetables on a sloping plot above the harbor. He measured each row with a length of rope and marked the ends with chipped blue tiles. One morning, the tiles were gone, and a narrow trench cut across his neat beds. The gardener from next door blamed rain, but the ground was dry and the trench walls stood crisp. Gideon bent to inspect them, then glanced at the footprints leading toward the old boathouse. He asked at the harbor office whether anyone had been working nearby. The clerk shrugged, so Gideon went home and planted his remaining lettuce seeds in pots by the kitchen window. He left the outdoor beds untouched for a day. At dusk, a lantern flickered once in the boathouse, then vanished. Gideon locked his back gate before turning in.

After retiring from the high school cafeteria, I started a garden in the community lot beside the railway. I made a chart for each bed and wrote down every seed I planted. The first carrots came up in tidy rows, but someone had clipped their tops with scissors. My fellow gardeners offered guesses: rabbits, children, careless boots. I found no paw prints, only a square of clean earth where my small stool had stood. The next day, I carried the stool home. A man I’d never met asked whether I had planted anything valuable. I told him turnips, and he laughed too quickly. Now I water at different hours, sometimes from the alley, sometimes from the path. When I spot a figure near the fence, I keep my face pleasant and my keys threaded between my fingers.

Marta had spent her retirement in a quiet Colorado town, where she turned a patch of lawn into a vegetable garden. She installed a rain barrel and carefully labeled her tomato varieties. Then the barrel’s lid appeared on the ground, though its clasp was intact. A neighbor said raccoons were clever, but Marta found no muddy marks on the barrel or nearby fence. She began bringing her labels inside each evening. When a delivery driver asked whether she lived alone, she answered by asking what company he worked for. He glanced at his clipboard and left without delivering a parcel. That night, Marta placed a bell on the garden gate. Before dawn, it rang once. She opened the back curtain and saw the gate closed, the bell still, and a wheelbarrow parked beside the shed in a place she had not left it.

I retired from the navy with a habit of checking doors twice, and my new vegetable garden gave that habit plenty to do. The allotment sits behind a church in Liverpool, where I planted onions and broad beans. Someone kept shifting my water jug a few inches each time I visited. It was a small thing, easy to dismiss, but the handle always faced the wrong way. I marked its position with a chalk line. The following morning, the jug stood beyond the line, and the chalk had been rubbed from the paving. I asked the caretaker if he’d been near the plot. He said no while staring at my boots. I started carrying the jug with me. A week later, a folded note appeared under my gate, asking me to stop digging near the brick wall. I had never touched the wall.

At sixty-eight, Clarence bought a modest house outside Atlanta and planted okra, collards, and tomatoes in the backyard. His first harvest disappeared overnight, leaving only a few cut stems. He suspected deer at first, until he saw the garden gate still secured and a clean slice on each stalk. Clarence bought a motion light and mounted it above the shed. The next evening, it flashed toward the back fence, though nothing showed in the yard. He walked out with a flashlight and found the battery cover hanging open. Rather than complain to his neighbors, he invited them over for lemonade and listened as they discussed who had keys to the alley gate. One guest knew exactly where the spare was kept. Clarence kept smiling, but when the visit ended, he moved the key to a drawer inside his house.

I came home to Vermont after retiring from a museum, eager to grow vegetables where my parents once kept lilacs. The soil was rich, but the first week brought a surprise: every new plant had a tag bearing the wrong name. My zucchini was labeled cucumber; my basil said mint. I corrected them and tucked the marker box into the greenhouse. Two days later, the tags were mixed again. I asked the hardware clerk whether anyone had bought the same markers, and he said a woman from my road had. I hadn’t mentioned my project to anyone there. I began planting extra seeds in trays indoors and leaving one empty bed outside. On a misty morning, I found fresh boot prints circling the empty bed. I stepped backward, shut the greenhouse door, and watched the road until a car rolled past without slowing.

Rafiq, a retired machinist in Manchester, built a vegetable garden from reclaimed timber behind his narrow terrace. He fitted each board with screws of the same length, then noticed one had been replaced by a bright new bolt. The change seemed too precise to be an accident. He ran a finger over the threads and found a fleck of green paint, matching nothing in his yard. Rafiq asked the landlord about repairs; the man said no one had entered. After that, Rafiq kept the shed key on a chain beneath his shirt. One morning, the key was still there, yet a packet of beet seeds had shifted from the shelf to the floor. He left a thin layer of flour across the shed threshold. By midday, a single shoe print crossed it, pointing inward. Rafiq closed the door and called his niece.

I retired to a small island off the coast of Washington and planted potatoes where the previous owner had kept a boat. The first few weeks went smoothly, until a neighbor began leaving fish heads beside my compost bin. He said they would enrich the soil. I thanked him, though I hadn’t asked for them, and buried the remains far from the beds. Then I noticed the same blue twine tied around the bin and around a stake marking my property line. I untied both pieces and put them in a jar. The neighbor stopped by to ask whether I’d seen any seals. I said no and watched his eyes move past me toward the shed. That evening I moved my seed potatoes indoors. At sunrise, a wheelbarrow track led from the shore to the garden gate, then stopped abruptly on the path.

Evelyn, seventy-six and newly retired from a dental practice, turned her Phoenix patio into a compact garden of peppers, eggplant, and citrus. The building’s maintenance man complimented her pots, then asked whether she would be away during the summer. She replied that her plans were not settled. After his visit, she noticed a thin line of dust missing from the storage cupboard, as if something had been slid out and replaced. She counted her seed envelopes and found them all present, but arranged in a different order. Evelyn put a small strip of tape across the cupboard door and began watering before dawn. One morning the tape remained unbroken, yet the garden hose had been turned on. She followed it to the courtyard drain, where a wet footprint faced her patio. She brought the hose nozzle inside and set a chair beside the window.

The envelope was waiting beneath my apartment door, though the hallway camera showed no one arriving. My name was typed neatly across the front, and the stamp bore a postmark from the town where my brother had vanished years ago. I held it by one corner and checked the paper for powder, wires, anything that belonged in a thriller. Then I called the building manager and asked him to come upstairs. He laughed at first, until I read him the return address: a parcel locker that had been demolished. I opened the flap with a kitchen knife, keeping the envelope pointed away from me. Inside was a photograph of my brother standing outside my building, taken that morning. On the back, in his handwriting, were four words: Don’t tell them yet. I looked toward the peephole and heard the elevator stop.

At the post office, Nia was handed a cream-colored letter with no return address. The clerk said it had been found wedged behind the sorting machine, although the postmark was clear and recent. Nia turned it over twice before accepting it. She had spent the past month reporting missing mail, and this envelope was addressed in the same blue ink as the complaints she had filed. At home, she set it on the counter and watched it while making tea. The paper seemed too thick to fold naturally. She photographed both sides, then called her sister and asked her to stay on the line. Inside was a single key and a note directing Nia to a storage unit she had never rented. She didn’t touch the key again. Instead, she checked the window locks and searched the storage company’s name online.

I found the letter tucked inside a library book I had returned three days earlier. It carried no stamp, only my full name and the address of the house I’d moved out of when I was twelve. The handwriting looked familiar, but the loops were too careful, as if someone had copied it from an old card. I took the book to the librarian and asked who had checked it out after me. She glanced at the computer, then said the record had been erased during a system update. That answer made my palms damp. I unfolded the note beside the reference desk, where the cameras could see me. It said my father had hidden something beneath the loose floorboard in his workshop. He had been dead for six years. I called my cousin before going anywhere near that house.

When the letter arrived at the ranch, Mateo recognized the return address as the county courthouse, though he had never been summoned there. The envelope was sealed with a strip of clear tape that crossed the flap and continued onto the paper. He carried it to the barn, where the light was good, and examined the tape for fingerprints. His wife asked why he was pacing around a piece of mail. He told her the county had sent him a notice last week, and this one had no case number. The message inside claimed that someone had filed a deed transferring part of his land. Mateo called the courthouse from the number printed on its official website, not the one in the letter. The clerk found no such filing. By sunset, Mateo had photographed the envelope, locked it in the feed safe, and driven to town to speak with a lawyer.

A letter addressed to me appeared in the mailbox of the ferry terminal, where I worked nights. The handwriting was blocky, and the postmark came from a city I had never visited. Inside, someone claimed to know why the old lighthouse lamp had gone dark on the night my partner fell overboard. I read the sentence twice, then checked the staff room for anyone listening. The door was open, but the corridor stood empty. I folded the page into my pocket and finished my shift without telling the captain. At dawn, I called the sender’s return address from a pay phone across the harbor. The number belonged to a seafood shop that had closed years ago. When I returned to the terminal, my locker stood open. The letter was gone, but the lock was still intact, and a wet footprint marked the floor beneath it.

Priya received the envelope during a meeting at the museum, where every visitor was logged at the front desk. It was addressed in her mother’s handwriting, although her mother had been living abroad and denied sending anything. Priya asked the courier for identification and wrote down his badge number while he waited. He said the delivery had been arranged by the museum director. The director, when asked, looked genuinely puzzled and suggested it might be a prank. Priya kept the letter unopened until she reached the conservation lab. Inside was a photograph of a painting that had vanished from the collection decades before, resting on a table in the director’s private office. The date on the image was yesterday. She slid the photograph into an evidence sleeve and checked the lab’s access log. The director’s keycard had opened the room at midnight.

The letter came to my bakery in a hand-delivered brown envelope, though the shop had been locked since closing. I noticed it when I switched on the lights, lying beside the register with no flour on it and no sign of a forced door. It told me to stop buying eggs from my new supplier because the farm was hiding a disease outbreak. I didn’t throw it away or take it at face value. I checked the supplier’s invoices, searched public inspection records, and called the farm using the number on its website. The owner answered, but he knew my name before I introduced myself. I hung up and stood very still, listening to the refrigerator hum. Then I looked at the back door. Its bolt was engaged, yet a smear of wet clay crossed the tile and ended beside the envelope.

At seventy-four, Eleanor had grown used to bills and holiday cards, not a letter delivered by hand after midnight. The young courier wore no uniform and left before she could ask who had hired him. She watched from the curtain until his bicycle vanished beyond the corner, then checked the street in both directions. The envelope contained a list of dates and amounts matching withdrawals from her late husband’s account. At the bottom, someone had written that the bank teller knew where the rest of the money was buried. Eleanor didn’t call the bank. She placed the note in a biscuit tin, drove to her daughter’s house, and asked her to look at the handwriting. Her daughter recognized it as her father’s, but the ink looked fresh. Together they opened the account records. Every listed withdrawal had occurred after his funeral.

I received the letter at the university, in a mailbox I rarely checked because the department secretary usually sorted everything. The envelope had no stamp, and someone had written my office number under my name. Inside was a copy of a student’s exam, with several answers circled in red and a message accusing me of changing grades. I knew the handwriting on the circles: it resembled mine, but the capital R leaned the wrong way. I locked my office door and checked the drawer where I kept old exams. Nothing was missing. Then I asked the secretary who had accessed the mailroom. She said the department chair had been there before dawn. I looked through the window toward his office, where the blinds had just been drawn. Before replying to the note, I made a scan and sent it to the university’s academic integrity officer.

When a letter arrived at the remote weather station, Ivo assumed the mail plane had dropped it by mistake. The envelope was addressed to him in a language he had not used since childhood, and the return address belonged to a village submerged by a reservoir. He set it beside the radio and waited for the next scheduled call before opening it. The message claimed that the station’s readings had been altered and instructed him to destroy the last month of logs. Ivo read the paper under a lamp, checking for a second page or a hidden code. Then he compared the figures with the backup records stored on a separate drive. They matched. He keyed the radio and asked headquarters who had requested the logs. The operator went quiet for several seconds, then asked Ivo to repeat the question. Outside, someone knocked once on the locked weather door.

The letter landed on my windshield while I was parked at the hospital, though the security guard insisted no one had approached the car. It was addressed to me, not tucked under the wiper but sealed against the glass with a strip of clear tape. Inside, a stranger warned me not to trust the doctor treating my father. I read it in the parking garage, where the fluorescent lights flickered above me. The note included details about Dad’s medication that only family and staff should know. I took a photo, then went straight to the nurses’ station and asked for the medication record. The nurse’s smile tightened when I mentioned the letter. She said she would get the doctor. While she was gone, I checked the chart myself. One dose had been signed out, but its box was still sealed in the cabinet.

Darius opened the unexpected letter at his repair shop and found a photograph of his own front door, taken from across the street. The picture was dated that morning, although he had been at work since dawn. No return address appeared on the envelope, and the stamp had been canceled in a town two states away. He stopped the radio and listened to the shop’s quiet machinery ticking as it cooled. On the back of the photograph, a sentence told him to bring the blue suitcase to the old bus depot at nine. Darius owned no blue suitcase. He called the depot’s public number and asked whether any event was scheduled; the clerk said the building had been closed for renovation. He put the photo in a drawer, then checked the security footage from the shop. At 8:14, a person in his own jacket had entered and left without being recorded.

I arrived early to find our championship uniforms laid out in neat rows, except my jersey had been turned inside out. The equipment manager shrugged when I asked about it, but his eyes flicked toward Coach Danner before he answered. During drills, I watched him pass the water bottles. Mine had a loose cap and smelled faintly of oranges, though the team usually drank plain water. I set it aside and took another. By halftime of practice, two players were complaining about stomach cramps. I checked the bottle I’d left untouched and noticed a strip of tape under its label, marked with someone else’s initials. I showed Coach, who went quiet and called the manager over. The man insisted it was a mix-up, but he kept rubbing his thumb over a fresh ink stain. I stayed beside the bottle until the athletic trainer arrived.

Mara noticed the championship playbook on the bench was open to a page her team had never practiced. Someone had penciled a route in the margin, then rubbed it away so roughly the paper had gone thin. She asked the assistant coach who had borrowed the book. He said nobody, though he glanced at the locked office door. At dinner, Mara sat with the playbook beneath her chair and watched the visiting team’s captain stroll past their table, smiling at the diagrams projected on the wall. She pulled the book out and found a tiny blue thread caught in its binding, matching the captain’s warm-up jacket. Rather than accuse anyone, she asked the coach to change the final signals. The next morning, when the opposing defense shifted exactly as if expecting the old call, Mara met her teammates’ eyes and gave the new one.

I’m the oldest player on our community basketball squad, and I’ve learned that championship week makes everyone generous with advice. Still, I didn’t like finding our practice schedule taped outside the gym, where anyone could read it. The paper had been folded around a note saying our starting center would miss the final. I checked the roster; he was healthy and shooting baskets across the court. When I asked who posted it, our volunteer coordinator said she’d never seen the sheet. Her hands were full of fresh tape, and one corner of the schedule clung to her sleeve. I said nothing. Instead, I moved our next practice to a schoolyard and told only the players. That evening, a delivery driver showed up at the empty gym with a crate of recovery drinks addressed to our team. I took the label to the league office.

At sixteen, Omari had earned a place as goalkeeper for the regional final, but the spare gloves in his locker were damp when he opened it. He touched the lining, then checked his own gloves, which had been hanging on a hook nearby. A faint line of mud crossed the locker floor toward the equipment room. When he mentioned it, the kit attendant joked that the building was old and the pipes leaked. Omari watched the man’s face instead of laughing. Before warm-ups, he asked a teammate to stay with him while he tested every buckle and seam. One glove had a pinhole near the thumb, too small to notice until he flexed his hand. He handed it to the trainer without making a scene. The attendant kept his distance for the rest of practice, and Omari guarded his bag until the team bus arrived.

I help coach a girls’ softball team in a coastal town, and championship day was supposed to be our first game under new lights. The electrician arrived during batting practice and asked to inspect the control box, though he had already signed off on it. I noticed a new padlock on the fence gate and no matching key on his ring. When I asked about the change, he said the groundskeeper had requested it. The groundskeeper was away, and nobody could reach him. I walked the perimeter, listening to the lights hum overhead. One bank blinked twice, then went dark. The electrician immediately offered to fix it, but I asked him to wait for the league supervisor. He smiled too broadly and packed his tools. Before he left, I photographed the lock and found its brand matched a receipt left beside our team’s discarded batting helmets.
