Mina opened a carton of linens and found a faded picture wedged between two pillowcases. The dog’s ears stood up in the sun, and their father’s young face was visible beside him. Dev stared at it for a long moment before wrapping the frame in a towel. They went down together, careful not to bend the photograph.

My sister Becca and I had to sort the attic before our parents returned from a weekend away. I was twelve, old enough to know the wobbly ladder wasn’t safe, but Becca had climbed it anyway. She reached for a carton on the top shelf, and the ladder shifted against the wall. I grabbed its sides so hard my knuckles turned pale. “Come down first,” I said. She told me she was fine, then the box tipped and sent a rain of old postcards around her shoes. I couldn’t tell whether the wood would hold her weight. Becca stopped, looked at my face, and climbed down without arguing. We moved the ladder to a clear patch of floor and brought the cartons down one at a time. The postcards were scattered, but none had fallen through the ceiling or been crushed.

After moving back from overseas, siblings Darius and Simone sorted the boxes their late uncle had stored in the attic. Simone needed to find a set of keys before a locksmith arrived to change the locks downstairs. Darius opened cartons of sports gear, while she searched a row of battered tins. Every few minutes, she went to the window to check the street for the locksmith’s van. The appointment was nearly over, and the front door still would not latch. Darius suggested they cancel, but Simone pictured the house sitting unsecured overnight. She sifted through a box of sewing supplies, keeping the keys she found separate from loose pins and buttons. A brass key caught on a spool of thread. She tested it against the lock on the attic trunk, not the front door. Darius spotted a small tag tied to its ring: FRONT. Simone hurried downstairs.

I reached the north field before sunrise, carrying a lantern and the rain gauge from the porch. The radio had called for hail by noon, and my young corn still stood thin as pencils. I walked each row, pressing soil between my fingers and lifting leaves to look for torn edges. At the far end, one stalk had bent beneath a clod. I straightened it, then checked the sky again, though the clouds had not changed. My phone showed a message from the grain buyer asking whether the crop would be ready. I typed a reply, erased it, and tucked the phone away. When the wind rattled the dry beans against their poles, I went back for twine and began tying the weakest plants. The lantern shook in my hand. By the time the first drops struck my hat, I had covered only half the field.

Marta Velez left the kitchen with her coat still unbuttoned, keeping one eye on the dark shelf of clouds beyond the orchard. The storm forecast had shifted west overnight, placing her peach rows directly in its path. She checked the irrigation ditch first, clearing a plug of leaves with a shovel, then hurried between trees to inspect the fruit. Several peaches had split after the heat, and she gathered them into her apron before they could bruise beneath the coming rain. Her brother called from the barn to ask if they should move the ladders. Marta answered too quickly, then glanced at the sky and changed her mind. She stacked them under cover herself, counting each one twice. A gust lifted the orchard netting, and she grabbed its edge with both hands. The first thunder rolled while she was still tying knots.

I took my grandfather’s pocketknife into the barley field, though there was nothing to cut yet. The weather service had issued a severe-storm alert, and I kept rereading the message as if its wording might soften. My boots sank in the low ground where the crop had already grown heavy. I checked the drainage furrows, poking mud loose with the knife, then climbed the fence to see how far the creek had risen. It was still below the bank, but the water moved faster than it had at breakfast. My daughter waved from the tractor and asked whether we should harvest early. I looked at the green heads, then at the stacked grain sacks waiting in the shed. “Give me ten minutes,” I said. I spent those minutes tightening a gate latch that was already secure, listening for the next crack of thunder.

At sixty-eight, Harlan Price knew the sound of rain on every roof he owned, but the sharp wind snapping the sunflower stalks was new. He walked the field with a notebook, marking patches where the heads had begun to droop. The approaching storm could flatten the crop before the seeds finished filling, and his loan payment was due on Monday. He stopped beside a row and rubbed one seed between thumb and forefinger. Still pale. His wife called from the truck that the tarp was ready, but he kept moving, checking another head, then another. A gust sent his cap skittering into the weeds. He chased it, laughing once without humor, and pinned it under his arm. When the clouds swallowed the last strip of blue, he finally waved for the tarp. His hands fumbled at the knots.

I had promised the cooperative that my rice paddies would be ready for inspection, but the storm clouds arrived a day early. I walked the levee in rubber boots, testing weak spots with a bamboo pole. At each soft patch, I pressed down harder than necessary, then marked it with a scrap of red cloth. The water level looked right, yet I returned to the first gate to make sure I had shut it. My cousin called from the house, asking whether to bring the drying racks inside. I said yes, then changed the answer to no, then told him to wait for me. The wind pushed rain-scented air across the paddies, and a heron lifted suddenly from the reeds. I flinched at the rush of wings. I checked the gate once more before heading back, pole clenched so tightly my palm ached.

Nia Okafor had planted okra on a rented plot behind the railway, hoping the harvest would pay for her nursing course. Before the storm, she moved quickly down the rows, examining pods and turning leaves to spot pests. The forecast mentioned flash flooding, and the plot sat in a shallow dip. She dug a narrow channel toward the roadside drain, but muddy water kept flowing back. Her neighbor offered a ride home; Nia thanked him and stayed, shifting crates onto the highest patch of ground. She checked the drain again, then crouched beside a young plant whose roots showed through the soil. Thunder sounded over the tracks. Nia pressed the earth around the stem with both palms, though the next gust loosened it almost at once. When her neighbor returned with a spade, she snatched it from him and began cutting a deeper trench.

The storm warning came through while I was feeding the hens, and I left the pail beside the coop. My apple trees were already carrying more fruit than their branches could bear. I walked the rows with a ladder, checking each support post and tightening the straps around the heaviest limbs. One branch creaked overhead; I froze, then reached up to steady it as though my hands could hold back the weather. My son asked if we should pick the apples early. They were still hard and green, so I shook my head. A sheet of cloud had covered the sun, turning the orchard the color of old tin. I kept glancing toward the barn, where the harvest crates were stacked beneath a roof that leaked last spring. Before I could decide what to move first, rain began ticking against the ladder.

Jonah Bell took a thermos into the potato field and set it on the hood of his pickup, untouched. The storm was expected to bring heavy rain, and the low rows had flooded twice that summer. He walked the furrows, watching for blocked outlets, and kicked clumps of earth away from each one. At the far corner, he found a broken pipe. He crouched over it, turning the cracked piece in his hands while the wind pressed his shirt against his back. His sister called that the barn doors were banging loose. Jonah said he would come in a minute, then stayed to lash the pipe together with wire. When lightning flashed beyond the ridge, he dropped the wire and hurried toward the truck. The thermos tipped off the hood and rolled into the grass. He did not stop to retrieve it.

I checked the vineyard just after lunch, carrying pruning shears I never opened. A line of thunderstorms was moving toward our valley, and the grapes had only recently begun to darken. I examined the trellis wires, tugging each one until my fingertips stung. At the lowest slope, water was already gathering around the posts. I scraped a channel with my boot, then walked uphill to see whether it had worked. The puddle remained. My partner asked from the shed if I wanted the harvest bins moved under cover. I nodded, then stood staring at the vines, trying to judge how much wind they could take. A leaf struck my cheek. I wiped it away and checked the weather app again, though the signal had vanished. The shears clicked open in my hand, then shut, then opened once more.

Evelyn Cho drove her old tractor along the pumpkin patch, stopping every few yards to inspect the broad leaves. A storm system had been building all morning, and the forecast warned of strong gusts. She checked each vine for pumpkins resting in shallow water, nudging them onto dry straw with the toe of her boot. One fruit rolled back into the mud. Evelyn set down her coffee and tried again, breathing through her teeth as the wind picked up. Her grandson asked whether the patch would survive. She told him to bring in the empty crates, then watched him run toward the shed without his jacket. A low branch scraped across the tractor’s roof. Evelyn looked up at the clouds, then down at the vines, measuring the distance to the nearest shelter. She climbed aboard and drove slowly toward the far rows, where the leaves were already turning over.

I went out to inspect the flax when the sky turned the strange yellow that comes before hail. The plants were nearly ready, but their stems still bent easily beneath my hand. I checked the field edges for loose fencing, fastening a wire that had held all season. Then I walked back to the center and found my bootprints filling with water. My sister texted that the cellar had started leaking again. I read her message twice, thumb hovering over the reply, while I watched the flax ripple in gusts. If I left, I could help with the cellar; if I stayed, I might save the crop from the worst wind. I typed that I was coming, deleted it, and called instead. “Get the buckets ready,” I said. My voice came out thin. I kept walking toward the house, turning around every few steps.

Pavel Sokolov had spent the morning checking his small field of lentils, though the storm was still several hours away. He knelt to examine the pods, then brushed dirt from his trousers and inspected the drainage ditch. A fallen branch blocked one end. He dragged it free, paused to listen to the distant rumble, and dragged it farther than necessary. His wife stood by the gate with a basket, asking whether the crop should be cut now. Pavel studied the plants, their leaves fluttering in the rising breeze, and shook his head. There was no time to harvest them properly. He carried the basket to the shed, returned for a coil of rope, and checked the gate latch twice. When rain began pattering on the metal roof, he remained outside, looking over the rows as though he might spot the exact moment the storm would turn.

I found the crack in my bicycle’s rear tire halfway to the river, just as the clouds swallowed the afternoon sun. My phone showed one bar, then none, and the last bus had already passed. I crouched beside the wheel and pressed the rubber with my thumb, as if that could make the split disappear. The repair kit in my backpack was missing its smallest wrench. When a car slowed behind me, I stood too quickly and nearly dropped the bike into the ditch. I kept checking the road for headlights, then the wheel, then the road again. At last I used a coin to loosen the stubborn bolt and patched the tube with trembling fingers. The tire held air, but I walked the bicycle all the way home, listening for every faint hiss.

Mina, a retired postal carrier, heard a sharp clank as she pedaled up the hill toward her apartment. The chain had slipped between the gears, and the pedals spun uselessly beneath her feet. She glanced at the sky, where rain was already stippling the pavement, then at the paper bag of groceries balanced in her front basket. Her hands fumbled with the chain. Grease streaked her sleeve, and she pressed her lips together whenever a passing cyclist glanced over. The small repair shop would close in twenty minutes; she knew because she had checked its hours twice that morning. Mina turned the bicycle upside down against a bus shelter and eased the chain back into place. When it caught, she tested each pedal slowly, shoulders still raised as she headed for the shop.

I was supposed to lead the school’s charity ride, but my handlebars suddenly twisted sideways when I rolled my bicycle out of the shed. The start time was written on my wrist in blue marker, already smudged by sweat. I fetched a spanner from the kitchen drawer and tried to tighten the stem bolt. It would not budge. Dad was at work, and the other riders were gathering at the park without me. I kept picturing their empty faces at the starting line, then made myself read the tiny instructions on the repair leaflet. My fingers slipped twice. On the third try, the bolt turned with a squeak. I pushed the bike around the yard, gripping the bars hard and testing every bump. When I reached the park, I gave everyone a bright wave, though my stomach still felt tightly knotted.

At the edge of the desert trail, Yusef noticed that his bicycle’s front brake lever sank all the way to the handlebar. His younger sister was already far ahead, and the sun flashed white off the rocks. He pulled the bike into the shade of a lone signpost and opened his tool roll. The cable had frayed near its clamp. Yusef wiped his palms on his shorts, leaving dusty streaks, and tried to remember what the mechanic had shown him. Each minute brought the distant rattle of his sister’s wheels closer, then farther away. He called her name, but the wind carried his voice down the trail. With pliers, he trimmed the damaged end and tightened the cable. The brake finally bit. He squeezed it several times before riding after her at a cautious pace.

I had borrowed the bicycle for my first shift delivering meals, and the rear wheel began scraping before I reached the first address. A metal fender had bent inward, rubbing the tire with every turn. I pulled over beside a laundromat and checked the clock on my dashboard app; the customer had already sent a message asking where I was. My cheeks warmed as I typed that I was fixing a problem. The fender sprang back each time I pushed it away. I searched my pockets for a tool and found only a house key and a paper clip. A woman leaving the laundromat offered a small adjustable wrench. I thanked her twice, then carefully bent the metal clear. The wheel spun freely. I rode on, glancing down at it at every stoplight, afraid the scrape would return.

Priya’s bicycle was her only way to reach the nursing home where her father was recovering. On the morning of his first day out of bed, she discovered a flat tire and a valve that would not hold air. She knelt on the apartment courtyard stones, turning the pump handle with quick, uneven strokes. Her lunch sat untouched on the windowsill, and the clock above the mailboxes seemed louder than usual. A neighbor offered to drive her, but Priya shook her head, then immediately looked toward the street to see whether a taxi was coming. She removed the tube and found a tiny thorn embedded in the rubber. After patching the hole, she inflated the tire and pressed it with both thumbs. It felt firm. She mounted the bicycle, then stopped at the gate to check the wheel once more before setting off.

I was taking my old bicycle to the station when the pedal came loose and clattered onto the pavement. My train ticket was folded in my shirt pocket, soft from the rain, and departure was less than half an hour away. I picked up the pedal and stared at the bare crank arm, trying to recall which direction the threads turned. A cyclist passed without slowing. I wiped the metal with my sleeve and found a wrench in the small pouch under the seat. The pedal resisted, and my jaw tightened as I leaned my weight against it. When it finally threaded in, I spun it with one finger, then rode a cautious circle around the block. The train announcement echoed from the station speakers. I pedaled hard, keeping one hand near the crank, and reached the platform just before the doors closed.

On the farm road, Tomas heard a pop and felt his bicycle chain snap loose. He was carrying a jar of medicine for the calf in the barn, and the veterinarian had asked him to deliver it before noon. He set the jar upright in the grass and turned the bicycle over. The chain had separated at a link, but his multitool was buried somewhere in the saddlebag beneath a coil of rope. Tomas dug through it, glancing repeatedly toward the farmhouse where his grandmother might be waiting for his call. His fingertips shook enough that the chain slipped twice. He found the tool, pressed the pin through the link, and tested the repair by turning the pedals slowly. The connection held. He wrapped the medicine in his jacket, climbed aboard, and rode with a careful eye on the chain all the way to the barn.

At the campground, Elsie discovered that the bicycle she had rented would not shift into its easiest gear. The steep road to the cabins climbed through dark pines, and dusk was draining color from the trail. She leaned the bike against a picnic table and examined the cable near the rear derailleur. Her map lay open beside her, its corner lifting in the breeze. Elsie kept rubbing her thumb over a chipped patch of nail while she followed the cable with her eyes. A family nearby packed up their dinner, and their departing headlights left the clearing dimmer. She turned the barrel adjuster a quarter turn, then pedaled the bike by hand. The chain clicked into the lower gear. She repeated the test several times before loading her backpack, then climbed toward the cabins at a measured pace, listening for any new clatter.

My bicycle’s saddle dropped an inch every time I hit a pothole, and I had to get across town for an audition. In the rehearsal-room mirror, I had already imagined myself arriving late, flushed and unable to focus. I stopped outside a hardware store and asked to borrow a wrench, but the clerk pointed to a display of tools instead. My pockets held enough coins for one small spanner. I bought it, crouched beside the curb, and loosened the seat clamp. The bolt turned too easily, which made me pause and inspect the whole fitting. I tightened it firmly, then pressed down on the saddle with both hands. It stayed put. I rode on, testing the seat after every rough patch. At the theater door, I tucked the wrench into my bag like a lucky charm and took several slow breaths before going in.

When the bicycle’s back wheel jammed outside the ferry terminal, Abdul saw the departure sign change to boarding. A strip of plastic had wound itself around the axle, wedged between the spokes and frame. He set down his canvas case and tugged at the material, but it stretched without tearing. The ferry crew began folding the ramp, and Abdul’s gaze bounced between the boat and the wheel. He tried his pocketknife, then stopped when the blade slipped close to a spoke. A dockworker brought over a pair of snips. Together they cut the plastic into short pieces and pulled them free. Abdul spun the wheel; it turned, though one spoke trembled. He tightened his grip on the handlebars and rolled the bicycle toward the ramp. At the top, he looked back at the wheel before following the crew aboard.

I set my violin case beside the church hall’s folding stage and checked the clock for the fourth time. The concert was meant to begin in twenty minutes, but the accompanist’s chair remained empty. I ran the opening passage under my breath, then stopped when my fingers began tapping the bow against my knee. The sound carried farther than I intended. Mrs. Bell, who had come early to arrange programs, glanced over. “He’ll make it,” she said. I nodded, though I kept looking toward the entrance. My phone showed no new message. I loosened the violin strings a fraction, tightened them again, and rubbed the damp spot on my palm against my skirt. When a car door slammed outside, I stood so quickly that my chair scraped the floor. It was only the caretaker arriving with a box of candles. I sat back down and began the passage again, slower this time.

At sixty-eight, Nirmala had played the bamboo flute at family gatherings for decades, but the library’s little concert room felt different. A row of unfamiliar faces waited beyond the open door, and her music stand kept slipping on the uneven floor. She tightened its screw, tested it, and watched it tilt again. Her grandson offered to hold it, but she waved him off and pressed her lips together. The first piece began with a breathy high note she sometimes missed. She tried it once, then once more, each time lifting the flute from her mouth to listen for a flaw. A librarian appeared with a folded towel and tucked it beneath one stand leg. The metal stayed firm. Nirmala’s shoulders lowered by a small degree. She turned the pages carefully, set a glass of water within reach, and counted the opening measures silently while the audience settled.

I had promised myself the trumpet solo would feel easy by the time I reached the school auditorium. Instead, every note in the rehearsal room seemed to bounce back with an accusation. My lips had gone dry, and I kept pressing them together before starting again. From the stage, I could see the front row filling with parents, including my father, whose camera was already raised. I wiped my mouth on my sleeve and checked the valves for the third time. They moved smoothly. The accompanist tapped the piano lid. “Ready?” I lifted the horn but let it fall to my side. A tiny squeak escaped when I tested the first note. My ears burned. I breathed in for four counts, as my teacher had shown me, then played the whole opening phrase without stopping. The final note held steady. I kept the trumpet raised a moment longer, listening until the room went quiet.

Mateo, a busker who usually played beneath the train station clock, had been invited to perform at a neighborhood café. The room was so small that the tables nearly touched the stool where he tuned his guitar. He kept twisting the pegs, although each string already sounded right, and glanced at the handwritten set list tucked into his pocket. The café owner had asked him to include a new song, one he had only finished the night before. Mateo mouthed its first line without making a sound. When a spoon clattered in the kitchen, his hand jerked against the strings. He laughed with the owner, then rubbed the reddened spot on his knuckle. A little girl at the nearest table leaned forward, watching him. Mateo smiled at her and began the new song from the top, quietly at first. By the second verse, his fingers had found their path.

I arrived at the retirement home an hour early with my cello, my music, and a spare endpin rubber tucked into my coat pocket. The residents were still finishing lunch, but I kept hearing the squeak the endpin had made during my last practice. I crouched to inspect it, then set up the chair and tested the instrument against the carpet. My bow hand felt slick. I wiped it on a cloth and checked the tuning app, though the notes were already centered. The activities director told me everyone was looking forward to the concert. I smiled, then asked whether the room’s heater could be turned down; the air seemed close and warm. While staff moved chairs into a semicircle, I played the first few bars so softly that I could barely hear them. A resident near the window hummed along. I looked up, and the bow stopped trembling against the strings.

At the community theater, Saba balanced her qanun on its stand and counted the audience chairs twice. Only forty people could fit, yet the sight of them arranged in neat rows made the stage seem enormous. She adjusted the small brass levers, plucked a string, and frowned when it rang longer than she expected. The tuner showed the correct pitch. Still, she leaned closer and tested it again. Her brother carried in a cup of tea, but she forgot to drink it while checking the first page of her score. One corner had curled beneath the clip. She smoothed it flat, then secured the other pages as well. A stagehand called that the doors would open in five minutes. Saba’s fingers folded around the plectra in her palm. She flexed them, placed each one beside the instrument, and began a familiar scale, letting its measured pattern fill the waiting room.

My clarinet rehearsal was supposed to be a quick run-through in the bakery after closing. The owner had cleared a space between the flour sacks and the counter, but the oven timer kept ringing at odd moments. I lost my place each time it sounded. The concert was tomorrow, and the fast section still tangled beneath my fingers. I took the mouthpiece apart, wiped it, and put it back together, even though nothing was wrong with it. A tray scraped in the kitchen, and my shoulders jumped. “Take the tempo down,” my teacher said over the phone. I set the metronome slower and watched its red light blink. At that pace, the notes came out clean. I tried once more at the concert tempo, stumbling near the end. My jaw tightened. Then the bakery owner placed a warm roll beside my score, and I gave myself one bite before starting again.

Eli had spent the afternoon rehearsing his drums in the apartment basement, where a low ceiling made every cymbal crash feel twice as loud. The small concert would take place in the building courtyard, and he kept picturing a neighbor asking him to stop halfway through a song. He tightened a wing nut, tested the snare, and tightened it again. His set list fluttered whenever the ventilation fan started. When he reached for a stick, one rolled beneath the washing machine. Eli crouched to retrieve it, then stayed there a moment, listening to footsteps cross the floor overhead. His bandmate came down carrying a pair of earplugs and a grin. “The courtyard crowd asked for the loud songs,” she said. Eli stood and rolled his shoulders. He played a measured beat, then let the rhythm build. The old pipes rattled in time, and he gave a short laugh as the sound filled the basement.

I rehearsed my vocal solo in the empty school music room, standing so close to the piano that my skirt brushed its bench. My voice kept catching on the first high note. I drank water, cleared my throat, and tried again, but the second attempt came out thinner. Through the window I could see students carrying chairs into the gym for the evening concert. My music lay open, though I had memorized every word. I traced the printed lines with one finger and pressed my thumbnail into the edge of the paper. The choir director came in and asked me to sing the verse as if telling it to one person. I chose the custodian stacking chairs by the door. This time the phrase rose without breaking. I lowered my eyes quickly and turned to the next page, although there was nothing written on its back. The custodian gave me a quiet thumbs-up.

Farah was the youngest musician on the bill at the seaside arts center, where she would play a short oud piece before the local storyteller. She had rehearsed in her bedroom, but the stage’s lights made the strings shine and blurred the notes on her page. She moved the stand closer, then shifted it back because it blocked her view of the audience. A technician asked whether she wanted more light. Farah said yes, then watched him adjust the lamp with tight hands clasped around her plectrum. Her father waited near the exit, holding her coat. She checked the tuning pegs and quietly repeated the opening phrase, stopping at the same ornament each time. The storyteller approached and asked to hear it. Farah played the phrase slowly while he listened without interrupting. He nodded at the finish. She returned to the first measure and let the ornament ring to its end.

I was rehearsing my harmonica set in the back room of a small bookshop, where the concert chairs were still stacked against the wall. The owner had told me not to fret about the turnout, but I kept glancing at the ticket sheet on the counter. Only six names were written there. I wiped the harmonica on my sleeve and ran through the first blues tune. The notes came out too breathy, so I changed reeds, then changed back. My watchband felt too tight; I unfastened it and left the watch beside the books. The front door bell chimed, and I stopped mid-note. A customer wandered in to return a novel. I began again while he browsed, keeping the melody low. He paused by the poetry shelf and tapped one foot. When he smiled, I lowered the harmonica and let out a breath I had been holding.

Jun rehearsed the final movement of his piano piece in a hotel lounge while a conference crew arranged chairs for the evening concert. Every few minutes, someone crossed behind him with a cart, and he lost his place in the rapid passage. He sat very straight, hands hovering above the keys, and waited for the hallway to clear. The event manager said the guests would arrive early. Jun nodded, then checked the score for a measure he had already marked in red. His phone buzzed with a message from his daughter: a drawing of him at the piano, with a huge audience made of stick figures. He smiled, but his fingers still pressed hard into his knees. He played the difficult section at half speed, then gradually increased the tempo. On the next attempt, he reached the final chord cleanly. He kept his hands resting on the keys as the first guests entered.

The train sighed into Bellweather, and I stepped onto the platform with my suitcase bumping against my knees. The address on my phone belonged to a street that the station map did not show. I tried the name at the ticket desk, but the clerk pointed toward three exits without looking up. Outside, rain blurred the signs, and my battery slipped from twelve percent to nine. I ducked beneath an awning and unfolded the paper directions my sister had insisted I carry. A gust snatched them from my hands. I caught one corner, then flattened the damp sheet against a wall, tracing each turn with a shaking finger. A bus hissed past before I could flag it down. When a woman selling chestnuts offered to help, I held out the address, speaking too quickly. She studied it, then beckoned me toward a tram stop, and I followed close behind.

At twenty, Sanaa had crossed the ocean for a nursing placement, but the first view of Marseille left her speechless for reasons she could not explain. The taxi dropped her beside a square crowded with scooters, and the lodging instructions listed a door number that seemed to skip from six to fourteen. She checked the message again, then the street sign, then the message once more. Her aunt’s scarf was knotted around the suitcase handle, and Sanaa tightened it until her fingertips paled. A group of students laughed nearby; she flinched, certain they had noticed her circling the same block. She called the host, heard only a recorded greeting, and swallowed before trying again. At last, an elderly baker recognized the address and led her through a narrow passage. Sanaa thanked him, still glancing over her shoulder at every turning.

I had imagined arriving in Kyoto as a graceful beginning: a train, a map, a quiet walk to my guesthouse. Instead, the station swallowed me in voices and arrows. My backpack strap twisted under one arm, and I kept stepping aside for people moving with purpose. The pin on my map hovered over a river, though the booking email promised a place near a temple. I opened the email, closed it, and opened it again, as if the words might rearrange themselves. My mother’s last message sat unread at the top of the screen. I couldn’t bring myself to answer until I knew where I was. A station attendant pointed me toward the bus lanes, but I wrote the route on my palm before leaving. On the bus, I watched each stop pass and counted them under my breath, gripping the rail even while seated.

Marek arrived in Accra just before dusk, carrying a cello case and a paper invitation to a music workshop. The driver who had promised to meet him was nowhere near the terminal doors. Marek kept the case upright between his shoes while he scanned each face, then checked the time, then scanned again. The numbers on his phone blurred in the glare. He approached a uniformed guard, rehearsing his request silently before forcing it out. The guard called someone, but the connection crackled and ended. Around them, families reunited in bright embraces; Marek stood very still, his thumb rubbing a dent in the cello’s handle. A young woman noticed the invitation and recognized the workshop’s logo. She directed him to a shared taxi, writing the destination in large letters on his hand. He repeated it twice before getting in.

By the time I reached Lisbon, the little hotel had changed its name online, and my reservation showed an address across town. I stood beneath a blue awning with two bags and read the screen until the letters seemed to drift. The street sloped away toward a maze of tiled lanes. I started downhill, turned back, then pretended I had meant to do that when a cyclist passed. My brother had given me a pocket notebook; I opened it to his neat list of emergency numbers. The page stuck to my damp thumb. A tram bell rang, and I jumped hard enough to drop my key pouch. An older man picked it up and asked where I was headed. I showed him the address. He nodded toward a nearby café, where the owner called the hotel and spoke slowly while I watched the battery icon shrink.

Lina, a retired school librarian, reached Reykjavík with a wool hat, a carefully folded itinerary, and no idea which bus stop served her rented cottage. Wind pushed at her coat as she stood by the terminal map. She leaned close to the glass, following the colored lines, then stepped back to make room and lost her place. A suitcase rattled across the pavement; she gripped her own handle until the ache reached her wrist. She could have asked the couple beside her, but they were speaking Icelandic, and she feared interrupting. Instead, she took out the small phrase card her grandson had made. The paper shook between her hands. A driver noticed her searching and came over, pointing out the right route with patient gestures. Lina climbed aboard, chose a seat near the door, and kept the cottage address visible on her lap.

When I arrived in Mexico City, my cousin’s directions led me to a plaza with two streets bearing almost identical names. The taxi had already disappeared into traffic, leaving me beside a fountain and a row of unfamiliar stalls. I called my cousin, but the line went straight to voicemail. My suitcase wheel snagged on a crack as I crossed the plaza, and every few steps I stopped to compare the buildings with a blurry photograph. A vendor offered me a bottle of water. I thanked him, though my voice came out thin, then asked him to read the address aloud. He recognized the neighborhood but not the number. I wrote it on a napkin and showed it to a traffic officer. She pointed toward a metro entrance and drew a quick route, while I copied every station name as if there might be a test.

At thirty-two, Pavel had moved often for construction jobs, yet arriving in Nairobi with a feverish toddler made every ordinary task feel enormous. The bus station roared around him, and his daughter slept against his chest, cheek damp with sweat. His sister’s directions had stopped at a landmark that was now hidden behind scaffolding. Pavel read the message again, shifting the child’s weight from one arm to the other. A taxi queue stretched around the corner. He searched his pockets for the clinic number and found only a receipt. His jaw worked while he stared at it. A woman carrying a basket saw the child and asked where he needed to go. Pavel answered in short bursts. She called a driver she knew, then waited beside him until the car arrived, making sure he had the correct address before he climbed in.

I stepped off the ferry in Istanbul with a canvas bag, a cracked phone, and a reservation written in a language I could barely read. The waterfront was crowded, and the hotel’s pin placed it somewhere beyond the rising streets. I asked a shopkeeper for directions, but the ferry horn swallowed his answer. Nodding as if I understood, I walked toward the nearest staircase. Halfway up, my phone went black. I sat on a low wall and searched my bag for the charger, spilling coins and a folded map onto the stones. People streamed around me. I lined the coins up by size, then forced myself to stand and enter a tea shop. The owner let me charge the phone behind the counter. While it flickered back to life, I practiced the hotel name under my breath, afraid I would lose it again.

Nia came to Oslo for an architecture conference and found that the airport train had taken her to the wrong side of the city. She stood beneath the departure board, checking her conference badge against the venue’s address. Each time a platform announcement sounded, she looked up sharply. Her suitcase was light, but she held its handle with both hands. She had promised her team she would arrive early to present their model; now the first session was less than an hour away. Nia typed a message, erased it, and typed another. A student noticed the badge and recognized the building name. He showed her a faster route involving a tram and a short walk. Nia repeated the stops aloud, then took a photograph of the map. When the tram doors opened, she waited for the student’s nod before stepping inside.

The streets of Bogotá climbed more steeply than I expected, and by the time I reached the hostel address, the front door was locked. I pressed the bell once, waited, then pressed it again, counting the seconds between attempts. My backpack tugged at my shoulders. The booking site showed a message from the host, but the last line had vanished when the signal dropped. I walked to a corner shop and asked to use their Wi-Fi. The owner pointed me toward a table, and I arranged my maps and receipts in a tidy row while the connection loaded. My hands kept returning to the door key, though it belonged to another hotel. At last, the host replied: the entrance was around the block, through a courtyard marked with a painted bird. I thanked the owner and hurried there, checking every wall for the small blue wings.

Elias, a visiting chef from Beirut, arrived in Copenhagen with a suitcase of knives packed safely in his checked luggage and a recipe notebook tucked under his arm. The apartment key was supposed to be in a lockbox, but the code provided by the landlord opened nothing. He tried it slowly, then quickly, then wiped the keypad with his sleeve and began again. Behind him, bicycles zipped along the lane. He kept glancing at the darkening sky and at the notebook, which contained the address of tomorrow’s kitchen trial. Calling the landlord produced no answer. Elias paced to the corner and back, rubbing the bridge of his nose. A neighbor carrying groceries stopped to help, spotted a digit transposed in the message, and tested the corrected code. The box clicked open. Elias let out a long breath and thanked her with both hands wrapped around the key.

When the message flashed on my screen—Please come to Ms. Patel’s office—I read it twice, then closed the spreadsheet without saving. My palms left damp marks on the mouse. I had been covering the late shift at the pharmacy and couldn’t remember whether I’d logged the refrigerator temperature after the delivery. In the hallway, I rehearsed three versions of an explanation, each less convincing than the last. Ms. Patel pointed to a chair and turned her monitor toward me. The temperature entry was missing, but she had also found a supplier’s receipt tucked beneath the clipboard. “You caught the incorrect shipment code,” she said. I let out a breath I hadn’t noticed holding. She asked me to show the new hire how I checked deliveries, and I nodded, still feeling my pulse in my fingertips.

Darius kept his hands beneath the break-room table after the supervisor’s assistant told him to report to the manager’s office. A stack of invoices had gone missing from his desk, and he had been the last person in the accounting suite on Friday. On the walk upstairs, he counted the floor tiles, lost track, and started again. Mr. Chen didn’t accuse him. Instead, he asked about a courier’s signature on one invoice. Darius recognized the handwriting as his own: he had signed for the envelope, then placed it in a cabinet while moving files for a maintenance crew. His cheeks warmed as he explained. The manager listened, then asked him to retrieve the papers and help revise the delivery log. Darius’s shoulders lowered only after the cabinet door swung open and the invoices appeared.

I was halfway through labeling jars when the store director called my name and asked me to come upstairs. The label printer kept clicking after I had switched it off. I wiped my fingers on my apron and followed her past the shelves, trying to remember every customer complaint from the morning. At her desk, a chart showed that my department’s sales had fallen. I began listing broken displays and short staffing, but she raised a hand. She had noticed that I’d been staying late to train the seasonal staff and wanted me to explain the new layout. My voice came out thin at first. Then I showed her the customer notes I’d collected. She studied them, made a few marks, and asked me to lead a trial of my idea. My apron strings felt suddenly tight against my back.

Leena was sorting paint samples at the design studio when a calendar alert summoned her to her manager’s office. She checked the project board, then checked it again, though nothing there had changed. The client’s presentation was due in the morning, and one of the color files had failed to upload. In the office, Mr. Alvarez folded his hands and asked why the client had received an empty attachment. Leena’s throat tightened as she described the upload error and admitted she had not checked the outgoing email. He studied the screen, then said the client had replied with a revised deadline and wanted a second option. Leena volunteered to build it that evening. When she returned to her desk, she placed both feet flat on the floor and opened the backup folder.

The call came just as I was closing the café for the night: my manager wanted me in her office before I left. I checked the till receipt, then the safe, then the till receipt again. A customer had complained that I’d charged twice for a meal, and I could picture the crowded lunch rush in flashes—steam, clattering plates, my hand reaching for the register. In the office, I kept my coat on and perched at the edge of the chair. My manager showed me the transaction. The duplicate charge had come from the card reader, not my entry, and the customer had already been refunded. She wanted me to help test a new checkout procedure. I agreed, though my fingers stayed curled around my coat zipper until I got back to the empty dining room.

At thirty-eight, Mateo had worked at the print shop long enough to recognize the manager’s serious voice over the phone. “Come by my office when you can,” she said. He glanced at the giant banner on the cutting table, where a thin white line ran through the center. The client was arriving that afternoon. Mateo’s stomach gave a small, hard twist as he followed her inside, certain the flaw had appeared after his final inspection. The manager asked whether he knew why the machine had paused. He explained that he’d stopped the run when the paper shifted, but hadn’t mentioned the brief jam in his report. She tapped the service log and said the technician needed that detail. Together they found a loose roller. Mateo returned to the floor with a repair schedule and a fresh roll of material.

My manager sent a message asking me to come in, and I spent the next ten minutes searching my calendar for something I might have missed. I worked at a small museum, where even a misplaced key could set off a chain of forms. In her office, the director had an envelope beside her keyboard. She asked whether I had taken a donation receipt home. My mouth went dry; I remembered slipping paperwork into my tote after a late event, but I couldn’t picture which sheet it was. I emptied the bag onto the chair. The receipt was folded inside my sketchbook. She thanked me for bringing it back and said the donor needed a copy by noon. I offered to scan it. As I walked to the copier, I held the paper carefully by its corners.

Nia heard the announcement over the warehouse intercom and stopped with a box in her arms. The manager wanted to see her in the office. She set the box down too quickly, and a roll of tape bounced across the floor. Two weeks earlier, a shipment had gone to the wrong branch after she entered an address from an outdated form. In the office, the manager had a delivery map spread across his desk. Nia’s fingers pressed together as he asked her to identify a handwritten note. She recognized her own initials, but the note had been added after she submitted the order. They checked the timestamp and found that a routing change had been made by the carrier. The manager asked her to update the form anyway. Nia picked up the tape on her way back, one strip at a time.

“Could you step into my office?” my supervisor asked while I was arranging flowers at the hotel entrance. I looked at the vase in my hands and set it down before the stems could slip. A guest had complained about a missing bouquet, and I had delivered the morning orders through the ballroom without checking each table. On the way upstairs, I kept rubbing a green smudge from my thumb. My supervisor showed me a photograph from the event. The bouquet was there, but it had been placed behind a tall centerpiece. The guest wanted it moved, not replaced. I explained that I could fix it before the reception began. She handed me the room key and asked me to check every table while I was there. I took the key with both hands, careful not to drop it.

Elliot was repairing a laptop when the operations manager asked him to come by. He left the tiny screw beside the keyboard and wiped his palms on his jeans. A staff member had reported that confidential files remained on a loaner machine. Elliot had erased the drive according to the checklist, but the machine had been returned sooner than expected. In the office, he sat upright while the manager opened a security report. His first answer came out too fast, so he stopped and asked to see the device number. It belonged to a different laptop, one he had not handled. The manager thanked him for catching the mismatch and asked him to verify the inventory records. Elliot nodded, then wrote the number on his wrist with a marker so it would not vanish from his mind before he reached the storage room.

The message arrived while I was teaching a beginner’s pottery class: please see the studio manager after cleanup. I kept glancing at it between demonstrations, and my clay bowl began to lean as I pressed too hard on one side. I had recently ordered supplies, and the invoice total looked higher than the quote. When I entered the office, my manager slid a printed bill across the desk. I recognized the amount and felt heat climb into my face. The supplier had charged for express shipping, though I had selected standard. I explained that I’d noticed the discrepancy but hadn’t contacted them yet. She asked me to make the call with her there. My voice shook through the first sentence, then steadied when the supplier confirmed the mistake. I returned to class with the corrected order number written on my sleeve.

At the airport café, Priya was restocking cups when her manager beckoned her toward the staff office. The rush had been relentless, and she had left a handwritten note about a broken freezer on the counter instead of filing it. Now a tray of pastries had spoiled. She held her apron at the seams as she followed him inside, replaying the moment she’d seen the temperature display. The manager asked when the unit first began to warm. Priya gave him the time and described the note. He checked the maintenance log and found that the repair request had never been entered. He did not raise his voice; he asked her to help document the loss and call the technician. Priya took a pen, but her first mark landed crooked. She drew a neat line beneath it and started again.

I was updating the community center’s staff schedule when the director asked me to come to her office. My cursor hovered over the same empty shift box while I tried to recall whether I’d confirmed the substitute. The evening caretaker had called in sick, and I had left two messages without hearing back. In the office, the director pointed to a note from a parent asking if the building would be open for a youth rehearsal. I explained what I knew, then checked my phone. A reply had arrived: the substitute could cover, but only until seven. The director asked me to call the group and arrange an earlier end time. I stumbled over the first number, erased it, and dialed again. When someone finally answered, I read the updated plan slowly, keeping my free hand pressed against the desk.

I have read the clinic’s wall clock so often that I can tell when its second hand catches. My blood test was supposed to take ten minutes; the nurse said results might need an hour. I sit with my coat still buttoned, though the room is warm, and turn my phone face down whenever it lights up. Across from me, a child builds a tower from paper cups. I count each cup, then lose track when the receptionist calls another name. My sister texts, “How’s it going?” I type “Fine,” erase it, and send a photograph of the vending machine instead. When a doctor finally appears at the doorway, I stand too quickly and my knees give a small, unsteady dip. He checks the chart in his hand before looking up.

At seventy-two, Mr. Okafor had learned to bring a crossword to every appointment, but today the clues would not stay in his head. He wrote “river” into a space meant for “bird,” then pressed so hard the pencil snapped. The clinic had taken his sample before breakfast, and the specialist was meant to call him into a consultation room once the report arrived. He watched the corridor through the gap between two chairs. Each time footsteps approached, he folded his newspaper into a smaller square. His daughter offered to fetch tea; he asked her to stay close instead. When the nurse finally stepped out, Mr. Okafor rose, smoothed his tie, and tucked the broken pencil into his pocket as if it might still be useful.

I keep rubbing the faint blue ink mark on my thumb, although it has already smeared. The clinic assistant said the scan report would be ready by noon, and the digital clock now shows 11:58. My son is coloring beside me, making a green dog with purple ears. I smile when he holds it up, but my gaze keeps sliding to the closed door at the end of the hall. I rehearse what I will ask the doctor, then forget the questions as soon as I picture his face. A cart rattles past, and I sit straighter. When the receptionist says my name, my mouth feels dry enough that I have to clear my throat before answering. I take my son’s hand and follow her.

Linh had arrived at the neighborhood clinic straight from her bakery shift, flour still caught in the seams of her sleeves. The doctor had ordered a test after she mentioned the recurring pain, and now she waited beneath a poster about handwashing, tapping one shoe against the tile. She checked the time, then checked it again as if the digits might have changed in the few seconds between glances. Her phone held a message from her brother asking whether she could bring home sesame rolls. She began a reply, stopped, and slipped the phone away. When the lab technician opened the door, Linh stood so quickly that her paper cup tipped over. She caught it before it spilled, then followed the technician down the hall with her fingers curled around the cup.

The little speaker above the reception desk crackles whenever someone is called. I jump at the first burst, then pretend I was only adjusting my scarf. My test results are somewhere in the clinic’s computer system, and the doctor is running behind. I study a framed photograph of a beach, tracing the shoreline with my eyes until the pale sand blurs. My friend has offered to pick me up, but I keep telling her not to leave work yet. The receptionist gives me a kind nod; I answer with a smile that feels pinned in place. Then the door opens and a nurse steps out holding a folder. I stand, sit again when she calls another patient, and fold my appointment card into a narrow strip between my fingers.

Rashida’s bus pass lay in her palm, its plastic edge digging into the same spot while she waited for the clinic to finish reviewing her test. She had planned to meet her grandson after school, but the clock above the reception desk had already passed the pickup time. She called her neighbor and asked if he could collect him, then listened twice to make sure she had heard the answer. Around her, people turned pages and scrolled through their phones. Rashida kept hers dark, afraid she might miss the doctor’s call if it buzzed. A nurse appeared with a clipboard, and Rashida rose before the name was spoken. When it belonged to someone else, she lowered herself carefully, smoothing the creases in her skirt.

I brought a book to the clinic, but I have read the same paragraph four times without reaching the end. The test was routine, the nurse said, yet the doctor asked me to wait for a conversation, and that changed the shape of the morning. I rest my hands on the open pages and press my thumbs against the paper. A toddler drops a toy truck nearby; its wheels spin across the floor until his father retrieves it. I glance toward the hallway at every sound, then scold myself silently for doing it. My partner sends a heart, and I hold the phone against my chest for a moment before putting it away. At last, a receptionist gestures toward the consultation room. I close the book without marking my place.

Sixteen-year-old Mateo had insisted he could wait alone while his mother parked the car. In the clinic lobby, though, he kept his backpack on his lap and gripped both straps. The doctor had taken a blood sample after a week of unexplained fevers, and the results were expected that afternoon. Mateo opened a game on his phone, but the bright colors made his eyes ache, so he shut it down. He watched a janitor mop a clean patch of floor and tried to follow the careful pattern of each stroke. When his mother came in, he asked whether she had found a space, though he had heard her say yes. A nurse called them both. Mateo stood, then reached back to pick up a pencil he had dropped.

I sit nearest the window because the clinic’s air conditioner seems to blow straight at my neck. Outside, rain slides down the glass in crooked lines. The doctor ordered a test after I fainted at work, and now I keep replaying the moment I woke on the office carpet, hearing my coworkers call my name. I tell myself the results could explain everything, but my stomach tightens whenever the hallway door swings open. The woman beside me offers a mint. I take it and thank her, then hold it in my cheek without tasting it. When the physician finally comes out, she checks the chart and asks me to come in. I wipe my damp palms on my jeans before following her.

At the rural clinic, Elsie’s name was written on a paper slip beside the receptionist’s keyboard. She had driven forty miles for the follow-up and arrived before the doors opened, carrying a thermos of coffee she had barely touched. Her test results were delayed because the lab had sent them from another town. To pass the time, she sorted the receipts in her purse by date, then mixed them together again when her hands began to shake. The receptionist apologized and offered to call the doctor. Elsie nodded, keeping her eyes on the small green plant beside the desk. When a phone rang in the back office, she rose halfway from her chair. A moment later, she sat down and wrapped both hands around the cooling thermos.

I keep checking the pocket where I put the clinic’s appointment slip, though I know it is there. The nurse said the test had gone smoothly and the doctor would discuss the numbers as soon as they came through. My foot moves beneath the chair, making the metal leg tick against the floor. I try to breathe slowly, counting four beats in and four out, but I lose count whenever someone walks behind the reception desk. A man in a blue jacket laughs at something on his phone; the sound makes me jump, and I pretend to adjust my glasses. When my name is called, I gather my bag, drop a pen, and bend to retrieve it before looking up. The doctor waits by the open door.

Amina had brought a knitting project to the clinic, hoping it would keep her hands occupied while she waited for the results of her thyroid test. Instead, she had unraveled the same row three times. The yarn pooled in her lap, a loose tangle she kept trying to straighten. Her aunt called from another city, and Amina answered with cheerful details about the waiting room’s faded murals, avoiding the question about when she would hear from the doctor. After the call ended, she set the needles carefully on her bag and watched the hallway. A nurse appeared carrying a tablet. Amina’s shoulders lifted before the nurse even spoke. When she was invited inside, she wound the yarn around her fingers and followed, leaving the unfinished scarf on the chair.

I kept checking the buckle on Lila’s life vest, even after the instructor said it was secure. At the shallow end, she stood with one hand on the ladder and watched the other children kick across the pool. “We can just practice blowing bubbles,” I told her, though my own fingers had gone cold. She looked up at me, waiting for the promise I had made in the car. I stepped into the water and held out both hands. Lila lowered her face, blew one tiny stream of bubbles, then popped upright, sputtering. I laughed too loudly and reached for her shoulder. She asked if I would stay right beside her. “Every second,” I said. On her next try, she floated between my palms for three breaths. I counted each one silently, afraid to blink, until she grabbed my wrist and grinned.

Mateo had taught his daughter to ride a bicycle without holding the seat, but the lake seemed like a different kind of test. He waded beside Rosa, keeping his palm beneath her back as she kicked. Each time a boat sent a small wave toward them, his jaw tightened and his eyes darted to the shore. Rosa noticed. “Papa, you’re making the same face as when the dentist comes,” she said. He tried to smile, then showed her how to breathe out slowly into the water. She copied him, bubbles trembling across the surface. When he loosened his support, she floated for a moment, arms spread. Mateo’s hand hovered inches away, ready to catch her. Rosa paddled toward the dock by herself. He exhaled only when her fingers touched the wood, then clapped so hard a nearby duck flapped away.

The indoor pool smelled of chlorine and the orange slices I had packed for afterward. My son, Benji, clung to the tiled wall while I crouched in the water beside him. He was eight and had promised his cousins he would jump in during our cabin trip. Now he kept asking how deep the pool was, though I had answered three times. I showed him how to hold the edge, push off, and kick toward me. My voice sounded steady; my knees did not. When he finally let go, he moved less than a foot before grabbing my shirt. I swallowed the sharp reply that rose in my throat and reset my hands beneath his elbows. “We’ll do one tile at a time,” I said. By closing time, he had crossed four tiles, and I had stopped glancing toward the clock.

Amina brought her six-year-old, Idris, to a quiet cove before the fishing boats arrived. She had promised him that the sea would hold him, but as he edged toward the water, she watched the tide line and every shifting patch of foam. She tied a bright scarf around his waist as a marker and knelt to show him how to float on his back. Idris pressed both hands over his ears when a gull cried overhead. Amina started humming the tune her mother used at bedtime, though her breath kept catching between notes. He tried leaning back against her forearms. For a heartbeat, his shoulders rested on the water; then he sat up and clutched her neck. She held him close, resisting the urge to end the lesson. When he asked to try again, she nodded, eyes fixed on his small face.

At the community center, I laid two towels beside the pool and lined up Maya’s goggles, cap, and favorite plastic turtle. She kept rolling the turtle between her palms instead of putting on her swimsuit. I told her we would stay where she could stand, then tested the depth with my foot anyway. The water reached only my waist, but my stomach remained knotted. Maya finally climbed down the steps and gripped the rail. I demonstrated a slow kick, making a ridiculous splash that drew a brief smile from her. Then she tried, one hand still wrapped around the metal bar. A whistle sounded across the pool, and her shoulders jumped. I nearly called the lesson off. Instead, I asked her to find the blue tile beneath her toes. She did, and together we counted kicks until her grip softened.

On the ranch, Eli had learned to cross creeks on horseback, but teaching his son to swim felt far less predictable. Noah stood at the edge of the farm pond in borrowed trunks, staring at the dark water. Eli tested the wooden dock with his heel and checked the rope tied to the ladder. He had brought a foam board, two towels, and a thermos of cocoa, yet kept wiping his palms on his jeans. “You’ll catch me if I sink?” Noah asked. Eli crouched until their faces were level. “I’ll be right here.” He guided Noah through floating on his belly, supporting his chest while the boy kicked. A dragonfly landed on the foam board; both watched it until it lifted away. Noah paddled back to the ladder without Eli’s hands beneath him. Eli gripped the dock rail, then offered his son the cocoa with a hand that still trembled.

My daughter Noor had watched swimming videos all winter, but when we reached the hotel pool, she wouldn’t remove her sandals. I sat beside her on the tiles, pretending to read the safety rules while tracking every splash nearby. She asked if the drain could pull her under. I explained that it couldn’t, then checked the grate myself before leading her down the steps. The water barely reached her waist. Still, she pinched the straps of her swimsuit and kept her chin lifted. I showed her how to cup her hands and push water behind her. She copied me, sending a little wave against the wall. A boy shrieked as he jumped from the diving board; Noor backed up one step. I offered my hand, and she squeezed it hard. After a while, she released my fingers long enough to paddle to the next ladder rung.

Tessa chose the warm therapy pool for her first lessons with her grandson, Leon. The doctor had said the shallow water would be suitable, but Tessa still read the posted depth markers twice. She brought a waterproof pouch for his inhaler and set it on a chair where she could see it. Leon bounced on his toes, eager to practice the strokes he had invented in the bathtub. Tessa smiled, though her gaze kept returning to the pool’s edge. She showed him how to blow bubbles, then guided his hands along the rail. When he slipped and splashed, she caught his elbow before he could call out. He looked surprised, not hurt. Tessa rubbed his shoulder and asked whether he wanted another try. Leon nodded and began counting his kicks aloud. She joined the count, her voice growing steadier as he moved from one marker to the next.

I had taught my niece Priya to bake, garden, and mend a torn kite, but the river pool made me feel clumsy. I stood knee-deep while she held the bank with both hands. A lifeguard watched from the rocks, and I kept glancing over to make sure he was still there. Priya wanted to learn how to float, so I placed one hand beneath her shoulders and asked her to look at the clouds. She stared at the water instead, breathing in quick little pulls. “What if I can’t get back up?” she asked. I showed her how to roll onto her side and find the bank, demonstrating twice before inviting her to try. Her legs stiffened, then loosened. For a few seconds she floated. When she sat up, I felt my shoulders drop and realized I had been holding my breath longer than she had.

Darius and his son, Omari, arrived at the beach before sunrise, when the water was still and the sand cool. Darius had chosen a spot near the lifeguard stand, but he kept looking at the horizon for waves. Omari wore a bright green swim shirt and carried a toy boat. His father explained how to kick while holding the boat, then walked beside him through ankle-deep water. A sudden swell lifted the toy and tipped it over. Omari froze, eyes fixed on the bobbing boat. Darius retrieved it at once, hiding how quickly his pulse had leapt. He suggested they practice in the shallows again, using his hands as a steady target. Omari kicked toward him, splashing his father’s shirt. Darius laughed and pretended to stagger backward. The boy laughed too, and they kept going until the sun reached the lifeguard’s umbrella.

When my son Pavel said he wanted to swim before the school trip, I signed us up for an early-morning lesson at the YMCA. In the locker room, he kept asking whether the pool had a shallow lane. I pointed out the signs and walked him there, though I had already studied the layout online. He held my hand down the steps and pressed close to my side. I showed him how to make a star on his back, supporting his neck with one palm. His body went stiff, and I felt every muscle in my own arm tighten. “Look at the ceiling,” I said, trying to keep my voice light. Pavel found a painted cloud and studied it. Slowly, his ears touched the water. He floated for two seconds before grabbing my sleeve. I smiled, but my fingers were numb from gripping the pool edge.

At a seaside hotel in Greece, Niko promised his granddaughter Eleni that he would teach her to swim before their flight home. She watched the pool’s blue lane rope sway and asked whether it could break. Niko checked its knots, then guided her to the steps. He had spent years captaining a ferry, yet the small distance between them seemed enormous when Eleni let go of the rail. He held a kickboard beneath her arms and walked backward, watching her face more than her feet. She kicked unevenly, sending water into his eyes. For an instant he lost sight of her, and his hands shot forward. Eleni surfaced laughing at his wet hair. Niko laughed with her, then wiped his eyes and suggested they rest on the steps. After a drink of water, she asked to cross the pool again. He checked the lane rope once more before nodding.

I had six parcels left and twenty minutes before the pharmacy closed. The traffic lights along Mercer Street seemed to hold red longer each time I reached one. I checked the delivery app at a stop, then checked it again, though the map had not changed. A paper bag of groceries slid across the passenger seat when I turned, and I caught it with my elbow. The last address belonged to an older man who needed his prescription that evening. I called the depot, listened to the ringing, and rubbed the damp edge of my steering wheel with my thumb. When a lane finally opened, I eased the van through, eyes flicking from the clock to the street signs. At the curb, I grabbed the parcel and ran.

Nadia’s van was already forty minutes behind when a road crew closed the bridge she needed. She pulled into a gas station and spread the route sheet across the hood, pinning its corners beneath her keys. Her supervisor’s message flashed on the phone: three customers had called. Nadia read it, locked the screen, and unlocked it a moment later. She found a detour through narrow streets, but the first turn was blocked by a delivery truck. As rain ticked against the windshield, she tapped the steering wheel in quick, uneven beats. The final package was a birthday cake, carefully boxed and labeled. She pictured its frosting shifting with every sudden stop, then eased back into traffic, leaving extra room between the van and the car ahead.

By noon, I was behind schedule and the navigation screen had gone black. I held my phone near the windshield, searching for a signal while the van crawled through the old quarter of town. A box of ceramic bowls rattled behind me with every pothole. I kept glancing at it in the mirror, then at the names on my clipboard. One customer had written that she would be leaving for work at two. I tried to call, but my thumb slipped against the screen twice before the number dialed. No answer. At the next intersection, I missed the turn and let out a tight breath. I pulled over, studied the street map, and traced the route with one finger before starting again.

Malik’s route had been simple until a parade filled the main avenue with drums, banners, and stopped cars. His delivery app stacked late notices in bright red along the edge of the screen. He silenced the alerts, then reached over to turn the volume back up, afraid he might miss a customer’s call. A small package for a hospital ward sat beside him, marked for a patient waiting on a replacement charger. Malik asked a traffic officer for another way through. The officer pointed toward a steep side street, and Malik nodded twice before pulling away. At the top, he checked the clock again and pressed his lips together. The hospital entrance was crowded, so he parked farther down and carried the parcel at a brisk walk.

I was supposed to deliver the new sewing machine before the shop owner locked up, but a flat tire had eaten half an hour. I crouched beside the van while a passing car sprayed muddy water onto my trousers. The spare was on, yet my hands still smelled of rubber as I drove toward the address. Each time the phone buzzed, my shoulders jumped. The customer had sent a message asking whether I was close. I typed, “Ten minutes,” then erased it and wrote, “I’m on my way,” because the traffic ahead had stopped again. I watched the brake lights stretch down the road and flexed my fingers around the wheel. When the line began moving, I followed it carefully, counting the blocks aloud.

Eloise was late with a shipment of seedlings, and the greenhouse manager had called twice to ask whether they were still on the truck. A sudden hailstorm had forced her off the highway, where she waited beneath an overpass with the hazards blinking. She kept one hand on the insulated cargo compartment’s temperature gauge and wiped condensation from its display with her sleeve. The storm eased, but traffic stayed packed beyond the ramp. Eloise leaned forward, searching for a gap, then sat back when a horn sounded behind her. She pictured the young plants bouncing in their trays. At the next exit, she chose a slower country road, stopping once to secure a loose strap. The greenhouse’s lights appeared at last, and she hurried to the loading door.

I had promised to bring the replacement laptop to a student before her evening exam, and now the delivery van was inching through a tunnel. A dashboard light blinked, then disappeared. I turned the radio off so I could hear the engine, though every passing truck made that difficult. The clock crept forward. I called the depot and asked whether another driver could meet me at the far end; my voice came out thin, and I cleared my throat before repeating the address. No one was available. I gripped the wheel at ten and two and watched the tunnel lights pass overhead, one after another. When I emerged, I took the first legal turn toward campus and searched the sidewalks for the building number.

Rafael was running late with a bundle of wedding flowers when the lift at his apartment building stopped between floors. He had to carry the arrangements down seven flights, holding each box level while his phone vibrated in his pocket. The florist kept sending updates about the ceremony’s start time. At the curb, he set the flowers in the van and checked every ribbon for damage. A delivery truck blocked the narrow street outside the venue, so Rafael circled the block, jaw clenched against the ticking clock. He called the wedding planner at a red light and listened to the clipped instructions. When he reached the back entrance, he lifted the boxes one by one, moving carefully despite his quick steps.

My route fell apart when a school bus broke down across the only road to the village. I checked the map, checked the parcel labels, then checked the map again. The next delivery was a box of insulin supplies, packed in a cooler that I kept glancing at from the driver’s seat. I called the recipient to explain, but the line crackled and cut out before I could finish. My stomach tightened as I searched for a farm track marked on the paper atlas. The van bumped over gravel, and I held the cooler steady with one hand at the first sharp bend. At the village, I parked beside the post office and hurried to the door, rehearsing what I would say if nobody answered.

June’s delivery truck was late to the film set, where a crate of costume jewelry had to be ready before the actors arrived. A security guard waved her toward a distant entrance, then disappeared into the crowd. She called the production office and listened to a recorded menu while crew members hurried past with cables and folding chairs. June’s eyes kept returning to the crate in the back, its seal intact but its label smudged by rain. She wiped the label with a tissue and read the address again. When the office finally answered, she spoke quickly, then repeated her truck’s color and location. A runner came waving from across the lot. June locked the doors and jogged toward him, clutching the delivery paperwork.

I was late with a birthday present, a hand-carved chess set, and the recipient had already sent a cheerful message saying everyone was waiting. The van’s route took me through a neighborhood where roadwork had removed the street signs. I stopped at a corner shop and asked for directions, trying to keep my eyes from darting back to the clock in my cab. The shopkeeper pointed down an alley. I thanked him, then checked the parcel’s padding before driving on. At the next junction, a cyclist shouted that the alley ended at a locked gate. I reversed slowly, palms damp against the wheel, and found another way around. When I finally reached the house, I carried the box with both hands, careful not to let it bump the doorframe.

Tomas had three stops left when the warning light on his refrigerated van began flashing. He pulled into a supermarket lot and opened the back doors just enough to read the temperature display. The final delivery was seafood for a restaurant preparing its dinner service. Tomas called the fleet mechanic, pacing beside the van while a queue of carts rattled past. The mechanic talked him through a reset, but the light returned after a few minutes. Tomas wrote the readings on the back of a receipt and kept checking them as he drove. At the restaurant, the chef met him at the curb with a towel over one shoulder. Tomas handed over the log along with the crates, watching the chef inspect each one.

At sixty-eight, I traded my accounting desk for a patch of ground behind my bungalow. The seed packets promised neat rows, but the soil clung to my shovel in heavy slabs, and the forecast showed three dry weeks. I checked the weather app before breakfast, after lunch, and once more in bed. When my neighbor offered a hose, I thanked him too quickly and asked whether the pressure was strong enough for tomatoes. That evening I pressed a finger into the earth around every seedling, though the labels said not to disturb them. My hands smelled of damp dirt as I studied the tiny green shoots, counting each one twice. If even one row failed, I had no idea what I would tell my daughter, who had given me the seeds.

After retiring from the ferry service, Doreen rented a narrow allotment beside the railway. She brought home a packet of beans and a secondhand spade, then spent an hour measuring the bed with a ruler. The allotment steward said the plants would be fine, but Doreen kept glancing at the dark clouds gathering over the tracks. She had never grown anything beyond a windowsill herb, and the seed instructions seemed full of traps: too deep, too shallow, too soon. At night she left her boots by the door in case rain came, then rose twice to look through the kitchen window. By morning, the sky had cleared. Doreen loosened the soil carefully, pausing whenever a train rattled past, as though its vibration might undo all her work.

I retired from teaching at seventy and decided my first summer should include a vegetable garden. The raised bed looked simple in the catalog, but after I assembled it, the boards bowed at one corner. I kept a wrench in my pocket and tightened the bolts whenever I passed. My grandson planted radishes with me, then asked if they would be ready for his birthday picnic. I smiled and said yes, although the calendar left little room for error. Every morning I lifted the leaves to check for holes and searched the soil for signs of sprouts. When a cold night was forecast, I dragged an old blanket outside and covered the bed. At dawn, I hurried back with my tea untouched, lifting one edge to see whether the seedlings were still standing.

Hector, a retired bus mechanic, chose a sunny strip behind his apartment building for his first vegetable plot. The building manager had approved it, but the patch sat close to a busy alley where delivery vans clipped the curb. Hector staked out the edges with string and returned every afternoon to see if anyone had moved it. He planted lettuce, then reread the packet while standing over the row, unable to settle on whether he had spaced the seeds correctly. When a van backed toward the curb, he hurried outside and waved both arms until the driver stopped. The driver apologized; Hector nodded, then inspected the freshly turned soil for tire marks. He took a folding chair to the plot at sunset, listening for engines and watching the fragile green tips.

When my nursing career ended, I was sixty-six and suddenly had long mornings to fill. I planted carrots in tubs on the balcony, where wind curled around the railings. The first storm warning sent me outside with a roll of tape, securing each pot as if it might sail away. My sister called to ask how the garden was going, and I described the leaves in precise detail, avoiding the fact that no carrots had appeared. I pulled one seedling up by mistake while checking beneath it, then sat on the kitchen floor with the little root in my palm. For the next week I watered only with a measuring cup.
