She moved the most delicate plants beneath a workbench, then called her neighbor, who repaired houses between shifts at the ferry terminal. While waiting, she kept pressing a cloth to the damp plywood and checking the weather radar on her tablet. The colored bands showed rain moving closer. Her neighbor arrived with a ladder and a coil of flashing. Together they located a loose seam where an old skylight had been removed. Nia held the flashlight from below as he patched it. A few drops still fell into the tray, making her shoulders jump, but soon the ceiling was quiet. She carried the seedlings back one by one.

I was closing the library when a drip landed on the return desk, right beside a stack of books due for cataloging. I moved everything to a cart and fetched the custodian, who was already mopping near the west wall. The storm had knocked a branch against the roof, and our usual repair company was booked. I kept glancing at the darkening ceiling while calling other contractors, my pencil tapping the desk until its eraser split. One agreed to come before morning. He climbed up, removed the branch, and replaced several torn shingles. I stayed below, holding a plastic sheet over the books despite his promise that the leak was fixed. The next day, the ceiling remained dry, and I returned every volume to its place.

At seventy-six, Beatrice refused to leave her cottage just because rainwater had found a path through the roof. She put a saucepan beneath the drip and called her grandson, then sat beside the window with her coat on, ready to move if the ceiling worsened. The repairer was coming from two villages away. She checked the clock, then the stain, then the clock again, twisting a ring around her finger. When the van finally arrived, she insisted on holding the ladder steady despite his protests. He traced the leak to a cracked tile and replaced it with one from his truck. Beatrice watched the clouds thin over the fields. Before he drove off, she offered him tea and checked the bedroom ceiling once more.

I was halfway through an online exam when a cold drop landed on my shoulder. The leak came from the roof above my rented attic room, directly over the desk where my laptop sat. I shoved it aside, stacked textbooks around the spreading puddle, and called the landlord. His message said a repairer would come tomorrow. I paced the narrow room, then carried my notes downstairs to the laundromat, checking my phone every few minutes for updates. By evening, the landlord had arranged an emergency visit. The roofer found a slipped slate and set it back in place before darkness. I climbed upstairs slowly, listening for drips. My desk was damp at one corner, but the laptop worked, and I finished the exam with a towel beside me.

On the island, Farid’s roof leaked just as the radio announced another squall. He shifted his sewing machine away from the window and spread a blue tarp over the fabric stacked beneath it. The only roofer on that side of the harbor was finishing another job, and the ferry had stopped running. Farid kept walking to the porch to scan the gray water, though he knew no boat could cross it safely. His hands fumbled with a cup of tea, leaving a brown ring on the table. After the wind eased, the roofer arrived by skiff and climbed onto the low house. He found a seam lifted by salt and weather, then nailed down a fresh strip. Farid stayed outside until the final cloud drifted past.

I heard the leak before I saw it: a soft plink inside the closet where my father’s violin rested. I pulled the case out and set it on the bed, then called the building manager with my voice held tight and level. Water had begun to stain the ceiling near the attic hatch. The repair crew was working on another apartment, so I placed a bowl under the drip and sat on the floor beside the violin case. Every few seconds I checked the lid, though it was securely closed. When the roofer arrived, I helped him move a chair so he could reach the hatch. He found a cracked vent collar and sealed it. I carried the violin downstairs only after the rain stopped.

At the coastal clinic, Dr. Sato kept glancing up whenever wind rattled the windows. A leak had appeared above the supply cupboard, where boxes of bandages were stored. She asked the receptionist to move them, then called the maintenance crew between appointments. Their technician was delayed by a road closure. Meanwhile, Sato positioned a basin beneath the drip and shifted patients to the opposite hallway, explaining the change in a brisk, careful voice. She checked the ceiling after every consultation, pressing her lips together when the stain widened. The technician arrived with a ladder and traced the water to a gap around a roof vent. He sealed it from above and tested the area with a hose. Sato watched the dry plaster, then returned to her waiting patients.

At the summit, I unfolded the map for the fourth time, though the inked trail could not explain why the clouds had swallowed the ridge behind me. My brother was supposed to meet me at the lower shelter by dusk; his last text had arrived before the signal vanished. I checked my phone, tapped the dark screen, then tucked it away and pulled it out again. The wind snapped the map against my gloves. I tried to eat a granola bar, but each bite turned to paste in my mouth. From the peak, the trail looked simple enough, a pale line dropping through stone. Still, I set a timer, marked my location on the paper, and left a note beneath a cairn in case anyone came looking. Before descending, I listened for a bell from the shelter. Only the wind answered, and I started down carefully, counting each switchback.

Mara reached the summit just as the sun slipped behind a bank of clouds. The view should have been the reward, but she kept glancing at the narrow path where her daughter had gone ahead. Their plan had been to wait together at the marker; now the peak was empty except for Mara and a red scarf snagged on a rock. She called out, then called again, her voice thinning in the gusts. Her fingers fumbled over the emergency whistle at her collar. She examined the footprints, trying to tell old prints from fresh ones, and set her pack beside the cairn so it would be easy to spot. When a distant shape appeared on the ridge, she stood so quickly that her knee struck stone. It was only a cloud shadow. Mara began following the trail downward, stopping every few steps to scan the slope and call her daughter’s name.

I had trained for months to reach the summit, but the first thing I noticed was the crack in my water bottle. A thin stream ran over the rock beneath my boot. The descent was long, the afternoon was hot, and the guidebook’s next water source was marked miles away. I turned the bottle upside down, hoping the leak had stopped, then wrapped it in my spare shirt. My mouth already felt dry. At the peak, I checked the map against the ridgeline and traced the route with one finger. A shortcut looked tempting, but the loose scree beneath it shifted whenever the wind pushed at my pack. I took a photograph of the route notes and sent them to my partner while the phone still had a bar of service. Then I drank a careful mouthful, tightened the bottle inside the pack, and chose the longer marked trail.

At the summit, Dev found the small metal case he had carried all morning was missing. It held his father’s old compass, the one he planned to leave beside the peak’s register as a tribute. He searched every pocket, then emptied his pack onto the flat stone, sorting gear with quick, stiff movements. The wind lifted a snack wrapper and sent it skittering toward the edge. Dev caught it, but his eyes kept returning to the steep path below. He pictured the compass bouncing down the slope, its needle still pointing north while he stood helpless above it. A fellow hiker offered to help retrace the last section. Dev nodded, swallowing before he could answer. Together they followed his footprints back to a patch of snow, where the case lay half buried. He pressed it to his chest for a moment, then secured it inside his jacket.

The summit marker was less dramatic than I had imagined: a rusted post, a stone pile, and a view of the valley where my bus would leave without me if I missed the last connection. I checked my watch, though the hands seemed to move faster whenever I looked. The descent sign pointed toward two routes, and the one I had planned was partly obscured by a fallen branch. I unfolded my notes and compared the contour lines, wiping sweat from the page before it blurred. A group nearby laughed over their photographs; I smiled when one of them offered to take mine, then hurried through the shot. I called the bus station, but the call dropped after one ring. Rather than gamble on the shorter, unmarked slope, I chose the established trail and began moving briskly, stopping at each junction to confirm the symbols matched my map.

Niko stood on the summit with a bright orange kite tucked under one arm. His younger cousin had asked him to launch it there, but the wind had sharpened and the clouds were thickening over the western ridge. He studied the sky, then the narrow trail leading back to the village. The kite’s string trembled between his fingers. He imagined the gusts pulling it free and dragging him toward the exposed edge, so he coiled the line twice around his wrist before reconsidering and unwound it again. His phone showed no service. Niko tried to make a joke for the hikers nearby, but the words came out clipped. He packed the kite carefully, securing its frame beneath his jacket, and checked that his cousin’s handwritten note was still dry in his pocket. The summit could wait for another visit; he started down before the weather made the choice for him.

I reached the peak and found the trail register open to a page with my name already written on it. Someone had mistaken me for another hiker, and beside the name was a note saying they had gone down the north face. My friend Lena had planned to meet me here, but there was no sign of her. I read the entry twice, searching for a time or a description. Then I scanned the slopes, turning slowly so I would not miss a moving figure. A gust blew grit into my eyes. I blinked hard and kept looking. My phone had enough battery for one call, so I left Lena a short message with my location and the route I intended to take. Before leaving, I added my own entry with the hour and direction, pressing the pencil so firmly it nearly snapped. Then I followed the safer marked trail at a steady pace.

At the mountain’s highest point, Celia discovered that the clasp on her climbing harness would not close. She had used it only as a backup on the final scramble, but the return route crossed the same exposed ledge. She crouched beside the summit cairn and worked the metal gate with numb fingers, opening and closing it until the motion felt familiar. Each click sounded weaker than the last. Her partner was already farther down, beyond the bend, and she called for him to wait. Her voice cracked on the final word. Celia clipped the harness to her pack instead of trusting the faulty clasp, then checked the route for an alternate descent. A pair of climbers offered to accompany her to the next junction. She accepted, holding the map between both hands as they studied the terrain and chose a broad, less exposed path.

When I stepped onto the summit, I expected to feel triumphant. Instead, I noticed the empty space where my camera should have been. I had brought it to photograph the glacier, and its strap was no longer looped around my wrist. I retraced my final steps, checking the cracks between stones and the snow beside the marker. Each time a shadow shifted, I turned sharply, thinking I had spotted the black camera body. The rest of the group waited while I searched. I apologized, then apologized again, though nobody complained. Finally, I asked them to continue toward the first shelter while I checked the last sheltered spot below the peak. I left my bright hat on a boulder to mark where I had gone. The camera was wedged behind a slab, its lens cap still on. I let out a breath and hurried to catch up.

Rafi reached the summit as the first flakes began to fall. His gloves were damp from the climb, and he kept flexing his fingers as he examined the clouds gathering over the ridge. The weather forecast had promised a clear afternoon. He took out the paper map and tried to keep it flat against the wind, but the edges folded over his route. Down below, the trail split near a stand of dark pines; he could not see which branch was marked for the shelter. Rafi asked another hiker if the signs were visible from the junction. The question came out too quickly, and he had to repeat it. He packed the map inside his jacket, checked his compass, and wrote the shelter’s bearing on his wrist with a pencil. Then he began the descent while the markers were still visible, pausing at every turn to verify the direction.

At the summit, Beatrice realized the small dog she had been hiking with was gone. She had unclipped its lead only for a moment while filling her bottle, but the peak was ringed with boulders and pockets of scrub. She crouched to look beneath them, calling in a calm voice that grew thinner each time it carried away. Her hands shook as she checked the trail for paw prints. A loose stone clicked down the slope, and she froze, listening for any sound that might follow. Beatrice set her red jacket on the cairn so it would be visible from below, then asked two hikers to watch the eastern path while she searched along the safer western side. She kept the dog’s favorite treat in her open palm. A soft bark came from behind a cluster of rocks. She knelt, and the dog trotted out, tail low but wagging.
